## 2. Electric Vehicles (EV) — two-wheelers and four-wheelers, charging infrastructure, and the battery/nickel ecosystem
**Kategori**: Industry & Energy (industrial policy, automotive manufacturing, energy transition, critical minerals downstreaming)

📊 Predominantly Laggard, but of a specific and important subtype: dependent/compressed adoption rather than developmental catch-up. Indonesia is adopting the consumer output of China's transition very quickly (4-year lag on BEV car share) while remaining a decade or more behind on the productive capability that generated it. Secondary classifications by segment: Laggard-compressing on four-wheel BEVs (transplant-driven); Laggard-severe and currently regressing on electric two-wheelers (sales falling); Simultaneous/Reverse on upstream nickel and battery materials, where Indonesia is a co-located and indispensable part of the Chinese supply chain rather than a follower — Indonesia holds the resource but not the technology, so this is 'reverse' in position and 'laggard' in value capture. Not a Leapfrog: the leapfrog thesis (skip ICE, go straight to electric) fails because Indonesia's incumbent ICE two-wheeler fleet, refuelling habits and Japanese-dominated aftermarket are already deeply installed, and because coal-heavy electricity blunts the case for switching. | 🎯 Prob: Very High / Tinggi for four-wheel BEVs and for Chinese battery-supply-chain investment (both are already realised, not forecast). Medium / Sedang for electric two-wheelers at mass scale (demand economics work for high-mileage users but the policy support is absent). Low / Rendah for the transfer of genuine technological capability — cells, power electronics, e-drive design and vehicle software — in Chinese-equivalent depth. | 🔍 Keyakinan: Tinggi (High) for the core structural narrative and for headline figures on both sides: China's 2025 NEV volume and penetration (CAAM), charging counts (NEA/EVCIPA-derived reporting), policy chronology, price-war and consolidation dynamics; Indonesia's 2025 vehicle and BEV sales (GAIKINDO-derived), electric-motorcycle sales (Kemenhub SRUT), SPKLU counts (PLN), incentive and TKDN schedule, and the CATL/BYD investment facts. Sedang (Medium) for brand-level market shares (period-dependent: Jan-May vs full-year, wholesale vs retail), employment estimates in both countries, the 2019-2025 nickel-smelter casualty tallies (NGO-compiled rather than official), and lag quantification. Rendah (Low) for all forward projections — Indonesian mainstream and peak years, the two-wheeler inflection date, and the durability of the nickel-battery investment thesis — and for the China two-wheeler fleet total, where estimates range from ~300 million to ~380 million depending on source and whether unregistered units are counted.

> **Status di Indonesia**: Entered and accelerating rapidly on four wheels; stalled and shrinking on two wheels; structurally advanced but export-oriented on batteries. This is a split-status domain: Indonesia is a fast-follower in BEV car adoption (13.3% of 2025 vehicle sales), a laggard in electric motorcycles (~0.8% of a 6.55 million unit market, with sales falling 28.6% in 2025 after subsidies ended), an emerging global node in battery raw materials (nickel), and almost entirely dependent on Chinese firms across all three.

### Basic Info

**Tahun Mulai China**

> 2009 as policy start (the 'Ten Cities, Thousand Vehicles' / 十城千辆 demonstration programme launched by four ministries, targeting 10 pilot cities x 1,000 electric vehicles).
> 2012 as strategic codification (State Council Energy-Saving and New Energy Vehicle Industry Development Plan 2012-2020).
> 2014-2015 as the first commercial take-off (purchase-tax exemption from September 2014; China became the world's largest NEV market in 2015).
> 2020-2021 as the mass-market explosion (NEV penetration jumped from 5.4% in 2020 to 13.4% in 2021).
> For electric two-wheelers the timeline is much earlier: mass adoption began in the late 1990s-2000s, driven by city-level gasoline motorcycle bans (禁摩令) in 100+ cities rather than by climate policy.

**Pemain Kunci China**

> Automakers: BYD (dominant, ~4.6 million deliveries in 2025 with >1.05 million exports), Geely/Zeekr/Galaxy, SAIC (MG, and SAIC-GM-Wuling for micro-EVs), Changan/Deepal/Avatr, Chery/Omoda/Jaecoo/iCAR, GAC Aion, Great Wall/Ora, Dongfeng, NIO, XPeng, Li Auto, Xiaomi Auto (entered 2024), Leapmotor, Seres/AITO (with Huawei), Hongqi/FAW; failed players Neta/Hozon, WM Motor, HiPhi, Jidu, Qoros, Niutron.
> Batteries and materials: CATL (Contemporary Amperex, global #1), BYD FinDreams (Blade LFP), CALB, Gotion, EVE, SVOLT, Ganfeng and Tianqi (lithium), Huayou Cobalt, GEM, Lygend, Tsingshan (nickel).
> Electric two-wheelers: Yadea, Aima, Tailg, Luyuan, Niu, Segway-Ninebot.
> Charging/energy: TELD (特来电), Star Charge (星星充电), State Grid, NIO Power (battery swap), CATL EVOGO/Choco-SEB swap.
> Tech/supply: Huawei (HarmonyOS Intelligent Mobility, e-drive), Horizon Robotics, DJI Automotive.
> State actors: NDRC, MIIT, Ministry of Finance, MOST, SAMR, CAAM and CPCA as data authorities.

### China Trend Detail

**Apa Yang Terjadi Di China**

> China executed the most complete state-directed industrial transition of the modern era: it did not merely adopt electric vehicles, it built an entire vertically integrated ecosystem — minerals, cathode/anode chemistry, cells, power electronics, motors, software, vehicles, charging and recycling — and then used it to displace a century-old foreign-dominated automotive order at home and to become the world's largest vehicle exporter.
> The mechanism had five reinforcing layers.
> (1) Sequenced state demand creation: the 2009 'Ten Cities, Thousand Vehicles' pilot used government fleets (buses, taxis, sanitation trucks) to guarantee early volume when consumer demand did not exist; central subsidies of up to RMB 50,000 per vehicle, purchase-tax exemption from 2014, and government procurement mandates de-risked the first decade.
> (2) Non-fiscal incentives that proved stronger than cash: in megacities with licence-plate quotas and rationing (Beijing, Shanghai, Shenzhen, Hangzhou, Guangzhou), NEVs received free or fast-tracked plates worth tens of thousands of RMB and exemption from driving restrictions — academic work using synthetic control finds this plate exemption had a larger adoption effect than purchase subsidies.
> (3) Regulatory forcing rather than permanent subsidy: as fiscal support tapered, the dual-credit / NEV mandate (finalised September 2017, effective 1 April 2018, modelled on California's ZEV rule) shifted the burden onto automakers via tradable NEV credits — 10% of the conventional PV market in 2019, 12% in 2020 — which converted a subsidy programme into a permanent structural obligation.
> (4) Supply-chain capture: China chose LFP chemistry (cheaper, cobalt-free, safer), locked up upstream lithium, nickel and cobalt assets abroad — including Indonesia's nickel — and built the cell-manufacturing base that now underwrites the whole global industry.
> (5) Ruthless domestic competition: with 100+ brands fighting, a price war that began when Tesla cut prices in January 2023 turned into structural 'involution' (内卷) — 227 models cut prices in 2024, industry profit margin fell from 7.8% in 2017 to 4.3% in 2024 — which destroyed weak firms but drove genuine cost and technology gains (800V architectures, megawatt charging, cell-to-body, sub-USD 10,000 BEVs).
> The consequences went far beyond cars: an electrified two-wheeler fleet of roughly 380 million units, the world's largest charging network (19.32 million points by November 2025), a battery industry employing ~737,000 people, a NEV skills gap of 1.03 million forecast by MIIT, the hollowing of the ICE supply chain and its dealer network, gas-station closures, and an export surge (2.62 million NEVs in 2025, double 2024) that is now reshaping automotive markets across Southeast Asia, Latin America and Europe — Indonesia among them.

**Fase Tren Di China**

> Mature, consolidating and now partially de-subsidised — with a regulated shakeout underway.
> Adoption is past the inflection point (47.9% of new sales, heading to ~55% in 2026) so the growth story has shifted from penetration to (a) export expansion, (b) technology differentiation (fast charging, autonomy, software) and (c) survival economics.
> Three simultaneous phase markers: the state is actively suppressing the trend's own excesses through the 'anti-involution' (反内卷) campaign named in Premier Li Qiang's March 2025 work report and the June 2025 State Council rule forcing 60-day supplier payment terms; fiscal support is being deliberately withdrawn (purchase tax halved from January 2026, prompting a pre-deadline order rush of up to +60% at some dealerships and an expected early-2026 air pocket); and the industry is consolidating hard (738 → 591 makers; Neta/Hozon in bankruptcy restructuring; WM Motor, HiPhi, Jidu, Qoros and Niutron failed).
> Electric two-wheelers are in a mature/re-regulated phase — near-total category dominance, with policy attention now on lithium-battery fire safety, standard GB 17761 compliance and trade-in-driven fleet replacement rather than on growth.

**Puncak Tren China**

> Multiple peaks depending on the metric.
> Growth-rate peak: 2021 (NEV sales grew roughly 150-160% and penetration jumped from 5.4% to 13.4%).
> Symbolic penetration peak: July 2024, when NEVs first exceeded 50% of monthly retail sales — the moment electric became the majority of new cars in the world's largest market.
> Policy-generosity peak: 2015-2018 (maximum subsidy plus licence-plate privileges), after which support shifted to mandates.
> Profitability trough / competitive-intensity peak: 2024-2025 (price war, 4.3% margins, mass brand failure).
> Absolute volume peak: not yet reached — 16.49 million in 2025 heading to a forecast 19 million in 2026 — but growth is decelerating and the January 2026 tax change is the first genuine demand headwind in a decade.
> Geographic centres of the peak: Shenzhen (fully electrified buses by 2017 and taxis by 2019, BYD's home base), Shanghai (Tesla Gigafactory 3, plate-quota effect), Hangzhou and Beijing (plate rationing), Liuzhou (the Wuling Hongguang Mini EV micro-mobility model, the most transferable template for developing markets), Hefei (NIO), Changzhou and Ningde (battery cluster), Xi'an and Changsha (BYD plants).

### Status Indonesia Saat Ini

**Status Di Indonesia**

> Entered and accelerating rapidly on four wheels; stalled and shrinking on two wheels; structurally advanced but export-oriented on batteries.
> This is a split-status domain: Indonesia is a fast-follower in BEV car adoption (13.3% of 2025 vehicle sales), a laggard in electric motorcycles (~0.8% of a 6.55 million unit market, with sales falling 28.6% in 2025 after subsidies ended), an emerging global node in battery raw materials (nickel), and almost entirely dependent on Chinese firms across all three.

### Analisis Lag

**Bukti Historical Lag**

> (1) Automotive motorisation generally: China's domestic car market took off after 2001 WTO accession and passed 10 million units in 2009; Indonesia passed 1 million only in 2013 and has since fallen back to ~800,000 — a structural scale gap, not merely a time lag.
> (2) Motorcycle-to-car transition: China largely completed it in coastal cities in the 2000s; Indonesia remains motorcycle-dominant with a ~6.5 million unit annual two-wheeler market versus ~800,000 cars, so the sequencing is different rather than delayed.
> (3) Prior Chinese consumer-durable waves reached Indonesia with 4-7 year lags (smartphones: Xiaomi/Oppo/Vivo entered Indonesia around 2014-2016, roughly 4-5 years after their Chinese take-off; e-commerce and livestream commerce showed 4-6 year lags).
> The EV car lag of ~4 years fits this pattern precisely.
> (4) Direct-transplant compression is observable: BYD announced Indonesian entry in January 2024 and was market leader within roughly 12 months — comparable to TikTok Shop's compressed entry in e-commerce, and evidence that when a Chinese firm ships the same product itself, the lag collapses to the logistics and homologation timeline.
> (5) Counter-evidence of non-convergence: Indonesia's electric-motorcycle sales actually fell 28.6% in 2025 when subsidies lapsed, and the 2 million-unit 2025 production target was missed by ~97% — showing that in the absence of either sustained fiscal support or a structural forcing mechanism, the trend does not diffuse on its own.
> (6) Infrastructure lags have historically been the longest in Indonesia (mobile payments, broadband, cold chain), which is consistent with the 10-12 year charging-infrastructure gap estimated here.
> (7) The nickel downstreaming ban (2020 export ban on nickel ore) shows Indonesia can move fast when it holds a resource lever — a partial 'reverse' element in this domain.

**Tipe Lag**

> Predominantly Laggard, but of a specific and important subtype: dependent/compressed adoption rather than developmental catch-up.
> Indonesia is adopting the consumer output of China's transition very quickly (4-year lag on BEV car share) while remaining a decade or more behind on the productive capability that generated it.
> Secondary classifications by segment: Laggard-compressing on four-wheel BEVs (transplant-driven); Laggard-severe and currently regressing on electric two-wheelers (sales falling); Simultaneous/Reverse on upstream nickel and battery materials, where Indonesia is a co-located and indispensable part of the Chinese supply chain rather than a follower — Indonesia holds the resource but not the technology, so this is 'reverse' in position and 'laggard' in value capture.
> Not a Leapfrog: the leapfrog thesis (skip ICE, go straight to electric) fails because Indonesia's incumbent ICE two-wheeler fleet, refuelling habits and Japanese-dominated aftermarket are already deeply installed, and because coal-heavy electricity blunts the case for switching.

### Probabilitas Transfer ke Indonesia

**Probabilitas Transfer**

> Very High / Tinggi for four-wheel BEVs and for Chinese battery-supply-chain investment (both are already realised, not forecast).
> Medium / Sedang for electric two-wheelers at mass scale (demand economics work for high-mileage users but the policy support is absent).
> Low / Rendah for the transfer of genuine technological capability — cells, power electronics, e-drive design and vehicle software — in Chinese-equivalent depth.

**Alasan Probabilitas**

> Four factors make consumer-side transfer nearly certain.
> (1) Supply push: Chinese overcapacity is structural — 591 makers, 4.3% margins, ~50 loss-making firms expected to retrench in 2026 — so exporting is survival, and NEV exports doubled to 2.62 million units in 2025.
> Indonesia is the largest ASEAN market, right-hand drive, ASEAN-China FTA covered, and politically welcoming.
> (2) Policy pull: Indonesia has explicitly traded market access for factories.
> Perpres 79/2023 and the CBU import-relief scheme allowed Chinese brands to import duty-free against binding local-production commitments, and the TKDN escalator (40% in 2026, 60% by 2027-2028, 80% by 2030) converts market share into plant construction — BYD Subang, XPeng-Erajaya, GAC Aion, Chery, VinFast.
> (3) The nickel lever: Indonesia holds the world's largest nickel reserves and banned ore exports in 2020, forcing Chinese processors on-shore (IMIP, IWIP, the CATL/CBL-ANTAM-IBC USD 6 billion project).
> This creates a mutual dependency that guarantees continued Chinese capital and personnel flows regardless of consumer demand.
> (4) Price convergence: Chinese BEVs now compete on sticker price with equivalent Japanese ICE models in Indonesia's upper-middle segments, and running costs are dramatically lower, so the middle-class purchase decision no longer requires a green premium.
> Conversely, capability transfer is unlikely: TKDN is measured largely by assembly value, cells and power electronics remain imported or made in wholly Chinese-controlled JVs, R&D stays in China, and Indonesia's ~800,000-unit market cannot support independent platform development.
> Electric two-wheelers sit in the middle: the total cost of ownership case is compelling for ojol riders (fuel savings of roughly Rp 200,000-350,000 per month) but the Rp 20-35 million purchase price against a Rp 18-20 million Honda, financing scarcity, resale uncertainty, battery-swap fragmentation and the withdrawal of the Rp 7 million subsidy have stalled it — which is exactly why 2025 sales fell 28.6%.

**Vektor Transmisi**

> (a) Direct entry by Chinese firms — overwhelmingly dominant.
> BYD, Wuling (SAIC-GM-Wuling), Chery, GAC Aion, Geely, MG, Neta, XPeng and Denza entered with their own brands, dealer networks, financing arms and, increasingly, their own plants; BYD went from market entry (January 2024) to BEV market leader within about a year and to top-six overall car brand.
> This is not diffusion, it is corporate transplantation.
> (b) Chinese capital and joint ventures in the upstream — CATL/CBL with ANTAM and IBC (USD 6 billion, East Halmahera groundbreaking 29 June 2025, plus 6.9 GWh in Karawang), Tsingshan's IMIP (Morowali) and IWIP (Weda Bay), Huayou, Lygend, GEM, QMB New Energy Materials.
> Belt and Road framing, state-bank financing, and Chinese EPC contractors move the whole industrial package, not just money.
> (c) State-to-state and resource-for-investment bargaining — Indonesia's 2020 nickel-ore export ban plus the TKDN escalator are deliberate policy levers that force Chinese firms to localise; the transmission is therefore partly pulled by Indonesian industrial policy rather than only pushed by China.
> (d) Local partners and copycat/assembly imitation — Indomobil, Erajaya (PT Era Industri Otomotif with XPeng), Handal (Chery), Polytron (an Indonesian consumer-electronics brand that became the largest e-motorcycle seller using Chinese-sourced components and platforms), Volta, Selis and United all build on Chinese componentry, cells and design; the 'local' two-wheeler industry is largely a CKD/SKD localisation of Chinese supply.
> (e) Personnel, diaspora and technical labour — thousands of Chinese engineers, technicians and managers work at IMIP/IWIP and in EV plants; Mandarin-capable Indonesian-Chinese business networks broker sourcing; Indonesian graduates of Chinese universities and BYD/CATL training programmes return with process knowledge; conversely, Chinese firms run in-house academies rather than transferring knowledge to Indonesian institutions.
> (f) Algorithmic content diffusion — TikTok/Douyin and YouTube EV review culture, Chinese charging-tech content and 'BYD vs Toyota' comparison media shaped Indonesian consumer expectations well ahead of dealer availability; this is a secondary but real vector for demand formation, particularly among urban middle-class buyers.
> (g) Component and aftermarket import channels — Chinese e-motorcycle kits, LFP battery packs, controllers, BMS boards and charging hardware flow through Alibaba/1688 and Shenzhen/Wuxi supply channels into Indonesian conversion workshops and small assemblers, seeding a grey-market ecosystem beneath the formal one.

### Faktor Pendorong

**Prasyarat Struktural**

> Threshold conditions and Indonesia's position relative to China at the equivalent stage.
> (1) GDP per capita: China was at roughly USD 8,000-10,500 when NEV penetration crossed 5-13% (2016-2021); Indonesia is at ~USD 5,000 with 13.3% BEV share — Indonesia is achieving Chinese-2021 penetration at roughly half the income level, which is only possible because Chinese overcapacity has collapsed vehicle prices and because Indonesian BEV buyers are a narrow affluent urban slice, not the median household.
> Indonesia does NOT meet the income threshold for broad-based adoption.
> (2) Electricity supply and carbon intensity: China's grid was and is coal-heavy but had massive surplus capacity, nationwide reliability and a state utility able to cross-subsidise charging; Indonesia's PLN has surplus capacity in Java-Bali (a genuine enabler) but a grid that is roughly 60%+ coal, weak outside Java, and a tariff structure that has only recently supported charging economics.
> Partially met, and the coal intensity undermines the environmental rationale.
> (3) Charging density: a practical threshold is roughly 1 public charger per 10-20 EVs plus widespread home charging.
> China had 19.32 million points for its fleet by late 2025; Indonesia has ~4,655 public points for ~136,000 electric cars — thin but not yet binding because most Indonesian BEV owners have private garages and home charging (PLN home-charging installations doubled in 2025).
> Binding constraint arrives at roughly 300,000-500,000 e-cars.
> (4) Urban form and parking: China's apartment-block density made both charging-pile allocation and battery-swap networks viable; Indonesia's mix of landed housing (favourable for home charging among the affluent) and dense kampung (unfavourable — no dedicated parking for motorcycles) creates a split.
> This is the single biggest structural obstacle for electric two-wheelers, and it is why battery swap rather than plug-in charging is the only viable Indonesian two-wheeler architecture.
> Not met for the mass two-wheeler market.
> (5) Domestic manufacturing and supply-chain depth: China had a complete cell-to-vehicle chain before mass adoption; Indonesia has world-leading nickel processing but almost no cathode-to-cell-to-pack integration under domestic control, and its component industry is ICE-oriented and shrinking.
> Not met.
> (6) Fiscal capacity: China spent well over RMB 200 billion in cumulative direct NEV subsidies across a decade plus enormous local-government support; Indonesia's Rp 7 million per-unit motorcycle subsidy lapsed after two years and was not renewed, and CBU import relief ended in 2025.
> Not met — Indonesia cannot buy adoption at Chinese scale and must rely on regulation and price convergence instead.
> (7) Non-fiscal forcing levers: China's licence-plate quotas and driving restrictions in megacities were, empirically, more powerful than subsidies.
> Indonesia has only weak analogues (Jakarta odd-even exemption for EVs, some parking and toll concessions) and no vehicle-quota regime to exempt from.
> Not met — and this is the most under-appreciated missing prerequisite.
> (8) Financing and consumer credit: China's adoption ran on cash and bank auto loans; Indonesian two-wheeler purchases run overwhelmingly on multifinance credit, and multifinance companies remain reluctant to underwrite electric motorcycles because residual values are unproven.
> Not met, and it is a decisive brake.
> (9) Standards and interoperability: China standardised charging (GB/T) and progressively regulated two-wheeler batteries (GB 17761, effective 1 September 2025); Indonesia has SNI standards but fragmented battery-swap formats across Volta, SWAP, Oyika and others.
> Not met.
> Net: Indonesia clears the demand-side threshold for affluent four-wheel buyers and the resource-side threshold for upstream investment, but fails on income breadth, charging density for two-wheelers, financing, fiscal capacity, forcing levers and supply-chain depth — which precisely predicts the observed split outcome.

**Indikator Pemantauan**

> Already fired: BYD reaching top-six overall car brand and >39% BEV share within a year of entry; BEV share of car sales crossing 10% (13.3% in 2025); CATL/CBL groundbreaking in East Halmahera (June 2025); BYD's Subang plant nearing production; XPeng's acquisition of PT Era Industri Otomotif; SPKLU count passing 4,655 (+44% YoY); the TKDN escalator taking legal effect from January 2026; the RUKN decree quietly cutting the 2030 e-motorcycle target.
> Still to monitor, roughly in order of diagnostic value: (a) multifinance/leasing companies publicly offering standard credit for electric motorcycles with published residual values — the single best leading indicator that two-wheeler adoption is about to inflect; (b) whether any Indonesian city introduces a real forcing lever (low-emission zone, ICE motorcycle restrictions in a CBD, parking or registration surcharges, mandatory electric ojol fleets) — the Chinese experience says this matters more than subsidies; (c) Gojek/Grab electric fleet share and whether their unit economics disclosures show positive TCO at scale; (d) battery-swap network density and any move toward a national swap standard (SNI for swappable packs); (e) TKDN certification filings showing cell-level or cathode-level local content rather than assembly-only; (f) PLN SPKLU count outside Java-Bali as a share of total; (g) new KBLI codes and SKKNI competency standards for EV/high-voltage technicians and battery handling; (h) SMK concentration keahlian and polytechnic programme approvals specifically for kendaraan listrik and battery technology, and their enrolment numbers; (i) job-posting volume for 'teknisi kendaraan listrik', 'battery engineer', 'BMS', 'power electronics' on Indonesian job boards; (j) trademark and PT registrations by Chinese EV, charging and battery firms; (k) Chinese-brand dealer network counts outside Jabodetabek; (l) used-BEV auction prices and insurance premium differentials — the early warning for the demand-side problems China hit; (m) GIAMM/GIAMM-member reports of ICE component plant closures and layoffs; (n) whether Indonesia introduces any dual-credit-style mandate on automakers; (o) IMIP/IWIP incident reporting and environmental enforcement actions, which govern the political sustainability of the whole nickel bargain.

### Hambatan & Faktor Pembatal

**Hambatan Transfer**

> Purchasing power — the median Indonesian household buys a Rp 18-25 million motorcycle, not a Rp 200-500 million car, so BEV adoption is confined to a thin affluent segment.
> Withdrawal of incentives — the Rp 7 million electric-motorcycle subsidy expired in December 2024 and was not renewed, and CBU import relief ended in 2025; sales fell 28.6% immediately, demonstrating that demand was subsidy-dependent.
> Financing — multifinance companies will not underwrite electric two-wheelers at normal terms because residual values are unproven, and Indonesian two-wheeler sales are overwhelmingly credit-financed.
> Charging and parking — kampung and dense urban housing lack dedicated parking or safe overnight charging for motorcycles; apartment buildings resist charger installation; public charging outside Java is thin.
> Grid and geography — 17,000+ islands, weak transmission outside Java-Bali, and a coal-heavy generation mix that both weakens the environmental argument and exposes EV policy to 'coal cars' criticism.
> Battery-swap fragmentation — competing incompatible formats prevent network effects.
> Aftermarket and service — Indonesia's enormous informal bengkel network is trained on carburettors and small ICE engines and has neither the tools nor the high-voltage safety training for EVs; owners fear being stranded.
> Resale and residual value anxiety — no established used-EV market or valuation benchmark.
> Incumbent lock-in — Honda and Yamaha hold roughly 95% of the motorcycle market with 40 years of dealer, parts and financing infrastructure and strong incentives to slow-walk electrification.
> Component-industry resistance — GIAMM and the local supplier base face a shrinking domestic market (from ~1 million to ~800,000 units) and low local content in EVs, giving them reason to lobby against rapid transition.
> Policy volatility and TKDN cost — the escalating local-content requirement (40% → 60% → 80%) raises costs and may deter entrants or push them to import-heavy workarounds.
> Institutional capacity — weak enforcement of safety, battery-disposal and homologation standards.
> Trade politics — protecting Japanese-invested manufacturing employment is a genuine constraint on how fast Jakarta can favour Chinese EVs.

**Faktor Pembatal Transfer**

> Structural conditions under which the Chinese pattern will NOT reproduce in Indonesia.
> (1) The two-wheeler substitution path is not available.
> China's ~380 million electric two-wheelers did not replace gasoline motorcycles by consumer preference — they filled a vacuum created by administrative bans on gasoline motorcycles (禁摩令) imposed by well over 100 cities from the 1990s, combined with a bicycle-replacement dynamic and a low-speed, low-cost vehicle class regulated as a bicycle rather than as a motor vehicle.
> Indonesia's ~120 million-strong motorcycle fleet is the backbone of household mobility and informal livelihoods; no Indonesian government can ban gasoline motorcycles, and Indonesian riders need 60-100 km/h highway-capable machines, not 25 km/h e-bikes.
> The Chinese two-wheeler model is therefore structurally untransferable in its original form — Indonesia must invent a different one (battery swap for high-mileage commercial riders), and this is why the 13 million-by-2030 target was fantasy and has already been cut to 2.9-3.8 million.
> (2) No forcing lever equivalent to licence-plate rationing.
> China's most effective instrument was exempting NEVs from plate quotas and driving restrictions in megacities — a lever that costs the state nothing and is worth tens of thousands of RMB to the buyer.
> Indonesia has no vehicle-quota system to exempt from, and creating one is politically impossible.
> Without it, Indonesia must rely on fiscal subsidies it cannot afford.
> (3) Fiscal asymmetry.
> China sustained a decade of subsidies plus local-government support at a scale (well over RMB 200 billion centrally, plus fraud losses of RMB 9.27 billion absorbed without derailing the programme) that Indonesia's fiscal space cannot approach; Indonesia's two-year, Rp 7 million motorcycle subsidy lapsed and its withdrawal immediately reversed the market.
> (4) Market scale forecloses domestic capability.
> China's ~30 million-unit domestic market could support 100+ brands, multiple cell chemistries and genuine R&D competition; Indonesia's ~800,000-unit market cannot amortise platform development, so no Indonesian BYD is possible and the realistic ceiling is assembly, components and upstream materials.
> (5) Coal-dominated grid.
> With roughly 60%+ coal generation and new captive coal plants built specifically to power nickel smelters, the well-to-wheel case for Indonesian EVs is far weaker than China's (where hydro, nuclear, wind and solar shares are much larger and rising), which both limits the climate benefit and exposes the policy to legitimate criticism.
> (6) Value capture inverted.
> In China the transition created domestic champions capturing design, brand, software and cell margins; in Indonesia the same transition transfers vehicle margins to Chinese OEMs, cell margins to CATL, and leaves Indonesia with mining and assembly — plus the environmental and occupational costs at IMIP/IWIP.
> The trend arrives, the industrial upgrading does not.
> (7) Incumbent ICE employment as a political constraint.
> Indonesia's automotive and component industry employs on the order of 1.5 million people directly and indirectly and EV production is estimated to absorb only about a third of that; a Chinese-speed transition would be a net job destroyer in the medium term, which sets a political speed limit no technology curve can override.
> (8) Archipelagic charging economics.
> Building a China-density charging network across 17,000 islands with a fraction of the EV fleet has no commercial logic outside Java-Bali and a handful of Sumatran and Sulawesi corridors, so a genuinely national EV market — as opposed to a Jakarta-Bandung-Surabaya-Bali market — is not achievable on Chinese timescales.

### Prediksi Timeline di Indonesia

**Tahun Masuk Indonesia**

> Already entered, in three distinct waves.
> 2019-2021: policy foundation (Perpres 55/2019), Wuling's Cikarang plant, Hyundai Ioniq 5 (2022), and the first Indonesian-assembled BEV (Wuling Air ev, 2022).
> 2023-2024: the subsidy-driven electric-motorcycle wave (Rp 7 million subsidy; sales 62,409 in 2023 and 77,078 in 2024) plus BYD's January 2024 entry, which reset the four-wheel market.
> 2025-2026: institutionalisation — BEV share reaching 13.3%, CATL groundbreaking, BYD Subang, the end of CBU import relief and the start of the TKDN escalator.
> The domain is past entry and into the localisation phase.

**Skenario Percepatan**

> A binding urban forcing lever (Jakarta low-emission zone, ICE restrictions in the CBD, or mandatory electrification of ojol and logistics fleets); multifinance companies offering standard-term credit for electric motorcycles once residual values are established, possibly backstopped by a government residual-value guarantee; a national battery-swap standard making packs interchangeable across operators; battery-as-a-service pricing that removes the battery from the purchase price and undercuts a Honda outright; a fuel-subsidy reduction that widens the running-cost gap; BYD's Subang plant and other localised production cutting sticker prices by 15-25%; LFP cell production actually landing in Indonesia rather than only cathode materials; PLN aggressive off-peak charging tariffs and mass home-charger rollout; a renewed and better-designed purchase incentive tied to local content; Chinese OEM price wars spilling into Indonesia as export pressure intensifies; and cheap Chinese micro-EVs on the Liuzhou model entering the Rp 100-150 million segment.

### Dampak Sosial-Ekonomi

**Dampak Kelas Menengah**

> For the upper-middle class (roughly the top decile), the effect is straightforwardly positive: Chinese BEVs deliver features and performance previously reserved for premium European models at Toyota Innova prices, with running costs a fraction of petrol — which is exactly why BEV share reached 13.3% while the overall car market shrank 7%.
> This is a genuine consumption upgrade and helps explain why EV adoption has proceeded despite a weak macro environment.
> For the broad middle class and the aspirational lower-middle class — the motorcycle-owning majority — the picture is far less favourable: the electric motorcycle that would actually serve them costs Rp 20-35 million against a Rp 18-20 million Honda, cannot be financed on normal multifinance terms, has no proven resale value, and often cannot be charged safely at home.
> The subsidy that briefly closed the gap was withdrawn, and sales fell 28.6%.
> So the EV transition is currently regressive in access: it upgrades the mobility of the affluent while leaving the mass market on petrol and exposed to future fuel-subsidy reform.
> There is a second, sharper channel: the middle class in this domain is disproportionately made up of small automotive entrepreneurs — bengkel owners, spare-parts traders, component SME operators, driving-school and fleet businesses — and these are precisely the livelihoods the transition erodes.
> A third channel is favourable: ojol drivers and small logistics operators, who sit at the lower-middle boundary, are the one mass segment where electric economics already work (fuel savings on the order of Rp 200,000-350,000 per month for a high-mileage rider), so a well-designed battery-swap and financing scheme could deliver a real income gain to several million households.
> Net: consumption benefit concentrated at the top, livelihood risk concentrated in the middle, and a large unrealised income opportunity at the bottom of the middle class that current policy is failing to capture.

**Dampak Daerah Non Jawa**

> This domain produces the sharpest Java / non-Java asymmetry of any trend studied, and it runs in an unusual direction.
> Consumption is overwhelmingly Javanese: BEV sales, dealer networks and the SPKLU network are concentrated in Jabodetabek, Bandung, Surabaya and Bali, and charging density outside Java-Bali is too thin to make an EV a rational purchase.
> Production of the raw materials, however, is overwhelmingly non-Javanese: Sulawesi (Morowali/IMIP), North Maluku (Weda Bay/IWIP and the East Halmahera CATL project), and Southeast Sulawesi carry the mining, smelting and HPAL processing.
> Vehicle and cell assembly, meanwhile, sits back in Java (Karawang, Subang, Cikarang).
> The result is a three-way split in which non-Java regions supply the ore and absorb the environmental and occupational costs, Java captures the manufacturing value-added and the consumption benefit, and the technology margin leaves the country entirely.
> The costs borne by non-Java are documented and serious: between 2019 and 2025, 104 workplace accidents in Indonesian nickel smelters caused 107 deaths and 155 injuries; the December 2023 IMIP explosion alone killed 21 (including eight Chinese workers); multiple tailings dams breached at IMIP in March 2025 (PT Huayue Nickel Cobalt and PT QMB New Energy Materials) causing water pollution; IMIP tailings of ~11.5 million tonnes per year were projected to grow more than fourfold to ~47 million tonnes by 2026, containing sulphuric acid and hexavalent chromium; captive coal plants power the smelters; deforestation and coastal pollution are widespread; and tensions between Chinese and Indonesian workers have repeatedly turned violent.
> Non-Java regions do gain substantial formal employment and local economic activity — Morowali's economy was transformed — but the jobs are hazardous, the environmental liabilities are long-lived, and the region will not host the higher-value cell, power-electronics or vehicle-software activity.
> There is also a positive path that is currently under-used: island and remote grids in eastern Indonesia are the places where electric two- and three-wheelers plus solar charging would deliver the largest fuel-cost savings, since diesel and petrol logistics costs there are highest — but no policy currently targets this.

### Kaitan Pendidikan

**Jurusan Terancam**

> Programmes whose current content, not whose discipline, is at risk.
> SMK Teknik Kendaraan Ringan Otomotif (TKRO) and Teknik dan Bisnis Sepeda Motor (TBSM) as presently taught — curricula built around internal combustion engines, fuel systems, carburettors and injection, transmissions, exhaust and engine tuning; these programmes produce the largest single cohort of Indonesian vocational graduates in the automotive field and are the most directly exposed.
> D3 Teknik Mesin Otomotif and Teknik Otomotif diploma programmes oriented to engine overhaul and powertrain machining.
> Teknik Mesin (S1) tracks specialising in internal combustion, thermodynamics of engines, and fuel-injection systems without electrification content.
> Teknik Perawatan Mesin and heavy-equipment maintenance programmes tied to diesel powertrains (partially protected, since mining and heavy equipment electrify last).
> Teknik Pengelasan and metal-forming programmes tied to exhaust, muffler and engine-block component manufacture.
> Manajemen Bisnis Otomotif curricula built around spare-parts distribution and periodic-service revenue models that EVs largely eliminate.
> Petroleum-adjacent programmes with a downstream retail focus.
> Two important qualifications: first, none of these disciplines disappears — mechanical engineering, materials and manufacturing become more important, not less, in a battery and e-drive industry; what expires is the powertrain assumption embedded in the syllabus.
> Second, Indonesia's ICE fleet of ~120 million motorcycles and ~20 million cars will need servicing for two to three decades, so the demand for conventional skills declines slowly, not abruptly — the real risk is graduating a cohort into a shrinking, deflating trade rather than into an expanding one.

**Jurusan Dibutuhkan**

> Highest-leverage and most under-supplied: Electrochemistry and Battery Materials Engineering (cathode, anode, electrolyte, cell design) — Indonesia processes the world's nickel yet has almost no domestic cell-science capability, which is the single clearest national skills gap.
> Metallurgical Engineering and Hydrometallurgy (HPAL, RKEF, refining, impurity control) — directly employable at IMIP, IWIP and the CATL project, and currently filled substantially by Chinese engineers.
> Power Electronics and Electric Drive Engineering (inverters, motors, converters, thermal management).
> Battery Management Systems and embedded systems/firmware.
> Mechatronics and vehicle electrical systems for the vocational tier — the direct replacement for engine-focused TKRO/TBSM content, including mandatory high-voltage safety certification.
> Electrical Engineering with a power-systems and EVSE specialisation (charging infrastructure design, grid integration, distributed energy, V2G) — critical given PLN's rollout.
> Energy Storage Science and Engineering as a distinct programme, mirroring China's 储能科学与工程 major.
> Automotive/vehicle software, telematics, ADAS and connected-vehicle systems.
> Battery recycling, second-life and circular-economy engineering — an area where Indonesia can build capability before the waste arrives rather than after, avoiding China's informal-recycling failure.
> Environmental engineering, tailings management, industrial safety and occupational health — given the documented IMIP record, this is both an ethical and a commercial necessity.
> Supply-chain and industrial engineering for battery and vehicle manufacturing.
> Mining engineering with ESG and traceability competence (battery-passport, EU CBAM and responsible-sourcing compliance) — a genuine export-relevant differentiator.
> Industrial Mandarin combined with any of the above, since the entire counterpart ecosystem is Chinese-speaking.
> And on the commercial side: EV product management, fleet electrification and TCO analysis, and EV financing and residual-value risk analytics — the last of these directly addresses the financing bottleneck that is currently strangling two-wheeler adoption.

**China Education Response**

> China's education system was retooled deliberately and at speed, in tight coupling with industrial policy.
> Vocational tier: the number of higher vocational colleges offering the New Energy Vehicle Technology major (新能源汽车技术) rose from 298 in 2018 to 716 in 2023 — out of 1,545 such colleges nationally, meaning nearly half the vocational system added the programme within five years.
> MIIT's Manufacturing Talent Development Plan projected a shortfall of 1.03 million NEV specialists by 2025, and this published gap functioned as the coordinating signal that drove programme openings, provincial funding and enrolment.
> The content and its partners evolved with the industry: early programmes focused on EV sales and after-sales maintenance, then shifted toward订单-style directed cooperation with BYD, Geely, BAIC and others to supply production-line technical talent.
> Undergraduate and postgraduate tier: universities added Energy Storage Science and Engineering (储能科学与工程, first approved 2020 at Xi'an Jiaotong University and then diffused widely), New Energy Materials and Devices (新能源材料与器件), Intelligent Vehicle Engineering (智能车辆工程) and Robotics/AI tracks feeding autonomous-driving work, while classical Vehicle Engineering (车辆工程) departments rebuilt their curricula around electric powertrains, batteries and software.
> Industry-run pipelines: BYD, CATL, NIO and others operate their own academies, dual-track apprenticeships and school partnerships at large scale, and CATL-linked training feeds its overseas plants — including, now, Indonesia.
> Repair-side response: a high-wage market emerged for NEV maintenance technicians because the existing ICE mechanic base could not service high-voltage systems, and vocational retraining programmes were launched specifically to convert them.
> Sequencing lesson for Indonesia: China published a quantified national talent-gap figure, tied it to an industrial roadmap, and let that number pull curriculum, funding and enrolment behind it.
> Indonesia has industrial targets (2 million cars, 13 million motorcycles by 2030, TKDN escalators) but no published, credible EV workforce-gap estimate — which is precisely the missing coordinating instrument.

### Pelajaran Kebijakan dari China

**Respons Kebijakan China**

> China's regulatory arc contains both the instruments that made the transition work and the corrections it needed once the trend matured — Indonesia can borrow both, and should note that the second category arrived only after significant damage.
> Enabling instruments: the 2009 'Ten Cities, Thousand Vehicles' demonstration using public fleets to create guaranteed early demand; consumer subsidies up to RMB 50,000 with a technology-linked, progressively tightening qualification threshold (range, energy density, efficiency) so that support pulled technology forward rather than merely subsidising volume; purchase-tax exemption from 2014, extended repeatedly and only now being tapered (halved from 1 January 2026, cap cut from RMB 30,000 to RMB 15,000) — a decade-long glide path rather than a cliff, which is exactly the design Indonesia failed to apply to its motorcycle subsidy; licence-plate quota exemption and driving-restriction exemption in megacities, empirically more powerful than cash subsidies and fiscally free; the dual-credit / NEV mandate finalised September 2017 and effective 1 April 2018, converting subsidy dependence into a permanent tradable obligation on manufacturers (10% of the conventional PV market in 2019, 12% in 2020, tightened repeatedly since); charging-infrastructure targets with public-capacity metrics (28 million points and >300 GW public capacity by end-2027) rather than only unit counts; and rural EV promotion (新能源汽车下乡) extending adoption beyond tier-1 cities.
> Corrective instruments, each marking a problem: the 2016 subsidy-fraud crackdown — 93 companies investigated, 72 found fraudulent, 76,374 phantom vehicles, RMB 9.27 billion involved — after which subsidies were switched to post-verification disbursement tied to actual mileage accrual, a design Indonesia should adopt preemptively; the 'anti-involution' (反内卷) campaign named in the March 2025 government work report, and the June 2025 State Council rule mandating 60-day payment terms to suppliers, both responses to a price war that pushed industry margins to 4.3% and pushed the pain onto SMEs; battery-recycling regulation strengthened repeatedly and again in January 2026 because 70-75% of retired packs were flowing to unlicensed workshops — a failure Indonesia can still avoid; the revised electric two-wheeler national standard GB 17761 (issued 31 December 2024, mandatory from 1 September 2025) responding to lithium-battery fires and illegal modification; and mandatory NEV data reporting to national monitoring platforms.
> What Indonesia should adopt preemptively rather than reactively: mileage-verified subsidy disbursement; extended producer responsibility and licensed-recycler requirements written now, before the first large battery cohort retires around 2030-2033; a battery-swap interoperability standard before proprietary networks entrench; two-wheeler battery safety standards with enforcement (Indonesia's kampung charging conditions make fire risk higher than China's); supplier-payment protection for the component SME base; and a taper-not-cliff design for every incentive.

**Rekomendasi Kebijakan Indonesia**

> (1) Replace the on-off subsidy with a multi-year, declining, mileage-verified incentive.
> The Rp 7 million motorcycle subsidy's abrupt expiry cut sales 28.6% and destroyed investment confidence; China's decade-long taper is the correct template, and post-verification disbursement tied to actual usage forecloses the fraud that cost China RMB 9.27 billion.
> (2) Fix financing before adding purchase subsidies.
> The binding constraint on two-wheelers is that multifinance companies will not lend against unproven residual values; a government or IBC-backed residual-value guarantee or battery buy-back floor would unlock credit at far lower fiscal cost per unit than a purchase subsidy, and should be the single highest priority.
> (3) Mandate battery-swap interoperability now.
> Legislate an SNI standard for swappable two-wheeler packs covering form factor, connector, voltage and communication protocol before Volta, SWAP, Oyika and OEM networks entrench incompatible fleets — this is a one-time, low-cost intervention with compounding returns.
> (4) Target commercial fleets rather than private buyers.
> Ojol, last-mile logistics, government fleets and postal services have the mileage economics that make electric two-wheelers profitable today; a fleet electrification mandate with a phased timetable, mirroring China's public-fleet-first sequencing, would build volume, charging demand and technician demand simultaneously.
> (5) Introduce a supply-side obligation.
> Consider a simplified dual-credit-style mandate on manufacturers above a volume threshold; it shifts cost off the budget and onto firms, is the mechanism that carried China after subsidies tapered, and is more durable than annual fiscal decisions.
> (6) Make TKDN measure capability, not assembly.
> The 40%/60%/80% escalator will otherwise be met through low-value localisation; weight local content toward cells, cathode, power electronics, BMS and software, and pair it with mandatory technology-transfer and Indonesian-engineer-training clauses in every incentive-linked investment agreement.
> (7) Legislate battery extended producer responsibility now.
> Require OEMs to fund take-back, license recyclers, and register every pack — China is losing a 'battle' against a 70-75% informal recycling share it tried to fix after the fact; Indonesia's first large retirement wave arrives around 2030-2033 and the rules must exist before it.
> (8) Enforce two-wheeler battery safety standards, adapting GB 17761's logic to Indonesian conditions, with enforcement against uncertified conversion kits and imported cells — Indonesia's dense kampung housing makes fire risk materially higher than China's.
> (9) Introduce non-fiscal forcing levers, since Indonesia cannot afford Chinese-scale subsidies: EV-only or low-emission zones in Jakarta's core, parking and toll differentials, registration-tax escalation on high-emission vehicles, and priority ojol licensing for electric fleets.
> (10) Clean the grid in parallel and be honest about it.
> Publish well-to-wheel emission factors, accelerate renewables in the RUPTL, and stop permitting new captive coal for smelters — otherwise the EV programme is a coal programme with extra steps and will be attacked as such domestically and by export markets.
> (11) Regulate the nickel bargain properly.
> Enforce smelter safety and tailings standards, publish incident data, require independent environmental monitoring and community compensation at IMIP/IWIP, and build traceability for EU battery-passport compliance — this is both an ethical obligation given 107 deaths in 2019-2025 and a commercial necessity for accessing Western markets.
> (12) Fund a just transition for the ICE component sector and the bengkel economy: retooling grants for GIAMM members, mass high-voltage certification for informal mechanics through BLK and SMK networks, and a published national EV workforce-gap estimate to coordinate the education response the way MIIT's 1.03 million figure did in China.
> (13) Diversify beyond nickel exposure.
> LFP chemistry is displacing nickel-rich cathodes globally; Indonesia's entire strategy is levered to a mineral whose demand share is shrinking, so policy should actively court LFP, sodium-ion and recycling capacity rather than assume nickel dominance persists.

### Peluang & Rekomendasi Aksi

**Peluang Bisnis**

> (1) Battery-swap network operations for commercial riders — the highest-conviction opportunity, since ojol and logistics economics already work and the missing piece is density and standardisation; the winner is whoever reaches critical station density in Jabodetabek first.
> (2) Battery-as-a-service and residual-value underwriting — separating the battery from the purchase price attacks the exact bottleneck (financing and resale anxiety) that is throttling the two-wheeler market.
> (3) EV-specific multifinance and insurance products, including used-EV valuation data services — a genuine white space, and China's RMB 5.7 billion NEV underwriting loss in 2024 shows the pricing problem is real and solvable with data.
> (4) High-voltage technician training and certification — Indonesia has hundreds of thousands of ICE-trained mechanics and no scaled EV certification pipeline; training-as-a-service to dealers, fleets and BLKs is capital-light and immediately monetisable.
> (5) Charging infrastructure development and operation, especially destination charging (malls, hotels, offices) and Java-Bali highway corridors, plus home-charger installation and electrical upgrade services.
> (6) Fleet electrification consulting and TCO analytics for logistics, mining, plantation and government fleets.
> (7) EV component manufacturing under the TKDN escalator — wiring harnesses, thermal management, BMS assembly, motor housings, charging cables and connectors — with a guaranteed local market created by the 40/60/80% rules.
> (8) Battery second-life and recycling — build the licensed capacity before the retirement wave, and capture stationary-storage demand from telecom towers, mini-grids and rooftop solar in eastern Indonesia.
> (9) Conversion kits for existing motorcycles, done properly with certified batteries and SNI compliance, addressing the ~120 million-unit installed base that no new-vehicle strategy can reach.
> (10) Micro-EVs and low-speed vehicles on the Liuzhou model for gated communities, campuses, industrial estates, resorts and plantations.
> (11) Electric three-wheelers and light commercial vehicles for last-mile logistics — a segment Chinese suppliers serve well and Indonesian assemblers can localise cheaply.
> (12) Solar-plus-storage charging for islands and remote areas where diesel and petrol logistics costs are highest — the strongest unit economics in the country and completely unserved.
> (13) Mandarin-capable technical brokerage, ESG/traceability compliance services, and industrial safety consulting to the nickel-battery complex — demand created directly by the IMIP incident record and by EU battery-passport requirements.
> (14) Aftermarket and parts for the growing Chinese-brand parc, where independent service capacity lags dealer network expansion badly.
> (15) EV-specific used-vehicle marketplaces with battery-health certification.

**Rekomendasi Individu Mahasiswa**

> Build depth in the electrical and electrochemical layer, not the mechanical one.
> Core technical: high-voltage safety certification (the fastest-payback credential available in this domain), battery fundamentals (cell chemistry, degradation, thermal runaway, BMS logic), power electronics (inverters, converters, motor control), and vehicle electrical diagnostics — these are employable at dealer, fleet and plant level within months, not years.
> Second layer, for engineering students: electrochemistry, materials science and metallurgy for the battery-materials complex, or embedded software and CAN-bus/telematics for the vehicle side; Indonesia has an acute shortage in both and currently imports the expertise.
> Third layer, commercially differentiating: total-cost-of-ownership modelling, fleet economics, and residual-value/battery-health analytics — the financing bottleneck is the single largest constraint on the Indonesian market and almost nobody can model it credibly.
> Fourth layer: energy-systems literacy (grid integration, EVSE design, distributed solar) since charging is where the infrastructure money will be spent.
> Language and network: functional Mandarin is disproportionately valuable here — the entire counterpart ecosystem, from CATL and BYD to IMIP contractors, operates in Chinese, and Indonesian engineers who can work directly with Chinese technical teams capture the knowledge transfer that institutions are failing to broker; consider CATL/BYD training programmes, Chinese-university scholarships in energy storage, and internships at Karawang/Subang/Cikarang plants.
> Practical path: get hands on actual vehicles and packs early (student EV teams, conversion projects, dealer internships), document diagnostics work, and prefer plant, fleet or charging-operator roles over generic automotive-sales tracks.
> Strategic caution: do not build a career on ICE powertrain specialisation alone — the servicing demand persists for two to three decades but the wage and investment trend is downward; and do not assume the nickel boom is permanent, since LFP chemistry is eroding nickel's share and Indonesia's entire industrial bet is levered to it.
> Non-obvious durable skill: industrial safety and environmental compliance for battery and smelter operations — given 107 deaths in Indonesian nickel smelters between 2019 and 2025 and tightening European sourcing rules, this is both scarce and structurally growing.

**Rekomendasi Perguruan Tinggi**

> Open or expand: Energy Storage / Battery Technology as a standalone programme at S1 and D4 level, modelled on China's 储能科学与工程 (approved 2020 and rapidly diffused) — Indonesia processes the world's nickel and has essentially no cell-science teaching capacity, which is the country's clearest strategic education gap; Battery Materials and Electrochemical Engineering within existing chemical-engineering and metallurgy faculties, sited near Morowali, Halmahera and Karawang rather than only in Bandung and Jakarta; D3/D4 Teknologi Kendaraan Listrik with real high-voltage labs and OEM-supplied training vehicles; Power Electronics and Electric Drive tracks in electrical engineering; EVSE and grid-integration specialisation in partnership with PLN; battery recycling and circular-economy engineering; and industrial safety, tailings and environmental management programmes tied to the nickel complex.
> Restructure rather than close: SMK TKRO and TBSM must be rebuilt around electrical systems, battery handling and high-voltage safety as core rather than elective content — this is the largest single curriculum-change task in Indonesian vocational education and it affects the biggest cohort; Teknik Mesin should shift from combustion thermodynamics toward thermal management, lightweight materials and manufacturing systems; Teknik Elektro should add automotive-grade power electronics; Manajemen Bisnis Otomotif should replace parts-and-service revenue models with fleet, subscription and BaaS economics.
> Delivery reforms that matter more than the programme list: binding industry co-design with BYD, CATL, Wuling, Hyundai, PLN and GIAMM including equipment donation and instructor secondment (China's 订单班 directed-cohort model with BYD and Geely is the working template); mandatory instructor retraining, since most automotive lecturers were themselves trained on ICE; stackable micro-credentials in high-voltage safety and battery diagnostics so the existing informal mechanic workforce can be certified without a full degree; campus battery and EV labs as shared regional facilities rather than duplicated per-institution; and regional siting so that Sulawesi and Maluku institutions serve the industrial estates in their own provinces instead of importing Javanese and Chinese engineers.
> Institutional prerequisite: Indonesia needs a published, credible national EV workforce-gap estimate — the coordinating function that MIIT's 1.03 million figure performed in China — and Kemnaker SKKNI competency standards for EV technicians and battery handling, without which curricula will proliferate without recognised occupational standing.

### Faktor Risiko & Sisi Gelap

**Dampak Negatif China**

> (1) Destructive involution.
> The price war that began in January 2023 pushed industry profit margins from 7.8% (2017) to 4.3% (2024) and 4.4% (2025) — the two worst years on record — with 227 models cutting prices in 2024 alone and discounts reaching 34%.
> This is now officially recognised as harmful: 'involution' appeared in Premier Li Qiang's March 2025 work report and the regulator called for rectifying involutionary competition.
> (2) Supply-chain squeeze onto SMEs.
> Automakers routinely demanded ~10% annual price reductions from suppliers and stretched payment terms via IOUs, forcing the State Council in June 2025 to mandate 60-day payment.
> The cost of the price war was pushed down onto the smallest, least protected firms.
> (3) Mass corporate failure and stranded consumers.
> Manufacturer count fell from 738 (2023) to 591 (2024); Neta's parent Hozon entered bankruptcy restructuring leaving owners without service or parts; WM Motor, HiPhi, Jidu, Qoros and Niutron also failed; roughly 50 loss-making makers are expected to retrench in 2026.
> Consumers who bought from failed brands lost warranty, software updates and resale value entirely.
> (4) Subsidy fraud on a large scale.
> The 2016 investigation found 72 of 93 companies defrauding the programme across 76,374 vehicles and RMB 9.27 billion — including selling vehicles to themselves to claim subsidies.
> (5) A failing battery-recycling regime.
> 70-75% of retired packs flow to unlicensed workshops that outbid certified recyclers precisely because they skip safe dismantling and pollution control, earning around RMB 10,000 per vehicle; researchers describe the state's containment effort as a 'losing battle', with documented poisoning, fires and explosions from improper dismantling and wastewater dumped into rivers and soil.
> Retired batteries will exceed 1 million tonnes by 2030.
> (6) Insurance sector losses and cost transfer to owners.
> Chinese insurers lost RMB 5.7 billion (~USD 802 million) underwriting NEV policies in 2024 after at least three straight loss-making years; EV owners pay 20-100% higher premiums and file roughly twice as many claims, and older EVs are more likely to be written off entirely due to battery damage.
> (7) Employment disruption inside the winners.
> Even BYD, the transition's greatest success, reportedly cut around 100,000 jobs (~10% of its workforce) in 2025 as growth slowed — a warning that EV manufacturing employment is neither stable nor monotonically increasing.
> (8) Displacement of the ICE ecosystem — dealer failures, gas-station closures, and the erosion of the conventional parts and service trade.
> (9) Capital misallocation — local governments competing to host EV plants funded projects that failed, leaving idle capacity and debt.

**Risiko Sosial Indonesia**

> (1) Deindustrialisation without reindustrialisation.
> Indonesia risks losing the ICE component base (which supports on the order of 1.5 million direct and indirect jobs and is already squeezed by a market that shrank from ~1 million to ~800,000 units) while gaining only assembly and mining employment estimated at roughly a third of that — a net job loss layered on top of an already weakening manufacturing sector.
> (2) Permanent value-chain subordination.
> Without enforceable technology-transfer conditions, TKDN will be satisfied by assembly-level localisation while cells, power electronics, software and brand margins stay Chinese — Indonesia becomes a market plus a quarry, which is precisely the outcome the downstreaming policy was designed to prevent.
> (3) Nickel-complex human and environmental costs escalating.
> 104 accidents with 107 deaths and 155 injuries in nickel smelters between 2019 and 2025; the December 2023 IMIP explosion killed 21; tailings dam breaches in March 2025; tailings volumes projected to quadruple to ~47 million tonnes annually containing sulphuric acid and hexavalent chromium; captive coal power; deforestation and coastal pollution; and repeated Chinese-Indonesian worker violence.
> Without enforcement this becomes both a humanitarian failure and, eventually, a market-access problem as EU and US sourcing rules tighten.
> (4) Battery waste crisis by the 2030s.
> Indonesia has no functioning EPR regime; given that China — with far greater regulatory capacity — is losing control of informal battery recycling at 70-75%, Indonesia's informal-sector scale makes a worse outcome likely, with lead-acid recycling's existing contamination record as the local precedent.
> (5) Two-wheeler battery fires in dense housing.
> Kampung charging conditions, uncertified imported cells and conversion kits, and weak enforcement create a fire risk materially higher than China's — and China needed a full national standard revision (GB 17761, mandatory from September 2025) to address it.
> (6) Regressive mobility policy.
> Public money and policy attention flowing to Rp 300-700 million cars used by the top decile while the motorcycle-owning majority gets no viable electric option is a distributional failure that will become politically toxic, especially if paired with fuel-subsidy reform.
> (7) Stranded consumers from brand failure.
> Neta's Indonesian buyers already face the consequences of its parent's bankruptcy; with ~50 Chinese makers expected to retrench in 2026, more Indonesian owners will be left without warranty, parts or software support, and there is no local regulatory mechanism protecting them.
> (8) Grid and coal lock-in.
> EV growth justifying new coal capacity — including captive plants for smelters — would make the transition carbon-negative in effect while creating decades of stranded-asset and emissions liability.
> (9) Fiscal exposure.
> Incentives, TKDN concessions and infrastructure spending directed toward a sector whose value capture is largely foreign, at a moment when nickel prices and nickel-rich chemistry demand are both under pressure from LFP substitution.
> (10) Informal mechanic displacement.
> Hundreds of thousands of small bengkel operators face gradual obsolescence with no retraining pathway and no social protection.

**Kelompok Rentan**

> (1) Nickel smelter and mine workers in Morowali, Weda Bay and Southeast Sulawesi — 107 deaths and 155 injuries across 104 accidents (2019-2025), documented complaints about safety equipment, overwork and pay cuts (including from Chinese workers themselves), and repeated ethnic-tinged labour conflict.
> (2) Communities adjacent to the industrial parks — tailings dam breaches, water and air pollution, hexavalent chromium and sulphuric acid exposure, coastal fisheries damage, and land dispossession; often with limited information about what is being released.
> (3) ICE component-sector workers — concentrated in Bekasi, Karawang, Cikarang and Tangerang, with skills tied to engine, transmission and exhaust manufacture, facing a shrinking market and low EV local content.
> (4) Informal bengkel owners and mechanics — hundreds of thousands of micro-enterprises with no retraining pathway, no social protection, and capital sunk in ICE-specific tools and parts inventory.
> (5) SPBU attendants, fuel logistics workers and spare-parts traders.
> (6) Current SMK TKRO/TBSM students — the cohort most at risk of graduating into a declining trade because their curriculum has not been rebuilt.
> (7) Ojol drivers — simultaneously the biggest potential beneficiaries and the most exposed: they may be pushed into electric fleets by platform mandates while bearing the financing risk, battery degradation cost and swap-network dependency, with no bargaining power over swap pricing.
> (8) Low-income buyers of uncertified electric motorcycles or conversion kits — exposed to fire risk in dense housing and to worthless warranties.
> (9) Owners of failed brands — Neta buyers already, more to follow.
> (10) Residents of eastern Indonesia generally — bearing the extraction externalities while having the least access to the vehicles, charging and industrial value-added.

### Contoh Kasus Konkret

**Padanan Indonesia**

> (1) BYD Indonesia — entered January 2024, became the best-selling BEV brand with ~39.7% of BEV wholesales by mid-2025 and 51% of full-year 2025 BEV sales including Denza, reached top-six overall car brand, and is building a ~USD 1 billion, 150,000-unit plant at Subang for 2026 production.
> The closest analogue to the TikTok Shop pattern in e-commerce: direct corporate transplantation producing market leadership within roughly twelve months.
> (2) Wuling Air ev — the first BEV mass-produced in Indonesia (Cikarang, 2022), a direct descendant of the Liuzhou micro-EV playbook and proof that the Chinese small-EV model can be localised, though it has since lost share to BYD.
> (3) The CATL/CBL-ANTAM-IBC USD 6 billion integrated project — groundbreaking in East Halmahera on 29 June 2025 with a 6.9 GWh first-phase cell plant in Karawang, projecting 8,000 direct and 35,000 indirect jobs; Indonesia's attempt to convert nickel into battery-chain participation, and the test case for whether downstreaming delivers capability or only extraction.
> (4) The Rp 7 million electric-motorcycle subsidy (2023-2024) and its aftermath — sales rose to 62,409 (2023) and 77,078 (2024), then fell 28.6% to 55,059 in 2025 when the subsidy lapsed; the sharpest available evidence that Indonesian EV demand is currently policy-manufactured rather than self-sustaining, and the exact opposite of China's decade-long taper.
> (5) Polytron — an Indonesian consumer-electronics brand that took a claimed ~60% share of a shrinking electric-motorcycle market with roughly 33,000 units, built on Chinese componentry; the closest thing to a domestic champion, and a reminder that 'local' in this domain means localised assembly of Chinese technology.
> (6) IMIP Morowali — the Indonesian counterpart to China's industrial clusters, but with the costs concentrated locally: 21 deaths in the December 2023 explosion, tailings dam breaches in March 2025, and tailings volumes projected to reach ~47 million tonnes a year.
> (7) Neta Indonesia — stranded by its parent's bankruptcy, the local instance of China's brand-failure risk.
> (8) The TKDN escalator (40% 2026, 60% 2027-2028, 80% 2030) — Indonesia's substitute for China's dual-credit mandate: a localisation lever rather than an electrification lever, which is a meaningful design difference.
> (9) PLN's SPKLU network — 4,655 units at 3,007 locations by end-2025, +44% YoY, roughly China's 2013-2014 position.
> (10) The RUKN decree cutting the 2030 electric-motorcycle target from 13 million to 2.9-3.8 million — the moment the government formally conceded that the Chinese two-wheeler pattern will not reproduce here.
