### Tingkat Keyakinan & Kualitas Sumber

**Catatan Kontradiksi Data**

> (1) China MCN agency count varies materially by definition: CAPA reports approximately 29,000 'online performance (livestream and short video) brokerage institutions' as of May 2025, while other sources cite 24,000-30,000+ for 2024 and one search result referenced 290,000 (almost certainly a decimal/unit error, and inconsistent with the same report's own 180-fold growth from 160 in 2015).
> The research brief's '>30,000 MCN (2024)' is at the upper edge of defensible but is not the CAPA figure; RMB 63.6 billion for 2024 market size IS the CAPA figure and is well corroborated.
> (2) China MCN market size for 2023 is cited as both RMB 61.0 billion and RMB 72.6 billion by different vendors, which cannot both be reconciled with a 2024 figure of RMB 63.6 billion — the RMB 72.6 billion figure likely uses a broader definition including agency-mediated ad spend rather than agency revenue.
> Treat MCN market size as definition-dependent.
> (3) China short-video market size for 2024 is cited as both RMB 420 billion and RMB 480 billion (+15.6%) — different scope (platform revenue versus total industry including commerce commissions).
> (4) Indonesian TikTok user counts range from 108 million (18+ users, 2025) to 157 million (2026 users) to 180 million (advertising reach, 18+, late 2025) — these are three different metrics routinely quoted interchangeably; the 180 million figure is advertising reach and overstates real users, and the 157.6 million figure attributed to July 2024 in some sources appears to be advertising audience rather than active users.
> (5) The estimate of 12-15 million active Indonesian content creators comes from secondary commentary with no stated methodology and should not be treated as reliable; no BPS or Kemnaker count exists.
> (6) The Indonesian MCN market size of USD 887 million (2025) growing to USD 2.74 billion (2034) is a single vendor projection with no visible methodology.
> (7) Indonesian creative-economy figures (27.4 million workers, >8% of GDP, Rp 450 trillion) cover the entire creative-economy sector as officially defined — which includes culinary, fashion and crafts — and are frequently misquoted as creator-economy figures; the only rigorous creator-specific quantification available is YouTube's Rp 8.4 trillion GDP contribution and 190,000 FTE jobs.
> (8) China's professional streamer count of 15.08 million is dated end-2023 and is often quoted as current; the same figure appears in 2024, 2025 and 2026 reporting without update.
> (9) The 19.4 million 'talent gap by 2025' figure is a forecast from an industry report, not an observed statistic.
> (10) Douyin DAU is variously reported at 760 million, 800 million and 907 million MAU — DAU and MAU are frequently conflated in secondary sources.
> (11) The research brief's framing of Indonesia's lag as 'very short' is correct for consumption and platform adoption (1-3 years) but understates the industrialization and institutional lag (5-7 years), which is where the policy-relevant risk sits; presenting a single lag number for this domain is misleading.

## 5. Fintech & Digital Payment (QR payment, BNPL/paylater, neobank/digital bank, financial super-app)
**Kategori**: Keuangan / Digital Economy

📊 MIXED — Leapfrog on the payment rail, Laggard on the credit cycle, and a genuine 'risk leapfrog' in between. Indonesia leapfrogged the card era via a state-owned interoperable QR standard (QRIS), which is institutionally ahead of China's fragmented, platform-owned QR of 2014-2018. But Indonesia simultaneously imported China's embedded-credit business model years before building China's credit-bureau, capital and enforcement infrastructure — so household debt risk arrived faster than the guardrails. In other words: infrastructure leapfrog + regulation laggard = risk leapfrog. On P2P/pinjol social harm Indonesia is arguably already at or past China's 2018 severity level relative to income, which is a partial 'Reverse' case. | 🎯 Prob: Tinggi / High — for the remaining un-transferred components (Alipay+-style cross-border wallet interoperability, AI-driven alternative credit scoring, super-app wealth distribution, e-CNY-style CBDC, and post-boom credit re-regulation). The core payment and BNPL trends have already transferred. | 🔍 Keyakinan: Tinggi / High for the core quantitative claims — Indonesian BNPL and pinjol figures come directly from OJK monthly statistics reported consistently across ANTARA, Kontan, Katadata/Databoks and Republika, and the Chinese figures (Ant IPO suspension, Huabei/Jiebei RMB 1.7tn, P2P peak-to-zero, Ant's RMB 7.12bn fine, market shares) are well documented in primary regulatory and major-media sources. Sedang / Medium for market-size projections, e-wallet share percentages, forward-looking peak-timing estimates and the lag quantification, which involve judgement and vendor-dependent methodology.

> **Status di Indonesia**: SUDAH MASUK MASIF pada lapisan pembayaran (QR sudah mainstream, sebagian leapfrog karena rail-nya milik bank sentral), TAPI masih BOOMING TANPA REM pada lapisan kredit (BNPL + pinjol) — yaitu fase yang di China sudah berakhir sejak 2020. Neobank: sudah masuk masif dan mulai profitable. Financial super-app: sudah ada tetapi terfragmentasi, belum ada pemenang tunggal seperti Alipay/WeChat. Ringkasnya: Indonesia LEAPFROG pada infrastruktur pembayaran, tetapi LAGGARD pada regulasi kredit — kombinasi yang melahirkan 'leapfrog dalam risiko'. (English: mass adoption on the payment layer, partly leapfrogged via a central-bank-owned rail; still in an un-braked boom on the credit layer, the exact phase China exited in 2020; neobanks are mainstream and turning profitable; the financial super-app remains fragmented with no single winner.)

### Basic Info

**Tahun Mulai China**

> 2011-2014 for QR payment (Alipay and WeChat Pay launched proprietary QR codes in 2011; the 2014 WeChat 'hongbao' red-envelope campaign was the mass-adoption tipping point).
> 2014-2015 for consumer BNPL and micro-lending (Ant's Huabei launched April 2015, Jiebei 2015; JD Baitiao February 2014).
> 2013 for the fintech super-app / wealth layer (Yu'ebao money market fund, June 2013).
> 2014-2015 for internet-only banks (WeBank December 2014, MYbank June 2015).

**Pemain Kunci China**

> Payments and super-apps: Ant Group / Alipay (Alibaba), Tencent WeChat Pay / Weixin Pay, UnionPay & UnionPay Cloud QuickPass, Meituan Pay, Douyin Pay, JD Pay.
> Credit / BNPL: Ant Huabei (花呗) and Jiebei (借呗), JD Baitiao (白条), Ant Consumer Finance Co (Chongqing Ant Consumer Finance), Lufax, 360 DigiTech, Qudian, LexinFintech (Fenqile), Weilidai (WeBank).
> Digital banks: WeBank (Tencent), MYbank (Ant), aiBank (Baidu/CITIC), XW Bank (Xiaomi/New Hope).
> Wealth/insurance layer: Yu'ebao (Tianhong Asset Management), Ant Fortune, Zhong An Online (insurtech), Xianghubao (mutual aid, closed 2022).
> Infrastructure and regulators: PBOC, NUCC/Nets Union (网联), Baihang Credit (百行征信), PBOC Credit Reference Center, CBIRC/NFRA, e-CNY Digital Currency Research Institute.

### China Trend Detail

**Apa Yang Terjadi Di China**

> China skipped the card era entirely and built a QR-code-first, wallet-native payment stack that then became the distribution rail for credit, savings, insurance and investment.
> Four layers stacked on top of each other.
> (1) Payment rail: Alipay and WeChat Pay made static and dynamic QR codes free-to-cheap for merchants, so a street vendor with a printed paper code could accept digital money with zero hardware.
> The 2014 WeChat red-envelope campaign converted hundreds of millions of users into wallet-holders overnight by tying payment to a social ritual; Jack Ma called it a 'Pearl Harbor moment' for Alipay.
> By 2016-2018 cash had effectively disappeared from tier-1/2 city retail.
> (2) Data-to-credit layer: because the wallets saw every transaction, they could underwrite consumers with no bank credit file.
> Huabei (a revolving 'virtual credit card', 30-40 day interest-free) and Jiebei (cash instalment loans) were embedded one tap away from the checkout button on Alipay and Taobao — the archetypal BNPL model.
> Ant did this asset-light: it originated loans and sold ~98% of the risk to partner banks and ABS investors, keeping only ~2% on balance sheet while taking most of the fee.
> (3) Deposit/wealth layer: Yu'ebao (2013) let users sweep idle wallet balance into a money-market fund with one tap and became briefly the world's largest MMF (peak ~RMB 1.69 trillion, 2018), pulling deposits away from banks.
> Internet-only banks WeBank and MYbank then used wallet data to lend to consumers and micro-merchants with fully automated underwriting (WeBank's 'Weilidai' approves in seconds).
> (4) Backlash and re-regulation: the parallel P2P lending industry (peak 5,970 platforms, >USD 218bn outstanding in 2018) collapsed in fraud and runs, wiping out retail investors and forcing regulators to reduce the sector to literally zero platforms by mid-November 2020.
> That trauma is the direct cause of the crackdown on Ant: the record USD 34.5bn IPO was suspended on 3 November 2020, days after new online micro-lending draft rules; Ant was ordered to restructure as a financial holding company, fold Huabei/Jiebei into a licensed consumer finance subsidiary, meet bank-like capital rules, contribute at least 30% of each co-lent loan from its own capital, cut the 'improper linkage' between the payment app and its credit products, connect to the national credit reporting system, and separate its data business.
> Ant was fined RMB 7.12bn (~USD 985m) in July 2023, formally closing the campaign.
> In parallel PBOC forced all third-party payment flows off direct bank connections onto the Nets Union (NUCC) clearing house ('断直连', completed 2018-2019), imposed 100% reserve requirements on customer float, pushed barcode interoperability so Alipay/WeChat/UnionPay codes must be mutually scannable, and rolled out e-CNY as a state-controlled alternative rail (~180 million personal wallets, RMB 7.3 trillion cumulative transactions by July 2024).
> Net effect: China now has the world's deepest digital payment penetration, but the credit layer is licensed, capitalised, rate-capped and credit-bureau-reported — a mature, heavily-regulated regime.

**Fase Tren Di China**

> Payment layer: MATURE / SATURATED — near-universal adoption, growth now comes from cross-border (Alipay+ in 56 countries, 19m merchants onboarded) and from format upgrades (palm-print, e-CNY, tap-to-pay), not from new domestic users.
> Credit/BNPL layer: REGULATED / POST-BACKLASH — after the 2020-2023 crackdown, growth is licensed, capital-constrained and rate-capped; volumes stopped compounding and youth-debt discourse turned negative.
> P2P sub-sector: EXTINCT by regulatory fiat (zero platforms since Nov 2020).
> Neobank layer: MATURE and profitable but capped by licence scarcity (no new internet bank licences issued for years).
> Net: China is simultaneously mature on payments and in the post-backlash regulated phase on consumer credit — which is exactly the phase Indonesia has not yet reached.

**Puncak Tren China**

> Payment adoption peak: 2017-2019, epicentre Hangzhou, Shenzhen, Shanghai and Beijing, then diffusing to tier-3/4 cities and rural counties by 2019-2020.
> Consumer credit/BNPL peak: 2019 to first half of 2020 — Huabei/Jiebei at RMB 1.7 trillion facilitated and Ant's IPO priced at a ~USD 315bn valuation in October 2020.
> The absolute peak moment was 3 November 2020, when the IPO was suspended 48 hours before listing; that date marks the top of the unregulated Chinese consumer-fintech cycle.
> P2P peak: 2017 (5,970 platforms) with blow-up concentrated in 2018-2019 in Shanghai, Hangzhou, Shenzhen.
> Wealth-layer peak: Yu'ebao AUM peak 2018.

### Status Indonesia Saat Ini

**Status Di Indonesia**

> SUDAH MASUK MASIF pada lapisan pembayaran (QR sudah mainstream, sebagian leapfrog karena rail-nya milik bank sentral), TAPI masih BOOMING TANPA REM pada lapisan kredit (BNPL + pinjol) — yaitu fase yang di China sudah berakhir sejak 2020.
> Neobank: sudah masuk masif dan mulai profitable.
> Financial super-app: sudah ada tetapi terfragmentasi, belum ada pemenang tunggal seperti Alipay/WeChat.
> Ringkasnya: Indonesia LEAPFROG pada infrastruktur pembayaran, tetapi LAGGARD pada regulasi kredit — kombinasi yang melahirkan 'leapfrog dalam risiko'.
> (English: mass adoption on the payment layer, partly leapfrogged via a central-bank-owned rail; still in an un-braked boom on the credit layer, the exact phase China exited in 2020; neobanks are mainstream and turning profitable; the financial super-app remains fragmented with no single winner.)

**Contoh Konkret Indonesia**

> Payment rail: QRIS (Quick Response Code Indonesian Standard, Bank Indonesia, launched 2019, mandatory interoperability from 1 January 2020), QRIS Cross-border (live with Thailand, Malaysia, Singapore, Japan, South Korea and China), QRIS TAP (NFC tap-in/tap-out, launched October 2025).
> E-wallets: GoPay (GoTo), DANA (part-owned by Ant Group, Sinar Mas/Emtek, Lazada), ShopeePay (Sea Group), OVO (Grab), LinkAja (BUMN consortium).
> BNPL: Kredivo (FinAccel), Akulaku/Akulaku PayLater (Ant Group investor), SPayLater (Shopee), GoPayLater / GoPayLater Cicil, Atome, Traveloka PayLater, Home Credit, Indodana, plus bank-issued paylater from BCA, BRI, Mandiri, BNI.
> P2P/pinjol: Investree (collapsed/licence revoked), TaniFund, AdaKami, Easycash, Kredit Pintar, Julo, Amartha, Modalku.
> Neobanks: Bank Jago (GoTo ecosystem), SeaBank (Shopee), Superbank (Grab/Emtek/Singtel/KakaoBank), blu by BCA Digital, Bank Neo Commerce, Krom Bank, Bank Saqu, Allo Bank (CT Corp), Bank Raya, Jenius (BTPN), LINE Bank, Bank Aladin Syariah.
> Wealth super-app analogue: Bibit, Ajaib, Bareksa, Stockbit, Pluang.
> Regulators/enforcement: OJK POJK 32/2025 on BNPL (effective 15 December 2025, full eligibility rules by 1 January 2027), OJK SLIK credit bureau, Satgas PASTI (anti-illegal-lending task force), BI Proyek Garuda (digital rupiah, still at proof-of-concept).

### Analisis Lag

**Bukti Historical Lag**

> 1) E-money/QR: Alipay QR from 2011 and mass adoption by 2014-2016; QRIS only launched in 2019 and only crossed 50 million users in 2025 — a ~5-8 year offset consistent with the e-commerce and ride-hailing lags.
> 2) Ride-hailing/super-app: Didi Chuxing consolidated 2015-2016; Gojek/Grab consolidated in Indonesia around 2019-2021 (GoTo merger May 2021) — ~5 years.
> 3) P2P lending precedent is the sharpest evidence: China's P2P boomed 2013-2017, blew up 2018-2019, was zeroed in 2020.
> Indonesia's licensed P2P boomed 2018-2021, entered its stress phase 2023-2026 (Investree licence revocation, TWP90 rising from 2.52% to 4.52% in a year, Rp 101tn outstanding) — a lag of roughly 5-6 years on exactly the same curve.
> 4) Consumer-credit regulation: China capped judicially-protected private lending rates and imposed the 30% co-lending capital rule in 2020-2021; Indonesia's OJK only introduced daily-rate caps for P2P in 2024 (SEOJK 19/2023, stepping down to 0.3%/day then 0.2%/day for consumptive loans) and BNPL eligibility rules in POJK 32/2025 — again ~4-5 years later.
> 5) Banking dis-intermediation: China's big-four banks began net headcount declines in 2016 driven by mobile payments; Indonesian banks only began meaningful branch rationalisation around 2021-2023.
> The consistency of a 5-8 year offset across five separate sub-trends is the strongest support for the estimate.

**Tipe Lag**

> MIXED — Leapfrog on the payment rail, Laggard on the credit cycle, and a genuine 'risk leapfrog' in between.
> Indonesia leapfrogged the card era via a state-owned interoperable QR standard (QRIS), which is institutionally ahead of China's fragmented, platform-owned QR of 2014-2018.
> But Indonesia simultaneously imported China's embedded-credit business model years before building China's credit-bureau, capital and enforcement infrastructure — so household debt risk arrived faster than the guardrails.
> In other words: infrastructure leapfrog + regulation laggard = risk leapfrog.
> On P2P/pinjol social harm Indonesia is arguably already at or past China's 2018 severity level relative to income, which is a partial 'Reverse' case.

### Probabilitas Transfer ke Indonesia

**Probabilitas Transfer**

> Tinggi / High — for the remaining un-transferred components (Alipay+-style cross-border wallet interoperability, AI-driven alternative credit scoring, super-app wealth distribution, e-CNY-style CBDC, and post-boom credit re-regulation).
> The core payment and BNPL trends have already transferred.

**Alasan Probabilitas**

> The transfer is already substantially complete, so the question is about residual components, and every enabling condition points to high probability.
> (1) Chinese capital is already inside the Indonesian cap table: Ant Group holds a stake in DANA and invested in Akulaku (USD 40m, then part of a ~USD 100m Series D); Tencent invested in Gojek; Alibaba controls Lazada Indonesia; Sea Group (Tencent-backed) owns Shopee, ShopeePay, SPayLater and SeaBank.
> (2) The demand side is textbook: ~200 million internet users, 85%+ smartphone penetration, tens of millions of thin-file adults with no credit card (credit card penetration is in the single digits), and a young median age (~30) matching China's 2015 profile.
> (3) The state actively wants the model: Bank Indonesia is negotiating QRIS interoperability with Chinese rails and has already opened a China corridor; Ant is in talks with Bank Mandiri and DANA to operate Alipay+ locally.
> (4) The margin logic is compelling for platforms — embedded credit is the only reliably profitable layer on top of near-zero-margin payments, so every Indonesian super-app has a structural incentive to push BNPL harder.
> (5) The main uncertainty is not whether the model comes but which version arrives — the pre-2020 Chinese growth version (already here) or the post-2021 regulated version (arriving now via POJK 32/2025).

**Vektor Transmisi**

> (a) Direct entry by Chinese players — strongest vector.
> Ant Group is a shareholder in DANA and an investor in Akulaku; Alipay+ is being negotiated with Bank Mandiri and DANA for local acceptance; Alipay+ already reaches 56 countries and ~19 million merchants; UnionPay acceptance and QRIS-China cross-border corridors bring Chinese rails directly to Indonesian merchants.
> Sea Group (Tencent-backed, Singapore-domiciled but Chinese-model) operates Shopee, ShopeePay, SPayLater and SeaBank as a single closed loop — an almost literal transplant of the Alipay-Huabei-MYbank stack.
> (b) Local copycat / model imitation — Kredivo's revolving credit line is a direct Huabei analogue; GoTo's GoPay + GoPayLater + Bank Jago is a conscious Alipay + Huabei + MYbank replication; Superbank (Grab/Emtek/Singtel/KakaoBank) copies the WeBank ecosystem-bank pattern; QRIS itself is a policy imitation of China's barcode payment model but with state-owned interoperability.
> (c) Chinese venture and strategic capital — Ant, Tencent, Alibaba, GGV, Qiming, Gobi and Chinese ABS/offshore lenders funding Indonesian lending books; Chinese-built lending-app software (many illegal pinjol apps are white-labelled Chinese SaaS with Chinese-language admin panels and Chinese-run collection call centres, a documented pattern since the 2018-2019 exodus of Chinese P2P operators after their domestic ban).
> (d) Talent and operator diaspora — ex-Ant/Tencent/Didi operators and Chinese-Indonesian founders seeding local fintechs; MBA/engineering alumni returning from Chinese firms.
> (e) Algorithmic and content diffusion — TikTok Shop and Douyin-style commerce normalising instalment checkout; influencer promotion of paylater; SEO/app-store diffusion of lending apps.
> (f) Regulatory learning — OJK and BI officials explicitly study PBOC/CBIRC precedents, which is the one benign vector: it transmits the *cure* rather than the disease.

### Faktor Pendorong

**Prasyarat Struktural**

> Threshold conditions and where Indonesia sits versus China at the equivalent moment.
> (1) Smartphone + mobile internet penetration above ~60% of adults: China crossed this around 2015-2016 (internet penetration ~50-53%, but urban smartphone use far higher); Indonesia is at ~80% of the population digitally connected and ~85% smartphone penetration in 2024 — condition MET and exceeded.
> (2) GDP per capita: China's mobile-payment explosion happened at ~USD 7,500-8,000 per capita (2015-2016); Indonesia sits at roughly USD 5,000-5,300 in 2025-2026 — condition PARTIALLY met, meaning Indonesia is adopting the same technology at ~65% of China's income level, which mechanically raises debt-service stress per rupiah of credit extended.
> (3) Low incumbent card penetration (the leapfrog precondition): China had ~0.3-0.4 credit cards per capita in 2015; Indonesia has roughly 17-18 million credit cards for ~190 million adults, i.e.
> under 10% penetration — condition STRONGLY MET, which is precisely why BNPL substitutes for credit cards rather than competing with them.
> (4) A large thin-file, unbanked or underbanked adult population: China had several hundred million; Indonesia had ~97.7 million unbanked adults (48% of adults) in the 2021 Findex with ~60 million of them holding mobile phones — condition MET.
> (5) Cheap merchant acceptance hardware: QR at near-zero cost — MET, and QRIS's 0% MDR for micro-merchants under Rp 500k is more aggressive than China ever was.
> (6) Urbanisation: China was ~56% urban in 2015; Indonesia is ~58-59% urban — condition MET.
> (7) An interoperable clearing layer: China only built this retroactively (Nets Union, 2017-2019); Indonesia built it up front (QRIS/BI, 2019-2020) — Indonesia AHEAD.
> (8) A functioning national credit bureau covering non-bank lenders: China built PBOC Credit Reference Center plus Baihang Credit and forced platforms to report; Indonesia's SLIK historically covered banks and multifinance but not all fintech lending, and BNPL reporting into SLIK is only being mandated now under POJK 32/2025 — condition NOT YET MET, the single biggest structural gap.
> (9) Regulatory capacity to supervise thousands of small non-bank lenders: China ultimately used administrative force to zero the sector; Indonesia's OJK relies on licensing plus Satgas PASTI blocking (14,006 entities blocked since 2017) which is whack-a-mole against offshore apps — condition WEAK.
> (10) A social safety net to absorb defaulters: both weak, but Indonesia's informal-sector share (~59% of workers) is far higher than China's at the equivalent moment, meaning income volatility is structurally worse.

**Indikator Pemantauan**

> Leading indicators that the next phase is arriving: (1) OJK monthly statistics — BNPL outstanding growth rate, TWP90 crossing the 5% ceiling, share of NPL held by the 19-34 age bracket (already 48.65%); a TWP90 print above 5% would be the trigger event.
> (2) Pefindo Biro Kredit and SLIK reporting coverage — the month BNPL exposures become fully SLIK-reported is the moment true multi-lender exposure (borrowing from one app to repay another) becomes visible; expect a one-off jump in reported NPLs.
> (3) Licensing signals — OJK approvals for financing companies to run BNPL under POJK 32/2025, new digital bank licences, ITSK (innovative credit scoring) sandbox graduations.
> (4) Chinese-player footprint — formal Alipay+ acquiring launch in Indonesia, Ant/Tencent stake increases in DANA/Akulaku/GoTo, UnionPay-QRIS full interoperability, Chinese ABS or offshore funding lines appearing in Indonesian lenders' funding mixes.
> (5) Trademark and entity registrations at DJKI plus new PT PMA registrations by Chinese fintech holdings.
> (6) Job postings — surge in vacancies for credit risk modeller, collections analytics, fraud/AML, and 'debt collection' roles; conversely a decline in teller and branch-operations hiring at BUKU-4 banks.
> (7) Search and app-store signals — Google Trends for 'paylater', 'galbay' (gagal bayar), 'joki pinjol', 'sedang butuh uang'; app-store ranking velocity of new lending apps.
> (8) Satgas PASTI monthly blocking counts (951 in Q1 2026) and the volume of phone numbers referred to Komdigi for blocking.
> (9) Bank Indonesia QRIS dashboards — merchant count, transaction volume, and the ratio of QRIS TAP to static QR.
> (10) University signals — new fintech/financial-engineering study programmes and Kampus Merdeka partnerships with fintechs.
> (11) Media and civil society — growth of debt-relief communities, class actions, and the emergence of an Indonesian analogue to China's 'Debtors Avengers' Douban groups (already visible on Reddit r/indonesia and Facebook 'korban pinjol' groups).

### Hambatan & Faktor Pembatal

**Hambatan Transfer**

> (1) Fragmented wallet market — no Indonesian player has above ~25% share, so none can achieve the data density and cross-subsidy power that made Alipay's underwriting work; this slows the shift from payment to credit monetisation.
> (2) Regulatory pre-emption — BI owns the QR standard and caps MDR, structurally denying platforms the payment-monopoly rents that funded Chinese fintech expansion; OJK's POJK 32/2025 arrived before Indonesian BNPL matured, unlike China.
> (3) Credit bureau incompleteness — without full multi-lender visibility, prudent lenders cannot price risk, so responsible players under-lend while aggressive ones over-lend; this depresses the quality but not the quantity of transfer.
> (4) Islamic finance sensitivities — riba concerns constrain interest-bearing BNPL among a meaningful segment; sharia-compliant structures (murabahah/ijarah) add cost and complexity.
> (5) Archipelagic geography and uneven connectivity — reliable 4G, agent networks and ID verification are much weaker in eastern Indonesia.
> (6) Identity infrastructure friction — although Dukcapil NIK/e-KTP verification exists, data quality issues and identity fraud (rented NIKs, syndicated account farming) inflate loss rates.
> (7) Funding cost — Indonesian lenders fund at far higher rates than Chinese platforms did, and lack Ant-scale ABS markets, capping loan-book growth.
> (8) Foreign ownership and data-localisation rules limiting direct Chinese control of licensed institutions.
> (9) Consumer trust damage — the pinjol scandal has already poisoned public sentiment toward digital credit, creating political resistance to further liberalisation.
> (10) Weak collections legal infrastructure — no equivalent of China's court-enforced 'laolai' blacklist, so unsecured recovery rates are low, which paradoxically pushes lenders toward abusive informal collection.

**Faktor Pembatal Transfer**

> Structural reasons the Chinese version will NOT arrive in the same form.
> (1) State ownership of the rail is irreversible: QRIS is a Bank Indonesia standard with mandated interoperability and administered MDR.
> China's model depended on two private duopolists owning the rail and monetising the float and the data for a decade before the state clawed it back (Nets Union, 100% float reserves).
> Indonesia pre-empted that, so no Indonesian Ant Group can ever accumulate equivalent rent, data or systemic leverage.
> Consequence: Indonesia will not produce a domestic Alipay-scale financial super-app.
> (2) Market fragmentation is stable, not transitional: GoTo, Sea/Shopee, Grab and DANA are each backed by different global sponsors (SoftBank/Tencent/Alibaba/Sea/Grab/Emtek/Singtel/KakaoBank) with no plausible merger path given competition and national-interest scrutiny; China's duopoly emerged from a domestic market closed to foreign competitors, a condition Indonesia does not replicate.
> (3) Absence of a universal, enforceable credit-identity plus judicial enforcement regime: China's social-credit adjacent enforcement (court blacklists restricting flights, trains and private schooling for judgment defaulters) gave unsecured consumer lending a recovery mechanism that Indonesia's legal system cannot and politically will not replicate.
> Without it, Indonesian unsecured lending economics must stay high-rate and low-ticket permanently.
> (4) Informality of income: ~59% of Indonesian workers are informal with no verifiable payslip, so the POJK 32/2025 requirement of documented Rp 3 million monthly income either excludes the majority of would-be borrowers (shrinking the formal market) or is met with fabricated documents (undermining the rule).
> China's urban formal-employment base at the equivalent moment was far larger.
> (5) Income level mismatch: adopting the same credit products at ~65% of China's per-capita income at the equivalent point means the ratio of instalment burden to income is structurally worse; the Indonesian market will therefore hit its default wall at a much lower absolute penetration than China did.
> (6) No manufacturing/e-commerce supply engine of equivalent depth to absorb credit into productive consumption — 93% of Indonesian BNPL is pure consumption, whereas a larger share of Chinese platform credit funded merchant working capital via MYbank/Weilidai.
> (7) CBDC divergence: e-CNY is partly a geopolitical instrument backed by an enormous domestic payment base; Digital Rupiah has no comparable strategic urgency and remains at proof-of-concept, so a Chinese-style state digital currency rollout is unlikely before the 2030s.
> (8) Demographics run the other way: China's fintech credit boom coincided with a peaking working-age population and a real-estate wealth effect; Indonesia's runs alongside a still-growing young cohort but without an asset-price wealth buffer, so household balance sheets have no collateral cushion.

### Prediksi Timeline di Indonesia

**Tahun Masuk Indonesia**

> Already entered, in phases: QR/e-money 2016-2019 (GoPay 2016, OVO 2017, DANA 2018, QRIS standard 2019); BNPL/paylater 2016-2018 (Kredivo 2016, Akulaku 2016, Traveloka PayLater 2018, SPayLater 2019); licensed P2P 2016-2018; neobanks 2020-2023 (Bank Jago transformation 2020-2021, SeaBank 2021, Superbank 2023).
> The Chinese-style *regulated* phase entered in December 2025 with POJK 32/2025.

**Skenario Percepatan**

> Formal Alipay+ / UnionPay acceptance launch in Indonesia plus full QRIS-China interoperability; a large Chinese strategic investment or control stake in DANA, Akulaku or a digital bank; completion of full BNPL and fintech-lending reporting into SLIK (which would unlock safe scale-up); Kartu Prakerja-style or government-to-person disbursements routed through wallets; nationwide QRIS TAP on iOS; a macro shock (subsidy cuts, layoffs) that pushes households toward instalment credit; and aggressive AI/alternative credit scoring approvals under OJK's ITSK sandbox.

### Dampak Sosial-Ekonomi

**Dampak Lapangan Kerja**

> Jobs disappearing or shrinking: bank tellers and branch service staff (China's precedent is stark — ICBC cut 14,090 tellers, CCB 30,007 and ABC 10,842 in a single year, with big-four headcount falling for the first time in six years in 2016; >84% of Chinese banking transactions moved outside branches by 2016; 1,126 Chinese branches closed in H1 2024 and ATMs fell by 8,358 in one quarter).
> Indonesia will follow with a lag: expect continued rationalisation of BRI/Mandiri/BNI/BCA branch and ATM networks, shrinking demand for cash-handling roles, cash-in-transit staff, ATM replenishment crews, and traditional teller/customer-service positions.
> Also at risk: manual credit analysts and survey-based field credit officers at multifinance companies (replaced by automated scoring), physical top-up/pulsa agents as wallets go bank-linked, and traditional insurance and mutual-fund agents displaced by app distribution.
> Jobs changing: bank relationship managers becoming advisory/complex-product specialists; branch staff shifting to onboarding/digital assistance; field collectors moving from door-knocking to omnichannel/telecollection under stricter conduct rules.
> Jobs being created: credit risk and machine-learning modellers, alternative-data scoring scientists, fraud/AML and financial-crime analysts, data engineers for real-time payment streams, API/platform engineers, mobile developers, product managers for embedded finance, compliance and regulatory-reporting specialists, cybersecurity and identity-verification specialists, customer-experience and dispute-resolution agents, merchant-acquiring field sales for QRIS onboarding (a genuinely large, geographically distributed job category), agent-banking (Laku Pandai/BRILink) operators, and — a dark category — a rapidly expanding debt-collection industry (both formal telecollection and informal field DC), which in China grew into a notorious 暴力催收 sector before being criminalised.
> Net national effect is likely mildly positive on headcount but sharply negative on job quality at the low-skill end and strongly positive at the analytics end — a barbell.

**Dampak Kelas Menengah**

> Double-edged and, on current trajectory, net negative for the aspiring middle class.
> Positives: near-frictionless payments cut transaction costs; access to credit without a credit card for the first time; higher deposit yields at digital banks (5-8% p.a.
> at Krom, Bank Neo Commerce, Superbank versus ~2-3% at incumbents); micro-investing via Bibit/Ajaib/Bareksa democratising mutual funds; small merchants gaining formal transaction records that can become credit history.
> Negatives, which currently dominate: 93.01% of BNPL outstanding is consumption financing, not productive investment — this is a consumption-smoothing tool being used as a consumption-*expansion* tool.
> Indonesia's middle class is already shrinking (World Bank/BPS data show the middle class falling from ~57.3 million in 2019 to ~47-48 million by 2024, with tens of millions sliding into the 'aspiring middle' vulnerable band), so layering unsecured instalment debt onto stagnant real wages accelerates that slide.
> The 'lifestyle inflation on credit' pattern — gadgets, fashion, travel, concert tickets, food delivery bought in twelve instalments — converts a one-off consumption boost into a permanent monthly cash-flow claim.
> Because BNPL is largely absent from SLIK today, a household can hold five or six simultaneous paylater lines and still appear creditworthy, meaning the first real signal is a mortgage or car-loan rejection.
> Indonesian banks have already begun rejecting KPR applications because of paylater records — a direct wealth-formation penalty: young middle-class Indonesians are trading future housing access for present consumption.
> China's precedent is exactly this: research on youth indebtedness there documents a debt-laden cohort curtailing consumption, delaying marriage and housing, and dampening aggregate demand — the 'death of consumption' effect.
> Indonesia risks reaching that state at a much lower income level.

**Dampak Daerah Non Jawa**

> Highly relevant outside Java, and in some respects the risk is greater there.
> QRIS is genuinely national — 42-44 million merchants cannot be a Java-only phenomenon, and BI's cross-border and tourism corridors (Bali, Manado, Labuan Bajo, Batam, Lombok) push acceptance into non-Java tourism economies.
> Agent banking (BRILink, ~700k+ agents) and Laku Pandai already give non-Java districts a cash-in/cash-out layer that wallets ride on, so payment access diffuses reasonably evenly and is arguably Indonesia's best inclusion success.
> The credit layer, however, diffuses unevenly and dangerously: pinjol default rates are highest in provinces where income is most volatile and financial literacy weakest, and Katadata's provincial rankings consistently show non-Java provinces among the highest TWP90 districts alongside Jabodetabek.
> Structural reasons: (a) incomes outside Java are more seasonal (harvest cycles, fisheries, commodity prices, mining shifts), which mismatches fixed monthly instalments; (b) financial literacy indices are materially lower outside Java-Bali (OJK's national literacy index sits around 65-66% versus inclusion near 75-80%+, and the literacy-inclusion gap is widest in eastern Indonesia); (c) illegal lending apps target exactly these markets because enforcement reach is thinnest; (d) there is no local advisory or legal-aid capacity when collection harassment starts.
> Counter-effect: for non-Java MSMEs, QRIS transaction history is the first credible path to formal working-capital credit, and productive P2P (Amartha, Modalku, Investree's original thesis) does reach rural women's groups and small traders.
> The policy conclusion is that the payment layer should be pushed harder outside Java while the consumptive credit layer needs *stricter* limits there, not looser ones — the opposite of what commercial incentives dictate.

### Kaitan Pendidikan

**Jurusan Terancam**

> Programmes whose relevance is eroding, though almost none disappear outright — they hollow out.
> (1) D3/Vokasi Perbankan, Keuangan dan Perbankan, and Administrasi Perbankan — these were built to supply teller, customer-service and back-office cash-handling roles, precisely the jobs China's data shows evaporating; Indonesian intake into these diplomas should be expected to fall sharply.
> (2) Akuntansi at the transactional/bookkeeping end — automated reconciliation from payment APIs removes routine journal work; the discipline survives only if it moves toward assurance, forensic accounting, and systems audit.
> (3) Manajemen Keuangan taught without any quantitative or programming content — graduates cannot compete for the credit-modelling roles that replace the analyst roles they trained for.
> (4) Sekretaris / Administrasi Perkantoran in financial institutions.
> (5) Ekonomi Pembangunan taught purely descriptively, without data skills.
> (6) Asuransi/Aktuaria taught without programming — actuarial science itself is in demand but only in its computational form.
> (7) Marketing/Manajemen Pemasaran generalist tracks in financial services, displaced by growth/performance-marketing and CRM analytics roles.
> The honest framing for students: the *sector* is growing while the *entry-level clerical ladder* into it is being removed, so the risk is not unemployment in finance but the disappearance of the low-credential entry point that historically let a D3 graduate enter a bank and rise.

**Jurusan Dibutuhkan**

> (1) Financial Engineering / Fintech / Computational Finance — an explicit cross-disciplinary programme combining finance, statistics, and software (China's template: 119 mainland universities now run a 金融科技 major built around programming, big data, blockchain and AI applied to finance).
> (2) Data Science and Statistics with a credit-risk specialisation — scorecard development, survival analysis, PD/LGD/EAD modelling, IFRS 9 expected-credit-loss modelling, model validation and model risk management; this is the single most under-supplied skill in Indonesian lending today.
> (3) Actuarial Science / Aktuaria in computational form.
> (4) Cybersecurity, digital identity and fraud analytics — social-engineering fraud, account takeover, synthetic identity and money-mule detection; Indonesia has an acute shortage.
> (5) Software engineering for high-availability distributed systems — real-time payment switching, idempotency, reconciliation, ledger design; QRIS/BI-FAST volumes make this a genuine specialism.
> (6) Law and regulatory technology — fintech law, data protection (UU PDP), consumer protection, AML/CFT, RegTech and SupTech; OJK/BI themselves need this pipeline.
> (7) Behavioural economics and consumer finance — designing products and disclosures that do not exploit present bias, plus financial-literacy programme design.
> (8) UX research and inclusive design for low-literacy and low-connectivity users.
> (9) Sharia fintech / Islamic finance structuring for compliant BNPL and takaful.
> (10) Collections and workout/restructuring as an ethical professional discipline — currently an unregulated informal trade that urgently needs a certified profession.
> (11) AI/ML engineering with explainability skills, since OJK's ITSK framework and consumer-protection rules will require explainable credit decisions.

**China Education Response**

> China's system responded institutionally and fast.
> (1) A dedicated undergraduate major, 金融科技 (Financial Technology, catalogue code 020310T), was formally approved by the Ministry of Education and first offered from the 2017-2018 cycle.
> Adoption then exploded: roughly 47 institutions offered it as of the 2023 rankings and about 119 mainland universities offer it now, with fintech ranking among the ten fastest-growing new majors in 2022 at a ~194% increase in offering institutions in a single year.
> (2) The curriculum is explicitly cross-disciplinary by design — economics and finance fused with statistics, software programming, big data, blockchain and artificial intelligence — rather than a finance degree with an IT elective bolted on.
> Central University of Finance and Economics (CUFE), University of International Business and Economics (UIBE), South China University of Technology, Beijing Institute of Technology and Dongbei University of Finance and Economics lead the rankings.
> (3) Elite finance institutes (Shanghai Advanced Institute of Finance/SAIF at SJTU, PBC School of Finance at Tsinghua, Peking University's Institute of Digital Finance) built research centres feeding regulators — PKU's Digital Financial Inclusion Index of China became the standard measurement instrument and directly informed policy.
> (4) Industry-academia coupling: Ant, Tencent, JD and the big banks fund joint labs, sponsor competitions, and hire aggressively, with reports of banks offering RMB 700,000 annual packages for fintech talent, which pulled enrolment.
> (5) Adjacent expansion in actuarial science, cyberspace security (a first-level discipline since 2015) and AI majors (~400+ universities added AI majors from 2018).
> (6) The corrective phase: after the P2P collapse and the Ant crackdown, curricula and regulator-facing programmes added heavy compliance, financial-consumer-protection, risk-management and financial-ethics content, and MOE/PBOC pushed financial literacy into secondary-school curricula — China moved financial education into schools *after* the damage, which is the mistake Indonesia can avoid by moving first.
> (7) Vocational retraining: banks redeployed displaced tellers into wealth-advisory and digital-support roles through internal academies rather than mass layoffs, a model Indonesian banks could copy.

### Pelajaran Kebijakan dari China

**Respons Kebijakan China**

> Regulations China imposed only AFTER the trend matured and blew up — this is Indonesia's preemptive-policy menu.
> (1) Total prohibition of unlicensed P2P lending: the sector went from 5,970 platforms (2017) to zero by mid-November 2020 after >USD 218bn of loans and ~USD 115bn of unpaid investor claims.
> Lesson: intermediating retail savings into unsecured consumer credit without bank-grade prudential rules always ends in runs.
> (2) Licensing and capital: online micro-lending draft rules (2 November 2020) plus the April 2021 rectification forced Ant into a financial holding company under PBOC supervision with bank-like consolidated capital requirements.
> (3) The co-lending skin-in-the-game rule: partners must fund at least 30% of each jointly-originated loan, ending the originate-and-distribute model where Ant held only ~2% of a RMB 1.7 trillion book.
> (4) Product licensing: Huabei and Jiebei were forced into a separately capitalised licensed consumer finance company (Chongqing Ant Consumer Finance).
> (5) Severing 'improper linkage' between the payment app and credit products — i.e.
> banning the design pattern where a credit line is the default payment method at checkout.
> (6) Mandatory credit reporting: platforms must feed the national credit reference system; Baihang Credit was created to cover non-bank consumer lending, ending invisible multi-lender stacking.
> (7) Interest-rate ceilings: the Supreme People's Court reset the judicially protected private-lending rate cap in August 2020 to four times the one-year LPR (~15.4%), far below the previous 24%/36% brackets, crushing high-rate consumer lending economics.
> (8) Protection of specific vulnerable groups: micro-lenders were banned from marketing to and lending to university students (2021), and platforms self-committed to no lending to minors and to blocking loan proceeds flowing into stocks or property.
> (9) Payment-rail nationalisation of clearing: all third-party payment flows forced onto Nets Union/NUCC ('断直连', 2018-2019) plus 100% reserve requirements on customer float, ending float income and giving the regulator full transaction visibility.
> (10) Mandatory barcode interoperability so no wallet can lock merchants in.
> (11) Advertising and marketing restrictions on consumer loan promotion, especially content that trivialises borrowing.
> (12) Criminalisation of violent debt collection and crackdowns on 'campus loans' and abusive collection.
> (13) Enforcement finale: the RMB 7.12bn (~USD 985m) fine on Ant in July 2023.
> What Indonesia can adopt preemptively: the 30% skin-in-the-game rule for co-lending and channelling arrangements; universal mandatory reporting of every consumer credit line (including BNPL) into SLIK before the next growth cycle; a hard ban on credit being the default checkout option; a statutory total-cost-of-credit cap covering fees, not just nominal interest; a prohibition on lending to students and minors; and a licensed, criminally-enforceable debt-collection regime.

**Rekomendasi Kebijakan Indonesia**

> (1) Make SLIK (or Pefindo/private bureaus with mandated reciprocity) reporting universal and real-time for every BNPL, paylater and P2P exposure, with no de-minimis exemption — this is the single highest-leverage intervention and must precede, not follow, the next credit expansion.
> (2) Impose a debt-service-to-income ceiling (e.g.
> total unsecured instalment obligations capped at 20-30% of verified monthly income) enforced at the bureau level across all lenders, not per-lender; this is more workable than POJK 32/2025's Rp 3 million income floor, which is easily gamed and excludes informal workers.
> (3) Adopt China's co-lending skin-in-the-game rule: any platform originating credit funded by banks or institutional lenders must retain a minimum first-loss share (20-30%), killing the originate-and-distribute incentive to inflate volume.
> (4) Legislate a total-cost-of-credit cap that captures late fees, admin fees, service fees and insurance, not just the headline daily rate — current fee stacking defeats the 0.2-0.3%/day caps.
> (5) Ban credit-by-default: paylater must never be the pre-selected payment method at checkout, and one-tap credit activation during a purchase flow should require a separate, cooled-off consent.
> (6) Prohibit lending to students and under-21s without independent verified income, following China's 2021 campus-loan ban.
> (7) Create a licensed, bonded and criminally-liable debt-collection profession with a statutory conduct code (contact-hours limits, no third-party contact, no social shaming, no device-contact-list access) and meaningful penalties — this addresses the most acute current harm.
> (8) Enforce data minimisation under UU PDP: lending apps must be legally barred from requesting contacts, gallery, SMS and location permissions, which is the technical root of collection harassment.
> (9) Strengthen Satgas PASTI with upstream powers — app-store takedown obligations, payment-rail blocking of illegal lenders' settlement accounts (choking the money flow is far more effective than blocking domains), and cross-border cooperation given the Chinese-origin illegal-app supply chain.
> (10) Mandate a standardised, plain-Bahasa Schumer-box-style disclosure with total rupiah repayable shown before confirmation.
> (11) Build a statutory personal debt-restructuring/workout mechanism so over-indebted households have a legal path other than default and harassment.
> (12) Fund national financial literacy through the formal curriculum now, before the peak — China's regret is that literacy came after the damage.
> (13) Preserve QRIS's interoperable, low-MDR public-rail design and resist pressure to let any single wallet accumulate rail-level rents; simultaneously ensure the 0% micro-merchant MDR is fiscally sustainable rather than cross-subsidised into higher consumer credit pricing.
> (14) Require regulatory approval and explainability for AI/alternative credit scoring models under the ITSK framework, with audit rights and anti-discrimination testing.
> (15) Set up macroprudential monitoring of aggregate household unsecured debt as a share of disposable income, publishing it quarterly — Indonesia currently has no authoritative single number for this.

### Peluang & Rekomendasi Aksi

**Peluang Bisnis**

> (1) Credit infrastructure, not credit: alternative data credit bureaus, ITSK-licensed scoring providers, income-verification-as-a-service for informal workers (using QRIS merchant flows, e-wallet cash-flow, telco data, and BPJS/payroll APIs).
> Every lender needs this and almost none can build it alone.
> (2) Collections technology and outsourced ethical collections — a compliant, recorded, audited telecollection platform is both a large market and the remedy for the sector's worst abuse; first mover with a certified conduct standard can win regulated demand.
> (3) Debt-relief, restructuring and financial-counselling services (B2C subscription or employer-paid benefit), currently served only by informal and often predatory 'joki galbay' operators.
> (4) MSME working-capital lending underwritten on QRIS transaction history — 44 million QRIS merchants generating verifiable daily cash-flow data is the largest un-monetised credit dataset in Indonesia; this is the productive-credit opportunity as opposed to the consumptive one.
> (5) Merchant services on top of QRIS: POS/inventory/bookkeeping SaaS bundled with settlement, plus dynamic QR reconciliation for multi-outlet chains.
> (6) Embedded finance for verticals under-served by generalist BNPL — education fees, healthcare, agricultural inputs, motorcycle repair, umrah/travel — where instalments genuinely fund productive or lumpy-but-necessary spending.
> (7) Sharia-compliant BNPL and takaful, structurally under-served relative to the size of the observant market.
> (8) Fraud, identity and AML infrastructure — liveness/KYC, device intelligence, money-mule graph detection, scam-payment interdiction; scam losses on instant rails are the next regulatory crisis and BI/OJK will mandate controls.
> (9) Cross-border acquiring and remittance on QRIS corridors — inbound Chinese, Japanese, Korean and ASEAN tourists, plus PMI (migrant worker) remittance flows.
> (10) Wealth-tech for the newly-banked — micro-investing, gold savings, and pension/JHT-adjacent products distributed through wallets.
> (11) RegTech/SupTech for OJK/BI reporting, which becomes a compliance necessity as POJK 32/2025 and SLIK expansion bite.
> (12) Insurtech attachment: credit-life and income-protection insurance embedded in instalment products (with strict mis-selling controls).
> (13) Financial literacy and edtech as B2G/B2B — mandated curriculum content and employer wellbeing programmes.
> (14) Contrarian but real: buying distressed loan books and licences during the 2027-2029 consolidation, exactly as consolidators did in China post-2019.

**Rekomendasi Individu Mahasiswa**

> Build the skill stack that survives both the growth and the cleanup phases.
> Technical core: SQL and Python (pandas, scikit-learn) to a genuinely working level; statistics and probability well enough to build and validate a scorecard; credit risk fundamentals (PD/LGD/EAD, roll rates, vintage analysis, IFRS 9 ECL); and enough software engineering to ship a model into production rather than leaving it in a notebook.
> Domain layer: understand the actual Indonesian regulatory stack — POJK 32/2025, SEOJK rate caps, SLIK mechanics, UU PDP, AML/CFT — because regulatory fluency is the scarcest complement to technical skill and is what turns an analyst into a decision-maker.
> Adjacent high-value: fraud analytics and cybersecurity; actuarial/computational insurance; API and payments-systems literacy (ISO 20022, QRIS/BI-FAST message flows, idempotency and reconciliation).
> Soft and ethical layer: behavioural economics and consumer-protection design, plus the ability to write clearly for regulators.
> Portfolio moves: build a public credit-scoring project on open data; do a magang/internship at a licensed multifinance, digital bank or the OJK/BI itself; get a recognised certification (FRM, CFA level 1, or Indonesian sertifikasi manajemen risiko/BSMR, AAMAI for insurance).
> Personal finance discipline: treat your own paylater usage as a career-relevant decision — a damaged SLIK record at 22 will block a KPR at 30, and Indonesian banks are already rejecting mortgage applicants over paylater history.
> Career judgement: prefer roles in credit *risk*, fraud, compliance and infrastructure over growth/acquisition roles — when the cycle turns in 2027-2029, growth teams are cut first and risk teams expand.
> Language: functional Mandarin is a real differentiator given Chinese capital, vendors and operators in the sector.

**Rekomendasi Perguruan Tinggi**

> Open: a cross-disciplinary Fintech / Financial Engineering programme (or at minimum a formal concentration) explicitly modelled on the Chinese 金融科技 template — finance plus statistics plus programming plus data engineering plus regulation — rather than a finance degree with an IT elective; a Credit Risk Analytics track inside Statistics/Mathematics; Cybersecurity and Digital Forensics; Actuarial Science in computational form; a Fintech Law and Regulatory Technology track in law faculties; and a professional certificate in Compliance/AML and in Ethical Collections & Debt Counselling (a genuinely new professional category Indonesia needs).
> Convert rather than close: D3 Perbankan should be repositioned from teller/back-office supply toward digital-banking operations, merchant acquiring and onboarding, dispute resolution, and agent-network management — the roles that actually grew; Akuntansi should shift weight from bookkeeping to assurance, systems audit and forensic accounting; Manajemen Keuangan must add mandatory quantitative and coding content or its graduates will be locked out of the roles that replace the ones they trained for.
> Curriculum-wide: make financial literacy and personal debt management a compulsory MKWU/general-education course for every student in every faculty — this is the cheapest, highest-return intervention available and directly addresses the fact that 18-34 year olds hold 48.65% of problem loans; require a data-literacy course across social science and economics faculties; and embed research ethics and consumer-protection ethics into any programme teaching credit modelling.
> Institutional moves: build joint labs and applied-research partnerships with OJK, BI, Pefindo and licensed fintechs (the Chinese industry-academia model); use Kampus Merdeka placements inside risk and compliance functions, not only marketing; create an Indonesian equivalent of PKU's Digital Financial Inclusion Index so policy debate has a domestic evidence base; and stand up campus debt-counselling services, since students are already among the affected population.

### Faktor Risiko & Sisi Gelap

**Dampak Negatif China**

> (1) The P2P catastrophe: an industry peaking at 5,970 platforms and >USD 218bn in outstanding loans collapsed, leaving roughly USD 115bn owed to retail investors unpaid; the Ezubao case alone defrauded around 900,000 investors of ~RMB 50bn; mass protests by defrauded savers in Beijing in 2018 were met with police cordons, and the political shock is a direct cause of the subsequent crackdown.
> Tens of millions of ordinary savers lost life savings.
> (2) Youth over-indebtedness: peer-reviewed work on China's 'Debtors Avengers' (债务人复仇者联盟) Douban communities documents a cohort of young adults trapped in rolling digital debt, borrowing from one platform to repay another; surveys have found a majority of post-90s consumers using credit products, with a substantial share using them to service other debt.
> SCMP reporting after the crackdown found borrowing remained 'too easy' and debt continued to plague young people.
> (3) Consumption and demographic drag: a debt-burdened youth cohort curtails spending, delays marriage, home purchase and childbearing — an under-appreciated contributor to China's demand weakness and fertility collapse.
> (4) Violent and abusive collection (暴力催收): contact-list harvesting, mass-shaming calls to family and employers, doctored nude images ('裸条' loans against nude photos, which drove documented suicides among female students), and organised harassment — severe enough that regulators criminalised the practice and banned campus lending outright in 2021.
> (5) Predatory campus lending: students taking high-rate loans for phones and cosmetics, with suicides and family bankruptcies widely reported before the 2021 ban.
> (6) Financial-stability risk from shadow credit: Ant originating RMB 1.7 trillion while holding ~2% of the risk transferred systemic exposure to banks that had not underwritten it.
> (7) Labour displacement: tens of thousands of bank teller jobs eliminated (ICBC -14,090, CCB -30,007, ABC -10,842 in one year), plus branch and ATM network contraction.
> (8) Financial exclusion of the elderly and cash-dependent: merchants refusing cash became widespread enough that PBOC issued repeated rules in 2018 and 2020 penalising cash refusal — a direct harm to elderly and rural citizens.
> (9) Privacy and surveillance: total transaction visibility concentrated first in two private firms and then in the state clearing house; the aborted Sesame/social-credit adjacency raised durable concerns.
> (10) Telecom and payment fraud at scale, prompting the 'card-cutting' (断卡) campaign against money-mule accounts.
> (11) Investor value destruction: Ant's suspended USD 34.5bn IPO wiped an estimated USD 100bn+ of expected valuation and chilled Chinese fintech investment for years.
> (12) Mutual-aid failure: Xianghubao grew to over 100 million participants and then shut down in 2022, stranding members who had treated it as health cover.

**Risiko Sosial Indonesia**

> (1) A household debt spiral arriving at a lower income level than China's: with 93.01% of BNPL outstanding funding consumption, 24.5 million users, ~Rp 41-56 trillion of paylater exposure and Rp 101 trillion of pinjol outstanding, and TWP90 nearly doubling to 4.52% within a year, Indonesia is running China's 2018 dynamics at roughly two-thirds of China's income.
> (2) Multi-lender stacking invisible to regulators: because BNPL has not been fully SLIK-reported, no one — including the lenders — knows how many simultaneous obligations a household carries; the true default rate is therefore almost certainly understated and will step-change upward when reporting becomes universal.
> (3) A generational credit scar: 18-34 year olds already hold 48.65% of problem loans; a damaged SLIK record blocks mortgages, car loans, and increasingly employment screening, permanently impairing wealth formation for the exact cohort Indonesia needs to build a middle class.
> (4) Debt-collection harassment and violence: contact-list harvesting, threats to family and employers, doctored images, and workplace shaming are already documented in Indonesia; without a licensed collection regime this scales with the loan book, and Indonesia has already seen suicides attributed to pinjol harassment.
> (5) Illegal offshore lending at scale: 951 entities blocked in Q1 2026 and 14,006 since 2017 shows enforcement is losing a whack-a-mole game against an industrialised, partly Chinese-origin supply chain; borrowers rejected by legal lenders under POJK 32/2025 will be pushed *into* this illegal segment — the most predictable unintended consequence of the new rules.
> (6) Data-protection catastrophe: lending apps demanding contacts, SMS, gallery and location permissions create a mass surveillance dataset on tens of millions of Indonesians, held by weakly-secured operators; a large breach is a matter of when, not if.
> (7) Scam and social-engineering fraud on instant rails (QRIS/BI-FAST irrevocability, APK-file scams, fake QRIS stickers already reported at mosques and charity boxes) with no chargeback mechanism, transferring losses entirely onto consumers.
> (8) Macro transmission: unsecured consumer credit growing 25-70% YoY against ~5% GDP growth and stagnant real wages is arithmetically unsustainable; the correction transmits into multifinance and small-bank balance sheets and into consumption at exactly the moment the middle class is already contracting.
> (9) Financial exclusion of the elderly and cash-dependent as merchants go QR-only, and of informal workers who cannot document Rp 3 million income.
> (10) Regulatory capture and enforcement gap: OJK supervises hundreds of licensed entities with limited examiner capacity while political economy favours 'digital inclusion' framing over restraint.
> (11) Gambling adjacency: Indonesia's online-gambling epidemic (judi online) intersects with paylater and e-wallet rails, converting consumer credit into gambling losses — a risk China largely avoided because gambling rails were suppressed.
> (12) Concentration of collection abuse in non-Java provinces where legal aid is unavailable.

**Unintended Consequences**

> (1) In China: zeroing P2P did not eliminate demand — it migrated borrowers to licensed consumer finance and, at the margin, to informal usury; and the crackdown on Ant chilled the entire private tech-investment climate far beyond fintech, contributing to the 2021-2023 valuation collapse and a measurable slowdown in innovation financing.
> (2) In China: forcing 100% float reserves and Nets Union clearing removed platform float income, which pushed platforms harder into *credit* monetisation — regulating the payment layer inadvertently accelerated the credit layer.
> (3) In China: the shift to cashless made cash refusal so common that the central bank had to legislate the right to pay in cash, harming the elderly.
> (4) In Indonesia: POJK 32/2025's Rp 3 million verified-income floor, applied to an economy where ~59% of workers are informal, will likely push a large excluded population toward illegal lenders rather than reduce borrowing — the rule may increase net harm while improving reported statistics.
> (5) In Indonesia: mandatory SLIK reporting of BNPL, while correct, will produce a visible one-off spike in recorded NPLs and a wave of mortgage and vehicle-loan rejections among young borrowers who had no idea their paylater history was being recorded — a political shock that could trigger backlash against the very transparency needed.
> (6) QRIS's 0% micro-merchant MDR removes acquiring revenue, so wallets recover margin from lending and float — a benign inclusion policy that quietly subsidises the growth of consumer credit.
> (7) Rate caps without total-cost-of-credit caps produced fee-stacking rather than cheaper credit.
> (8) Blocking illegal apps at the domain/app-store level drove them to WhatsApp and Telegram distribution, which is harder to police and removes even app-store-level accountability.
> (9) Digital-bank deposit rate competition (5-8%) raises funding costs for small conventional banks (BPR), accelerating their consolidation and reducing local relationship lending in the regions.
> (10) The success of instant payment rails made real-time irreversible fraud scalable, so financial inclusion and fraud victimisation grew together.
> (11) Financial inclusion metrics (85-90% inclusion index) look excellent while financial *health* deteriorates — the metric itself misleads policymakers.

**Kelompok Rentan**

> (1) Gen Z and young millennials aged 18-34 — ~70% of BNPL users, ~40% Gen Z, and 48.65% of P2P problem loans; the primary casualty group.
> (2) Students and fresh graduates with no verified income, targeted by both legal marketing and illegal apps; China's campus-loan tragedies are the direct precedent.
> (3) Informal-sector and gig workers (ojol drivers, couriers, market traders, day labourers) — volatile daily income against fixed monthly instalments, and structurally excluded by the Rp 3 million verified-income rule, so pushed toward illegal lenders.
> (4) Low-income women, who are heavily represented in both microfinance borrowing and in the most humiliating forms of collection harassment (social shaming to family and neighbours).
> (5) Households in non-Java provinces with seasonal or commodity-linked income and no access to legal aid or financial counselling.
> (6) Micro-merchants who take consumptive credit to plug working-capital gaps and end up with instalment obligations mismatched to their cash cycle.
> (7) The elderly and the digitally illiterate, excluded as merchants go QR-only and disproportionately victimised by QR-swap and social-engineering scams.
> (8) People whose contacts are harvested — a uniquely Indonesian and Chinese harm where the vulnerable group extends beyond borrowers to their entire phone book: family, employers and colleagues who never took a loan.
> (9) Online-gambling-affected households, where paylater converts directly into gambling losses.
> (10) BPR/rural bank employees and bank branch staff facing displacement.
> (11) Debtors already in default, who are pushed into 'gali lubang tutup lubang' cycles and into the hands of galbay/joki intermediaries who extract further fees.

### Contoh Kasus Konkret

**Kasus China**

> Ant Group is the definitive case.
> Founded out of Alipay (2004), it built the payment rail, then layered Yu'ebao (June 2013) which swept idle wallet balances into a money market fund that briefly became the world's largest at ~RMB 1.69 trillion; then Huabei (April 2015, a revolving virtual credit card embedded at Taobao/Alipay checkout) and Jiebei (cash instalment loans).
> By 30 June 2020 these two products had facilitated RMB 1.7 trillion (~USD 263bn) of consumer credit to about 500 million people while Ant retained only ~2% on its own balance sheet — the rest funded by roughly 100 partner banks and ABS investors.
> Ant priced a USD 34.5bn dual listing at a ~USD 315bn valuation, which would have been the largest IPO in history.
> On 24 October 2020 Jack Ma publicly criticised Chinese financial regulators as having a 'pawnshop mentality'; on 2 November regulators summoned him; on 2-3 November PBOC and CBIRC published draft online micro-lending rules requiring lenders to fund at least 30% of joint loans; on 3 November 2020, roughly 48 hours before listing, the Shanghai Stock Exchange suspended the IPO.
> In April 2021 Ant was ordered into a full rectification: convert to a financial holding company under PBOC supervision, fold Huabei and Jiebei into a separately licensed and capitalised consumer finance company (Chongqing Ant Consumer Finance), sever the 'improper linkage' between the payment app and credit products, connect to the national credit reporting infrastructure, and comply with bank-equivalent capital rules.
> In July 2023 Ant was fined RMB 7.12bn (~USD 985m), signalling the end of the campaign.
> The counterfactual case is the P2P sector — 5,970 platforms at peak (2017), >USD 218bn outstanding (2018), ~USD 115bn of unpaid investor claims, and exactly zero platforms remaining by mid-November 2020.
> Together these two cases define both the ceiling and the floor of what unregulated fintech credit does at scale.

**Padanan Indonesia**

> The closest structural analogues: (1) GoTo Financial = the Ant template in miniature — GoPay (payment) + GoPayLater/GoPayLater Cicil (BNPL, in partnership with Findaya/multifinance) + Bank Jago (deposit and lending licence), a conscious replication of Alipay + Huabei + MYbank, though at a fraction of the scale and without rail ownership.
> (2) Sea Group Indonesia = the tightest closed loop actually operating — Shopee (commerce) + ShopeePay (payment) + SPayLater (BNPL) + SeaBank (licensed bank), Tencent-backed and arguably the most complete Chinese-model transplant in Indonesia.
> (3) Kredivo (FinAccel) = the clearest Huabei analogue as a standalone revolving digital credit line for thin-file consumers.
> (4) Akulaku = the closest thing to a direct Ant-funded vehicle, with Ant Group investment (USD 40m, later part of a ~USD 100m Series D), a BNPL book, a bank stake (Bank Neo Commerce), and a securities arm.
> (5) DANA = Ant's own wallet position in Indonesia, >135 million registered users, expanding into lending, wealth and insurance and running QRIS cross-border to Malaysia, Singapore and Thailand.
> (6) Superbank = the WeBank pattern with Grab/Emtek/Singtel/KakaoBank ecosystem distribution.
> (7) QRIS = Indonesia's *divergent* analogue: where China let two private firms own the rail and only nationalised clearing afterwards, Bank Indonesia built the interoperable standard first — the one place Indonesia leads China.
> (8) Investree's licence revocation and the rising TWP90 are the early-stage analogue of China's 2018-2019 P2P stress, at a much smaller but rapidly growing scale.
> (9) Satgas PASTI's 14,006 blocked entities is the analogue of China's pre-2019 illegal-lending clean-up, but without China's capacity for total prohibition.
