## 6. Platform Food & Beverage (Ultra-Cheap Coffee & Tea Chains) - massive low-cost bubble tea / ice cream / coffee franchise networks built on central-kitchen and vertically integrated supply-chain platforms
**Kategori**: Consumption & Retail (Konsumsi & Ritel) - sub-domain: Food Service Platformization, Franchise Retail, Supply-Chain-as-a-Platform

📊 Simultaneous on the demand and storefront layer (near-zero lag, direct entry by Chinese operators), Laggard on the supply-chain/manufacturing and regulatory layer (6-12 year gap), with a narrow Reverse element - Indonesia-originated, Chinese-capitalized Tomoro Coffee has exported its model back into China, and Indonesia's warkop density (461,991 outlets) already exceeds China's on a per-outlet basis. | 🎯 Prob: Very high - already fully transferred. The relevant question is no longer whether it arrives but which sub-wave arrives next and how deeply the supply chain localizes. | 🔍 Keyakinan: High for the core thesis (near-zero lag, Indonesia as Mixue's largest overseas market, direct entry as the dominant transmission vector, and the 2025-2026 shakeout), because it rests on IPO-prospectus-grade disclosures, audited annual results, and multiple independent outlets. Medium for Indonesia-specific quantities (exact current outlet counts by brand, market size in rupiah, employment totals), which come from press reports and industry estimates rather than official statistics. Medium-low for forward-looking timeline predictions (peak years) and for the China vocational-education specifics (the two new MOE coffee majors could not be verified from the primary source, which returned HTTP 503).

> **Status di Indonesia**: Already massively present - Indonesia is the single largest overseas market for this trend and has now moved past the entry phase into the saturation and shakeout phase, roughly 1-2 years behind China's own shakeout. Not a laggard on arrival; a laggard on infrastructure and on regulatory preparedness.

### Basic Info

**Tahun Mulai China**

> Deep roots in 1997 (Mixue founded in Zhengzhou, Henan by Zhang Hongchao with a CN¥3,000 loan from his grandmother), but the trend became structurally significant in three waves: (1) 2007 - Mixue converts to a franchise model; (2) 2014 - Mixue builds its own logistics network and abolishes freight charges for franchisees, creating the 'supply-chain-as-platform' model; (3) 2017-2020 - explosive scale-up phase, when Mixue crossed 10,000 stores (2019), Luckin Coffee launched (2017) and IPO'd (2019), and Chagee was founded (2017).
> The mass-market/ultra-cheap phase (RMB 6-10 drinks) peaked as a national phenomenon in 2022-2024, when the 9.9-yuan coffee price war between Luckin and Cotti erupted (2023).

**Pemain Kunci China**

> Ultra-cheap tea/ice cream: Mixue Bingcheng (蜜雪冰城) - world's largest F&B chain by store count; Lucky Cup / Xingyunke (幸运咖) - Mixue's ultra-cheap coffee sister brand, crossed 10,000 stores in Nov 2025; Tianlala (甜啦啦); Bing Xue Shi Guang.
> Mid-tier tea: Guming (古茗), Chabaidao (茶百道), Auntea Jenny / Hushang Ayi (沪上阿姨), Shuyi Tealicious (书亦烧仙草), Yidiandian (一点点).
> Premium/'new Chinese tea': Chagee / Bawang Chaji (霸王茶姬, NASDAQ-listed April 2025), Heytea (喜茶), Nayuki (奈雪的茶).
> Coffee: Luckin Coffee (瑞幸咖啡) - 31,048 stores end-2025; Cotti Coffee (库迪咖啡) - founded 2022 by Luckin's ousted founders Lu Zhengyao and Jenny Qian.
> Enabling infrastructure: Meituan and Ele.me (delivery + subsidy engines), Douyin local services (group-buy coupons), and dedicated cold-chain/ingredient suppliers (Tianye Biotech, Jiahe Foods, Dehe Hengfeng).
> Capital vector into Indonesia: ATM Capital (Chinese VC, backer of J&T Express and Tomoro Coffee).

### China Trend Detail

**Apa Yang Terjadi Di China**

> China converted the beverage shop from an independent small business into an industrial platform.
> The mechanism has four layers.
> (1) Vertical integration of the supply chain: Mixue does not make money from franchise royalties - roughly 94-98% of its revenue comes from selling ingredients, packaging, and equipment to its own franchisees.
> It operates five production bases (Henan, Hainan, Guangxi, Chongqing, Anhui) covering 670,000 sqm with ~1.43 million tons of annual capacity, and 27 self-operated warehouses with ~3.5 million sq ft of space, so it manufactures its own syrups, milk powder, jam, and cones rather than buying them.
> This makes the cost of goods 10-25% below peers (e.g.
> lemons ~20%+ cheaper, milk powder ~10% cheaper).
> (2) Zero-friction franchising: since 2014 Mixue has delivered ingredients to franchisees for free, with ~12-hour delivery coverage to the vast majority of stores via ~40 last-mile logistics partners.
> Franchise fees are among the lowest in the industry, store footprints are tiny (median ~400 sq ft / ~37 sqm), and the process is deskilled - a store is a set of SOPs plus a machine, not a craft.
> 99.97% of the network is franchised.
> (3) Price as the moat: soft-serve at RMB 2-4 and tea drinks at RMB 4-8 put the product below the psychological threshold of 'a discretionary purchase', creating enormous volume per square metre and making the chain recession-proof and lower-tier-city-proof.
> Luckin and Cotti applied the same logic to coffee with the 9.9-yuan war from 2023.
> (4) IP and algorithmic distribution: the 'Snow King' mascot and its earworm theme song turned marketing into user-generated content on Douyin/Xiaohongshu, driving customer acquisition cost near zero.
> The combined effect was a store-count explosion into county towns and townships (下沉市场) that no Western chain had reached, followed by capital-markets validation - Mixue's Hong Kong IPO in March 2025 was massively oversubscribed.
> But the same mechanics produced brutal saturation: because entry is cheap and deskilled, thousands of franchisees enter, and the shakeout falls on them, not on the platform.
> By 2025 the sector had entered an elimination phase with high closure rates, thin franchisee margins, food-safety incidents traceable to franchise-level execution, and regulatory attention under Beijing's 'anti-involution' (反内卷) campaign.

**Data Skala China**

> Mixue: 59,823 stores globally as of 31 Dec 2025, of which 55,356 in mainland China and ~4,467 overseas; FY2025 revenue RMB 33.56 billion (~US$4.9bn, +35% YoY), net profit RMB 5.93 billion (+33% YoY); operating income RMB 7.29 billion.
> As of 30 June 2025 it had 53,014 stores (+22.7% YoY) and 23,400 franchisees (up from 19,300).
> Hong Kong IPO 3 March 2025: 17 million shares at HK$202.5, raising ~HK$3.45bn (US$444m).
> Lucky Cup (Mixue's coffee brand) crossed 10,000 stores in Nov 2025.
> Luckin Coffee: 31,048 stores at end-2025 (20,234 self-operated, 10,814 partnership), net +8,708 stores in 2025 (~24 new stores/day); FY2025 revenue RMB 49.29 billion (~US$7.18bn, +43% YoY), but Q4 2025 net profit fell ~39% YoY as delivery-platform subsidies contracted.
> Chagee: 6,440 stores and ~US$1.7bn revenue in 2024 (+83% stores, +167% revenue YoY); global network spanning 8 countries across 2 continents by end-2025, with annual tea procurement above 10,000 tons.
> Sector: China's freshly-made tea shop industry is projected at RMB 538.5 billion by 2028, ~63.4% of the total beverage-shop industry.
> Churn: in the 12 months to 15 Dec 2024, ~127,700 new milk tea shops opened nationwide but the net change was -17,800, implying more than 140,000 closures in a single year.
> Estimated market-wide closure rate ~20%.
> In 2025 national tea-shop count grew only 7.9% YoY while sector retail sales grew 9.5% - the first year growth came from productivity rather than store additions.
> Brand-level stress: Auntea Jenny closure rate up to 12.11%; Chabaidao franchisee attrition up to 17.06%.

**Fase Tren Di China**

> Mature, consolidating, and partially in backlash/regulated phase.
> The ultra-cheap tea/ice cream segment is past peak store-count growth (2025 store growth only 7.9% vs 9.5% retail sales growth) and is in an explicit elimination round (淘汰赛) where weak brands and over-leveraged franchisees exit.
> The coffee segment is one step behind - still expanding aggressively (Luckin +8,708 stores in 2025) but exiting the pure price war: Luckin raised prices in early 2026 and Cotti suspended its shop-in-shop franchise model, signalling the end of the 9.9-yuan era.
> Regulatory overlay: since the July 2025 Politburo elevation of 'involution' to a top-level risk, the State Administration for Market Regulation has cracked down on below-cost selling by delivery platforms, and the draft revised Pricing Law would prohibit irrational price wars.
> Simultaneously, brands are pivoting from price to health positioning (reduced sugar, real tea, calorie labelling) and from store count to same-store productivity.
> Overseas expansion has become the growth valve, but even that is now selective: Mixue closed 428 overseas stores in the 12 months to end-2025, mostly in Indonesia and Vietnam.

**Puncak Tren China**

> Store-count peak and cultural peak: 2023-2024, centred on lower-tier cities, county towns, and townships (三四线城市 / 县域市场) across Henan, Guangdong, Shandong, Sichuan and Hunan, plus university-adjacent and transit locations in tier-1/2 cities.
> The 9.9-yuan coffee price war peaked in 2023-2024 in tier-1 and tier-2 cities (Shanghai, Beijing, Shenzhen, Chengdu).
> Capital-markets peak: 2024-2025, when Chabaidao (Apr 2024), Guming (Feb 2025), Mixue (Mar 2025), Auntea Jenny (2025) listed in Hong Kong and Chagee listed on NASDAQ (Apr 2025).
> Post-peak inflection is visible from 2025: net store additions collapsed, closure rates hit ~20%, and the industry narrative shifted from 'roll out stores' (卷门店) to 'return to value competition'.
> Overseas expansion peak is later and still unfolding (2024-2027).

### Status Indonesia Saat Ini

**Status Di Indonesia**

> Already massively present - Indonesia is the single largest overseas market for this trend and has now moved past the entry phase into the saturation and shakeout phase, roughly 1-2 years behind China's own shakeout.
> Not a laggard on arrival; a laggard on infrastructure and on regulatory preparedness.

**Contoh Konkret Indonesia**

> Chinese platforms operating directly: Mixue Ice Cream & Tea via PT Zhisheng Pacific Trading (entered Oct 2019, first store at Cihampelas Walk, Bandung, March 2020); Cotti Coffee (first Indonesian store at Kuningan City Mall, Jakarta, 15 August 2023, drinks around IDR 18,000); CHAGEE (first store at PIK Avenue, Jakarta, 11 April 2025, operated with Erajaya Group; followed by Mall of Indonesia, FX Sudirman, and a Plaza Indonesia flagship on 27 Nov 2025); WeDrink and Ai-Cha (Ai-Cha under PT Nanyang Group Indonesia); Shuyi Tealicious (Shuyi Grass Jelly); Cooler City.
> China-capital-backed 'Indonesian' brands: Tomoro Coffee - founded in Jakarta in 2022 by Star Yuan (an OPPO alumnus and J&T Express co-founder) and Fish Sun, seeded with ~US$60 million from ATM Capital, a Chinese VC; it runs a Jakarta roastery with 2,400 tons/year capacity and has exported the model back into China, Singapore and the Philippines.
> Local copycats built on the same low-cost franchise template: Momoyo (Indonesian-owned, 529 branches within ~6 months of launching its franchise package in April 2023), Xi Yue (Indonesian-owned), Es Teh Indonesia, Haus!, Kopi Kenangan, Kopi Janji Jiwa, Kopi Kulo, Fore Coffee (IDX-listed 2025), Point Coffee (Indomaret's in-store coffee brand), Kopi Soe.

### Analisis Lag

**Bukti Historical Lag**

> Consistent pattern of shrinking lag in Chinese consumer-platform exports to Indonesia.
> E-commerce: Alibaba's Taobao scaled from 2003; Lazada/Tokopedia took Chinese capital from 2016-2018 (~13-15 year lag).
> Fintech/paylater: China's 2013-2015 wave reached Indonesia via Akulaku/Kredivo around 2016-2018 (~3-4 years).
> Short-video: Douyin launched Sept 2016, TikTok Indonesia from 2017 (~1 year).
> Logistics: J&T Express was founded in Indonesia in 2015 by Chinese-Indonesian OPPO alumni and exported back to China in 2020 - a reverse flow.
> EV: BYD's China takeoff 2021-2022, Indonesian launch Jan 2024 (~2 years).
> F&B specifically: Mixue China 10,000 stores in 2019, Indonesia entry Oct 2019 - simultaneous; Cotti founded Oct 2022, Jakarta store Aug 2023; Chagee's China breakout 2023-2024, Jakarta store April 2025.
> Each successive wave compresses the lag because the transmission channel is now direct corporate expansion plus Chinese venture capital plus TikTok-mediated demand creation, not slow imitation.
> The counter-evidence - and the reason the lag is not literally zero - is that Indonesia consistently receives the storefront but not the factory: Mixue serves ~2,600 Indonesian stores substantially from imported and centrally sourced inputs rather than five Indonesian production bases.

**Tipe Lag**

> Simultaneous on the demand and storefront layer (near-zero lag, direct entry by Chinese operators), Laggard on the supply-chain/manufacturing and regulatory layer (6-12 year gap), with a narrow Reverse element - Indonesia-originated, Chinese-capitalized Tomoro Coffee has exported its model back into China, and Indonesia's warkop density (461,991 outlets) already exceeds China's on a per-outlet basis.

### Probabilitas Transfer ke Indonesia

**Probabilitas Transfer**

> Very high - already fully transferred.
> The relevant question is no longer whether it arrives but which sub-wave arrives next and how deeply the supply chain localizes.

**Alasan Probabilitas**

> Six reinforcing reasons.
> (1) It has already happened at scale - Indonesia is Mixue's #1 overseas market with ~55.7% of its non-China stores, and three of the four major Chinese chain archetypes (ultra-cheap tea, ultra-cheap coffee, premium new-Chinese-tea) are physically present.
> (2) Demographic fit: a median age around 30, ~145 million people in the aspiring middle class, and a Gen Z cohort for whom a Rp8,000-25,000 drink is a legitimate affordable-luxury ritual.
> (3) Purchasing-power fit: Indonesia's GDP per capita (~US$5,335 in 2025) sits well below China's (~US$13,303), which means the ultra-cheap tier - not the premium tier - is exactly the right product for the market, mirroring Mixue's own lower-tier-city thesis.
> (4) Push factor from China: domestic saturation, ~20% closure rates, and the anti-involution campaign make overseas expansion the only credible growth story for Chinese chains, and Southeast Asia is the closest, largest, youngest target.
> (5) Capital channel is open: Chinese VC (ATM Capital) already funds Indonesian F&B directly, and Erajaya-style local conglomerate partnerships de-risk entry.
> (6) Zero regulatory friction: Indonesia's franchise regime (Permendag 71/2019) removed the percentage-based local content obligation, foreign franchise registrations (145 STPW) nearly match domestic ones (151) as of Aug 2024, and halal certification has proven to be a solvable, not prohibitive, requirement.
> The only genuine constraint is that the profitable ceiling in Indonesia is lower than in China, so the transfer expresses itself as fewer stores and earlier saturation, not as absence.

**Vektor Transmisi**

> All five vectors are active simultaneously, which is why the lag collapsed to near-zero.
> (a) Direct entry by Chinese players - the dominant vector: Mixue via PT Zhisheng Pacific Trading (a China-controlled Indonesian entity holding the master franchise), Cotti Coffee opening directly in Jakarta in Aug 2023, CHAGEE entering in April 2025 in partnership with a listed local conglomerate (Erajaya Group), plus WeDrink, Ai-Cha (PT Nanyang Group Indonesia), Cooler City and Shuyi.
> These bring not just a brand but the entire operating system - SOPs, POS software, store design, ingredient supply contracts and franchisee recruitment funnels.
> (b) Local copycats/imitators: Momoyo and Xi Yue are Indonesian-owned clones launched within months of Mixue's viral moment (Momoyo reached 529 branches in about six months from April 2023); Es Teh Indonesia and Haus! applied the same low-price, high-density, franchise-first template to Indonesian taste profiles; Kopi Kenangan and Janji Jiwa are the Luckin analogue built for Indonesia.
> (c) Algorithmic content diffusion: TikTok/Douyin and Instagram Reels are the primary demand-creation engine - the Snow King mascot, jingles, and 'gerai Mixue baru buka' content made queueing itself the product, and TikTok's Indonesian penetration meant Chinese-format F&B virality replicated with essentially no translation delay.
> This is also how the format reaches tier-3 Indonesian cities without any marketing spend.
> (d) Chinese venture capital: ATM Capital (also the backer of J&T Express) seeded Tomoro Coffee with ~US$60 million, effectively building a Luckin-clone in Indonesia with Chinese money, Chinese operating know-how and Indonesian branding; this vector is the most consequential because it produces companies that look local and therefore face no nationalist backlash.
> (e) Diaspora and alumni networks: Chinese-Indonesian business families provide master-franchise partners, shophouse property, and distribution; OPPO/J&T alumni networks supply the operator talent (Tomoro's founders); and returning Indonesian students from Chinese universities plus Chinese managers rotating through Zhengzhou/Shanghai HQs carry the SOPs.
> A sixth, under-appreciated vector is equipment and ingredient trade: Chinese soft-serve machines, sealing machines, cup suppliers and non-dairy creamer manufacturers now sell openly on Indonesian e-commerce, letting any UMKM assemble a Mixue-format store without any franchise at all.

### Faktor Pendorong

**Prasyarat Struktural**

> Threshold conditions and Indonesia's position against China at the moment the trend exploded.
> (1) Income threshold: the ultra-cheap format needs a large population whose disposable income makes a US$0.50-1.50 drink a routine purchase.
> When Mixue crossed 10,000 stores (2019) China's GDP per capita was ~US$10,100, but its target lower-tier counties were at roughly US$4,000-7,000 - almost exactly Indonesia's national level today (~US$5,335 nominal, ~US$14,500 PPP).
> Indonesia therefore clears the threshold for the cheap tier and does NOT clear it broadly for the premium tier (Chagee/Heytea remain a Jakarta/Surabaya mall phenomenon).
> (2) Urban density and shophouse supply: the model requires 30-50 sqm street-facing units at low rent within walking distance of foot traffic.
> Indonesia's ruko oversupply after the pandemic was the physical enabler - Mixue literally filled empty shophouses.
> (3) Youth cohort and smartphone penetration: internet penetration around 79-80% and near-universal short-video use among 15-34s is what replaces advertising spend.
> (4) Cashless payment rails: QRIS is the decisive Indonesian enabler, functionally equivalent to WeChat Pay/Alipay in enabling sub-Rp10,000 transactions without cash-handling friction.
> (5) Cold chain and central kitchen - the binding constraint: Mixue's edge rests on five production bases and 27 self-owned warehouses.
> Indonesia's national logistics cost is ~14.29% of GDP (~Rp3 quadrillion / US$189bn), its cold-chain market is only ~US$8.4bn (2026), and archipelagic geography makes a 12-hour national delivery promise impossible.
> Roughly 80% of Indonesia's raw milk is imported and per-capita dairy consumption is only ~16.3 litres/year, so the dairy input layer is import-dependent and FX-exposed.
> (6) Franchise-capital availability: the model needs tens of thousands of households able to deploy Rp250-800 million.
> Indonesia's shrinking middle class (46.7 million in 2025, down from 47.9 million in 2024) is the demand-side and franchisee-side ceiling simultaneously.
> (7) Regulatory permissiveness: mandatory halal certification (achievable - Mixue cleared it in Feb 2023), BPOM food-safety compliance, and Permendag 71/2019 which dropped the percentage-based domestic-content mandate.
> Net position: Indonesia clears prerequisites 1-4 and 7 fully, fails 5 badly, and is deteriorating on 6.

**Indikator Pemantauan**

> Leading indicators that the next sub-wave is landing.
> (1) Trademark and franchise registrations: new DJKI (Ditjen KI) filings by Chinese beverage brands, and new STPW/franchise registration letters at Kemendag for foreign principals - Chinese brands typically file trademarks 6-18 months before opening.
> Watch specifically for Guming, Tianlala, Auntea Jenny, Heytea, Luckin Coffee and Lucky Cup/Xingyunke (which has already entered Malaysia in Aug 2025 and Thailand - Indonesia is the logical next stop).
> (2) BPOM registration and MUI/BPJPH halal certificates issued to new Chinese-owned PTs.
> (3) BKPM/OSS foreign-investment filings for beverage manufacturing (KBLI 10-series) rather than trading - this would signal the shift from importing concentrate to building an Indonesian central kitchen, the single most important indicator.
> (4) Job-board signals: LinkedIn/Glints/JobStreet postings for 'Area Manager', 'Supply Chain Manager', 'Franchise Development' and Mandarin-required roles at newly registered PTs.
> (5) Google Trends and TikTok hashtag volume for brand names before official launch, plus 'franchise [brand] Indonesia' search volume - franchisee demand precedes store openings by ~3-6 months.
> (6) Shophouse/mall leasing data: new anchor-adjacent kiosk leases in tier-2 malls, and conversely rising ruko vacancy where the previous wave is dying.
> (7) Import statistics (BPS) for non-dairy creamer, HS-code milk powder, fruit concentrate, and PP/PET cups from China - a rising trend indicates network expansion; a stalling trend indicates the shakeout.
> (8) Equipment imports: soft-serve and sealing machines.
> (9) Education signal: new SMK/vocational barista and 'peracik minuman' programmes, and any polytechnic opening a beverage-technology or F&B supply-chain diploma.
> (10) Reverse indicator for the shakeout: volume of secondhand Mixue/Momoyo equipment listings on Tokopedia/Facebook Marketplace and 'takeover gerai' classifieds - a proven early signal of franchisee distress.

### Hambatan & Faktor Pembatal

**Hambatan Transfer**

> (1) Purchasing-power compression - Indonesia's middle class shrank to 46.7 million in 2025 and middle-class per-capita consumption grew only 4.1% (below the 4.6% national average), directly capping same-store sales for a discretionary beverage.
> (2) Cold-chain and archipelagic logistics - 14.29% of GDP logistics cost and no feasible national 12-hour delivery mean the free-freight franchisee subsidy that anchors Mixue's China model cannot be replicated outside Java, Sumatra and parts of Sulawesi.
> (3) Input import dependence - ~80% of raw milk imported, plus imported creamer, concentrate and packaging, exposing unit economics to rupiah depreciation in a way Chinese domestic operations never faced.
> (4) Halal compliance - mandatory certification adds cost, audit burden and ingredient-substitution constraints; any single lapse is a brand-lethal event in a Muslim-majority market, far more severe than China's food-safety incidents.
> (5) Franchisee capital scarcity and financing gap - Rp700-800 million entry against limited SME credit availability at reasonable rates.
> (6) Saturation already reached - the format's low barrier to entry means Indonesian imitators (Momoyo, Xi Yue, WeDrink, Ai-Cha) flooded the market within months, collapsing differentiation and driving the current closure wave.
> (7) Incumbent informal competition - 461,991 coffee-selling outlets including warkop and street es teh vendors selling at Rp3,000-5,000, a price floor Chinese chains cannot profitably undercut.
> (8) Sugary-drink excise (cukai MBDK) agreed for the 2026 state budget, with rates still undetermined - a tail risk to the entire category if it is extended beyond packaged drinks to freshly-made beverages.
> (9) Nationalist/UMKM-protection sentiment and periodic boycott dynamics that can attach to visibly Chinese brands.
> (10) Talent and management-depth shortage for multi-site operations outside Jakarta.

**Faktor Pembatal Transfer**

> Structural conditions that guarantee this trend will NEVER take the same form in Indonesia as in China.
> (1) Absent manufacturing base - Mixue's whole thesis is that it is a food manufacturer that happens to own stores; Indonesia's food-processing sector cannot supply syrups, non-dairy creamer, fruit concentrate, cones and cups at Chinese cost, and there is no realistic path to five Indonesian production bases when domestic dairy is 80% imported and sugar itself is import-regulated.
> The Indonesian instance of this trend is therefore permanently a distribution business, not a supply-chain platform - which means Indonesian franchisees pay platform margin to a Chinese manufacturer rather than to an Indonesian one, and the high-value jobs stay in Henan.
> (2) Archipelagic geography - 17,000 islands and 14.29%-of-GDP logistics cost make the free-freight, 12-hour, 27-warehouse density model economically impossible outside a few corridors; the trend will remain Java-Sumatra-Bali concentrated with thin, expensive coverage in Eastern Indonesia.
> (3) Population and density ceiling - China supports ~55,000 Mixue stores on 1.41 billion people with extreme urban density; Indonesia's realistic national ceiling for any single ultra-cheap beverage brand is plausibly in the 3,000-5,000 store range, meaning the growth runway ends far sooner and the shakeout arrives at a much lower absolute scale.
> (4) Pre-existing hyper-competitive informal sector - unlike China, where the modern chain displaced a relative vacuum, Indonesia already has a saturated, ultra-cheap informal beverage economy (warkop, es teh keliling, warung) at Rp3,000-5,000 with near-zero fixed cost, so the chain cannot win on price alone and must compete on air-conditioning, brand and hygiene - a fundamentally different, higher-cost proposition.
> (5) Halal and religious dietary regime - permanently constrains ingredient sourcing, gelatin/enzyme choices, and supplier switching speed, removing one of the platform's core levers (opportunistic input substitution).
> (6) No equivalent delivery-subsidy war chest - China's tea/coffee volumes were inflated by Meituan/Ele.me/Douyin subsidy wars funded by platform capital; GoFood/GrabFood/ShopeeFood in Indonesia operate under profitability discipline and will not fund an equivalent volume bubble.
> (7) Weaker consumer credit and lower discretionary frequency - Chinese consumers buy tea 3-5x/week in tier-1/2 cities; Indonesian frequency is structurally lower outside a narrow urban Gen Z segment.
> Net conclusion: the trend arrives fully, but as a franchise-retail phenomenon layered on imported inputs - it will not deliver China's industrial-upgrading side effects, and the value capture is asymmetric against Indonesia.

### Prediksi Timeline di Indonesia

**Tahun Masuk Indonesia**

> Already entered - staged arrival: 2019-2020 (Mixue: entity registered Oct 2019, first store Cihampelas Walk Bandung March 2020) for the ultra-cheap tea/ice-cream wave; 2022 for the China-capital coffee wave (Tomoro Coffee founded in Jakarta, first store Aug 2022); 2023 for the direct Chinese coffee wave (Cotti Coffee, Kuningan City Mall Jakarta, 15 Aug 2023); 2025 for the premium new-Chinese-tea wave (CHAGEE, PIK Avenue Jakarta, 11 April 2025).
> Expected next entries: Lucky Cup/Xingyunke, Guming, Auntea Jenny, Heytea and possibly Luckin Coffee in 2026-2028.

**Tahun Mainstream Indonesia**

> 2022-2023 for the ultra-cheap tea/ice-cream format - Mixue became a nationwide cultural phenomenon after the Feb 2023 MUI halal fatwa removed the last adoption barrier, and the 'Mixue in every ruko' meme plus Momoyo/Ai-Cha/WeDrink clones made the format ubiquitous within about 12 months.
> 2023-2024 for grab-and-go chain coffee (Kopi Kenangan overtook Starbucks Indonesia on outlet count in 2024; Tomoro passed 600 stores).
> Premium new-Chinese-tea (Chagee) is not yet mainstream and will likely become so only in 2027-2029, and only in tier-1/2 cities.

**Skenario Percepatan**

> Acceleration triggers: (a) intensified anti-involution pressure and price-war bans in China pushing every mid-tier Chinese chain overseas at once; (b) a Chinese chain building an actual Indonesian production base/central kitchen (a BKPM manufacturing FDI filing would signal this), which would collapse input costs and reopen the growth runway; (c) a large local conglomerate (Erajaya, Salim, MAP, CT Corp) taking master-franchise rights and using its property and distribution footprint for instant national scale; (d) renewed GoFood/GrabFood/ShopeeFood subsidy competition; (e) IDR appreciation or falling global dairy/sugar prices improving unit economics; (f) a TikTok Shop-style integration of beverage vouchers into short-video commerce; (g) recovery of middle-class purchasing power via wage growth or the free nutritious meal programme freeing household budget; (h) Chinese chains treating Indonesia as the manufacturing hub for ASEAN halal exports.

### Dampak Sosial-Ekonomi

**Dampak Kelas Menengah**

> Double-edged and currently net-negative.
> As consumers: the ultra-cheap format is genuinely pro-middle-class - it delivers an air-conditioned, hygienic, Instagram-legible affordable-luxury ritual at Rp8,000-25,000, exactly the kind of 'small indulgence' that survives a purchasing-power squeeze and substitutes for costlier outings.
> In a year when the middle class shrank to 46.7 million (from 47.9 million in 2024) and middle-class per-capita consumption grew only 4.1%, cheap chain beverages are a trade-down destination, not a casualty.
> As entrepreneurs: this is where the damage lands.
> The Rp700-800 million Mixue franchise (or Rp230-300 million for Ai-Cha, less for local clones) was marketed as a middle-class wealth-building vehicle, and thousands of households deployed savings, sold property, or borrowed against assets to buy in during 2022-2024.
> The saturation and closure wave of 2025-2026 converts that into destroyed household capital - the platform keeps its ingredient margin regardless of store-level profitability, so the downside is fully socialized onto franchisees.
> This is a middle-class balance-sheet event disguised as an entrepreneurship story.
> As employees: it offers abundant but low-ceiling jobs that do not build middle-class-sustaining income; a store crew role rarely progresses beyond area manager.
> Net effect: the trend makes middle-class consumption cheaper while making middle-class capital formation riskier - it cushions the symptom of the squeeze while accelerating one of its causes.

**Dampak Daerah Non Jawa**

> Genuinely national in reach, but with sharply unequal economics.
> Mixue explicitly positioned itself in Medan, Makassar, Palembang, Banjarmasin, Pontianak, Manado, Padang and many kabupaten-level towns, not only Jakarta/Surabaya/Bandung - the ultra-cheap price point works better in lower-income regions, exactly mirroring the Chinese 下沉市场 (lower-tier market) thesis, and the arrival of an air-conditioned branded outlet in a kabupaten town carries real symbolic and social value (a 'third place' for youth where none existed).
> However: (1) unit economics deteriorate with distance from Java-Sumatra logistics corridors, because ingredients must be shipped and the free-freight subsidy is unsustainable, so outlets in Eastern Indonesia (Papua, Maluku, NTT) are rare and expensive; (2) the closure wave hits residential-area and small-town outlets hardest, as those depend on thin local loyalty rather than mall footfall, so the shakeout is regionally regressive - Jakarta mall flagships survive while Kalimantan and Sulawesi neighbourhood stores close first; (3) displacement of local UMKM beverage vendors is proportionally more damaging in small towns where the local es teh or ice cream seller has no alternative livelihood; (4) the premium wave (Chagee, Heytea) will remain almost entirely Jabodetabek/Surabaya/Bali, widening the experiential gap.
> Positive regional counter-effect: the format creates local supply-chain demand for ice, packaging, sugar and delivery services, and the coffee sub-wave creates genuine upstream value for producing regions - Aceh Gayo, Toraja, Flores Bajawa, Java Preanger - because Indonesian chains such as Janji Jiwa, Kopi Kenangan, Fore and Tomoro source domestic robusta and arabica, unlike the tea chains whose inputs are imported.

### Kaitan Pendidikan

**Jurusan Terancam**

> Nothing is destroyed outright - this trend degrades the market value of certain skill sets rather than eliminating degree programmes.
> (1) Traditional culinary arts / Tata Boga (SMK) and classic Perhotelan (D3/D4 Hospitality) craft tracks - because the platform model deskills preparation into SOP execution with pre-mixed inputs and semi-automatic machines, an SMK Tata Boga graduate and an untrained hire perform identically behind a Mixue counter, collapsing the wage premium for formal culinary training.
> (2) Barista craft training as a standalone qualification - the artisanal barista skill set (manual brewing, latte art, sensory cupping) is commercially devalued in a market where 80% of volume is automated espresso plus syrup; the craft survives only in a small specialty niche.
> (3) Generic Manajemen / Business Administration undergraduate degrees - the franchise model outsources strategy, pricing, marketing and procurement to the platform, so the on-site 'manager' role requires compliance and scheduling skills rather than management theory, and these graduates are hired at crew-adjacent wages.
> (4) Independent-entrepreneurship-oriented Kewirausahaan programmes that teach 'open your own kedai' without teaching unit economics, cohort analysis, or franchise-contract literacy - they are actively producing graduates who become the losing side of the franchise trade.
> (5) Conventional Marketing/Advertising curricula built on ATL/BTL campaigns, since customer acquisition in this sector runs through short-video virality and mascot IP rather than media buying.
> (6) Sekretaris/Administrasi Perkantoran and similar clerical vocational tracks, whose graduates are absorbed into crew roles because no better formal-sector option exists - the trend does not threaten the major, it caps the ceiling for its graduates.
> The deeper threat is structural: the sector absorbs large volumes of diploma and SMK graduates into roles that do not require or reward their qualification, producing credential inflation and under-employment rather than unemployment.

**Jurusan Dibutuhkan**

> (1) Supply Chain Management and Logistics with a cold-chain specialization - the single largest capability gap; Indonesia needs people who can design multi-island cold-chain networks, warehouse siting, and demand forecasting, because this is the layer where value is captured and where Indonesia is 8-12 years behind.
> (2) Food Technology / Teknologi Pangan and Food Engineering - specifically formulation of syrups, non-dairy creamer, stabilizers, fruit concentrate, shelf-life extension, and halal-compliant ingredient substitution; this is what would let Indonesia build its own central kitchens instead of importing them.
> (3) Halal Science and Halal Assurance Management (Sistem Jaminan Produk Halal auditing) - a genuinely defensible Indonesian specialization with export potential to the entire OIC market.
> (4) Industrial Engineering applied to multi-site service operations - store layout, throughput optimization, labour scheduling, waste reduction.
> (5) Retail/Franchise Business Analytics - POS data, basket analysis, cohort retention, store-level P&L modelling, site-selection geospatial analysis (GIS).
> (6) Agribusiness and post-harvest processing for coffee, tea, sugar, dairy and fruit - the upstream localization opportunity, including plantation management, roasting technology and sensory science.
> (7) Social commerce and short-video content operations - the modern demand-generation function.
> (8) Franchise law and commercial contract literacy - Indonesia has almost no professional layer advising prospective franchisees on disclosure, territory protection, termination clauses and input-pricing risk.
> (9) Applied Mandarin plus F&B operations - a scarce, immediately monetizable combination given the number of China-headquartered principals.
> (10) Food safety, HACCP, and quality auditing for distributed franchise networks.
> (11) Sustainability/packaging engineering, given imminent single-use plastic regulation and the category's cup waste footprint.

### Pelajaran Kebijakan dari China

**Respons Kebijakan China**

> Regulation arrived only AFTER the trend matured and produced visible harm - the sequence Indonesia can learn from.
> (1) Anti-involution campaign: in July 2025 China's top leadership formally elevated 'involution' (内卷) to a high-level economic risk, launching a coordinated push against destructive below-cost competition.
> (2) Delivery-platform price-war crackdown: in May 2025 the State Administration for Market Regulation chief Luo Wen publicly vowed to curb involutionary competition among food-delivery firms after Meituan/Ele.me/JD subsidy wars distorted the entire F&B sector; platforms are now prohibited from forcing or indirectly forcing merchants to sell below cost.
> (3) Pricing Law revision: the draft amendment prohibits irrational price wars and contemplates minimum-price mechanisms to prevent predatory undercutting - this is what ended the 9.9-yuan coffee era (Luckin raised prices in early 2026; Cotti suspended its shop-in-shop franchise model).
> (4) Anti-Unfair Competition Law revision (2025), with wide-reaching provisions on platform conduct and merchant coercion.
> (5) Food-safety enforcement on franchise networks: after the March 2025 CCTV/Hubei 3.15 exposé of a Yichang Mixue store using overnight lemon and orange slices, and the 2023 Beijing Consumer Association finding that Mixue had roughly three times the food-safety violations of the next-worst brand, regulators intensified inspection of franchise chains and pressed brands to accept liability for franchisee conduct.
> (6) Health/labelling pressure: nutrition-grade labelling for freshly made drinks and sugar-reduction pushes were promoted from the Two Sessions onward, driving brands to 'healthy' repositioning.
> (7) Franchise disclosure enforcement under the Commercial Franchise Administration Regulation, including scrutiny of misleading return-on-investment claims to prospective franchisees.
> Preemptive lessons for Indonesia: mandate franchisor disclosure of real store-level survival rates and median franchisee P&L before any franchise sale; make the franchisor jointly liable for franchisee food-safety violations; regulate below-cost delivery subsidies before a subsidy bubble forms rather than after; and require front-of-pack sugar labelling for freshly made drinks, not only packaged ones.

**Rekomendasi Kebijakan Indonesia**

> (1) Franchise disclosure reform - amend Permendag 71/2019 to require every franchisor (domestic and foreign) to publish, in the prospectus and in Bahasa Indonesia, audited store-level median revenue, median time-to-breakeven, the survival rate of stores opened in the prior 36 months, and full disclosure of mandatory input pricing and mark-ups; ban unsubstantiated ROI claims.
> This is the single highest-impact intervention given that thousands of middle-class households have already lost Rp700-800 million each.
> (2) Cooling-off and territory protection - a mandatory 14-day cooling-off period, plus minimum radius protection between outlets of the same brand, to stop platforms from cannibalizing their own franchisees to sell more ingredient volume.
> (3) Joint liability for food safety - make the franchisor legally co-responsible with the franchisee for BPOM and halal violations, so quality control is enforced by the party with the capital.
> (4) Local-content by incentive, not mandate - rather than reinstating a percentage rule (removed in Permendag 71/2019), offer tax holidays and import-duty relief conditional on establishing an Indonesian production/central-kitchen facility and on sourcing a rising share of dairy, sugar, fruit and packaging domestically; the objective is to convert Indonesia from a distribution market into a manufacturing node for ASEAN halal beverage inputs.
> (5) Sugary-drink excise design - when the cukai MBDK takes effect in 2026, apply it on a tiered sugar-content basis and extend the framework to freshly made beverages over time, but pair it with a mandatory front-of-pack sugar disclosure at point of sale so it changes behaviour rather than only raising revenue; earmark part of the proceeds for diabetes prevention.
> (6) Cold-chain and logistics investment - treat multi-island cold chain as strategic infrastructure (national logistics cost is 14.29% of GDP); co-fund regional distribution hubs in Sumatra, Kalimantan, Sulawesi that any F&B network can use, which lowers the barrier for Indonesian brands specifically.
> (7) UMKM upgrading, not protection - fund a national programme giving independent kedai and warkop access to shared cold storage, group purchasing, QRIS-integrated POS, and basic hygiene certification, so they compete on the dimensions where chains currently win.
> (8) Dairy self-sufficiency - accelerate domestic milk production given 80% import dependence and 16.3 l/capita consumption, linking it to the free nutritious meal programme's demand.
> (9) Labour standards - enforce minimum wage, overtime, and BPJS enrolment for franchise crew, explicitly learning from China where tea-chain staff faced age discrimination, unpaid overtime, disputed employment status and social-insurance evasion.
> (10) Reciprocity and data - require foreign F&B principals to report store counts, closures and franchisee turnover annually to Kemendag, creating the statistical basis Indonesia currently lacks.

### Peluang & Rekomendasi Aksi

**Peluang Bisnis**

> (1) The picks-and-shovels layer - the highest-margin, lowest-risk position.
> Supply the platforms rather than joining them: halal-certified non-dairy creamer, syrups, fruit concentrate, jelly/topping manufacturing, PP/PET cups, lids, sealing film, paper straws.
> Every one of these is currently imported or import-dependent, and every one of the ~2,600 Mixue plus thousands of clone outlets consumes them daily.
> (2) Central kitchen / commissary-as-a-service - build shared regional production and cold-storage facilities that mid-sized Indonesian brands can rent, giving them Mixue-like unit economics without Mixue-like capex; this is the structural gap and the most defensible business in the category.
> (3) Cold-chain 3PL for multi-island F&B - specialized frozen/chilled distribution to Sumatra, Kalimantan, Sulawesi with SLA guarantees.
> (4) Franchise-management SaaS - POS, inventory, franchisee compliance, store-level P&L dashboards, mystery-shopper/quality audit workflow, priced for the Indonesian mid-market.
> (5) Distressed-asset consolidation - the closure wave is creating a large supply of nearly-new soft-serve machines, sealers, chillers, refrigerated display units and fitted-out ruko leases at deep discounts; a refurbishment-and-resale or equipment-leasing business is timely right now.
> (6) Domestic-origin premium positioning - the whitespace Chinese chains cannot occupy: Indonesian single-origin coffee (Gayo, Toraja, Bajawa, Kintamani), Indonesian tea (Cianjur, Wonosobo), and heritage flavours (kelapa, gula aren, pandan, cincau, kopi jahe) at Rp15,000-25,000, defensible because it depends on domestic sourcing relationships.
> (7) Upstream value capture in coffee - specialty roasting, post-harvest processing, and export-grade green bean trading serving both domestic chains and the Chinese market, which now imports significant volumes.
> (8) Halal certification and food-safety consulting for the wave of incoming Chinese principals - a service business created directly by the trend.
> (9) Sugar-reduction and functional-beverage formulation ahead of the 2026 cukai MBDK - reformulation services and low-GI sweetener supply.
> (10) Sustainable packaging manufacturing ahead of plastic regulation.
> (11) Franchisee advisory and due-diligence services - independent unit-economics analysis for prospective franchisees, a market that does not currently exist in Indonesia.
> (12) Micro-format and mobile units (gerobak/kios) for tier-3 towns where a Rp700 million ruko format cannot work but a Rp30-60 million kiosk can.

**Rekomendasi Individu Mahasiswa**

> Build capability in the layer that captures margin, not the layer that serves cups.
> Concretely: (1) Learn unit economics fluently - contribution margin per cup, break-even foot traffic, rent-to-revenue ratio, payback period; this single skill would have prevented most of the franchisee losses of 2023-2025 and is directly employable in franchise development and investment roles.
> (2) Master supply chain and cold chain - demand planning, inventory optimization, warehouse siting, S&OP; take Coursera/edX supply-chain certificates and, if possible, CSCP/CPIM, then target roles at F&B principals, 3PLs and FMCG distributors.
> (3) Get data-analytical - SQL, Python/pandas, spreadsheet modelling, Power BI/Tableau, plus GIS for site selection; retail analytics is the most transferable skill in this sector.
> (4) Acquire halal-assurance and food-safety credentials (HACCP, ISO 22000, Penyelia Halal certification) - scarce, regulation-backed, and immediately monetizable given every incoming brand needs it.
> (5) Learn Mandarin to working proficiency if you want to be in the room where decisions are made - the principals are Chinese-headquartered and bilingual operators are structurally scarce and better paid.
> (6) If you study food technology, specialize in formulation and shelf-life for beverage systems, not general food science.
> (7) If you want to be an operator, work 12-24 months inside a chain (Kopi Kenangan, Tomoro, Fore, Mixue) to learn the SOP machine from the inside before risking capital - treat it as paid apprenticeship, not a career.
> (8) Do NOT buy a franchise as a first business without independent unit-economics due diligence and without the ability to survive 18 months of negative cash flow; the platform earns from your ingredient purchases whether or not your store is profitable.
> (9) Build social-commerce and short-video content skills - demand generation in this category is content-driven and this is one of the few store-level skills with real wage leverage.
> (10) Consider the upstream: agribusiness, post-harvest processing and specialty coffee sourcing offer a more defensible Indonesian career than downstream retail service.

**Rekomendasi Perguruan Tinggi**

> OPEN or strengthen: (1) D3/D4 Cold Chain and Food Logistics - the clearest national capability gap, best sited at polytechnics in Surabaya, Medan, Makassar and Semarang, built with industry (Kemendag, ALFI, 3PLs, F&B principals).
> (2) D4 Food Processing Technology with a beverage-systems concentration - syrup, creamer, concentrate, stabilizer, and halal-compliant reformulation, explicitly aimed at enabling Indonesian central kitchens.
> (3) Retail and Franchise Management diploma with mandatory unit-economics, franchise law, site selection and store-level P&L modules - and require every graduate to build a real franchise due-diligence model.
> (4) Halal Assurance Management as a standalone applied programme with BPJPH-recognized certification embedded in the curriculum.
> (5) Applied Data Analytics for Retail as a cross-cutting minor available to all business and vocational students.
> STRENGTHEN and REORIENT: (6) Existing Tata Boga (SMK) and Perhotelan (D3/D4) programmes should add operations-management, inventory, hygiene-audit and POS-analytics content and reduce pure craft hours, since craft alone no longer commands a wage premium.
> (7) Kewirausahaan programmes must stop teaching aspirational business-plan writing and start teaching cash-flow survival, contract literacy and franchise-risk analysis.
> (8) Coffee and tea agribusiness programmes - build on the model of Politeknik Negeri Jember's D4 Pengelolaan Perkebunan Kopi (which already certifies graduates as coffee plantation assistant, production supervisor, roaster and barista) and replicate it in Aceh, North Sumatra, South Sulawesi and NTT, explicitly linking upstream agriculture to downstream retail in one curriculum - exactly the integration Zunyi Vocational College built in Guizhou.
> ADOPT FROM CHINA: (9) Industry-education integration (produk-pendidikan terpadu) - negotiate with major chains (Kopi Kenangan, Tomoro, Mixue Indonesia, Fore) to co-develop and donate standardized operations curricula and digital training platforms into SMK and polytechnic course standards, as Mixue did with Chinese vocational colleges, so training cost is shared and placement is guaranteed; and (10) create a recognized national occupational certification for 'peracik minuman'/beverage formulator through BNSP, mirroring China's 调饮师, so the role becomes a certified skill with a wage ladder rather than an interchangeable crew slot.
> DO NOT open: generic 'F&B Business' bachelor's degrees with no technical or supply-chain core - they would replicate the credential inflation already visible in generic management programmes.

### Faktor Risiko & Sisi Gelap

**Dampak Negatif China**

> (1) Franchisee capital destruction at industrial scale - in the twelve months to 15 Dec 2024, about 127,700 new milk tea shops opened but net store count fell by 17,800, implying more than 140,000 closures in a single year; each closure represents a household's lost deposit, fit-out and equipment.
> Brand-level attrition reached 12.11% closure rate (Auntea Jenny) and 17.06% franchisee attrition (Chabaidao).
> The platform's revenue model - selling ingredients to franchisees - means the parent profits from network expansion regardless of store-level profitability, structurally misaligning incentives.
> (2) Margin destruction across the sector from the 9.9-yuan price war, which compressed gross margins for everyone and forced Luckin to raise prices and Cotti to suspend its shop-in-shop franchising by early 2026.
> (3) Food safety failures traceable to deskilled franchise execution - the March 2025 Hubei 3.15 exposé of a Yichang Mixue store using overnight lemon and orange slices amid visible flies; a 2023 Beijing Consumer Association finding that Mixue had roughly three times the food-safety problems of the second-worst brand; a June Hong Kong finding of coliform and total bacteria counts exceeding legal limits in a frozen dessert sample.
> (4) Labour exploitation - franchise-store staff on roughly RMB 4,000/month with no onboarding training; Chagee starting base pay of RMB 2,420 topped up by performance and attendance allowances to RMB 5,000-7,000; standing shifts with no break during order surges; documented cases of workers re-hired three times in one year at the same store and then denied unpaid wages and holiday overtime because courts found no formal employment relationship existed; and industry-wide under-payment or non-payment of social insurance to cut costs.
> (5) Age discrimination - reports from 2023 of Mixue stores screening out applicants by age, with 26 already treated as 'too old' for crew work; similar practices at Heytea.
> (6) Public-health externality - normalizing multiple high-sugar drinks per week among young consumers, contributing to rising obesity and metabolic disease.
> (7) Homogenization of urban commercial streetscapes and displacement of independent tea houses and local dessert shops.
> (8) Enormous single-use packaging waste.
> (9) Delivery-subsidy distortion that inflated demand artificially and then collapsed, taking Q4 2025 profits down 39% at Luckin when subsidies contracted.

**Risiko Sosial Indonesia**

> (1) Mass middle-class capital destruction with no legal recourse - Indonesia has no franchise-disclosure regime requiring survival rates or median franchisee P&L, so households continue to buy Rp700-800 million franchises on the basis of marketing claims into an already-saturated market; the 428 overseas closures concentrated in Indonesia and Vietnam are the leading edge of this, and unlike in China there is no consumer-association reporting or regulatory follow-up.
> This is the highest-severity risk.
> (2) Youth employment trap - a large cohort of 18-25 year olds absorbed into minimum-wage, high-turnover, deskilled crew roles with no wage ladder, producing under-employment of SMK and diploma graduates and a lost decade of skill accumulation; without labour enforcement, Indonesia will import China's problems (unpaid overtime, disputed employment status, BPJS evasion, informal age screening) into a weaker enforcement environment.
> (3) Public health - Indonesia already faces a severe diabetes burden; normalizing 3-5 high-sugar drinks per week among adolescents, with no front-of-pack sugar disclosure on freshly made beverages and a cukai MBDK whose rate is still undetermined and which may not cover fresh drinks at all, is a slow-moving crisis.
> (4) UMKM displacement without transition support - independent es teh vendors, warkop and neighbourhood ice cream sellers lose footfall to branded chains and have no upgrading pathway.
> (5) Food-safety incident risk amplified by halal sensitivity - a single credible contamination or halal-violation event at a franchised outlet could cascade into brand collapse, boycott dynamics with ethnic and religious overtones, and abrupt mass unemployment across thousands of stores; Indonesia's regulatory capacity to inspect thousands of dispersed franchise outlets is far weaker than China's.
> (6) Value-capture asymmetry - Indonesia supplies the consumers, the shophouses, the franchisee capital and the low-wage labour while the manufacturing margin, R&D and IP remain in China, so the sector grows GDP consumption without building industrial capability; if this pattern persists, Indonesia converts household savings into Chinese manufacturing revenue.
> (7) Predatory financing - the risk that fintech lenders and paylater platforms begin financing franchise purchases, converting a business failure into a household debt crisis.
> (8) Environmental - a step-change in single-use cup and plastic waste in cities with weak waste management.
> (9) Regional inequality - the shakeout closes non-Java outlets first, leaving small-town franchisees with the largest relative losses.

**Kelompok Rentan**

> (1) Aspiring and lower-middle-class franchisee households - the group that deployed Rp230-800 million of savings, property proceeds or borrowed capital into a franchise between 2022 and 2024 and now faces closure; they bear 100% of the downside while the platform retains its ingredient margin, and Indonesia's shrinking middle class (46.7 million in 2025, down from 47.9 million) cannot absorb these losses.
> (2) Young crew workers aged 18-25, mostly SMA/SMK graduates, on minimum-wage contracts with high turnover, limited BPJS enrolment, and no skill accumulation - and they are the first to lose work in a closure wave; women are over-represented in these roles.
> (3) Informal beverage vendors - pedagang es teh keliling, warkop owners, neighbourhood ice cream sellers - who lose footfall to branded outlets and have no capital to upgrade and no social protection when displaced.
> (4) Small commercial property owners in secondary cities who leased to franchisees and now face vacancy and rent arrears.
> (5) Adolescents and children as a public-health cohort, given high sugar intake, aggressive youth-targeted marketing, and no point-of-sale sugar disclosure.
> (6) Non-Java and small-town franchisees, whose outlets have worse logistics economics, thinner catchments and are structurally first to close.
> (7) Delivery drivers, whose earnings depend on order volumes inflated by promotions that are now being withdrawn.
> (8) Local dairy farmers and sugar producers, who are bypassed by import-based supply chains and therefore capture none of the sector's growth despite it being a beverage industry.

### Contoh Kasus Konkret

**Kasus China**

> Mixue Bingcheng (蜜雪冰城) is the definitive case.
> Founded June 1997 in Zhengzhou, Henan by Zhang Hongchao with a CN¥3,000 loan from his grandmother, starting as a shaved-ice stall.
> It converted to franchising in 2007 and, critically, built its own logistics network in 2014 and became the first in the industry to abolish freight charges for franchisees.
> It is not principally a beverage retailer but a food manufacturer and distributor: roughly 94-98% of revenue comes from selling ingredients, packaging and equipment to its own franchisees, supported by five production bases (Henan, Hainan, Guangxi, Chongqing, Anhui) totalling 670,000 sqm with ~1.43 million tons of annual capacity, and 27 self-operated warehouses covering ~3.5 million sq ft, with last-mile delivery via ~40 local providers.
> Median store size is roughly 400 sq ft.
> Cost advantage: lemons sourced ~20%+ cheaper and milk powder ~10% cheaper than peers.
> Scale at end-2025: 59,823 stores globally (55,356 in mainland China), 99.97% franchised, FY2025 revenue RMB 33.56 billion (+35%) and net profit RMB 5.93 billion (+33%).
> It listed in Hong Kong on 3 March 2025 at HK$202.5 per share, raising about US$444 million, and surpassed McDonald's and Starbucks in global store count.
> Its ultra-cheap coffee sister brand Lucky Cup (幸运咖) crossed 10,000 stores in Nov 2025 and opened its first overseas store in Selangor, Malaysia in August 2025.
> The counter-case is Luckin Coffee: 31,048 stores at end-2025 after adding a net 8,708 in one year (~24/day) and FY2025 revenue of RMB 49.29 billion (+43%), yet Q4 2025 net profit fell 39% as delivery subsidies contracted - demonstrating that even the winner of the price war does not escape its economics.
> The systemic case is the shakeout: more than 140,000 milk tea shops closed in China in the twelve months to Dec 2024 against 127,700 openings, a net loss of 17,800 stores.

**Padanan Indonesia**

> Direct instances: Mixue Indonesia (PT Zhisheng Pacific Trading) - entered Oct 2019, first store at Cihampelas Walk Bandung in March 2020, ~2,600-2,667 outlets by 2025 representing ~55.7% of Mixue's entire overseas network, ~12,800 direct jobs, 1,400+ franchise partners, MUI halal certification since Feb 2023, franchise entry Rp700-800 million - and now the epicentre of Mixue's 428 overseas store closures.
> Cotti Coffee (first store Kuningan City Mall Jakarta, 15 Aug 2023, ~IDR 18,000 per drink).
> CHAGEE (PIK Avenue Jakarta, 11 April 2025, with Erajaya Group; Plaza Indonesia flagship Nov 2025).
> WeDrink, Ai-Cha (PT Nanyang Group Indonesia, 14 principal plus 160 partner outlets, franchise Rp230-300 million), Cooler City, Shuyi.
> The most important structural analogue is Tomoro Coffee - Indonesia's Luckin: founded in Jakarta in 2022 by J&T Express co-founder Star Yuan with ~US$60 million from Chinese VC ATM Capital, 600+ Indonesian outlets by Oct 2024 targeting 1,000, a 2,400-ton/year Jakarta roastery, and expansion into China, Singapore and the Philippines - Chinese capital and operating know-how wearing an Indonesian brand.
> Domestic imitators: Momoyo (Indonesian-owned, 529 branches within ~6 months of launching franchising in April 2023) and Xi Yue; Es Teh Indonesia (945+ outlets); Haus!; Kopi Kenangan (900+, overtook Starbucks Indonesia on outlet count in 2024); Kopi Janji Jiwa (900+); Fore Coffee (210+, IDX-listed 2025); Kopi Kulo; Point Coffee.
> Sector backdrop: ~461,991 coffee-selling outlets nationwide as of Nov 2025 including warkop, the highest absolute count globally, with a modern coffee shop market of roughly US$2.1 billion growing about 10% annually.

### Tingkat Keyakinan & Kualitas Sumber

**Catatan Kontradiksi Data**

> (1) Mixue global store count varies by reporting date and is often quoted without one: 45,302 (Sept 2024 prospectus), ~46,000 (end-2024), 53,014 (30 June 2025), 59,823 (31 Dec 2025).
> The Jakarta Post (June 2026) says 'over 45,000 globally', which is stale by roughly 15,000 stores.
> Reports citing '59,823 in 2025' and '53,014 in 2025' are both correct but refer to different dates.
> (2) Mixue Indonesia outlet count: reported as 2,667 (55.7% of overseas) in one source, 'more than 2,600 as of February 2025' in another, and 'nearly 2,600 by end-2025' by the company - the direction is flat-to-declining, but the precise figure is unresolved, and no source discloses how many of the 428 overseas closures were Indonesian specifically.
> (3) Mixue overseas total: 4,895 (end-2024) vs 4,733 (H1 2025) vs an implied ~4,467 (59,823 minus 55,356 at end-2025) - the last is a derived figure and may not be directly comparable.
> (4) Tomoro Coffee outlet count is reported as both '600+ in Indonesia (Oct 2024)' and '1,000+ branches', likely conflating Indonesian and global counts or different dates.
> (5) Mixue Indonesia entry year is given as both 2019 (entity registration, October) and 2020 (first store, March, Bandung); Wikipedia says 'Indonesia followed in 2020'.
> (6) Mixue franchise cost in Indonesia ranges across sources from Rp700 million to Rp840 million depending on inclusions.
> (7) Indonesia's 461,991 'coffee shops' figure counts warkop and street vendors and is not comparable to modern chain-outlet counts used for China.
> (8) The Rp170 trillion Indonesian contemporary beverage market figure comes from a commercial franchise-promotion site and could not be corroborated against a statistical authority - treat as indicative only.
> (9) The cukai MBDK is agreed in principle for the 2026 budget but the rate and the scope (whether freshly made drinks are covered) remain undetermined as of this writing.
> (10) The two new Ministry of Education vocational coffee specialties are reported by a Tencent News aggregation dated Jan 2026, but the primary page returned HTTP 503 and the exact programme names and levels could not be confirmed.
