## 7. Consumer Downgrade / Trading Down (消费降级 / 反向消费) — the mass shift from premium to value consumption, the rise of hard-discount and white-label retail, and the parallel 'emotional upgrade' in low-ticket affective spending
**Kategori**: Konsumsi & Ritel (Consumption & Retail) — with cross-cutting exposure to Macroeconomics (deflation/disinflation), Labour Markets, and Consumer Finance

📊 Hybrid — best described as Simultaneous-with-Structural-Laggard. The consumer-behaviour dimension is close to Simultaneous (both economies are downgrading in 2024-2026, from different causes: China from a property-wealth shock at ~USD 13,000 GDP per capita, Indonesia from deindustrialisation, weak formal job creation and rising taxes at ~USD 5,000). The supply-side response is a clear Laggard (Indonesia lacks the hard-discount, white-label and C2M retail infrastructure China built, and is importing it via Chinese chains). The emotional-upgrade dimension shows near-Leapfrog behaviour (Labubu reached Indonesia within months). And there is a Reverse element: Indonesia's middle-class contraction is measurably older (from 2019) than China's structural downgrade (from 2021-2022). The most consequential asymmetry is not timing but sequence — China is trading down AFTER a mass premium consumption era, while Indonesia is trading down BEFORE ever having one. | 🎯 Prob: Tinggi (High) — and largely already realised for consumer behaviour. For the Chinese-style organised discount/white-label retail infrastructure specifically, probability is Sedang-Tinggi (Medium-High) over 2026-2030, driven more by Chinese operator entry than by domestic invention. | 🔍 Keyakinan: Tinggi (High) for the core structural narrative and for all headline quantitative claims, which come from official statistics (China NBS via Xinhua and State Council releases, Indonesia BPS, Bank Indonesia consumer confidence, Kemnaker layoff counts) and from primary corporate disclosure (MR.DIY Indonesia press releases, Pop Mart results, Alfamart financials) corroborated by top-tier research (Bain China Shopper Report, Kantar/Worldpanel, Rhodium, OECD, Asia Society). Sedang (Medium) for the lag quantification (4-6 years), for the causal attribution of Indonesian down-trading to specific drivers versus general macro weakness, and for China's education-response detail, where programme-withdrawal counts vary by source. Rendah (Low) for the 2027-2030 Indonesian peak projection and for any claim about how the two cycles will interact after 2027.

> **Status di Indonesia**: Already entered at scale on the demand side (sudah masuk masif) but only partially on the supply side. Indonesian consumers are demonstrably trading down — measurable in cigarette down-trading, FMCG downtrading, pack-size reduction, promotion dependence, minimarket over hypermarket, and value-chain retail expansion — while the organised hard-discount/white-label retail infrastructure that China built to serve downgrade is still embryonic. Indonesia is therefore in the 'demand arrived, supply lagging' phase, which is precisely the gap Chinese value operators (Mixue, Miniso, Chagee, Cotti) are entering to fill.

### Basic Info

**Tahun Mulai China**

> Two distinct starts.
> (a) 2018 — the term 消费降级 ('consumption downgrade') entered mainstream Chinese discourse as Pinduoduo's rise made cheap-goods commerce visible; PDD IPO'd on NASDAQ in July 2018 only 2 years 11 months after founding, the fastest ever for a Chinese internet company, and retail sales growth visibly slowed that year.
> This first wave was largely a discovery of the 'sinking market' (下沉市场) rather than a genuine national income shock.
> (b) 2021-2022 — the structural phase, triggered by the property-developer crisis (Evergrande, August 2021), the zero-COVID shutdowns of 2022, the education/platform crackdowns, and the collapse of the housing wealth effect.
> From 2023 onward downgrade became the default consumption regime rather than a niche behaviour, and by 2024-2026 it hardened into a deflationary equilibrium.

**Pemain Kunci China**

> Value platforms: Pinduoduo (PDD Holdings) with its 百亿补贴 '10 Billion Subsidy' programme (launched June 2019), Taobao Tejia/Taobao Special Offer, Douyin low-price channel, Xianyu (闲鱼, Alibaba's second-hand marketplace), Zhuanzhuan.
> Hard discount and snack-collection chains: 鸣鸣很忙 Ming Ming Hen Mang group (零食很忙 Snack Is Busy + 赵一鸣零食 Zhao Yi Ming), 万辰集团 Wanchen Group (好想来 Hao Xiang Lai) — each operating roughly 15,000-20,000 outlets; 好特卖 HotMaxx and 嗨特购 HitGoo (near-expiry discount stores); 奥乐齐 ALDI China (Shanghai RMB 9.9 own-label line); Pang Donglai (胖东来) as the quality-value counter-model.
> Membership warehouse clubs: Sam's Club China, Costco China — the 'trade down by trading channel' format.
> Value F&B: 蜜雪冰城 Mixue Bingcheng (world's largest F&B chain by outlet count, RMB 4-8 drinks), 库迪咖啡 Cotti Coffee and Luckin Coffee (the RMB 9.9 coffee price war), Wallace (华莱士), Tastien (塔斯汀), plus the 穷鬼套餐 'poor man's meal deal' menus at McDonald's, KFC and Haidilao's small-portion lines.
> White-label/C2M manufacturers in Yiwu, Guangzhou, Quanzhou and Baiyun supplying unbranded 白牌 goods.
> On the emotional-upgrade side: Pop Mart (Labubu / The Monsters), Miniso and TOP TOY, Bandai/guzi retailers, Jellycat, and the 谷子经济 anime-merchandise malls in Shanghai, Chengdu and Wuhan.
> Regulators shaping the response: NDRC, MOFCOM, SAMR (Pricing Law amendment), Ministry of Finance (trade-in subsidies).

### China Trend Detail

**Apa Yang Terjadi Di China**

> China is running a full-economy trading-down cycle in which consumers buy the same or larger physical volume while paying materially less per unit — a volume-up, price-down regime that is structurally different from a simple demand recession.
> Bain's China Shopper Report shows FMCG value growth of just +0.8% in 2024 (the weakest in four years) built from +4.4% volume growth and a -3.4% collapse in average selling price, the sharpest ASP fall in four years; Q1 2025 continued the pattern (+2.7% value, +5.3% volume, -2.5% ASP).
> The mechanism has four interlocking parts.
> (1) A negative wealth shock rather than an income shock: the property crash removed the collateral and the wealth effect that underwrote a decade of aspirational spending, so households with intact incomes still cut discretionary outlays and raised precautionary savings — household savings deposits rose from about RMB 82 trillion in 2019 to roughly RMB 152 trillion in 2024.
> (2) A channel migration: spending re-routed out of department stores, hypermarkets and premium brand outlets into formats explicitly engineered for cost-per-unit — snack collection stores (+51% YoY), discount stores (+92% YoY), membership warehouse clubs (+40% YoY, buyer counts +26%), Pinduoduo (+11% in Q1 2025) and Douyin's low-price channel (which overtook JD.com to become China's second-largest e-commerce platform at 23% online share).
> (3) A brand-equity collapse in the mid-market: 平替 ('dupe' / affordable substitute) became the organising consumer concept, with search volume up 237% YoY in 2025 and the RMB 50-300 price band growing about 150%; surveys report 74% of young consumers refusing to pay brand premiums and 87.1% prioritising value-for-money.
> White-label (白牌) goods produced directly by OEM factories now compete head-on with the national brands those same factories manufacture for.
> (4) A cultural re-coding in which frugality became a status performance rather than a shame: 反向消费 ('reverse consumption'), 穷鬼套餐 ('poor man's meal deals'), 抠门 (deliberate stinginess) and 省钱 money-saving communities on Xiaohongshu and Douban carry more than 1.5 million posts and 130 million views.
> Second-hand commerce normalised, with roughly 100 million users on resale platforms and ~79% penetration among 16-34s.
> The critical nuance — and the reason 'downgrade' is a partial misnomer — is that this coexists with an aggressive emotional upgrade: Chinese consumers cut RMB 200 off a skincare basket and then spend RMB 99 on a blind box.
> The emotional economy reached about RMB 2.3 trillion in 2024, the guzi (anime merchandise) segment RMB 168.9 billion (+40% YoY), and Pop Mart's revenue jumped 185% to RMB 37.12 billion in 2025 with the Labubu-bearing Monsters IP up 668% YoY in H1 2025.
> Consumers are not spending less on everything; they are re-allocating from functional/status categories to affective ones, and from brand rent to unit utility.
> The macro consequence is a deflationary feedback loop: cheaper consumer demand forces price wars, price wars compress corporate margins (industrial profits fell 13.1% YoY in November 2025), compressed margins force wage freezes and layoffs, and weaker labour income reinforces downgrading.
> Beijing named this loop 内卷 (involution) and launched an explicit 反内卷 anti-involution campaign in July 2025, including a Pricing Law amendment barring below-cost selling.

**Fase Tren Di China**

> Mature and structurally entrenched, now moving into a policy-contested phase.
> The trend is no longer 'emerging' — it is the baseline consumption regime and has been for roughly four years.
> Three markers of maturity: (a) supply has fully reorganised around it (hard-discount formats, white-label C2M, RMB 9.9 coffee, snack chains at 15,000-20,000 stores each) rather than treating it as a temporary demand dip; (b) it has produced its own institutional counter-reaction — the 反内卷 anti-involution campaign from July 2025, Pricing Law amendments banning below-cost selling, and successive consumption-stimulus rounds; (c) the trend has begun to bifurcate rather than deepen uniformly, splitting into hard downgrade on functional categories and simultaneous upgrade on emotional/experiential ones (services retail +5.3% vs goods +1.1% in H1 2026).
> It is not in backlash or decline: the June 2026 rebound to +1.0% was festival- and base-effect-driven, and the underlying volume-up/price-down structure remains intact.
> Best description: 'mature / regulated / deflation-locked, with an internal bifurcation into value-seeking plus affective premiumisation'.

### Status Indonesia Saat Ini

**Status Di Indonesia**

> Already entered at scale on the demand side (sudah masuk masif) but only partially on the supply side.
> Indonesian consumers are demonstrably trading down — measurable in cigarette down-trading, FMCG downtrading, pack-size reduction, promotion dependence, minimarket over hypermarket, and value-chain retail expansion — while the organised hard-discount/white-label retail infrastructure that China built to serve downgrade is still embryonic.
> Indonesia is therefore in the 'demand arrived, supply lagging' phase, which is precisely the gap Chinese value operators (Mixue, Miniso, Chagee, Cotti) are entering to fill.

**Contoh Konkret Indonesia**

> Value retail expansion: MR.DIY Indonesia — the country's fastest-expanding retailer, opening its 1,200th store in December 2025, reaching 1,278 stores in Q1 2026 and 1,349 by H1 2026, with Q1 2026 revenue of IDR 2.4 trillion (+31.0% YoY) and profit after tax +35.5% YoY on an explicit 'Everyday Value' positioning.
> Chinese value F&B and retail: Mixue Bingcheng (entered 2020, ~2,600 outlets by end-2025, Indonesia's largest freshly-made beverage chain by store count, then began streamlining outlets in H1 as the market saturated), Miniso (150+ stores), Chagee (launched April 2025 at PIK Avenue via a joint venture with an Erajaya subsidiary, halal-certified, three-hour opening queues), Cotti Coffee, Wallace, Naixue and Yao Yao — more than half of enquiries to Indonesian mall landlords now come from F&B, dominated by Chinese chains.
> Local value players: Tomoro Coffee, Kopi Kenangan and Esteh Indonesia in the sub-Rp 20,000 beverage tier; Rocket Chicken and Sabana in value QSR.
> Format shift in grocery: minimarkets keep expanding (Indomaret 22,682 stores in 2024 to 23,441 by Q3 2025; Alfamart 20,120 to 20,925; combined 44,366 outlets by February 2026) while hypermarkets contract (336 outlets in 2019 to 244 in 2024, with Lulu Hypermarket exiting Indonesia on 30 April 2025).
> Category down-trading: cigarette Group I (highest excise) production collapsed about 10% while Group II rose 1.3% and Group III rose 7% — the textbook down-trading signature, with national output at 307.9 billion sticks in 2025, the lowest in years.
> Promotion dependence: 39% of cooking-oil purchases were promotion-driven in 2024, up from 22% in 2022 (Nielsen).
> Kantar Worldpanel documents Indonesian shoppers buying less, shrinking baskets and downtrading to cheaper brands, with explicit downtrading in baby care and volume declines in beverages, dairy and home care.
> Retail earnings stress: Alfamart net income -7% in 2024 and -3.5% YoY in 9M 2025, with ready-to-drink beverage sales down roughly 20%.
> Policy responses: repeated purchasing-power stimulus packages — transport-fare and toll discounts, a 50% electricity tariff discount for over 79 million households under 1,300 VA, food aid to 18.3 million families (June 2025); a Rp 12.8 trillion (~USD 763 million) Q1 2026 package; and a Rp 26.34 trillion (~USD 1.48 billion) H2 2026 package combining transport incentives, internships/vocational training and food assistance.
> Protectionist response: Kominfo blocked Temu in October 2024 to shield MSMEs from direct factory-to-consumer Chinese pricing.
> Emotional-upgrade counterpart: the Labubu/blind-box craze, sold-out concerts and strong iPhone demand coexisting with falling retail sales — Indonesian commentators explicitly invoke 'doom spending' and the lipstick effect.

### Analisis Lag

**Bukti Historical Lag**

> (1) Value-format retail: Miniso launched in China in 2013 and reached Indonesia meaningfully around 2017-2018 (now 150+ stores) — a 4-5 year gap.
> (2) Value F&B: Mixue scaled in China from roughly 2018-2019 and entered Indonesia in 2020, reaching ~2,600 outlets by 2025 — a 2-3 year entry lag but a 5-6 year lag to comparable density.
> (3) Discount/near-expiry retail: HotMaxx and the snack-collection chains scaled in China 2019-2023; Indonesia has no equivalent chain at scale in 2026 — an unresolved 6+ year gap.
> (4) Cheap-goods e-commerce: Pinduoduo's group-buying value model took off in China 2016-2018; the Indonesian copycat cohort (KitaBeli, Super, Chilibeli) tried 2020-2022 and largely failed, showing that value-commerce transfer is format-dependent, not automatic.
> (5) Blind-box/IP merchandise: Pop Mart scaled in China from 2019-2020; the Labubu wave hit Indonesia in 2025 — a 5-year lag on the category but near-zero lag on the specific viral product, evidence that algorithmic diffusion has collapsed the lag on emotional consumption while leaving the retail-infrastructure lag intact.
> (6) Coffee price wars: Luckin's RMB 9.9 war ran 2023-2024; Indonesia's sub-Rp 20,000 coffee war (Tomoro, Kopi Kenangan, Fore) intensified 2024-2026 — roughly a 1-2 year gap, the fastest-transferring sub-trend.
> (7) Macro precedent: China's post-2018 retail deceleration preceded Indonesia's post-2023 consumption stall by about five years, matching the general 4-7 year China-Indonesia lag observed across e-commerce, fintech and gig-economy domains.
> (8) Counter-evidence: Indonesia's middle-class contraction started in 2019, before China's property-driven downgrade — so on the raw demand side Indonesia was not behind, it was simply less visible because the absolute levels were lower.

**Tipe Lag**

> Hybrid — best described as Simultaneous-with-Structural-Laggard.
> The consumer-behaviour dimension is close to Simultaneous (both economies are downgrading in 2024-2026, from different causes: China from a property-wealth shock at ~USD 13,000 GDP per capita, Indonesia from deindustrialisation, weak formal job creation and rising taxes at ~USD 5,000).
> The supply-side response is a clear Laggard (Indonesia lacks the hard-discount, white-label and C2M retail infrastructure China built, and is importing it via Chinese chains).
> The emotional-upgrade dimension shows near-Leapfrog behaviour (Labubu reached Indonesia within months).
> And there is a Reverse element: Indonesia's middle-class contraction is measurably older (from 2019) than China's structural downgrade (from 2021-2022).
> The most consequential asymmetry is not timing but sequence — China is trading down AFTER a mass premium consumption era, while Indonesia is trading down BEFORE ever having one.

### Probabilitas Transfer ke Indonesia

**Probabilitas Transfer**

> Tinggi (High) — and largely already realised for consumer behaviour.
> For the Chinese-style organised discount/white-label retail infrastructure specifically, probability is Sedang-Tinggi (Medium-High) over 2026-2030, driven more by Chinese operator entry than by domestic invention.

**Alasan Probabilitas**

> High, for five reinforcing reasons.
> (1) The demand condition already exists independently: Indonesia does not need to import trading-down behaviour because its own middle class has been contracting since 2019 (57.33m to 46.7m), household consumption growth has been under 5% for eight straight quarters, retail sales turned negative in April-May 2026, and layoffs reached 88,519 in 2025.
> Down-trading is already measurable in cigarettes, FMCG and promotion dependence.
> (2) The supply vector is actively pushing: Chinese value operators whose entire business model was forged in China's downgrade era are expanding into Indonesia precisely because their home market is saturated and deflationary — Mixue at ~2,600 outlets, Miniso at 150+, Chagee via an Erajaya JV, Cotti, Wallace, Naixue, with Chinese F&B dominating mall leasing enquiries.
> China's overcapacity and price deflation make Indonesia an outlet market for both cheap goods and cheap-goods business models.
> (3) The playbook is portable in a way that livestream commerce or community group buying was not: a Rp 8,000 ice-cream cone or a Rp 15,000 fixed-price homeware SKU requires no super-app, no dense apartment-block grid and no next-day national logistics — MR.DIY's 1,349-store run-rate and +31% Q1 2026 revenue growth in a market where overall retail sales fell 3.7% is direct proof of format-market fit.
> (4) The emotional-upgrade half transfers even faster through algorithmic content diffusion — Labubu, blind boxes and IP merchandise reached Indonesian malls within months of their Chinese peak.
> (5) Structural macro conditions in Indonesia are worsening, not improving: contracting real wages in manufacturing/trade/construction, textile-sector layoffs, consumer confidence at a nine-month low, and Gen Z online-lending exposure at 34%.
> The main reason the supply side is only Medium-High rather than High is Indonesia's political economy: the Temu block in October 2024 shows that any format perceived as an unmediated conduit for Chinese factory goods into the MSME base will attract regulatory action, so the transfer will occur through licensed, franchised, halal-certified, locally-partnered formats rather than through raw cross-border discount platforms.

**Vektor Transmisi**

> (a) Direct entry by Chinese value operators — the dominant vector, and unusually literal here because the exported product IS the downgrade business model.
> Mixue transplanted its RMB 4-8 pricing architecture (franchise-plus-supply-chain-margin, not store-margin) and reached ~2,600 Indonesian outlets in five years; Miniso exported the Japanese-styled Chinese value-variety format to 150+ stores; Chagee entered April 2025 through a joint venture with an Erajaya subsidiary with halal certification secured upfront; Cotti Coffee, Wallace, Naixue and Yao Yao follow the same route, now accounting for the majority of F&B leasing enquiries to Indonesian mall landlords.
> (b) Supply-push from Chinese overcapacity — the most underrated vector.
> Deflation and involution at home mean Chinese manufacturers must dump volume abroad; Indonesia becomes a destination for cheap white-label goods through Shopee/TikTok Shop cross-border listings, Yiwu/1688 sourcing agents, and grey-channel imports, which mechanically enables Indonesian consumers to trade down even where domestic supply cannot support it.
> This vector is what triggered the October 2024 Temu block and the recurring textile-import controversies.
> (c) Local copycat and defensive repositioning — MR.DIY (Malaysian-origin but running the same hard-value playbook), Tomoro, Kopi Kenangan and Esteh in sub-Rp 20,000 beverages, Alfamart and Indomaret expanding private label and dark stores (50 in 2025, doubling in 2026), Alfagift at 25 million members; incumbents copying the format to defend share.
> (d) Algorithmic content diffusion — the fastest vector for the emotional-upgrade half and for frugality culture itself.
> TikTok, Instagram Reels and Xiaohongshu carry Chinese 平替/省钱 content conventions (dupe reviews, haul-comparison videos, 'racun TikTok' cheap-find culture, blind-box unboxing) into Indonesian feeds with near-zero lag; Labubu's Jakarta queues followed Shanghai's within months.
> (e) Chinese venture and franchise capital — Chinese-backed F&B franchises, Chinese-funded logistics (J&T), and Chinese capital behind Indonesian value brands lower the cost of building discount infrastructure.
> (f) Diaspora, sourcing intermediaries and franchise brokers — Indonesian-Chinese trading families and Mandarin-capable sourcing agents connecting Indonesian franchisees to Chinese master franchisors and Yiwu supply, plus master-franchise consultancies actively marketing Chinese value brands to Indonesian investors.
> (g) Macro-financial transmission — Chinese deflation exported through goods prices contributes to Indonesia's own disinflation/deflation prints, reinforcing the price expectations that make consumers postpone purchases.

### Faktor Pendorong

**Prasyarat Struktural**

> Threshold conditions, with Indonesia's position benchmarked against China at the moment its downgrade cycle turned structural (2021-2022).
> (1) A prior mass premium-consumption base to trade DOWN from.
> China had one: GDP per capita ~USD 12,600 in 2021, a decade of luxury growth, and a household sector with roughly RMB 82 trillion in savings.
> Indonesia does NOT meet this — GDP per capita is roughly USD 4,900-5,000, about 39% of China's 2021 level.
> Indonesia is trading down from a base that was never premium, so the downgrade takes a different form: not luxury-to-mass but mass-to-subsistence, and not brand-to-white-label but branded-to-smaller-pack or branded-to-illicit (as in cigarettes).
> (2) A wealth-effect shock transmission channel.
> China's driver was property (roughly 60-70% of household wealth).
> Indonesia's property market is far less financialised and homeownership less leveraged, so the Indonesian shock arrives through the labour market instead — 88,519 layoffs in 2025, textile-sector collapse, contracting real wages — which is slower-moving but harder to reverse with monetary policy.
> Partially met, via a different channel.
> (3) Retail modernisation sufficient to host organised discount formats.
> China had roughly 65-70% modern-trade penetration when discount chains scaled.
> Indonesia's modern trade is heavily minimarket-weighted (44,366 Alfamart+Indomaret outlets) with general trade / warung still dominant in many categories, and only 244 hypermarkets.
> Partially met — the minimarket network is a viable discount rail, but there is no big-box discount or membership-club density.
> (4) Domestic manufacturing depth for white-label supply.
> China's Yiwu/Guangzhou/Quanzhou clusters make 白牌 goods viable at margin-free prices.
> Indonesia's manufacturing base is narrower and its textile sector is contracting.
> NOT met — this is the binding constraint, and it means Indonesian trading down channels demand toward imports rather than toward domestic private label, which is economically and politically corrosive.
> (5) Logistics cost enabling low-ticket, high-frequency retail.
> China moves parcels nationally in 1-3 days at RMB 2-3.
> Indonesia's archipelagic geography makes non-Java distribution structurally costly.
> NOT met outside Java-Sumatra-Bali — which is why value formats cluster on Java and why national hard discount is harder than in China.
> (6) Consumer price transparency and comparison behaviour.
> China: >70% of consumers compare prices across platforms; 平替 search +237%.
> Indonesia: promotion-driven purchasing rising sharply (cooking oil 22% to 39%), heavy marketplace price comparison, high social-media dupe culture.
> MET and rising.
> (7) Urban density supporting small-format store economics.
> China ~67% urbanisation; Indonesia ~58% — below threshold but sufficient in Java.
> Partially met.
> (8) A young, digitally-native cohort willing to perform frugality as identity.
> China: 74% of young consumers refuse brand premiums.
> Indonesia: strong 'racun TikTok' cheap-find culture, thrift/preloved culture, and heavy price-comparison behaviour.
> MET.
> (9) Social-safety-net weakness driving precautionary saving.
> China's downgrade is precautionary (savings up to RMB 152 trillion).
> Indonesia's is closer to forced — with roughly 59% informal employment, low savings buffers and 34% of Gen Z using P2P/online loans, Indonesian households cannot save their way through; they down-trade and borrow instead.
> NOT met, in a way that makes the Indonesian version more socially dangerous.
> Net reading: Indonesia clears the demand and cultural thresholds, fails the supply-side and logistics thresholds, and critically fails the 'prior affluence' threshold — predicting exactly the observed outcome of visible consumer down-trading served largely by imported formats and imported goods rather than by a domestic value-manufacturing complex.

**Indikator Pemantauan**

> Already fired: BPS middle-class series (57.33m to 46.7m, 2019-2025); cigarette excise-group mix (Group I -10%, Group III +7%); retail sales index turning negative (-3.7% April 2026, -3.9% May 2026); consumer confidence at 117.8 (June 2026); Kantar/Worldpanel downtrading and basket-shrinkage findings; promotion-driven cooking-oil purchases at 39%; MR.DIY's +31% revenue growth against a shrinking retail market; hypermarket count falling 336 to 244 and Lulu's exit; Alfamart's -20% RTD beverage sales; Mixue reaching ~2,600 outlets then streamlining; Chinese F&B dominating mall leasing enquiries.
> Still to monitor as leading signals: (a) private-label share of Alfamart/Indomaret/Superindo revenue crossing 10% — the single cleanest indicator that Indonesia is building a domestic value stack rather than importing one; (b) the first Indonesian hard-discount grocery chain (fixed-price or near-expiry format) exceeding 200 outlets; (c) registration of PT entities and trademarks containing 'diskon', 'grosir hemat', 'harga pabrik', 'outlet', or master-franchise filings for Chinese discount brands; (d) Google Trends and TikTok hashtag volumes for 'harga termurah', 'dupe', 'barang KW', 'preloved', 'thrifting', 'promo', 'skincare murah'; (e) growth of preloved/second-hand platforms (Carousell, Tinkerlust, thrift markets) and pawnshop (Pegadaian) lending volumes; (f) pack-size downsizing ('shrinkflation') incidence tracked by BPOM/YLKI; (g) illicit-cigarette prevalence as a proxy for terminal down-trading; (h) motorcycle and car sales mix shifting to entry-level and used units; (i) mall vacancy rates and premium-tenant churn in Jakarta/Surabaya; (j) BNPL and P2P delinquency at OJK, particularly among under-30s; (k) SP2KP/BPS deflation prints in volatile-food and core categories; (l) Kemnaker layoff (PHK) counts in retail and F&B specifically, not just manufacturing; (m) the arrival of a Chinese-style membership warehouse club or a licensed Temu-equivalent; (n) whether beauty's +16% growth outlier persists (the lipstick-effect signal); (o) blind-box/IP merchandise retail floorspace in Indonesian malls as the emotional-upgrade counterpart.

### Hambatan & Faktor Pembatal

**Hambatan Transfer**

> Regulatory protectionism against cheap Chinese supply — the October 2024 Kominfo block of Temu is the template, justified explicitly as MSME protection against factory-direct pricing, and the same reflex constrains any pure import-arbitrage discount format.
> Import licensing, SNI standards, halal certification (mandatory for food and increasingly for consumer goods) and safeguard duties on textiles raise the cost floor beneath which Chinese-style discount pricing cannot go.
> Logistics economics: archipelagic freight makes low-ticket, high-frequency national discount retail arithmetically difficult outside Java-Sumatra-Bali, capping the addressable market for the format.
> Absence of a domestic white-label manufacturing base means Indonesian private label has no cost engine — retailers cannot replicate ALDI or Pang Donglai economics with imported inputs and a weakening rupiah.
> Fragmented general trade: warung and traditional markets still carry a large share of FMCG volume, and they compete on credit relationships and proximity rather than price, blunting organised discounters' advantage.
> Capital scarcity: China's discount chains scaled on abundant domestic venture and franchise capital; Indonesian retail capital is thinner and post-2022 funding conditions are tight.
> Real-estate constraints: prime retail space in Java is expensive relative to discount-format unit economics, though hypermarket vacancies create an opening.
> Consumer trust and quality anxiety: 'murah' still carries a KW/counterfeit stigma in categories like cosmetics, pharma and baby products, and enforcement of product-safety standards is weaker than China's.
> Weak deflationary tolerance: unlike China, Indonesia's government treats falling prices as a political emergency and responds with demand stimulus, which partially offsets down-trading pressure.
> Labour-cost structure: minimum-wage increases and UMP regulation limit the labour-cost compression that Chinese discounters used.
> Finally, the cultural pattern of social consumption (Lebaran, weddings, arisan, gengsi/status signalling) creates categories where Indonesians will not trade down even under severe pressure — a genuine dampener on the format's ceiling.

**Faktor Pembatal Transfer**

> Structural conditions guaranteeing that Chinese-style consumption downgrade will NOT replicate in the same form.
> (1) No prior premium base to fall from.
> China's downgrade is a descent from mass affluence — luxury -20%, cosmetics -26.4% in Beijing and Shanghai, high-end restaurants halving in Shanghai — because those markets existed at scale.
> Indonesia's premium consumer segment is small (the entire middle class is 46.7 million people and shrinking, at 16.6% of population), so there is far less to cannibalise: the Indonesian version manifests as pack downsizing, brand-to-unbranded switching, deferral of durables, and shifts into the informal/illicit economy rather than luxury-to-mass migration.
> Analytically, Indonesia risks 'trading down before ever trading up' — a middle-income-trap consumption pattern with no Chinese equivalent.
> (2) No C2M/white-label manufacturing complex.
> China's discount formats are ultimately a distribution layer on top of the world's deepest factory base; the value captured stays domestic.
> Indonesia has no equivalent, so the same formats become import channels, converting consumer savings into an import bill and a current-account drag while destroying domestic MSME producers.
> This is why the Indonesian state blocks rather than embraces the model, and it is the single most consequential asymmetry.
> (3) Archipelagic logistics.
> Hard discount depends on dense, cheap national distribution; Indonesian freight to eastern regions can exceed the value of a low-ticket basket, so the format will remain Java-centric indefinitely without subsidy.
> (4) Different shock channel and therefore different reversibility.
> China's downgrade is wealth-effect driven and could partially reverse if property stabilises; Indonesia's is labour-market and deindustrialisation driven, which is structurally slower to reverse and less responsive to consumption stimulus — meaning Indonesia may get the downgrade without the eventual Chinese-style recovery optionality.
> (5) Precautionary saving is not available.
> Chinese households absorb the shock by saving (deposits at RMB 152 trillion); Indonesian households, with roughly 59% informal employment, low savings buffers, and 34% of Gen Z on P2P/online loans, absorb it by borrowing and by exiting formal consumption entirely.
> The Indonesian downgrade is therefore more debt-financed and more socially corrosive than China's.
> (6) Deflation politics.
> China tolerated four years of PPI deflation as an industrial-policy byproduct; Indonesia's political system treats deflation prints as a legitimacy problem and responds with repeated demand-side packages (Rp 12.8 trillion in Q1 2026, Rp 26.34 trillion in H2 2026), which will keep the Indonesian cycle shallower but longer and fiscally costlier.
> (7) MSME political economy.
> MSMEs represent the majority of Indonesian employment and have organised representation (Kadin, HIPMI, IKAPPI); any discount format that visibly destroys warung and pasar livelihoods will be regulated, as Temu was.
> (8) Religious and social consumption floors.
> Lebaran, hajj/umrah saving, weddings and halal certification create categories that resist down-trading and that have no Chinese analogue in scale.

### Prediksi Timeline di Indonesia

**Tahun Masuk Indonesia**

> Already entered.
> Phasing: 2019-2023 latent phase (middle-class contraction begins in BPS data; Mixue enters 2020; cigarette down-trading emerges); 2024 statistical confirmation (BPS confirms 9.48 million people dropped out of the middle class; Kantar records downtrading; Temu blocked in October); 2025 acceleration (deflation in January and February; 88,519 layoffs; middle class down to 46.7 million; Chagee launches; MR.DIY opens its 1,200th store); 2026 entrenchment (retail sales negative in April and May; consumer confidence at a nine-month low; MR.DIY revenue +31% against a shrinking market — the classic discount-format-outperforms-in-downturn signature).

**Tahun Mainstream Indonesia**

> 2025-2027.
> It is arguably already mainstream on the demand side — eight consecutive quarters of sub-5% consumption growth, negative retail sales, measurable category down-trading — but 'mainstream' in the supply-side sense (organised value retail as the default shopping mode, private label at double-digit share, a domestic hard-discount chain at scale) is more likely 2027-2028.
> The tipping markers to watch are private-label share crossing 10% at the major minimarket chains and the first Indonesian fixed-price/near-expiry chain passing a few hundred stores.

**Skenario Percepatan**

> Further textile and labour-intensive manufacturing layoffs deepening the income shock; rupiah depreciation raising imported input costs and squeezing real purchasing power further; expansion of the VAT base or new consumption taxes; removal or narrowing of fuel and electricity subsidies; a global commodity-price downturn hitting Indonesia's export earnings and regional incomes; aggressive entry by additional Chinese value chains and a licensed cross-border discount platform; Chinese overcapacity intensifying goods dumping into ASEAN; rapid MR.DIY-style format proliferation proving the unit economics and pulling in copycat capital; further BNPL/P2P expansion that lets stressed households sustain volume while trading down on price; a property or BNPL credit event among the urban lower-middle class; and — the most underrated accelerant — social-media normalisation of frugality as identity, which converts down-trading from a reluctant necessity into a durable preference that persists even after incomes recover, exactly as happened with China's Gen Z.

### Dampak Sosial-Ekonomi

**Dampak Kelas Menengah**

> This trend is not merely something that happens TO the Indonesian middle class — the middle class is its subject and its casualty.
> BPS data are unambiguous: 57.33 million people (21.4% of population) in 2019 fell to 47.85 million (17.13%) in 2024 and roughly 46.7 million (16.6%) in 2025, with 9.48 million people dropping out over five years, mostly into the 'aspiring middle class' (137.5 million, 49.22%) and vulnerable-poor (67.69 million) cohorts.
> Because the middle class plus aspiring middle class generate over 81% of household consumption (36.88% and 44.34% respectively), their down-trading is the transmission mechanism for the entire consumption slowdown.
> Concretely: (1) Expenditure recomposition — housing, education, transport and health costs are rising faster than incomes, forcing discretionary compression; nearly half of surveyed middle-class workers report falling purchasing power, with 85% blaming essential-goods prices.
> (2) Savings depletion and 'makan tabungan' — households that once saved now run expenditure deficits, and the buffer that defines middle-class status is being consumed; unlike Chinese households, who responded to the same shock by saving more (deposits from RMB 82 trillion to RMB 152 trillion), Indonesian households lack the buffer to do so.
> (3) Debt substitution — 34% of Gen Z respondents used online loans or P2P lending within six months; BNPL fills the gap between aspiration and income, converting a consumption problem into a balance-sheet problem.
> (4) Status-anxiety spending — the paradox of empty malls alongside sold-out concerts, Labubu queues and strong iPhone demand is the lipstick effect and doom spending: households abandon the large aspirational purchase (house, car, overseas travel) and redirect a fraction of the freed cash into small affective purchases, which is rational despair, not recovery.
> (5) Aspiration foreclosure — the deepest harm is not the current basket but the closing of the upward path: the aspiring middle class is growing faster than the middle class, meaning Indonesia is accumulating people who will not convert into middle-class consumers, which forecloses the domestic-demand-led growth model.
> (6) Entrepreneurial squeeze — middle-class small businesses (boutiques, cafés, convection workshops, distributorships) face simultaneous demand contraction and cheap-import competition.
> Net assessment: the Indonesian middle class is experiencing a downgrade that is more debt-financed, less cushioned, and occurring at roughly 39% of the per-capita income level at which China's began — a materially more fragile position.

**Dampak Daerah Non Jawa**

> Asymmetric and, unusually for a China-transfer trend, partly favourable to non-Java on the demand side but exclusionary on the supply side.
> Demand side: down-trading behaviour is if anything more entrenched outside Java, where incomes are lower and the middle class thinner; regions dependent on commodity cycles (Kalimantan coal, Sulawesi nickel, Sumatra palm oil) experience sharper consumption swings, and BPS poverty and vulnerable-poor concentrations sit disproportionately in eastern Indonesia and rural areas.
> The Chinese parallel is instructive but inverted: in China, downgrade was deepest in Tier-1 cities (Beijing and Shanghai cosmetics -26.4%, retail declines) while Tier-3/Tier-4 markets grew (+8% and +7.3% in mini-store channels) because they had less premium consumption to lose; in Indonesia the equivalent effect means Jakarta and Surabaya show the most visible premium destruction while regional markets see relatively resilient low-ticket volume.
> Supply side: value-retail infrastructure is Java-concentrated because archipelagic freight destroys low-ticket unit economics — this is the binding constraint.
> Indomaret and Alfamart are expanding into eastern Indonesia (Indomaret targeting 1,000 new stores with explicit eastern focus), and MR.DIY's 1,349-store network is spreading, but hard-discount and membership formats will remain Java-centric.
> Consequence: non-Java consumers face the worst of both worlds — they trade down like everyone else but pay a geographic price premium and get less format choice, so their effective real-income loss is larger.
> Where non-Java could gain: local production substitution.
> If down-trading redirects demand from imported branded goods to local unbranded equivalents, regional producers of food, coffee, snacks, textiles and household goods could capture volume — but only with deliberate intervention (regional fulfilment hubs, freight equalisation, SNI/halal certification support, aggregator platforms).
> Absent that, the trend widens the Java/non-Java gap by making outer regions consumption markets for Java-distributed imported cheap goods rather than producers of them.
> The most concrete non-Java risk is regional retail and distributor employment: as brand principals cut distribution layers to fund price competition, the regional distributor and sales-agent network — a major source of formal-sector employment outside Java — is the first cost line to be cut.

### Kaitan Pendidikan

**Jurusan Terancam**

> The framing matters: almost no discipline becomes obsolete, but several curricula rest on assumptions that a trading-down economy invalidates.
> (1) Manajemen Pemasaran taught as brand-equity building, premium positioning and above-the-line advertising — the entire pedagogical apparatus of Kotler-style brand management assumes consumers will pay for brand, which 74% of young Chinese consumers now refuse and Indonesian consumers increasingly do too; the discipline survives only if retooled toward price architecture, promotion mechanics and value engineering.
> (2) Periklanan/Advertising and Desain Komunikasi Visual programmes oriented to campaign-led brand building, as A&P budgets are reallocated to trade promotion and price.
> (3) Manajemen Ritel curricula built on department-store and hypermarket formats — a format losing outlets in Indonesia (336 to 244).
> (4) Perhotelan dan Pariwisata programmes aimed at the premium and MICE segments, where domestic discretionary travel is the first cut; the value/domestic tourism segment is where demand actually is.
> (5) Tata Boga and Culinary Arts oriented to fine dining — China's evidence is brutal (nearly 3 million food-service closures, half of Shanghai's high-end restaurants gone) and Indonesian premium F&B is under similar pressure.
> (6) Fashion Design and Tata Busana programmes premised on domestic branded apparel manufacturing, in a sector already contracting under import pressure and carrying the bulk of Indonesian layoffs.
> (7) Manajemen Bisnis (general) and D3 administrative programmes without cost, sourcing or data content — the generic business degree is the most exposed credential in a margin-compressed economy.
> (8) Ilmu Komunikasi tracks built on mass-media brand communication rather than performance and community mechanics.
> (9) Programmes whose graduates were absorbed by the branded-FMCG and premium-retail management-trainee pipelines, which are shrinking as those employers cut structural costs.
> The systemic risk is subtler than obsolescence: in a low-margin economy, employers stop paying a graduate premium for credentials that do not demonstrably reduce cost or increase volume, so the return on a generalist degree falls.
> China's answer to that pressure — 3.72 million applicants for 38,100 civil-service posts — is the warning: credential inflation plus a weak private labour market channels a generation into rent-seeking stability rather than productive work, and Indonesia's CPNS/PPPK application volumes show the same reflex forming.

**Jurusan Dibutuhkan**

> The demand shifts from creating willingness-to-pay to removing cost while preserving perceived value.
> Rising: (1) Supply Chain Management, Procurement and Logistics — the highest-leverage gap in Indonesia given that archipelagic freight is the binding constraint on value retail; includes landed-cost modelling, cold chain, network design and freight optimisation.
> (2) Cost Engineering / Value Engineering / Industrial Engineering applied to product — the discipline of taking cost out of a SKU without destroying it, which is exactly what white-label and private-label economics require and which Indonesia barely teaches.
> (3) Private Label and Own-Brand Product Development — sourcing, specification writing, OEM management, QC, packaging cost optimisation, and the regulatory layer (SNI, BPOM, halal).
> (4) Retail Analytics and Category Management — price elasticity, promotion effectiveness, assortment optimisation, basket analysis; the skill that separates a discounter that survives from one that burns margin.
> (5) Pricing Strategy and Revenue Management, including pack-price architecture and shrinkflation ethics.
> (6) Consumer Behaviour, Behavioural Economics and Consumer Psychology — specifically the psychology of value perception, scarcity, and the emotional-upgrade paradox; understanding why the same consumer buys a Rp 8,000 drink and a Rp 300,000 blind box is now a commercial competency.
> (7) Franchise Management and Multi-Unit Operations — the operating model of Mixue, MR.DIY and every value chain; Indonesia has enormous franchise activity and almost no formal franchise-management education.
> (8) Manufacturing Engineering, Automation and Lean Production — the only durable Indonesian answer to import-driven down-trading is competitive domestic light manufacturing.
> (9) Halal Supply Chain and Certification — a genuine Indonesian differentiator and a required capability for every entering Chinese chain (as Chagee's pre-launch certification shows).
> (10) Data Analytics and SQL/BI fluency as a general-purpose competency for margin management.
> (11) Consumer Finance, Credit Risk and Financial Literacy — urgent given 34% Gen Z online-lending exposure.
> (12) IP, Licensing and Character Merchandising — the emotional-economy skill set behind Pop Mart, guzi retail and the RMB 168.9 billion Chinese merchandise market.
> (13) Mandarin plus sourcing capability, for direct China supply-chain negotiation.
> Highest-value combinations rather than single skills: supply chain + data analytics; product development + regulatory compliance; consumer psychology + pricing.

### Pelajaran Kebijakan dari China

**Respons Kebijakan China**

> China's response evolved through three stages, and the sequencing is the lesson.
> Stage 1 — demand stimulus (2024-2026, ongoing): the consumer-goods trade-in programme (以旧换新) scaled from RMB 150 billion in 2024 to roughly RMB 300 billion in 2025, with RMB 62.5 billion in ultra-long-term special bonds front-loaded to local governments for Q1 2026; coverage expanded from autos and home appliances into smart devices.
> A consumption-loan interest subsidy ran from 1 September 2025 to 31 August 2026 for verified consumption borrowing (excluding credit cards).
> The March 2025 Special Action Plan to Boost Consumption identified childcare subsidies, social-security strengthening, income growth and service-consumption expansion as the five priorities.
> Verdict: these measures pull demand forward and distort category mix (note the June 2026 collapse in appliance sales as trade-in subsidies rolled off) without addressing the underlying wealth and income problem.
> Stage 2 — recognising the supply-side cause (July 2025 onward): the 反内卷 anti-involution campaign, targeting destructive below-cost competition; amendments to the Pricing Law explicitly barring below-cost selling; capacity-consolidation pressure across autos, solar, e-commerce and food delivery.
> This is the pivotal conceptual move — Beijing reclassified consumption downgrade from a demand-deficiency problem into a price-war/margin-destruction problem, recognising that involutionary price competition destroys the corporate profits and wages that fund consumption (industrial profits -13.1% YoY in November 2025).
> Stage 3 — structural rebalancing (15th Five-Year Plan, 2026-2030): elevating household consumption's share of GDP, strengthening the social safety net (childcare, education, healthcare, eldercare, skills training) to reduce precautionary saving, and expanding service consumption — which is already outperforming goods (+5.3% vs +1.1% in H1 2026).
> What Indonesia can adopt preemptively: (a) do not treat down-trading as purely cyclical — build the safety-net capacity that reduces precautionary and forced saving BEFORE the middle class is hollowed out, since China's biggest regret is that a thin safety net made the wealth shock far more contractionary; (b) legislate against sustained below-cost predatory pricing in retail and platform commerce before a price war destroys domestic producer margins, rather than after; (c) avoid subsidy programmes that merely pull demand forward and create cliff effects (China's appliance sales fell 8.7% and autos 16.1% in June 2026 as subsidies lapsed); (d) recognise emergent value-retail and service occupations early so that labour standards attach before exploitative norms set; (e) protect against imported deflation systematically (anti-dumping capacity, de minimis enforcement) rather than through ad hoc platform blocks like the Temu ban; (f) monitor and act on the corporate-margin channel — falling profits cause falling wages cause falling consumption, and the loop is easier to break early.

**Rekomendasi Kebijakan Indonesia**

> (1) Stop treating purchasing power as a stimulus problem and start treating it as a job-quality problem.
> Rp 12.8 trillion and Rp 26.34 trillion packages of transport discounts and food aid buy quarters, not recovery; the binding constraint is 88,519 layoffs in 2025, contracting real wages in manufacturing/trade/construction, and roughly 59% informal employment.
> Prioritise formal job creation in labour-intensive manufacturing over transfer payments.
> (2) Build the domestic value-supply base rather than blocking the demand for value.
> The Temu block protected MSMEs from a platform but not from the underlying price gap.
> Instead: an SME contract-manufacturing and private-label programme linking domestic producers to Alfamart, Indomaret, Superindo and MR.DIY-style retailers; certification cost subsidies (SNI, BPOM, halal) that currently price small producers out of modern trade; and shared industrial facilities for packaging and QC.
> If Indonesians are going to trade down, the goods they trade down to should be Indonesian.
> (3) Legislate against sustained below-cost predatory pricing in retail and platform commerce, adapting China's Pricing Law amendment and giving KPPU an explicit standard — pre-empting rather than following an involutionary price war.
> (4) Strengthen anti-dumping and import-surveillance capacity as a permanent institution rather than through ad hoc bans, with particular attention to textiles, footwear, ceramics and household goods where Chinese overcapacity is being exported.
> (5) Reduce precautionary and forced saving through the safety net: expand BPJS Kesehatan and Ketenagakerjaan coverage to informal and platform workers, strengthen unemployment insurance (JKP) coverage and adequacy, and expand childcare/eldercare provision — China's clearest retrospective lesson is that a thin safety net converts an income shock into a consumption collapse.
> (6) OJK guardrails on BNPL and P2P lending targeted at the under-30 cohort (34% Gen Z usage), including affordability checks, aggregate-exposure limits and cooling-off rules — Indonesia's downgrade is debt-financed in a way China's was not, which is the single most dangerous divergence.
> (7) Freight equalisation and regional fulfilment hubs so that non-Java consumers are not paying a geographic premium on an already-shrunken basket, and so value formats can serve outer islands.
> (8) Fix the excise structure driving cigarette down-trading and illicit-market growth: the Group I/II/III tariff gap is producing exactly the substitution effect (-10% / +1.3% / +7%) that erodes revenue while sustaining consumption; simplify the tiers.
> (9) Improve measurement: publish a regular official trading-down dashboard (pack-size mix, private-label share, promotion dependence, brand-tier migration by category) so policy responds to structure rather than to headline retail prints.
> (10) Preserve the middle-class ladder explicitly — the aspiring middle class at 137.5 million is the policy target; the metric that matters is conversion rate into the middle class, not aggregate consumption growth.
> (11) Prepare for the emotional-economy adjacency: it is a genuine growth sector (China's RMB 2.3 trillion emotional economy, RMB 168.9 billion guzi market) and Indonesia has strong local IP potential, but it also needs consumer-protection rules on blind-box and gacha mechanics, particularly for minors — China introduced blind-box regulation in 2023 and Indonesia has none.
> (12) Resist the reflex to declare the problem solved when a stimulus quarter prints well; China's June 2026 +1.0% rebound was festival and base effects, and Indonesia's Q1 2026 5.61% headline sat atop contracting real wages.

### Peluang & Rekomendasi Aksi

**Peluang Bisnis**

> (1) Domestic hard-discount grocery — no Indonesian chain occupies the ALDI/HotMaxx position; a limited-assortment, high-private-label, low-cost-to-serve format built for Java's density is the largest open space in Indonesian retail, validated by MR.DIY's +31% growth in a market where retail sales fell 3.7%.
> (2) Private-label manufacturing and OEM services — supplying Alfamart, Indomaret, Superindo and value chains with locally-made own-brand SKUs; the structural gap that currently forces value retail to import.
> (3) Fixed-price and value-variety retail beyond MR.DIY's categories — beauty, stationery, kitchenware, pet, baby.
> (4) Near-expiry and surplus-inventory retail — the HotMaxx model, currently near-absent in Indonesia, with a strong ESG story and a genuine cost advantage.
> (5) Value F&B franchising — both master-franchising Chinese brands into Indonesia and building Indonesian equivalents; the sub-Rp 20,000 beverage and Rp 15,000-25,000 meal tiers are where volume is migrating, and the Mixue model (make margin on supply chain, not store) is the template.
> (6) Supply-chain and landed-cost services — freight consolidation, regional fulfilment hubs, customs and certification-as-a-service; the highest-leverage adjacency given Indonesia's logistics constraint.
> (7) Second-hand, preloved and refurbished commerce — apparel, electronics, furniture, phones; China's ~100 million second-hand platform users show the ceiling, and Indonesian thrift culture is already strong but unorganised and unbranded.
> (8) Repair and refurbishment services — phone, appliance and footwear repair scales when replacement cycles lengthen.
> (9) Rental and access models — appliances, baby equipment, tools, formalwear, vehicles.
> (10) Cost-engineering and value-engineering consultancy for FMCG and manufacturing clients under margin pressure.
> (11) Retail and pricing analytics SaaS — promotion effectiveness, elasticity modelling, assortment optimisation for chains that must now manage margin to the basis point.
> (12) The emotional-upgrade play: Indonesian IP and character merchandising, blind-box and collectible retail, local designer toys — a market Pop Mart proved and that Indonesia currently serves almost entirely with imports despite deep local IP potential (wayang, local animation, music and football fandom).
> (13) Affordable indulgence categories — local beauty (the +16% growth outlier), snacks, RTD beverages engineered to the Rp 5,000-15,000 price point.
> (14) Consumer financial wellness — budgeting, debt consolidation and income-smoothing tools for a cohort with 34% P2P exposure.
> (15) Halal certification and compliance services, made non-optional by every entering Chinese chain.
> (16) Sourcing and QC agency work connecting Indonesian retailers directly to Chinese factories at factory prices, capturing the intermediation margin domestically.

**Rekomendasi Individu Mahasiswa**

> Reorient from 'how do I make customers pay more' to 'how do I take cost out without destroying value' — that is the economy Indonesia is entering, and it is the opposite of what most business curricula teach.
> Core skills to build now: (1) supply-chain and landed-cost literacy — freight, duties, inventory carrying cost, network design, cold chain; in an archipelago this is the highest-paid scarce competency; (2) data fluency — spreadsheets to a professional standard, SQL, basic BI, elasticity and promotion analysis; margin management is an analytical job; (3) sourcing and procurement — supplier identification, specification writing, negotiation, QC, and the regulatory stack (SNI, BPOM, halal); (4) product cost engineering — understanding a bill of materials well enough to redesign it; (5) pricing and pack architecture — how the Rp 5,000 sachet, the Rp 8,000 cone and the Rp 15,000 SKU actually work; (6) multi-unit and franchise operations — the operating discipline behind every value chain in the country; (7) consumer psychology of value and emotion — why the same person trades down on shampoo and up on a blind box; (8) functional Mandarin plus China sourcing capability, a rare and immediately monetisable combination as Chinese chains and suppliers flood in; (9) personal financial discipline as a professional signal — in an economy where 34% of Gen Z carry P2P debt, the individual who avoids it preserves optionality.
> Career positioning: value retail, discount F&B, private-label manufacturing, logistics and repair/second-hand services are the sectors hiring against the trend — MR.DIY opened 130 stores in a half-year while premium retail contracted.
> Avoid over-indexing on brand-building, premium hospitality and premium F&B roles, which are the first cut.
> Study the Chinese case directly (Mixue's supply-chain-margin model, MR.DIY's SKU economics, Pang Donglai's value-through-service model, Pop Mart's IP monetisation) — Indonesia is running roughly four to six years behind on the supply side, so what works in Zhengzhou or Changsha today is a preview of what Indonesian operators will need.
> Non-obvious durable advantage: the ability to build a profitable low-price business in a high-logistics-cost archipelago is a genuinely hard problem that very few Indonesian graduates are trained to solve, and solving it is worth more than any brand-management credential.

**Rekomendasi Perguruan Tinggi**

> Open or expand: Supply Chain and Logistics Management as a full S1 programme with explicit archipelagic, cold-chain and landed-cost content — Indonesia's single largest applied-skills gap; D3/D4 Retail and Chain-Store Operations (連鎖經營管理 equivalent) with real store-based capstones, covering category management, private-label development, shrinkage, promotion mechanics and multi-unit P&L; Cost/Value Engineering as an applied track within Industrial Engineering; Private-Label and Product Development (specification, OEM management, QC, packaging cost, SNI/BPOM/halal compliance); Franchise and Multi-Unit Business Management; Retail and Pricing Analytics; Consumer Finance and Financial Literacy as a mandatory general-education module given Gen Z debt exposure; IP, Licensing and Character Merchandising for the emotional economy; Halal Supply Chain as an export-differentiating specialisation.
> Restructure rather than close: Manajemen Pemasaran toward price architecture, trade promotion, value engineering and performance marketing rather than brand-equity theory; Manajemen Ritel toward discount, minimarket, quick-commerce and omnichannel formats rather than department-store models; Tata Boga toward value and volume F&B operations rather than fine dining; Perhotelan toward domestic and value tourism; Ilmu Komunikasi toward community and performance mechanics.
> Consolidate: generic Manajemen Bisnis and D3 administrative programmes without cost, sourcing or data content — the credential most exposed to margin-compressed hiring.
> Delivery reforms that matter more than the programme list: (a) make programme continuation contingent on measured graduate employment outcomes, adopting China's MOE optimisation criterion rather than enrolment demand; (b) co-design curricula with the actual employers now hiring — MR.DIY, Alfamart, Indomaret, Mixue's franchise network, logistics operators; (c) require capstones measured in real unit economics (a student-run store's gross margin, a sourced SKU's landed cost) rather than in marketing plans; (d) build stackable micro-credentials so working retail and logistics staff can upskill without leaving employment; (e) prioritise campuses outside Java for logistics and regional-sourcing specialisations, since the freight constraint is where non-Java value creation actually lies; (f) lobby Kemnaker to define SKKNI competency standards for retail operations, category management, procurement and franchise management — China's precedent is that occupational recognition precedes and enables curriculum, and Indonesia currently has demand without standards.

### Faktor Risiko & Sisi Gelap

**Dampak Negatif China**

> (1) Deflationary lock-in: China has run the longest deflationary stretch since the 1990s, with PPI negative from late 2022 into early 2026, because cheap-seeking demand and involutionary supply reinforce each other.
> Deflation raises real debt burdens, delays purchases (why buy today if it is cheaper tomorrow), and is far harder to exit than inflation.
> (2) Corporate profit destruction: industrial profits fell 13.1% YoY in November 2025, wiping out nearly all of the year's earlier profit gains; below-cost competition means market-share wars that no one wins, which is precisely what the 反内卷 campaign names.
> (3) Mass small-business failure: nearly 3 million food-service establishments closed in 2024; over half of Shanghai's high-end restaurants shut within a year; Michelin-starred venues and major chains alike failed, taking employment and entrepreneurial capital with them.
> (4) The wage-consumption doom loop: compressed margins force wage freezes and layoffs, which reduce household income, which deepens down-trading — an equilibrium that stimulus alone cannot break.
> (5) Brand and innovation erosion: when 74% of young consumers refuse to pay brand premiums and white-label goods compete directly with the national brands the same factories produce, the returns to brand-building and product innovation collapse, pushing the whole economy toward commoditisation.
> (6) Labour-market distortion: a record 3.72 million applicants for about 38,100 central civil-service posts in 2026 represents an enormous diversion of human capital into exam preparation and rent-seeking stability rather than production — Caixin called the exam 'the new gaokao'.
> (7) Youth withdrawal: 'lying flat' (躺平) and its successors are a rational response to poor returns on effort, but they compound the demographic and demand problems and correlate with delayed family formation.
> (8) Erosion of the mid-market: the hollowing-out of mid-price products and services eliminates the segment where most employment and most SME value creation sits, leaving a barbell of cheap goods and affective luxuries.
> (9) Exported deflation: Chinese overcapacity dumping into ASEAN, Latin America and Europe destabilises trading partners' manufacturing bases — an externality Indonesia is directly absorbing.
> (10) Quality and safety degradation in the race to the bottom, with recurring scandals in near-expiry retail, white-label food and low-cost cosmetics.
> (11) The emotional economy's own dark side: blind-box mechanics are structurally gambling-adjacent, drove documented compulsive spending and minor-protection concerns severe enough that China introduced blind-box regulation in 2023, and Pop Mart's ~40% share decline from its August 2025 peak shows how fragile affective demand is when it is the only thing growing.

**Risiko Sosial Indonesia**

> (1) A downgrade without a floor.
> China's households absorbed the shock by saving (deposits from RMB 82 trillion to RMB 152 trillion); Indonesian households, with roughly 59% informal employment and minimal buffers, absorb it by depleting savings ('makan tabungan'), then by borrowing — 34% of Gen Z using online loans or P2P within six months.
> Indonesia is running a debt-financed downgrade, which converts a consumption problem into a household-balance-sheet crisis and, at scale, into a financial-stability risk via BNPL and fintech-lending delinquency.
> (2) Permanent middle-class foreclosure.
> 9.48 million people have already dropped out of the middle class; the aspiring middle class (137.5 million) is growing faster than the middle class it is supposed to feed.
> If down-trading persists to 2030, Indonesia risks locking in a consumption structure incompatible with its own middle-income-exit ambitions — the consumption analogue of the middle-income trap.
> (3) Import-driven deindustrialisation.
> Because Indonesia lacks a white-label manufacturing base, every rupiah of consumer down-trading disproportionately buys imported goods, accelerating the collapse of domestic light manufacturing that is already producing the bulk of 88,519 (2025) and 23,000+ (2026) layoffs — a self-reinforcing loop in which the workers made redundant become the consumers who can only afford imports.
> (4) Growth of the illicit and informal economy.
> Cigarette down-trading is already spilling into illicit product; the same substitution logic applies to unregistered cosmetics, counterfeit pharmaceuticals, unsafe food and grey-market electronics, in an enforcement environment weaker than China's.
> (5) Job-quality degradation without headline unemployment.
> Value retail and value F&B replace better jobs with lower-paid, higher-turnover ones, so the labour market deteriorates faster than the unemployment rate shows.
> (6) Regional divergence.
> Non-Java consumers trade down while paying a freight premium and receiving less format choice — a compounding real-income penalty that widens inequality.
> (7) Gambling and predatory-mechanic adjacency.
> Indonesia already has a severe online-gambling problem; the combination of financial desperation, doom spending and unregulated blind-box/gacha mechanics is a materially worse risk profile than China faced, and Indonesia has no blind-box regulation where China introduced one in 2023.
> (8) Deflation politics and policy overreaction.
> Repeated demand-stimulus packages (Rp 12.8 trillion, Rp 26.34 trillion) consume fiscal space without addressing job quality, raising the risk of fiscal strain alongside an unresolved consumption problem.
> (9) Social and political volatility.
> The 2025 protests over official allowances against a backdrop of falling purchasing power showed how quickly consumption stress converts into political stress; a shrinking middle class is historically the least stable configuration.
> (10) Aspiration-status stress.
> A generation that cannot afford housing or vehicles but is continuously exposed to consumption signalling on social media is a documented driver of doom spending, over-indebtedness and mental-health deterioration.

**Kelompok Rentan**

> (1) The lower-middle class and 'aspiring middle class' (137.5 million people, 49.22% of the population) — the cohort with just enough income to have adopted middle-class consumption commitments (motorcycle instalments, private schooling, BPJS top-ups, digital subscriptions) and no buffer to sustain them; this is where the 9.48 million who dropped out came from.
> (2) Gen Z and young workers — 34% carrying P2P/online-loan exposure, entering a labour market with contracting real wages and degraded job quality, and the group most exposed to doom spending, blind-box mechanics and status-anxiety consumption.
> (3) Textile, garment and footwear workers — the epicentre of Indonesian layoffs and the direct casualties of import-driven down-trading.
> (4) Warung owners and traditional market traders — losing volume to minimarket and value-chain formats while their own household finances deteriorate; they are simultaneously displaced producers and stressed consumers.
> (5) Retail and F&B workers in mid-market and premium formats — hypermarket employees (336 to 244 outlets, Lulu's exit), department-store staff, casual-dining crew.
> (6) Regional distributors and sales agents outside Java — the first cost line cut when brand principals fund price competition, and a major source of formal non-Java employment.
> (7) Small domestic manufacturers and convection workshops — unable to match imported price points and unable to access modern-trade shelves without certification they cannot afford.
> (8) Non-Java consumers generally — trading down while paying a freight premium and receiving less format choice.
> (9) Fresh graduates — entering a market where the graduate premium is compressing and where, as in China, the rational response is to queue for CPNS/PPPK rather than produce.
> (10) Households dependent on commodity-cycle regional economies, whose incomes swing hardest.
> (11) Children and adolescents — exposed to gambling-adjacent blind-box and gacha mechanics that Indonesia, unlike China since 2023, does not regulate.

### Contoh Kasus Konkret

**Kasus China**

> (1) Mixue Bingcheng (蜜雪冰城) — the definitive downgrade-era business model.
> Drinks at RMB 4-8, profit made on supply-chain margin to franchisees rather than on retail margin, scaled to become the world's largest F&B chain by outlet count and then exported wholesale to Southeast Asia, reaching ~2,600 Indonesian outlets by end-2025.
> It proves that in a trading-down economy the winning structure is supply-chain ownership plus franchise density, not brand premium.
> (2) The snack-collection duopoly — 鸣鸣很忙 (零食很忙 + 赵一鸣零食) and 万辰集团 (好想来), each at roughly 15,000-20,000 stores, having built a national retail format from nothing in about five years by stripping brand rent out of the snack category; the discount-store channel grew 92% YoY and snack-collection stores 51%.
> (3) Pinduoduo — the origin case: NASDAQ IPO in July 2018 just 2 years 11 months after founding, the RMB 10 billion subsidy programme from June 2019, and continued +11% growth in Q1 2025 when the rest of e-commerce stalled; PDD made 'cheap' respectable and forced Alibaba and JD to build their own value channels.
> (4) The RMB 9.9 coffee war — Luckin versus Cotti through 2023-2024, which reset China's entire coffee price expectation downward and destroyed the mid-tier café segment, a direct preview of Indonesia's sub-Rp 20,000 coffee war.
> (5) The 2024 food-service extinction event — nearly 3 million establishments closed, over half of Shanghai's high-end restaurants gone, Michelin-starred venues failing within months of opening; the clearest measure of how fast premium consumption capacity can disappear.
> (6) Beijing and Shanghai cosmetics -26.4% YoY in 2024 alongside Bain's -20% luxury contraction — evidence that the downgrade hit hardest at the top, inverting the usual assumption that value-seeking starts at the bottom.
> (7) Pop Mart / Labubu — the counter-case and the paradox: revenue RMB 37.12 billion in 2025 (+185%), The Monsters IP +668% YoY in H1 2025, one figure auctioned for RMB 1.08 million, the stock up ~200% then down ~40% from its August peak.
> Affective consumption boomed precisely as material consumption contracted, and then proved fragile — the lipstick effect at national scale, with a warning attached.
> (8) The 2026 civil-service exam — 3.72 million qualified applicants for about 38,100 posts; the human-capital cost of a low-margin private economy.
> (9) November 2025's +1.3% retail print and the -13.1% industrial-profit fall in the same month — the two numbers that together define the wage-margin-consumption doom loop and that triggered the elevation of consumption in the 15th Five-Year Plan.

**Padanan Indonesia**

> (1) MR.DIY Indonesia — the closest structural analogue to China's hard-discount formats and the clearest proof of format-market fit: 1,200th store in December 2025, 1,278 in Q1 2026, 1,349 by H1 2026, Q1 2026 revenue IDR 2.4 trillion (+31.0% YoY) with PAT +35.5%, achieved in the same months that national retail sales fell 3.7-3.9% YoY.
> A discounter growing 31% while the market contracts 4% is the textbook signature of a trading-down economy.
> (2) Mixue Indonesia — the direct import of the Chinese downgrade playbook: entered 2020, ~2,600 outlets by end-2025, then began streamlining as the market saturated; Indonesia compressed China's five-year value-beverage cycle into roughly the same span.
> (3) Cigarette down-trading — the cleanest quantitative Indonesian evidence: Group I (highest excise) production -10%, Group II +1.3%, Group III +7%, with total output at 307.9 billion sticks in 2025, the lowest in years, plus rising illicit prevalence.
> Excise policy inadvertently built the down-trading ladder.
> (4) The hypermarket-to-minimarket migration — hypermarkets from 336 (2019) to 244 (2024) with Lulu exiting on 30 April 2025, while Indomaret and Alfamart reached 44,366 combined outlets; Indonesia's version of China's channel migration, though toward proximity-convenience rather than toward hard discount.
> (5) Alfamart's earnings as the middle-class barometer — net income -7% in 2024 and -3.5% YoY in 9M 2025, with RTD beverage sales down about 20%: the discretionary top-up purchase is the first casualty.
> (6) The BPS middle-class series — 57.33 million (2019) to 46.7 million (2025), 9.48 million people dropping out; Indonesia's structural equivalent of China's property-wealth shock, arriving through the labour market instead.
> (7) Promotion dependence — 39% of cooking-oil purchases promotion-driven in 2024, up from 22% in 2022; the Indonesian analogue of China's 87.1% value-first consumers.
> (8) The Labubu queues, sold-out concerts and strong iPhone demand alongside falling retail sales — Indonesia's version of the emotional-upgrade paradox, explicitly discussed domestically as doom spending and the lipstick effect, with beauty's +16% value growth in 2024 as the measurable carve-out.
> (9) The October 2024 Temu block — Indonesia's structural divergence from China: with no domestic white-label base, the state blocks the value supply rather than absorbing it, which is the single most consequential difference between the two trajectories.
> (10) Chagee's April 2025 PIK Avenue launch via an Erajaya JV with pre-secured halal certification — the template for how Chinese value formats will actually enter: licensed, partnered and certified, not cross-border and unmediated.

### Tingkat Keyakinan & Kualitas Sumber

**Catatan Kontradiksi Data**

> (1) The 'downgrade' label is contested.
> Bain, Premia Partners and Baiguan all argue that China is not simply consuming less but consuming differently — volume rose +4.4% in 2024 even as ASP fell -3.4%, and services retail (+5.3% in H1 2026) far outpaced goods (+1.1%).
> Xinhua's official position explicitly disputes the downgrade framing.
> Both readings are supportable; the honest description is 'volume-preserving, price-destroying re-composition', not a demand collapse.
> (2) Indonesian middle-class figures diverge by definition.
> BPS uses the World Bank 3.5-17x poverty-line expenditure band and reports 47.85 million (2024) / 46.7 million (2025); other analysts using different income cutoffs report larger middle classes and milder declines, and some (including FULCRUM/ISEAS) argue the 'shrinking middle class' narrative overstates the case because the aspiring middle class grew simultaneously.
> The direction is unambiguous; the magnitude is not.
> (3) Indonesian headline growth contradicts consumer data.
> Q1 2026 GDP printed 5.61% — the highest since 2022 — while retail sales fell 3.7-3.9% YoY in April-May 2026, consumer confidence hit a nine-month low, and real wages contracted in the largest employing sectors.
> Government and critical analysts read these facts oppositely; the discrepancy likely reflects government-consumption and investment contributions masking household weakness.
> (4) China's November 2025 retail figure is variously cited at +1.3% (TrendForce, CNBC, SCMP) and as an eight-month or three-year low depending on the series used (goods only versus goods-and-services, and whether services retail is included); Chinese statistical practice changed in 2025 to headline 'goods and services retail', which makes year-on-year comparisons with pre-2025 series unreliable.
> (5) The H1 2026 figure of +1.3% for consumer-goods retail sits alongside +2.7% for goods-and-services retail — these are different aggregates and are frequently conflated in secondary reporting.
> (6) Layoff counts for Indonesia vary widely: Kemnaker recorded 88,519 for 2025 while mid-2025 reporting cited about 70,000 by that point and unions claim substantially higher figures; official counts capture only formally reported terminations and systematically understate informal-sector job loss.
> (7) Pop Mart's trajectory is contradictory within a single year: revenue +185% in 2025 with the stock up ~200%, then a ~40% drawdown from the August peak and a 22% single-day plunge in March 2026 — the emotional economy is real but its durability is unproven, so any Indonesian forecast built on it is fragile.
> (8) Mixue's Indonesian store count (~2,600 at end-2025) is followed by reports of outlet streamlining in Indonesia and Vietnam during the subsequent half-year, so the expansion narrative and the saturation narrative are both currently true and depend on the reference date.
> (9) China's programme-withdrawal counts in the MOE major-optimisation cycle differ by source (figures around 1,700 for 2024 are commonly cited but not consistently sourced), so the education-response section is marked uncertain.
> (10) The lag framing itself is contestable for this domain: Indonesia's middle-class contraction began in 2019, before China's structural downgrade (2021-2022), so on the pure demand dimension Indonesia may be leading rather than lagging — the lag is genuine only on the supply-side infrastructure and policy-response dimensions.
> (11) Indonesian FMCG data show simultaneous downtrading (baby care, beverages, dairy, home care) and premiumisation (beauty +16% in 2024), which some analysts, including Bain's 2026 outlook, read as evidence that Indonesia is premiumising rather than trading down; the reconciliation is category polarisation, not a contradiction, but headline claims in either direction are unreliable.
