## 8. Cross-border E-Commerce & Chinese Brand Expansion (出海 / chuhai) into ASEAN and Indonesia — export of an integrated system (supply chain + capital + culture + lifestyle), not merely export of products
**Kategori**: Digital Economy

📊 Hybrid: Simultaneous on the consumption side, Laggard on the production/capability side. Indonesia consumes the trend at near-Chinese speed while remaining structurally unable to originate it. There is no leapfrog available here because the trend's foundation is a manufacturing base Indonesia has not built. Reverse elements exist only at the margins: J&T Express (founded in Indonesia in 2015, now regionally dominant and HKEX-listed) is the one case where the Indonesia-China flow ran outward. | 🎯 Prob: Tinggi (Very High) — the transfer has already occurred and is deepening. The forward-looking question is not whether but in what regulated form, and whether Indonesia captures value or only absorbs cost. | 🔍 Keyakinan: Sedang-Tinggi (Medium-High). High confidence on: China's cross-border e-commerce trade values (official GAC data), Mixue's Indonesian store counts and financials (HKEX-listed disclosures), the Temu block and its stated rationale, Permendag 31/2023 and 19/2026 provisions, the ByteDance-Tokopedia transaction, Sritex's bankruptcy and layoff count, BYD and SAIC market positions, Indonesia's macro indicators (GDP per capita, internet penetration), and China's anti-involution policy actions. Medium confidence on: TikTok Shop Indonesia GMV and market-share figures (third-party trackers with differing methodologies, not audited platform disclosures), the 6-million-seller / 7-million-affiliate figures (2023 platform-supplied numbers, likely inflated and now dated), Chinese FDI ranking adjusted for Singapore/Hong Kong routing, and the China education-response specifics for cross-border e-commerce programmes (no comprehensive national enrolment statistics were located). Low confidence and explicitly marked uncertain: all forward-looking peak-year projections, the exact peak year of the outbound wave in China, and specific franchise unit-economics claims for Indonesian Mixue operators (no audited franchisee-level data is public).

> **Status di Indonesia**: Already massively present, but selectively filtered. Indonesia is the single largest destination of Chinese consumer-brand expansion in ASEAN by absolute volume, while simultaneously being the region's most aggressive regulator of pure cross-border marketplace models. Status is best described as: physical brands and manufacturing FDI = massively in; algorithmic social commerce = massively in via a forced local joint venture; direct cross-border parcel marketplaces (Temu/Shein) = blocked or restricted.

### Basic Info

**Tahun Mulai China**

> 2013-2015 as policy foundation (first cross-border e-commerce Comprehensive Pilot Zone approved in Hangzhou, March 2015; Belt and Road Initiative announced 2013).
> Consumer-brand 'chuhai' wave becomes significant 2018-2020 (Shein pivots to global fast fashion, Mixue opens first overseas store in Vietnam 2018, Temu launched September 2022).
> The phase relevant to Indonesia — full system export including localized supply chain and franchise networks — begins 2020 and accelerates sharply 2022-2026.

**Pemain Kunci China**

> Cross-border marketplaces: Temu (PDD Holdings), Shein, AliExpress/Alibaba International Digital Commerce, TikTok Shop (ByteDance), Lazada (Alibaba-controlled), JD Global.
> F&B and retail chains: Mixue Ice Cream & Tea (蜜雪冰城), Chagee (霸王茶姬), Luckin Coffee, Haidilao/Super Hi International, Miniso, Cotti Coffee.
> Automotive: BYD, SAIC-GM-Wuling (Wuling, MG), Chery, Great Wall Motor, Neta/Hozon, Geely, Aion (GAC).
> Electronics/handsets: Xiaomi, OPPO, vivo, realme, Transsion, Huawei.
> Logistics and infrastructure enablers: Cainiao, J&T Express (Indonesia-founded but built on Chinese OPPO-network DNA), SF Express, YunExpress, JD Logistics.
> Supply clusters: Yiwu, Shenzhen (Huaqiangbei, Shahe), Guangzhou (Panyu garment cluster), Dongguan, Zhengzhou (Mixue's Snow King supply base).
> Capital: Tencent, Alibaba, PDD, ByteDance, Hillhouse, Sequoia China/HongShan, MSA Capital, GGV/Granite Asia.

### China Trend Detail

**Apa Yang Terjadi Di China**

> China converted three decades of manufacturing overcapacity plus a decade of domestic platform warfare into an exportable commercial operating system.
> The mechanism has four stacked layers.
> (1) Manufacturing base: dense industrial clusters (Yiwu for small commodities, Panyu/Guangzhou for garments, Shenzhen for electronics, Zhengzhou for beverage inputs) that can compress design-to-shelf cycles to 7-14 days and accept order sizes of 100-200 units — the 'small-order quick-response' (小单快反) model that Shein industrialized.
> (2) Platform and algorithm layer: fully-managed (全托管) marketplace models where the platform, not the seller, owns pricing, marketing, logistics and returns.
> Temu's fully-managed model reduced the seller to a factory supplying goods at a bid price, letting Temu arbitrage Chinese factory-gate prices directly against foreign retail prices while owning the customer relationship.
> TikTok Shop added algorithmic discovery: short video and livestream turn passive scrolling into impulse purchase, collapsing awareness-to-checkout into seconds.
> (3) Logistics layer: consolidated air/sea freight, bonded warehouses inside China's 165 cross-border e-commerce pilot zones, overseas warehouses, and last-mile partnerships.
> (4) Capital and franchise layer: for physical brands like Mixue, Luckin, Chagee, Haidilao and Miniso, the export is not the product but the franchise system — centralized procurement, self-built cold chain and factories, a proprietary ERP, standardized store fit-out, and low franchise fees that recruit local small capital while the Chinese parent monetizes through selling ingredients and equipment to franchisees rather than through royalties.
> Mixue makes roughly 95%+ of revenue selling raw materials and packaging to its own franchisees, which means every new overseas store is a new node in a Chinese supply chain, not merely a licensed logo.

Crucially, what crosses the border is a bundle.
> The product carries a price point (Mixue's sub-Rp10,000 ice cream, Temu's sub-USD 5 items), a supply chain that localizes production but keeps the recipe, standards and IT centrally Chinese, an aesthetic (Snow King mascot, Douyin-derived store design, 'new Chinese style' tea), a consumption ritual (livestream haul, flash-sale gamification, milk-tea-as-daily-affordable-luxury), and a labor model (franchisee-operator with thin margins, affiliate creator paid on commission, gig courier).
> Chinese domestic 'involution' (内卷) — margin-destroying price war amid overcapacity and weak domestic demand — is the engine pushing this outward: brands that cannot earn a return at home go abroad, and they carry the price-war logic with them.
> The result for recipient markets like Indonesia is simultaneous consumer surplus (cheaper goods and treats) and producer destruction (import-competing manufacturers and retailers).

Beijing has actively subsidized the export of this system: 165 cross-border e-commerce comprehensive pilot zones with simplified customs, VAT rebates on 9710/9810 export codes, overseas warehouse subsidies, and RCEP/ACFTA tariff coverage.
> Since 2024-2025 the US tariff wall and de minimis repeal made ASEAN — and Indonesia as its largest consumer market — the primary redirection target.

**Data Skala China**

> Cross-border e-commerce trade (General Administration of Customs): RMB 2.63 trillion in 2024, of which exports RMB 2.15 trillion (+16.9% YoY, first time above RMB 2 trillion); RMB 2.75-2.84 trillion in 2025 (~USD 418 billion), roughly +4.8% YoY and about +70% versus 2020.
> The United States absorbed 36.2% of China's cross-border e-commerce exports in 2024 — the concentration that tariff action is now dispersing toward ASEAN.
> Cross-border e-commerce shoppers inside China reached 140 million in H1 2026.
> Institutional footprint: 105 pilot zones approved in five batches from March 2015, expanded to 165 zones covering most provinces after November 2022.

Platform scale: Temu launched September 2022, reached ~50 countries within two years, global app downloads +69% in 2024 (ahead of Shein).
> Shein annual revenue in the USD 30-38 billion range with a Guangzhou-centric supplier network of several thousand factories.
> TikTok Shop global GMV growth is the fastest of any commerce channel of the decade; its Southeast Asia GMV doubled to USD 45.6 billion in 2025.

Brand-chain scale: Mixue exceeded 45,000 stores globally, listed on HKEX 3 March 2025 at HKD 109.3 billion market capitalization with a 43.21% first-day gain — the most valuable freshly-made-beverage company in the world; 66% of IPO proceeds earmarked for supply chain expansion, particularly Southeast Asian localized production.
> Mixue 2025 revenue RMB 33.56 billion (+35%), net profit RMB 5.93 billion (+33%).
> Overseas stores ~4,800 across 11 countries by September 2024, ~70% concentrated in Southeast Asia.
> Luckin Coffee passed its 30,000th store.
> Haidilao operates ~1,300 restaurants across 14 countries.
> BYD expects overseas sales to exceed 25% of total volume in 2026.

**Fase Tren Di China**

> Booming externally, regulated and consolidating internally.
> The outbound (出海) motion is in its steepest growth phase — 2024-2026 is the peak-acceleration window driven by domestic overcapacity, deflationary price war, and the closure of the US channel.
> Simultaneously the domestic base of the same trend is in a 'regulated/backlash' phase: since Xi Jinping elevated 'anti-involution' (反内卷) at the Central Financial and Economic Affairs Commission in July 2025, Beijing has issued 50+ measures across solar, EV batteries, cement, food delivery and e-commerce to curb below-cost competition, and is redrafting the E-Commerce Law and Price Law to prohibit irrational price wars and platform-coerced discounting.
> Net effect: the price-war logic is being suppressed at home and exported abroad.
> Expect the outbound phase itself to enter consolidation/shakeout around 2027-2029.

### Status Indonesia Saat Ini

**Status Di Indonesia**

> Already massively present, but selectively filtered.
> Indonesia is the single largest destination of Chinese consumer-brand expansion in ASEAN by absolute volume, while simultaneously being the region's most aggressive regulator of pure cross-border marketplace models.
> Status is best described as: physical brands and manufacturing FDI = massively in; algorithmic social commerce = massively in via a forced local joint venture; direct cross-border parcel marketplaces (Temu/Shein) = blocked or restricted.

**Contoh Konkret Indonesia**

> TikTok Shop: after Permendag 31/2023 banned social-commerce transactions (September-October 2023), ByteDance paid USD 1.5 billion for a 75% stake in Tokopedia (December 2023) and merged operations — the clearest case of regulation converting a cross-border entrant into a domestically incorporated one.
> Temu: blocked by Kominfo/Komdigi from October 2024; app still downloadable but without rupiah support or domestic shipping.
> Shein: pre-emptively targeted for the same treatment.
> Mixue Ice Cream & Tea: first Indonesian outlet in Bandung 2020 via franchisee PT Zisheng Pacific Trading; now the country's largest freshly-made beverage chain by store count, halal-certified (MUI, 2023) as the key market-entry unlock.
> Chagee, Cotti Coffee, Miniso, Haidilao (pursuing halal certification), Luckin (pipeline) follow the same route.
> Automotive: BYD (entered January 2024, plant in Subang, West Java), SAIC-GM-Wuling (Cikarang plant since 2017, Wuling Air ev as the G20 Bali official vehicle in 2022), Chery, Neta, GWM, Aion.
> Handsets: OPPO, vivo, Xiaomi, realme collectively dominate the Indonesian smartphone market.
> Logistics: J&T Express (built on the OPPO Indonesia distribution network, now a HKEX-listed regional giant), Cainiao and JD Logistics warehouses.
> Industrial: Morowali and Weda Bay nickel-downstreaming complexes as the heavy-industry counterpart of the same capital flow.

### Analisis Lag

**Bukti Historical Lag**

> Handsets: Chinese brands took roughly 8-10 years (2014-2023) to move from marginal to dominant share of Indonesian smartphone sales after achieving the same at home — the template of 'win China on price and channel, then replicate'.
> Ride-hailing/super-app: Didi's model matured in China 2014-2016; Gojek and Grab scaled the equivalent in Indonesia 2016-2019 with Chinese capital (Tencent, JD, Meituan alumni) — a 2-3 year exposure lag but a much longer capability lag, since Indonesia never built the domestic mapping, payments and merchant-SaaS stack that Meituan/Alipay have.
> Livestream commerce: Taobao Live launched May 2016 and peaked in China around 2020-2021; Indonesian livestream commerce became mainstream 2022-2023 — roughly a 5-6 year lag that has since compressed to near-zero because TikTok's algorithm removes the diffusion delay.
> EV: BYD achieved domestic dominance in 2021-2022 and reached Indonesian top-5 status by 2026 — a 4-year lag.
> Tea/coffee chains: Mixue crossed 10,000 domestic stores in 2020-2021 and became Indonesia's largest beverage chain by 2024-2025 — a 3-4 year lag.
> Every observed lag has been shortening, and the shortening is itself caused by this domain: cross-border commerce and algorithmic content are the mechanism that collapses lag for all other trends.

**Tipe Lag**

> Hybrid: Simultaneous on the consumption side, Laggard on the production/capability side.
> Indonesia consumes the trend at near-Chinese speed while remaining structurally unable to originate it.
> There is no leapfrog available here because the trend's foundation is a manufacturing base Indonesia has not built.
> Reverse elements exist only at the margins: J&T Express (founded in Indonesia in 2015, now regionally dominant and HKEX-listed) is the one case where the Indonesia-China flow ran outward.

### Probabilitas Transfer ke Indonesia

**Probabilitas Transfer**

> Tinggi (Very High) — the transfer has already occurred and is deepening.
> The forward-looking question is not whether but in what regulated form, and whether Indonesia captures value or only absorbs cost.

**Alasan Probabilitas**

> Five reinforcing drivers.
> (1) Push from China: domestic overcapacity, deflation and anti-involution enforcement make overseas margin the only growth story for consumer brands and mid-tier manufacturers.
> (2) US tariff wall and de minimis repeal (2025) force redirection of goods that were priced for the American market — Indonesia, with 280+ million people and rising middle-income consumption, is the largest available substitute demand pool in ASEAN.
> (3) ACFTA/RCEP tariff coverage plus the Indonesia-China Comprehensive Strategic Partnership give preferential access.
> (4) Indonesian consumer price sensitivity: a large lower-middle segment for whom a Rp8,000 ice cream or a Rp30,000 imported gadget is a genuine consumption unlock.
> (5) Algorithmic pull: TikTok's Indonesian user base is among the world's largest, so Chinese content aesthetics and product trends propagate without any deliberate distribution effort.
> The only counterweight is Indonesian regulatory nationalism, which has proven willing to block (Temu) but not to close the market — it channels rather than stops.

**Vektor Transmisi**

> All five vectors from the framework are active, in a specific hierarchy of importance.
> (a) Direct entry by Chinese players — dominant vector.
> Wholly-owned or majority-owned entities: BYD (Subang plant), SAIC-GM-Wuling (Cikarang), Mixue via master-franchise PT Zisheng Pacific Trading, Miniso, Chagee, Haidilao, plus Chinese-owned logistics warehouses.
> Regulation has forced this vector to mutate from cross-border parcel into local incorporation and local manufacturing — the ByteDance-Tokopedia deal is the canonical example, and Permendag 19/2026's KP3A representative-office threshold institutionalizes it.
> (b) Algorithmic content diffusion — the fastest and least controllable vector.
> TikTok's recommendation engine transmits Chinese product formats (labubu-style blind boxes, Chinese-style tea, jelly grip phone cases, whatever is trending on Douyin) to Indonesian consumers within days, creating pull-demand before any brand formally enters.
> This is the vector that has collapsed the historic lag.
> (c) Local copycats — very high volume, low differentiation.
> Indonesian beverage and retail chains explicitly reverse-engineer the Mixue playbook (dense low-price franchising, mascot branding, standardized kiosk); Indonesian sellers on Shopee/TikTok Shop source from 1688/Alibaba and rebrand.
> Esteh Indonesia and Haus! (both 2018) predate Mixue's Indonesian entry but converged on the same low-price mass model.
> (d) Chinese venture and strategic capital — Tencent, Alibaba, JD and ByteDance stakes across Indonesian platforms (Tokopedia, GoTo historically, Bukalapak historically), plus Chinese-linked industrial capital in Morowali/Weda Bay; a large fraction routed through Singapore and Hong Kong vehicles, which understates China's apparent FDI rank.
> (e) Diaspora, alumni and intermediary networks — Indonesian-Chinese business families as master franchisees and importers; a growing cadre of Indonesian graduates of Chinese universities and of Chinese-company Indonesian operations (the 'OPPO mafia' that produced J&T Express is the archetype); Yiwu- and Guangzhou-based Indonesian sourcing agents; Mandarin-speaking supply-chain managers as the human interface layer.
> A sixth vector deserves naming: (f) state-to-state infrastructure and industrial policy — nickel downstreaming, the Jakarta-Bandung high-speed rail, and industrial-park MOUs create the physical and diplomatic substrate that makes commercial entry easier and politically protected.

### Faktor Pendorong

**Prasyarat Struktural**

> Threshold conditions and Indonesia's position against China at the moment the trend exploded there.

(1) Consumer income floor.
> Mixue's sub-USD 1 price point and Temu-style ultra-cheap goods work in markets with GDP per capita roughly USD 3,000-12,000 — Indonesia at USD 4,960 (2024) sits squarely in the sweet spot; China was at roughly USD 8,000-10,000 when its own low-price chains and community group-buying exploded (2018-2020).
> Indonesia is therefore MORE, not less, susceptible to the low-price format than China was.

(2) Internet and smartphone penetration.
> Indonesia 80.66% internet penetration, 229 million users (2025) versus China's ~70-75% when livestream commerce peaked (2020-2021).
> Threshold already exceeded.

(3) Digital payments rails.
> QRIS national interoperability, e-wallet ubiquity (GoPay, OVO, DANA, ShopeePay) — Indonesia crossed this threshold around 2021-2022; China crossed it around 2015-2016 with Alipay/WeChat Pay.
> This is roughly a 6-year lag that no longer binds.

(4) Logistics density and cost.
> This is the binding constraint.
> Indonesia's logistics cost is roughly 14-23% of GDP versus China's ~14% and falling; archipelagic geography imposes inter-island freight costs and low drop density outside Java.
> Chinese ultra-cheap commerce economics assume sub-USD 0.5 last-mile cost, achievable in contiguous high-density China but not across 17,000 islands.
> Indonesia's e-commerce logistics market is only ~USD 5.3 billion (2025).

(5) Urbanization.
> Indonesia ~58-59% urban versus China ~64-66% when the outbound wave began.
> Close enough not to be binding for tier-1/2 formats, binding for tier-4/5 replication.

(6) Manufacturing base and cluster density — Indonesia's decisive deficit.
> Manufacturing is ~18-19% of Indonesian GDP and falling (deindustrialization), versus China's ~27-28% at the equivalent stage.
> Indonesia has no small-order quick-response apparel cluster, no component ecosystem for consumer electronics, no domestic cold-chain sufficient for a 3,000-store beverage network without imported concentrate.

(7) Regulatory permissiveness.
> China's trend required a permissive early-stage regulator that later tightened.
> Indonesia has inverted the sequence — tightening first (Permendag 31/2023, Temu block, Permendag 19/2026).
> This shapes the form of arrival rather than preventing it.

(8) Halal certification infrastructure.
> Uniquely Indonesian prerequisite: MUI/BPJPH halal certification is the gate for any Chinese F&B brand.
> Mixue cleared it in 2023 and its Indonesian growth inflected immediately; Haidilao is pursuing it now.
> Any Chinese F&B brand that cannot clear it is structurally excluded.

**Indikator Pemantauan**

> Leading indicators to watch, in rough order of lead time.
> (1) Trademark filings at DJKI (Ditjen Kekayaan Intelektual) by Chinese applicants — typically 12-24 months ahead of store openings; a spike in Chinese-origin class 30/32/43 (food, beverage, F&B services) filings signals the next chain-brand wave.
> (2) KP3A representative-office registrations under Permendag 19/2026 — this is now a legally mandated, publicly checkable tripwire for any foreign platform crossing 1,000 transactions, 1,000 shipped packages, or 1% of Indonesian internet users.
> (3) BKPM investment-realization data by country and KBLI sector, particularly wholesale/retail trade, F&B, and transport-warehousing rather than base metals — a shift of Chinese FDI from nickel into consumer sectors is the signal that system export, not resource extraction, is the driver.
> (4) Mandarin-requiring job postings on JobStreet/Glints/LinkedIn Indonesia, especially in supply chain, warehouse operations, quality control and country-manager roles.
> (5) Google Trends and TikTok search volume in Indonesia for Chinese brand names before they open (Chagee, Luckin, Haidilao, Pop Mart) — algorithmic pre-demand is visible months ahead.
> (6) Import statistics from BPS by HS code for consumer goods from China, especially textiles, footwear, ceramics, small appliances — the Jan-Apr 2025 figures (TPT +8.84%, footwear +30.89%) were an early warning of the current wave.
> (7) New franchise registrations (STPW) at Kemendag with Chinese principals.
> (8) Container throughput and the composition of parcels at Soekarno-Hatta and Tanjung Priok bonded zones.
> (9) University program launches: new Mandarin business, cross-border e-commerce, or supply-chain-management study programs approved by Kemendikbudristek/Kemdiktisaintek.
> (10) Announcements of Chinese localized production facilities for inputs (Mixue's Indonesian ice-cream/coconut-cream plants; BYD component localization) — this marks the transition from export to embedded system.

### Hambatan & Faktor Pembatal

**Hambatan Transfer**

> Regulatory: Permendag 19/2026 (effective 8 June 2026) imposes a USD 100 FOB per-unit minimum on cross-border e-commerce imports (Article 23, carried over from Permendag 50/2020), mandatory legalized business licences, SNI/product-standard proof, Bahasa Indonesia product descriptions, local bank accounts, and — critically — an algorithmic obligation to surface domestic products (especially MSME goods) in initial search results with dedicated local-product pages.
> Sanctions escalate through five tiers to blacklisting, platform blocking and licence revocation.
> Permendag 31/2023 separated social media from transaction.
> Import safeguards and antidumping duties: final safeguard on imported cotton fabric effective 10 January 2026 to 9 January 2029; antidumping duty (BMAD) on Chinese ceramic tiles; mandatory SNI under Permenperin 36/2024.
> Halal certification (BPJPH) as a non-tariff gate for all F&B.
> Local-content requirement (TKDN) for EVs and electronics.
> Economic and infrastructural: archipelagic logistics costs, low drop density outside Java, port congestion, warehousing scarcity in Kalimantan/Sulawesi/Papua, and a rupiah that periodically depreciates against the yuan.
> Cultural: halal sensitivity, taste localization (sweetness levels, spice, pork and alcohol exclusion), religiously and nationalistically charged anti-China sentiment that periodically surfaces in political cycles and social media boycott campaigns, and consumer preference for cash-on-delivery and physical inspection in lower-income segments.
> Political economy: an organized domestic manufacturing lobby (API, APSyFI, HIPPINDO, Kadin) with direct access to the Ministry of Industry, plus a Prabowo administration that has framed import flooding as a threat to hundreds of thousands of jobs.

**Faktor Pembatal Transfer**

> Conditions under which this trend will never replicate in Indonesia in its Chinese form.

(1) Absence of a manufacturing base and cluster economics.
> The Chinese model's core is not the app — it is the ability of Panyu or Yiwu to quote, tool, produce and ship a 200-unit order in ten days at a price no other geography can match.
> Indonesia's manufacturing share of GDP has been declining since roughly 2002 and the textile sector is actively collapsing (Sritex bankruptcy, March 2025).
> Indonesia can host assembly and localized final-stage production but cannot generate the supplier density that makes ultra-fast, ultra-cheap iteration possible.
> Therefore Indonesia will be a consumption node in someone else's supply chain, not an origin node.

(2) Archipelagic geography and permanent logistics cost floor.
> Chinese ultra-low-price commerce is a function of contiguous landmass, world-class rail/expressway networks, and 1.4 billion people within trucking range.
> Indonesia's 17,000 islands impose an irreducible inter-island freight cost.
> Formats that require sub-USD 0.5 last-mile economics or 3-4 store density per 500 metres cannot survive outside Jabodetabek, Bandung, Surabaya, Medan and a handful of other cities.
> Mixue's own 428 overseas store closures in 2025, concentrated in Indonesia and Vietnam, are the empirical proof: it over-densified into markets whose drop economics could not support it.

(3) Population-scale mismatch.
> Chinese platforms are engineered around 1.4 billion users generating enough tail demand to make long-tail SKU economics work.
> Indonesia's 280 million, with a much smaller genuinely-transacting middle class (arguably 50-60 million households with discretionary spend), cannot support the same SKU depth or the same subsidy-burn-to-scale strategy.

(4) Religious and halal architecture.
> A meaningful share of the Chinese consumer format — pork-based hotpot, alcohol-adjacent beverages, certain ingredient sourcing — cannot be transplanted without reformulation, and reformulation breaks the central-kitchen standardization that makes the model cheap.

(5) Regulatory pre-emption.
> Unlike China's own permissive-then-restrictive sequence, Indonesia is restricting first.
> The USD 100 FOB floor structurally forecloses the Temu/Shein direct-parcel model in Indonesia — not slow it, foreclose it.
> Any Chinese platform wanting Indonesian volume must localize, and localization destroys the very cost arbitrage that made it disruptive.

(6) Absence of a domestic sovereign platform.
> China had Alibaba, Tencent, ByteDance and PDD as national champions capturing the value.
> Indonesia's equivalents were acquired or minority-diluted (Tokopedia 75% ByteDance; Shopee is Singaporean; Lazada is Alibaba).
> Indonesia therefore cannot run the Chinese playbook of using domestic platform monopoly rents to fund outward expansion.

Net judgement: the CONSUMPTION side of this trend will fully arrive; the PRODUCTION and PLATFORM-OWNERSHIP side will not.
> That asymmetry is the central risk for Indonesia.

### Prediksi Timeline di Indonesia

**Tahun Masuk Indonesia**

> Already entered — 2020 for the physical brand wave (Mixue Bandung, 2020; Wuling Cikarang plant 2017 as the industrial precursor), 2021-2023 for algorithmic social commerce (TikTok Shop Indonesia launch 2021, mainstream by 2022-2023), 2024 for the EV wave (BYD entry January 2024), and 2022-2024 for the attempted direct cross-border parcel wave (Temu, blocked October 2024).
> The system-export phase — localized Chinese supply chain plus Chinese-owned platform plus Chinese franchise network operating as an integrated whole — dates from 2023-2024.

### Dampak Sosial-Ekonomi

**Dampak Lapangan Kerja**

> Jobs destroyed.
> Import-competing manufacturing is the primary casualty: PT Sri Rejeki Isman (Sritex) was declared bankrupt in March 2025 with 10,965 workers laid off; the Confederation of Indonesian Trade Unions (KSPI) counted 38 manufacturers ceasing operations in Q1 2025, majority textile and footwear; China accounts for roughly half of Indonesia's textile imports.
> Traditional wholesale and retail intermediation is the second casualty: Tanah Abang traders reported turnover declines of around 50% as livestream commerce disintermediated the wholesale-to-kiosk chain; the same pressure hits Pasar Baru, Cipulir, ITC-format malls, and provincial distributors.
> Third: local brand-owning SMEs squeezed out by white-label Chinese goods with better unit economics.
> Fourth: conventional automotive component suppliers tied to Japanese ICE platforms as the market shifts to Chinese EVs with different (and initially imported) component sets.

Jobs transformed.
> Retail work migrates from counter service to on-camera livestream hosting, affiliate content production and customer-service chat operations.
> Warehouse and courier work expands but with gig-contract terms and piece-rate pay.
> Trading businesses shift from importing-and-reselling to sourcing-agent and fulfilment roles.
> Franchise ownership becomes a mass-market small-capital job: thousands of Indonesians are now Mixue, Chagee or Miniso franchisees — technically business owners, functionally operators inside a Chinese supply chain with thin, centrally-determined margins.

Jobs created.
> Roughly 6 million sellers and about 7 million affiliate creators were reported active on TikTok Shop Indonesia (2023 platform figure).
> Last-mile courier employment (J&T, SiCepat, Ninja, Shopee Express, Anteraja) numbers in the hundreds of thousands.
> New categories: cross-border compliance and customs specialists, halal-certification consultants for foreign principals, Mandarin-Indonesian supply-chain and QC managers, EV service technicians and battery specialists, warehouse automation technicians, marketplace-operations and performance-marketing specialists, and localization staff (translation, product-description compliance under Permendag 19/2026).

Net assessment: strongly negative for formal, unionized, benefit-bearing manufacturing jobs; strongly positive in raw count for informal, commission-based, low-security service jobs.
> This is a job-quality downgrade disguised as job-count growth — the same substitution China itself experienced but from a much higher industrial base.

**Dampak Kelas Menengah**

> Bifurcated.
> As consumers, the lower-middle class gains substantially: Mixue makes a branded café-style treat accessible at Rp8,000-10,000, Chinese handsets deliver flagship-adjacent specs at mid-range prices, and Chinese EVs put a new car within reach of households previously priced out.
> This is a genuine, measurable welfare gain and explains the political durability of Chinese brands despite periodic anti-China sentiment.
> As producers and earners, the same class loses: Indonesia's middle class shrank from roughly 57.3 million (2019) to about 47-48 million (2024) by BPS measures, and the destruction of formal manufacturing and traditional trading jobs — the two classic ladders into the Indonesian middle class — is a contributing mechanism.
> The replacement jobs (affiliate creator, courier, franchise operator, marketplace seller) offer no pension, no health-benefit floor, no severance, and income volatility.
> A further effect is the franchise trap: middle-class households deploy Rp300-600 million of savings or bank credit into a Chinese-system franchise whose margins are compressed by over-density and by the parent's control of input pricing — Mixue's 2025 closure of 428 overseas outlets, concentrated in Indonesia and Vietnam, represents real capital losses borne by Indonesian franchisees, not by the Chinese parent.
> Net: consumption standard rises while income security and asset formation fall — a pattern that shows up as rising consumption ratios and falling savings rates.

**Dampak Daerah Non Jawa**

> Genuinely national, but asymmetric.
> Chinese brand penetration is not confined to Java: Mixue outlets are present in Medan, Makassar, Palembang, Pontianak, Banjarmasin, Manado and district capitals, and Chinese handsets and small appliances dominate everywhere Shopee and TikTok Shop deliver.
> The low-price format is in fact BETTER suited to non-Java purchasing power than premium Western brands are, which is why penetration outside Java has been fast.
> Three region-specific dynamics matter.
> (1) Consumption gain is largest outside Java, where prior access to branded goods was thinnest — this is the most positive distributional effect of the whole trend.
> (2) Production loss is concentrated in Java, since Indonesian textile, footwear and ceramics manufacturing is concentrated in West Java, Central Java and Banten — meaning the job destruction is a Javanese phenomenon while the consumption gain is national.
> (3) Logistics economics cap the depth of penetration: inter-island freight, low drop density and warehouse scarcity in Kalimantan, Sulawesi, Maluku and Papua mean delivery times and costs remain materially higher, and ultra-cheap SKUs that work in Jabodetabek are unprofitable in Eastern Indonesia.
> Separately, the resource-extraction leg of Chinese capital (Morowali in Central Sulawesi, Weda Bay in North Maluku) creates a distinct non-Java impact: enclave industrial employment with documented labour-safety and environmental controversies, and local-versus-migrant-worker tensions.
> Papua and Eastern Indonesia remain the least-penetrated on the consumer side and the most exposed on the extractive side.

### Kaitan Pendidikan

**Jurusan Terancam**

> Programs whose core value proposition is being eroded.
> (1) Teknik Tekstil / Teknologi Tekstil and Politeknik STTT Bandung-type programs — the domestic industry they serve is contracting, with Sritex's bankruptcy and 38 Q1-2025 factory closures as the signal; the skills remain valid but the domestic employer base is shrinking.
> (2) Manajemen Ritel and conventional Bisnis Ritel curricula built around store-format, planogram and physical merchandising, now displaced by algorithmic and content-driven retail.
> (3) Manajemen Pemasaran taught around the classical 4P and mass-media advertising, without content, creator or marketplace-algorithm competence.
> (4) Administrasi Bisnis / Administrasi Niaga in its clerical, document-processing form — increasingly absorbed by ERP and AI.
> (5) Ilmu Ekspor-Impor and Kepabeanan taught as manual documentation rather than digital customs, bonded-logistics and cross-border platform compliance.
> (6) Desain Produk / Desain Komunikasi Visual programs oriented to slow, agency-style production cycles that cannot compete with rapid Chinese design iteration and AI-assisted asset generation.
> (7) Teknik Mesin Otomotif specialized in internal combustion engines without electrification, battery or power-electronics content.
> (8) Akuntansi and Manajemen at the generic, non-specialized undergraduate level — the largest enrolment categories in Indonesia and the most exposed to both automation and oversupply.
> Important framing: none of these disciplines becomes worthless; what dies is the version of them that is domestic-only, analogue and non-quantitative.

**Jurusan Dibutuhkan**

> Supply Chain Management and Logistics Engineering — the single highest-leverage gap, covering cold chain, bonded warehousing, multimodal and inter-island freight, demand planning and S&OP; Indonesia's binding constraint is precisely here.
> Cross-border E-Commerce and Digital Trade — customs regimes, HS classification, incoterms, marketplace operations, fulfilment models, and now compliance with Permendag 19/2026 including algorithmic-transparency and AI-disclosure obligations.
> Business Mandarin combined with a technical or commercial discipline (not Mandarin literature alone) — the bilingual supply-chain manager is the scarcest role in Chinese-invested operations across manufacturing, logistics and retail.
> Halal Industry Management and halal supply-chain assurance — a genuinely Indonesian comparative advantage and the mandatory gate every foreign F&B principal must pass; Indonesia can export this expertise regionally.
> Data Analytics and Growth/Performance Marketing — marketplace and platform analytics, attribution, pricing and inventory optimization.
> Content and Creator Economy skills — livestream hosting, short-video production, affiliate operations, creator management (MCN-equivalent), which is the actual employment growth category.
> EV and Battery Engineering, power electronics, battery management systems, EV diagnostics and battery second-life/recycling — Indonesia's nickel position makes this strategically central.
> Industrial Engineering with automation, robotics and quick-response manufacturing focus — the discipline needed to build Indonesian cluster capability rather than only host assembly.
> Trade Law, Competition Law and Digital Platform Regulation — Indonesia is under-supplied with lawyers and analysts capable of running antidumping and safeguard cases, which is a direct national-capability deficit.
> Product Design with rapid-iteration and manufacturing-for-cost competence.
> Fintech, cross-border payments and trade finance.

### Pelajaran Kebijakan dari China

**Respons Kebijakan China**

> Regulations China imposed AFTER the model matured and produced damage — the pre-emptive menu for Indonesia.
> (1) Anti-involution (反内卷) campaign: elevated by Xi Jinping at the Central Financial and Economic Affairs Commission in July 2025, followed by 50+ measures across solar, EV batteries, cement, food delivery and e-commerce to curb below-cost selling and coerced discounting.
> (2) E-Commerce Law and Price Law revision (draft, 2025-2026): prohibits irrational price wars, contemplates minimum-price mechanisms to prevent undercutting, and redefines price collusion, price gouging and price discrimination.
> Directly relevant because it bans platforms from forcing sellers below cost — the precise mechanism that destroyed Chinese Temu and Meituan-ecosystem sellers.
> (3) Antitrust enforcement: SAMR summoned Meituan, JD.com and Alibaba's Ele.me over subsidy warfare and extracted a public commitment to 'rational competition'; the State Council Anti-Monopoly and Anti-Unfair Competition Commission opened a food-delivery market investigation in January 2026; Trip.com was fined RMB 5.2 billion (USD 765 million) for monopolistic practices.
> The earlier Alibaba RMB 18.2 billion fine (2021) established the precedent that platform exclusivity ('choose one of two', 二选一) is illegal.
> (4) Platform-labour and algorithm rules: algorithmic transparency obligations for delivery-time setting, minimum social-insurance coverage pilots for gig couriers, and 2025 rules requiring platforms to disclose recommendation-algorithm logic.
> (5) Livestream commerce regulation: mandatory host real-name registration, prohibition of false discount claims and fabricated 'lowest price' claims, joint liability of platforms and MCNs for product quality, and high-profile tax-evasion penalties against top hosts (Viya, RMB 1.34 billion in 2021) that reset the industry's compliance norms.
> (6) Seller-protection rules: 2025 measures curbing platforms' punitive fine regimes ('refund without return' policies that were bankrupting small Temu/Pinduoduo sellers) and requiring reasonable, appealable penalty mechanisms.

What Indonesia can adopt pre-emptively, before the damage rather than after: platform prohibition on below-cost coerced pricing; mandatory seller-protection and appealable penalty rules; algorithmic transparency and non-discrimination duties (Permendag 19/2026 already takes a first step by mandating domestic-product surfacing and AI disclosure); joint platform liability for product safety and SNI conformity on cross-border listings; social-insurance floors for couriers and affiliate creators; franchise-disclosure regulation requiring publication of average and median franchisee unit economics and territorial-density limits.

**Rekomendasi Kebijakan Indonesia**

> (1) Enforce Permendag 19/2026 with a published, narrow exemption list.
> The USD 100 FOB floor is meaningless if the exemption list is broad or unpublished; publish it, review it annually, and instrument compliance via the KP3A registration threshold.
> (2) Regulate franchising, not just importing.
> Require Chinese-principal franchisors to disclose median franchisee payback period, average unit economics and closure rates, and impose minimum territorial-density rules — the Mixue over-density collapse (428 overseas closures in 2025, concentrated in Indonesia and Vietnam) destroyed Indonesian household capital, not Chinese capital, and current STPW rules do not address it.
> (3) Build antidumping and safeguard capacity as permanent institutional muscle.
> KADI and KPPI are chronically under-resourced; Indonesia should target a standing caseload capability comparable to India's or Brazil's, since the cotton-fabric safeguard (10 Jan 2026 - 9 Jan 2029) and ceramic-tile BMAD show the instruments work when actually used.
> (4) Convert market access into localization, explicitly and with deadlines.
> The ByteDance-Tokopedia outcome shows Indonesia has leverage; formalize it as a tiered rule — above a defined GMV or user threshold, a platform must locally incorporate, hold data onshore, and meet a rising domestic-sourcing ratio.
> Apply the same logic to EVs via TKDN with credible enforcement rather than repeated deferrals.
> (5) Pre-empt the platform price-war damage China had to fix retrospectively: prohibit platform-coerced below-cost pricing and unappealable seller penalties NOW, using China's own draft Price Law and 2025 seller-protection rules as the template.
> (6) Establish social-insurance floors (BPJS Ketenagakerjaan and Kesehatan) for couriers, warehouse gig workers and full-time affiliate creators, with platform contribution obligations.
> (7) Fix the industrial base rather than only blocking imports — protection without upgrading merely raises consumer prices.
> Direct restructuring finance and machinery-modernization credit at surviving textile, footwear and ceramics firms, conditional on productivity and export milestones, and build at least one genuine quick-response apparel cluster (candidate: Central Java) with shared testing, dyeing and design services.
> (8) Invest in logistics as the binding constraint: inter-island freight subsidy reform, bonded logistics centres outside Java, and a national cold-chain plan — without this, no Indonesian brand can replicate the Chinese model even domestically.
> (9) Mandate halal as strategic leverage: keep certification rigorous and use it as both a consumer-protection tool and a negotiating asset, while building halal-certification services as an export industry.
> (10) Treat education-industry alignment as policy: create an annual national programme add/close cycle at Kemdiktisaintek modelled on China's MoE catalogue revision, informed by actual labour-market data.
> (11) Data and monitoring: publish a quarterly dashboard of Chinese-origin trademark filings, KP3A registrations, consumer-goods import penetration by HS code, and manufacturing closures, so that policy responds to leading rather than lagging indicators.

### Peluang & Rekomendasi Aksi

**Peluang Bisnis**

> (1) Fulfilment, warehousing and cold chain — the highest-certainty opportunity.
> Every localizing Chinese brand needs Indonesian 3PL, bonded warehousing, inter-island consolidation and, for F&B chains, cold chain.
> This is capital-intensive but demand is contracted and visible; Mixue alone requires cold-chain capacity for thousands of outlets and is already localizing ingredient production.
> (2) Halal certification, formulation and compliance consulting — a mandatory, non-substitutable gate with foreign principals as willing payers; extendable into a regional export service.
> (3) Localized ingredient and component manufacturing for Chinese chains — coconut cream, dairy, sweeteners, cups, packaging, store fit-out for F&B; wiring harnesses, seats, interior trim and charging hardware for EVs.
> Being a tier-1/2 supplier to a Chinese principal is a real, achievable industrial upgrade path.
> (4) Master-franchise and multi-unit operator businesses — but only with disciplined site selection and density limits, exactly the discipline Mixue's Indonesian franchise base lacked.
> (5) Sourcing-agent, QC and compliance services for Indonesian sellers buying from 1688/Alibaba — inspection, consolidation, HS classification, SNI conformity, now heavier under Permendag 19/2026.
> (6) Regulatory-compliance SaaS for marketplaces and sellers — Bahasa product-description generation, SNI/halal document management, KP3A registration, AI-disclosure logging.
> (7) Creator-economy infrastructure — Indonesian MCN-equivalent agencies, livestream studio rentals, affiliate-management and creator-payout platforms.
> Indonesia has 7 million-plus affiliate creators and almost no professional infrastructure serving them.
> (8) EV aftermarket — charging networks, battery diagnostics, independent service centres, battery second-life and recycling; the installed base is growing far faster than the service base.
> (9) Genuinely differentiated Indonesian consumer brands that compete on identity rather than price — the one competitive axis where Chinese scale is not decisive; local F&B, modest fashion and halal beauty with authentic Indonesian provenance.
> (10) Reverse cross-border: exporting Indonesian products (coffee, spices, halal food, natural cosmetics, handicraft) into China via Douyin, Xiaohongshu and Tmall Global — the trade flow that Indonesian policy talks about and almost nobody operationalizes; the missing piece is Mandarin-capable operators, which is itself an opportunity.
> (11) Data and market intelligence on Chinese-brand movement in Indonesia — currently no one publishes it systematically.

**Rekomendasi Individu Mahasiswa**

> Build a stack, not a single skill.
> Layer 1 — a hard technical or operational core: supply chain and logistics operations, industrial engineering, data analytics, or EV/battery/power-electronics engineering.
> Layer 2 — Mandarin at genuine working proficiency (HSK 4-5 minimum, HSK 5-6 to be valuable), paired with the technical core rather than studied alone; the bilingual supply-chain or QC manager is the scarcest and best-paid intersection in Chinese-invested operations in Indonesia.
> Layer 3 — platform and regulatory literacy: how marketplace algorithms rank and price, how customs and HS classification work, what Permendag 19/2026 actually requires, how halal certification is obtained.
> Layer 4 — content and commerce execution: the ability to produce short video, run a livestream, and read attribution data; this is now baseline commercial literacy, not a specialism.
> Practical moves while still a student: run a real store on Shopee or TikTok Shop sourcing from 1688 and learn the full loop including returns and customs; take an internship at a Chinese-invested operation (BYD, Wuling, Mixue, J&T, a Morowali contractor) specifically to see how a Chinese system is actually run; learn Excel/SQL to a genuinely operational standard; get an exchange or short programme in China if possible — the alumni-and-diaspora vector is real and career-defining.
> What to avoid: a generic management or accounting degree with no language, no data skill and no domain; and betting a career on a domestic-market-only trading business with no defensible sourcing or brand advantage.

**Rekomendasi Perguruan Tinggi**

> Open or strengthen: Supply Chain Management and Logistics Engineering as full programmes (not electives inside Manajemen), with cold-chain, bonded-logistics and multimodal inter-island content; Cross-border E-Commerce / Digital Trade as an applied programme at both vocational (D3/D4) and undergraduate level, following the Chinese higher-vocational model where operating a real store is coursework; Halal Industry Management and halal supply-chain assurance as a national strategic specialization; EV and Battery Technology within Teknik Mesin/Elektro, with battery second-life and recycling; Business Mandarin as a mandatory paired minor for supply chain, industrial engineering, international business and logistics students, taught for workplace use rather than literature; Trade Remedy and Digital Platform Law as a concentration in Fakultas Hukum, since Indonesia cannot run antidumping and safeguard cases it has no lawyers for; Creator Economy and Digital Commerce Production within Ilmu Komunikasi, replacing legacy advertising curricula.

Restructure rather than close: Teknik Tekstil toward technical textiles, functional fabrics and quick-response manufacturing; Manajemen Ritel toward omnichannel and marketplace operations; Manajemen Pemasaran toward performance marketing, pricing analytics and creator-channel management; Ekspor-Impor toward digital customs and platform compliance; Otomotif toward electrification.

Institutional reforms, which matter more than any single programme: (1) adopt an annual programme add/close cycle informed by real labour-market data, mirroring China's MoE catalogue revision — Indonesia's inability to close saturated programmes is a structural defect; (2) build order-based classes and industrial colleges with Chinese-invested firms operating in Indonesia (BYD, Wuling, Mixue, J&T, CATL-linked ventures), with curriculum co-design and guaranteed placement; (3) require every business and engineering student to complete a real cross-border transaction as coursework; (4) establish a national research centre on Chinese industrial and platform policy — Indonesia has extensive Chinese investment and almost no independent domestic analytical capacity to interpret it; (5) build reverse-direction capability: train Indonesian operators who can sell INTO China via Douyin, Xiaohongshu and Tmall Global.

### Faktor Risiko & Sisi Gelap

**Dampak Negatif China**

> (1) Margin destruction and seller bankruptcy.
> Fully-managed platform models transferred all pricing power to the platform; Temu/Pinduoduo-ecosystem sellers faced 'refund without return' policies and punitive fine regimes severe enough to drive small businesses to collapse, prompting 2025 regulatory intervention on seller protection.
> (2) Labour conditions in the supply base.
> Investigations of Guangzhou factories supplying Shein documented 11-12 hour days, seven days a week, some workers earning around USD 556 per month against quotas of hundreds of garments daily, with widespread subcontracting into unregulated 'handshake building' workshops that flout labour law and pose fire risk.
> (3) Involution as a macro pathology.
> Cutthroat price competition across solar, EV batteries, cement, e-commerce and food delivery destroyed industry-wide profitability, suppressed wages, and became severe enough that the top leadership named it a national economic problem in July 2025 — an explicit admission that the model's domestic version was self-harming.
> (4) Platform-labour precarity.
> Algorithmic delivery-time compression produced documented courier injury and death rates and triggered the 'trapped in the system' public backlash from 2020 onward.
> (5) Consumption downgrade and deflation.
> Persistent price war contributed to entrenched consumer-price and producer-price deflation, weak household demand, and a national mood of pessimism that manifests culturally as 'lying flat' (躺平) and 'involuted youth'.
> (6) Environmental cost.
> Ultra-fast fashion produced enormous textile waste, high air-freight carbon intensity and packaging volumes; parcel volumes in the tens of billions annually.
> (7) Franchise-system risk transfer.
> The low-fee franchise model transfers capital risk to small franchisees while the parent earns on input sales — profitable for the brand even when individual stores fail, which is precisely what showed up as 428 overseas closures in 2025 while Mixue's own profit rose 33%.
> (8) Trade retaliation.
> The success of the model provoked de minimis repeal in the US, EU parcel-duty proposals, and bans and investigations across multiple markets — a strategic cost to Chinese exporters generally.

**Risiko Sosial Indonesia**

> (1) Accelerated premature deindustrialization.
> Indonesia's manufacturing share of GDP is already falling; textile, footwear and ceramics are actively contracting, with Sritex's March 2025 bankruptcy (10,965 workers) and 38 Q1-2025 factory closures as evidence.
> Without effective safeguards, Indonesia risks locking in a consumption-only role — importing goods, exporting raw nickel, and manufacturing neither.
> (2) Job-quality collapse disguised as job growth.
> Millions of new affiliate, courier and micro-seller roles with no BPJS coverage, no severance and volatile income substituting for formal factory employment that had all three.
> (3) Household capital destruction via franchising.
> Middle-class savings and bank credit deployed into over-densified Chinese franchise networks with no disclosure of realistic unit economics; the risk sits entirely with the Indonesian franchisee.
> (4) MSME displacement.
> Indonesia has roughly 65 million MSMEs, overwhelmingly trading and micro-manufacturing; ultra-cheap imported substitutes and platform algorithms that favour scale sellers erode both.
> Permendag 19/2026's domestic-product surfacing mandate is a direct response but its enforcement is untested.
> (5) Consumer-safety exposure.
> Cross-border listings that bypass SNI, halal and BPOM verification — cosmetics, food, children's toys, electrical goods — with no accountable domestic entity when harm occurs.
> (6) Data sovereignty.
> Chinese-owned platforms holding transaction, location and behavioural data on the majority of Indonesian consumers, with data-localization enforcement still weak.
> (7) Financial risk to consumers.
> Ultra-cheap goods paired with paylater and pinjol products drive youth debt; Indonesian paylater delinquency among under-25s is already a supervisory concern.
> (8) Political and communal risk.
> Economic displacement attributed to Chinese competition is combustible in Indonesia's specific history; anti-Chinese sentiment can be mobilized against Chinese-Indonesian citizens who have no connection to PRC capital.
> This is the most severe non-economic risk and the one least addressed by trade policy.
> (9) Cultural-consumption homogenization.
> Local food, fashion and retail formats displaced by algorithmically-amplified Chinese trends, and Indonesian creative production reduced to localizing someone else's product.
> (10) Environmental burden.
> Packaging waste, textile waste and unregulated e-waste from ultra-cheap electronics, arriving in a country with far weaker waste infrastructure than China's.

**Unintended Consequences**

> (1) Regulation produced ownership transfer rather than protection.
> Banning social commerce (Permendag 31/2023) did not remove ByteDance from Indonesian e-commerce — it caused ByteDance to buy 75% of Tokopedia for USD 1.5 billion, converting Indonesia's national e-commerce champion into a Chinese-controlled asset.
> The nationalist policy achieved the opposite of its nationalist intent.
> (2) Blocking Temu strengthened incumbents rather than local manufacturers.
> The blocked demand flowed to Shopee, TikTok Shop and Lazada — all foreign-controlled — and much of the merchandise still arrives from China through those channels.
> (3) The USD 100 FOB floor is arbitraged.
> Consolidation, undervaluation, misdeclaration, personal-shipment routing and jastip (jasa titip) channels absorb a share of the flow; enforcement capacity, not the rule, is the binding variable.
> (4) Protection raises consumer prices for the very class it claims to protect.
> Safeguard duties on cotton fabric and antidumping on ceramic tiles raise input costs for downstream Indonesian garment makers and construction, potentially destroying more downstream jobs than they save upstream.
> (5) The franchise boom created a new class of leveraged micro-capitalists whose failures are individually invisible and collectively significant, with no data collection tracking them.
> (6) Halal certification became a competitive moat FOR Chinese brands.
> Mixue's early MUI certification let it outcompete Chinese rivals and reassure Muslim consumers — a regulation meant as a domestic religious safeguard functioned as a market-entry advantage for the best-resourced foreign player.
> (7) Cheap Chinese EVs are decarbonizing Indonesian transport faster than any domestic policy did, while simultaneously undermining the Japanese-anchored component industry that employed far more Indonesians.
> Environmental win, industrial loss, neither planned.
> (8) China's anti-involution campaign, intended to fix a domestic problem, functions as an export-push policy — suppressing price war at home while intensifying it abroad.
> Indonesia is absorbing a policy externality it had no part in creating.
> (9) The creator economy became a genuine social-mobility channel for young Indonesians outside Java and outside elite education — a real, underappreciated positive that no policy designed.
> (10) J&T Express: Chinese distribution methods transplanted into Indonesia produced an Indonesian-founded regional champion that now competes against Chinese incumbents — proof that the system, once transferred, can be locally recompiled.

**Kelompok Rentan**

> (1) Textile, garment, footwear and ceramics factory workers, concentrated in West Java, Central Java and Banten — the group already suffering measured, documented losses (Sritex's 10,965; 38 factory closures in Q1 2025).
> Predominantly women, often with only secondary education and few transferable skills.
> (2) Traditional wholesale and market traders — Tanah Abang, Cipulir, Pasar Baru and provincial equivalents, reporting turnover declines around 50%; typically middle-aged, low digital fluency, with capital tied up in physical inventory and shop leases.
> (3) Small franchisees and micro-entrepreneurs who deployed household savings or credit into over-densified franchise networks.
> (4) Micro-manufacturers and home-industry producers within Indonesia's ~65 million MSMEs, competing directly against imported substitutes with structurally lower cost.
> (5) Gig couriers and warehouse workers — high injury exposure, piece-rate income, minimal social-insurance coverage.
> (6) Young affiliate creators and livestream hosts — income entirely dependent on platform algorithm changes, no contract, no benefits, and high burnout; a policy shift or algorithm update can eliminate income overnight, as the 2023 TikTok Shop closure demonstrated.
> (7) Fresh graduates of oversupplied generic programmes (management, accounting, communication) entering a labour market whose formal-sector entry ladder is narrowing.
> (8) Consumers in low-income and non-Java households exposed to unverified imported goods and to paylater debt.
> (9) Chinese-Indonesian citizens, structurally exposed to displaced economic anger they did not cause — a risk requiring explicit political management, not merely economic policy.
> (10) Communities around Chinese-invested extractive and industrial enclaves (Morowali, Weda Bay) facing environmental and occupational-safety exposure.

### Contoh Kasus Konkret

**Kasus China**

> Mixue Ice Cream & Tea (蜜雪冰城) is the cleanest illustration of system export versus product export.
> Founded in Zhengzhou, it exceeded 45,000 stores globally and listed on HKEX on 3 March 2025 at HKD 109.3 billion market capitalization, rising 43.21% on debut to become the world's most valuable freshly-made-beverage company; 66% of IPO proceeds were allocated to supply chain expansion, explicitly including Southeast Asian localized production.
> 2025 revenue reached RMB 33.56 billion (+35%) with net profit RMB 5.93 billion (+33%).
> The economics are the point: Mixue earns almost entirely from selling ingredients, packaging and equipment to its own franchisees, not from royalties — so its overseas store network is functionally a distribution system for a Chinese supply chain.
> It began overseas expansion in 2018 (Vietnam first), reached ~4,800 overseas stores across 11 countries by September 2024 with roughly 70% in Southeast Asia, and is now building localized production of ice cream base and coconut cream in Indonesia and the Philippines plus regional warehousing hubs to cut cross-border shipping dependence.
> The failure mode is equally instructive: aggressive franchising with lowered entry thresholds and relaxed site-approval standards produced three to four Indonesian stores within a 500-metre radius, a four-month supply shortage during the 2023 Eid peak that damaged franchisee confidence, and 428 overseas store closures during 2025 concentrated in Indonesia and Vietnam — while group profit still rose 33%, because the risk sat with franchisees.

The complementary case is Temu (PDD Holdings, launched September 2022), which industrialized the fully-managed model: the platform sets price, owns marketing, logistics and returns, and the Chinese factory becomes an anonymous bid-taking supplier.
> It scaled to roughly 50 countries within two years with global downloads up 69% in 2024.
> Its collision with Indonesia — blocked from October 2024 on the explicit ground that its model excises local resellers and shippers from the supply chain — is the sharpest statement any government has made of what is actually at stake: not the price of goods, but who is permitted to exist in the value chain.
> And Shein supplies the labour-cost case: Guangzhou supplier factories documented at 11-12 hour days, seven days a week, with subcontracting into unregulated workshops.

**Padanan Indonesia**

> Indonesia has recipients and imitators, not originators.
> Local imitation of the model: Esteh Indonesia and Haus! (both founded 2018, predating Mixue's 2020 Indonesian entry) already ran the dense low-price mass-beverage model and are the closest structural analogues; Kopi Kenangan, Fore and Goola compete on adjacent positioning but Kopi Kenangan deliberately does not franchise externally, which capped its store-count growth against Mixue's franchise army.
> Mixue overtook Kopi Kenangan to become Indonesia's largest freshly-made drinks chain by end-2025.
> Platform side: Tokopedia is the padanan that was absorbed rather than replicated — 75% acquired by ByteDance for USD 1.5 billion in December 2023 — while Bukalapak retreated from physical-goods marketplace entirely.
> The one genuine Indonesian success inside this system is J&T Express, founded in Indonesia in 2015 by alumni of OPPO's Indonesian distribution network: Chinese operating method, Indonesian founding, regional scale, HKEX listing — the single clearest case of Indonesia recompiling the transferred system rather than only consuming it, and the model most worth studying.
> On the manufacturing side there is no padanan: Indonesia has no Yiwu, no Panyu, no quick-response cluster, and its largest integrated textile manufacturer went bankrupt in March 2025.
> On the outbound side, Indonesian brands going to China (Kopiko, Indomie into ASEAN, some coffee and spice exporters via Tmall Global) exist but at a scale two orders of magnitude below the inbound flow.

### Tingkat Keyakinan & Kualitas Sumber

**Catatan Kontradiksi Data**

> (1) China's 2025 cross-border e-commerce trade value is reported inconsistently: RMB 2.75 trillion in one framing (cited as +69.7% versus 2020) and RMB 2.84 trillion (~USD 418 billion, +4.8% YoY) in another; the discrepancy likely reflects different scope definitions (goods-only versus goods-plus-services, or customs-supervised codes versus broader estimates).
> Both are cited.
> (2) Mixue Indonesia store counts vary: 2,667 as of February 2025 versus 'almost 2,600' at end-2025 — consistent with net closures during 2025 but the closure count specific to Indonesia was never disclosed by the company, only that 428 overseas stores closed group-wide with 'many' in Indonesia and Vietnam.
> (3) Indonesia's e-commerce GMV for 2025 ranges from USD 71 billion to USD 75+ billion depending on source and whether video commerce is counted separately; total digital economy GMV is variously 'approaching USD 100 billion' or already at it.
> (4) BYD's Indonesian ranking is reported as both 5th and 6th in different April 2026 sources, likely reflecting wholesale versus retail registration bases.
> (5) Chinese FDI rank in Indonesia is officially third (Q3 2025) but this materially understates the position because a large share of Singapore and Hong Kong inflows is Chinese capital routed through holding companies — no official reconciliation exists.
> (6) TikTok Shop's ~32% Indonesian FMCG platform-GMV share is from a single tracked-panel source and should not be read as total-market share.
> (7) Reporting on whether Shein formally operates in Indonesia is inconsistent — some sources state it does not operate there at all, others treat it as a target of prospective blocking; the practical position appears to be limited or informal availability without local incorporation.
> (8) Historical data on Chinese-brand Indonesian entry dates occasionally conflicts (Mixue's first Indonesian outlet is dated 2020 consistently, but the specific first-city attribution to Bandung appears in some sources and not others).

## 9. AI & Labor Automation (state-driven AI diffusion causing white-collar displacement, entry-level job collapse, and 'quiet layoffs')
**Kategori**: Ketenagakerjaan (Labor & Employment) - with strong spillovers into Education Policy, Industrial Policy, and Social Protection

📊 MIXED — LAGGARD on state-driven diffusion and enterprise-scale deployment (3-4 years behind), SIMULTANEOUS on individual/worker-level AI use and model access (0-1 year), and potentially REVERSE on labor-protection regulation (Indonesia is debating AI-displacement clauses in its Labor Law revision at roughly the same time China announced its first AI-employment document, and before the shock has fully landed). There is also a genuine LEAPFROG risk in the negative direction: because Indonesia has a much thinner white-collar layer and a much thicker informal economy, AI may skip the 'orderly white-collar restructuring' phase China is managing and instead directly choke the entry-level rungs that Indonesian graduates use to enter the formal economy — displacement without the compensating industrial upgrade. | 🎯 Prob: TINGGI (HIGH) — for the technology and for entry-level white-collar displacement. SEDANG-RENDAH (MEDIUM-LOW) for the specific Chinese form (state-mandated penetration targets + administratively suppressed layoffs + SOE absorption). | 🔍 Keyakinan: SEDANG-TINGGI (MEDIUM-HIGH). High confidence on: China's policy architecture and dates (State Council AI+ 27 Aug 2025 with 70%/90% targets; MOHRSS 27 Jan 2026; Dec 2025 Beijing arbitration precedent), the Zhaopin -22%/+8% graduate posting data, Chinese corporate headcount changes from 2025 annual reports, China's education restructuring numbers (12,200 closed / 10,200 opened; 600+ AI programs; 38 new 2026 majors), and Indonesian BPS February 2026 labour statistics. Medium confidence on: AI-agent market-size figures (consultancy estimates diverge by more than 2x), the causal attribution of Chinese and Indonesian layoffs to AI specifically rather than to post-boom correction and macro weakness, and Indonesian enterprise AI-adoption percentages (different surveys measure different things). Low confidence on: all forward-looking timeline projections for Indonesia (tahun_mainstream, tahun_puncak), the '>160,000 Indonesian tech workers laid off' figure, the illustrator/translator job-loss percentages, and the US$15bn Chinese retraining figure.

> **Status di Indonesia**: BARU MULAI / EARLY ENTRY WITH A DIFFERENT MECHANISM. AI-attributed layoffs and hiring freezes have begun in Indonesia's tech, e-commerce, BPO-adjacent, and creative sectors, and AI agents are commercially available and being deployed (banking, e-commerce, logistics). But unlike China there is no state diffusion mandate, no numeric penetration target, and no evidence yet of economy-wide white-collar displacement. Population-level AI adoption is only ~18.2% (APJII 2026) and organizational AI implementation ~26%. Indonesia is roughly at China's 2023-2024 stage on displacement, but is AHEAD of most peers on individual worker AI usage (33% of Indonesian workers classed as 'Frontier Professionals', more than double the global average of 16% — Microsoft Work Trend Index 2026) and is moving on regulation earlier in the cycle than China did (draft AI Perpres 2026, DPR Commission IX explicitly demanding AI-displacement clauses in the Labor Law revision).

### Basic Info

**Pemain Kunci China**

> STATE ACTORS: State Council (issuer of the 'AI+' Action Plan, 27 Aug 2025); Ministry of Human Resources and Social Security (MOHRSS / 人社部) — Minister Wang Xiaoping, announced the AI-employment policy document on 27 Jan 2026 and runs the unemployment-risk monitoring system; MIIT (Vice-Minister Zhang Yunming: 'restructuring is not disappearance, iteration is not replacement'); National Development and Reform Commission; Central Party School (Study Times, Nov 2025, floated legislation on AI-driven displacement); All-China Federation of Trade Unions.
> MODEL/PLATFORM COMPANIES: DeepSeek (whose Nov 2025 statement that AI success means 'replacing the vast majority of human jobs' triggered national debate), Alibaba (Qwen; 'Wukong' one-person-company automation platform; ~34% headcount reduction in 2025), Tencent, ByteDance (Doubao), Baidu (Ernie; ~7% headcount down by end-2025), Moonshot/Kimi, Zhipu AI, MiniMax, iFlytek.
> INDUSTRIAL AUTOMATION: Foxconn, BYD (~100,000 jobs cut in 2025, ~10%), Xiaomi (Changping 'dark factory'), Midea, Haier, Estun/Siasun/Inovance (domestic robot makers), Unitree (humanoids).
> LABOR-MARKET INFRASTRUCTURE: Zhaopin (智联招聘) and BOSS Zhipi (BOSS直聘) — the recruitment platforms whose data made the entry-level collapse visible; MyCOS (麦可思) for graduate-employment tracking.
> EDUCATION: Ministry of Education (2026 undergraduate major catalogue; 600+ universities with AI undergraduate programs).

### China Trend Detail

**Apa Yang Terjadi Di China**

> China is running the world's first deliberate, state-orchestrated, economy-wide AI diffusion program while simultaneously discovering that the same program is the main threat to its most politically sensitive metric — youth employment.
> The mechanism has five interlocking parts.

(1) TOP-DOWN DIFFUSION MANDATE.
> The State Council's 'AI+' Action Plan (27 Aug 2025) sets hard numeric penetration targets — next-generation intelligent terminals and AI agents to exceed 70% penetration by 2027, 90% by 2030, with a fully 'intelligent society' by 2035 — across six domains: science & technology, industry, consumption, public welfare, governance, and international cooperation.
> The 2026 Government Work Report wrote 'intelligent agents' (智能体) into policy text for the first time.
> This is not a market outcome that the state is reacting to; it is a target the state is pushing enterprises and SOEs to hit, with provincial governments and SASAC-supervised SOEs graded on adoption.

(2) CHEAP MODELS MADE DIFFUSION REAL.
> DeepSeek's early-2025 releases collapsed inference costs domestically, so AI agent deployment stopped being a big-tech luxury and became affordable for mid-size firms and even individual contractors.
> Chinese enterprise AI-agent deployment reached roughly 79% of surveyed enterprises with ~23% at full production scale, with penetration above 30% in finance and e-commerce and near 20% in manufacturing.

(3) DISPLACEMENT SHOWS UP FIRST AT THE ENTRY LEVEL, NOT AS MASS LAYOFFS.
> Chinese labor law requires government approval for layoffs exceeding 10% of a workforce, and Beijing has reportedly directed large tech firms to avoid visible mass layoffs.
> The result is 'quiet layoffs' (隐形裁员): attrition without backfill, performance-management exits, forced internal transfers, contractor non-renewal, and above all a freeze on entry-level hiring.
> Alibaba's headcount fell about 34% in 2025; Baidu's by nearly 7%; BYD cut roughly 100,000 (≈10%); nearly half of listed Chinese firms reduced headcount in 2025; aggregate employment growth at listed companies fell from 6.4% (2021) to 1% (2024), recovering only to 1.9% (2025).
> Micro-drama and content studios report departments shrinking from 30-40 people to about 10 after AI adoption.
> A fintech firm largely replaced marketing and front-end roles with AI.

(4) THE BURDEN LANDS ON FRESH GRADUATES.
> Zhaopin data show job postings targeting new graduates fell 22% in H1 2025 while the number of graduate job-seekers rose 8% — a scissors gap arriving exactly as record cohorts graduate (12.22 million in 2025, ~12.7 million in 2026).
> Youth (16-24, excluding students) unemployment hit 16.3% in April 2026, near record.
> Citi estimates 9.6% of all Chinese jobs (~70 million) are at high risk of AI displacement, rising to 13.6% for workers in their 20s.
> Paradoxically, AI-related job postings surged 74% in 2025 — the new jobs are real but are senior/technical and far fewer than the entry-level rungs being removed.
> The displaced flow downward into the 280-million-strong flexible/gig economy: cities have run subsidy schemes paying new graduates up to ~29,000 yuan to take food-delivery work, and a graduate can earn ~160 yuan on a good delivery day against ~93,190 yuan/year for an average office worker.

(5) THE STATE IS NOW BUILDING A LABOR-SIDE COUNTERWEIGHT.
> Beijing's position, articulated by MIIT, is 'human-machine coordination' (人机协同) — restructuring, not elimination.
> Concretely: Chinese labor arbitration and courts have already ruled in at least three cases that adopting AI is NOT lawful grounds for termination; a Beijing arbitration decision in December 2025 required employers to consider contract modification, retraining, and internal transfer first, and one worker was awarded 260,000 yuan (~US$38,000) for an unlawful AI-substitution dismissal.
> On 27 January 2026 MOHRSS announced a forthcoming national document on responding to AI's employment impact, bundled with a 'stabilize-expand-upgrade employment' action, sectoral employment-support measures, a dedicated graduate/youth employment document, basic-rights protection measures for new-form employment workers, and an interim regulation on over-age workers.
> Proposals under discussion include AI-specific unemployment insurance, 6-12 month grace periods before AI-driven layoffs take effect, mandatory upskilling funding, and regional employment-monitoring pilots.
> China is therefore attempting something novel: maximum-speed AI adoption plus administratively suppressed layoffs, absorbing the slack through SOEs, gig work, civil-service exam demand, and delayed labor-market entry via graduate school.

**Fase Tren Di China**

> BOOMING on the technology/diffusion side, simultaneously entering EARLY REGULATED/BACKLASH on the labor side — a rare split-phase condition.
> Diffusion is in a state-accelerated boom (2025-2027 target window, 70% agent penetration by 2027).
> Labor impact has moved through emerging (2023-2024) → visible and contested (2025, graduate posting collapse, 'quiet layoffs', DeepSeek's 'replace most jobs' remark) → into the pre-regulatory phase (Dec 2025 arbitration precedent; 27 Jan 2026 MOHRSS announcement of a dedicated AI-employment document).
> Notably, China is regulating the LABOR consequences of AI without slowing AI ADOPTION — the opposite sequencing from its platform-economy crackdown (2020-2022), where the state slowed the industry itself.
> Expect 2026-2028 to be the 'managed displacement' phase: mandatory retraining, layoff grace periods, judicial hostility to AI-substitution dismissals, SOE absorption, and expanded unemployment insurance, all layered on top of an unchanged 90%-by-2030 adoption target.

### Status Indonesia Saat Ini

**Status Di Indonesia**

> BARU MULAI / EARLY ENTRY WITH A DIFFERENT MECHANISM.
> AI-attributed layoffs and hiring freezes have begun in Indonesia's tech, e-commerce, BPO-adjacent, and creative sectors, and AI agents are commercially available and being deployed (banking, e-commerce, logistics).
> But unlike China there is no state diffusion mandate, no numeric penetration target, and no evidence yet of economy-wide white-collar displacement.
> Population-level AI adoption is only ~18.2% (APJII 2026) and organizational AI implementation ~26%.
> Indonesia is roughly at China's 2023-2024 stage on displacement, but is AHEAD of most peers on individual worker AI usage (33% of Indonesian workers classed as 'Frontier Professionals', more than double the global average of 16% — Microsoft Work Trend Index 2026) and is moving on regulation earlier in the cycle than China did (draft AI Perpres 2026, DPR Commission IX explicitly demanding AI-displacement clauses in the Labor Law revision).

**Contoh Konkret Indonesia**

> LAYOFFS & RESTRUCTURING: Tokopedia under ByteDance — four rounds of cuts since operational control (≈450 in June 2024, ≈180 in July 2025, ≈240 in August 2025, ~200 accepting packages in July 2026), with the July 2026 '90% layoff' rumour triggering direct government intervention after the Tokopedia Lite launch; GoTo (1,300 in 2022; 600 in March 2023); Bukalapak (<5% of workforce, Aug 2023); Shopee and Lazada framing cuts as a shift from growth to productivity with investment redirected to AI.
> Global employers cutting Indonesian-relevant white-collar work: Accenture (AI made data analysis, system testing, report preparation more efficient, reducing entry/mid-level need), Salesforce (Einstein absorbing routine customer communication, support docs, daily content).
> AI AGENT DEPLOYMENT: a national logistics firm in Surabaya reports ~75% of document verification, delivery scheduling, and customer-complaint handling running without human intervention on an AI-agent platform; AI-agent subscriptions from Rp1-2 million/month with ready-made WhatsApp agents now within reach of mid-size UMKM.
> BANKING: Bank Mandiri applies AI to business improvement, operational efficiency, and operational risk, with ~4,500 staff in its IT directorate — but explicitly states headcount reduction is not under consideration near-term; state banks (BRI, Mandiri, BNI) remain a job-stability anchor, so no visible AI-driven banking layoff wave yet.
> CHINA-LINKED TRANSMISSION: Alibaba Cloud AI Talent Development Program roadshows in 9 cities (Jakarta, Bandung, Yogyakarta, Malang, Makassar, Aceh, Padang, Bali, Papua), 60+ communities/universities, 500+ participants, 500+ cloud certifications, pushing Qwen LLM and Wan video-generation models into the local creative industry; Telkom AI Center of Excellence (launched 2025) partnering with Alibaba Cloud on AI talent; Huawei Partner Summit 2026 building an Indonesian AI partner ecosystem.
