> INFRASTRUCTURE: Nvidia-Indosat US$200 million AI centre; Nvidia-backed AI hub in Batam; Microsoft US$1.7 billion cloud/AI commitment and Indonesia Central Cloud Region; DAMAC Digital US$2.3 billion Jakarta data centre; pipeline of ~1.3 GW of planned data-centre capacity on top of ~580 MW operating.
> EDUCATION: Universitas Indonesia's Fasilkom AI undergraduate program approved by Academic Senate 3 Oct 2025, first intake 2026/2027, ~16 designated lecturers; ITS Rekayasa Kecerdasan Artifisial; BINUS and UPH AI programs.
> POLICY: Komdigi's National AI Roadmap White Paper (public consultation Aug 2025) and two draft Presidential Regulations (National AI Roadmap 2026-2030 and AI Ethics/Governance) targeted for Q1 2026 — reportedly without sanctions, prioritising governance and public trust; Kemnaker using AI itself for labour-market analysis and training planning (webinar 17 July 2026, Secretary-General Cris Kuntadi); DPR Commission IX member Pulung Agustanto arguing the Labor Law revision must protect workers from automation and AI; Apindo pushing the RUU Ketenagakerjaan toward job creation and layoff prevention.

### Analisis Lag

**Tipe Lag**

> MIXED — LAGGARD on state-driven diffusion and enterprise-scale deployment (3-4 years behind), SIMULTANEOUS on individual/worker-level AI use and model access (0-1 year), and potentially REVERSE on labor-protection regulation (Indonesia is debating AI-displacement clauses in its Labor Law revision at roughly the same time China announced its first AI-employment document, and before the shock has fully landed).
> There is also a genuine LEAPFROG risk in the negative direction: because Indonesia has a much thinner white-collar layer and a much thicker informal economy, AI may skip the 'orderly white-collar restructuring' phase China is managing and instead directly choke the entry-level rungs that Indonesian graduates use to enter the formal economy — displacement without the compensating industrial upgrade.

### Probabilitas Transfer ke Indonesia

**Probabilitas Transfer**

> TINGGI (HIGH) — for the technology and for entry-level white-collar displacement.
> SEDANG-RENDAH (MEDIUM-LOW) for the specific Chinese form (state-mandated penetration targets + administratively suppressed layoffs + SOE absorption).

**Alasan Probabilitas**

> HIGH-probability drivers: (a) Generative AI is delivered as software over the internet — no ports, no factories, no import licences, no physical logistics; the same models Chinese firms use are available in Jakarta on release day.
> (b) Indonesia's internet penetration (81.72%) already exceeds China's (80.1%) and 33% of Indonesian workers are advanced AI users versus a 16% global average — the demand-side conditions are already met.
> (c) The transmission is already underway through multinational employers (Accenture, Salesforce), platform owners restructuring around AI (ByteDance/Tokopedia, Shopee, Lazada), and Chinese cloud vendors actively selling agents (Alibaba Cloud's Qwen and Wan models, 9-city roadshows, Telkom AI CoE partnership; Huawei's 2026 partner ecosystem build).
> (d) AI-agent pricing has already fallen to Rp1-2 million/month — inside the budget of Indonesian UMKM, meaning diffusion does not depend on large-enterprise capex.
> (e) Indonesia's tertiary-graduate unemployment is ALREADY rising (+23,085 YoY, Feb 2026) against falling national unemployment — the entry-level squeeze has structurally begun even before AI is the dominant cause.

Why the CHINESE FORM transfers only partially: (i) There is no Indonesian analogue to a State Council document setting a 70%-by-2027 penetration target, and the draft AI Perpres is reportedly sanction-free and governance-focused rather than a diffusion mandate.
> (ii) China's suppression mechanism — layoffs above 10% requiring government approval, courts ruling AI substitution an unlawful ground for dismissal, SOEs instructed to absorb surplus labour — depends on state capacity over the corporate sector that Indonesia does not possess; the Cipta Kerja framework made severance cheaper and dismissal easier, so Indonesian displacement will be more visible and faster, not quieter.
> (iii) China's displacement is happening inside a large, formal, white-collar economy (though still under 25% of its 725m workforce); in Indonesia 57.70% of workers are informal and the automatable white-collar layer is proportionally much smaller — so the absolute number displaced will be far lower, but the damage will be concentrated on precisely the group Indonesia is counting on for mobility: urban tertiary graduates.
> (iv) Indonesia lacks China's absorption channels — no comparable SOE hiring capacity, no civil-service exam absorbing millions, no municipal subsidy programs paying graduates to enter delivery work.

**Vektor Transmisi**

> (a) DIRECT ENTRY BY GLOBAL AND CHINESE PLAYERS — the dominant vector.
> Chinese cloud/AI vendors are selling agent capability into Indonesia now: Alibaba Cloud is running an AI Talent Development Program across 9 cities (Jakarta, Bandung, Yogyakarta, Malang, Makassar, Aceh, Padang, Bali, Papua) with 60+ communities and universities, 500+ certifications, pushing the Qwen LLM family plus Wan/'Happy Horse' video-generation models explicitly aimed at the creative industry — i.e.
> selling the exact tool that displaces Indonesian illustrators and video editors; Huawei's Partner Summit 2026 is assembling an Indonesian AI partner ecosystem; DeepSeek's open-weight models are freely deployable by any Indonesian firm.
> Simultaneously ByteDance controls Tokopedia and is restructuring it around AI-driven efficiency, and Western vendors (Microsoft US$1.7bn, Nvidia-Indosat US$200m, DAMAC US$2.3bn) are building the compute substrate.

(b) EMPLOYER-SIDE POLICY IMPORT VIA MULTINATIONALS AND GCCs — Accenture, Salesforce and similar firms make global decisions to cut entry and mid-level roles after AI adoption, and those decisions propagate to Indonesian delivery centres and back-offices without any local deliberation.
> This is the fastest and least visible vector.

(c) LOCAL COPYCAT / SaaS RESELLING — Indonesian AI-agent vendors packaging foreign models into WhatsApp-native agents at Rp1-2m/month for UMKM; the Surabaya logistics case (75% of document verification, scheduling, and complaint handling automated) is the template being sold to every mid-size Indonesian firm.

(d) ALGORITHMIC CONTENT DIFFUSION — Chinese-origin AI narratives, tools, and 'one-person company' workflows spread through TikTok, Xiaohongshu-derived content, and Indonesian tech media; Alibaba's 'Wukong' one-person-company automation concept is a directly copyable playbook for Indonesian solopreneurs, which accelerates both productivity and the hollowing-out of junior support roles.

(e) CHINESE VENTURE CAPITAL AND INFRASTRUCTURE FINANCE — less central here than in e-commerce or fintech, but relevant through data-centre and cloud-region investment that lowers local inference cost.

(f) DIASPORA / ALUMNI AND TALENT PROGRAMS — Indonesian graduates of Chinese universities, Alibaba Cloud/Huawei certification alumni, and Telkom's AI Center of Excellence trainees carry Chinese-style AI deployment practices into Indonesian corporates.

(g) POLICY EMULATION — Indonesia's Komdigi roadmap and Kemnaker's own AI-based labour-market analysis show the state is watching the Chinese and global playbooks; the risk is importing the ADOPTION target while omitting the LABOR-PROTECTION counterweight.

### Faktor Pendorong

**Prasyarat Struktural**

> WHAT MUST BE TRUE FOR THE CHINESE PATTERN TO ARRIVE, AND WHERE INDONESIA STANDS:

1) INTERNET / DIGITAL SUBSTRATE — threshold: >75% penetration.
> China at 'AI+' launch (2025): 80.1%.
> Indonesia (2026): 81.72%, 235.3m users.
> STATUS: MET AND EXCEEDED.
> This is the single most important reason the lag will be shorter than for any previous China trend.

2) A LARGE ENOUGH WHITE-COLLAR / FORMAL SERVICES LAYER TO DISPLACE — China: white-collar <25% of a 725m workforce, i.e.
> roughly 150-180m people, inside a formal economy.
> Indonesia: informal employment 57.70%; formal workers 59.93m; only ~1.03m unemployed tertiary graduates but a tertiary-educated workforce far smaller in share.
> STATUS: PARTIALLY MET, MUCH SMALLER.
> This caps the absolute scale of displacement but concentrates it on the urban graduate class.

3) INCOME LEVEL WHERE LABOUR COST EXCEEDS AI COST — the decisive economic threshold.
> China's GDP per capita at 'AI+' launch: ~US$13,866; average office salary ~93,190 yuan (~US$13,700/yr) — automating that worker saves real money.
> Indonesia (2026): GDP per capita ~US$5,362, about 39% of China's; entry-level white-collar salaries in Jakarta are a fraction of Chinese equivalents.
> STATUS: NOT MET AT THE SAME MARGIN.
> Cheap human labour is Indonesia's structural brake on AI substitution — but that brake WEAKENS every year as inference costs fall faster than Indonesian wages rise.
> The crossover for routine admin/CS work is plausibly 2027-2029.

4) ENTERPRISE DIGITAL MATURITY (cloud, structured data, workflow digitisation) — agents cannot automate processes that are not digitised.
> China: ~79% enterprise agent deployment, ~23% at full production.
> Indonesia: ~23-26% organizational implementation, only 16% daily generative-AI use among workers despite 69% having tried it.
> STATUS: NOT MET — this is the true 3-4 year gap.

5) COMPUTE / DATA-CENTRE CAPACITY AND LOCAL INFERENCE COST — Indonesia: ~580 MW operating, ~1.3 GW planned, up to US$20bn of announced investment, Microsoft cloud region live, Nvidia-Indosat and Batam hubs.
> STATUS: IN PROGRESS, adequate for agent workloads by ~2027.

6) TALENT TO BUILD AND OPERATE — Indonesia needs 9 million digital talents by 2030, has ~500,000, and produces only 100,000-200,000/year.
> STATUS: SEVERELY UNMET — a shortfall of 400,000-500,000/year.
> Perverse consequence: Indonesia may be BETTER at consuming foreign AI agents (which displace jobs) than at building domestic AI capability (which creates them).

7) URBANISATION — China ~66%, Indonesia ~60.3%.
> STATUS: BROADLY MET for the affected white-collar geography (Jabodetabek, Bandung, Surabaya).

8) A STATE WILLING TO MANDATE DIFFUSION — China: State Council targets of 70% (2027) and 90% (2030), SOE and provincial accountability.
> Indonesia: draft Perpres reportedly without sanctions, roadmap-and-ethics oriented.
> STATUS: NOT MET, AND UNLIKELY TO BE.
> Indonesian diffusion will be market-paced, which slows arrival but also removes the political ownership of the resulting displacement.

**Indikator Pemantauan**

> HIGH-FREQUENCY LEADING INDICATORS (check quarterly):
1) Entry-level job postings on JobStreet/SEEK Indonesia, Glints, Kalibrr, and LinkedIn Indonesia for the exposed roles — customer service, admin, data entry, content writer, junior graphic designer, QA tester, junior programmer, translator, junior accountant.
> The single most predictive signal is the RATIO of fresher-tagged postings to total postings; China's -22% Zhaopin shock is the template.
2) BPS Sakernas: TPT for D4/S1/S2/S3 specifically.
> It rose +23,085 YoY to 1,033,737 in Feb 2026 while national unemployment FELL — if this divergence widens for three consecutive releases, the AI channel is confirmed.
3) Kemnaker layoff registrations disaggregated by sector and by stated reason; watch for 'efisiensi/restrukturisasi teknologi' as a coded reason.
> Baseline: 88,000+ (2025), 23,470 (Jan-May 2026).
4) Fresh-graduate starting salaries in Jakarta for administrative and creative roles — nominal stagnation or decline is the clearest displacement signal in a market where layoffs are less visible than hiring freezes.
5) Time-to-first-job for new graduates (tracer study data from major universities, and BPS 'lama mencari kerja' series).

STRUCTURAL / MEDIUM-FREQUENCY INDICATORS:
6) Chinese and global AI vendor commercial footprint: Alibaba Cloud enterprise-agent customer counts, Qwen/Wan adoption in Indonesian creative firms, Huawei partner-ecosystem announcements, new Indonesian AI-agent SaaS launches and their pricing (watch for the Rp1-2m/month tier falling below Rp500k — the UMKM inflection point).
7) Data-centre capacity actually energised (MW live, not announced) and Indonesian-region availability of frontier models — local inference availability is a step-change trigger.
8) BPO/shared-services headcount in Indonesia and the region; the Philippine BPO downgrade (from a projected 2.5m jobs in 2028 to as few as 1.85m) is the regional early-warning system for Indonesia's own outsourcing ambitions.
9) New study programs: count of PT opening AI/data-science prodi (UI 2026/2027, ITS, BINUS, UPH already) versus closures/mergers in translation, secretarial/administration, and basic design programs — China's 12,200 closures vs 10,200 openings is the pattern to watch for locally.
10) Trademark and business-permit registrations (DJKI/OSS) containing 'AI agent', 'automation', 'agentic' — early commercial-formation signal.
11) Google Trends Indonesia for 'AI agent', 'diganti AI', 'PHK AI', 'prompt engineer', and job-loss-anxiety search terms; China's RedNote 'AI anxiety' hashtag hit 7.8m views before policy responded.
12) Regulatory tripwires: signature of the two AI Perpres; whether AI/automation clauses survive into the final RUU Ketenagakerjaan; any Indonesian labour-court or PHI ruling on AI-substitution dismissal (China's Beijing arbitration precedent and the 260,000-yuan award are the comparator).
13) Corporate disclosure: headcount lines in annual reports of GoTo, Bukalapak, Telkom, the big four banks, and major BPO/insurance firms — Chinese-style 'quiet layoffs' show up as attrition without backfill, not as announcements.

### Hambatan & Faktor Pembatal

**Hambatan Transfer**

> 1) WAGE ARBITRAGE RUNS THE OTHER WAY.
> Indonesian white-collar wages are low enough that the ROI on replacing an admin clerk or CS agent with an AI agent is far weaker than in China.
> At GDP per capita ~39% of China's, the automation payback period is roughly 2-3x longer.
> This is the strongest single brake.
2) LOW ENTERPRISE DIGITAL MATURITY.
> Agents automate digitised workflows; Indonesian mid-market firms still run on spreadsheets, WhatsApp, and paper.
> Only ~23-26% of organizations have implemented AI and only 16% of workers use generative AI daily despite 69% having tried it — the gap between trial and embedded process use is the real barrier.
3) SEVERE AI/DATA TALENT SHORTAGE.
> 9 million digital talents needed by 2030 versus ~500,000 today and 100,000-200,000 produced per year.
> Firms cannot deploy agents they cannot configure, integrate, or govern.
4) NO STATE DIFFUSION MANDATE.
> Without a State Council-style 70%/90% target, Indonesian adoption is left to individual firm ROI calculations, which are unfavourable in the near term.
5) LANGUAGE AND DATA THINNESS.
> Bahasa Indonesia and especially regional languages (Javanese, Sundanese, Minang, Bugis) are under-represented in training data; domain data for Indonesian regulation, tax, and legal contexts is scarce, so agent accuracy in local workflows lags English/Mandarin performance.
6) ELECTRICITY AND INFRASTRUCTURE CONSTRAINTS.
> Only ~580 MW of data-centre capacity operating; grid reliability and power cost outside Java constrain local inference.
7) LABOUR-RELATIONS FRICTION AND POLITICAL SENSITIVITY.
> PHK is politically explosive in Indonesia; the government intervened within days over an unverified Tokopedia rumour.
> Firms have strong incentives to avoid AI-attributed layoffs becoming a public story, which pushes displacement into slow hiring freezes rather than visible cuts.
8) SME/UMKM STRUCTURE.
> Indonesia's economy is dominated by ~65 million MSMEs, most micro and family-run, with no formal white-collar staff to displace and limited capacity to adopt agents beyond a WhatsApp chatbot.
9) TRUST, SECURITY AND DATA-PROTECTION UNCERTAINTY.
> UU PDP implementation, unclear liability rules, and the sanction-free draft Perpres leave enterprises hesitant on customer-facing autonomous agents.
10) INTERNAL RESISTANCE AND SKILL GAPS ACROSS GENERATIONS.
> PwC's Indonesian findings show a productivity boost concentrated in Gen Z with persistent skill gaps across older cohorts — the people who would have to redesign processes are the least AI-fluent.

**Faktor Pembatal Transfer**

> STRUCTURAL REASONS THE CHINESE VERSION WILL NEVER FULLY ARRIVE IN INDONESIA — and why the Indonesian outcome will be a different, in some ways worse, shape:

1) THE WHITE-COLLAR BASE IS TOO THIN.
> China's AI displacement is dramatic because it has an enormous formal white-collar economy — even at under 25% of a 725-million workforce, that is 150-180 million people in exactly the jobs agents automate.
> Indonesia has 59.93 million FORMAL workers total and 57.70% of all workers in the informal sector.
> There simply is not an Indonesian equivalent of 'tens of millions of office jobs' to eliminate.
> The absolute displacement will be an order of magnitude smaller.
> But the corollary is harsh: the jobs at risk are the SAME jobs that constitute Indonesia's only reliable ladder from tertiary education into the middle class.
> Small absolute numbers, catastrophic distributional significance.

2) NO MANUFACTURING BASE TO AUTOMATE.
> China's 30-million-job manufacturing decline (115m → <85m, 2013-2025) is inseparable from its 2-million-robot installed base and 392+ robot density.
> Indonesia's manufacturing is labour-intensive, low-margin (textiles, footwear, food processing) with robot density in the low tens, and its recent job losses (Sritex and the textile collapse) are about competitiveness and import pressure, NOT automation.
> The Chinese blue-collar automation story is largely inapplicable; Indonesia will lose manufacturing jobs to Chinese and Vietnamese automated factories abroad rather than to robots at home.
> This is displacement by TRADE, not by domestic AI.

3) NO STATE CAPACITY TO SUPPRESS OR ABSORB.
> China's model rests on instruments Indonesia does not have: layoffs above 10% requiring government approval; courts ruling AI substitution unlawful grounds for dismissal (three-plus cases, 260,000-yuan award); SOEs directed to absorb surplus labour; municipal subsidies of up to 29,000 yuan pushing graduates into delivery work; a civil-service exam channel absorbing millions of applicants.
> Indonesia's Cipta Kerja framework moved in the OPPOSITE direction — easier, cheaper dismissal.
> Indonesian displacement will therefore be faster, more visible, and less cushioned than China's.

4) THE INFORMAL SECTOR IS ALREADY THE ABSORBER, AND IT IS ALREADY FULL.
> China pushed displaced workers into a 280-million gig economy that had spare capacity for a while (until dozens of cities issued saturation warnings).
> Indonesia's informal sector at 57.70% is not a shock absorber with slack — it is the default state, with 47.42 million already non-full-time.
> Displaced graduates will not fall into gig work as a novel cushion; they will fall into an already-saturated ojol/informal market, driving down incomes for people who were already there.
> The distributional damage lands twice.

5) ARCHIPELAGIC GEOGRAPHY AND GRID CONSTRAINTS CAP DIFFUSION OUTSIDE JAVA.
> Compute, enterprise IT, and the white-collar workforce are overwhelmingly concentrated in Jabodetabek plus a handful of Java cities.
> There is no realistic path to a nationally uniform 90%-penetration outcome.

6) COST STRUCTURE INVERSION.
> In China, automating a 93,190-yuan office worker is obviously profitable.
> In Indonesia, a junior admin costs a fraction of that, and the fully loaded cost of an enterprise AI agent (licence + integration + local-language tuning + governance) can EXCEED the human's salary for several more years.
> Rational Indonesian firms will keep humans longer — which delays the shock but also delays the productivity gain, leaving Indonesia with neither the jobs China lost nor the output China gained.

7) NO DOMESTIC FRONTIER-MODEL INDUSTRY.
> China's displacement is at least paired with capturing the upside: DeepSeek, Qwen, Doubao, a 182-billion-yuan agent industry, and 74% growth in AI job postings.
> Indonesia will import the agents (largely from Chinese and US vendors) and export the value — absorbing the labour-market cost of AI without the compensating creation of an AI industry.
> This is the core asymmetry and the single most important policy problem.

### Prediksi Timeline di Indonesia

**Tahun Masuk Indonesia**

> 2025-2026 — ALREADY ENTERING.
> Evidence that entry has begun: AI-attributed restructuring at ByteDance/Tokopedia, Shopee, and Lazada; Accenture and Salesforce cutting entry/mid-level roles globally with Indonesian exposure; AI agents commercially deployed in Indonesian banking, e-commerce, logistics (the Surabaya 75%-automation case) and priced at Rp1-2m/month; UI approving an AI undergraduate program (Oct 2025, intake 2026/2027); Komdigi's AI roadmap consultation (Aug 2025) and two draft Perpres targeted for Q1 2026; DPR Commission IX debating AI-displacement clauses in the Labor Law revision (2026); and — the clearest labour-market fingerprint — tertiary-graduate unemployment rising +23,085 YoY to 1,033,737 in Feb 2026 while national unemployment fell.

**Skenario Percepatan**

> Acceleration triggers, roughly in order of impact: (1) a sharp further fall in inference/agent cost — Rp1-2m/month dropping below ~Rp500k, putting agents inside UMKM budgets and below the cost of a junior staffer; (2) strong Bahasa Indonesia performance in an open-weight model (Qwen, DeepSeek, or a Sahabat-AI-type national model) removing the language barrier; (3) an economic shock or margin squeeze forcing cost-cutting — recession, rupiah stress, or an e-commerce profitability push, which converts optional automation into mandatory cost reduction; (4) the government adopting a Chinese-style adoption TARGET (an 'AI+ Indonesia' penetration goal) without the corresponding labour safeguards; (5) a single high-profile Indonesian corporate publicly proving large savings from agent deployment — the herd effect in Indonesian corporate governance is strong; (6) data-centre capacity energising ahead of schedule (Batam/Nvidia, Microsoft region) cutting latency and local inference cost; (7) aggressive Chinese vendor pricing — Alibaba Cloud and Huawei subsidising Qwen-based agents to win share, exactly as Chinese platforms subsidised their way into Indonesian e-commerce and payments; (8) BPO clients offshore mandating AI-first delivery in contracts, importing displacement directly into Indonesian delivery centres.

### Dampak Sosial-Ekonomi

**Dampak Daerah Non Jawa**

> ASYMMETRIC AND, IN THE SHORT RUN, PROTECTIVE — but that protection is itself a form of exclusion.

Why non-Java is less exposed initially: the automatable white-collar employment base — corporate HQs, banking back-offices, BPO centres, digital agencies, professional services — is overwhelmingly concentrated in Jabodetabek, with secondary clusters in Bandung, Surabaya, Semarang, Medan, and Makassar.
> Regional economies outside Java are dominated by agriculture, mining and resource extraction, fisheries, plantation, trade, construction and public administration, none of which are near-term targets for AI agents.
> Informality is also higher outside Java, and informal work is by definition outside the digitised workflows agents automate.

Why that protection is not good news: (1) It reflects the ABSENCE of the very formal white-collar jobs regional graduates want.
> Regional tertiary graduates already face weaker local labour markets and migrate to Java for formal employment — AI shrinks exactly the Java-based entry-level pool they were migrating into, so the shock reaches non-Java regions through blocked out-migration and returning graduates rather than through local layoffs.
> (2) COMPUTE AND CAPABILITY CONCENTRATION WIDENS THE GAP.
> Data-centre capacity, cloud regions, and AI talent programs cluster in Java, Batam and Bali; the ~1.3 GW pipeline and the Nvidia/Microsoft/DAMAC investments create high-value technical jobs in a handful of locations.
> Alibaba Cloud's roadshow reach into Makassar, Aceh, Padang, and Papua is notable precisely because it is unusual — most AI capability-building stops at Java.
> (3) LANGUAGE AND DATA MARGINALISATION.
> Models perform worst in regional languages and on regional contexts, so AI services will be least useful where they are most needed, reinforcing a digital-capability divide.
> (4) THE ONE GENUINE REGIONAL OPPORTUNITY.
> Data annotation, AI training-data collection, local-language corpus building, and remote AI-assisted services are geographically footloose and could be deliberately sited in Yogyakarta, Malang, Makassar, Padang or Manado where costs are lower — this is the clearest policy lever for making AI a regional development tool rather than a Java-concentration tool.
> (5) POWER AND CONNECTIVITY REMAIN THE HARD CONSTRAINT: grid reliability and cost outside Java-Bali cap any serious compute decentralisation this decade.

### Kaitan Pendidikan

**Jurusan Terancam**

> Direct read-across from what China is actually closing (12,200 programs ended or suspended 2021-2025) plus Indonesian labour-market exposure:

HIGHEST RISK — programs whose core vocational output is now a model capability:
- Sastra/Bahasa Asing and Penerjemahan (foreign languages and translation).
> China's evidence is unambiguous: a May 2026 survey of 70 universities found 8 Japanese majors, 5 German majors and 5 translation programs eliminated; a 60-year-old Swahili translation course at a Chinese university was redesigned so students 'direct and manage AI translators'.
> In Indonesia ~36% of translators already report losing work.
> Sastra Inggris, Sastra Jepang, Sastra Mandarin, and D3/D4 Penerjemahan as currently taught are the single most exposed cluster.
- Sekretaris / Administrasi Perkantoran / Manajemen Perkantoran (D3) — the job the degree names is the job agents do first.
- Desain Komunikasi Visual and Desain Grafis at the production-skill level (~26% of illustrators report lost work).
> Note China's Communication University of China cut five programs including photography, comics, and visual communication design while adding 'Intelligent Imaging Art' — the lesson is redesign, not closure.
- Ilmu Komunikasi / Jurnalistik / Periklanan taught as content production rather than strategy, audience science, or verification.
- Akuntansi at the bookkeeping/processing level (D3 Akuntansi, entry-level AP/AR roles) — the analytical and assurance track survives; the processing track does not.

HIGH RISK — programs that survive only with substantial curricular change:
- Manajemen and Administrasi Bisnis taught as generic theory without data, analytics, or AI-tool fluency — Indonesia's single largest enrolment block and its most generic graduate output.
- Ilmu Perpustakaan/Kearsipan; D3 Perbankan and teller-track programs; Public Relations taught as press-release writing; Statistika/Matematika taught without computation; Teknik Informatika taught as syntax-level programming without systems, data, or ML depth (junior coding and QA are explicitly among the first automated).
- Hukum at the document-drafting and paralegal-review level (the advocacy, negotiation, and judgment core is safe).

CRITICAL CAVEAT — the real threat is not the field, it is the LEVEL.
> AI is removing junior TASKS, not whole professions.
> A translation graduate who becomes an AI-translation quality director is employable; one trained only to translate is not.
> The correct institutional response is the Chinese one — restructure the curriculum around directing, verifying, and being accountable for AI output — not mass closure.
> Indonesia should be far more cautious than China about eliminating humanities capacity outright, because verification, ethics, cultural judgment, and language stewardship become MORE valuable as generation becomes free.

**Jurusan Dibutuhkan**

> TECHNICAL CORE: Artificial Intelligence / Kecerdasan Artifisial as a standalone undergraduate degree (UI's Fasilkom program, first intake 2026/2027; ITS Rekayasa Kecerdasan Artifisial; BINUS and UPH already running) — China went from 35 approved institutions in 2018 to 600+ universities with AI undergraduate programs by 2026, which is the scaling benchmark; Machine Learning Engineering and MLOps; Data Engineering (distinct from data science — Indonesian enterprises' binding constraint is un-digitised, unstructured data, not model availability); Data Science and applied statistics; Cybersecurity (agent deployment expands the attack surface); Cloud and distributed systems engineering.

THE HIGHEST-LEVERAGE NEW CATEGORY — AI DEPLOYMENT AND ORCHESTRATION, not AI research.
> Indonesia will not build frontier models; it will integrate them.
> The scarce, well-paid, non-automatable skill is agent orchestration, systems integration, workflow redesign, evaluation, and accountability.
> Programs should be built around: AI product management, business-process redesign for agentic workflows, AI evaluation and quality assurance, and human-AI interaction design.

GOVERNANCE AND ASSURANCE — a genuine growth field created by regulation: AI governance, audit and compliance; AI ethics and policy; technology law (UU PDP, the incoming AI Perpres and sectoral derivatives, AI-content labelling/watermarking obligations); algorithmic accountability and model risk management for financial institutions.

PHYSICAL AND INFRASTRUCTURE — where the ~1.3 GW data-centre pipeline creates real jobs: data-centre engineering, electrical and thermal/cooling systems, power systems engineering, industrial automation and robotics technicians (China's model: robotics technicians, AI trainers, and cybersecurity professionals are the named growth roles alongside its automation build-out), embodied intelligence/robotics (9 Chinese universities were authorized for 'embodied intelligence' in the 2026 catalogue).

DOMAIN-PLUS-AI HYBRIDS — the highest-return combination for a country that imports models: AI in health and clinical informatics; agritech and precision agriculture (directly relevant outside Java); AI in mining, energy and geoscience; fintech and credit risk modelling; AI for logistics and maritime; AI in education.
> China's 2026 catalogue explicitly created 'AI for business' and 'data intelligence' as applied hybrids rather than pure CS variants — this is the model Indonesia should copy.

HUMAN-PREMIUM SKILLS THAT RISE IN VALUE: complex negotiation, sales and relationship management; care, health and education delivery; skilled trades and technical maintenance; creative DIRECTION (as distinct from creative production); verification, fact-checking, and information integrity; cross-cultural and multilingual judgment work; and any role where legal or professional accountability must attach to a named human.

STRATEGIC NICHE WITH EXPORT POTENTIAL: AI training-data services — annotation, evaluation, red-teaming, RLHF, and low-resource-language corpus construction for Bahasa Indonesia and regional languages.
> This is labour-intensive, geographically footloose, suited to Indonesia's cost structure and demographic bulge, and is one of very few ways Indonesia captures value from the AI stack rather than only paying for it.

**China Education Response**

> China has executed the fastest and most centrally directed higher-education restructuring of any major country in response to AI, and it is a direct policy template.

SCALE OF RESTRUCTURING: Between 2021 and 2025, Chinese universities ended or suspended approximately 12,200 undergraduate degree programs and introduced approximately 10,200 new ones — a churn of over 22,000 programs in five years, executed through the Ministry of Education's annual undergraduate major catalogue rather than through market attrition.

AI PROGRAM EXPANSION: AI undergraduate programs went from 35 approved institutions in 2018 to more than 600 universities by 2026.
> The MOE's 2026 catalogue added 38 new undergraduate majors effective for the 2026 gaokao intake, including AI for business (商业人工智能), embodied intelligence (具身智能), brain-computer science and technology, data intelligence, low-altitude economy management, semiconductor equipment engineering, and rare-earth science and engineering.
> Nine universities were specifically authorized to offer embodied intelligence.
> Eleven existing majors including Future Robotics and Interdisciplinary Engineering, plus four new ones, were for the first time placed under a new 'interdisciplinary studies' category — an explicit structural admission that AI-era fields do not fit the old disciplinary taxonomy.
> The 2025 catalogue had already added 29 new majors covering AI and frontier technologies.

WHAT IS BEING CUT: foreign languages and translation are the clearest casualties.
> A May 2026 survey of 70 universities found 8 Japanese-language majors, 5 German majors, and 5 translation studies programs eliminated, alongside broader foreign-language cuts.
> MyCOS, the main Chinese graduate-employment consultancy, notes that foreign-language majors were among China's fastest-growing programs for years and are now being forced to rethink their training model by AI translation tools.

CURRICULAR REDESIGN RATHER THAN PURE CLOSURE — the most transferable lesson: Communication University of China cut five programs (photography, comics, visual communication design among them) but simultaneously created 'Intelligent Imaging Art'.
> A 60-year-old Swahili translation course was redesigned so students learn to DIRECT AND MANAGE AI translators rather than translate themselves.
> The pattern is: keep the domain, move the human up the value chain to direction, verification, and accountability.

MECHANISM AND SPEED: this happened because China's MOE controls the national major catalogue and enrolment quotas, allowing annual, centrally-timed realignment of higher education to industrial policy — an instrument Indonesia's Kemendiktisaintek has in weaker form through prodi accreditation and quota approval.

WHAT CHINA IS ARGUABLY GETTING WRONG: the volume and speed of humanities and language cuts is already generating concern that China is eliminating exactly the interpretive, cultural, and verification capacity that becomes scarce when machine generation is free — and that 600+ AI programs will produce a glut of mediocre AI graduates chasing a smaller number of genuinely technical roles.
> Indonesia should copy the RESTRUCTURING MECHANISM and the DIRECT-THE-AI curricular philosophy, but not the scale of humanities elimination.

### Pelajaran Kebijakan dari China

**Rekomendasi Kebijakan Indonesia**

> 1) LEGISLATE THE SAFEGUARD BEFORE THE SHOCK — the core recommendation.
> Insert into the RUU Ketenagakerjaan revision an explicit provision that technological or AI-driven substitution is not, by itself, a lawful ground for PHK absent a documented offer of retraining, redeployment, or enhanced transition compensation.
> This mirrors the Chinese judicial doctrine (Beijing arbitration, Dec 2025; 260,000-yuan award) but arrives preemptively.
> DPR Commission IX (Pulung Agustanto) and Apindo are already discussing exactly this — the window is open in 2026 and closes once the shock lands.
2) BUILD AI-EXPOSURE LABOUR MONITORING NOW.
> Have BPS publish a quarterly AI-exposure series: entry-level vacancy counts by occupation, tertiary-graduate TPT disaggregated by field of study, time-to-first-job, and real starting salaries — plus a mandatory field in Kemnaker's PHK reporting capturing whether technology substitution was a cause.
> China built monitoring only as the shock hit; Indonesia can have the instrument ready by 2027.
3) DO NOT COPY THE 'AI+' PENETRATION TARGET WITHOUT THE LABOUR COUNTERWEIGHT.
> If Indonesia sets adoption targets, pair every diffusion target with a transition obligation.
> Adopting China's 70%/90% ambition without China's judicial and administrative brakes would produce the worst combination available.
4) MAKE THE PERPRES ENFORCEABLE ON THE LABOUR DIMENSION.
> The draft AI Perpres is reportedly sanction-free and governance-oriented; at minimum add a mandatory workforce-impact disclosure for large-scale AI deployment in regulated sectors (banking, telco, insurance, public services), and require human review and named accountability for automated decisions affecting employment or benefits.
5) FUND A NATIONAL RESKILLING INSTRUMENT WITH A REAL BUDGET LINE.
> Repurpose and expand Kartu Prakerja from a general voucher into a targeted AI-transition program with certified AI-deployment, data-engineering, and AI-governance tracks; consider a modest levy on large-scale enterprise AI deployment to fund it.
> Kemnaker is already using AI to map skill gaps and design training — connect that analytical capacity to actual funded programs.
6) CAPTURE PART OF THE STACK, DO NOT ONLY CONSUME IT.
> Tie data-centre incentives (the ~1.3 GW pipeline, Nvidia/Microsoft/DAMAC investments) to binding local-hiring, technology-transfer, and training commitments.
> Fund Bahasa Indonesia and regional-language corpora as public digital infrastructure so domestic models and evaluation services become viable, and deliberately build a national AI training-data and evaluation industry as an export sector.
7) PROTECT THE FIRST RUNG EXPLICITLY.
> Consider hiring incentives or wage subsidies tied specifically to fresh-graduate entry-level roles in AI-exposed occupations — the failure mode is not mass firing, it is the disappearance of the ladder.
> Any such scheme must be time-bound to avoid subsidising jobs that are genuinely obsolete.
8) GIVE KEMENDIKTISAINTEK AN ANNUAL PROGRAM-REALIGNMENT MECHANISM.
> China restructured 22,000+ programs in five years because MOE controls the national major catalogue.
> Indonesia should create a faster, evidence-driven prodi realignment cycle — but with a deliberate bias toward CURRICULAR REDESIGN over closure, and explicit protection for humanities capacity that becomes more valuable as generation becomes free.
9) PREPARE THE GIG/INFORMAL SAFETY NET FOR A SECOND WAVE.
> Displaced graduates will land in an ojol and informal market that is already saturated.
> Extend JKP eligibility toward platform and non-standard workers, and treat platform-worker protection (which China formalised for 200m+ workers) as connected policy, not a separate file.
10) REGIONAL DECONCENTRATION AS DESIGN, NOT HOPE.
> Site AI training-data operations, annotation centres, and AI skills academies deliberately outside Java (Makassar, Padang, Manado, Malang, Yogyakarta), and use Alibaba Cloud/Huawei/Telkom partnerships to require regional reach as a condition, extending the precedent of Alibaba Cloud's 9-city roadshow.

### Peluang & Rekomendasi Aksi

**Peluang Bisnis**

> 1) AI AGENT INTEGRATION AND DEPLOYMENT SERVICES FOR MID-MARKET AND UMKM — the largest and most immediate opportunity.
> Indonesian organizational AI implementation is only ~23-26% against ~79% in China; closing that gap is a services market.
> The proven wedge is already visible: WhatsApp-native agents at Rp1-2 million/month, and the Surabaya logistics case automating ~75% of document verification, scheduling and complaint handling.
> The winner will be whoever productises vertical agents (for klinik, distributor, ekspedisi, sekolah, koperasi, toko online) rather than selling generic chatbots.
> Indonesia's 65 million MSMEs are the addressable base.
2) AI TRAINING-DATA, ANNOTATION, EVALUATION AND RED-TEAMING SERVICES — the clearest way for Indonesia to sell INTO the AI stack rather than only buy from it.
> Labour-intensive, cost-advantaged, geographically footloose (deployable in Makassar, Padang, Malang), and with a defensible niche in Bahasa Indonesia and low-resource regional languages that global labs cannot source elsewhere.
3) BAHASA INDONESIA AND REGIONAL-LANGUAGE MODEL TUNING, EVALUATION, AND DOMAIN DATA — fine-tuned models and benchmark suites for Indonesian legal, tax, healthcare, syariah-finance, and government contexts, where global models underperform and where accuracy is legally consequential.
4) AI GOVERNANCE, AUDIT AND COMPLIANCE — a market created by regulation.
> The two Perpres, sectoral derivatives, AI-content labelling/watermarking obligations, UU PDP interaction, and OJK model-risk expectations will generate demand for audit, documentation, and assurance services that barely exists today.
5) RESKILLING AND CERTIFICATION AT SCALE — the 9-million-by-2030 talent target against ~500,000 today and 100,000-200,000 produced annually is a 400,000-500,000/year shortfall.
> Bootcamps, corporate academies, and certification partnerships (the Alibaba Cloud model: 9 cities, 500+ certifications) are a durable business, especially if tied to employer hiring commitments.
6) DATA-CENTRE ADJACENT SERVICES — with ~580 MW operating, ~1.3 GW planned, and up to US$20bn of announced investment, the picks-and-shovels opportunities are cooling, power engineering, electrical contracting, colocation operations, security, and specialised staffing.
> This is physical, local, and non-offshorable.
7) VERTICAL AI SaaS IN INDONESIA-SPECIFIC DOMAINS — agritech and plantation intelligence, maritime and fisheries, mining operations optimisation, halal supply-chain verification, syariah finance, and public-service delivery.
> These are markets where foreign vendors have no local data advantage.
8) 'HUMAN-VERIFIED' PREMIUM SERVICES — as AI-generated content floods the market, verified-human creative direction, editorial assurance, provenance, and audit become a differentiated premium, particularly in advertising, publishing, and professional services.
9) AI-NATIVE ONE-PERSON AND MICRO-COMPANIES — the Alibaba 'Wukong' pattern applied locally: individual professionals running agency-scale operations with agents.
> This is simultaneously the biggest personal opportunity and a driver of junior-role destruction.
10) TRANSITION AND OUTPLACEMENT SERVICES — as PHK volumes rise (88,000+ in 2025, 23,470 in Jan-May 2026), employer-funded reskilling, outplacement, and career-transition services become a real B2B market, especially if a retraining obligation enters the Labor Law.
11) EDGE AND SOVEREIGN AI FOR REGULATED SECTORS — on-premise and sovereign deployments for banks, government, and healthcare that cannot send data offshore.

**Rekomendasi Individu Mahasiswa**

> 1) ASSUME THE ENTRY-LEVEL RUNG WILL BE MISSING, AND BUILD PROOF OF WORK THAT SUBSTITUTES FOR IT.
> The mechanism of harm is not being fired; it is never being hired.
> Portfolio, shipped projects, internships, freelance clients, and open-source or community contributions are now the entry credential — the transcript alone is not.
> Indonesian tertiary-graduate unemployment (6.13%) already exceeds the national rate (4.68%) and is rising in absolute terms.
2) BECOME THE PERSON WHO DIRECTS AND VERIFIES AI, NOT THE PERSON WHO COMPETES WITH IT.
> This is precisely how Chinese universities redesigned their translation programs — students learn to direct and manage AI translators.
> Whatever the domain, the durable skill is specification, evaluation, correction, and taking accountability for AI output.
3) STACK DOMAIN EXPERTISE + AI FLUENCY.
> Pure AI skills will commoditise; pure domain knowledge is exposed.
> The defensible position is domain-plus-AI: health + AI, agriculture + AI, law + AI, finance + AI, logistics + AI.
> China's own 2026 catalogue reflects this by creating 'AI for business' and 'data intelligence' rather than only more computer science.
4) LEARN DATA ENGINEERING AND SYSTEMS INTEGRATION, NOT JUST PROMPTING.
> Indonesian enterprises' binding constraint is messy, un-digitised data and unintegrated systems.
> The scarce, well-paid, non-automatable work is making organizational data usable and wiring agents into real workflows.
5) DEVELOP THE ACCOUNTABILITY SKILLS AI CANNOT HOLD: negotiation, client relationships, stakeholder management, judgment under ambiguity, and professional or legal responsibility.
> Roles where a named human must be answerable are structurally protected.
6) TREAT ENGLISH PLUS AI FLUENCY AS AN EXPORT LICENCE.
> Remote work for foreign employers is one of the few ways an Indonesian graduate escapes a compressed local entry-level market — and 33% of Indonesian workers are already advanced AI users, an unusual national advantage to build on.
7) GET CERTIFIED WHERE THE EMPLOYERS ARE LOOKING — cloud and AI certifications from Alibaba Cloud, AWS, Google, Microsoft; the Alibaba Cloud AI Talent Development Program and Telkom's AI Center of Excellence are free or low-cost local entry points.
8) CONSIDER THE PHYSICAL AND INFRASTRUCTURE TRACK.
> Data-centre engineering, power and cooling systems, industrial automation and robotics maintenance are growing (the ~1.3 GW pipeline), are non-offshorable, and face far less credential inflation than generic business degrees.
9) DO NOT ABANDON HUMANITIES CAPABILITY — REPOSITION IT.
> Verification, cultural judgment, ethics, and communication become scarcer and more valuable as machine generation becomes free.
> The failure mode is being a humanities graduate with no technical fluency; the winning position is a humanities graduate who can audit and direct AI systems.
10) BUILD AN INCOME FLOOR EARLY.
> Given a saturated ojol/informal market and delayed formal entry, freelance capability, a small AI-leveraged business, or a niche service practice is a rational hedge — the Alibaba 'Wukong' one-person-company pattern is directly available to Indonesian students today.

**Rekomendasi Perguruan Tinggi**

> OPEN / EXPAND: Kecerdasan Artifisial as a standalone S1 (follow UI Fasilkom's 2026/2027 model and ITS's Rekayasa KA); Data Engineering and MLOps as a distinct track from Data Science; Cybersecurity; AI Governance, Audit and Technology Law; Data Centre and Power Systems Engineering; Robotics and Industrial Automation (with an eye on China's 'embodied intelligence' category); and applied hybrids explicitly modelled on China's 2026 catalogue — AI for Business, Data Intelligence, AI in Health, AI in Agriculture, AI in Mining and Energy.

REDESIGN RATHER THAN CLOSE (the most important recommendation): Sastra/Bahasa Asing and Penerjemahan should be rebuilt around directing, evaluating, and being accountable for AI translation and localisation — exactly the Chinese Swahili-course redesign.
> DKV and Desain Grafis should move from production skill to creative direction, art direction, and AI-assisted pipeline management (Communication University of China's replacement of five production programs with 'Intelligent Imaging Art' is the template).
> Ilmu Komunikasi should shift toward audience science, verification and information integrity.
> Akuntansi should move from processing to assurance, forensic and advisory.
> Manajemen must embed data and AI fluency or it becomes the largest producer of unemployable graduates in the country.

CONSOLIDATE OR PHASE DOWN: D3 Sekretaris and Administrasi Perkantoran as currently constituted; D3 teller-track banking programs; pure data-entry and clerical vocational tracks.
> Do this through merger and curricular conversion, not abrupt closure — and note that China's 12,200 closures over 2021-2025 came with 10,200 openings, i.e.
> redeployment of capacity rather than contraction.

CROSS-CUTTING CURRICULAR REFORMS: (1) Make AI literacy a compulsory general-education course for every prodi, including non-technical ones — this is the single highest-return intervention.
> (2) Rewrite assessment: if an assignment can be completed by an agent, it no longer measures anything; move to oral defence, in-person work, process assessment, and critique of AI output.
> (3) Mandate a capstone or internship producing verifiable work product, because employers can no longer infer capability from grades.
> (4) Build employer co-design into curricula through the Telkom AI CoE, Alibaba Cloud, Huawei and Microsoft programs — but negotiate for genuine capability transfer and regional reach, not just vendor certification pipelines.
> (5) Establish tracer studies that specifically measure AI displacement of alumni — the sector currently has no visibility into its own obsolescence.
> (6) Create fast mid-career reskilling routes (micro-credentials, RPL/recognition of prior learning) for the 35-50 cohort, which PwC data indicate is the least AI-fluent and most exposed.
> (7) Deliberately site AI programs and data-annotation training outside Java to prevent the capability gap from widening.

### Faktor Risiko & Sisi Gelap

**Dampak Negatif China**

> 1) DESTRUCTION OF THE GRADUATE ENTRY PATHWAY.
> Graduate job postings fell 22% in H1 2025 while graduate job-seekers rose 8%, against record cohorts of 12.22 million (2025) and ~12.7 million (2026).
> Youth unemployment (16-24, ex-students) reached 16.3% in April 2026, near record.
> The social contract that a degree buys mobility has visibly broken.
2) DOWNWARD OCCUPATIONAL MOBILITY AND CREDENTIAL HUMILIATION.
> Graduates are absorbed into food delivery and gig work — cities have paid subsidies of up to 29,000 yuan to push new graduates into delivery, where a good day yields ~160 yuan against ~93,190 yuan/year for an average office job.
> Roughly a quarter of delivery riders now hold tertiary qualifications.
> This is a measurable waste of national human-capital investment and a documented source of individual despair.
3) 'QUIET LAYOFFS' AS A HIDDEN HARM.
> Because layoffs above 10% require government approval and firms are pressured to avoid visible cuts, displacement takes the form of attrition without backfill, performance-managed exits, forced transfers, and contractor non-renewal.
> Workers get less notice, less severance, and no public accounting.
> Alibaba's ~34% headcount decline in 2025, Baidu's ~7%, BYD's ~100,000, and headcount reductions at nearly half of all listed firms occurred with almost no formal redundancy process.
4) MASS PSYCHOLOGICAL STRESS.
> 'AI anxiety' reached ~7.8 million views as a hashtag on RedNote; the prevailing worker sentiment is captured by 'those who don't use AI will be eliminated'.
> This compounds an existing involution (内卷) and lying-flat (躺平) culture.
5) THE 30-MILLION MANUFACTURING JOB LOSS.
> Manufacturing employment fell from ~115 million (2013) to below ~85 million (2025) even as exports hit records — an automation-driven decoupling of output from employment that removed the historical absorption channel for less-educated workers.
6) DEFENSIVE INEFFICIENCY AND MISALLOCATION.
> As one fintech manager put it, 'private companies will need to make room for inefficiency to avoid mass layoffs.' Administrative suppression of layoffs converts a labour problem into a productivity and balance-sheet problem, with SOEs absorbing surplus labour they do not need.
7) HUMANITIES AND LANGUAGE CAPACITY DESTRUCTION.
> Eliminating Japanese, German, and translation programs at scale (and 12,200 programs overall) risks removing interpretive, cultural and verification capacity precisely when machine generation makes such capacity scarce — plus the near-term human cost to students and faculty in closed programs.
8) WAGE COMPRESSION AND EXPECTATION COLLAPSE.
> Engineering roles advertised at ~100,000 yuan/year and declining entry-level pay indicate that even 'safe' technical work is being repriced downward.
9) POLICY WHIPLASH RISK.
> The state is simultaneously demanding 90% AI penetration by 2030 and prohibiting AI-based dismissal — a contradiction firms resolve through opacity, which degrades the quality of the labour statistics the state relies on.

**Risiko Sosial Indonesia**

> 1) A LOST GRADUATE COHORT WITH NO ABSORPTION CHANNEL.
> Indonesia has China's problem without China's cushions.
> Tertiary-graduate unemployment is already 6.13% (1,033,737 people) and rising even as national unemployment falls; youth unemployment is 16.36%, essentially identical to China's 16.3%; NEET stands at ~8.9 million.
> But Indonesia has no SOE hiring capacity at Chinese scale, no civil-service exam absorbing millions, no municipal subsidies channelling graduates into delivery work, and a gig sector that is already saturated.
> If the entry-level rung disappears in 2027-2029, there is nowhere for that cohort to go.
2) FASTER, HARSHER, MORE VISIBLE DISPLACEMENT THAN CHINA'S.
> China's Cipta-Kerja-equivalent went the other way: Chinese courts treat AI substitution as unlawful dismissal grounds and require approval for large layoffs, while Indonesia's post-Cipta Kerja framework made dismissal cheaper and easier.
> Without an explicit statutory safeguard, Indonesian employers face far less friction in AI-attributed PHK.
3) DOUBLE-HIT INFORMALISATION.
> Displaced formal workers pushed into an informal sector already at 57.70% will compete with people already there, depressing incomes for the most vulnerable.
> BPS data already show more work shifting to the informal sector.
> The harm is regressive twice over.
4) HOLLOWING WITHOUT UPGRADING.
> China at least captured the upside — DeepSeek, Qwen, a 182-billion-yuan agent industry, 74% growth in AI job postings.
> Indonesia risks absorbing the labour-market cost while importing the technology, paying rent to foreign vendors, and creating few compensating high-value jobs.
> The 9-million talent gap against ~500,000 today means Indonesia is far better positioned to CONSUME agents than to BUILD them.
5) INTRA-CLASS POLARISATION AND SOCIAL RESENTMENT.
> The 33% of Indonesian workers who are advanced AI users will pull sharply ahead; the rest will not.
> Combined with an already-shrinking middle class and visible foreign ownership of the technology, this is fertile ground for economic nationalism and anti-technology politics — the #TolakGambarAI illustrator backlash is an early, small-scale example.
6) REGULATORY VACUUM DURING THE CRITICAL WINDOW.
> The draft AI Perpres is reportedly sanction-free; the RUU Ketenagakerjaan revision is unresolved.
> If the shock lands in 2027-2028 with no statutory retraining or redeployment obligation, the transition cost falls entirely on workers.
7) CREATIVE-SECTOR COLLAPSE AT THE ENTRY LEVEL.
> With roughly 26% of illustrators and 36% of translators already reporting lost work, and Alibaba Cloud actively marketing Wan/'Happy Horse' video models into the Indonesian creative industry, the junior tier of a sector Indonesia had positioned as a growth area (ekonomi kreatif) may be eliminated before it matures.
8) EDUCATION-SYSTEM MISMATCH BECOMING PERMANENT.
> Universities producing 100,000-200,000 digital talents a year against a need for 9 million by 2030, while continuing to graduate large volumes into the most exposed generic programs, converts a temporary mismatch into a structural one.
9) DATA, SURVEILLANCE AND GOVERNANCE RISKS from AI agents deployed in HR, credit, and public-service decisions without meaningful sanction or appeal rights under the current draft framework.
10) FISCAL AND SOCIAL-PROTECTION STRAIN: JKP and BPJS coverage are calibrated to formal-sector job loss, not to a cohort that never enters formal employment at all — the safety net misses precisely the population most affected.

**Unintended Consequences**

> OBSERVED IN CHINA: (1) Suppressing layoffs administratively produced 'quiet layoffs' that are worse for workers — no notice, no severance, no public record — and simultaneously degraded the reliability of official employment statistics; the headline urban unemployment rate stayed near 5% while the underlying entry-level market collapsed.
> (2) Firms began deliberately preserving inefficiency to avoid triggering approval thresholds, converting a labour problem into a productivity drag.
> (3) The graduate-to-delivery-rider pipeline created a highly educated gig workforce, which then made platform-labour conditions a politically explosive issue and forced a separate regulatory intervention for 200m+ platform workers.
> (4) Explosive growth to 600+ university AI programs risks producing an AI-graduate glut chasing a much smaller pool of genuinely technical roles — credential inflation reproducing itself one field over.
> (5) Cutting 12,200 programs including language and translation may have destroyed verification and cultural-judgment capacity that becomes scarcer as generation becomes free.
> (6) DeepSeek's own public statement that AI success means 'replacing the vast majority of human jobs' undermined the government's 'human-machine coordination' messaging and amplified public anxiety — the industry's candour worked against the state's framing.
> (7) AI-related postings rose 74% while overall graduate postings fell 22%, producing a labour market that is simultaneously desperately short of talent and full of unemployed graduates.

PREDICTED FOR INDONESIA: (1) AI may INCREASE measured employment in the short run by enabling more one-person businesses and freelancers, masking the destruction of stable formal entry-level jobs behind a rising count of precarious self-employment.
> (2) Cheap AI agents may extend the life of low-productivity Indonesian firms rather than raise productivity — automating around bad processes instead of fixing them, so Indonesia gets the job losses without the growth.
> (3) The talent shortage may perversely SLOW displacement: firms cannot deploy agents they cannot configure, so Indonesia's weakness becomes a temporary shield — and a permanent handicap.
> (4) Universities may over-rotate into AI programs, producing a glut of mediocre AI graduates while the actual scarce skills are data engineering, integration, and governance.
> (5) Preemptive labour regulation, if written clumsily, could push AI deployment offshore — Indonesian firms buying automated services from foreign providers rather than automating domestically, exporting the jobs entirely.
> (6) Data-centre investment may deliver far fewer jobs than the headline dollar figures imply (data centres are capital- not labour-intensive) while consuming scarce grid capacity, generating disappointment and backlash.
> (7) Because AI arrives via foreign vendors, a labour backlash could take an economic-nationalist form aimed at Chinese and US technology firms rather than at the displacement mechanism itself.
> (8) Remote work may become the escape valve for the AI-fluent 33%, producing a brain drain of exactly the people needed to build domestic capability.

**Kelompok Rentan**

> 1) FRESH TERTIARY GRADUATES, ESPECIALLY IN GENERIC PROGRAMS — the primary victims.
> 1,033,737 D4/S1/S2/S3 holders already unemployed (TPT 6.13% vs 4.68% national), a figure that rose +23,085 YoY even as national unemployment fell.
> Most exposed: manajemen, administrasi, akuntansi (processing track), komunikasi, sastra/bahasa, DKV, and non-elite informatics graduates.
> They face a market where the first rung is being removed.
2) WOMEN IN ADMINISTRATIVE AND CLERICAL ROLES — administrative assistants, secretaries, data entry, and first-line customer service are disproportionately female in Indonesia and sit at the very top of the automation-exposure list.
> This is a gendered shock that current policy discussion has not addressed.
3) BPO, CALL-CENTRE AND SHARED-SERVICES WORKERS — the segment where routine, script-driven work is most exposed; analysts project AI could affect up to half of global contact-centre jobs by 2030, and the Philippines has already downgraded its 2028 BPO employment projection from 2.5 million to as low as 1.85 million.
> Indonesia's smaller BPO sector faces the same physics.
4) JUNIOR CREATIVE WORKERS AND FREELANCERS — illustrators (~26% reporting lost work), translators (~36%), junior copywriters, video editors, and entry-level designers.
> Freelancers have no severance, no JKP, and no collective representation, and are being directly targeted by vendor marketing of generative video and image models into Indonesia.
5) MID-CAREER WORKERS AGED 35-50 IN WHITE-COLLAR SUPPORT ROLES — PwC's Indonesian data show the AI productivity gain concentrated in Gen Z with persistent skill gaps in older cohorts.
> This group has financial obligations (mortgages, children's education), the least AI fluency, and the weakest access to reskilling.
6) EXISTING INFORMAL AND GIG WORKERS — the second-order victims.
> They will absorb the displaced without any increase in demand, so ojol and informal incomes fall for people who were already the most precarious.
> Indonesia's informal share is 57.70% and 47.42 million workers are already non-full-time.
7) REGIONAL AND NON-JAVA GRADUATES — insulated from local AI displacement only because there were never many formal white-collar jobs locally; their route to mobility was migration to Java, which is exactly the pathway being narrowed.
8) STUDENTS CURRENTLY ENROLLED IN PROGRAMS BEING OBSOLETED — those two or three years into translation, secretarial, or production-design degrees have already sunk the investment and cannot easily switch; China's program closures show how fast institutions move once the shift is recognised.
9) LOW-SKILL FORMAL WORKERS IN LABOUR-INTENSIVE MANUFACTURING — not directly automated in Indonesia, but exposed to displacement-by-trade as Chinese and Vietnamese automated production (2m+ robots, 392+ density) undercuts Indonesian textile and footwear employment; the Sritex collapse is the template.
10) PEOPLE WITH LIMITED ENGLISH AND LOW DIGITAL LITERACY — locked out of the AI-fluent 33% and out of the remote-work escape valve, in a market where model performance in Bahasa Indonesia and regional languages remains weaker.

### Contoh Kasus Konkret

**Kasus China**

> CASE 1 — THE ZHAOPIN SCISSORS (H1 2025).
> Job postings targeting new graduates fell 22% year-on-year while the number of graduate job-seekers rose 8%, into a record cohort of 12.22 million (2025).
> Simultaneously AI-related job postings surged 74%.
> This single data pairing is the cleanest available evidence anywhere that AI destroys entry-level rungs faster than it creates entry-level replacements, and it is the specific statistic that put AI-employment on the Chinese policy agenda.

CASE 2 — ALIBABA'S ~34% HEADCOUNT DECLINE IN 2025, WITHOUT A MASS-LAYOFF ANNOUNCEMENT.
> Executed through attrition, offline business-unit reduction, and non-backfill rather than declared redundancies — the definitive example of 'quiet layoffs' (隐形裁员) under a legal regime requiring government approval for cuts above 10%.
> Alibaba simultaneously markets 'Wukong', a platform explicitly enabling one-person-company automation, i.e.
> selling the tool that removes the roles it is itself removing.
> Baidu (~-7%) and BYD (~-100,000, ~10%) show the same pattern; nearly half of all listed Chinese firms cut headcount in 2025.

CASE 3 — THE MICRO-DRAMA STUDIO COLLAPSE.
> Entertainment and micro-drama production departments reported shrinking from 30-40 people to about 10 after AI adoption — a ~70-75% reduction in a single function.
> This is the most concrete Chinese evidence of what generative video and content models do to creative-sector employment, and it is directly relevant to Indonesia because Alibaba Cloud is marketing the same class of models (Wan, 'Happy Horse') into the Indonesian creative industry.

CASE 4 — THE BEIJING AI-DISMISSAL ARBITRATION (DECEMBER 2025).
> Labour arbitration held that adopting AI is not valid grounds for termination and that employers must first consider contract modification, retraining, and internal transfer; across at least three cases Chinese courts have ruled against AI-substitution dismissals, with one worker awarded 260,000 yuan (~US$38,000).
> This established the world's first meaningful judicial doctrine allocating AI transition costs to the employer capturing the gain — the single most copyable instrument for Indonesia.

CASE 5 — MOHRSS, 27 JANUARY 2026.
> At a regular press conference the Ministry announced China would issue a dedicated document on responding to AI's employment impact, alongside a stabilise-expand-upgrade employment action, sectoral support measures, a graduate/youth employment document, and basic-rights protections for new-form and over-age workers, with Minister Wang Xiaoping directing the build-out of unemployment-risk monitoring across key regions, industries, enterprises and groups.
> This is the first time a major economy formally opened an AI-specific labour policy file.

CASE 6 — THE EDUCATION PIVOT.
> 600+ universities with AI undergraduate programs by 2026 (from 35 institutions in 2018); 12,200 programs ended or suspended and 10,200 introduced over 2021-2025; 38 new majors in the 2026 catalogue including embodied intelligence and AI for business; and a 60-year-old Swahili translation course redesigned so students direct and manage AI translators rather than translate.
> Communication University of China cut photography, comics and visual communication design while creating 'Intelligent Imaging Art'.

CASE 7 — THE GRADUATE-TO-RIDER PIPELINE.
> Municipal subsidies of up to 29,000 yuan for new graduates entering food delivery, against average office pay of 93,190 yuan/year and delivery earnings of ~160 yuan on a good day, inside a 280-million-person flexible-employment sector that is nearly 40% of the urban workforce and already issuing city-level saturation warnings.

**Padanan Indonesia**

> Indonesia has partial analogues to each Chinese case, all at an earlier stage:
- ZHAOPIN SCISSORS → BPS February 2026: tertiary-graduate unemployment rose +23,085 YoY to 1,033,737 (TPT 6.13%) while TOTAL national unemployment FELL by 34,702 (TPT 4.68%).
> Youth unemployment 16.36%, almost exactly China's 16.3%.
> Indonesia lacks an equivalent published entry-level vacancy series, which is itself the most urgent measurement gap.
- QUIET LAYOFFS → ByteDance/Tokopedia's four rounds of cuts (≈450 June 2024; ≈180 July 2025; ≈240 August 2025; ~200 packages July 2026), the July 2026 '90% layoff' rumour that provoked immediate government intervention, and Shopee and Lazada framing reductions as a shift from growth to productivity with investment redirected to AI.
> Kemnaker recorded 88,000+ layoffs in 2025 and 23,470 in January-May 2026.
- MICRO-DRAMA STUDIO COLLAPSE → Indonesia's creative-sector damage: ~26% of illustrators and ~36% of translators reporting lost work, the #TolakGambarAI backlash, and Alibaba Cloud actively marketing Qwen, Wan and 'Happy Horse' generative models to the Indonesian creative industry across a 9-city roadshow.
- AGENT DEPLOYMENT → the Surabaya national logistics firm running ~75% of document verification, delivery scheduling and complaint handling without human intervention; AI agents priced at Rp1-2 million/month with WhatsApp-native deployment now inside UMKM budgets; Bank Mandiri applying AI to efficiency and risk while explicitly declining near-term headcount reduction — the clearest signal that Indonesia is at the deployment-without-displacement stage China passed through in 2023-2024.
- JUDICIAL DOCTRINE → no Indonesian equivalent yet.
> No known PHI ruling on AI-substitution dismissal.
> This is the most important missing piece.
- MOHRSS POLICY FILE → Komdigi's two draft Perpres (National AI Roadmap 2026-2030 and AI Ethics/Governance), targeted for Q1 2026 and reportedly sanction-free; DPR Commission IX (Pulung Agustanto) arguing the Labor Law revision must protect workers from automation and AI; Apindo pushing the RUU Ketenagakerjaan toward job creation and PHK prevention; Kemnaker using AI for labour-market analysis and training design (webinar 17 July 2026).
> Indonesia is debating labour safeguards at roughly the same time as China but BEFORE the shock — a genuine timing advantage.
- EDUCATION PIVOT → UI Fasilkom's AI undergraduate program (Senate approval 3 Oct 2025, first intake 2026/2027, ~16 designated lecturers), ITS Rekayasa Kecerdasan Artifisial, BINUS and UPH AI programs — a handful of institutions versus China's 600+, and no national program-realignment mechanism comparable to the MOE catalogue.
- ABSORPTION CHANNEL → Indonesia's ojol/informal sector (57.70% informality, 47.42 million non-full-time) is the analogue of China's 280-million gig economy, but it is already saturated and has no equivalent of the 29,000-yuan graduate subsidy.

### Tingkat Keyakinan & Kualitas Sumber

**Catatan Kontradiksi Data**

> 1) DID AI CAUSE THE CHINESE LAYOFFS? Directly contradicted in-source.
> Professor Sun Zhongwei argues the headcount cuts are 'much more about adjusting to a downturn after that cycle of growth than being about AI displacing jobs,' and headhunter Claire Deng says 'I don't think AI has had a systemic impact yet — it's still quite fragmented.' Against this, the same reporting documents micro-drama departments collapsing from 30-40 people to ~10 and a fintech firm replacing marketing and front-end roles with AI.
> Most defensible reading: AI is an accelerant and a justification layered on top of a post-internet-boom correction, not yet the primary cause.
2) ENTRY-LEVEL POSTINGS — DIRECT CONTRADICTION.
> Zhaopin reports graduate-targeted postings down 22% in H1 2025, while BOSS Zhipin reports entry-level postings holding steady at ~7% of listings.
> These are different metrics (absolute graduate-targeted volume vs entry-level share of all listings) and different platforms, but the divergence is large enough that the -22% figure should not be treated as a settled national statistic.
3) HEADLINE UNEMPLOYMENT VS THE UNDERLYING MARKET.
> China's urban surveyed unemployment sits stably near 5% (below the 5.5% target) with ~3 million jobs added in Q1 2026, while youth unemployment is 16.3% and graduate postings collapsed.
> The headline series is not capturing the phenomenon — a caution that applies equally to reading Indonesia's falling 4.68% national TPT while tertiary-graduate unemployment rises.
4) AI-AGENT MARKET SIZE — WIDE DIVERGENCE.
> 182.34bn yuan (2025, Guanyan) vs 212bn yuan (2025, enterprise-grade) vs projections ranging from 852bn yuan (2028) to 3.32 trillion yuan (2029).
> CAGRs quoted between 72.7% and 107%.
> These are vendor and consultancy estimates with incompatible definitions of what counts as the 'agent market'.
5) INDONESIAN AI-ADOPTION FIGURES ARE MUTUALLY INCONSISTENT.
> APJII says 18.2% population adoption; Microsoft says 33% of workers are Frontier Professionals (double the global average); PwC says 69% have used AI for work but only 16% daily; Pertama Partners says ~26% organizational implementation; IBM/Advisia says 23% of enterprises are at the investment stage.
> One source cites '92% adoption' [almost certainly a vendor-marketing figure and not credible].
> These measure different populations and different intensities and must not be compared directly.
6) THE '>160,000 INDONESIAN TECH WORKERS LAID OFF IN 2026' FIGURE almost certainly reflects a GLOBAL tech-layoff tracker rather than Indonesian layoffs; Kemnaker's own national figures are 88,000+ (all of 2025, all sectors) and 23,470 (Jan-May 2026).
> Do not use the 160,000 figure as an Indonesian statistic.
7) CREATIVE-SECTOR JOB-LOSS PERCENTAGES (26% of illustrators, 36% of translators) appear in Indonesian media without a clearly identified survey population; they may be international figures circulated locally.
> Treat as directional only.
8) UNEMPLOYMENT TOTALS FOR INDONESIA differ across reports (7.24 million vs 7.35 million) because of different reference periods (February vs later 2026 releases) — always cite the reference month.
9) CHINA'S POLICY POSTURE IS INTERNALLY CONTRADICTORY BY DESIGN: the State Council mandates 90% AI penetration by 2030 while courts rule AI substitution an unlawful ground for dismissal and MIIT insists 'iteration is not replacement.' Both are real policy; firms resolve the tension through opacity, which degrades data quality.
10) TOKOPEDIA'S JULY 2026 '90% LAYOFF' CLAIM was a social-media rumour; the verified figure was roughly 200 employees accepting packages.
> Widely circulated Indonesian layoff numbers require verification against Kemnaker or company filings.
11) INDONESIA'S INTERNET PENETRATION (81.72%) EXCEEDS CHINA'S (80.1%), which cuts against the intuitive assumption of a large technology lag and is the strongest single reason to compress lag estimates for software-delivered automation relative to prior China-to-Indonesia trends.
