## 10. Real Estate & Housing Crisis — the deflation of a debt-financed property bubble (property as savings vehicle and local-government fiscal engine), the systemic collapse of leveraged developers (Evergrande, Country Garden, Vanke), the emergence of negative-equity mortgages and unfinished pre-sold homes, and the exclusion of a whole generation from home ownership
**Kategori**: Properti & Demografi (Property & Demographics) — with heavy cross-cutting exposure to Public Finance (local-government land revenue), Banking & Financial Stability, Construction Labour Markets, Household Wealth & Consumption, and Higher-Education Demand

📊 Hybrid: LAGGARD on the affordability/generational-exclusion dimension (≈10-15 years behind China's arrival at mass youth exclusion), SIMULTANEOUS-TO-SLIGHTLY-AHEAD on the stalled-pre-sold-project dimension (Meikarta 2018 vs China's 2021-2022 烂尾楼 peak), and REVERSE on the systemic property-crash dimension (Indonesia had its property-driven banking collapse in 1997-98, twenty-plus years before China, and built macroprudential defences as a result). The dominant framing for policy purposes should be: Indonesia is NOT going to import China's crash — it is at risk of importing China's *pre-crash structure* (pre-sale leverage, investor-driven high-rise supply, state-designated mega-estates, housing as the only savings vehicle) while lacking China's fiscal and banking capacity to absorb the consequences. | 🎯 Prob: Split verdict. HIGH (Tinggi) for the affordability crisis, generational exclusion and inheritance-based ownership — already arriving. MEDIUM-HIGH (Sedang-Tinggi) for localised unfinished-project crises and consumer-loss scandals — already recurring and likely to intensify as the 3-million-homes programme accelerates weak developers into the market. MEDIUM (Sedang) for a segment-specific price correction in Jakarta/Tangerang high-rise investor stock. LOW (Rendah) for a China-style systemic developer-debt collapse, nationwide nominal price decline, or mass negative-equity mortgages within the next decade. | 🔍 Keyakinan: Sedang-Tinggi (Medium-High). HIGH confidence in: the China macro aggregates (property share of GDP, land revenue collapse, investment/starts/completions declines, NBS price indices, Goldman's demand projections, migrant-worker construction share) — these come from official statistics and top-tier institutions and are mutually corroborating; the developer case histories (Evergrande, Country Garden, Vanke); the Chinese education response (multiple independent outlets, consistent direction and magnitude); the Indonesian structural indicators (mortgage/GDP ~3.4%, IDR 807tn outstanding, IHPR +0.83% YoY, KPR NPL 2.88%, construction 9.82% of GDP, 8.7 million construction workers, FLPP 22.15% execution); and the Indonesian case studies (Meikarta, LRT City, Hanson, Country Garden's Tangerang towers). MEDIUM confidence in: the exact magnitude of China's peak-to-trough price declines (the -30% national and >40-50% city figures come from listing data and commentary rather than an official index, and China's official indices are widely believed to understate declines); negative-equity projections (3.3 million homes by 2027 is a single modelled estimate); the specific -7.6% YoY second-hand figure for October 2025, which is consistent with private 100-city indices but not with the NBS 70-city aggregate; and Indonesian backlog figures, which range from 9.9 million (BPS 2023) to ~15 million (Wamen PKP 2025). LOW confidence in: all forward-looking Indonesian timeline estimates (entry, mainstream, peak years); the lag estimates in years, which are analytical judgements rather than measurements; the Zhengzhou 500,000-default figure; and the Wuhan University architecture-cohort anecdote.

> **Status di Indonesia**: Mixed and asymmetric — NOT a single status. Decompose into four sub-trends: (1) HOUSING AFFORDABILITY / GENERATIONAL EXCLUSION — already massively present, arguably worse than China on a price-to-income basis for the bottom half of the income distribution, but produced by supply failure and low incomes rather than by a credit bubble. (2) STALLED PRE-SOLD PROJECTS (烂尾楼 equivalent) — already present in miniature and accelerating: Meikarta, LRT City, dozens of PKPU'd apartment towers, syariah-property fraud. (3) DEVELOPER DEBT CRISIS AT SYSTEMIC SCALE — has NOT arrived and is unlikely in the Chinese form; Indonesian developers are far less leveraged and the mortgage system is far shallower. (4) NEGATIVE-EQUITY MORTGAGES / NATIONAL PRICE CRASH — essentially absent; Indonesian nominal house prices have not fallen, they have merely stopped growing (IHPR +0.83% YoY in Q4 2025, the slowest since the series began in 2003), which is a stagnation signal rather than a crash signal. Overall label: 'sudah masuk secara parsial (affordability + mangkrak), belum ada dan mungkin tidak akan ada dalam bentuk yang sama (bubble crash + negative equity)'.

### Basic Info

**Tahun Mulai China**

> Three distinguishable start dates.
> (a) 1998 — the abolition of the danwei welfare-housing allocation system (State Council Document 23) created a private housing market from scratch and launched the commodification of urban housing; this is the true origin of the asset class.
> (b) 2008-2009 — the RMB 4 trillion stimulus turned housing into the primary macro-policy transmission channel and the primary household savings vehicle; land-finance (土地财政) became the fiscal backbone of local governments.
> (c) August 2020 — the 'three red lines' (三道红线) leverage caps mark the start of the crisis phase proper; Evergrande's liquidity failure followed in Q3 2021, and the sector has contracted every year since.
> For the purposes of this research the 'trend' being studied is the crisis, so 2020-2021 is the operative start date, with the bubble build-up running 1998-2020.

**Pemain Kunci China**

> Developers: China Evergrande Group (恒大, defaulted Dec 2021 on >US$300bn of liabilities, ordered into liquidation by the Hong Kong court in Jan 2024, delisted 2025); Country Garden / Bigui Yuan (碧桂园, the largest developer by contracted sales 2017-2022, defaulted on offshore debt Oct 2023, ~3,121 pending projects); China Vanke (万科, the last major developer to have avoided default, repeatedly rescued by its state shareholder Shenzhen Metro Group and by bondholder grace-period extensions in late 2025 / 2026); Sunac, Shimao, Kaisa, Logan, Sino-Ocean (all defaulted); the surviving state-linked tier — China Overseas Land & Investment (COLI), Poly Developments, China Resources Land, China Merchants Shekou, Greentown — which now dominates land auctions.
> Brokerage / data: KE Holdings / Beike-Lianjia (贝壳找房·链家, >140,000 agents nationwide, the de facto price index for the resale market), China Index Academy (中指研究院) and CRIC/Kerry for the 100-city indices.
> State actors: the National Bureau of Statistics (70-city index), MOHURD (住建部), the People's Bank of China, the National Financial Regulatory Administration (NFRA, whitelist lending), the Ministry of Finance (land revenue), and municipal governments as monopoly land sellers.
> Banks: ICBC, CCB, ABC, BOC (holders of ~RMB 38 trillion of mortgages at peak) plus the trust and LGFV shadow-finance complex.

### China Trend Detail

**Apa Yang Terjadi Di China**

> China built the largest housing bubble in history and is now living through its controlled deflation.
> The mechanism had four interlocking legs.
> (1) A land monopoly: municipal governments were the sole legal seller of urban land-use rights, and auction revenue became their dominant discretionary income — land-use-rights sales reached roughly 40% of local government revenue at their 2021 peak.
> Local governments therefore had a structural interest in high and rising land prices.
> (2) A pre-sale (期房) system: buyers paid in full, usually with a mortgage, for apartments that were holes in the ground, and developers recycled that cash into buying more land.
> This turned developers into leveraged maturity-transformation machines that were solvent only while sales grew.
> (3) A household balance sheet almost entirely composed of housing: more than 70% of urban household wealth sits in residential and commercial real estate, versus roughly 30% in advanced economies, because capital controls, a shallow equity market and negative real deposit rates left households with no alternative store of value.
> Housing became a savings account, a marriage prerequisite, a school-admission ticket (学区房) and a hukou-linked entitlement all at once.
> (4) A social norm that made ownership non-optional: surveys found around 83% of rural respondents believed a young man needed to own a city apartment before he could marry, producing the 'six wallets' (六个钱包) phenomenon in which two sets of grandparents plus both parents pooled savings for a down payment.

The bubble was punctured deliberately.
> In August 2020 the 'three red lines' capped developer leverage on three ratios (liabilities/assets ex-advances, net debt/equity, cash/short-term debt).
> Financing dried up almost overnight for the most leveraged players.
> Evergrande missed offshore coupon payments in late 2021; Country Garden — until then treated as the 'safe' private developer — followed in 2023; by 2024-2025 essentially every large private developer had defaulted or restructured, and only Vanke, propped up by its Shenzhen state shareholder, was still technically current, and only after bondholders granted grace-period extensions in late 2025 and 2026.

What followed was not a single crash but a five-year grind with several distinct waves of damage.
> Wave 1 (2021-2022): developer credit collapse and construction stoppages, producing the 烂尾楼 (unfinished-building) crisis and the summer-2022 mortgage boycott movement (停贷潮) in which buyers of stalled projects across dozens of cities collectively refused to service mortgages on apartments that would never be delivered.
> Wave 2 (2022-2024): the collapse of new construction and of land sales, which detonated local-government finances, triggered public-sector wage arrears, and removed roughly 2 percentage points from annual GDP growth in both 2024 and 2025.
> Wave 3 (2023-2026): the resale market broke.
> Because new-build prices were administratively floored ('限跌令', price-drop bans) while resale prices were not, the second-hand market became the true price signal, and it fell continuously.
> In September and October 2025 second-hand prices fell in all 70 major cities for two consecutive months — the first time this has happened since the series began in 2011.
> Wave 4 (2025 onward): the balance-sheet phase.
> Households who bought at the 2020-2021 peak with 70-80% loan-to-value mortgages are now in negative equity; mortgage NPLs are climbing; foreclosure (法拍房) listings have surged while the auction clearance rate collapsed to around 15% in H1 2025, forcing banks to hold or quietly discount repossessed stock.
> Buyers now rationally refuse to catch a falling knife, so the market has entered a self-reinforcing expectations trap: prices fall because buyers wait, and buyers wait because prices fall.

The state response has evolved from denial to triage to managed shrinkage.
> 'Houses are for living in, not for speculation' (房住不炒, 2017) framed the ideological turn.
> 保交楼 ('ensure delivery of homes') mobilised policy banks and commercial banks to complete pre-sold units — by 2025 authorities claimed 7.5 million previously sold unfinished homes had been completed, with roughly RMB 7 trillion of 'whitelist' project loans approved.
> Purchase restrictions were dismantled almost everywhere, mortgage rates and down payments were cut to historic lows, and governments were told to buy unsold inventory for conversion into subsidised rental housing (though less than 4% of unsold stock has actually been repurchased).
> In January 2026 Beijing quietly retired the 'three red lines' framework itself.
> The declared destination is a 'new development model' (新发展模式): completed-home sales instead of pre-sales, a project-company system, lead-bank supervision of project accounts, 'good houses' (好房子) quality standards, and a much larger subsidised/rental segment.
> In practice this is an orderly downsizing of a sector that will never return to its former size, not a rescue.

**Fase Tren Di China**

> Late-stage managed decline / balance-sheet recession, moving from acute crisis toward chronic structural shrinkage.
> Mapping to the phase vocabulary: the BOOM ran 1998-2020; the BACKLASH/REGULATED phase was 2020-2022 (three red lines, 房住不炒, mortgage boycotts); the DECLINING phase has been continuous since 2021 and is now in its sixth year.
> As of mid-2026 the sector is simultaneously (a) still declining on every physical indicator — starts -22.6%, completions -23.4%, investment -16.2% — and (b) partially re-regulated in the loosening direction, with the three red lines retired in January 2026 and purchase restrictions largely gone.
> Crucially, the crisis has migrated from the corporate balance sheet (2021-2024, developer defaults) to the household balance sheet (2025-2026, negative equity, mortgage NPLs, foreclosures) and to the fiscal balance sheet (local-government land revenue collapse).
> The most useful single label is 'controlled deleveraging into a permanently smaller steady state' — an L-shaped, Japan-1990s-style adjustment rather than a US-2008-style banking panic, because the state controls the banks, the land supply and the price disclosure.

**Puncak Tren China**

> Peak of the bubble: 2020-2021.
> Precise markers — (a) volume peak: 2021, when total property sales reached roughly RMB 18 trillion and residential land revenue peaked at ~40% of local-government income; (b) price peak: mid-2021 for the national second-hand index, though tier-1 cities (Shenzhen, Shanghai, Beijing) peaked slightly earlier, around mid-2021 for Shenzhen after its 2020 surge; (c) new-home demand peak: 2017 by unit volume (Goldman uses 2017 as the reference peak, ~9.4 million urban units a year through the 2010s); (d) macro-share peak: 2020, at 33.3% of GDP for the residential stock and 12.3% of GDP for housing investment.
> Geographically the bubble peaked hardest in the tier-3/4 cities of Henan, Hebei, Guangxi and the north-east — Zhengzhou, Langfang, Beihai, Hebi, Shenyang, Harbin — where shantytown-redevelopment monetised compensation (棚改货币化, 2015-2018) pushed prices far above local income capacity; these are the cities now 40-50% below peak.
> Tier-1 cities peaked later and have fallen less in percentage terms but from far higher absolute levels.
> The turning point event is precisely datable: the three-red-lines circular of 20 August 2020, followed by Evergrande's public liquidity failure in September 2021.

### Status Indonesia Saat Ini

**Status Di Indonesia**

> Mixed and asymmetric — NOT a single status.
> Decompose into four sub-trends: (1) HOUSING AFFORDABILITY / GENERATIONAL EXCLUSION — already massively present, arguably worse than China on a price-to-income basis for the bottom half of the income distribution, but produced by supply failure and low incomes rather than by a credit bubble.
> (2) STALLED PRE-SOLD PROJECTS (烂尾楼 equivalent) — already present in miniature and accelerating: Meikarta, LRT City, dozens of PKPU'd apartment towers, syariah-property fraud.
> (3) DEVELOPER DEBT CRISIS AT SYSTEMIC SCALE — has NOT arrived and is unlikely in the Chinese form; Indonesian developers are far less leveraged and the mortgage system is far shallower.
> (4) NEGATIVE-EQUITY MORTGAGES / NATIONAL PRICE CRASH — essentially absent; Indonesian nominal house prices have not fallen, they have merely stopped growing (IHPR +0.83% YoY in Q4 2025, the slowest since the series began in 2003), which is a stagnation signal rather than a crash signal.
> Overall label: 'sudah masuk secara parsial (affordability + mangkrak), belum ada dan mungkin tidak akan ada dalam bentuk yang sama (bubble crash + negative equity)'.

**Contoh Konkret Indonesia**

> STALLED / DISTRESSED PROJECTS.
> Meikarta (Lippo Cikarang, Bekasi) — the flagship Indonesian 烂尾楼 case: launched 2017 with an enormous marketing blitz, entangled in a permit-bribery scandal, thousands of buyers left without units, buyers who complained sued by the developer in 2023, and by January 2026 the Housing Ministry was floating a plan to convert parts of the stalled complex into subsidised rusun.
> LRT City (Adhi Commuter Properti — LRT City Ciracas, LRT City Tebet, LRT City Bekasi) — structures topped out but interior and facilities work halted from mid-2025; by July 2026 around 2,400 consumers were still without units, some being chased by debt collectors for KPA instalments on apartments they will never receive, with the Housing Ministry and Danantara brought in to resolve it.
> Regional cases: a stalled Bandung Barat housing project with 103 consumers and Rp 62.3 billion of losses (May 2026); repeated 'properti syariah' fraud schemes documented by FKBI.
> PT Hanson International (MYRX) — a public developer with a claimed ~5,000 ha landbank (Citra Maja Raya, Forest Hill, Millenium City) that collapsed into bankruptcy in 2020 after the Jiwasraya/Asabri scandal and an OJK finding of unlicensed public fund-raising: Indonesia's closest analogue to a landbank-leverage blow-up.

LEGAL/REGULATORY ANALOGUE.
> SEMA No.
> 3/2023 (Supreme Court Circular) effectively bars apartment/rusun buyers from using the 'simple proof' bankruptcy/PKPU route against developers — a state intervention to protect developer balance sheets that structurally mirrors China's 保交楼 logic of prioritising project completion over creditor enforcement, but without the compensating whitelist financing.

CHINESE PLAYERS ALREADY ON THE GROUND.
> Country Garden (碧桂园) has Indonesian projects worth roughly RMB 1.8 billion (~Rp 3.8 trillion), including Sky House BSD+ and Sky House Alam Sutera+ in Tangerang — meaning Indonesian buyers already hold units in towers built by a defaulted Chinese developer.
> China Fortune Land Development (CFLD) committed roughly Rp 19 trillion to residential and industrial-city projects around Tangerang/Karawang from 2016, including a 2,800-home, 60-hectare scheme, and saw its projects stall from 2018 when its own liquidity problems began.
> Chinese FDI into Indonesia hit ~US$8.1 billion in 2024, more than half of it linked to industrial/warehouse facilities with 10-15 year leases and worker housing — a different, industrial channel of Chinese property capital.

DOMESTIC MEGA-PROJECTS WITH LAND-FINANCE CHARACTERISTICS.
> PIK 2 / Pantai Indah Kapuk Dua (Agung Sedayu + Salim) — a ~Rp 40 trillion (US$2.6bn) coastal tourism estate north-west of Jakarta granted National Strategic Project (PSN) status, which is Indonesia's clearest structural echo of the Chinese model in which state designation, land assembly and a single mega-developer combine to create value; it became a political flashpoint in 2025 over sea fences and land acquisition.
> Similar dynamics attach to IKN Nusantara, BSD City (Sinar Mas Land) and Kota Deltamas.

POLICY MACHINERY.
> Program 3 Juta Rumah (Prabowo/Kementerian PKP), FLPP via BP Tapera, PPN DTP housing VAT relief (PMK 90/2025), and BI's 100% LTV / 0% down-payment macroprudential stance — a demand-stimulus stack that, taken together, resembles the Chinese playbook for propping up housing demand.

### Analisis Lag

**Bukti Historical Lag**

> (a) 1997-1998 ASIAN CRISIS PRECEDENT — Indonesia has already had its property-and-banking collapse, twenty-four years before China's.
> Property lending, dollar-denominated developer debt and Jakarta office/condo overbuilding were central to the 1998 banking collapse; the resulting institutions (BI's LTV macroprudential rules from 2012, the 20-25% down-payment regime, conservative bank property exposure limits, IBRA's asset disposals) are precisely why Indonesian banks entered the 2020s with far less property leverage than Chinese banks.
> On this dimension Indonesia is a REVERSE case: it learned first.
> (b) THE E-COMMERCE/FINTECH ANALOGUE DOES NOT APPLY WELL — in digital sectors Indonesia typically runs 5-8 years behind China because transmission is via platforms, capital and copycat product.
> Property does not transmit that way; it transmits via land law, fiscal design and credit systems, which are country-specific and change on decadal timescales.
> This is why the property lag is longer and less reliable than digital-sector lags.
> (c) THE MEIKARTA-EVERGRANDE PARALLEL — Meikarta's 2017 launch-and-fail sequence (aggressive pre-sales, permit scandal, buyers stranded, developer sues complaining buyers) predates Evergrande's public failure by four years, demonstrating that the pre-sale-without-escrow failure mode is endogenous to Indonesia and not imported.
> (d) SHOPHOUSE/APARTMENT INVESTOR CYCLES — Jakarta's 2012-2015 apartment boom, driven by investor buyers rather than end-users, produced the current >5,000-unit unsold overhang and 2-3 years of flat secondary prices; this is a compressed, local rehearsal of the same investor-demand-collapse mechanism China experienced at national scale.
> (e) LAND-FINANCE ANALOGUE IS PARTIAL — Indonesian local governments derive revenue from PBB-P2 and BPHTB (recurring and transaction property taxes) rather than from selling land-use rights, so the single most explosive Chinese mechanism has no Indonesian counterpart; PSN designation for private estates (PIK 2) is the nearest thing and is far smaller in fiscal terms.

**Tipe Lag**

> Hybrid: LAGGARD on the affordability/generational-exclusion dimension (≈10-15 years behind China's arrival at mass youth exclusion), SIMULTANEOUS-TO-SLIGHTLY-AHEAD on the stalled-pre-sold-project dimension (Meikarta 2018 vs China's 2021-2022 烂尾楼 peak), and REVERSE on the systemic property-crash dimension (Indonesia had its property-driven banking collapse in 1997-98, twenty-plus years before China, and built macroprudential defences as a result).
> The dominant framing for policy purposes should be: Indonesia is NOT going to import China's crash — it is at risk of importing China's *pre-crash structure* (pre-sale leverage, investor-driven high-rise supply, state-designated mega-estates, housing as the only savings vehicle) while lacking China's fiscal and banking capacity to absorb the consequences.

### Probabilitas Transfer ke Indonesia

**Probabilitas Transfer**

> Split verdict.
> HIGH (Tinggi) for the affordability crisis, generational exclusion and inheritance-based ownership — already arriving.
> MEDIUM-HIGH (Sedang-Tinggi) for localised unfinished-project crises and consumer-loss scandals — already recurring and likely to intensify as the 3-million-homes programme accelerates weak developers into the market.
> MEDIUM (Sedang) for a segment-specific price correction in Jakarta/Tangerang high-rise investor stock.
> LOW (Rendah) for a China-style systemic developer-debt collapse, nationwide nominal price decline, or mass negative-equity mortgages within the next decade.

**Alasan Probabilitas**

> The high-probability components transfer because their drivers are already present and independent of China: urban land prices in Jabodetabek, Bali, Surabaya and Makassar rising faster than wages; a young workforce concentrated in informal or contract employment that cannot document income for a KPR; a subsidised-mortgage system delivering only ~22% of its annual quota by mid-year; and a cultural expectation of ownership as a marriage and adulthood marker identical to China's.
> The result — 51% of Gen Z declaring they cannot afford a house, inheritance as the dominant acquisition route — is the same social outcome as China's, reached by a different mechanism (supply and income failure rather than credit-fuelled price inflation).

The unfinished-project component transfers because Indonesia runs the same pre-sale (PPJB) architecture with weaker safeguards: buyers pay deposits and start servicing KPA before completion, developer project accounts are not ring-fenced by a mandatory escrow with bank supervision, and SEMA 3/2023 removes the consumers' bankruptcy lever.
> Meikarta and LRT City demonstrate the failure mode is live.
> Adding a 3-million-unit political target with FLPP quota pressure creates exactly the incentive structure — volume targets, thin developers, front-loaded cash collection — that manufactures 烂尾楼.

The low-probability components fail to transfer for four structural reasons.
> First, credit depth: mortgages are 3.4% of GDP in Indonesia versus a Chinese household mortgage stock an order of magnitude larger relative to GDP; you cannot have a mass negative-equity event when most homes are not mortgaged.
> Second, fiscal architecture: Indonesian local governments do not monopolise and auction land-use rights, so there is no land-finance flywheel to reverse.
> Third, tenure and informality: a very large share of Indonesian housing is self-built (rumah swadaya) on inherited or informally titled land, outside the developer-and-mortgage system entirely — this is a shock absorber China does not have.
> Fourth, demography: Indonesia's population and urbanisation are still rising, so the terminal demand cliff that makes China's oversupply permanent does not apply for decades.

The residual risk is a compositional one: the *segments* of Indonesian property that most resemble China (investor-owned high-rise apartments in Jakarta/Tangerang, PSN mega-estates, syariah/kavling speculative land schemes) can and probably will experience Chinese-style outcomes at their own scale, without dragging the national economy down with them.

**Vektor Transmisi**

> (a) DIRECT ENTRY BY CHINESE PLAYERS — the most literal channel, and it has already produced negative outcomes.
> Country Garden holds ~RMB 1.8 billion (Rp 3.8 trillion) of Indonesian projects including Sky House BSD+ and Sky House Alam Sutera+ in Tangerang; China Fortune Land Development committed ~Rp 19 trillion from 2016 to residential and industrial-city projects near Tangerang and saw them stall when its own liquidity failed from 2018.
> The transmission here is not a business model but contagion: a Chinese parent's default strands Indonesian buyers.
> Expect more of this as surviving Chinese developers (COLI, Poly, Greentown) and Chinese contractors seek overseas volume to replace a domestic market that has halved.
> (b) CHINESE CAPITAL VIA INDUSTRIAL REAL ESTATE — the largest and least discussed channel: US$8.1 billion of Chinese FDI in 2024, more than half tied to factories, warehouses and worker housing on 10-15 year leases, pushing industrial yields to 7-7.5%.
> This is Chinese property capital arriving in Indonesia in its healthiest form, and it is genuinely additive; the risk is concentration of industrial-estate exposure with single-tenant Chinese occupiers whose own domestic finances are fragile.
> (c) LOCAL COPYCAT OF THE MODEL, NOT THE CRISIS — Indonesian developers and provincial governments imitating the Chinese 'new city' template: PSN-designated private mega-estates (PIK 2), integrated township land banking (BSD, Deltamas, Meikarta), TOD-branded high-rise (LRT City), and the marketing grammar of pre-sale with heavy discounts and 0% down payment.
> This is the most consequential vector because it reproduces the *structure* that later fails.
> (d) POLICY EMULATION — Indonesian policymakers copying Chinese demand-stimulus instruments (PPN DTP VAT relief, 100% LTV / 0% DP, subsidised fixed-rate mortgages, state-directed volume targets) while not copying the Chinese safeguards that were added later (escrow supervision of pre-sale proceeds, whitelist project financing, completed-home sales).
> Copying the accelerator without the brakes is the specific danger.
> (e) FINANCIAL-MARKET AND SENTIMENT SPILLOVER — a further leg down in China depresses commodity demand (coal, nickel, CPO), weakens the rupiah and Indonesian fiscal revenue, and tightens KPR conditions indirectly; this is a macro rather than a sectoral vector.
> (f) DIASPORA AND DEMONSTRATION EFFECT — Chinese-Indonesian and mainland Chinese buyers concentrated in PIK 2 and Batam, plus mainland investors seeking offshore property after being burned at home; this can inflate specific micro-markets and then withdraw abruptly.
> (g) ALGORITHMIC CONTENT DIFFUSION — a soft but real channel: Chinese-language and Indonesian-language short-video content about 烂尾楼, negative equity and 'lying flat' rather than buying property is already reshaping young Indonesians' expectations, feeding the emerging 'why bother buying' narrative that CNBC Indonesia documented in 2026.

### Faktor Pendorong

**Indikator Pemantauan**

> TIER 1 — EARLY WARNING OF THE UNFINISHED-PROJECT CHANNEL (watch monthly/quarterly): number of new PKPU petitions filed against property developers in the Commercial Courts of Jakarta Pusat, Surabaya and Semarang; volume of consumer complaints to BPKN/YLKI and to Kementerian PKP citing 'proyek mangkrak'; media counts of stalled TOD/apartment projects; whether any national escrow/rekening penampungan requirement for pre-sale proceeds is drafted.
> TIER 2 — CREDIT AND PRICE STRESS: BI's IHPR quarterly YoY (a first-ever negative print would be the regime-change signal — it hit +0.83% in Q4 2025, the lowest in the series' 22-year history); KPR NPL ratio in OJK's SPI (2.88% in Q1 2025; a move above 4% would be significant); restructured-KPR share; KPR approval rejection rates; growth of outstanding KPR (below 5% and falling); developer bond and sukuk yields for APLN, LPKR, PWON, CTRA, SMRA; the property sector's share of bank credit.
> TIER 3 — SUPPLY/OVERSUPPLY: Colliers/Cushman/Knight Frank quarterly Jakarta apartment unsold-inventory counts (>5,000 units in 2025) and take-up (~150 units in H1 2025 Jakarta); condo occupancy (~88%); months-of-supply in Tangerang/Bekasi landed housing; number of new tower launches versus handovers.
> TIER 4 — POLICY AND FISCAL: FLPP disbursement rate versus the 350,000 quota (only 22.15% by mid-June 2026 — a chronic under-execution signal); the fiscal cost of PPN DTP extensions; whether BI keeps LTV at 100%/0% DP (a rollback would signal stress); Tapera contribution enforcement and any expansion of the 3% deduction to private-sector workers; new PSN designations for private property estates.
> TIER 5 — CHINESE PLAYER ENTRY: BKPM/Kementerian Investasi filings of new Chinese-origin PMA in the real estate sector; trademark and brand registrations by Chinese developers; job postings in Indonesian for Mandarin-speaking property sales staff; announcements by COLI, Poly, Greentown, CSCEC or Chinese contractors of Indonesian residential ventures; Chinese construction-materials dumping into the Indonesian market (steel, glass, ceramics, aluminium) as excess Chinese capacity seeks outlets.
> TIER 6 — SOCIAL/DEMAND: Google Trends for 'sewa vs beli rumah', 'rumah subsidi', 'KPR ditolak', 'proyek mangkrak'; share of Gen Z declaring they will not buy (51% in 2025); marriage registration counts at Kemenag; the co-living and long-term rental market's growth; growth in 'rumah subsidi' resale listings.

### Hambatan & Faktor Pembatal

**Hambatan Transfer**

> (a) CREDIT SHALLOWNESS — with mortgages at 3.4% of GDP and >55% informal employment, the leverage channel that turns a price fall into a systemic event simply is not there; this is the single strongest brake.
> (b) MACROPRUDENTIAL MEMORY OF 1998 — Bank Indonesia and OJK have run LTV caps, developer-exposure limits and single-obligor rules since 2012 precisely because of the 1997-98 property-banking collapse; Indonesian banks are structurally less property-concentrated than Chinese banks.
> (c) LAND MARKET FRICTION — fragmented private ownership, adat and overlapping claims, slow BPN certification and endemic land litigation make Chinese-style rapid, large-scale land assembly nearly impossible outside PSN designation; this caps the speed of supply expansion (and therefore also caps the bubble).
> (d) SELF-BUILT HOUSING (RUMAH SWADAYA) — a large majority of Indonesian housing is built incrementally by households outside the developer/mortgage system, insulating most of the stock from the developer cycle entirely.
> (e) FISCAL CAPACITY — Indonesia cannot fund a 保交楼-scale bailout: China deployed roughly RMB 7 trillion in whitelist project loans and completed 7.5 million unfinished units; Indonesia's entire annual FLPP programme is a rounding error by comparison, and the state's willingness to intervene (Danantara being brought into the LRT City mess) is ad hoc.
> (f) INTEREST-RATE ENVIRONMENT — Indonesian mortgage rates are structurally 7-11% after teaser periods versus China's 3-4%, which mechanically limits how much price a given income can support, keeping speculation costly.
> (g) ABSENCE OF A DEMAND CLIFF — a growing, urbanising population with a 9.9-15 million unit backlog means genuine end-user demand persists even when investor demand collapses.
> (h) POLITICAL SALIENCE — Indonesian housing policy is redistributive and electoral (3 million homes, FLPP, PPN DTP), oriented toward the bottom of the market, whereas the Chinese bubble was built at the top; the political economy pushes toward subsidised supply rather than speculative demand.

**Faktor Pembatal Transfer**

> Conditions that make a full-strength Chinese-style crisis structurally impossible in Indonesia, rather than merely delayed.
> (1) NO LAND-FINANCE FLYWHEEL.
> The Chinese crisis is fundamentally a *fiscal* crisis wearing a property costume: municipalities monopolised land supply, sold it to leveraged developers, and spent the proceeds.
> Remove that mechanism and you remove the amplifier.
> Indonesian regions raise property revenue from recurring taxes on existing stock (PBB-P2) and transaction taxes (BPHTB) — revenue that falls only modestly when transaction volume falls, and does not depend on ever-rising auction prices.
> This single institutional difference caps the size of any Indonesian property shock.
> (2) NO CLOSED CAPITAL ACCOUNT.
> Chinese households were fiscally conscripted into housing.
> Indonesian savers have SBN, deposits, gold, offshore assets and crypto.
> Housing will never be 70% of Indonesian urban household wealth.
> (3) ARCHIPELAGIC GEOGRAPHY AND FRAGMENTED URBAN SYSTEM.
> China's bubble was propagated by a hierarchical, connected urban system in which tier-1 price signals cascaded to 300+ tier-3/4 cities via a national developer oligopoly and a national mortgage market.
> Indonesia's property markets are physically and financially segmented — Jakarta, Surabaya, Medan, Makassar, Bali and Batam are almost separate markets with different developers, buyers and price dynamics.
> A Jakarta apartment glut cannot propagate to Makassar the way a Shenzhen boom propagated to Hebi.
> High inter-island logistics costs also prevent the standardised, industrialised national homebuilding that made Chinese supply expansion so fast.
> (4) INFORMALITY AS A SHOCK ABSORBER.
> A majority-informal labour force cannot be mortgaged, so it cannot be foreclosed; the same feature that causes the affordability crisis prevents the debt crisis.
> (5) NO DEMOGRAPHIC CLIFF FOR DECADES.
> China's 2022 population peak and the end of household formation make its oversupply permanent.
> Indonesia's population is still growing and urbanising; today's oversupply in one segment is tomorrow's absorbed stock.
> (6) DEVELOPER SCALE.
> Country Garden alone had ~3,121 pending projects; Indonesia's entire listed property sector is a fraction of one Chinese top-five developer's balance sheet, so no single failure is systemically threatening.
> (7) NO STATE PRICE-SUPPRESSION APPARATUS.
> China's 限跌令 (price-drop bans) and administrative new-home pricing created the distorted gap between new and second-hand prices that made the resale collapse so violent.
> Indonesia has no such apparatus, so prices adjust continuously and gently — the observed pattern of stagnant nominal prices eroding in real terms rather than crashing.

CONCLUSION: what Indonesia can import is the *social* crisis (generational exclusion, stranded buyers, wealth transmitted only by inheritance), not the *macro-financial* crisis.
> Any policy framing that prepares only for the latter will miss the actual risk.

### Prediksi Timeline di Indonesia

**Skenario Percepatan**

> Accelerators that would pull the crisis forward: (1) a sharp BI rate cycle reversal or rupiah crisis pushing KPR rates into the mid-teens, freezing the primary market and stranding developers mid-project; (2) political over-delivery on the 3-million-homes target — quota pressure onboarding undercapitalised developers, producing a mass 烂尾 event within 24-36 months; (3) a deeper Chinese downturn hitting commodity revenue (coal, nickel, CPO), squeezing regional economies where property demand is commodity-financed (Kalimantan, Sulawesi, Riau); (4) failure or scandal at BP Tapera that collapses public trust in the subsidised-housing channel; (5) aggressive entry of surviving Chinese developers and contractors dumping capacity and pre-sale marketing techniques into Indonesian metros; (6) an OJK/BI decision to keep 0% down payments in place through a downturn, which would maximise the number of Indonesian buyers with negative equity in any correction; (7) rapid financialisation of housing via property crowdfunding, tokenisation or REIT/DIRE retail products that import investor-driven demand into a market that currently lacks it.

### Dampak Sosial-Ekonomi

**Dampak Lapangan Kerja**

> WHAT CHINA SHOWS.
> The property complex was China's largest employer of low-skilled male labour and its collapse has been the country's biggest quiet labour shock.
> Migrant workers in construction fell from 15.4% of ~300 million migrants in 2023 to 14.3% in 2024 and 13.8% by December 2025 — the lowest share since 2008, implying several million net exits from the sector; construction output contracted ~1% in real terms in 2025 while new starts fell 22.6%.
> The jobs that disappeared: site labourers, formwork and rebar crews, crane and concrete operators, interior finishing trades, and the vast tier of subcontracted 包工头 gang bosses.
> The jobs that were transformed: real estate agents (Beike/Lianjia still has >140,000 agents but their income model shifted from new-home commissions to a brutally competitive resale and rental market), developer sales staff (mass layoffs), architects and structural engineers (the share of graduates entering construction engineering fell 46% in five years, the largest fall among 46 occupational categories), and property managers (now the only growing part of the value chain).
> The jobs that were created: renovation and retrofit (旧改), property management and facilities services, elderly-adapted housing, long-term rental operations, distressed-asset workout and foreclosure disposal, prefabricated/industrialised construction, and building-energy retrofit — but at perhaps a fifth of the headcount and lower wage levels than new-build construction.
> A meaningful share of displaced construction labour was absorbed by delivery platforms and ride-hailing, which is the direct causal link between the property crash and China's gig-economy glut.

WHAT THIS MEANS FOR INDONESIA.
> Indonesian construction employs more than 8.7 million people (5.97% of all workers, Sakernas Feb 2025), and the wider property ecosystem was estimated at ~13.8 million jobs (~10.2% of employment).
> Construction is 9.82% of GDP (Q3 2025).
> Indonesia is nowhere near a Chinese-scale contraction, but three specific exposures matter.
> First, IKN and PSN-driven construction employment is politically contingent — a budget reallocation can strand tens of thousands of workers quickly, and much of this labour is migrant, informal and unprotected.
> Second, if the 3-million-homes push falters, the incremental construction jobs it created (largely low-skilled, in the subsidised segment, spread across Java, Sumatra and Sulawesi) will evaporate faster than they appeared.
> Third — and most underrated — Chinese overcapacity is already exporting deflation into Indonesian construction inputs (steel, glass, aluminium, ceramics, sanitary ware); this lowers Indonesian build costs but threatens jobs in domestic building-materials manufacturing, a sector with real employment weight in Java.
> Conversely, growing job families in Indonesia mirror China's post-crisis pattern: property management and strata management, rental/co-living operations, renovation contracting, building inspection and QS/claims work, distressed-asset and PKPU workout specialists, and — the biggest — construction workers for industrial estates and warehousing serving relocating Chinese manufacturers (>half of US$8.1bn Chinese FDI in 2024).

**Dampak Kelas Menengah**

> The Indonesian middle class is being squeezed from a different direction than China's, with a similar end result.
> In China the middle class was made by property and is now being unmade by it: with >70% of urban household wealth in real estate and existing-home prices roughly 30% below the 2021 peak (40-50% in the worst cities), the negative wealth effect has been the primary driver of the consumption downgrade — estimates suggest a 10% fall in home prices cuts household spending by 1.5-2.3%, implying a 2-4% of GDP consumption loss at observed price declines.
> Chinese middle-class households that bought at peak with 70-80% LTV mortgages now service debt on a depreciating asset; the mortgage-payment-to-income ratio had already risen from 16.2% in 2004 to 57.4% in 2021.

Indonesia's middle class is not being decapitalised — it is being *excluded from capitalisation*.
> Because only ~3.4% of GDP is mortgage credit and only 10% of young buyers use a KPR, most Indonesian middle-class households never got the leveraged asset in the first place.
> The result is a bifurcation: households that already own (usually through inheritance or a 2000s-2010s purchase) hold an asset appreciating slowly in nominal terms and roughly flat in real terms, while the entering cohort is permanently priced out.
> Bank Indonesia's IHPR growing at 0.83% YoY in Q4 2025 — below inflation — means the middle class's main asset is quietly losing real value while remaining unattainable for new entrants.
> That is the worst of both worlds: no wealth effect for owners, no access for non-owners.

The practical consequences already visible: 51% of Gen Z and 40% of millennials say they cannot afford a house; only 18% bought with savings; inheritance is the dominant route; Deloitte finds Indonesians deferring marriage and home purchase for financial reasons.
> Expect the Indonesian middle class to rotate spending away from a housing down-payment they cannot reach and toward consumption, travel, education and 'emotional' spending — the same behavioural signature that appears in China's consumption-downgrade data, but arriving through frustration rather than through loss.
> A secondary effect is the rise of housing-adjacent debt: paylater, multiguna loans and kredit renovasi taken by households that cannot get a KPR, concentrating middle-class leverage in expensive unsecured credit rather than cheap secured credit.

**Dampak Daerah Non Jawa**

> Highly differentiated, and the non-Java story is not a smaller version of the Java story.
> (1) COMMODITY-CYCLE PROPERTY MARKETS — Balikpapan, Samarinda, Pekanbaru, Palembang, Jambi, Sorowako/Morowali and Kendari have property markets financed by coal, nickel, CPO and their multipliers.
> A deeper Chinese property/industrial downturn transmits to these cities through commodity revenue, not through mortgages: when coal and nickel prices fall, local house prices, shophouse rents and construction activity fall with them.
> This is the most direct Chinese-crisis transmission channel to non-Java Indonesia, and it is macro rather than sectoral.
> (2) TOURISM-DRIVEN LAND SPECULATION — Bali (Canggu, Ubud, Uluwatu), Lombok (Mandalika), Labuan Bajo and Batam exhibit the most genuinely Chinese-style dynamics in Indonesia: rapid land price escalation, off-plan villa sales to foreign investors, thin developer capitalisation, and yield promises of 15-20% that resemble the pre-sale-and-promise model.
> These markets are the most likely site of an Indonesian 烂尾 cluster, and Bali land prices have already outrun local wages so severely that Balinese under-35s are effectively excluded from their own island.
> (3) IKN NUSANTARA — the closest Indonesian analogue to a Chinese state-led new city, with the same failure mode: if central budget commitment wavers, East Kalimantan is left with infrastructure without population, the Indonesian version of a 鬼城 (ghost city).
> This risk is concrete and near-term.
> (4) LOW-DENSITY EASTERN INDONESIA — NTT, Maluku, Papua: the housing problem here is quality and legality (rumah tidak layak huni, uncertified land), not price bubbles; the 2-million-unit rural renovation leg of Program 3 Juta Rumah is the relevant instrument and it is chronically under-executed.
> The 'Chinese trend' is largely irrelevant here except as a source of building materials.
> (5) SUBSIDISED-HOUSING OVERSUPPLY RISK — the FLPP programme builds heavily in peri-urban and non-Java locations where land is cheap; if units are built far from employment, Indonesia risks creating its own remote unsold inventory, the low-income mirror of China's tier-3/4 glut.
> This is a genuine, monitorable risk given FLPP delivery of only 22.15% of quota by mid-2026 alongside pressure to hit volume targets.

BOTTOM LINE: the affordability crisis is a metro-Java-plus-Bali phenomenon; the commodity transmission of China's crisis is a Kalimantan/Sulawesi/Sumatra phenomenon; and the ghost-city/stranded-infrastructure risk is an IKN and Bali/Mandalika phenomenon.
> Different regions need different policy responses.

### Kaitan Pendidikan

**Jurusan Dibutuhkan**

> Skills and disciplines that grow as property shifts from development to stewardship — validated by what actually grew in China after the crash.
> (1) BUILDING RETROFIT, RENOVATION AND URBAN REGENERATION — China's 旧改/城中村改造 programmes became the only growing construction segment; Indonesia's equivalent is the 2-million-unit rural renovation leg of Program 3 Juta Rumah plus kampung upgrading.
> Needs: renovation project management, structural assessment of existing buildings, retrofit cost estimation.
> (2) PROPERTY AND FACILITIES MANAGEMENT — the single most reliably growing job family in a stock-dominated (rather than flow-dominated) property economy: strata/PPPSRS management, building systems, energy management, tenant services.
> Indonesia has almost no dedicated degree programmes here.
> (3) DISTRESSED ASSET, INSOLVENCY AND CONSUMER-PROTECTION LAW — PKPU/kepailitan practice, escrow and pre-sale regulation, consumer class actions; the LRT City and Meikarta cases demonstrate acute demand and acute supply shortage.
> (4) HOUSING FINANCE AND CREDIT RISK — mortgage underwriting for informal-income borrowers, alternative credit scoring, secondary-mortgage markets (SMF), housing microfinance, mortgage servicing and workout.
> Indonesia's 3.4% mortgage/GDP is a market development problem, not just a policy problem.
> (5) URBAN ECONOMICS, LAND VALUE CAPTURE AND PUBLIC FINANCE — how to fund cities without land-finance: PBB-P2 reform, betterment levies, TOD value capture, land-value taxation.
> China's crisis is fundamentally about this and Indonesia has almost no domestic expertise.
> (6) INDUSTRIALISED CONSTRUCTION AND MODULAR/PREFAB — the only way to deliver subsidised housing at scale and cost; also the direction Chinese construction moved.
> (7) GEOSPATIAL, LAND ADMINISTRATION AND CADASTRE — BPN certification, land dispute resolution, digital land registry; Indonesia's binding supply constraint is land legality.
> (8) GREEN BUILDING AND CLIMATE-RESILIENT HOUSING — BI is already offering LTV incentives tied to green certification; coastal adaptive housing is in the 3-million-homes design.
> (9) DATA AND VALUATION — automated valuation models, market analytics, property data science; the resale market is where the action moves, and Indonesia lacks a trustworthy price index at neighbourhood granularity.
> (10) RENTAL AND CO-LIVING OPERATIONS — the sector young Indonesians will actually use, currently dominated by informal kos operators.

**China Education Response**

> China's education system responded to the property collapse faster and more mechanically than any other country's, and the response has three visible layers.
> LAYER 1 — MARKET-DRIVEN COLLAPSE IN DEMAND.
> Students voted with their feet before any ministry acted: transfers out of civil engineering exceeded transfers in at Tongji; nearly 100 of 440 major-transfer applicants at Hunan University in 2022 came from the civil engineering college with zero inbound; the share of graduates entering construction engineering fell 46% in five years, the largest decline among 46 occupational categories.
> Elite universities cut gaokao entry thresholds for civil engineering in Hebei, Shandong, Henan and Chongqing and still failed to fill seats (Tongji, Jilin).
> Southeast University, second-ranked in architecture nationally, opened its architecture programme to humanities-stream applicants to fill capacity.
> LAYER 2 — ADMINISTRATIVE PROGRAMME RATIONALISATION.
> The Ministry of Education's programme-adjustment mechanism (专业设置调整优化) has been used to close, merge or suspend enrolment in thousands of undersubscribed majors while approving thousands of new ones; the reported pattern is large-scale withdrawal of construction-adjacent programmes at 985/211 and provincial universities alongside approval of programmes in AI, integrated circuits, biomanufacturing, low-altitude economy, elderly care, new energy and 'future technology' fields.
> Several universities have publicly phased out civil engineering enrolment entirely.
> LAYER 3 — CURRICULAR REPOSITIONING RATHER THAN ELIMINATION.
> Surviving civil engineering programmes have been re-badged toward intelligent construction (智能建造), prefabricated/industrialised building, infrastructure maintenance and inspection, underground and transport engineering, and 'new infrastructure' (data centres, rail, energy).
> Architecture has pivoted toward urban renewal (城市更新), heritage retrofit, interior and 'good houses' (好房子) quality standards, and the elderly-adapted housing market (适老化改造), in line with MOHURD's declared new development model.

LESSON FOR INDONESIA: China's education system responded *after* the sector collapsed, not before, and the adjustment fell hardest on students who had already enrolled — a cohort of civil engineering and architecture graduates entered a market that had lost half its jobs.
> The preemptive lesson is to diversify the *content* of construction-related programmes now, while Indonesian demand is still strong, so that graduates are employable in infrastructure, industry, retrofit and maintenance rather than exclusively in residential development.

### Pelajaran Kebijakan dari China

**Respons Kebijakan China**

> SEQUENCE OF CHINESE POLICY, AND WHICH PARTS ARE WORTH PRE-EMPTING.
> (1) 2016-2017, 房住不炒 ('houses are for living in, not for speculation') — the ideological turn, plus purchase restrictions (限购), price caps (限价), sale restrictions (限售).
> Verdict: right principle, applied through administrative quantity controls that distorted the market.
> (2) August 2020, THREE RED LINES (三道红线) — hard leverage caps on developers.
> Verdict: correct diagnosis, catastrophic timing and sequencing.
> It was applied abruptly, to a sector whose entire business model was maturity mismatch, without any parallel mechanism to protect pre-sale buyers.
> It caused the crisis it was meant to prevent.
> It was quietly retired in January 2026.
> THE LESSON IS ABOUT SEQUENCING: deleverage developers only *after* ring-fencing buyer money.
> (3) 2022 onward, 保交楼 ('ensure delivery') AND PRE-SALE FUND SUPERVISION — the response to mass unfinished buildings and the 2022 mortgage boycotts: mandatory supervision of pre-sale proceeds in dedicated project accounts, policy-bank special loans, and from 2024 the 'whitelist' (白名单) real-estate financing coordination mechanism under which local governments nominate viable projects for guaranteed bank credit.
> By September 2025 commercial banks had approved ~RMB 7 trillion under the whitelist and authorities claimed 7.5 million pre-sold unfinished homes completed.
> THIS IS THE SINGLE MOST TRANSFERABLE POLICY: escrow supervision of pre-sale money, adopted preemptively, is cheap; adopted after the fact it costs trillions.
> (4) 2023-2025, DEMAND RESTORATION — removal of purchase restrictions in nearly all cities, historic-low mortgage rates, minimum down payments cut to 15%, existing-mortgage rate repricing, hukou liberalisation in most cities.
> Verdict: necessary but ineffective once expectations turned; you cannot rate-cut your way out of a belief that prices will keep falling.
> (5) 2024-2026, INVENTORY ABSORPTION AND THE NEW MODEL — PBoC relending facilities for local SOEs to buy unsold homes for conversion into affordable/rental housing (execution poor: <4% of unsold stock repurchased), the shift toward completed-home sales (现房销售) replacing pre-sales, a project-company system, lead-bank supervision, 'good houses' quality standards, urban village renovation, and a much larger subsidised rental segment.
> Verdict: this is the correct destination and Indonesia should aim directly at it rather than passing through the pre-sale model first.
> (6) PROPERTY TAX — the one reform China conspicuously failed to execute: pilots in Shanghai and Chongqing since 2011 at 0.4-1.2% on second and luxury homes, an expanded pilot announced in 2021 and then shelved in 2022 because falling prices made new taxes politically impossible.
> THE LESSON IS TIMING: a recurring property tax must be introduced during a boom, when it dampens speculation and builds a local revenue base; once prices fall, the political window closes permanently and local governments are left with no replacement for land revenue.

WHAT INDONESIA SHOULD ADOPT PREEMPTIVELY: mandatory escrow/rekening penampungan with bank supervision and milestone-based release for all pre-sale residential projects; a completed-home-sale requirement for developers below a capital threshold; strengthening rather than weakening consumer insolvency remedies (revisiting SEMA 3/2023); a functioning recurring property tax and vacant-property levy while prices are still rising; a genuine public/social rental housing stock rather than an ownership-only subsidy model; and developer leverage rules introduced gradually and counter-cyclically, never abruptly.

**Rekomendasi Kebijakan Indonesia**

> (1) MANDATORY PRE-SALE ESCROW LAW — the highest-return, lowest-cost intervention available.
> Require all PPJB proceeds and KPA disbursements for pre-sold units to enter a bank-supervised escrow released against independently verified construction milestones, with automatic refund triggers.
> This directly prevents the Meikarta/LRT City failure mode and costs the state nothing.
> Pair it with a completed-home-sale (rumah jadi) requirement for developers below a capital/track-record threshold.
> (2) REVISIT SEMA No.
> 3/2023 — restoring a workable insolvency remedy for apartment buyers, or replacing it with a statutory buyer-protection fund funded by a small levy on pre-sale volume, so that protecting developers does not mean abandoning consumers.
> (3) FIX FLPP EXECUTION BEFORE EXPANDING TARGETS — 22.15% of quota disbursed by mid-June 2026 is the binding constraint, not the quota size.
> Audit the bottleneck (developer eligibility, bank channelling, land availability, buyer documentation for informal-income applicants) and publish monthly disbursement data by province.
> Volume targets pursued without execution capacity are exactly what manufactures thin developers and stalled projects.
> (4) BUILD MORTGAGE ACCESS FOR INFORMAL INCOME — Indonesia's 3.4% mortgage/GDP is the firewall against a Chinese crash but also the cause of exclusion.
> Develop alternative-data underwriting, housing microfinance, rent-to-own, and gradual-payment products for the ~55%+ informal workforce, with prudential guardrails so this deepens access without importing leverage risk.
> Strengthen SMF's secondary-mortgage function.
> (5) TAX THE STOCK, NOT THE TRANSACTION — reform PBB-P2 into a genuine recurring value-based tax with progressive rates and a vacant/idle-land levy, while reducing BPHTB transaction friction.
> Do it now while prices still rise; China's shelved property tax proves the window closes permanently once prices fall.
> This also gives regions a land-independent revenue base, pre-empting the fiscal dependence that made China's crisis systemic.
> (6) LAND SUPPLY AND LEGALITY — accelerate BPN systematic registration (PTSL), publish land price data, enforce idle-land (tanah terlantar) rules, and use land value capture around MRT/LRT/KRL corridors to fund transit and affordable units.
> Supply failure, not credit shortage, is Indonesia's primary affordability driver.
> (7) BUILD A PUBLIC RENTAL STOCK — Indonesia's housing policy is almost exclusively ownership-subsidy.
> Given that a large cohort will never buy, a professionally managed social and market rental sector (rusunawa reform, institutional rental, regulated kos) is essential.
> Meikarta's conversion into subsidised rusun is a useful precedent if executed transparently.
> (8) COUNTER-CYCLICAL, GRADUAL MACROPRUDENTIAL POLICY — retain LTV/DP flexibility but re-tighten during upswings rather than only easing; avoid China's abrupt three-red-lines shock.
> Publish a developer leverage dashboard.
> (9) REGULATE SPECULATIVE LAND AND SYARIAH-PROPERTY SCHEMES — OJK and Satgas PASTI enforcement against kavling and 'properti syariah' Ponzi structures, with a mandatory disclosure and licensing regime for off-plan land sales, concentrated on Bali, Lombok, Batam and peri-urban Java.
> (10) CHINESE-CAPITAL SCREENING — require Indonesian-domiciled project subsidiaries with ring-fenced funding and completion bonds for foreign developer projects, so that a parent's offshore default (Country Garden, CFLD) cannot strand Indonesian buyers.
> (11) IKN CONTINGENCY PLANNING — publish an explicit plan for the scenario in which IKN population targets are not met, to avoid a state-built ghost city.

### Peluang & Rekomendasi Aksi

**Peluang Bisnis**

> (1) PROPERTY AND FACILITIES MANAGEMENT AT SCALE — the structurally growing segment in any stock-dominated property economy, and Indonesia's strata sector is chronically badly run.
> Professionalised PPPSRS management, building systems maintenance, and energy management for the ~decade of apartment stock already delivered.
> (2) RENOVATION AND RETROFIT — Program 3 Juta Rumah includes 2 million rural renovations; add urban kampung upgrading and the ageing 1990s-2000s housing stock.
> Opportunities in standardised renovation packages, materials retail (the Indonesian equivalent of a Home Depot/Mitra10 expansion), financing for renovation, and contractor marketplaces.
> (3) INSTITUTIONAL RENTAL AND CO-LIVING — the market for the 51% of Gen Z who say they will not buy.
> Professionalised kos/co-living operators, build-to-rent, corporate housing for industrial estates (particularly serving Chinese manufacturers on 10-15 year leases), and rental-management platforms.
> (4) INDUSTRIAL AND LOGISTICS REAL ESTATE — the strongest segment in Indonesian property, with yields at 7-7.5% driven by relocating Chinese manufacturing; warehouses, worker dormitories, cold chain and industrial estate services.
> (5) PROPTECH FOR THE RESALE AND RENTAL MARKET — Indonesia has no trustworthy granular price index; the Beike/Lianjia model (verified listings, transaction data, agent standards) is directly transferable and currently unfilled between Rumah123, 99.co, Pinhome and Lamudi.
> (6) HOUSING FINANCE INNOVATION — alternative-data underwriting for informal incomes, rent-to-own, housing microfinance, developer construction finance, and mortgage servicing/workout.
> This is the largest untapped financial market in Indonesia by size.
> (7) DISTRESSED ASSET AND WORKOUT SERVICES — legal, valuation and asset-management practices around PKPU'd projects and stranded consumers; a real and growing demand documented by LRT City, Meikarta and dozens of PKPU'd towers.
> (8) INDUSTRIALISED/MODULAR CONSTRUCTION — the only route to delivering subsidised units at target cost and speed; also a hedge against skilled-labour shortages.
> (9) BUILDING MATERIALS ARBITRAGE — Chinese overcapacity in steel, glass, aluminium, ceramics and sanitary ware is deflating input costs; importers and integrators can capture this, though domestic manufacturers need trade-remedy protection.
> (10) LAND LEGALITY AND GEOSPATIAL SERVICES — due diligence, cadastral survey, title insurance (essentially non-existent in Indonesia) and land dispute resolution.
> (11) ELDERLY-ADAPTED AND ACCESSIBLE HOUSING — a decade early for Indonesia but China's fastest-growing retrofit niche; first movers can build the standards.

**Rekomendasi Individu Mahasiswa**

> (1) IF YOU ARE IN TEKNIK SIPIL OR ARSITEKTUR, DO NOT PANIC AND DO NOT QUIT — Indonesia is not China; infrastructure, industrial facilities and water/disaster works will absorb graduates for at least another decade.
> But actively steer your specialisation away from residential high-rise development and toward infrastructure, industrial and energy facilities, geotechnics, water, retrofit/maintenance, and disaster-resilient construction.
> Chinese students who stayed generalist in property-oriented civil engineering were the ones who got hurt.
> (2) LEARN THE ASSET-MANAGEMENT SIDE, NOT JUST THE BUILD SIDE — property and facilities management, building systems, energy management, strata law.
> In a stock economy the money moves from building to operating.
> (3) ACQUIRE FINANCIAL AND LEGAL LITERACY IN PROPERTY — PPJB and AJB mechanics, escrow, PKPU/kepailitan, LTV rules, valuation, mortgage credit risk.
> This makes you employable in banks, regulators, funds and law firms, not just contractors.
> (4) BUILD DATA SKILLS APPLIED TO PROPERTY — SQL, Python, GIS, automated valuation modelling, scraping and cleaning listing data.
> Whoever builds Indonesia's credible neighbourhood-level price index will own a valuable position.
> (5) BIM, DIGITAL TWIN AND MODULAR CONSTRUCTION COMPETENCE — the productivity frontier in a cost-constrained subsidised-housing market.
> (6) FOR NON-ENGINEERS: study urban economics and public finance — land value capture, property taxation, municipal finance.
> Indonesia will need people who can answer 'how do we fund cities' and almost nobody is trained for it.
> (7) PERSONALLY: do not treat home ownership as a mandatory life milestone or as a guaranteed investment.
> Indonesia's IHPR grew 0.83% YoY in Q4 2025, below inflation; a house bought at a stretch, with a floating rate after the teaser period, in a peri-urban location without transit, is a bad investment and a mobility trap.
> Prioritise income growth, liquidity and geographic flexibility in your twenties; rent deliberately; buy when the purchase is affordable at a payment-to-income ratio you can survive a job loss with.
> This is precisely the lesson Chinese millennials learned too late.
> (8) WATCH THE WARNING SIGNS BEFORE BUYING OFF-PLAN — verify PBG/IMB, developer track record, escrow arrangements and construction progress; the LRT City buyers were servicing loans on buildings that stopped at the shell stage.

**Rekomendasi Perguruan Tinggi**

> OPEN OR EXPAND: (1) a dedicated Real Estate & Facilities Management programme (D4/S1) — Indonesia has scattered courses inside Teknik Sipil and Manajemen but no serious professional pipeline for the fastest-growing part of the value chain; (2) Urban Economics & Municipal Finance concentrations within economics and public administration faculties, covering land value capture, property taxation, PBB-P2 reform and infrastructure finance; (3) Housing Finance & Credit Risk tracks in finance and banking programmes, focused explicitly on underwriting informal incomes; (4) Insolvency, Restructuring & Consumer Protection Law modules in law faculties, with live clinics on PKPU cases and stranded-buyer representation; (5) Industrialised/Modular Construction and Construction Productivity labs within civil engineering; (6) Land Administration, Cadastre & Geospatial programmes in partnership with BPN/ATR and STPN; (7) Urban Regeneration & Retrofit studios in architecture, replacing part of the new-build design studio load — mirroring China's pivot to 城市更新.

RESTRUCTURE RATHER THAN CLOSE: Teknik Sipil should be explicitly re-balanced from a developer-employment assumption toward infrastructure, industrial, water, energy, maintenance and resilience; Arsitektur should shift studio weight from greenfield towers toward renovation, heritage, affordable housing typologies and coastal/climate-adaptive design; Manajemen Properti/Pemasaran Properti curricula should stop being sales-oriented and become asset-management oriented.
> Do NOT close civil engineering or architecture — that would be importing China's outcome without China's cause, and Indonesia's infrastructure pipeline still needs these graduates.

INSTITUTIONAL PRACTICES TO ADOPT: publish graduate employment outcomes by programme so that student demand can adjust on evidence rather than rumour (China's adjustment was chaotic partly because it was rumour-driven); build a standing MOU pipeline with Kementerian PKP, BP Tapera, BTN, OJK and the developer associations (REI, APERSI) for internships in subsidised-housing delivery; and establish a national housing-research centre producing a credible independent price and affordability index — the absence of trustworthy data is itself a structural weakness relative to China, which had NBS 70-city and Beike data throughout its crisis.

### Faktor Risiko & Sisi Gelap

**Risiko Sosial Indonesia**

> (1) A STRANDED-BUYER CRISIS AT SCALE — the clearest and most imminent risk.
> Indonesia runs pre-sale without mandatory escrow, and SEMA 3/2023 has removed buyers' bankruptcy leverage.
> LRT City's ~2,400 stranded buyers being chased by debt collectors for loans on undelivered apartments is a direct rehearsal of China's 2022 mortgage boycott, at 1/1000th of the scale.
> If the 3-million-homes push draws in undercapitalised developers under volume pressure, Indonesia could produce tens of thousands of such cases within three years — with no fiscal capacity for a 保交楼-scale rescue.
> (2) PERMANENT GENERATIONAL EXCLUSION AND ITS DEMOGRAPHIC ECHO — 51% of Gen Z already say they cannot afford a house; inheritance is the dominant acquisition route; Deloitte finds marriage and home purchase both being deferred.
> China's experience shows this hardens into a norm that does not reverse when affordability improves.
> Indonesia is running this risk while still inside its demographic bonus window, which is the worst possible timing: deferred household formation now compounds the fertility decline that will define Indonesia's 2050s.
> (3) ENTRENCHMENT OF INHERITED WEALTH — if ownership passes mainly by inheritance, property becomes the mechanism that freezes the Indonesian class structure, converting an aspirational middle class into a rentier/excluded binary.
> This is more socially corrosive in Indonesia than in China because Indonesian inequality is already higher and land ownership more concentrated.
> (4) PREDATORY SUBSTITUTE CREDIT — households locked out of KPR turn to paylater, pinjol, and multiguna loans at far higher rates; the affordability crisis converts into an unsecured-debt crisis among exactly the households least able to bear it.
> (5) SPECULATIVE LAND FRAUD — kavling and 'properti syariah' Ponzi schemes proliferate precisely when ownership is unattainable and yields are promised at 30-50%; OJK has recorded hundreds of illegal entities in the property and land sector.
> Victims are typically lower-middle-class savers with no recourse.
> (6) FOREIGN-PARENT CONTAGION — Indonesian buyers already hold units in projects by Country Garden (a defaulted Chinese developer) and CFLD (which stalled its Tangerang projects from 2018).
> Without ring-fencing rules, an offshore parent's collapse strands Indonesian households.
> (7) STRANDED STATE INFRASTRUCTURE — an under-populated IKN, or Mandalika/coastal estates built ahead of demand, is the Indonesian ghost-city risk, with the added feature that the losses land on the state budget rather than on private developers.
> (8) DISPLACEMENT AND LAND CONFLICT — the PSN mechanism used for private mega-estates (PIK 2 sea fences, land acquisition disputes) risks reproducing China's demolition-and-relocation conflicts without China's compensation capacity, in a democracy where such conflicts are electorally explosive.
> (9) CONSTRUCTION LABOUR PRECARITY — 8.7 million construction workers, overwhelmingly informal, with no unemployment insurance; a project-finance freeze transmits to household income within weeks.

**Unintended Consequences**

> IN CHINA: (a) The three red lines, designed to prevent a crisis, precipitated it — a textbook case of correct diagnosis destroyed by wrong sequencing.
> (b) Administrative price-drop bans (限跌令) on new homes pushed price discovery entirely into the resale market, which then fell harder and faster, inverting the normal relationship where new homes trade at a premium and creating the bizarre situation of new-build prices holding while identical second-hand units nearby fell 30-40%.
> (c) 保交楼 succeeded at completing 7.5 million homes but, by adding finished supply into a falling market, accelerated the price decline it was partly meant to arrest.
> (d) The property crash pushed millions of displaced construction workers into food delivery and ride-hailing, creating the gig-labour glut and wage deflation that is now a separate policy problem.
> (e) The wealth destruction converted a high-savings, high-investment economy into a deflationary one, making the property crisis the proximate cause of China's consumption downgrade, youth unemployment and export-dependence — all of which then generated trade conflicts abroad.
> (f) Excess construction capacity and materials overcapacity are now being exported, deflating global building-materials prices and threatening manufacturers in importing countries including Indonesia.
> (g) The shelving of the property tax in 2022 left local governments with no replacement for land revenue and no politically feasible path to create one — a permanent fiscal wound caused by a temporary market condition.
> (h) Falling home prices did not improve fertility; the deferral behaviours had already become normalised, so the demographic damage outlived its cause.

PREDICTED FOR INDONESIA: (a) 0% down-payment/100% LTV policy, maintained for years to stimulate demand, maximises the number of buyers with no equity buffer — if any correction occurs, Indonesia will have manufactured its own negative-equity cohort using a policy meant to expand access.
> (b) SEMA 3/2023, intended to protect housing supply by preventing opportunistic bankruptcy petitions, has instead removed the main deterrent against developers taking buyer money and not delivering — protecting the supply side by disarming the demand side.
> (c) The 3-million-homes volume target, if pursued through quota pressure, will select for developers willing to promise cheaply rather than build reliably, manufacturing exactly the stalled-project problem it is meant to solve.
> (d) PPN DTP and other demand subsidies in a supply-constrained market are largely capitalised into land prices, transferring public money to landowners rather than to buyers.
> (e) Subsidised housing built where land is cheap — far from jobs and transit — creates remote unsold or abandoned estates, Indonesia's low-income version of China's tier-3 glut, and locks poor households into high commuting costs.
> (f) Tapera's mandatory 3% deduction, intended to fund housing, functions as a regressive payroll tax on workers who will never qualify for the housing it funds, and its funds' allocation to government bonds rather than housing has already drawn analyst criticism.
> (g) Chinese materials deflation lowers construction costs — good for affordability, bad for Indonesian building-materials employment — an unintended industrial-policy collision.

**Kelompok Rentan**

> (1) URBAN GEN Z AND YOUNGER MILLENNIALS WITHOUT PROPERTY-OWNING PARENTS — the single most affected group; 51% of Gen Z and 40% of millennials already report inability to buy, only 10% obtained a KPR, and inheritance is the dominant route, meaning those without inheritable property face permanent exclusion.
> (2) INFORMAL AND GIG WORKERS (>55% of the workforce, plus ~4-5 million platform drivers and couriers) — structurally unbankable for a KPR regardless of actual income; excluded from FLPP by documentation requirements; simultaneously the group most exposed to construction-sector job losses.
> (3) BUYERS OF UNFINISHED PRE-SOLD UNITS — the LRT City and Meikarta cohorts: households servicing KPA instalments and being pursued by debt collectors for assets that do not exist, with SEMA 3/2023 blocking their strongest legal remedy.
> This group faces total loss of a lifetime's savings.
> (4) LOW-INCOME (MBR) HOUSEHOLDS — 83.3% of the 9.9-15 million unit backlog, dependent on an FLPP programme that delivered only 22.15% of quota by mid-2026, and on remote subsidised estates with poor jobs access.
> (5) CONSTRUCTION WORKERS — 8.7 million people, overwhelmingly informal, without unemployment insurance, whose incomes stop within weeks of a project-finance freeze; disproportionately migrant, male, low-education, and supporting rural households through remittances.
> (6) SMALL SAVERS TARGETED BY LAND AND SYARIAH-PROPERTY SCHEMES — typically lower-middle-class, religiously motivated, and outside OJK-supervised products; hundreds of illegal entities recorded in the property and land sector.
> (7) RESIDENTS DISPLACED BY PSN AND MEGA-ESTATE LAND ACQUISITION — fishing and farming communities around PIK 2, Mandalika, Rempang and coastal estates, with weak title and weak bargaining power.
> (8) BALINESE AND OTHER LOCAL POPULATIONS IN TOURISM PROPERTY HOTSPOTS — priced out of their own land by foreign and Jakarta capital, the most extreme local affordability gap in Indonesia.
> (9) SANDWICH-GENERATION HOUSEHOLDS — young workers simultaneously supporting parents and attempting to save a down payment, for whom Tapera's 3% deduction is a direct income loss with a distant and uncertain benefit.
> (10) SMALL AND REGIONAL DEVELOPERS — thinly capitalised firms pulled into subsidised-housing volume targets, who bear the residual risk when land, materials or financing costs move against them.

### Contoh Kasus Konkret

**Padanan Indonesia**

> MEIKARTA (Lippo Cikarang) is Indonesia's Evergrande-in-miniature and its clearest 烂尾楼 analogue: a Rp 278 trillion 'city' announced in 2017 with saturation advertising, sold aggressively off-plan, entangled in a permit-bribery prosecution, delivering only a fraction of promised units, and by 2023 suing its own complaining buyers; by January 2026 the government was proposing to convert parts of it into subsidised rusun.
> LRT CITY (Adhi Commuter Properti) is the 2025-2026 sequel and the closer parallel to China's mortgage-boycott moment: TOD-branded towers at Ciracas, Tebet and Bekasi topped out but abandoned at the finishing stage from mid-2025, ~2,400 buyers left without units in July 2026, some pursued by debt collectors for KPA instalments, with the Housing Ministry and Danantara brought in — the first time an Indonesian sovereign-fund vehicle has been used to resolve a stranded-buyer crisis.
> PT HANSON INTERNATIONAL (MYRX) is the landbank-leverage analogue: a claimed ~5,000 hectare landbank (Citra Maja Raya, Forest Hill, Millenium City), unlicensed public fund-raising flagged by OJK in 2019, entanglement in the Jiwasraya and Asabri scandals, and bankruptcy in 2020.
> THE JAKARTA APARTMENT GLUT is the investor-demand-collapse analogue: >5,000 unsold units, roughly 150 units sold in Jakarta in H1 2025, and secondary prices flat for 2-3 years — a small, contained version of what happened across Chinese tier-3 cities.
> PIK 2 is the state-designated mega-estate analogue: a ~Rp 40 trillion PSN-designated coastal project by Agung Sedayu/Salim that has generated land-acquisition and sea-fence conflict, structurally echoing the Chinese pattern of state designation plus single-developer land assembly.
> IKN NUSANTARA is the state-built new-city analogue and Indonesia's clearest ghost-city risk.
> THE AFFORDABILITY DATA is the human analogue and the most advanced of all: 51% of Gen Z and 40% of millennials unable to buy, only 10% using a KPR, inheritance the dominant route, marriage and home purchase both being deferred — precisely the social pattern China produced a decade earlier.
> Finally, COUNTRY GARDEN'S SKY HOUSE BSD+ / ALAM SUTERA+ AND CFLD'S TANGERANG PROJECTS are the literal transmission: Indonesian households holding units in projects owned by Chinese developers that have already defaulted or stalled at home.
