### Tingkat Keyakinan & Kualitas Sumber

**Catatan Kontradiksi Data**

> (1) THE -7.6% YoY SECOND-HAND FIGURE.
> The research brief cites -7.6% YoY for October 2025, but this cannot be matched to the NBS 70-city aggregate: the NBS October 2025 release shows second-hand YoY indices of 95.3-96.7 for tier-1 cities and worst-case readings of 91.7 (tier-2) and 91.0 (tier-3), while Reuters/Caixin reporting put the December 2025 national second-hand decline at -6.1% YoY.
> A -7.6% figure is plausible for a private 100-city index (China Index Academy/CRIC) or for a particular tier, and by June 2026 the CIA 100-city readings had reached -6.95% (tier-1), -8.21% (tier-2) and -7.48% (tier-3/4), bracketing -7.6%.
> Treat the number as directionally correct but index-ambiguous.
> (2) OFFICIAL VS MARKET PRICE DECLINES.
> The NBS 70-city index shows cumulative declines of roughly 10-20% from peak, while listing data, brokerage data and market commentary indicate 30-50% in many cities.
> This gap is systematic, not random: administrative price-drop bans, developer 'gift' incentives that disguise effective discounts, and index-construction choices all bias official data upward.
> Any analysis relying solely on NBS numbers will understate the crisis; any analysis relying solely on commentary will overstate it.
> (3) INDONESIAN BACKLOG.
> BPS 2023 gives 9.9 million units; the Deputy Minister of PKP cited ~15 million households in 2025; industry sources (Majalah REI) explicitly note the absence of an agreed definition (ownership backlog vs occupancy backlog vs habitability).
> The 3-million-homes programme's target rests on a number nobody agrees on.
> (4) MORTGAGE/GDP COMPARISONS.
> The Indonesia ~3.4% figure is current; the comparison set found (Malaysia 31%, India 7%, China 15%) is from 2008 and is not contemporaneous — China's household mortgage stock is now far above 15% of GDP.
> The direction of the comparison is robust; the specific ratios should not be quoted together.
> (5) INDONESIAN APARTMENT MARKET NARRATIVE.
> Sources conflict sharply: some consultancies describe 'stabilisation', 88% occupancy and 'disciplined supply', while Bisnis Indonesia reports >5,000 unsold units and only ~150 Jakarta units sold in H1 2025.
> The reconciliation is that occupancy (of delivered, largely rented stock) and primary sales (of new stock) are different things; the sales figure is the stress signal.
> (6) INDONESIAN CIVIL ENGINEERING OUTLOOK.
> Indonesian career-guidance sources uniformly describe civil engineering as a low-unemployment major with strong prospects, which is currently true given infrastructure spending; this sits in direct tension with the Chinese experience and with the medium-term risk if property development stalls.
> Both can be true at different horizons.
> (7) CHINA'S 保交楼 CLAIMS.
> The 7.5 million completed homes and RMB 7 trillion whitelist figures are state-reported and not independently verifiable; independent researchers (Jamestown, Asia Society) emphasise a persistent policy-reality gap.
> (8) VANKE'S STATUS.
> Reporting varies between 'averted default', 'near-default' and 'default risk resurfacing' depending on the date and on whether offshore or onshore instruments are meant; the accurate framing is repeated grace-period extensions rather than a resolution.

## 11. Youth Unemployment & Anti-Hustle Culture (the involution -> lying-flat -> let-it-rot -> rat-people continuum: mass graduate under-employment producing a self-organised culture of withdrawal, anti-productivity and nocturnal social retreat)
**Kategori**: Ketenagakerjaan (Labour & Employment) — with heavy spillover into Pendidikan (Higher Education), Kesehatan Mental (Public Mental Health), Ekonomi Konsumsi (Consumption/Demand) and Stabilitas Sosial-Politik

📊 HYBRID, and the mix is the whole story: LEAPFROG/SIMULTANEOUS on the symbolic layer (memes of refusal arrive within months via algorithmic diffusion), LAGGARD by 2-3 years on the labour-market structure and by 4-6 years on policy machinery, PARTIALLY CANCELLED on the specific behavioural end-state (mass withdrawal requires family wealth Indonesia lacks), and REVERSE on the expression channel (Indonesian youth externalise the same grievance into street protest and emigration years before Chinese youth internalised theirs into withdrawal — Hirschman's EXIT and VOICE where China got LOYALTY-as-passivity). The most consequential asymmetry is not timing but income: Indonesia is reaching Chinese-level youth unemployment at roughly USD 5,000 GDP per capita, whereas China hit its record at roughly USD 12,600-13,000 — a 'worse-outcome laggard' pattern, i.e. the same distress with a much thinner cushion. | 🎯 Prob: Tinggi (High) for the cultural/discursive form and for anti-hustle norms in the workplace; Sedang (Medium) for a genuinely mass, sustained withdrawal behaviour among urban educated youth; Rendah-Sedang (Low-Medium) for the full Chinese end-state of long-run family-financed non-participation ('full-time children' as a recognised social role). | 🔍 Keyakinan: Sedang-Tinggi (Medium-High). Tinggi (High) for: the Chinese cultural genealogy and its dating (involution 2020, tang ping April-May 2021, bai lan 2022, rat literature/Kong Yiji 2023, rat people March-April 2025), all official labour statistics on both sides (NBS youth unemployment series including the 21.3% June 2023 record and the 18.9% August 2025 record; BPS 15-24 TPT of 16.26% Nov 2025 and 16.36% Feb 2026; 1,033,737 unemployed tertiary graduates Feb 2026), the Chinese education-policy response (12,200 programmes cut 2021-2025, the March 2023 20% adjustment guideline, 2,600 micro-majors), the Chinese employment-policy package (17 measures April 2025), the exam data (3.718 million 2026 civil-service applicants; 3.43 million kaoyan), the anti-involution campaign's official status (1 July 2025, Fourth Plenum October 2025), and the Indonesian cultural facts (#KaburAjaDulu, the August 2025 protests, I-NAMHS 2022 baselines, DataReportal digital figures). Sedang (Medium) for: the view-count magnitudes of the 老鼠人 meme (Chinese marketing-industry estimates that vary by an order of magnitude), the Indonesian survey figures on quiet quitting and burnout (single-vendor online panels), the 9.9 million NEET figure (2023 vintage, definitional sensitivity), and all lag quantification. Rendah (Low) for: the forward timeline (mainstream 2027-2029, peak 2030-2034), the claim about relative strength of the withdrawal versus protest channel in Indonesia, and any estimate of how large an Indonesian withdrawal cohort could become.

> **Status di Indonesia**: Split status. The AESTHETIC/DISCURSIVE layer has already arrived (masif, effectively simultaneous): Indonesian media, TikTok and campus discourse covered 'manusia tikus' during 2025, and the domestic vocabulary of refusal — mager, rebahan, healing, self-reward, nolep, quiet quitting, #KaburAjaDulu — is already mainstream. The STRUCTURAL condition (record youth unemployment, graduate under-employment, credential devaluation) is also already present and worsening. What has NOT arrived at scale is the specific Chinese end-state — full economic withdrawal financed by family wealth, sustained nocturnal isolation as a mass lifestyle, and voluntary exit from the labour force by educated urban youth. Indonesian youth today mostly cannot afford to withdraw: they convert the same despair into gig work (ojol, freelancing), migration ambitions, informal hustling, or street politics. So: 'baru mulai' on the behavioural layer, 'sudah masuk masif' on the meme layer, 'sudah masiv' on the underlying labour-market condition.

### Basic Info

**Pemain Kunci China**

> This is a bottom-up cultural trend, so the 'key players' are platforms, symbolic originators, and the institutions reacting to it.
> Platforms/amplifiers: Douyin (抖音) — the single largest carrier of 老鼠人 vlogs; Xiaohongshu (RED/小红书) — where '低能量' topped the trending list; Bilibili (B站) — home of 鼠鼠文学 and 摆烂 video culture; Baidu Tieba (百度贴吧) — birthplace of both 躺平 (Luo Huazhong, 2021) and much rat-literature; Weibo (微博) — mainstreaming and state-media pushback; Zhihu (知乎) — the long-form debate layer; Kuaishou (快手) — small-town/rural variant.
> Symbolic originators: Luo Huazhong (骆华忠, the original 'lying-flat master'); anonymous Chinese overseas students in the UK who coined the 'rat person' day-in-the-life vlog format.
> Commercial actors that monetised the meme (March-April 2025): Meituan (美团), Tmall (天猫), Alibaba 1688, Midea (美的), Guoquan Shihui (锅圈食汇), snack and tissue brands, plus the sleep-economy/宅经济 cluster (short-lease studio rentals, cheap meal boxes, sleep aids, mobile/idle games).
> Institutional actors: National Bureau of Statistics (NBS), Ministry of Human Resources and Social Security (MOHRSS), Ministry of Education (MOE), Xinhua/People's Daily/Guangming Daily (the discourse-management arm), the Communist Youth League, and from July 2025 the Central Financial and Economic Affairs Commission which turned '反内卷' (anti-involution) into official macro policy.

### China Trend Detail

**Apa Yang Terjadi Di China**

> China has produced, in roughly five years, the world's most articulated youth counter-culture of refusal — and the underlying driver is a labour-market arithmetic failure, not laziness.
> Mechanism: (a) Higher-education expansion outran the creation of graduate-grade jobs.
> Annual college graduates rose from ~8.7 million (2019) to 11.79 million (2024), 12.22 million (2025) and a record 12.7 million (2026), while the sectors that historically absorbed them — internet platforms, private tutoring, real estate, finance — were simultaneously hit by regulatory crackdowns (2021), a property bust (2021-) and cost-cutting.
> (b) The result is 'involution' (内卷): more credentials, more hours, more test-taking for the same or shrinking prize.
> Master's degrees and civil-service exams become defensive purchases rather than upgrades.
> (c) When effort stops paying, the rational individual response is to reduce effort and consumption to the point where the system cannot extract more — 躺平 (lie flat): minimal work, minimal spending, no marriage, no mortgage, no children.
> (d) 摆烂 (let it rot, 2022) radicalised this from strategic rest to demonstrative self-abandonment.
> (e) 鼠鼠文学 (2023) supplied the emotional grammar — speaking of oneself in the third person as a sewer rat, a creature with no claim on dignity — which pairs with 孔乙己文学 (March 2023), where a degree becomes a gown you cannot remove to take a manual job.
> (f) 老鼠人 (2025) is the behavioural end-state: a nocturnal, low-stimulus, low-desire, delivery-fed existence in a rented room — wake around 11:00, scroll in bed, first meal around 15:00, no daylight, no social contact, sleep after midnight, repeat.
> It is not primarily protest and it is not clinical hikikomori; it is a self-mocking identity (自黑) that converts economic humiliation into shareable comedy.
> Scale of the phenomenon is genuinely mass: Douyin generated more than a dozen related hashtags in 2025, with a single topic passing 1.47 billion views and cross-platform totals reported in the multi-billions.
> Critically, the state's response evolved from moral condemnation (Xinhua calling lying flat 'shameful' in 2021, censorship of tang-ping forums) to partial adoption of the youth diagnosis: by July 2025 Xi Jinping's own agenda item was '反内卷' — rectifying 'involutionary competition' — applied to firms and local governments rather than to individuals.
> In other words, the state accepted the word the youth invented, then redirected it at industrial price wars.
> Meanwhile the material adaptations institutionalised: 全职儿女 ('full-time children' paid an allowance by parents for domestic labour and companionship), 慢就业 ('slow employment' — deliberately delaying entry), mass exam-taking (3.718 million applicants cleared screening for the 2026 civil-service exam, ~2.9x the 2019 level, against ~38,100 posts), and a shift of graduates into delivery, livestream and other flexible work inside a ~200-million-strong flexible-employment pool.

**Fase Tren Di China**

> Mature and institutionalised, moving into a managed/co-opted phase rather than declining.
> Evidence for 'mature': the vocabulary has completed a full generational cycle (involution -> lie flat -> let it rot -> rat literature -> rat people) with each stage more behavioural and less rhetorical than the last; the 2025 rat-people wave was commercialised by mainstream brands within roughly a month of going viral, which is the classic signature of a subculture crossing into mass culture.
> Evidence for 'managed/co-opted': the state stopped fighting the diagnosis and adopted the word — '反内卷' became formal economic policy from July 2025 (Central Financial and Economic Affairs Commission, 1 July 2025) and was written into the Fourth Plenum decision of October 2025 — while public-opinion units (e.g.
> provincial 舆情 monitoring reports in mid-2025) now analyse 老鼠人 as a sentiment indicator rather than as deviance to be censored.
> Evidence against 'declining': youth unemployment set a new record under the current methodology in August 2025, i.e.
> after the meme peaked, and although the rate fell through the first half of 2026 (14.9% in June 2026), the graduate cohort keeps hitting records.
> The cultural form will keep mutating (a successor label after 老鼠人 should be expected roughly every 12-24 months); the underlying condition is structural and will outlast any one label.

### Status Indonesia Saat Ini

**Status Di Indonesia**

> Split status.
> The AESTHETIC/DISCURSIVE layer has already arrived (masif, effectively simultaneous): Indonesian media, TikTok and campus discourse covered 'manusia tikus' during 2025, and the domestic vocabulary of refusal — mager, rebahan, healing, self-reward, nolep, quiet quitting, #KaburAjaDulu — is already mainstream.
> The STRUCTURAL condition (record youth unemployment, graduate under-employment, credential devaluation) is also already present and worsening.
> What has NOT arrived at scale is the specific Chinese end-state — full economic withdrawal financed by family wealth, sustained nocturnal isolation as a mass lifestyle, and voluntary exit from the labour force by educated urban youth.
> Indonesian youth today mostly cannot afford to withdraw: they convert the same despair into gig work (ojol, freelancing), migration ambitions, informal hustling, or street politics.
> So: 'baru mulai' on the behavioural layer, 'sudah masuk masif' on the meme layer, 'sudah masiv' on the underlying labour-market condition.

### Analisis Lag

**Bukti Historical Lag**

> (1) Meme diffusion is already near-zero-lag: the Labubu/Pop Mart wave reached Indonesia in 2025 against a Chinese scale-up of 2019-2020 for the product, but the CONTENT wave moved within months; likewise 'brain rot', 'quiet quitting' and 'doom spending' entered Indonesian usage within one year of their Anglophone/Chinese peaks.
> Cultural lag has compressed from years to months since TikTok/Reels reached ~180 million Indonesian reach.
> (2) Labour-market consequence lag runs 3-5 years, consistent with the sibling analysis in this research set: China's algorithmic-exploitation reckoning peaked September 2020 and produced binding guidance by July 2021, while Indonesia's equivalent reached presidential level only in 2025-2026; China's youth-unemployment record was mid-2023, Indonesia's graduate-unemployment issue became a headline political fight in 2025.
> (3) Credential devaluation followed the same path with a lag: China's 孔乙己文学 (the useless-degree lament) went viral in March 2023; Indonesia's mass 'sarjana menganggur' discourse and the data showing tertiary TPT (6.13%) above the national average (4.68%) became a standing national argument in 2025-2026 — a 2-3 year gap.
> (4) Education-system response lag is wider: China's Ministry of Education ordered ~20% of programmes optimised in March 2023 and cut 12,200 undergraduate programmes over 2021-2025; Indonesia closed 122 programmes in 2026 — the same policy instinct, roughly three years later and two orders of magnitude smaller.
> (5) Counter-evidence for a REVERSE element: Indonesia's youth political explosion (August 2025, 30+ provinces, ~3,195 detained) has no Chinese analogue at all; on the 'voice' dimension Indonesia is ahead, not behind.

**Tipe Lag**

> HYBRID, and the mix is the whole story: LEAPFROG/SIMULTANEOUS on the symbolic layer (memes of refusal arrive within months via algorithmic diffusion), LAGGARD by 2-3 years on the labour-market structure and by 4-6 years on policy machinery, PARTIALLY CANCELLED on the specific behavioural end-state (mass withdrawal requires family wealth Indonesia lacks), and REVERSE on the expression channel (Indonesian youth externalise the same grievance into street protest and emigration years before Chinese youth internalised theirs into withdrawal — Hirschman's EXIT and VOICE where China got LOYALTY-as-passivity).
> The most consequential asymmetry is not timing but income: Indonesia is reaching Chinese-level youth unemployment at roughly USD 5,000 GDP per capita, whereas China hit its record at roughly USD 12,600-13,000 — a 'worse-outcome laggard' pattern, i.e.
> the same distress with a much thinner cushion.

### Probabilitas Transfer ke Indonesia

**Probabilitas Transfer**

> Tinggi (High) for the cultural/discursive form and for anti-hustle norms in the workplace; Sedang (Medium) for a genuinely mass, sustained withdrawal behaviour among urban educated youth; Rendah-Sedang (Low-Medium) for the full Chinese end-state of long-run family-financed non-participation ('full-time children' as a recognised social role).

**Alasan Probabilitas**

> High for the cultural layer because every precondition is already satisfied: 230 million internet users, 180 million TikTok-reachable people, ~22 hours a week of social video, a youth unemployment rate (16.36%, Feb 2026) statistically comparable to China's, tertiary graduates whose unemployment rate (6.13%) exceeds the national average, ~9.9 million NEET Gen Z, a shrinking middle class, and an existing native vocabulary (mager, rebahan, nolep, healing, quiet quitting) that the Chinese frame slots into without translation friction.
> Memes of refusal are cheap to adopt and socially rewarding — they convert private failure into shared comedy.
> Medium for the behavioural layer because Indonesia lacks the two enabling conditions that made Chinese lying-flat survivable: (i) household wealth — Chinese urban parents hold property and savings that can fund a non-working adult child, whereas Indonesian households were still drawing down savings (76.3%) merely to cover normal expenses in 2026; and (ii) a dense, cheap, delivery-plus-rental infrastructure that makes a room-bound life logistically possible at low cost across many cities.
> Low-Medium for full withdrawal because Indonesian informal-sector absorption gives young people an always-available fallback (ojol, warung, freelance, family enterprise) — the Indonesian equivalent of lying flat is not lying in bed, it is under-employment that looks like work.
> Additional accelerant: Indonesia's own political channel means grievance can convert into mobilisation rather than resignation, which paradoxically slows the withdrawal culture while raising political risk.

**Vektor Transmisi**

> (c) ALGORITHMIC CONTENT DIFFUSION is the dominant vector and it is already operating: the 老鼠人/低能量 format is a highly portable video grammar (POV shot from bed, dark room, delivery bag, reversed clock) that survives translation, and TikTok — the same ByteDance recommendation stack that carried it in China — reaches ~180 million Indonesians.
> Indonesian-language explainers of 'manusia tikus' appeared in 2025 and the raw local equivalents (mager, rebahan, nolep) provide instant subtitling.
> (b) LOCAL COPYCAT/RELABELLING is the second vector: Indonesian creators will not import the Chinese word; they will mint a local one — expect a bahasa-gaul successor to 'kaum rebahan' and 'nolep' with an explicit economic-futility framing.
> (a) DIRECT ENTRY OF CHINESE PLAYERS matters indirectly rather than directly: it is not that Chinese firms export the culture, but that the Chinese-platform consumption stack that makes withdrawal survivable (ultra-cheap food delivery, sub-Rp 15,000 meal bundles, Shopee/TikTok Shop/Temu-style cheap goods, cloud/idle gaming, short-drama apps — several of them Chinese-origin) is being installed in Indonesia now; that infrastructure is the true carrier.
> (d) CHINESE VENTURE CAPITAL is a weak vector for the culture but a strong one for the infrastructure (short-drama, mini-game, live-stream and cheap-delivery investment).
> (e) DIASPORA/ALUMNI is a real but narrow channel — the rat-person vlog was itself invented by Chinese students abroad, and Indonesian students in China (and in Australia, UK, Japan, Korea) plus the large Indonesian TikTok-Chinese-content translation ecosystem carry the frame home.
> A SIXTH vector specific to this topic: ACADEMIC AND MEDIA IMPORT — Indonesian universities, think-tanks and journalists have begun using 'tang ping', 'involution' and 'rat people' as analytical labels for Indonesian conditions, which legitimises the frame faster than organic adoption would.

### Faktor Pendorong

**Prasyarat Struktural**

> THRESHOLDS AND INDONESIA'S POSITION VERSUS CHINA AT ITS TRIGGER POINT.
> (1) Higher-education mass participation outrunning graduate-job creation.
> China: gross tertiary enrolment ~60.8% (2024) and 12.2-12.7 million graduates a year when lying flat matured.
> Indonesia: gross tertiary enrolment ~45% (2023), projected to add ~4.3 million students over the next decade toward ~13 million enrolled.
> Indonesia is BELOW the Chinese threshold but rising, and is projected to become the world's third-largest university system by 2035 — meaning the graduate-oversupply pressure will intensify structurally through the 2030s.
> (2) Income level at onset.
> China's lying-flat moment came at roughly USD 12,000-13,000 GDP per capita; Indonesia is around USD 5,000.
> This is the single biggest divergence: Indonesia is hitting Chinese-level youth unemployment at roughly one-third the income, which makes withdrawal materially unaffordable but makes the emotional content MORE resonant, not less.
> (3) Urbanisation and rental-room living.
> China's rat-people archetype presupposes a single young adult living alone in a rented urban room.
> China is ~67% urban; Indonesia ~58-59% and, crucially, Indonesian urban youth far more often live in the family home or a kos with dense social surveillance — which suppresses invisible withdrawal.
> (4) Cheap delivery and low-cost consumption stack.
> A room-bound life requires sub-USD 2 meal delivery at national scale.
> Indonesia has this in Jabodetabek and major cities via GoFood/GrabFood/ShopeeFood promotions, but at higher real cost relative to income than China.
> (5) Digital saturation.
> Indonesia already exceeds the threshold: 80.5% internet penetration, ~22 hours/week of social video.
> (6) Family safety net without state safety net.
> China's version is financed by parental property wealth; Indonesia has neither the parental wealth nor unemployment insurance of meaningful duration (JKP coverage is narrow and formal-sector only) — so the Indonesian variant must be work-adjacent.
> (7) A salient credential-devaluation signal.
> Indonesia already has it: tertiary TPT (6.13%) above national TPT (4.68%), and 1.03 million unemployed degree-holders.

**Indikator Pemantauan**

> Leading indicators that the trend is arriving in force: (1) BPS Sakernas — sustained rise in the 15-24 TPT above 17% AND, more diagnostically, a FALL in the youth labour-force participation rate alongside it (withdrawal shows up as LFPR decline, not unemployment); track also the 'never worked' share of young unemployed (2.81 million of 3.93 million in Aug 2024).
> (2) The NEET series — movement of the ~9.9 million Gen Z NEET figure toward 11-12 million, and a rising MALE share (currently female-dominated for care reasons; a male shift signals genuine discouragement, not domestic work).
> (3) Google Trends / TikTok hashtag volumes in Indonesian for a native withdrawal label (successors to 'mager', 'nolep', 'kaum rebahan'; watch for a coined term such as 'manusia tikus', 'generasi gelap' or a fresh slang noun) and for 'burnout', 'resign', 'kerja gak worth it', '#KaburAjaDulu'.
> (4) Emigration proxies: BP2MI/KP2MI placement data, working-holiday and Japan/Korea/Germany visa applications, IELTS test volumes, passport issuance among under-30s.
> (5) Employer-side indicators: JobStreet/Kalibrr posting-to-application ratios for fresh graduates, starting-salary stagnation in real terms, and the share of graduate hires in non-graduate roles.
> (6) Consumption tells: growth in single-serving cheap meal bundles, kos/co-living occupancy at the low end, night-time delivery order share (22:00-04:00), mobile-game and short-drama night-time DAU, sleep-aid and instant-noodle volumes.
> (7) Institutional tells: universities creating career-anxiety/mental-health units; Kemnaker or Kemendiktisaintek publishing a youth-specific employment package; the appearance of an Indonesian 'anti-involution' or 'anti-hustle' policy vocabulary.
> (8) Mental-health system load: national helpline volumes, campus counselling waiting lists, and any repeat of I-NAMHS showing deterioration from the 34.9% baseline.

### Hambatan & Faktor Pembatal

**Hambatan Transfer**

> (1) ECONOMIC: Indonesian young people mostly cannot afford non-participation.
> Household savings are already being drawn down (76.3% dipping into savings), the middle class shrank to 46.7 million in 2025, and there is no unemployment benefit of meaningful scope — so the cost of a month in bed is borne directly by a family that cannot absorb it.
> (2) SOCIAL-STRUCTURAL: extended-family and neighbourhood density (kos culture, RT/RW, mosque and church networks, kampung sociality) makes invisible withdrawal socially expensive in a way that atomised Chinese one-child urban households do not.
> (3) RELIGIOUS-NORMATIVE: work-as-ibadah framing and strong intergenerational obligation norms give idleness a moral charge that Chinese secular-Confucian achievement culture frames differently (China's youth rebelled against a productivity ethic; Indonesia's youth face a religious-familial obligation ethic that is harder to satirise publicly).
> (4) LABOUR-MARKET SHAPE: an ~59-60% informal sector plus a huge gig layer means there is almost always SOMETHING to do for cash, which converts would-be lying-flat into underemployment.
> (5) DEMOGRAPHIC-STRUCTURAL: Indonesia's tertiary participation (~45%) is still well below China's (60.8%), so the specific pathology of surplus graduates is at maybe two-thirds of Chinese intensity today.
> (6) POLITICAL-CHANNEL SUBSTITUTION: an open (if contested) protest space means grievance has a public outlet; passive withdrawal competes with active mobilisation for the same energy.
> (7) LANGUAGE/PLATFORM: Chinese-origin memes still require translation and re-anchoring; the specific rat imagery (sewer rat, 鼠鼠) carries connotations that do not map cleanly onto Indonesian symbolic registers.

**Faktor Pembatal Transfer**

> Conditions that mean the Chinese form will NOT be replicated one-to-one in Indonesia, however severe youth unemployment becomes.
> (1) NO PARENTAL WEALTH BUFFER.
> The Chinese variant is quietly financed by a generation of urban parents who own appreciated property, hold high savings rates, and — because of the one-child policy — concentrate all resources on a single child; this is what makes 全职儿女 ('full-time children' on a parental allowance) possible.
> Indonesian families have low home equity in liquid terms, ~2.3-2.5 children per household historically, and are themselves net dissavers right now.
> A paid 'full-time child' is not a viable Indonesian social role at scale.
> (2) NO STATE INCOME FLOOR FOR THE YOUNG.
> China at least offers dense subsidised training, hiring subsidies and rural fallback (village land rights, hukou-linked homestead); Indonesian youth have neither land-right fallback of similar strength nor a youth benefit — Kartu Prakerja is a training stipend, not income support.
> (3) DIFFERENT LABOUR-MARKET GEOMETRY.
> China's distress is a graduate-glut problem inside a formalised urban economy; Indonesia's is a formal-job-scarcity problem inside an informal economy with premature deindustrialisation.
> Indonesia's youth are more likely to be invisibly under-employed than visibly unemployed, so the culture that emerges will valorise 'working hard for nothing' (a hustle-fatigue culture) rather than 'refusing to work' (a withdrawal culture).
> (4) ARCHIPELAGIC GEOGRAPHY AND LOGISTICS COST.
> The room-bound life is subsidised in China by a delivery network of extreme density and cost efficiency.
> Outside Jabodetabek, Surabaya, Bandung, Medan and Makassar, Indonesian delivery economics cannot support a Rp 10,000-15,000 hot meal at scale — the rat-person life is not logistically available in most of the country.
> (5) HOUSING PATTERN.
> Solo occupancy in a private flat is a Chinese urban norm and an Indonesian exception; Indonesian young adults live with family or in shared kos far longer, and cohabitation destroys the privacy withdrawal requires.
> (6) YOUNGER DEMOGRAPHIC POSITION.
> China's youth despair is amplified by a shrinking cohort facing an ageing dependency burden; Indonesia is still inside a demographic bonus window to roughly 2035-2045, which changes the emotional register from terminal decline to squandered opportunity — anger rather than resignation.
> (7) OPEN EXIT OPTION.
> Indonesians can, and increasingly do, emigrate (#KaburAjaDulu); Chinese youth face harder exit friction, which pushes their coping inward.

### Prediksi Timeline di Indonesia

**Tahun Masuk Indonesia**

> Already entered — 2024-2025.
> The discursive entry point is December 2024 to February 2025 (#KaburAjaDulu going viral) plus the 2025 Indonesian-language coverage of China's 'manusia tikus'.
> The structural entry point is 2024-2026: youth TPT at 16.26-16.36%, ~9.9 million NEET Gen Z, and unemployed degree-holders crossing 1 million and still rising in February 2026.
> Treat 2025 as the year the frame became legible in Indonesia and 2026 as the year the data made it undeniable.

**Skenario Percepatan**

> Fastest accelerants, roughly in order of impact: (1) AI displacement of entry-level white-collar work (admin, customer service, junior analytics, content) removing the very rungs graduates use to enter; (2) a macro shock — rupiah/commodity crisis or a large-scale manufacturing/textile layoff wave — that pushes national TPT above 6%; (3) a viral Indonesian-language withdrawal label plus a hit short-drama or creator archetype that makes it aspirational-ironic; (4) continued real-wage stagnation with rising costs (VAT/tax changes, subsidised-fuel adjustments, housing costs) so that working full-time visibly fails to deliver a livable outcome; (5) closure of the emigration valve (visa tightening in Japan/Korea/Australia/Germany) which would redirect #KaburAjaDulu energy from exit back into withdrawal; (6) repression of the protest channel, which converts VOICE into passive refusal — the single most likely mechanism by which Indonesia would move from the 2025 protest mode toward the Chinese withdrawal mode; (7) cheap, dense delivery and micro-living infrastructure reaching tier-2 cities, making the room-bound life logistically affordable outside Jabodetabek.

### Dampak Sosial-Ekonomi

**Dampak Kelas Menengah**

> This trend is a middle-class disease specifically — it attacks the class whose entire strategy is credential-based mobility.
> Indonesia's middle class shrank to ~46.7 million in 2025 (-1.1 million y/y, worse than 2024's -400,000) with ~142 million 'aspiring middle class' below it; the household bargain — sell land or take debt to fund a degree, expect a formal salaried job in return — is visibly failing when tertiary TPT (6.13%) exceeds national TPT (4.68%).
> Consequences: (1) INTERGENERATIONAL CONFLICT — parents who paid for the degree read withdrawal as ingratitude, producing exactly the family friction Chinese 'full-time children' households report; (2) DELAYED FAMILY FORMATION — Indonesian marriage registrations and fertility are already trending down, and China's experience shows youth economic despair translating into a decade of falling marriages and a birth collapse; Indonesia risks compressing its demographic-bonus window from the demand side; (3) CONSUMPTION DOWNGRADE AND DOOM SPENDING SIMULTANEOUSLY — the same cohort trades down on staples (frugal living, makan tabungan at 76.3%) while spending disproportionately on small emotional purchases (coffee, gacha/blind box, mobile games, short-form entertainment), which is precisely the Chinese 'emotional consumption' pattern; (4) SAVINGS AND ASSET FORMATION COLLAPSE — a cohort that never accumulates housing equity in its twenties will be structurally poorer at fifty, converting a cyclical problem into a permanent class demotion; (5) POLITICAL VOLATILITY — the August 2025 protests were disproportionately a middle-class-adjacent youth phenomenon, and thwarted middle-class expectation is historically the most politically combustible condition in Indonesia.

**Dampak Daerah Non Jawa**

> Not a Java-only phenomenon, but it takes two different forms.
> IN BIG CITIES (Jabodetabek, Bandung, Surabaya, Semarang, Yogyakarta, plus Medan, Makassar, Denpasar, Balikpapan, Pekanbaru): the full Chinese-style pattern is possible — rented kos, delivery-fed, nocturnal, socially isolated — because the delivery, co-living and mobile-entertainment infrastructure exists.
> Yogyakarta and Malang are particularly exposed: student cities with huge graduate outputs, low local wage ceilings and cheap kos, i.e.
> the exact conditions for post-graduation stasis.
> OUTSIDE THOSE CITIES: the withdrawal form is materially unavailable (no cheap delivery density, no solo housing, high family surveillance), so the same economic distress expresses as (a) return migration to the family home and absorption into farm, fishery or family-trade work that looks like employment but is disguised underemployment; (b) out-migration to Java or abroad (PMI placement); (c) NEET status among young women in particular, which is already the dominant Indonesian NEET pattern.
> There is also an important regional asymmetry in the DATA: provinces with high youth unemployment (Aceh, West Java, Banten, Maluku, North Sulawesi have historically ranked high) will show the labour symptom first, while the CULTURAL symptom will appear first in Java's student cities and be exported outward by returning graduates and by TikTok.
> Policy implication: an anti-withdrawal strategy targeted only at Jakarta will miss the larger, quieter non-Java version, where the failure mode is invisible underemployment and female NEET status rather than viral nocturnal vlogs.

### Kaitan Pendidikan

**Jurusan Terancam**

> Programmes whose value proposition is 'generic white-collar credential' are the most exposed, because they are exactly what China cut.
> Chinese precedent is explicit: information management and information systems, and public affairs management, were the two most frequently revoked undergraduate programmes (100 and 97 universities respectively, 2018-2022), and management and arts programmes dominated the cuts, with low employment rates the stated criterion.
> Indonesian analogues at risk: (1) Manajemen and Administrasi Bisnis/Administrasi Publik/Administrasi Niaga in the vast non-selective private-university tier — enormous enrolment, weak differentiation, entry roles most exposed to AI automation; (2) Akuntansi at the transactional end (bookkeeping, AP/AR) as automation and shared-service centres absorb the work; (3) Ilmu Komunikasi in its generic form — massively over-enrolled relative to the shrinking number of paid media/PR entry roles; (4) Sekretari, Perkantoran and general D3 office administration; (5) Pendidikan (teacher-training) beyond the number of actual teacher vacancies, which is why Indonesia's 2026 programme-closure round explicitly avoided touching education programmes — a political constraint China did not face in the same way; (6) low-selectivity Hukum, Sosiologi, Ilmu Politik and Sastra where the programme does not connect to a licensed profession; (7) generic Sistem Informasi/Informatika at institutions without real project or lab capacity — the credential exists but the capability does not, which is the fastest route to a devalued degree.
> The deeper threat is not the discipline but the TIER: Indonesia has thousands of small private institutions whose graduates carry the credential cost without the credential's labour-market power, which is the structural engine of Kong-Yiji-style despair.

**Jurusan Dibutuhkan**

> Follow China's replacement pattern, adapted to Indonesia's industrial base.
> China cut 12,200 programmes over 2021-2025 while opening ~10,200, plus 2,600+ 'micro-majors' and 1,100+ professional training courses, concentrated in AI, integrated circuits, robotics, biomanufacturing, low-altitude economy, new energy, elderly care and digital health.
> Indonesia's high-demand set: (1) AI/machine learning and data engineering — already appearing (UI's S1 Kecerdasan Artifisial from 2026/2027, Unesa's S1 AI, D4 Teknologi Informasi dan Kecerdasan Artifisial) but at tiny quotas relative to need; (2) applied engineering tied to real industry — mechatronics, industrial automation, electrical/energy systems, mining and mineral processing (hilirisasi nickel/copper/bauxite), petrochemicals; (3) healthcare and care work — nursing, physiotherapy, geriatric and mental-health care, plus care-work qualifications recognised in Japan/Germany/Korea, which doubles as an emigration pathway; (4) mental-health professionals — Indonesia's psychologist-to-population ratio is grossly inadequate against a 34.9% adolescent mental-health problem rate; this trend itself creates the demand; (5) agri-food technology, aquaculture and food processing — the sectors that can absorb non-Java graduates where they live; (6) skilled trades with formal certification (welding, HVAC, electrical, marine, aviation MRO) — the Indonesian answer to China's vocational-undergraduate push; (7) cross-cutting employability skills as credentialed micro-programmes: applied English/Mandarin/Japanese, AI-tool fluency, project delivery, sales — the 'micro-major' instrument China deployed at scale.
> Crucially, the demanded skill for THIS trend specifically is the ability to work in low-supervision, output-based, hybrid environments — self-management, not endurance.

**China Education Response**

> China's education system responded with unusual bluntness and speed, and it is the most transferable part of the Chinese playbook.
> (1) SUPPLY-SIDE PURGE: a March 2023 guideline from the Ministry of Education plus four other departments required roughly 20% of higher-education discipline and programme offerings to be optimised or adjusted; between 2021 and 2025 universities ended or suspended 12,200 undergraduate programmes and introduced about 10,200 new ones, affecting more than 30% of all undergraduate programmes nationally.
> Low employment rates and misalignment with industrial upgrading were the explicit criteria; management and arts bore the brunt (information management and information systems, and public affairs management, were the most-revoked programmes).
> (2) REDIRECTION TOWARD AI AND STRATEGIC INDUSTRY: new and renamed programmes cluster in artificial intelligence, integrated circuits, robotics, new energy, biomanufacturing and elderly care; even elite 985 institutions cut legacy majors while adding thousands of new ones.
> (3) MODULARISATION: 2,600+ 'micro-majors' (微专业) and 1,100+ professional training courses were created to retrofit employability onto existing degrees without waiting for full curriculum reform — a fast, cheap instrument Indonesia could copy immediately.
> (4) VOCATIONAL ELEVATION: expansion of vocational undergraduate (职业本科) capacity and a revised Vocational Education Law to reduce the stigma that pushes everyone into academic degrees.
> (5) EMPLOYMENT-LINKED ACCOUNTABILITY: graduate employment outcomes became a formal input into programme approval and continuation — with the well-documented side effect of statistical gaming (see unintended_consequences).
> (6) MASS RETRAINING: a target to train 1 million graduates and youths in 2025 for employability, alongside subsidised internships/apprenticeship placements (就业见习).
> Indonesia's 2026 closure of 122 study programmes and 1,200+ new programme openings is the same instinct at roughly 1% of the Chinese scale and three years later.

### Pelajaran Kebijakan dari China

**Respons Kebijakan China**

> Sequence and content, with the pre-emptive lesson for Indonesia at each step.
> (1) 2021 — MORAL CONDEMNATION AND CENSORSHIP: Xinhua called lying flat 'shameful', tang-ping forums and groups were restricted.
> This FAILED: the term survived, mutated into 摆烂 and 鼠鼠文学, and the state lost the framing initiative.
> LESSON: do not attempt to shame or suppress the discourse; it converts a coping meme into a political symbol.
> (2) 2021 — LABOUR-STANDARD ENFORCEMENT: the Supreme People's Court and MOHRSS jointly declared 996 (9am-9pm, six days) illegal in August 2021 via published typical cases, giving the anti-overwork sentiment a legal channel.
> LESSON: this is the single most adoptable pre-emptive policy — enforce existing working-hour and overtime law loudly and publicly BEFORE the anti-hustle sentiment turns anti-system.
> (3) 2023 — EDUCATION SUPPLY-SIDE ADJUSTMENT (see china_education_response): cut what does not employ, fund what does, modularise the rest.
> (4) 2023 — DATA GOVERNANCE, HANDLED BADLY: suspending the youth-unemployment series for six months after it hit 21.3% destroyed credibility and became an international story larger than the number itself; resumption on a student-excluding methodology invited permanent suspicion.
> LESSON FOR INDONESIA: never suspend or redefine an embarrassing labour series; publish it and pair it with a policy response.
> (5) 2025 — DEMAND-SIDE HIRING INCENTIVES: 17 inter-ministerial measures (April 2025) from MOHRSS, MOE and MOF — one-off job-expansion subsidies for employers hiring 2025 graduates, graduates unemployed within two years, and registered unemployed youth aged 16-24; social-insurance subsidies; tax and fee reductions; extension of SOE graduate-hiring subsidies to 31 December 2026; a further package in March 2026.
> (6) 2025 — REFRAMING THE PROBLEM AS SYSTEMIC, NOT INDIVIDUAL: the '反内卷' (anti-involution) campaign launched from Xi's 1 July 2025 Central Financial and Economic Affairs Commission remarks and enshrined in the October 2025 Fourth Plenum decision, targeting destructive competition among firms and local governments.
> LESSON: naming the structure rather than blaming the young is what finally de-escalated the discourse — Beijing effectively conceded the youth's diagnosis and moved the target.
> (7) THROUGHOUT — CHANNELLING: rural revitalisation placements, grassroots service schemes, SOE hiring quotas and expanded postgraduate places to warehouse cohorts.
> LESSON: warehousing buys time but inflates the next cohort's credential arms race, as China's exam-application data now shows.

**Rekomendasi Kebijakan Indonesia**

> (1) MEASURE HONESTLY AND MONTHLY.
> Publish youth (15-24) unemployment, youth LFPR, NEET counts by sex and province, and graduate-underemployment (graduates in non-graduate jobs) as a standing quarterly release.
> The decisive early-warning variable is youth LFPR FALLING while unemployment rises — that is withdrawal, and Indonesia currently has no timely indicator for it.
> Do not repeat China's 2023 suspension error.
> (2) ENFORCE WORKING-HOUR LAW NOW, PUBLICLY.
> Kemnaker should run a visible campaign of overtime and working-hour enforcement (UU Ketenagakerjaan/Cipta Kerja provisions) plus a right-to-disconnect norm for white-collar employers, before anti-hustle sentiment hardens into anti-work sentiment.
> This is the highest-yield pre-emptive move and it is nearly free.
> (3) TARGETED DEMAND-SIDE HIRING SUBSIDY.
> Copy the Chinese instrument precisely: a time-limited BPJS-contribution subsidy plus a wage subsidy for employers hiring first-time workers aged 18-24, with a heavier rate for non-Java placements and for SMEs — cheaper and faster-acting than another training scheme.
> (4) FIX PRAKERJA'S THEORY OF CHANGE.
> Shift from generic online course vouchers to employer-committed apprenticeships (magang bersertifikat with a hiring commitment), modelled on China's 就业见习; pay employers for conversion to permanent hire, not for training delivery.
> (5) HIGHER-EDUCATION SUPPLY DISCIPLINE WITH TRANSPARENCY.
> Kemendiktisaintek should publish programme-level graduate employment and earnings outcomes (a tracer-study mandate with audited data) and tie new-programme approval and accreditation to them — but avoid China's error of making employment rate a pure survival metric, which produced systematic falsification.
> Pair closure with funded transition for affected students and staff.
> (6) MICRO-CREDENTIALS AT SCALE.
> Deploy an Indonesian equivalent of China's 2,600 micro-majors — 1-2 semester stackable certificates in AI tooling, data, industrial automation, care work, applied languages — retrofittable onto existing degrees within one year.
> (7) BUILD YOUTH MENTAL-HEALTH CAPACITY BEFORE THE PEAK.
> Against a 34.9% adolescent mental-health-problem baseline and a severe psychologist shortage, fund campus counselling, a national youth helpline, and BPJS Kesehatan coverage for outpatient mental health — the cheapest intervention with the highest social return if withdrawal culture arrives.
> (8) KEEP THE VOICE CHANNEL OPEN.
> The August 2025 protests and the repression response are directly relevant: closing the political outlet is the surest way to convert Indonesian youth anger into Chinese-style withdrawal.
> Institutionalised youth consultation (a standing national youth employment council with real agenda power) is cheaper than the alternative.
> (9) TREAT EMIGRATION AS POLICY, NOT LEAKAGE.
> #KaburAjaDulu is a pressure valve; formalise it — bilateral labour agreements with Japan, Korea, Germany, Australia and the Gulf for skilled and care roles, with certification, protection and remittance/return incentives, instead of moralising about disloyalty (the same mistake Xinhua made about lying flat).

### Peluang & Rekomendasi Aksi

**Peluang Bisnis**

> (1) AFFORDABLE MENTAL HEALTH AT SCALE — teletherapy, group therapy, campus-embedded counselling, corporate EAP for mid-size Indonesian employers, and AI-assisted triage; a 34.9% adolescent problem rate against a tiny professional supply is the widest service gap this trend creates.
> (2) THE STAY-AT-HOME ('rebahan') ECONOMY — night-window delivery (22:00-04:00 order share is a leading indicator and an underserved slot), single-serving cheap meal bundles, ready-to-eat and frozen at sub-Rp 20,000 price points, comfort/sleep goods, micro-living and co-living operators offering dignified small-format urban rooms.
> (3) LOW-COMMITMENT ENTERTAINMENT — short dramas (the fastest-growing Chinese format and already entering Indonesia), idle and hyper-casual mobile games, audio and podcast, cloud gaming: the products of an economy where time is abundant and money is not.
> (4) 'DIGNIFIED EXIT' SERVICES — emigration and study-abroad services, IELTS/JLPT/TOPIK prep, care-worker and welder certification for Japan/Germany/Korea placement, and remittance/fintech products for a young overseas cohort; #KaburAjaDulu is a market, not just a hashtag.
> (5) EMPLOYABILITY INFRASTRUCTURE — bootcamps with hiring guarantees, apprenticeship-brokerage platforms, skills-verification and portfolio credentials, and AI-tool fluency training; also HR-tech for output-based management, which employers will need as presence-based supervision collapses.
> (6) SECOND-HAND, REPAIR AND RENTAL — the consumption pattern of a cohort with time but no income (already visible in the thrift/preloved boom); the Chinese analogue (Xianyu) is a multi-hundred-million-user platform.
> (7) CREATOR ECONOMY AROUND THE AESTHETIC ITSELF — Indonesian brands that speak in the exhausted-non-striver voice will out-perform hustle-coded advertising with under-30s; the Chinese precedent (Meituan, Tmall, 1688, Midea joining the rat-people meme within weeks in March-April 2025) shows this is a first-mover advantage measured in weeks.
> (8) FINANCIAL PRODUCTS FOR IRREGULAR INCOME — micro-savings, income-smoothing and insurance designed for gig/irregular earners rather than salaried workers.
> CAUTION: several of these monetise distress; the reputational line between serving and exploiting a demoralised cohort is thin, and predatory paylater/gambling products are already occupying the same emotional space.

**Rekomendasi Individu Mahasiswa**

> (1) BUILD A VERIFIABLE PORTFOLIO, NOT JUST A TRANSCRIPT — in a credential-devalued market (tertiary TPT 6.13% above national 4.68%), demonstrable output beats the degree; ship real projects, internships, freelance work, open-source or community work with evidence.
> (2) BECOME AI-COMPLEMENTARY, FAST — the roles most at risk are the entry-level white-collar rungs; the defensible position is being the person who directs AI tools within a domain (finance, health, logistics, agriculture, law), not the person who does the task AI now does.
> (3) ACQUIRE ONE PHYSICALLY OR REGULATORILY ANCHORED SKILL — care work, industrial maintenance, electrical, welding, aquaculture, medical technology, or a licensed profession; these resist both automation and offshoring, and they are the skills with formal overseas demand.
> (4) LANGUAGE AS AN OPTION ON EXIT — English to professional level plus one of Japanese/Korean/German/Mandarin converts the emigration option from fantasy into a plan; this is rational hedging, not disloyalty.
> (5) TREAT YOUR FIRST JOB AS A LEARNING PURCHASE, NOT AN IDENTITY — but refuse unpaid overtime as a norm; the anti-hustle instinct is correct in substance and needs to be expressed as boundary-setting and output discipline rather than disengagement, because quiet quitting damages the quitter's skill accumulation most.
> (6) PROTECT SLEEP, DAYLIGHT AND ONE OFFLINE SOCIAL ANCHOR — the rat-person trajectory begins with reversed sleep and ends with unemployability; circadian collapse and social withdrawal are the two mechanisms that turn a bad year into a lost decade.
> Concretely: fixed wake time, morning daylight, one weekly in-person commitment.
> (7) BUILD A SMALL INCOME FLOOR EARLY — 3-6 months of expenses, however modest, is what converts 'I must accept this exploitative job' into 'I can choose'; without it, anti-hustle sentiment has no material backing.
> (8) FIND OR FORM A COHORT — the single strongest protective factor against withdrawal is a peer group with shared structure (study group, co-working, community organisation, religious or sports community).
> (9) READ THE MACRO — track BPS releases on youth employment and sectoral hiring; choosing a sector with structural tailwinds (energy transition, healthcare, food, defence-adjacent industry, downstream minerals) beats optimising a CV inside a shrinking one.

**Rekomendasi Perguruan Tinggi**

> (1) PUBLISH PROGRAMME-LEVEL OUTCOMES AND ACT ON THEM — mandatory audited tracer studies with employment and earnings by programme, published; then close, merge or radically redesign the bottom decile, following China's 2021-2025 purge logic but with student-transition funding attached.
> (2) SHRINK GENERIC MANAGEMENT/ADMINISTRATION/COMMUNICATION INTAKE and reallocate the seats to applied engineering, health and care, agri-food technology and AI/data — mirroring the specific programmes China revoked (information management and information systems; public affairs management).
> (3) INTRODUCE MICRO-CREDENTIALS WITHIN 12 MONTHS — a stackable 1-2 semester certificate layer (AI tooling, data analysis, industrial automation, care work, applied Japanese/German/Mandarin, sales and project delivery) retrofitted onto existing degrees; this is China's 2,600-micro-major instrument and it is the fastest, cheapest lever an Indonesian university actually controls.
> (4) MAKE INDUSTRY PLACEMENT A GRADUATION REQUIREMENT, NOT A BONUS — a minimum one-semester supervised placement with a named employer partner for every applied programme; convert the MBKM legacy into enforceable employer commitments rather than administrative reporting.
> (5) BUILD REAL CAREER AND MENTAL-HEALTH SERVICES — a funded ratio of counsellors and career advisers per 1,000 students, with proactive outreach to students who stop attending (attendance drop-off is the earliest detectable signal of withdrawal); Indonesian campuses currently detect this far too late.
> (6) ELEVATE VOCATIONAL PATHWAYS AND DESTIGMATISE THEM — expand applied/vocational bachelor capacity (Indonesia's 2026 programme growth is already vocational-weighted) and give it parity in funding, faculty quality and employer recognition, as China did with 职业本科.
> (7) TEACH THE ECONOMICS OF THEIR OWN SITUATION — a required module on labour-market reality, AI displacement, financial resilience and boundary-setting at work; students who understand the structural cause are measurably less likely to internalise failure as personal defect, which is the psychological mechanism the Chinese rat-people culture runs on.
> (8) STOP SELLING DEGREES THE MARKET DOES NOT WANT — the ethical core: small private institutions charging tuition for programmes with known-poor outcomes are manufacturing the Indonesian Kong Yiji cohort, and accreditation policy should make that unprofitable.

### Faktor Risiko & Sisi Gelap

**Risiko Sosial Indonesia**

> (1) LOST GENERATION AT A LOWER INCOME LEVEL: Indonesia is reaching Chinese-level youth unemployment (16.36%) at roughly one-third of China's income per capita and without unemployment insurance, family property wealth or a state training system of Chinese density — the same distress with a far thinner cushion, meaning worse and faster human damage.
> (2) WASTE OF THE DEMOGRAPHIC BONUS: with Gen Z at ~74.93 million (27.94% of the population) and the bonus window closing around 2035-2045, a decade of youth disengagement would mean the bonus expires unconverted — Indonesia would become old before it becomes rich, which is precisely the trap China is now in.
> (3) POLITICAL VOLATILITY, NOT QUIET WITHDRAWAL: the more likely Indonesian failure mode is not bedrooms but streets — August 2025 (30+ provinces, ~3,195 detained, a death that catalysed nationwide anger) is the template; economically hopeless, digitally coordinated youth are the most combustible political input Indonesia has, and repression would accelerate rather than resolve it.
> (4) MENTAL-HEALTH SYSTEM OVERWHELM: a 34.9% adolescent mental-health-problem baseline meeting mass graduate unemployment, against a psychologist shortage, points to rising self-harm and suicide risk with almost no service capacity to absorb it.
> (5) PREDATORY ECONOMY CAPTURE: demoralised, time-rich, cash-poor young people are the target market for online gambling (already a national crisis), illegal paylater and pinjol, crypto/trading gambling, MLM and 'quick money' scams, and — most seriously — trafficking into Southeast Asian scam compounds, which already recruits heavily from unemployed Indonesian graduates via fake overseas job offers.
> This is the single most dangerous Indonesian-specific pathway, and it has no Chinese equivalent in the same form.
> (6) RADICALISATION AND EXTREMIST RECRUITMENT: idle, alienated, online-native young men are a historically documented recruitment pool for both religious extremism and organised crime in Indonesia.
> (7) GENDERED WITHDRAWAL BECOMING PERMANENT: Indonesia's ~9.9 million NEET Gen Z are already female-dominated; an anti-hustle norm risks re-domesticating young women permanently under a voluntary-sounding label, entrenching a labour-force participation gap.
> (8) EMIGRATION OF THE MOST CAPABLE: #KaburAjaDulu selects for the employable — English-speaking, skilled, mobile — so the withdrawal culture stays home while the talent leaves, a doubly adverse selection.

**Unintended Consequences**

> IN CHINA: (a) statistical gaming — tying programme survival to graduate employment rates produced widespread falsification of employment records (students pressured to submit fake employment contracts), corrupting the very data the policy depended on; (b) the suspension of the youth-unemployment series made the number MORE famous, not less; (c) suppressing lying-flat discourse simply generated successor vocabulary every 12-24 months (摆烂, 鼠鼠, 孔乙己, 老鼠人) — an unkillable semantic hydra; (d) commercial co-optation defanged the politics but also normalised the identity: when Meituan and Tmall market to 'rat people', being one becomes a consumer segment rather than a crisis; (e) expanding postgraduate places to absorb unemployment inflated the next cohort's credential requirements, making the arms race worse — and the 2026 data (kaoyan applications falling for a third year while civil-service applications hit a record) shows students have now priced in that a master's no longer helps; (f) the anti-involution campaign aimed at firms has begun to be read by youth as vindication, which improves sentiment but raises expectations the economy may not meet.
> IN INDONESIA (predicted): (a) hustle-culture backlash could be absorbed by employers as an excuse to offer worse jobs ('Gen Z does not want to work anyway') rather than better ones — blaming the worker for a demand-side failure; (b) closing under-performing study programmes without transition funding would strand exactly the low-income students the policy is meant to help; (c) promoting entrepreneurship as the answer to graduate unemployment (the standard Indonesian policy reflex) tends to push young people into under-capitalised micro-businesses with high failure rates, producing a second layer of disillusionment; (d) an anti-hustle norm arriving BEFORE Indonesia has completed industrialisation could suppress the labour intensity a catching-up economy needs — Indonesia may get the anti-work culture of a rich country while still having the income of a middle one; (e) the emigration valve, if it works, will hollow out precisely the skilled cohort needed to fix the domestic problem; (f) the aesthetics of withdrawal are monetisable, so Indonesian creators and brands have a commercial incentive to spread a norm that is socially costly.

**Kelompok Rentan**

> (1) FRESH GRADUATES OF LOW-TIER PRIVATE UNIVERSITIES (PTS) — carrying tuition debt or family sacrifice with a credential the market discounts; the core Kong-Yiji cohort, and the most likely first Indonesian rat-people population, concentrated in Java's student cities (Yogyakarta, Malang, Bandung, Semarang, Jabodetabek).
> (2) SMK GRADUATES — the highest unemployment rate of any education level (7.74%, Feb 2026), trained for manufacturing jobs that premature deindustrialisation is not creating.
> (3) YOUNG WOMEN — already the majority of Indonesia's ~9.9 million Gen Z NEET; withdrawal that is culturally legible as 'helping at home' is invisible to policy and hardest to reverse.
> (4) YOUNG MEN AGED 18-25 WITHOUT STABLE WORK — the group most exposed to online gambling, pinjol, scam-compound trafficking, extremist recruitment and street-level political mobilisation.
> (5) FIRST-GENERATION-TO-UNIVERSITY YOUTH FROM LOWER-MIDDLE-INCOME FAMILIES — the family bet all its savings on the degree; failure carries the heaviest shame load and the least material fallback, and this group sits inside the ~142 million 'aspiring middle class'.
> (6) YOUTH OUTSIDE JAVA AND IN HIGH-UNEMPLOYMENT PROVINCES — where neither graduate jobs nor the gig fallback exist at scale, so the only options are migration or invisible underemployment.
> (7) YOUNG PEOPLE WITH EXISTING MENTAL-HEALTH CONDITIONS — against the I-NAMHS baseline (34.9% with a problem, 2.45 million with a disorder) and near-zero service capacity, the withdrawal lifestyle is a clinical accelerant.
> (8) OJOL AND GIG WORKERS UNDER 30 — the absorbing layer for graduate under-employment, with falling real earnings and no social protection; the death of a 21-year-old ojol driver was the spark for the largest youth unrest in a decade, which is a precise measure of this group's exposure.

### Tingkat Keyakinan & Kualitas Sumber

**Catatan Kontradiksi Data**

> (1) THE 17.6% (SEP 2024) FIGURE IN THE BRIEF COULD NOT BE VERIFIED AGAINST A NAMED SOURCE.
> BPS publishes Sakernas in February and August rounds, not September; the August 2024 round gives ~3.93 million unemployed aged 15-24 and a rate commonly reported as ~16%, while the modelled ILO/World Bank estimate for Indonesia in 2024 is 13.14% and the most recent BPS prints are 16.26% (Nov 2025) and 16.36% (Feb 2026).
> The brief's 17.6% is plausible for a specific sub-definition (urban only, or a particular quarterly/harmonised series) but should be cited carefully; the safest defensible statement is 'roughly 16-17%, the highest of any age group'.
> (2) CHINA'S YOUTH-UNEMPLOYMENT SERIES IS NOT COMPARABLE ACROSS THE 2023 BREAK: 21.3% (June 2023) includes job-seeking students; the post-Dec-2023 series excludes them, so the 18.9% record of August 2025 is NOT lower than 2023 in like-for-like terms.
> Any lag comparison using both numbers must flag this.
> (3) INDONESIAN HEADLINE UNEMPLOYMENT FOR FEB 2026 APPEARS IN SOURCES AS BOTH 4.68% and 4.91% (the latter is the August 2024 figure being recycled), and the unemployed count as both 7.24 million (Feb 2026) and 7.35 million (Nov 2025) — check the reference period before quoting.
> (4) 老鼠人 VIEW COUNTS DIVERGE BY AN ORDER OF MAGNITUDE: the research brief cites '>2 billion views'; Chinese marketing sources cite a single Douyin topic at 1.47 billion and aggregate cross-platform figures approaching 20 billion.
> None are audited platform disclosures.
> Use '>2 billion' as the conservative floor.
> (5) CHINA'S 2025 BIRTH FIGURE (7.92 million, down from 9.54 million in 2024) implies an unusually sharp one-year fall; the 2024 number was inflated by the dragon-year effect, but the magnitude should be treated as provisional.
> (6) INDONESIAN QUIET-QUITTING AND BURNOUT PERCENTAGES (63% disengaged, 41% refusing out-of-hours work, one third burnt out before 25) come from commercial online panels with undisclosed sampling frames and are mutually non-comparable.
> (7) INDONESIAN TERTIARY GROSS ENROLMENT is quoted as ~45% (World-Bank-style GER, 2023) but as ~31-35% in some Kemendikbud APK PT reporting because of different age-band and institution-coverage definitions — the China comparison (60.8%) should use the same definition on both sides.
> (8) THE 20-MILLION-JOBLESS-GEN-Z FIGURE for urban China is a media-derived estimate, not an NBS series.
> (9) INTERPRETIVE CONTRADICTION, not a data one: some analyses read the 2026 fall in Chinese youth unemployment (to 14.9% in June) as genuine improvement, others as the statistical effect of discouraged workers leaving the labour force — which is precisely what a withdrawal culture would produce, and the two readings cannot be distinguished from the published series.

## 12. Higher Education Restructuring (state-directed culling and re-engineering of university degree programmes: 'discipline and major setting adjustment and optimisation' / 学科专业设置调整优化). The Chinese case: 12,200 undergraduate programme points revoked or suspended versus 10,200 newly created across the 14th Five-Year Plan (2021-2025), against a Ministry of Education target of adjusting roughly 20% of all national programme points. Generic business management, design, humanities and foreign-language programmes were cut; artificial intelligence, robotics, embodied intelligence, low-altitude technology and engineering, carbon neutrality science and engineering, integrated circuits and brain-computer science were created in their place.
**Kategori**: Pendidikan (Higher Education Policy). Cross-cutting with Industrial Policy (majors are set to feed 16 designated strategic industries), Labour Market Policy (programme survival tied to graduate employment rates), and Demography (shrinking birth cohorts will eventually shrink the student base). This item is the 'supply-side' mirror of the AI/Automation and Youth Unemployment items in this research set: those describe the labour-demand shock, this describes the state's attempt to re-engineer labour supply through the university catalogue.

📊 LAGGARD (dominant), with a SELECTIVE-ADOPTION overlay and one REVERSE sub-dimension. Indonesia is a clear laggard on the state-directed, quota-driven, industrial-policy-aligned restructuring of the programme portfolio (6-9 years behind on policy, 10-15 on capability). It is a shorter-lag follower on opening new strategic majors (~7 years and compressing). It is roughly SIMULTANEOUS on vocational-education reform and on the general diagnosis of graduate mismatch. And it is REVERSE — ahead of China — on student-level curricular flexibility (MBKM/Kampus Merdeka, 2020) and on the political acceptability of defending humanities and basic sciences, which Indonesia's ministry states explicitly and China's ministry only implies through a counterweight action line. The most likely end state is not convergence but SELECTIVE ADOPTION: Indonesia imports the growth half of the Chinese model (open AI, robotics, semiconductor, green-energy programmes) and does not import the destruction half (forced closure of 20% of programmes), because the growth half is revenue-positive for institutions and the destruction half is existential for them. This produces a distinctive Indonesian failure mode — portfolio inflation rather than portfolio rotation — which is analysed under unintended_consequences. | 🔍 Keyakinan: TINGGI for the China side; SEDANG-TINGGI for the Indonesia side; SEDANG for the lag estimates and RENDAH-SEDANG for the post-2030 timeline projections.

HIGH CONFIDENCE (multiple official or first-tier sources, mutually consistent): the 12,200 / 10,200 / >30% / 10.1% figures (MOE via Xinhua, corroborated by SCMP, Forbes, VnExpress and Chinese outlets); the annual breakdowns for 2023 and 2024 (gov.cn Q&A); the 2025 and 2026 catalogue structures and named new majors (MOE releases); the 16 target industry fields (MOE notice); the February 2023 20% target and the August 2025 Action Plan with its six action lines (MOE and Central Education Work Leading Group); the most-revoked majors ranking (consistent across several independent Chinese compilations); Fudan's intake figures (institutional data, precisely reported); Jiangxi's red/yellow card thresholds and its +312/-335 five-year net (provincial education department); the 12.7 million 2026 graduate cohort (Xinhua). On the Indonesian side: the 122 closures and the eight most-closed programmes (ministerial statement to parliament, 2 June 2026); the 6,844 education and 6,127 engineering programme counts (Directorate of Institutional Affairs, May 2026); the 490,000/20,000 teacher figures (Secretary-General, April 2026); UI's AI programme approval date and intake year (multiple outlets); February 2026 unemployment rates by education level (BPS).

MEDIUM CONFIDENCE: the total count of Indonesian study programmes and institutions (the most recent precise national totals I could confirm come from the 2020 statistics — 29,413 programmes, 4,593 institutions; current figures are inferred and marked uncertain); the number of Chinese universities offering AI (sources give 406, 499 and 621 for different definitions and dates — registration versus approval versus currently enrolling); the 55% field-relevant employment figure for 2024 Chinese AI graduates (widely circulated, original survey not verified); the estimated lag decomposition, which rests on defensible but arguable choices about which milestones to compare.

LOW CONFIDENCE: the humanities 7:1 supply-demand ratio and 2.3x unemployment multiple (Chinese commercial media, no official source); all timeline projections beyond 2030; the probability percentages, which are structured judgements rather than measurements; and the claim that no Indonesian equivalent exists for low-altitude/carbon-neutrality/embodied-intelligence degree programmes — this is a negative finding from search and could be wrong at an institution I did not sample.

METHOD NOTE: the China evidence is unusually strong for this research set because the policy is executed through published catalogues and annual ministerial releases, so figures are official rather than estimated. The main analytical risk is not data accuracy but interpretation — Chinese official framing presents restructuring as successful modernisation, and critical evidence (herd behaviour, faculty displacement, gaming, weak outcomes for new majors) had to be assembled from secondary Chinese sources that are individually less authoritative than the ministry but collectively consistent.

> **Status di Indonesia**: BARU MULAI / EARLY AND VOLUNTARY, NOT A DIRECTED CAMPAIGN. Indonesia in mid-2026 has (a) the diagnosis, (b) ministerial rhetoric, (c) a small volume of bottom-up closures, and (d) the first strategic new programmes — but no quota, no national target, no employment-rate kill switch, and an explicit ministerial denial that programme closure is government policy. 122 study programmes were closed during 2026, all on the proposal of the host institutions themselves (both public and private), mostly because enrolment collapsed or the institution wanted to swap the programme for a more attractive one. Minister of Higher Education, Science and Technology Brian Yuliarto has publicly reframed the issue as 'transformation, not closure' — for example electrical engineering evolving into AI, machine learning or robotics tracks, with evaluation every 3-4 years — and has stated that closure is a last resort only where a programme fails quality standards and cannot be rescued through mentoring or transformation. Simultaneously the ministry defends basic sciences, social sciences, humanities and education programmes as holding an 'important position in the national talent architecture', explicitly rejecting the view of higher education as a narrow labour supplier. So Indonesia has arrived at the same problem statement as China circa 2019-2022 but has chosen, so far, the opposite instrument: persuasion, performance contracts and curriculum reform ('Diktisaintek Berdampak' / 'Kampus Berdampak', performance contracts signed for 2026) rather than catalogue control and forced exit. On the creation side Indonesia is genuinely moving: Universitas Indonesia's Academic Senate approved a standalone S1 Artificial Intelligence programme on 3 October 2025 for the 2026/2027 intake, UNIKOM opened S1 Robotics Engineering and AI for 2025/2026, and roughly 16 institutions now offer robotics-related programmes.

### Basic Info

**Tahun Mulai China**

> Layered start dates.
> (1) 2018-2019 — the quiet beginning: MOE began publishing annual programme registration/approval results in which revocations became conspicuous, and in March 2019 approved the first batch of 35 universities to run the standalone Artificial Intelligence undergraduate major (code 080717T).
> (2) 2022 — provincial exit mechanisms: Jiangxi and Fujian pioneered employment-rate-based warning systems (yellow card / red card) that suspend enrolment in low-placement programmes.
> (3) FEBRUARY 2023 — THE DECISIVE POLICY MOMENT: five ministries led by MOE issued the 'Reform Plan for Adjusting and Optimising Discipline and Major Setting in Ordinary Higher Education Institutions' (普通高等学校学科专业设置调整优化改革方案), setting the explicit target of optimising and adjusting roughly 20% of national discipline-major setting points by 2025.
> (4) 28 AUGUST 2025 — escalation: the Central Education Work Leading Group (a Party body above the ministry, signalling top-level political ownership) issued the 'Action Plan for Adjustment and Optimisation of Discipline and Major Setting in Higher Education (2025-2027)', extending the campaign for another three years with six named action lines.
> (5) 2026 — institutionalisation: the 2026 undergraduate catalogue created an entirely new 'Interdisciplinary' (交叉学科) degree category, the first structural change to the catalogue's top-level architecture in decades.

**Pemain Kunci China**

> STATE / PARTY ACTORS (this is a state-led trend with no private prime mover): Central Education Work Leading Group (中央教育工作领导小组) — issuer of the 2025-2027 Action Plan, which places the campaign under direct Party supervision rather than ministerial administration; Ministry of Education, Department of Higher Education (教育部高等教育司) — owner of the annual programme registration/approval cycle and the undergraduate major catalogue; National Development and Reform Commission and MIIT — suppliers of the 16 priority industry list that majors must map onto; provincial education departments (Jiangxi, Fujian, Anhui, Sichuan, Heilongjiang, Zhejiang, Chongqing and 8 pilot provinces) — operators of the red/yellow card employment-rate exit mechanisms and of regional 'major cluster' matching; MOHRSS — supplier of graduate placement (毕业去向落实率) data that determines which programmes die.
> UNIVERSITIES AS VISIBLE MOVERS: Fudan University (president Jin Li, who cut the humanities share of undergraduate intake from 30-40% to 20% in 2025 — the single most-cited symbolic act of the campaign); Beihang / Beijing University of Aeronautics and Astronautics and Harbin Institute of Technology (first movers on Low-Altitude Technology and Engineering, and on Embodied Intelligence); Renmin University, Tianjin University (brain-computer science), Sichuan University (integrated circuits plus 6 other new majors); the 499-621 institutions that now run an AI undergraduate major.
> DATA / INTERMEDIARY ACTORS: MyCOS (麦可思) — the graduate-employment survey firm whose 'red card major' lists shape public perception; Zhaopin and BOSS Zhipin — recruitment platforms whose data is used to justify cuts; gaokao advisory media (高考直通车, 自主选拔在线, 中国教育在线) which transmit the signal to families and thereby drive application behaviour faster than the formal policy does.

### China Trend Detail

**Apa Yang Terjadi Di China**

> China is running the largest deliberate re-engineering of a national university curriculum portfolio in modern history, and it is doing it top-down, on a quota, against an industrial-policy target list, using graduate employment rates as the kill switch.

(1) THE HEADLINE NUMBERS.
> Across the 14th Five-Year Plan (2021-2025), Chinese universities added roughly 10,200 undergraduate programme points (专业点 — one major at one institution) and revoked or suspended roughly 12,200.
> Net contraction of ~2,000 programme points, cumulative churn exceeding 30% of the national stock.
> The annual adjustment ratio crossed 10% for the first time in 2025 (10.1%).
> This exceeded the original 2023 target of adjusting 'roughly 20%' by 2025 — the campaign overshot its own quota by half again.

(2) THE MECHANISM IS A QUOTA PLUS A CATALOGUE PLUS A KILL SWITCH.
> The catalogue: MOE maintains a binding national list of permitted undergraduate majors.
> Nothing can be taught that is not on it, and getting onto it requires ministerial approval.
> The 2025 catalogue contained 845 majors; the 2026 catalogue contains 883 majors across 13 categories and 92 major classes, with 38 new majors added in one year.
> The quota: the February 2023 five-ministry reform plan instructed the system to adjust ~20% of programme points by 2025, converting what would elsewhere be a slow academic process into a measurable administrative KPI with a deadline.
> The kill switch: provinces run employment-based exit rules.
> Jiangxi issues a yellow card (with enrolment-quota deductions) to any programme whose graduate destination rate falls below 50%, and a red card forcing enrolment suspension if it stays below 50% for two consecutive years.
> Anhui and Jiangxi also apply a rule that programmes with employment rates below 60% for 2-3 consecutive years are revoked outright.
> Jiangxi alone added 312 programme points and stopped or revoked 335 over five years.

(3) WHAT DIED.
> The casualty list is remarkably consistent year after year.
> Over 2020-2024 the five most-revoked majors were Information Management and Information Systems (160 programme points revoked — first place four years running), Public Affairs/Public Utilities Management (138), Information and Computing Science (123), Marketing (104), and Product Design (93).
> Extending back to 2018-2022 adds Clothing and Apparel Design (70) and Educational Technology (51).
> In 2024 alone the top five revoked were Information Management and IS (38), Marketing (34), Information and Computing Science (27), Network Engineering (26) and Product Design (24).
> The pattern: generic, low-differentiation, easy-to-open, cheap-to-run programmes in management, applied design, and soft-IT — precisely the programmes that mass-expansion-era universities opened because they needed no laboratories.

(4) WHAT WAS BORN.
> The 2025 catalogue added 29 majors including Low-Altitude Technology and Engineering (低空技术与工程), Carbon Neutrality Science and Engineering (碳中和科学与工程), Integrated Circuit Science and Engineering, Artificial Intelligence Education, Area and Country Studies, Ocean Science and Technology, Intelligent Molecular Engineering, and Medical Device and Equipment Engineering.
> The 2026 catalogue went further and created a thirteenth top-level degree category — 'Interdisciplinary' (交叉学科) — populating it with 11 relocated majors plus 4 brand-new ones: Embodied Intelligence (具身智能), Brain-Computer Science and Technology (脑机科学与技术), Future Robotics (未来机器人) and Interdisciplinary Engineering (交叉工程).
> Nine universities were approved for embodied intelligence in the first batch; six for low-altitude technology and engineering in 2025 under an explicitly 'extraordinary/fast-track' (超常规) approval procedure that bypassed the normal multi-year approval cycle.

(5) THE PROGRAMME PORTFOLIO IS NOW EXPLICITLY AN INDUSTRIAL-POLICY INSTRUMENT.
> A 30 June 2025 MOE notice instructed universities to aim programme setting at 16 designated industry fields: integrated circuits, artificial intelligence, biomanufacturing, quantum technology, new energy, new materials, low-altitude economy, embodied intelligence, autonomous driving, international law and foreign-related legal affairs, international communication, international organisations, fintech, health and eldercare services, culture and tourism, and modern logistics.
> Since 2024, eight provinces (Heilongjiang, Zhejiang, Chongqing among them) run a pilot matching programme setting to regional industrial clusters, producing 247 designated 'characteristic advantage major clusters' aligned to 100-billion- and trillion-yuan regional industries.
> The degree catalogue and the industrial plan are now the same document read in two directions.

(6) ELITE INSTITUTIONS ARE MOVING FASTEST AND MOST SYMBOLICALLY.
