> Fudan University's president Jin Li announced that undergraduate humanities and social science intake would fall from 30-40% to 20% of the class, under the slogan 'refine the humanities, sharpen the sciences, strengthen engineering, renew medicine, enliven the interdisciplinary' (文科做精、理科做尖、工科做强、医科做新、交叉做活).
> The 2025 intake of 3,820 delivered exactly that: humanities and social sciences 776 (20.3%), sciences 737 (19.3%), engineering 778 (20.4%), medicine 765 (20.0%), interdisciplinary 764 (20.0%).
> When China's most prestigious liberal-arts university caps the humanities at one fifth, every provincial university reads it as permission.

(7) THE 2025-2027 ACTION PLAN EXTENDS THE CAMPAIGN WITH SIX ACTION LINES: extraordinary/fast-track layout of urgently needed disciplines for strategic emerging and future industries; strengthening of basic disciplines inside excellence-building schemes; incubation of emerging and interdisciplinary fields including demonstration interdisciplinary centres; optimisation of existing programmes, with formal warnings and mandated remediation for programmes showing insufficient social demand, declining training quality, or inadequate conditions; modernisation of curricular content with AI-empowered teaching; and reform of training models via National Excellence Engineer Academies.

(8) THE PARALLEL VOCATIONAL TRACK.
> The same logic is applied below the university tier: 27 new vocational education majors were added in 2026 covering AI, the low-altitude economy and humanoid robotics (first intake 2027), following ~40 new vocational majors added in the previous cycle, with a target of vocational undergraduate places reaching at least 10% of vocational higher education enrolment by 2025 and 33 new undergraduate-level vocational colleges approved, roughly half upgraded from existing vocational schools.
> The stated driver is a projected shortage of ~30 million skilled manufacturing workers.

(9) THE FORCING CONTEXT IS A GRADUATE JOBS CRISIS.
> China will produce 12.7 million higher education graduates in the 2026 cohort, up 480,000 year on year, into a campus recruitment market of roughly 5.67 million posts against 15 million-plus job seekers.
> Urban youth unemployment has run around 16%.
> The restructuring is therefore not only industrial policy — it is a legitimacy response to visible graduate unemployment, and it lets the state attribute the mismatch to bad majors rather than to weak aggregate demand.

**Fase Tren Di China**

> BOOMING and INSTITUTIONALISED, moving toward MATURE-WITH-EARLY-BACKLASH.
> Phase reading by dimension: (a) POLICY INTENSITY — peak and still rising: the campaign was escalated in August 2025 from a ministerial reform plan to a Central Education Work Leading Group action plan running to 2027, which means the political ceiling has been raised, not lowered.
> (b) EXECUTION — booming: the 2025 adjustment ratio crossed 10% for the first time, and the 2026 catalogue introduced a wholly new degree category, so the machinery is accelerating rather than settling.
> (c) CRITICAL DISCOURSE — early backlash is now visible and tolerated: Chinese academic and mainstream media openly debate whether the humanities will 'disappear', whether AI programmes are being opened by herd behaviour at institutions without faculty or laboratories, what happens to teachers whose programmes are cut, and whether employment-rate metrics are a legitimate way to judge basic disciplines.
> Notably the 2025-2027 Action Plan itself contains a counterweight action line on strengthening basic disciplines — an implicit acknowledgement that the cutting had overshot.
> (d) OUTCOME EVIDENCE — immature: the first cohorts from the new majors have not graduated, and the one early datapoint available (55% field-relevant employment for 2024 AI graduates) suggests the new programmes may reproduce the mismatch they were built to solve.
> Expect the phase to shift to 'regulated/consolidating' around 2027-2028 when the Action Plan expires and the quality problems in the newly opened programmes become measurable.

**Puncak Tren China**

> Two distinct peaks.
> POLICY PEAK: 28 August 2025, when the Central Education Work Leading Group — not merely MOE — issued the 2025-2027 Action Plan, elevating programme restructuring from education administration to Party-level strategic policy.
> VOLUME PEAK: 2025, the first year in which the annual adjustment ratio exceeded 10% of all programme points, closing a five-year period with >30% cumulative churn.
> SYMBOLIC PEAK: March 2025, Fudan University's announcement capping humanities and social science undergraduate intake at 20%, which functioned as the permission signal for the rest of the system and generated the largest public debate.
> CATALOGUE-ARCHITECTURE PEAK: 28 April 2026, creation of the 'Interdisciplinary' degree category with Embodied Intelligence, Brain-Computer Science and Technology and Future Robotics — the point at which the catalogue stopped being amended and started being rebuilt.
> GEOGRAPHIC CONCENTRATION: the cutting is heaviest in second- and third-tier provincial and private undergraduate institutions (Jiangxi, Anhui, Fujian, Henan, Shandong) that expanded fastest during the 1999-2015 massification and have the weakest programmes; the creation of new majors is concentrated in Beijing, Shanghai, Jiangsu, Guangdong, Zhejiang and Hubei where the target industries and the qualified faculty actually exist.
> The campaign therefore simultaneously downgrades the periphery and upgrades the core.

### Status Indonesia Saat Ini

**Status Di Indonesia**

> BARU MULAI / EARLY AND VOLUNTARY, NOT A DIRECTED CAMPAIGN.
> Indonesia in mid-2026 has (a) the diagnosis, (b) ministerial rhetoric, (c) a small volume of bottom-up closures, and (d) the first strategic new programmes — but no quota, no national target, no employment-rate kill switch, and an explicit ministerial denial that programme closure is government policy.
> 122 study programmes were closed during 2026, all on the proposal of the host institutions themselves (both public and private), mostly because enrolment collapsed or the institution wanted to swap the programme for a more attractive one.
> Minister of Higher Education, Science and Technology Brian Yuliarto has publicly reframed the issue as 'transformation, not closure' — for example electrical engineering evolving into AI, machine learning or robotics tracks, with evaluation every 3-4 years — and has stated that closure is a last resort only where a programme fails quality standards and cannot be rescued through mentoring or transformation.
> Simultaneously the ministry defends basic sciences, social sciences, humanities and education programmes as holding an 'important position in the national talent architecture', explicitly rejecting the view of higher education as a narrow labour supplier.
> So Indonesia has arrived at the same problem statement as China circa 2019-2022 but has chosen, so far, the opposite instrument: persuasion, performance contracts and curriculum reform ('Diktisaintek Berdampak' / 'Kampus Berdampak', performance contracts signed for 2026) rather than catalogue control and forced exit.
> On the creation side Indonesia is genuinely moving: Universitas Indonesia's Academic Senate approved a standalone S1 Artificial Intelligence programme on 3 October 2025 for the 2026/2027 intake, UNIKOM opened S1 Robotics Engineering and AI for 2025/2026, and roughly 16 institutions now offer robotics-related programmes.

**Contoh Konkret Indonesia**

> POLICY AND ACTORS: Kementerian Pendidikan Tinggi, Sains dan Teknologi (Kemdiktisaintek) under Minister Brian Yuliarto and Deputy Minister Fauzan; Secretary-General Badri Munir Sukoco, who put the teacher-education oversupply figures into public circulation at the National Population Symposium in April 2026; Director of Institutional Affairs Mukhamad Najib, source of the programme-count-by-field data (6 May 2026).
> Programme frameworks: 'Diktisaintek Berdampak' and 'Kampus Berdampak' (the successor framing to Kampus Merdeka), with 2026 performance contracts signed by hundreds of institutional leaders; new IKU (key performance indicators) for impact rather than graduate counts; vocational 'link and match with DUDIKA' curriculum grants for 2026.

CLOSURES (the Indonesian equivalent of China's 撤销): 122 programmes closed during 2026 on institutional proposal, discussed in parliament on 2 June 2026.
> The eight most frequently closed: D3 Midwifery (16 institutions), D3 Informatics Management (8), D3 Accounting (7), D3 Computer Engineering (3), D3 Nursing (3), D3 Finance and Banking (3), S1 Retail Management (3), S1 Mathematics (2).
> Note the pattern: overwhelmingly D3 diploma programmes being displaced by D4/S1, not a strategic cull.
> Separately, 84 private higher education institutions have been flagged for possible licence revocation for having unclear management, students or lecturers, and 23-25 private institutions have already had operating licences revoked for diploma fraud and phantom enrolment — this is Indonesia's real 'exit mechanism' and it is an integrity enforcement mechanism, not an industrial-policy one.

THE OVERSUPPLY CASE THAT COULD TRIGGER AN INDONESIAN VERSION: teacher education.
> Indonesia runs 6,844 education (kependidikan/keguruan) study programmes — the largest single field, ahead of engineering at 6,127 — producing roughly 490,000 graduates a year against roughly 20,000 teacher and early-childhood facilitator vacancies.
> Critics have described the ~6,000 education and religious studies programmes as a Ponzi structure that sustains itself by recruiting new students to pay for the last cohort.
> This is Indonesia's exact analogue of China's Information Management and Public Affairs Management problem, at larger scale.

NEW PROGRAMMES (the Indonesian equivalent of China's 新增): Universitas Indonesia S1 Kecerdasan Artifisial at Fasilkom, approved 3 October 2025, first intake 2026/2027, aligned to the National AI Strategy 2020-2045, taking Fasilkom to three undergraduate programmes (Computer Science, Information Systems, AI); UNIKOM S1 Teknik Robotika dan Kecerdasan Buatan from 2025/2026; roughly 16 institutions offering robotics-linked programmes; a national semiconductor talent programme coordinated through Kemenko Perekonomian and Kemdiktisaintek, including an Indonesia Semiconductor Hackathon 2026 and pushes for chip-design curricula and microelectronics laboratories; ITB's rare programmes such as Bioenergy and Chemurgy Engineering.
> At school level, Kurikulum Merdeka 2026 adds coding and artificial intelligence as elective subjects nationally — the pipeline precondition.

SYSTEM CONSTRAINTS THAT SHAPE ALL OF THIS: roughly 4,000+ higher education institutions, the great majority private; only about 6% of institutions hold 'Unggul' (excellent) accreditation as of end-2025; gross higher education participation rate around 32%.

### Analisis Lag

**Bukti Historical Lag**

> (1) THE AI MAJOR ITSELF — the cleanest single measurement in this entire research set.
> China: MOE approved the first 35 universities to run the standalone Artificial Intelligence undergraduate major in March 2019; by 2024 the count was 621 institutions, making it the most-added major of the decade.
> Indonesia: Universitas Indonesia's Academic Senate approved a standalone S1 Kecerdasan Artifisial on 3 October 2025 for first intake 2026/2027 — and this is the flagship national university, i.e.
> the earliest possible adopter.
> Lag: 6.5-7 years, measured first-mover to first-mover.

(2) DATA SCIENCE / BIG DATA MAJORS.
> China added 数据科学与大数据技术 to the catalogue in 2016 and it spread to hundreds of institutions within four years.
> Indonesian universities (Telkom University, ITS, IPB, Binus and others) opened Sains Data / Data Science programmes from roughly 2020-2021.
> Lag: 4-5 years.
> This shorter lag is instructive — it shows the creation lag has been compressing across successive technology waves, from ~5 years (data science) to ~7 years (AI, distorted by pandemic-era approval delays).

(3) MASSIFICATION AND THE OVERSUPPLY IT PRODUCES.
> China's higher education expansion began with the 1999 enrolment surge; the resulting oversupply of cheap-to-run management and soft-IT programmes became a visible policy problem around 2018-2022, i.e.
> roughly 20 years later.
> Indonesia's private higher education expansion accelerated through the 2000s-2010s; its oversupply crisis (teacher education, D3 programmes, phantom campuses) became a visible policy problem in 2024-2026, roughly 20 years later on its own clock.
> The structural rhythm is identical, offset by the difference in when massification started — which is where much of the 6-9 year headline lag actually comes from.

(4) VOCATIONAL EDUCATION REFORM.
> China revised its Vocational Education Law in 2022 to give vocational education legal parity with general education and approved 33 new undergraduate-level vocational colleges.
> Indonesia's vocational reform (Kampus Vokasi, D4 conversion, link-and-match with DUDIKA) has been running since 2019-2020 in policy but the 2026 closure list shows the D3-to-D4 conversion is still in progress — Indonesia is arguably NOT behind here, and on vocational-general parity may be roughly simultaneous.
> This is the one sub-dimension where the lag is near zero.

(5) THE COUNTER-EVIDENCE — an area where Indonesia is genuinely earlier.
> Indonesia introduced Kampus Merdeka/MBKM in 2020, a large-scale curriculum-flexibility reform allowing students to take up to three semesters outside their programme.
> China has nothing structurally equivalent at national scale; its reform runs through the catalogue rather than through student choice.
> So the lag is not uniform: Indonesia is behind on state-directed portfolio control and ahead on student-level curricular flexibility.
> Any lag estimate that ignores this will overstate Indonesian backwardness.

(6) SIGNAL-TRANSMISSION EVIDENCE.
> Indonesian mainstream coverage of the Chinese 12,200-programme cull appeared within days of the June 2026 international reporting, and Indonesian education commentators immediately used it in the domestic 'tutup prodi' debate.
> The idea now travels in near real time even though the institutional capacity to act on it does not — a recurring pattern across this research set.

**Tipe Lag**

> LAGGARD (dominant), with a SELECTIVE-ADOPTION overlay and one REVERSE sub-dimension.
> Indonesia is a clear laggard on the state-directed, quota-driven, industrial-policy-aligned restructuring of the programme portfolio (6-9 years behind on policy, 10-15 on capability).
> It is a shorter-lag follower on opening new strategic majors (~7 years and compressing).
> It is roughly SIMULTANEOUS on vocational-education reform and on the general diagnosis of graduate mismatch.
> And it is REVERSE — ahead of China — on student-level curricular flexibility (MBKM/Kampus Merdeka, 2020) and on the political acceptability of defending humanities and basic sciences, which Indonesia's ministry states explicitly and China's ministry only implies through a counterweight action line.
> The most likely end state is not convergence but SELECTIVE ADOPTION: Indonesia imports the growth half of the Chinese model (open AI, robotics, semiconductor, green-energy programmes) and does not import the destruction half (forced closure of 20% of programmes), because the growth half is revenue-positive for institutions and the destruction half is existential for them.
> This produces a distinctive Indonesian failure mode — portfolio inflation rather than portfolio rotation — which is analysed under unintended_consequences.

### Probabilitas Transfer ke Indonesia

**Alasan Probabilitas**

> WHY THE GROWTH HALF TRANSFERS EASILY (high probability): opening a programme in Indonesia is a revenue event for the institution and a prestige event for the rector, requires ministerial permit but no closure of anything, and is strongly pulled by student demand — Indonesian applicants track the same global signals about AI that Chinese applicants do, and rankings, accreditation KPIs and the 'Kampus Berdampak' performance contracts all reward visible modernity.
> Indonesia also has a genuine articulated national demand: the National AI Strategy 2020-2045, the semiconductor talent programme with Kemenko Perekonomian, the nickel/EV battery downstreaming agenda, and the renewable-energy transition all create at least a policy-level justification for new engineering programmes.
> The pipeline precondition is being laid at school level with coding and AI electives in Kurikulum Merdeka 2026.

WHY THE DESTRUCTION HALF TRANSFERS BADLY (low-to-medium probability): (1) OWNERSHIP STRUCTURE.
> The overwhelming majority of Indonesian institutions are private foundations (yayasan).
> A study programme is their product line and cash flow; closing it is not an administrative decision but a business death.
> China's cull worked because MOE controls enrolment quotas even at private institutions and because most of the affected capacity sat inside public provincial universities that the state funds directly.
> Indonesia's ministry has no equivalent lever over a yayasan's economics.
> (2) POLITICAL ECONOMY OF TEACHER EDUCATION.
> The single largest oversupply — 6,844 education programmes, ~490,000 graduates against ~20,000 vacancies — is also the most politically protected, entangled with LPTK institutional interests, PPG certification, honorary-teacher constituencies, professional associations and regional politics.
> Any move against it triggers immediate resistance, and the counter-narrative (Indonesia is short 679,000 teachers) is officially available from another ministry.
> (3) ACCESS EQUITY.
> With a gross participation rate of only ~32%, Indonesia's small regional private campuses are frequently the only tertiary access point in their kabupaten.
> Closing programmes there subtracts access in a country still trying to expand it, whereas China closed programmes in a system with a much higher participation rate and a shrinking birth cohort — China could afford contraction, Indonesia demographically cannot yet.
> (4) NO INDUSTRIAL DEMAND TO ROTATE INTO.
> China's cull was credible because the receiving industries — semiconductors, EVs, robotics, low-altitude aviation, renewables — actually exist at scale and hire.
> Indonesia lacks a domestic industrial base capable of absorbing large cohorts of AI, robotics or chip-design graduates, so a forced rotation would move students from a low-employment programme into a different low-employment programme.
> (5) STATE CAPACITY AND DATA.
> China's mechanism runs on annual, comparable, provincially audited graduate-destination data.
> Indonesia's tracer study coverage is uneven and self-reported; an employment-rate kill switch would be gamed within one cycle.
> (6) EXPLICIT MINISTERIAL POSITION.
> Kemdiktisaintek has stated that basic sciences, social sciences, humanities and education hold an important place in the national talent architecture and that higher education is not merely a labour supplier — the opposite of the framing that made China's cull possible.

NET: expect a high-volume, low-intensity Indonesian version — many new programmes, a slow trickle of voluntary closures concentrated in D3 programmes and in institutions that are already failing, and enforcement energy directed at integrity violations (phantom campuses, diploma fraud) rather than at strategic misalignment.

**Vektor Transmisi**

> This trend transfers primarily as POLICY IDEA and INSTITUTIONAL MIMICRY rather than as capital or product, which makes its transmission vectors different from the commercial items in this research set.

(a) POLICY DIFFUSION AND OFFICIAL LEARNING — the primary vector.
> Indonesian ministries and university leadership consume Chinese education policy through bilateral education cooperation, Ministry of Education comparative studies, delegations to Chinese universities, and multilateral framings (World Bank, OECD, ASEAN education ministers' meetings) that increasingly cite China's programme restructuring as a reference case.
> The June 2026 international reporting on the 12,200-programme cull was picked up in Indonesian media within days and immediately entered the domestic 'tutup prodi' debate.
> Expect the Chinese model to be cited explicitly in Indonesian policy documents and DPR hearings within 1-2 years.

(b) ALUMNI, SCHOLARSHIPS AND ACADEMIC DIASPORA — a strong and underrated vector.
> Indonesia sends a large and growing number of students to China on CSC scholarships, Belt and Road education programmes, and university partnerships (Tsinghua, Zhejiang, Harbin Institute of Technology, Southeast University and provincial universities).
> These returnees enter Indonesian faculties and ministries carrying the Chinese curricular template — including the assumption that a degree programme should map to a named industry.
> Chinese-language and China-studies programmes in Indonesia, plus Confucius Institute successors, provide additional channel capacity.

(c) CHINESE INDUSTRIAL PRESENCE CREATING DERIVED CURRICULAR DEMAND — the most concrete vector.
> Chinese firms operating in Indonesia (Wuling, BYD, CATL and the Morowali/Weda Bay nickel-battery complexes, Huawei, Xiaomi, TikTok/ByteDance, Mixue's supply chain, Chinese EPC contractors on rail and power projects) create direct employer demand for specific skills and frequently fund or co-design vocational and university programmes to secure their own labour supply.
> Huawei's ICT Academy programme with Indonesian universities and polytechnics is the template; nickel-industry technical academies in Sulawesi are the heavy-industry version.
> This vector delivers curriculum change without requiring any Indonesian policy decision at all, and it is the single most likely route by which battery/metallurgy/automation programmes appear in eastern Indonesia.

(d) EQUIPMENT, PLATFORM AND CERTIFICATION EMBEDDING.
> Chinese hardware and software vendors seed laboratories and certification tracks — robotics kits, industrial automation trainers, cloud and AI platform certifications — which then define what a programme can actually teach.
> Whoever supplies the teaching laboratory writes the curriculum in practice.
> Chinese vendors compete here with US platform incumbents, and in vocational and second-tier institutions where price dominates, Chinese equipment increasingly wins.

(e) GLOBAL RANKINGS AND ACCREDITATION ISOMORPHISM — an indirect but powerful vector.
> As Chinese universities climb QS/THE rankings on the back of engineering and computer science output, Indonesian institutions chasing rankings replicate the same portfolio logic: expand engineering and computing, protect research-productive units, deprioritise low-output humanities.
> This produces Chinese-style outcomes through a non-Chinese mechanism.

(f) STUDENT AND PARENT DEMAND VIA ALGORITHMIC CONTENT — the fastest-moving vector.
> Indonesian applicants and parents encounter 'jurusan masa depan' and 'jurusan yang akan hilang' content on TikTok, YouTube and Instagram, much of it derivative of Chinese gaokao advisory content.
> Application patterns shift years before ministries act, and enrolment collapse is precisely the trigger that produced Indonesia's 122 voluntary closures in 2026.
> Demand-side transmission is therefore running ahead of policy-side transmission — the reverse of the Chinese sequence.

(g) WHAT IS NOT A VECTOR: Chinese venture capital and direct market entry, which drive most other items in this set, are largely irrelevant here.
> Higher education programme approval is a sovereign function, and foreign providers face tight restrictions in Indonesia.
> This is why the trend will arrive as an idea, slowly, rather than as a company, quickly.

### Faktor Pendorong

**Indikator Pemantauan**

> LEADING INDICATORS, ROUGHLY IN THE ORDER THEY WOULD FIRE:

REGULATORY / POLICY
- Any Permendiktisaintek or ministerial regulation that ties programme permits or enrolment quotas to graduate placement rates — the single clearest signal that the Chinese mechanism is being imported
- Appearance of a numeric national target ('X% of prodi to be restructured by 20XX') in RPJMN, Renstra Kemdiktisaintek, or a DPR Commission X hearing
- Creation of a binding national programme catalogue or nomenclature list with a controlled add/remove process (Indonesia's current nomenclature is looser than China's)
- Moratorium announcements on specific programme families (teacher education, D3 business, generic management) — a moratorium on new permits is the politically cheapest first step and would likely precede any closure campaign
- Explicit citation of China's 12,200/10,200 figures in Indonesian government documents or ministerial speeches

ADMINISTRATIVE VOLUME
- Annual count of prodi closures rising from 122 (2026) through 300-500 toward 1,000+ — crossing ~1% of the national stock per year would mark a genuine regime change
- Ratio of closures to new permits: currently Indonesia almost certainly opens far more than it closes; the Chinese signature is closures exceeding openings
- Number of private institutions with revoked licences per year, and whether the stated grounds shift from integrity violations (phantom students, diploma fraud) toward strategic irrelevance and non-viability
- Share of closures that are S1 rather than D3 — the 2026 list is dominated by D3 conversions, which is not restructuring; S1 closures would be

PROGRAMME CREATION
- New prodi permits in: artificial intelligence, robotics, semiconductor/microelectronics and chip design, renewable and battery energy engineering, data engineering, biotechnology, and — as the frontier marker — any Indonesian equivalent of low-altitude/drone systems engineering, carbon-neutrality engineering, or embodied intelligence
- Whether second-tier and regional private institutions begin opening AI programmes en masse (the herd-behaviour signature China is now criticised for); a jump from a handful of institutions to 50+ within two years is the warning sign
- First Indonesian creation of an interdisciplinary degree category or faculty-crossing degree, mirroring China's 2026 catalogue restructuring

LABOUR AND DEMAND SIDE
- Job-posting volume on JobStreet, Kalibrr, Glints and LinkedIn Indonesia for AI/ML engineer, robotics engineer, MLOps, chip design, battery/energy systems roles — if programme creation outruns posting growth by a wide margin, Indonesia is inflating a credential bubble rather than closing a gap
- Graduate unemployment rate for D4/S1+ (6.13% in Feb 2026) and whether it keeps rising — sustained increase is the political trigger that would make closure politically possible
- Employer coalitions (Apindo, Kadin, the Employer Forum) formally demanding programme-level reform, as at the June 2026 Employer Forum

INSTITUTIONAL BEHAVIOUR
- Whether a flagship Indonesian university publicly caps humanities/social science intake, the Fudan-equivalent symbolic act — this has not happened and would be a major signal
- Faculty redeployment schemes (dosen transfer between prodi, retraining programmes) appearing in university regulations — China's 转岗 phenomenon
- Yayasan-level consolidation: mergers of small private institutions, which is how the private sector will actually contract if it does

DEMAND / SENTIMENT
- SNBP/SNBT and private-intake application ratios by programme: collapsing applications to teacher education, generic management and communications, and rising ratios for AI/computing — enrolment collapse is what actually killed the 122 programmes in 2026, so application data leads policy by about two years
- Google Trends and TikTok volume for 'jurusan yang akan hilang', 'jurusan masa depan', 'prodi ditutup'

CHINESE-PRESENCE INDICATORS
- Chinese firms (Huawei, BYD, CATL, Wuling, Xiaomi) signing curriculum or academy agreements with Indonesian universities and polytechnics
- Growth in Indonesian students on Chinese government scholarships in engineering fields, and their placement into Indonesian faculties on return

### Hambatan & Faktor Pembatal

**Hambatan Transfer**

> (1) OWNERSHIP AND FINANCE.
> Private foundations own most Indonesian capacity and depend on tuition per programme; closure is a solvency event, not an administrative one.
> There is no Indonesian equivalent of the state subsidy that let Chinese provincial universities absorb the shock of losing a programme.

(2) NO BINDING LEVER.
> Indonesia's ministry controls permits and accreditation but not enrolment quotas at private institutions.
> Accreditation was already weak leverage — only ~6% of institutions hold 'Unggul' status and the system tolerates the rest.
> Adding a new mandate to a regulator that cannot enforce existing standards is unlikely to work.

(3) ACCESS EQUITY AND GEOGRAPHY.
> At ~32% gross participation, closing regional programmes removes the only tertiary option in many districts, in an archipelagic country where students cannot easily relocate.
> China cut capacity from a position of abundance; Indonesia would be cutting from a position of scarcity.

(4) POLITICAL PROTECTION OF THE LARGEST OVERSUPPLY.
> Teacher education (6,844 programmes) is defended by LPTK institutional interests, teacher organisations, regional political interests, and by a competing official narrative that Indonesia is short 679,000 teachers.

(5) MISSING RECEIVING INDUSTRY.
> Rotating students into AI, robotics or semiconductors only helps if employers exist.
> With R&D at ~0.3% of GDP and an economy weighted toward commodities, construction and consumption, Indonesia risks rotating graduates from one unemployment queue into a better-branded one.

(6) FACULTY SCARCITY.
> Opening the new programmes requires PhD-qualified staff in fields where Indonesia has few.
> China is already criticised for staffing 621 AI programmes with retrained faculty; Indonesia would face a sharper version, and the quality gap would be invisible for four years until the first cohort graduates.

(7) DATA INFRASTRUCTURE.
> No standardised, audited, programme-level graduate destination data means no defensible basis for closure decisions and no defence against accusations of arbitrariness or politics.

(8) LEGAL AND PROCEDURAL FRICTION.
> Closing a programme requires teach-out arrangements for enrolled students, redeployment or termination of lecturers with attendant labour-law exposure, and creates litigation risk from foundations.
> Indonesia's administrative courts are an available venue for aggrieved yayasan.

(9) NORMATIVE RESISTANCE.
> Indonesian higher education discourse retains a strong commitment to education as public good, cultural formation and religious learning.
> Kompas and other outlets have already argued that 'what should be closed is not the prodi' — locating the problem in institutional quality and governance rather than in disciplinary choice.
> Islamic higher education (PTKIN under the Ministry of Religious Affairs) sits outside Kemdiktisaintek's authority entirely, fragmenting any national campaign.

(10) BUREAUCRATIC CAPACITY AND ATTENTION.
> Kemdiktisaintek is simultaneously running Diktisaintek Berdampak, performance contracts, curriculum reform, accreditation reform and the free-nutrition-adjacent budget environment.
> A restructuring campaign of Chinese intensity requires sustained administrative attention over 5+ years and multiple ministerial terms — Indonesia's education policy has changed direction with almost every minister since 2014, which is itself the deepest barrier.

**Faktor Pembatal Transfer**

> STRUCTURAL REASONS THIS TREND WILL NOT ARRIVE IN INDONESIA IN THE SAME FORM, EVER:

(1) DEMOGRAPHIC DIRECTION IS OPPOSITE.
> China restructures a system that must shrink: births have collapsed from ~18 million (2016) to under 10 million, so the 18-year-old cohort entering university from the mid-2030s will fall by roughly half, and the tertiary participation rate is already ~60%.
> Culling 20% of programmes is a rational response to guaranteed future contraction.
> Indonesia's participation rate is ~32% with a still-large youth cohort; its central problem is that too few young people reach university, not that too many programmes exist.
> A Chinese-style cull applied to Indonesia would be the right medicine for the wrong disease.
> This is the single strongest cancellation factor and it does not weaken until roughly the 2040s.

(2) THE INSTRUMENT REQUIRES A STATE-OWNED SYSTEM.
> China's mechanism is enrolment-quota control plus a closed national catalogue plus direct funding of the affected institutions.
> Indonesia's private-foundation system is structurally immune to all three.
> Absent constitutional-scale change in how private higher education is governed and financed, the mechanism cannot be transplanted; only its rhetoric can.

(3) NO INDUSTRIAL DEMAND SIGNAL TO ALIGN TO.
> China's 16 target industries are real, domestically owned, and hiring at scale.
> Indonesia's advanced-industry employment is dominated by foreign-owned assembly and by extraction/midstream processing, which demands technicians and operators far more than it demands AI researchers or chip designers.
> A faithful copy of China's target list would produce programmes whose graduates emigrate or work outside their field — which is what happens today with Indonesian engineering graduates.
> The correct Indonesian target list is different from the Chinese one, and that difference alone means the trend cannot transfer 'in the same form'.

(4) ARCHIPELAGIC GEOGRAPHY BLOCKS CONSOLIDATION.
> China can close a weak programme in one city because students can travel to another province.
> Indonesian students in Maluku, NTT, Papua or interior Kalimantan often cannot substitute a closed local programme with a distant one at any affordable cost.
> Consolidation logic that works on a contiguous landmass fails across 17,000 islands.
> Any Indonesian version must therefore work through upgrading and networking regional institutions rather than closing them — a fundamentally different policy.

(5) FISCAL ASYMMETRY.
> China's new majors are backed by state laboratory investment, National Excellence Engineer Academies, and industrial co-funding.
> Indonesia's education budget is constitutionally 20% of state spending but overwhelmingly committed to basic education and salaries, with higher education thinly funded and now competing against major new social programmes.
> Indonesia can rename programmes cheaply; it cannot equip them.
> A restructuring that changes names without changing laboratories produces credential inflation, not capability.

(6) FRAGMENTED AUTHORITY.
> Islamic higher education sits under the Ministry of Religious Affairs; vocational and secondary education under Kemendikdasmen; health professions programmes are co-governed with the Ministry of Health and professional colleges.
> No single Indonesian authority can execute a system-wide portfolio decision the way China's Central Education Work Leading Group can.
> Fragmentation is not a temporary weakness but a designed feature of Indonesian governance.

(7) POLITICAL COST STRUCTURE IS INVERTED.
> In China, closing a programme costs the state little and demonstrates decisiveness.
> In Indonesia, closing a programme creates identifiable, organised, locally-rooted losers (a yayasan, its lecturers, a district's only campus) and diffuse, unidentifiable winners.
> Indonesian democratic politics reliably resolves such asymmetries in favour of the concentrated losers.
> Expect moratoria on new permits rather than closures of existing ones — the same policy goal achieved through the only politically survivable instrument.

WHAT WILL ARRIVE INSTEAD: a hybrid — aggressive programme creation, rhetorical relevance-testing, integrity-driven closure of failing institutions, gradual D3-to-D4 conversion, and slow attrition of oversupplied programmes through enrolment collapse rather than administrative decision.
> Enrolment collapse is already the actual mechanism behind Indonesia's 122 closures in 2026, and it will remain the mechanism.
> The market will do quietly and inefficiently what the Chinese state does loudly and efficiently.

### Prediksi Timeline di Indonesia

**Skenario Percepatan**

> Accelerators, roughly by force: (1) a sustained rise in graduate unemployment above ~8% for D4/S1+, which would convert a technocratic issue into an electoral one; (2) a demographic or economic shock that collapses private-university enrolment, forcing consolidation from below — the most likely real accelerator; (3) an AI-driven contraction in white-collar entry hiring in Indonesia mirroring China's -22% graduate posting shock, which would delegitimise generic business and administration degrees within one admissions cycle; (4) large-scale Chinese or other FDI in advanced manufacturing (batteries, EV, electronics, semiconductors) creating visible, well-paid demand for specific skills, making rotation attractive rather than coercive; (5) a minister with a full five-year term who makes programme relevance a signature agenda and survives a cabinet reshuffle; (6) mandatory, published, programme-level tracer data, which would make the oversupply undeniable and mechanically generate closure pressure; (7) fiscal pressure that forces the state to ration higher education subsidy by programme; (8) a high-visibility scandal — mass unemployment of graduates from a specific programme family, or a diploma-mill collapse — that supplies political cover.

### Dampak Sosial-Ekonomi

**Dampak Lapangan Kerja**

> JOBS DESTROYED OR DEVALUED
- University lecturers in the cut fields.
> This is the most direct and least discussed effect.
> In China, revocation of thousands of programme points forced mass faculty redeployment (转岗): lecturers were moved to adjacent majors, pushed into teaching general/public foundation courses, transferred to administrative, laboratory or library posts, made student counsellors, or left for other institutions.
> Reports describe teachers 'looking for classes to teach' after 5,345 programme points were revoked.
> Humanities faculty are additionally disadvantaged in dynamic programme evaluations because the metrics (innovation competitions, 'Internet+' contests, patent and project counts) are engineering-weighted.
> In Indonesia the equivalent exposure sits with lecturers in ~6,844 education programmes, plus generic management, communications and D3 business faculties — a population in the tens of thousands, disproportionately non-PhD, disproportionately at private institutions with weak labour protection, and disproportionately outside Java.
- Administrative and support staff at institutions that shrink or merge.
- Downstream: the teaching profession itself becomes a rationed occupation.
> ~490,000 Indonesian teacher-education graduates a year against ~20,000 vacancies means the degree already functions as a consumption good rather than a labour-market credential; formalising that recognition destroys the implicit job promise that sustained enrolment.
- Test-prep, admissions consulting and private tutoring built around now-devalued programmes.

JOBS CHANGED
- Every lecturer in a surviving programme faces curriculum rewrite obligations: China's 2025-2027 Action Plan explicitly requires accelerated content iteration and AI-empowered teaching, meaning the job of 'teaching a stable syllabus for a decade' ends.
> Indonesia's Wamendiktisaintek made the same demand at the June 2026 Employer Forum.
- Career-services and industry-liaison roles move from peripheral to central, because graduate placement becomes the metric that determines programme survival.
- Institutional research, tracer-study and data roles become mandatory infrastructure.
- Accreditation and quality-assurance professionals gain leverage; in Indonesia, BAN-PT and the LAMs become the chokepoint.

JOBS CREATED
- Faculty and technical staff in the new fields: AI, machine learning, robotics, embodied intelligence, chip and integrated-circuit design, battery and energy-systems engineering, drone/low-altitude systems, carbon accounting and climate engineering, bioprocess engineering.
> China's 621 AI programmes alone imply tens of thousands of teaching posts.
- Laboratory technicians, simulation and equipment specialists, industry-embedded instructors — the National Excellence Engineer Academy model in China, the Center of Excellence and link-and-match model in Indonesia.
- Curriculum designers, EdTech and courseware developers for the new fields, and corporate-academy staff at firms that build their own pipelines (Huawei ICT Academy pattern).
- Retraining providers for displaced faculty — a market that barely exists in Indonesia and will need to.

THE CENTRAL CAVEAT: China's own data suggests the new jobs promise is oversold at the student level — only ~55% of 2024 AI graduates entered field-relevant work, and about half judged their curriculum outdated.
> Restructuring reallocates the mismatch rather than eliminating it unless the receiving industry is real.
> Indonesia's receiving industry is thinner than China's, so the Indonesian version will create fewer genuine graduate-level jobs per programme opened, while still destroying faculty jobs in the programmes it closes.
> The net employment effect in Indonesia is likely negative in the short run and positive only if industrial policy delivers actual employers.

**Dampak Kelas Menengah**

> Higher education is the primary technology of middle-class reproduction in Indonesia, so restructuring hits the middle class more directly than almost any other trend in this research set.

(1) THE DEGREE AS INSURANCE STOPS WORKING.
> The Indonesian middle-class bargain — pay for a bachelor's degree, receive a white-collar job — is already fraying, with D4/S1+ unemployment at 6.13% (Feb 2026) and rising from 5.38% three months earlier.
> Restructuring makes the failure explicit and official: when the state says a programme is 'not relevant', it retroactively devalues the credentials of everyone who already holds it.
> In China this produced open discussion of 'trap majors' (天坑专业) and of humanities graduates facing 7:1 supply-demand ratios; Indonesia's version will be sharper because Indonesian middle-class families carry more of the cost privately (tuition at private institutions, plus living costs) with far less state subsidy than Chinese families.

(2) THE COST OF CHOOSING WRONG RISES, AND FALLS HARDEST ON THE INFORMATIONALLY POOR.
> Upper-middle-class families in Jakarta, Surabaya and Bandung read the signals early, hire consultants, and route children to AI, computing, medicine or overseas study.
> Lower-middle-class families in secondary cities receive the signal late, through TikTok, and after their child has already enrolled.
> Restructuring therefore widens intra-middle-class stratification — the same dynamic China's gaokao advisory industry produced, where AI major cut-off scores rose sharply while humanities scores fell.

(3) THE LECTURER STRATUM IS DIRECTLY THREATENED.
> University lecturers are a core Indonesian middle-class occupation, especially outside Java where a private campus is often one of the few white-collar employers in a district.
> Programme closure converts secure middle-class professionals into displaced workers with narrow, non-transferable specialisation.
> In China this was managed through redeployment inside state-funded institutions; Indonesia's private sector offers no such cushion.

(4) THE YAYASAN OWNER CLASS FACES ASSET DESTRUCTION.
> Small private universities are middle-class family assets.
> A restructuring regime, or simply enrolment collapse, wipes out that capital.

(5) A COUNTERVAILING POSITIVE.
> For middle-class students who do land in genuinely well-built new programmes with real employers attached, restructuring is straightforwardly good: it is the difference between a marketing degree with no employer and a battery-engineering degree with three.
> The middle-class gain from this trend is real but narrow, concentrated in perhaps 15-20 institutions, and it will be captured disproportionately by those already advantaged.

(6) SECOND-ORDER: MIDDLE-CLASS FAITH IN EDUCATION AS MOBILITY.
> If the degree stops guaranteeing mobility, middle-class investment behaviour shifts — toward vocational certification, overseas study, entrepreneurship, or simply lower fertility and delayed family formation.
> China is already visibly experiencing all four.
> This is the mechanism by which an education-policy item becomes a demographic and consumption item, connecting directly to the Consumer Downgrade and Youth Unemployment items in this research set.

### Kaitan Pendidikan

**Jurusan Terancam**

> PROGRAMMES ALREADY DEMONSTRATED AS VULNERABLE — CHINA'S REVEALED LIST (programme points revoked 2020-2024):
1.
> Information Management and Information Systems (160) — the archetype: a 1990s-era hybrid of IT and business that is neither, cheap to run, impossible to differentiate
2.
> Public Affairs / Public Utilities Management (138)
3.
> Information and Computing Science (123)
4.
> Marketing (104)
5.
> Product Design (93)
6.
> Clothing and Apparel Design (70)
7.
> Educational Technology (51)
Also heavily cut: Network Engineering, Advertising, E-Commerce, Human Resource Management, Business English and minor foreign languages, Music Studies, Broadcasting and Hosting, generic Journalism/Communication, Tourism Management, Hotel Management, Public Administration.

INDONESIA'S REVEALED LIST — programmes actually closed in 2026:
D3 Midwifery (16), D3 Informatics Management (8), D3 Accounting (7), D3 Computer Engineering (3), D3 Nursing (3), D3 Finance and Banking (3), S1 Retail Management (3), S1 Mathematics (2).

INDONESIA'S EXPOSED LIST — programmes with the structural characteristics that killed their Chinese equivalents:
- TEACHER EDUCATION AND KEPENDIDIKAN, at massive scale: 6,844 programmes, ~490,000 graduates a year against ~20,000 vacancies.
> Highest-volume risk in the entire Indonesian system.
> Note the important nuance: the problem is quantity and distribution, not the discipline — Indonesia genuinely needs teachers, it does not need 490,000 new ones a year from programmes of uneven quality.
- All remaining D3 programmes in business, administration, accounting, secretarial studies, informatics management and banking — being displaced by D4/vocational bachelor's degrees, and separately by automation of the clerical work they feed.
- GENERIC MANAGEMENT AND BUSINESS ADMINISTRATION at institutions with no industry linkage, no research output and no distinctive specialisation.
> This is Indonesia's single largest undifferentiated block after teacher education.
- Communications, Public Relations, Advertising, Broadcasting — where generative AI is compressing entry-level production work fastest.
- Library and Information Science, Office Administration, generic Information Systems.
- Non-clinical health support programmes at diploma level where scope-of-practice has moved to D4.
- Generic Design (graphic, product, fashion) at non-elite institutions — mirroring China's Product Design and Apparel Design cuts, and now compounded by generative image tools.
- Minor foreign languages and literature programmes at institutions with tiny cohorts — though see the caveat below.
- Basic sciences (Mathematics, Physics, Chemistry, Biology) at institutions lacking laboratories: note S1 Mathematics already appears on Indonesia's 2026 closure list, which is a warning sign, because China's 2025-2027 Action Plan explicitly added a counterweight action to PROTECT basic disciplines after over-cutting them.
> Indonesia risks repeating China's mistake without China's corrective.

IMPORTANT CAVEATS, STATED DELIBERATELY:
(a) The threat is to the PROGRAMME AS CURRENTLY TAUGHT, not to the discipline.
> Marketing did not stop mattering; generic marketing degrees stopped signalling anything.
> The Chinese cuts fell hardest on programmes that were cheap to open and identical everywhere.
(b) 'Humanities are dying' is the wrong conclusion and China itself is retreating from it.
> The 2025-2027 Action Plan contains an explicit basic-disciplines action line; the 2025 catalogue added 'new humanities' programmes such as AI Education, Digital Drama and Area and Country Studies; and Fudan's slogan was 'refine the humanities' (文科做精), not eliminate them.
> What died was mass low-cost humanities provision, not humanities.
(c) Foreign languages are a special case worth flagging for Indonesia: machine translation has genuinely destroyed the routine translation job, but China simultaneously created Area and Country Studies, International Communication, International Law and International Organisations majors — i.e.
> it moved language study up the value chain rather than deleting it.
> Indonesia should copy the move, not the cut.

**Jurusan Dibutuhkan**

> WHAT CHINA CREATED — the revealed priority list, and the best available forward indicator for Indonesia:
From the 2025 catalogue (29 new majors): Low-Altitude Technology and Engineering, Carbon Neutrality Science and Engineering, Integrated Circuit Science and Engineering, Artificial Intelligence Education, Area and Country Studies, Ocean Science and Technology, Intelligent Molecular Engineering, Medical Device and Equipment Engineering.
From the 2026 catalogue (38 new majors, new Interdisciplinary category): Embodied Intelligence, Brain-Computer Science and Technology, Future Robotics, Interdisciplinary Engineering.
From the 16 designated priority industries (MOE, June 2025): integrated circuits, artificial intelligence, biomanufacturing, quantum technology, new energy, new materials, low-altitude economy, embodied intelligence, autonomous driving, international law and foreign-related legal affairs, international communication, international organisations, fintech, health and eldercare services, culture and tourism, modern logistics.
Vocational tier (27 new majors, 2026): AI applications, low-altitude economy operations, humanoid robotics maintenance.

WHAT INDONESIA ACTUALLY NEEDS — deliberately NOT a copy of the Chinese list, because Indonesia's industrial structure differs:
TIER 1 — high confidence, real domestic employers exist today:
- Applied AI / machine learning engineering and MLOps (finance, telco, platforms, government services)
- Data engineering and analytics (the volume job, more employable than 'data scientist')
- Cybersecurity and digital identity (mandated by regulation, chronically short-staffed)
- Battery, electrochemistry and metallurgical process engineering — Indonesia's genuine global comparative advantage via nickel; this is the one field where Indonesia could plausibly lead rather than follow
- Renewable energy systems, grid integration and geothermal engineering
- Industrial automation, mechatronics and maintenance engineering for the EV/electronics assembly base
- Agritech, food technology, aquaculture and marine technology — Indonesia's largest under-served technical demand, and where the archipelago is an asset rather than a liability
- Healthcare: Indonesia is short of doctors, nurses and specialists; health programmes need quality upgrading and clinical capacity, not closure
- Logistics, supply chain and maritime/port engineering
- Applied statistics and actuarial science
TIER 2 — build now for 2030 demand:
- Semiconductor and chip design (aligned to the national semiconductor talent programme and the 2026 Semiconductor Hackathon), microelectronics fabrication and testing
- Carbon accounting, climate risk, environmental engineering and ecosystem restoration — pulled by CBAM, carbon markets and Indonesia's forest/peat/blue-carbon assets; the strongest direct analogue to China's Carbon Neutrality Science and Engineering
- Robotics and drone/UAV systems engineering — Indonesia's realistic version of 'low-altitude economy' is agricultural and logistics drones and maritime surveillance across an archipelago, not urban eVTOL
- Biotechnology, bioinformatics and biomanufacturing
- Geospatial and remote sensing engineering (archipelagic state, disaster management)
- Disaster and resilience engineering
TIER 3 — the humanities move that China made and Indonesia should copy:
- Area and country studies (China studies, Middle East studies, Indo-Pacific studies) — Indonesia is a middle power with almost no institutional depth here
- International law, foreign-related legal practice, trade and investment law
- AI ethics, technology policy, and computational social science
- Digital humanities, digital heritage and creative technology, replacing generic design
- International communication and strategic communication, replacing generic PR
CROSS-CUTTING SKILLS regardless of programme: AI literacy and prompt/agent workflow competence in every discipline (China's Action Plan mandates AI-empowered teaching across the board); English plus one strategic language; statistical reasoning; laboratory and field capability; and demonstrable project portfolios, which are what employers actually screen on when degree signals stop working.

**China Education Response**

> THIS ITEM IS ITSELF THE CHINESE EDUCATION RESPONSE — the education system's answer to AI, automation, industrial upgrading and graduate unemployment, executed through the degree catalogue.
> Its full architecture:

(1) LEGAL/ADMINISTRATIVE ARCHITECTURE.
> A binding national undergraduate major catalogue (883 majors, 92 major classes, 13 degree categories as of 2026), revised annually, with every programme point at every institution requiring registration or ministerial approval.
> This is the instrument that makes everything else possible and that Indonesia does not have.

(2) THE QUOTA.
> February 2023, five ministries: optimise/adjust ~20% of national discipline-major setting points by 2025.
> Delivered >30% cumulative churn — 10,200 added, 12,200 revoked or suspended, with the 2025 single-year ratio at 10.1%.

(3) THE ESCALATION.
> 28 August 2025, Central Education Work Leading Group, Action Plan 2025-2027, with six action lines: extraordinary/fast-track layout of urgently needed disciplines; strengthening of basic disciplines (the explicit counterweight to over-cutting); incubation of emerging and interdisciplinary fields including demonstration interdisciplinary centres; optimisation of existing programmes with formal warnings and mandated remediation where social demand, training quality or conditions are inadequate; curriculum content modernisation with AI-empowered teaching; and training-model reform through National Excellence Engineer Academies.

(4) THE INDUSTRIAL ALIGNMENT.
> MOE notice of 30 June 2025 directing programme setting at 16 named industry fields.
> Since 2024, eight provinces run a pilot matching programme portfolios to regional industrial clusters, producing 247 'characteristic advantage major clusters' tied to 100-billion- and trillion-yuan regional industries.

(5) THE EXIT MECHANISM.
> Provincial employment-based red/yellow cards: Jiangxi issues a yellow card and cuts enrolment quota below a 50% graduate destination rate, a red card and enrolment suspension after two consecutive years below 50%; Anhui and Jiangxi revoke after 2-3 consecutive years below 60%.
> Jiangxi's five-year net: +312 programme points, -335 stopped or revoked.
> Fujian and Jiangxi pioneered the mechanism from 2022; it is now widespread.

(6) THE FAST-TRACK CREATION MECHANISM.
> 'Extraordinary' (超常规) approval for strategically urgent majors, bypassing the normal cycle — used for Low-Altitude Technology and Engineering (6 universities, 2025) and Embodied Intelligence (9 universities, 2026).
> China can now go from national priority to first student intake in roughly 12-18 months, which is the real capability being demonstrated.

(7) THE STRUCTURAL INNOVATION.
> The 2026 catalogue created a thirteenth top-level degree category, Interdisciplinary (交叉学科), populated with Future Robotics, Interdisciplinary Engineering, Embodied Intelligence and Brain-Computer Science and Technology, and explicitly designed to connect the undergraduate and postgraduate discipline catalogues.
> This is the deepest change: China stopped forcing new fields into old faculty boundaries.

(8) THE ELITE-INSTITUTION SIGNAL.
> Fudan capping humanities and social sciences at 20% of undergraduate intake under 'refine the humanities, sharpen the sciences, strengthen engineering, renew medicine, enliven the interdisciplinary', delivering an almost exactly 20/20/20/20/20 class in 2025.

(9) THE VOCATIONAL PARALLEL.
> 27 new vocational majors in 2026 (AI, low-altitude economy, humanoid robotics, first intake 2027), ~40 in the prior cycle, 33 new undergraduate-level vocational colleges approved with roughly half upgraded from vocational schools, a target of vocational undergraduate places at ≥10% of vocational higher education enrolment by 2025, and a 2022 legal revision giving vocational education parity with general education — all responding to a projected ~30 million skilled-worker shortage.

(10) THE SELF-CORRECTION ALREADY UNDERWAY.
> Chinese official and academic discourse now openly discusses the herd-behaviour problem (institutions opening AI programmes without faculty, laboratories or curriculum, sometimes by prefixing 'intelligent' to an existing major name), the outcome problem (only ~55% of 2024 AI graduates in field-relevant work; about half calling their curriculum outdated), the faculty-displacement problem, and the basic-disciplines problem.
> The 2025-2027 Action Plan's second action line exists because of the third of these.
> Indonesia's most valuable takeaway is not the cull but this correction: China is telling the world, in advance, which parts of the policy fail.

TRANSFERABLE VS NON-TRANSFERABLE: the mechanism (catalogue + quota + kill switch) is not transferable to Indonesia's private-dominant system.
> The DIAGNOSTIC APPARATUS is fully transferable and cheap — programme-level graduate destination data, published, comparable, annual.
> The REGIONAL MATCHING PILOT is transferable and desirable.
> The FAST-TRACK CREATION PROCEDURE is transferable and would fix Indonesia's slowest bottleneck.
> The FUDAN-STYLE HUMANITIES CAP is transferable but should not be copied.

### Pelajaran Kebijakan dari China

**Respons Kebijakan China**

> CHINA'S CORRECTIVE AND GUARD-RAIL POLICIES — the regulations imposed after the campaign started producing damage, which are the ones Indonesia should adopt preemptively:

(1) EXPLICIT PROTECTION OF BASIC DISCIPLINES.
> The 2025-2027 Action Plan's second action line strengthens basic disciplines inside excellence-building schemes — an admission that outcome-driven cutting had endangered mathematics, physics, chemistry, biology and core humanities, which have long payback periods and poor short-run employment metrics.
> LESSON FOR INDONESIA: ring-fence basic sciences and core humanities from any relevance test BEFORE the test is created, not after.
> Indonesia has already closed S1 Mathematics programmes in 2026 without such a guard-rail in place.

(2) FACULTY TRANSITION RIGHTS AND REDEPLOYMENT PATHWAYS.
> Chinese universities were required to build teacher-transition provisions into their own programme-adjustment regulations.
> Documented practice at one Hunan institution offers five redeployment tracks: teaching posts in adjacent programmes within the same school, other technical posts, administrative posts, student-counsellor posts, and posts in the innovation and entrepreneurship college.
> Experts additionally recommend visiting-scholar opportunities, a defined 'buffer zone' for transitioning teachers, and broadened evaluation systems so that teaching-track and teaching-research-track careers are viable.
> LESSON FOR INDONESIA: no programme closure regulation without a mandatory, funded lecturer transition scheme — otherwise closure means unemployment for a middle-class professional group with no cushion in the private sector.

(3) TEACH-OUT PROTECTION FOR ENROLLED STUDENTS.
> The Chinese distinction between 停招 (suspend new enrolment) and 撤销 (revoke) exists precisely so that enrolled cohorts complete their degrees; the standard sequence is warning, then enrolment suspension with a remediation period, then revocation.
> LESSON FOR INDONESIA: legislate the sequence — warning, remediation window, enrolment suspension, closure — never immediate termination, and guarantee transfer rights.

(4) WARNING BEFORE EXECUTION.
> Chinese provinces issue yellow cards with quota deductions before red cards with suspension, and the national Action Plan requires warnings plus improvement requirements rather than direct closure.
> LESSON FOR INDONESIA: build a graduated, published, appealable warning ladder — this also creates the political cover that makes closure survivable.

(5) MULTI-CRITERIA EVALUATION, NOT EMPLOYMENT RATE ALONE.
> The Action Plan's fourth line triggers on three criteria — insufficient social demand, declining training quality, AND inadequate conditions — not on employment rate alone.
> Chinese critics note that evaluation metrics weighted toward engineering-style outputs systematically disadvantage humanities faculty.
> LESSON FOR INDONESIA: never build a single-metric kill switch; a graduate-employment-only rule would be gamed instantly and would destroy disciplines whose value is not captured by first-job placement.

(6) REGIONAL MATCHING RATHER THAN UNIFORM NATIONAL TARGETS.
> The eight-province pilot aligning programmes to local industrial clusters (247 clusters) is the part of the Chinese design most suited to a diverse, decentralised country.
> LESSON FOR INDONESIA: any Indonesian version should be provincial and cluster-based from day one — nickel/battery in Sulawesi, marine in eastern Indonesia, geothermal in Sumatra — not a uniform Jakarta-issued percentage.

(7) CONTROLLING HERD BEHAVIOUR IN NEW PROGRAMME APPROVAL.
> China's most-criticised failure: hundreds of institutions opened AI programmes without adequate faculty, laboratories or curriculum, some merely renaming existing majors, producing only ~55% field-relevant employment for 2024 AI graduates.
> China's answer has been fast-track approval reserved for capable institutions plus conditions-based review.
> LESSON FOR INDONESIA — THE MOST URGENT ONE: gate new AI/robotics/semiconductor programme permits on verified faculty qualifications, laboratory capacity and named industry partners.
> Indonesia is at exactly the moment before this mistake, and can avoid it at zero cost.

(8) VOCATIONAL PARITY IN LAW.
> China's 2022 Vocational Education Law revision gave vocational education legal parity with general education, plus undergraduate-level vocational institutions.
> LESSON FOR INDONESIA: elevate applied/vocational bachelor's degrees in law, funding and civil-service recruitment rules, so that D4/vocational pathways become a destination rather than a consolation.

(9) MANDATORY, COMPARABLE, PUBLISHED OUTCOME DATA.
> The whole Chinese system runs on annual graduate destination rates per programme point.
> LESSON FOR INDONESIA: this is the cheapest, highest-leverage, least politically costly reform available, and it should come first — transparency will drive most of the adjustment through student choice before any closure power is ever needed.

(10) CURRICULUM ITERATION AS A STANDING OBLIGATION.
> The Action Plan's fifth line mandates accelerated content iteration and AI-empowered teaching across all programmes.
> LESSON FOR INDONESIA: the higher-return intervention is usually reforming what is taught inside an existing programme, not deleting the programme.

**Rekomendasi Kebijakan Indonesia**

> SEQUENCED, IN ORDER OF POLITICAL FEASIBILITY AND RETURN:

PHASE 1 (2026-2027) — BUILD THE EVIDENCE BASE BEFORE TOUCHING ANY PROGRAMME
1.
> Mandate standardised, audited, PUBLISHED programme-level graduate outcome data: employment rate, field-relevance, median salary, time-to-first-job, per prodi per institution, one year and three years after graduation.
> Publish on PDDikti as open data.
> This alone will trigger most of the necessary adjustment through student choice, and it is the single highest-leverage reform available.
2.
> Publish an annual national supply-demand map by field — Indonesia's version of the '490,000 vs 20,000' calculation, extended across all fields, produced jointly by Kemdiktisaintek, Kemnaker and BPS.
3.
> Create a public dashboard of prodi openings and closures so the churn rate becomes a visible national statistic, as it is in China.

PHASE 2 (2027-2028) — CONTROL THE INFLOW BEFORE ATTACKING THE STOCK
4.
> Impose a moratorium on NEW permits in demonstrably oversupplied fields — teacher education first, then generic management/administration and remaining D3 business programmes.
> Stopping the bleeding is politically far cheaper than amputation and delivers most of the benefit over a decade.
5.
> Gate new permits in strategic fields (AI, robotics, semiconductors, energy) on verified inputs: minimum PhD-qualified faculty in the field, laboratory capacity, named industry partners with signed placement commitments.
> This is the explicit lesson from China's herd-behaviour failure and it costs nothing to legislate now.
6.
> Create an Indonesian fast-track approval procedure — 12 months from national priority designation to first intake, for institutions that meet the input gates.
> Indonesia's approval slowness is as damaging as its lack of closure power.

PHASE 3 (2028-2030) — TRANSFORM RATHER THAN CLOSE
7.
> Fund a national PRODI TRANSFORMATION programme: competitive grants for institutions converting an oversupplied programme into an aligned one, covering curriculum redesign, laboratory equipment and — critically — lecturer retraining and further study.
> Make transformation more attractive than closure, in line with the minister's own 'transformation not closure' framing.
8.
> Legislate a mandatory LECTURER TRANSITION SCHEME before any closure authority is created: retraining funding, defined redeployment tracks (adjacent programme, general education, laboratory, administration, industry secondment), a minimum 3-year buffer, and portability of accumulated service.
> Adopt China's five-track model.
9.
> Legislate the closure sequence with teach-out and transfer guarantees: published warning → funded remediation window (minimum 2 years) → enrolment suspension → closure, with an appeal mechanism.
10.
> Ring-fence basic sciences (mathematics, physics, chemistry, biology), core humanities, and strategically necessary but low-volume fields from any employment-based test, with dedicated national funding — learning from China's need to add a basic-disciplines counterweight after the fact.

PHASE 4 (2029-2032) — REGIONAL MATCHING, THE MOST VALUABLE IDEA TO IMPORT
11.
> Run a provincial major-cluster pilot on the eight-province Chinese model: each province identifies 2-3 anchor industries and the institutions serving them receive targeted funding to build matched programmes.
> Priority pairings: Central/North Sulawesi with battery metallurgy and industrial automation; Maluku/NTT with marine technology, fisheries and port logistics; North Sumatra/NTT with geothermal and renewables; Riau/Kalimantan with bioprocess and biomass engineering; East Kalimantan with energy transition and reclamation engineering; Bali/NTB with tourism technology and creative industries; Batam/Karawang with electronics and semiconductor packaging.
> This ADDS capacity outside Java instead of subtracting it, and directly answers the equity objection.
12.
> Explicitly EXEMPT institutions that are the sole tertiary provider in their district from closure pressure, replacing closure with mandatory partnership, franchising of curriculum from stronger institutions, and shared-faculty arrangements.

CROSS-CUTTING
13.
> Mandate AI literacy across every programme rather than confining AI to AI degrees — China's Action Plan requires AI-empowered teaching system-wide and this is the higher-return intervention.
14.
> Resolve the teacher-education contradiction openly: reconcile the '490,000 graduates vs 20,000 vacancies' and 'short 679,000 teachers' figures through a single joint Kemdiktisaintek-Kemendikdasmen workforce plan, then set LPTK intake to the plan.
> The problem is a broken distribution and formation system, not the existence of teacher education.
15.
> Elevate vocational/applied degrees in law, funding and civil-service recruitment, following China's 2022 legal parity reform.
16.
> Protect against the credential-inflation failure mode: require every new strategic programme to publish its graduate outcomes from the first cohort, so that Indonesia detects its own 55%-field-relevance problem within four years rather than fifteen.
17.
> DO NOT adopt a national percentage target for programme restructuring.
> It fits a state-owned, contracting, high-participation system and fits none of Indonesia's conditions.
> Indonesia should import China's diagnostics, its guard-rails and its regional matching — and decline its quota.

### Peluang & Rekomendasi Aksi

**Peluang Bisnis**

> (1) LECTURER AND FACULTY RESKILLING — the clearest under-served market.
> Tens of thousands of Indonesian lecturers in oversupplied fields need credible retraining into adjacent teachable areas (data literacy, applied AI, industry-linked pedagogy).
> China ran this through state institutions; Indonesia has no dominant provider.
> Addressable via micro-credentials, industry certification partnerships, and cohort-based programmes sold to yayasan and to LLDIKTI.
> Demand is guaranteed by the arithmetic regardless of whether closures happen.

(2) TURNKEY PROGRAMME-IN-A-BOX FOR NEW MAJORS.
> Most Indonesian institutions want an AI, data, robotics or renewable-energy programme and cannot build one: no curriculum, no faculty, no laboratory, no industry partner.
> A packaged offering — accredited curriculum, laboratory specification and equipment, trained instructors, industry placement network, capstone project pipeline — sold per programme is a high-margin, sticky business.
> This is exactly the gap that produced China's herd-behaviour quality failure, which means the market will exist and the quality bar will be the differentiator.
> Adjacent: laboratory equipment supply and integration (robotics cells, embedded systems, power electronics, microfabrication teaching kits), where Chinese vendors will compete aggressively on price.

(3) GRADUATE OUTCOME DATA AND TRACER-STUDY INFRASTRUCTURE.
> If Indonesia mandates programme-level outcome reporting — the most likely first policy move — every institution needs instrumentation.
> Tracer-study platforms, alumni CRM, employer feedback systems, and analytics benchmarking a programme against national peers.
> Sells to institutions on compliance and to the ministry as national infrastructure.
> Small market today, mandatory market within three years.

(4) INDEPENDENT PROGRAMME RATINGS AND CAREER-OUTCOME GUIDANCE FOR FAMILIES.
> Indonesian families are making six-figure-rupiah-per-semester decisions with almost no outcome information.
> China's gaokao advisory industry is large and profitable.
> An Indonesian equivalent — programme-level ROI data, honest employability ratings, admissions advisory — has strong consumer demand and a clean media/subscription/lead-generation model.
> Ethical risk to manage: this business profits from fear.

(5) INSTITUTIONAL TURNAROUND AND M&A ADVISORY.
> With 84 private institutions flagged for possible licence revocation and structural consolidation coming, there is a professional services market in merger advisory, portfolio restructuring, accreditation remediation and distressed-asset transactions for yayasan — a market that essentially does not exist in Indonesia today.

(6) INDUSTRY-EMBEDDED ACADEMIES AND APPRENTICESHIP INTERMEDIATION.
> Employers in nickel/battery, EV assembly, electronics, renewables and digital services need technicians and engineers that universities do not produce.
> A firm that builds and operates corporate academies, or that intermediates structured apprenticeships between industrial estates and regional campuses, monetises the mismatch directly rather than waiting for universities to fix it.
> Strongest in Morowali, Weda Bay, Karawang-Cikarang, Batam and Gresik.

(7) ALTERNATIVE CREDENTIALS FOR THE DISPLACED.
> If the degree signal weakens as it has in China, demand shifts to shorter, employer-recognised credentials: bootcamps with verified placement, professional certifications, and portfolio-based assessment.
> The Indonesian bootcamp sector has already been through one hype cycle and a shakeout; the surviving model is employer-paid or income-share with genuine placement, not consumer-paid hope.

(8) SPECIALIST NICHE INSTITUTIONS.
> The Chinese pattern rewards differentiation and punishes generic provision.
> A small, focused, expensive Indonesian institution in one defensible field — battery and electrochemical engineering, marine technology, agritech, or health technology — with real industry ownership, is a more durable asset than a generic multi-faculty private university.
> Effectively, applying the Chinese lesson at the level of a single firm.

(9) EDTECH FOR CURRICULUM ITERATION.
> If curriculum must be updated continuously, institutions need tooling: courseware that updates, assessment banks, simulation and virtual laboratories (which also solve the equipment-cost problem for regional campuses), and AI teaching assistants.
> Virtual laboratories are especially well matched to an archipelagic country where equipment cannot be replicated everywhere.

(10) THE CONTRARIAN PLAY.
> When everyone rotates into AI, the scarce assets become the ones being abandoned: qualified mathematics and statistics teaching, laboratory-grade basic science, language and area-studies expertise, and skilled trades instruction.
> China's own corrective — adding a basic-disciplines action line after over-cutting — suggests these recover.
> Building capability in what is currently being discarded is a five-to-ten-year position with little competition.

**Rekomendasi Individu Mahasiswa**

> (1) CHOOSE THE INSTITUTION AND THE EVIDENCE, NOT THE PROGRAMME NAME.
> China's clearest lesson: 621 institutions offer AI, only ~55% of 2024 AI graduates found field-relevant work, and half called their curriculum outdated.
> A weak AI programme is worse than a strong mathematics programme.
> Before enrolling, demand evidence: how many faculty hold PhDs in the actual field, what laboratory exists, which employers hire from this programme, where did last year's graduates go.
> If the institution cannot answer, the programme is a name change.

(2) IF YOU ARE ALREADY IN A THREATENED PROGRAMME, DO NOT PANIC AND DO NOT TRANSFER REFLEXIVELY.
> Finish the degree — enrolled cohorts are protected in every closure regime — and build the complement rather than replacing the base.
> A teacher-education student who adds instructional design, EdTech and data skills is more employable than a mediocre computer science graduate.
> Marketing plus analytics, law plus technology regulation, communications plus AI-assisted production, design plus generative tooling: the pattern that survives is domain knowledge plus computational capability, and it beats both pure options.

(3) BUILD THE THREE THINGS THAT SURVIVE EVERY RESTRUCTURING.
> Quantitative reasoning (statistics and basic programming, whatever your field).
> Working fluency with AI tools as a collaborator, not a novelty — this is now mandated across the curriculum in China and will be assumed by Indonesian employers within three years.
> And demonstrated output: a portfolio, shipped projects, real internships.
> When degree signals weaken, portfolios become the signal.

(4) TARGET INDONESIA'S ACTUAL COMPARATIVE ADVANTAGES, NOT CHINA'S.
> Copying China's target list is a mistake: Indonesia has no domestic quantum industry and no eVTOL manufacturing base.
> Indonesia does have the world's largest nickel resource and a growing battery chain, an enormous marine and fisheries economy, a large agricultural sector ripe for technology, geothermal potential, a young digital consumer market, and a globally significant carbon and biodiversity asset base.
> Battery and electrochemical engineering, marine and aquaculture technology, agritech, geothermal and renewables, carbon and environmental measurement, and applied AI on top of any of these are fields where an Indonesian graduate can be globally relevant rather than a second-rate copy of a Chinese graduate.

(5) TAKE THE VOCATIONAL/APPLIED ROUTE SERIOUSLY.
> China legislated vocational parity and is expanding vocational bachelor's degrees against a projected 30-million skilled-worker shortage.
> Indonesia's industrial estates and processing plants have the same shortage today.
> A D4 or applied engineering qualification with real plant experience frequently out-earns a generic S1, and this gap will widen.

(6) LANGUAGES: MOVE UP THE VALUE CHAIN, DO NOT ABANDON.
> Routine translation is finished.
> But China created Area Studies, International Communication, International Law and International Organisations majors precisely as language study moved upward.
> Mandarin plus a technical or legal or commercial specialisation is a genuinely scarce Indonesian combination, especially with Chinese industrial investment concentrated in Indonesia.

(7) FOR HUMANITIES AND SOCIAL SCIENCE STUDENTS SPECIFICALLY.
> Do not accept the 'useless major' narrative uncritically — even China is correcting it.
> But do accept that generic provision is being devalued, and respond by specialising into something scarce: technology policy, AI ethics, computational social science, digital heritage, area studies, or research and evaluation methods.
> The Indonesian public sector, civil society and international organisations demand exactly these and cannot fill the roles.

(8) WATCH THE INSTITUTION'S SOLVENCY, NOT ONLY ITS RANKING.
> With 84 private institutions flagged for possible licence revocation, enrolling at a financially fragile campus is a real risk to your credential.
> Check accreditation status, enrolment trend and whether the institution has closed programmes recently.

(9) ASSUME A 40-YEAR CAREER WITH FOUR RESKILLINGS.
> Every specific technical skill taught today has a shorter half-life than your working life.
> The durable investments are learning capability, statistical and causal reasoning, writing and argument, and professional networks.
> Chinese graduates who over-optimised for a hot major in 2019 are discovering this in 2026.

**Rekomendasi Perguruan Tinggi**

> OPEN, WITH INPUT GATES ENFORCED FROM DAY ONE: applied AI and machine learning engineering; data engineering; cybersecurity; battery, electrochemical and metallurgical process engineering; renewable energy systems and geothermal engineering; industrial automation and mechatronics; agritech, food technology and aquaculture/marine technology; logistics and port engineering; applied statistics and actuarial science; semiconductor and microelectronics engineering (at the 5-8 institutions capable of it); biotechnology and bioinformatics; carbon accounting, climate risk and environmental engineering; geospatial and remote-sensing engineering; drone/UAV systems for agriculture, logistics and maritime surveillance — Indonesia's realistic version of China's 'low-altitude economy'; and on the humanities side, area and country studies, international and trade law, technology policy and AI ethics, and computational social science.
