Silver Economy (银发经济) — the commercialisation of population ageing: elderly healthcare and long-term care, senior living/CCRC real estate, senior tourism and leisure, age-adapted consumer products and assistive technology, elderly finance and pension products, and the age-tech/eldercare-robotics stack that China has turned from a welfare cost centre into a declared national industrial strategy
**Kategori**: Demografi & Sosial (Demography & Society) — with heavy cross-cutting exposure to Healthcare Services, Real Estate, Insurance & Financial Services, Tourism, Consumer Goods, Robotics/AI, Labour Markets (care work), and Fiscal Policy. Unlike most trends in this research set, this one is driven by a variable that is already locked in: people who will be 60 in 2045 have already been born.

📊 Laggard with two structural twists. Primarily Laggard: Indonesia trails China by roughly two decades demographically and institutionally. Twist 1 — Compressed and poorer-at-transition on the institutional dimension: Indonesia's fertility fell to replacement in 15 years without coercion, so its ageing will be fast, while its pension and care institutions are far less developed than China's were at the same demographic point; on care financing Indonesia is not merely behind, it has not started. Twist 2 — Reverse flow on care labour: Indonesia is a net exporter of eldercare labour to older, richer societies (Taiwan became the top destination for Indonesian migrant workers in Q1 2026, with 17.5% placed as caregivers; Japan is expanding intake) before it has built a domestic care industry. In this narrow respect Indonesia is upstream of China rather than downstream — Indonesian caregivers are already staffing the ageing societies China is trying to serve with robots. Partial Leapfrog is plausible on technology and product (Indonesia will import Chinese assistive devices, monitoring hardware and possibly eldercare robots without passing through a domestic manufacturing phase) and on service delivery (telemedicine and home-care platforms may skip the institutional-bed build-out that left China with 50% vacancy). | 🎯 Prob: Tinggi (High) — and unusually, near-certain in the demographic dimension. This is the most predictable trend in this research programme: the Indonesians who will be 60 in 2045 are already alive and counted. What is genuinely uncertain is not whether the silver economy arrives but which form it takes: a China-style state-financed care system (probability Rendah-Sedang / Low-Medium on current fiscal and political trajectory), a private premium market serving the top 5-10% (probability Tinggi / High, already happening), or a family-and-informal-labour absorption model with a thin commercial veneer (probability Tinggi / High, and the current default). | 🔍 Keyakinan: Tinggi (High) for the demographic core and for Chinese policy facts; Sedang (Medium) for market sizing on both sides; Rendah-Sedang (Low-Medium) for Indonesian industry scale and for all timeline predictions.

High confidence: Indonesia's demographic position (BPS SUPAS 2025, an official intercensal survey published May 2026: 11.97% aged 60+, TFR 2.13, population 284.67 million, working-age share peaked in 2020); China's demographic position (323 million aged 60+ / 23% and 223.65 million aged 65+ / 15.9% at end-2025, from official statistics reported through Chinese state media); China's policy chronology, which is exceptionally well documented (January 2024 State Council Opinions with 26 measures; January 2025 retirement-age implementation; January 2026 RMB 800 eldercare voucher; March 2026 LTC insurance nationalisation with a 2028 universal target); the Chinese education response (2020 major creation, 44 approved universities, SUES fill-rate and Shandong Women's University enrolment figures, 2024 kindergarten and preschool-teacher contraction numbers, all from Xinhua, Beijing Review, Sixth Tone, MoE statistical reports and SCMP); Indonesia's pension coverage gap (15.2 million participants as of August 2025, corroborated by UGM and ILO).

Medium confidence: silver-economy market sizes on both sides (see contradictions note); China's nursing-home vacancy figures, which come from a mix of 2020 national data, a 2023 Beijing survey and secondary syntheses; the eldercare robot market projections, which come from commercial research houses; Indonesia's facility counts, which come from an academic desk review rather than a registry.

Low-medium confidence: Indonesia's geriatric specialist count (two incompatible figures circulate — roughly 14-15 nationally versus 1.5 per 100,000 elderly, which would imply about 500); the ERIA US$7.5 billion Indonesian silver-economy estimate, whose definition and vintage I could not verify directly; all Indonesian timeline predictions (mainstream 2033-2040, peak 2045-2065), which hinge on an unpredictable political decision about care financing; the claim that Indonesia will be the world's third-largest silver economy, which appears in policy discourse without a stated methodology; the assessment of Chinese corporate entry vectors into Indonesian eldercare, where the evidence is thin and largely negative (absence of evidence rather than evidence of absence).

> **Status di Indonesia**: Baru mulai / pilot — but with a demographic trigger that has already fired. Indonesia formally became an ageing population in the 2025 Intercensal Survey (SUPAS 2025, published by BPS in May 2026), which recorded 11.97% of the population aged 60+, breaching the 10% threshold for the first time. The commercial silver economy, however, is at pioneer scale: a handful of senior living operators, a thin layer of private home-care and daycare firms, no long-term care insurance, minimal pension coverage, and an almost non-existent geriatric medical workforce. The gap between demographic status (already ageing) and industrial status (pre-commercial) is the defining feature of Indonesia's position — and it is wider than China's was at the equivalent demographic moment, because China's state began building the payment system within a decade of crossing the threshold whereas Indonesia has not begun.

### Basic Info

**Tahun Mulai China**

> Three distinct starting points, and conflating them is the main analytical error.
> (a) Demographic start — 1998-2000: China crossed the WHO 7% threshold for population aged 65+ in 1998, and the 2000 census recorded 10.33% of the population aged 60+, formally making China an 'ageing society'.
> (b) Commercial start — 2008-2015: Cherish-Yearn (亲和源) opened China's first membership-based senior community in Shanghai in 2008; Taikang Life received the first insurance-company approval to build continuing-care retirement communities (CCRCs) and opened Taikang Yanyuan in Beijing in 2015; Vanke, Sino-Ocean and Poly entered senior housing over 2010-2016.
> (c) Policy/industrial start — January 2024: the State Council General Office issued 'Opinions on Developing the Silver Economy and Improving the Well-being of the Elderly' — the first Chinese policy document ever named after the silver economy — containing 26 measures across four areas and mandating 10 dedicated silver-economy industrial parks.
> The 2024 document is the true inflection point: it reframed ageing from a social-welfare liability into a designated growth sector, and everything from 2024 to 2026 (long-term care insurance nationalisation, the eldercare consumption subsidy, silver trains, eldercare robotics pilots) descends from it.

**Pemain Kunci China**

> Insurance-led senior living (the dominant model): Taikang Life / Taikang Community (泰康之家) — pioneered the fusion of pension insurance, health insurance, asset management and CCRCs via a membership-card residency-rights model, now operating premium CCRCs in Beijing, Shanghai, Guangzhou, Chengdu and other tier-1/1.5 cities; Ping An (平安臻颐年 'Ping An Zhen Yi Nian' and the 'Ping An Butler' integrated payment-service-investment chain); China Life and Taiping also active.
> The insurance+eldercare value chain alone is estimated at over RMB 500 billion and is projected to reach trillion-yuan scale by 2030.
> Developer-led senior living: China Vanke (万科随园), Sino-Ocean Group (远洋椿萱茂), Poly Property (保利和熹会), Cherish-Yearn (亲和源, the Shanghai luxury pioneer).
> State/quasi-state: China Resources, China Merchants, and the Ministry of Civil Affairs' network of ~8,000+ licensed eldercare institutions.
> Eldercare robotics and age-tech: Unitree Robotics, UBTech Robotics, Fourier Intelligence (its care-centric humanoid GR-3, showcased at CES 2026, is positioned as the first full-size robot designed and marketed for eldercare at commercial scale), AgiBot, and the Chengdu Humanoid Robot Innovation Center.
> Platforms and consumer distribution: Alibaba/Taobao (dedicated 'Elder Mode' interfaces and senior shopping support lines), Douyin and Kuaishou (senior creator ecosystems and silver livestream commerce), Pinduoduo (value-priced elderly goods).
> Travel: China Railway Group's 'silver train' (银发旅游列车) network operated under a nine-agency action plan, plus Trip.com/Ctrip senior travel lines and hundreds of regional 旅居养老 (extended-stay retirement) operators in Yunnan, Hainan, Guangxi and Guizhou.
> Education: the National University for the Aged (国家老年大学, inaugurated March 2023) plus the nationwide 老年大学 network.
> Consumer goods: domestic adult-incontinence brands, hearing-aid makers, mobility-aid and massage-chair manufacturers, and the 适老化改造 (age-friendly home retrofit) contracting industry.

### China Trend Detail

**Apa Yang Terjadi Di China**

> China is executing the world's largest and fastest deliberate conversion of a demographic problem into an industrial policy.
> The mechanism has four interlocking layers.

Layer 1 — Demographic forcing.
> By end-2025 China had 323 million people aged 60+ (23.0% of the population) and 223.65 million aged 65+ (15.9%).
> Under the 15th Five-Year Plan (2026-2030) the elderly population is projected to grow 3.6% per year, taking the 60+ share to 27.8% by 2030, with the old-age dependency ratio crossing 40% during the plan period and reaching 46.1% by 2030.
> China will pass 400 million people aged 60+ around 2035 and enter what officials call the 'severe ageing' (重度老龄化) phase.
> Crucially, the one-child policy means each of these elders has on average roughly one child, producing the '4-2-1' structure in which one working adult faces four grandparents and two parents — a family-care supply collapse with no historical precedent at this scale.

Layer 2 — Care system construction.
> Because families cannot absorb the load, the state has built a care infrastructure around the '9073' service model (90% of seniors age at home, 7% receive community-based care, 3% institutional).
> The binding constraint was never beds but payment.
> China's answer is long-term care insurance (长期护理保险), piloted from 2016 in 49 cities, covering roughly 300 million people and paying benefits to over 3.3 million individuals, with designated providers growing tenfold to about 12,000.
> In March 2026 this was elevated into a national scheme — the widely reported 'sixth insurance' alongside pension, medical, unemployment, work-injury and maternity — with a three-year target (by 2028) of a unified system covering the entire population regardless of employment status, starting with the severely disabled and expanding downward in severity.
> In January 2026 the Ministry of Civil Affairs and Ministry of Finance added a national eldercare service consumption subsidy: monthly electronic vouchers worth up to RMB 800 per person for 12 months, usable on meal assistance, bathing, housekeeping, mobility support, emergency aid, medical assistance, rehabilitation nursing and daytime care.
> Over 1.05 million disabled seniors had received it by March 2026 and about 2 million during 2026.

Layer 3 — Consumption and industry.
> Chinese policymakers explicitly distinguish 养老 ('providing for the aged', a welfare frame) from 享老 ('enjoying age', a consumption frame).
> Today's Chinese retirees — the cohort that entered the workforce during reform and opening — hold urban property, receive urban pensions, and spend rather than hoard.
> The result is demand for senior tourism (over 100 million active senior travellers projected by end-2025), age-adapted housing retrofits, functional foods and TCM wellness, wearable health monitoring, hearing aids, adult incontinence products, smart-home safety systems, paid hobby instruction, and senior-targeted content and e-commerce.
> Seniors are now a major digital cohort: over 26% of Chinese netizens are aged 50+ versus 9% five years earlier, and a survey of 5,000+ older adults found roughly 90% watch short video for an average of about two hours daily.

Layer 4 — Technology substitution for care labour.
> China cannot hire its way out of the care-worker deficit, so it is attempting to automate part of it.
> New elderly-care service reform guidelines explicitly call for advancing humanoid robots, brain-computer interfaces and AI in senior care.
> Beijing launched what state media described as the world's first robot- and AI-powered eldercare centre in March 2026; the Chengdu Humanoid Robot Innovation Center is building lightweight humanoids to identify seniors, deliver medication, converse and assist with bathing; Fourier's GR-3 targets commercial eldercare deployment.
> This layer has no analogue in Japan's or Europe's ageing response at comparable scale.

Running alongside all of this is the supply-side adjustment: from 1 January 2025 China began gradually raising the statutory retirement age (male 60→63; female 55→58 and 50→55) over 15 years, with flexible early and late retirement windows of up to three years each — the first such increase since the 1950s.

**Fase Tren Di China**

> Booming, and — unusually — state-accelerated rather than state-restrained.
> The trend is past 'emerging' and nowhere near 'mature'.
> Three sub-phases coexist: (a) the care-payment system is in early build-out (LTC insurance only nationalised in March 2026, universal coverage targeted for 2028); (b) the consumption/leisure layer is in full boom (silver trains, senior tourism, senior e-commerce, senior content); (c) the technology layer is in hype-and-pilot phase (eldercare robots are in showcase and pilot deployment, not routine service).
> Simultaneously the institutional-care segment shows a mature-market pathology usually seen much later — roughly 50% bed vacancy nationally and 38% occupancy in Beijing — because supply was built ahead of affordable payment.
> So the honest classification is: policy phase = booming; demand phase = structurally guaranteed and accelerating; supply phase = oversupplied at the top and undersupplied at the affordable middle; technology phase = emerging.
> There is no meaningful backlash phase yet; the closest thing is regulatory crackdown on eldercare fraud, which targets abuse of the sector rather than the sector itself.

### Status Indonesia Saat Ini

**Status Di Indonesia**

> Baru mulai / pilot — but with a demographic trigger that has already fired.
> Indonesia formally became an ageing population in the 2025 Intercensal Survey (SUPAS 2025, published by BPS in May 2026), which recorded 11.97% of the population aged 60+, breaching the 10% threshold for the first time.
> The commercial silver economy, however, is at pioneer scale: a handful of senior living operators, a thin layer of private home-care and daycare firms, no long-term care insurance, minimal pension coverage, and an almost non-existent geriatric medical workforce.
> The gap between demographic status (already ageing) and industrial status (pre-commercial) is the defining feature of Indonesia's position — and it is wider than China's was at the equivalent demographic moment, because China's state began building the payment system within a decade of crossing the threshold whereas Indonesia has not begun.

### Analisis Lag

**Bukti Historical Lag**

> (1) Fertility transition sequencing: China's TFR fell below replacement around 1991-1992; Indonesia's reached 2.13 only in 2025 — a 33-year gap on that specific marker, though Indonesia's decline is now steeper relative to income.
> (2) Ageing threshold crossing: China 2000 (10.33% aged 60+), Indonesia 2020-2021 — a 20-21 year gap, and the single hardest piece of evidence in this analysis because both figures come from national censuses/intercensal surveys rather than models.
> (3) Pension system build-out: China's New Rural Social Pension pilot began in 2009 and reached near-universal rural coverage within roughly five years; Indonesia's contributory pension has been running since the 2015 BPJS Ketenagakerjaan reform and after a decade still covers under 25% of formal workers — a widening rather than closing gap.
> (4) Senior housing formats: Indonesia's first senior living community (RUKUN, 2012) followed China's first (Cherish-Yearn, 2008) by only four years, matching the 4-5 year format-transfer lag observed elsewhere in this research set (Miniso China 2013 to Indonesia 2017-2018; Mixue China scale-up 2018 to Indonesia 2020).
> Format transfer is fast; market depth is slow.
> (5) Health system response: China created a formal geriatric medicine specialty and built geriatrics departments into tertiary hospitals through the 2000s-2010s; Indonesia's geriatric specialist count remains in the low double digits in 2025-2026, indicating a clinical-capacity lag closer to 25-30 years.
> (6) Education-system response to falling fertility: China's kindergarten contraction began visibly in 2022-2023 and accelerated to 21,100 closures in 2024 and roughly 21,400 in 2025; Indonesia's TFR only hit replacement in 2025, so the equivalent school-contraction shock is roughly 10-15 years away — a directly forecastable lag with a known mechanism.

**Tipe Lag**

> Laggard with two structural twists.
> Primarily Laggard: Indonesia trails China by roughly two decades demographically and institutionally.
> Twist 1 — Compressed and poorer-at-transition on the institutional dimension: Indonesia's fertility fell to replacement in 15 years without coercion, so its ageing will be fast, while its pension and care institutions are far less developed than China's were at the same demographic point; on care financing Indonesia is not merely behind, it has not started.
> Twist 2 — Reverse flow on care labour: Indonesia is a net exporter of eldercare labour to older, richer societies (Taiwan became the top destination for Indonesian migrant workers in Q1 2026, with 17.5% placed as caregivers; Japan is expanding intake) before it has built a domestic care industry.
> In this narrow respect Indonesia is upstream of China rather than downstream — Indonesian caregivers are already staffing the ageing societies China is trying to serve with robots.
> Partial Leapfrog is plausible on technology and product (Indonesia will import Chinese assistive devices, monitoring hardware and possibly eldercare robots without passing through a domestic manufacturing phase) and on service delivery (telemedicine and home-care platforms may skip the institutional-bed build-out that left China with 50% vacancy).

### Probabilitas Transfer ke Indonesia

**Probabilitas Transfer**

> Tinggi (High) — and unusually, near-certain in the demographic dimension.
> This is the most predictable trend in this research programme: the Indonesians who will be 60 in 2045 are already alive and counted.
> What is genuinely uncertain is not whether the silver economy arrives but which form it takes: a China-style state-financed care system (probability Rendah-Sedang / Low-Medium on current fiscal and political trajectory), a private premium market serving the top 5-10% (probability Tinggi / High, already happening), or a family-and-informal-labour absorption model with a thin commercial veneer (probability Tinggi / High, and the current default).

**Alasan Probabilitas**

> (1) The driver is arithmetic, not preference.
> Fertility has already fallen to 2.13 and continues declining; the working-age share already peaked in 2020.
> No policy can reverse the 2045 age structure.
> (2) Indonesia is already over the threshold.
> At 11.97% aged 60+ (SUPAS 2025) the country is formally ageing; the trend does not need to be 'transferred' — it is endogenous.
> (3) The capital is already positioning.
> Bank Mandiri Taspen's July 2026 pivot toward a senior health-and-finance ecosystem, insurers launching age-specific products, and hospital groups adding geriatric services indicate that Indonesian financial institutions have read the demographic tables.
> (4) The format templates are proven and cheap to copy — CCRC, assisted living, daycare, home care and age-adapted retrofits require no technology transfer and have already been demonstrated locally by RUKUN and Hovi since 2012 and the late 2010s.
> (5) The product supply is frictionless.
> Chinese assistive devices, adult incontinence products, mobility aids, monitoring wearables and smart-home safety hardware already flow into Indonesia through Shopee, Tokopedia and TikTok Shop with no policy required.
> (6) The demonstration effect is regional and strong: Japan, Singapore, Thailand, Malaysia and Vietnam are all building senior-living and eldercare industries, with a Southeast Asian senior-living summit convened in Da Nang in May 2026 explicitly to position the region for the silver economy.

The counterweight — and the reason the *China-style* version specifically is not high probability — is payment.
> China's silver economy is underwritten by near-universal (if minimal) pensions, expanding LTC insurance, and a state willing to spend RMB 800 per person per month on care vouchers.
> Indonesia has 15.2 million pension participants, no LTC insurance, roughly 59% informal employment, and fiscal priorities skewed toward the young (free nutritious meals, education, job creation) in an electorate whose median age is still around 30.
> Without a payer, Indonesia gets the demographics without the economy.

### Faktor Pendorong

**Prasyarat Struktural**

> Threshold conditions, benchmarked against China at the moment each layer of its silver economy activated.

(1) Elderly share of population above 10%.
> China: crossed in 2000.
> Indonesia: crossed 2020-2021, at 11.97% in 2025.
> STATUS: MET.
> This is the only prerequisite Indonesia unambiguously satisfies, and it is the one that guarantees the trend arrives.

(2) GDP per capita at the crossing point.
> China was at roughly US$960 per capita in 2000 when it crossed 10% aged 60+; Indonesia was at roughly US$4,300 in 2021 and is near US$5,000-5,300 in 2025.
> Indonesia is therefore about four to five times richer than China was at the equivalent demographic milestone — a genuinely favourable fact that is almost never stated.
> The problem is the trajectory, not the level: China multiplied per-capita income roughly thirteenfold in the 24 years after crossing, which is what financed the silver economy.
> Indonesia growing at 5% per year doubles income in 14 years, not thirteenfold in 24.
> STATUS: MET on level, AT RISK on trajectory.

(3) Income level at which the silver economy becomes a commercial market.
> China's silver economy reached RMB 7 trillion (6% of GDP) at roughly US$12,600 per capita.
> Indonesia at about US$5,000 has an estimated US$7.5 billion silver economy, roughly 0.5% of GDP.
> To reach China's 6% intensity Indonesia plausibly needs both higher income and a payment mechanism.
> STATUS: NOT MET.

(4) A payer: pension coverage plus long-term care financing.
> China entered its silver-economy boom with effectively universal pension coverage (about 180 million rural recipients alone, however minimal at RMB 123-163/month) and a decade of LTC insurance pilots covering 300 million people.
> Indonesia has 15.2 million contributory pension participants (under 25% of formal workers), no LTC insurance, and roughly 59% informal employment.
> STATUS: NOT MET — this is the binding constraint, and nothing else compensates for it.

(5) Clinical and care workforce capacity.
> China built geriatrics into its tertiary hospital system and set a 300,000 professional eldercare nursing workforce target by 2025; it created a dedicated undergraduate major in 2020 with 44 approved universities and 300+ institutions offering related programmes.
> Indonesia has roughly 14-15 geriatric specialists nationally by one count and about 1.5 geriatricians per 100,000 elderly by another, minimal geriatric nursing content in curricula, and exports its trained caregivers.
> STATUS: NOT MET, severely.

(6) Urbanisation and household nuclearisation.
> China was about 36% urban in 2000 and 67% by 2025; the collapse of multigenerational co-residence in cities is what created institutional demand.
> Indonesia is roughly 58-59% urban — already more urban than China was at its crossing point — and Indonesian urban households are nuclearising and shrinking, with rising female labour-force participation removing the traditional unpaid caregiver.
> STATUS: MET and accelerating; this is the second-strongest driver after demography.

(7) Family care-supply ratio.
> China's one-child policy produced roughly one child per elder and the 4-2-1 structure — the mechanical forcing function behind institutionalisation.
> Indonesia's TFR of 2.13 (and higher for the cohorts now entering old age, whose children number three to five) means Indonesian elders will have materially more children available.
> STATUS: NOT MET — and this is a permanent structural difference, not a lag.

(8) Digital penetration among seniors.
> China: over 26% of netizens aged 50+, roughly 90% of surveyed older adults watching short video about two hours daily — which is what makes senior e-commerce and senior content commercially viable.
> Indonesia: rising fast via WhatsApp, Facebook and TikTok among the 50-65 cohort, though granular data are weak.
> STATUS: PARTIALLY MET and improving quickly.

(9) Property wealth among the elderly.
> Chinese urban retirees hold housing assets from the 1990s privatisation, which underwrites their consumption.
> Indonesian elderly homeownership is high but illiquid, with no functioning reverse-mortgage or home-equity-release market.
> STATUS: PARTIALLY MET — the asset exists, the liquidity mechanism does not.

**Indikator Pemantauan**

> Already fired (confirming the demographic trigger): BPS SUPAS 2025 recording 11.97% aged 60+ and TFR 2.13 (published May 2026); the working-age share peaking at 69.28% in 2020 and declining to 68.94% by 2025; Perpres 88/2021 establishing a national ageing strategy; BPJS Ketenagakerjaan's 2026 pension programme updates covering retirement age, benefit levels and the contribution wage ceiling; Taiwan becoming the top destination for Indonesian migrant workers in Q1 2026 with 17.5% placed as caregivers; the ILO's October 2025 brief on universal old-age pension feasibility.

Firing now (commercial entry): Bank Mandiri Taspen's July 2026 announcement of a senior product-and-health ecosystem built around a 70-million-elderly-by-2045 planning assumption; insurers launching over-60 and over-70 specific health and life products (Chubb 'Second Life', Great Eastern, Generali); the proliferation of BNSP-certified caregiver training providers (LSP Caregiver, Caregiver Indonesia, UI Academy/NTC FIK UI); Hovi Care's recognition at the Global Health Indonesia Awards in February 2025; growth in ASLI membership.

Watch next — the leading indicators that would signal genuine market formation: (1) a Ministry of Health or Ministry of Social Affairs licensing category for 'assisted living' or 'residensia lansia' distinct from panti sosial — the single most important regulatory unlock; (2) any BPJS Kesehatan or BPJS Ketenagakerjaan pilot covering long-term or home-based care, however small; (3) new S1 or D4 study programmes in Manajemen Layanan Lansia / gerontology at Indonesian universities and new geriatric-medicine residency slots (currently the hardest bottleneck); (4) OJK issuing rules for reverse mortgages, home-equity release or annuity products for retirees; (5) major developers (Ciputra, Sinar Mas Land, Summarecon, Agung Podomoro, Alam Sutera) announcing dedicated senior or 'multigenerational' residential products; (6) hospital groups (Siloam, Mayapada, Hermina, Bunda) opening branded geriatric centres or memory clinics; (7) trademark and business-permit filings containing 'senior living', 'lansia', 'geriatri', 'caregiver', 'homecare'; (8) job-posting volume for 'caregiver', 'perawat lansia', 'care coordinator' on Jobstreet/LinkedIn for domestic (not overseas) placement; (9) Google Trends and TikTok volume for 'panti jompo', 'senior living', 'homecare lansia', 'demensia', 'alzheimer' — destigmatisation is measurable; (10) entry of any Chinese, Japanese, Singaporean or Korean eldercare operator via joint venture; (11) imports of assistive devices and adult incontinence products (HS-code level customs data) as a proxy for household-level care spending; (12) Kemenkes data on the number of puskesmas classified as 'santun lansia' and hospitals with geriatric services; (13) any move to replace UU 13/1998 with a modern elderly law carrying budget authority.

### Hambatan & Faktor Pembatal

**Hambatan Transfer**

> (1) No payer — the decisive barrier.
> With 15.2 million pension participants, no LTC insurance, and BPJS Kesehatan already running structural deficits, there is no financing channel between the elderly who need care and the firms that could provide it.
> Every other barrier is downstream of this.
> (2) Cultural stigma against institutional care.
> Placing a parent in a panti jompo is widely read as filial failure ('anak durhaka'); the word panti itself carries connotations of charity and abandonment.
> China faced the same norm and it produced 50% national bed vacancy and 38% Beijing occupancy — a warning that supply built ahead of cultural change fails commercially.
> Indonesian stigma is arguably stronger, reinforced by Islamic teaching on birr al-walidayn (kindness to parents) and by the practical availability of more children per elder.
> (3) Affordability.
> Private senior living and daycare in Indonesia is priced in the tens of millions of rupiah per month at the premium end, against a median household income far below that; commercial operators can only address the top few percent.
> (4) Clinical workforce scarcity.
> Roughly 14-15 geriatric specialists nationally and about 1.5 per 100,000 elderly; almost no geriatric content in nursing curricula; the UGM finding that limited gerontic nursing skills threaten elderly care quality.
> (5) Care-labour drain.
> The best-trained Indonesian caregivers leave for Taiwan, Japan, Hong Kong and Singapore where wages are multiples of domestic pay — so the domestic sector cannot staff itself even as Indonesia trains thousands of caregivers a year.
> (6) Regulatory vacuum.
> UU 13/1998 predates the modern industry; there is no licensing category, staffing ratio, quality standard or inspection regime for assisted living, memory care or home care, which deters institutional capital and invites low-quality entrants.
> (7) Land, zoning and building-code friction for age-appropriate development, plus the absence of age-friendly building standards.
> (8) Fragmented governance: ageing policy sits across Kemensos, Kemenkes, Kemenko PMK, Bappenas, BPJS and local governments with weak coordination and no budget line commensurate with the strategy.
> (9) Political economy: the electorate's median age is around 30 and the flagship social programmes target children and youth; elderly voters are not yet a bloc that reallocates budgets.
> (10) Data poverty: no national long-term care needs survey, no disability-adjusted care-need registry, no silver-economy market statistic — which makes both policy design and private investment cases hard to build.

**Faktor Pembatal Transfer**

> Structural conditions guaranteeing that China's silver economy will NOT replicate in Indonesia in the same form.

(1) No 4-2-1 forcing function.
> China's institutional-care demand was manufactured by the one-child policy: one adult child facing two parents and four grandparents makes family care arithmetically impossible, which is why the Chinese state had to build a care system.
> Indonesia's TFR of 2.13 today — and three to five children for the cohorts now entering old age — means Indonesian elders will retain a family care option for at least another generation.
> Indonesia will therefore get the demographic ageing without the acute family-care collapse, and institutional demand will emerge far more slowly and remain far more concentrated in urban, small-family, dual-income households.
> This is not a lag; it is a permanent divergence.

(2) No fiscal capacity for a 'sixth insurance'.
> China nationalised long-term care insurance backed by decades of contributory surplus, a formalised urban workforce, and a state willing to fund RMB 800/month vouchers for over a million people.
> Indonesia's tax-to-GDP ratio is roughly 10-11%, BPJS Kesehatan is under chronic strain, and roughly 59% of workers are informal and outside any contributory base.
> A universal Indonesian LTC insurance on China's model is not fiscally reachable before the 2040s without a tax-base transformation.

(3) Archipelagic geography defeats network-scale formats.
> China's silver trains — a national network targeting 100+ routes and 2,500 annual trips by 2027 — exist because a continental rail grid connects a homogeneous domestic tourism market.
> Indonesia has no such grid across 17,000 islands; senior travel here will be air/sea-based, fragmented, higher-cost per trip and impossible to run as a state-coordinated national product.
> Likewise the 老年助餐 community-canteen model and community daycare networks depend on dense, walkable, administratively uniform urban neighbourhoods (China's 社区 grid) that Indonesian cities outside a few Jakarta and Surabaya districts do not have.

(4) No domestic manufacturing base for age-tech.
> China's silver-products economy — RMB 148.3 billion in adult incontinence products, RMB 200 billion in age-friendly retrofits, a US$3.5 billion eldercare robot industry — rests on its manufacturing complex.
> Indonesia will import essentially all of this, capturing distribution and service margin only.
> The 'silver economy' as an Indonesian *industrial* opportunity is therefore much smaller than as a *consumption* phenomenon, and will worsen rather than improve the trade balance.

(5) Care labour flows outward, not inward.
> China absorbs its rural surplus labour into urban care work.
> Indonesia's care workers are pulled abroad by wage differentials of 5-15x.
> As long as Taiwan, Japan, Korea, Hong Kong and Singapore are ageing faster and paying more, Indonesia's domestic care sector will be structurally understaffed — the opposite of China's position.

(6) No property-wealth effect to monetise.
> Chinese urban retirees are asset-rich from housing privatisation and can be marketed CCRC memberships and reverse-equity products.
> Indonesian elderly homeownership is high but the homes are in low-liquidity locations, often without clean title, with no reverse-mortgage market.
> The asset cannot be converted into care spending.

(7) Religious and kinship norms are load-bearing, not decorative.
> In China, filial-piety norms bent within two decades under one-child arithmetic and state encouragement.
> In Indonesia the norm is reinforced by religious obligation, by larger sibling sets that permit rotation of caregiving duty, and by continued multigenerational co-residence — including in cities, where housing costs make it economically rational.

(8) Indonesia is ageing without a preceding period of mass affluence.
> China's silver economy is being consumed by a cohort that experienced 1990s-2010s income growth and holds urban pensions.
> Indonesia's 2045 elderly will largely be today's informal workers with no pension, no savings and no property liquidity — meaning the 2045 elderly cohort could be poorer, relative to national income, than today's.
> The plausible Indonesian outcome is not a silver *economy* but a silver *dependency burden* with a small luxury market attached.

### Prediksi Timeline di Indonesia

**Tahun Masuk Indonesia**

> Already entered, in stages.
> 2012: pioneer commercial entry (RUKUN Senior Living, CCRC format).
> 2021: policy entry (Perpres 88/2021 Strategi Nasional Kelanjutusiaan, 14 September 2021).
> 2020-2021: demographic entry (60+ share crosses 10%).
> 2025-2026: statistical confirmation and capital entry — SUPAS 2025 (published May 2026) formally classifies Indonesia as an ageing population at 11.97% with TFR 2.13, and financial institutions begin building explicitly for the cohort (Bank Mandiri Taspen, July 2026).
> The correct framing for 2026 is that Indonesia has crossed the demographic threshold and is in the earliest commercial-pilot phase, roughly equivalent to where China stood around 2005-2010: the demand is visible, the payment system is absent, and the market is served by a handful of premium operators.

**Skenario Percepatan**

> A BPJS long-term-care or home-care benefit pilot (even in three or four cities) would compress the timeline by five to ten years by creating a payer overnight.
> Other accelerants: an OJK framework for reverse mortgages and retirement annuities unlocking illiquid elderly housing wealth; a Ministry of Health licensing category for assisted living and memory care, which would unlock institutional capital currently deterred by regulatory ambiguity; a major bank-insurer-hospital consortium (Mandiri Taspen, Siloam, Mayapada, Ciputra) launching an integrated senior product at scale; mass return of Indonesian caregivers from Taiwan and Japan as those markets tighten or automate, supplying a trained workforce cheaply; a viral destigmatisation moment on TikTok akin to China's nursing-home vlog genre; entry of a Japanese, Singaporean or Chinese operator via joint venture, which would validate the category for domestic capital; sharper-than-expected fertility decline (TFR falling below 2.0 before 2030) accelerating the whole schedule; and inclusion of ageing as a named priority sector — not a welfare programme — in the next RPJMN.

### Dampak Sosial-Ekonomi

**Dampak Lapangan Kerja**

> Jobs created — this is one of the few trends in this research set that is net job-creating, and job-creating in roles resistant to AI substitution because they require physical presence and trust.

Direct care: caregivers and home-care aides (the largest single category; China targeted 300,000 professional eldercare nursing staff by 2025 for 323 million elders, and Indonesia will need workers in the hundreds of thousands by 2040), geriatric nurses, nursing assistants, dementia-care specialists, palliative and hospice workers, respite-care providers.
> Clinical: geriatricians (from a base of roughly 14-15 nationally — the scarcest professional category in Indonesian healthcare relative to need), geriatric psychiatrists, geriatric pharmacists managing polypharmacy, geriatric physiotherapists and occupational therapists, speech and swallowing therapists, clinical nutritionists specialising in sarcopenia and dysphagia.
> Operations and management: senior-living community managers, care coordinators and case managers, admissions and family-liaison staff, quality and compliance officers for a licensing regime that does not yet exist.
> Built environment: age-friendly retrofit contractors and assessors (China's 适老化改造 industry alone is RMB 200 billion), accessibility auditors, universal-design architects.
> Technology and product: age-tech product managers, remote-monitoring and fall-detection service operators, telemedicine staff serving rural elders, assistive-device fitters and maintainers, medical-equipment distributors.
> Finance and insurance: retirement-income advisers, long-term-care underwriters and actuaries, reverse-mortgage and annuity specialists, elder-fraud compliance officers.
> Leisure and lifestyle: senior travel operators and escorted-tour guides with medical training, senior education and hobby instructors, senior fitness and mobility coaches, senior-focused content creators and community managers, funeral and estate-planning services.
> Household services: meal-delivery and therapeutic-nutrition services, medication-management and companionship services.

Jobs changed: general practice medicine shifts toward multimorbidity and polypharmacy management; general nursing shifts toward gerontic competence; insurance agency shifts from life-cover selling to retirement-income and care-cost planning; residential property development shifts from family units to age-adaptable and multigenerational units; retail and F&B adapt formats (lighting, signage, seating, portion sizes, payment interfaces).

Jobs lost or shrinking — the mirror image, and the part Indonesian planners consistently miss: falling fertility destroys demand at the young end long before the elderly market compensates.
> China's example is stark: kindergartens fell from 274,400 to 253,300 in 2024 (21,100 closures in one year) and by roughly another 21,400 in 2025; 241,800 preschool teachers lost their jobs in 2024 alone, more than 600 per day; primary schools fell by 5,645 to 143,500 in 2023; over 30,000 preschools and primary schools closed in 2025; kindergarten enrolment fell by about 12 million children between 2020 and 2024 from a peak of 48 million.
> Indonesia's TFR hit 2.13 only in 2025, so this shock is roughly 10-15 years out — but it is coming, and it will hit early-childhood and primary teaching, children's publishing and apparel, baby-products manufacturing and retail, paediatric services, and private school operators.
> Also shrinking: youth-oriented consumer marketing and the assumption of an ever-growing young workforce embedded in Indonesia's manufacturing FDI pitch.

**Dampak Kelas Menengah**

> The Indonesian middle class absorbs this trend as an unfunded liability before it experiences it as a market.
> Four specific effects.

(1) The sandwich squeeze.
> Urban middle-class Indonesians aged 35-50 in the 2030s will face simultaneous obligations to ageing parents with no pension (only about 15.2 million contributory pension participants nationally, so most of today's 50-somethings will retire with nothing) and to children in an increasingly expensive education market — while themselves being the first Indonesian generation to have two or fewer children and therefore no equivalent support in their own old age.
> China's middle class hit this wall with one child; Indonesia's will hit it with two, which softens but does not remove it.

(2) Out-of-pocket care costs become a middle-class impoverishment mechanism.
> Because there is no LTC insurance and BPJS Kesehatan does not cover long-term or custodial care, a stroke, dementia diagnosis or hip fracture in a parent converts directly into either lost income (usually a daughter or daughter-in-law leaving work) or cash outlay for a caregiver.
> This is the single most likely route by which middle-class Indonesian households slide down the income distribution in the 2030s — and it compounds the middle-class contraction already visible in BPS data.

(3) Female labour-force participation is the hidden variable.
> Care work in Indonesia is unpaid and gendered.
> As demand for elder care rises without a formal care sector, the adjustment mechanism is women leaving paid work — precisely the cohort whose rising participation Indonesia is counting on to offset the shrinking working-age share.
> This is a direct tax on middle-class household income and on national output.

(4) The upside is narrow and delayed.
> The middle class is the market for home care, daycare, assistive products and age-adapted housing — but at Indonesian income levels only the upper-middle segment (perhaps the top 10-15%) can pay commercial rates before 2035.
> For most of the middle class, the silver economy will initially mean paying an informal caregiver Rp 2-4 million a month out of pocket, not consuming a designed service.
> The class that funds the transition is therefore not the class that is served by it.

**Dampak Daerah Non Jawa**

> Highly asymmetric, and in a way that inverts the usual Java-centric pattern of this research set.

Ageing is already MOST advanced outside the biggest metros.
> Indonesia's oldest provinces by elderly share are DI Yogyakarta, Central Java, East Java and Bali — regions combining low fertility, high life expectancy and, crucially, decades of out-migration of working-age people.
> The same 'left-behind elderly' pattern that afflicts China's rural interior and Northeast is already visible in rural Java, NTT, West Sumatra, North Sulawesi and Maluku, where remittance-dependent elderly live alone while children work in Jakarta, Kalimantan or abroad.
> The demographic need is therefore highest exactly where the commercial market is weakest.

The commercial silver economy will be Java-and-Bali concentrated for at least a decade: Jabodetabek, Bandung, Surabaya, Semarang, Yogyakarta, Denpasar and Medan have the income density, hospital access and nuclear-family structure to support paid care.
> Bali has a distinct additional role as an international retirement and medical-tourism destination (Hovi Assisted Saba is in Bali, not Jakarta) serving foreign retirees and diaspora — a genuine non-Java export opportunity.

For eastern Indonesia and remote regions the realistic model is not senior living but public-health-led: strengthening Posyandu Lansia and 'puskesmas santun lansia', community health volunteers (kader), telemedicine and remote monitoring, and cash transfers.
> China's community canteen and grid-based neighbourhood care model does not port to dispersed archipelagic settlement; what does port is China's rural experience of a minimal universal pension (RMB 123-163/month reaching about 180 million people, over 70% farmers) — cheap, administratively simple, and transformative for rural elderly consumption even at low value.
> That, not senior living, is the non-Java policy lesson.

There is also a specific non-Java economic risk: regions whose economies depend on supplying young labour (NTB, NTT, East Java, West Java as sources of migrant workers; Central Java and West Java for manufacturing) face a double transition — their own populations age while the labour-export model that sustained them faces automation abroad, including by the very eldercare robots China is building.

### Kaitan Pendidikan

**Jurusan Terancam**

> The threat here is unusual: it comes not from the silver economy itself but from its demographic twin, collapsing fertility.
> Almost nothing is made obsolete by ageing; a great deal is made surplus by the disappearance of children.

(1) PGSD (Pendidikan Guru Sekolah Dasar) and PG-PAUD (early childhood education) — the most directly and severely exposed programmes in Indonesian higher education.
> China's data are the warning: 21,100 kindergartens closed in 2024 and roughly 21,400 in 2025, 241,800 preschool teachers lost their jobs in 2024 alone (over 600 per day), primary schools fell 3.8% in 2023, and kindergarten enrolment fell 12 million between 2020 and 2024.
> Indonesia produces PGSD and PAUD graduates at enormous volume from hundreds of LPTKs on the assumption of a permanently growing school-age cohort.
> With TFR at 2.13 and falling, primary enrolment will begin contracting in the 2030s.
> This is the clearest, most quantifiable oversupply risk in Indonesian higher education, and it is currently unmanaged.

(2) Pediatric-oriented health specialisations and midwifery at current production volumes — still needed, but the growth is over; the demand shift is decisively toward geriatrics.

(3) Secondary-education teacher training (all subjects) at current scale, on a 10-15 year lag behind primary.

(4) Programmes premised on a permanently abundant young workforce — labour-intensive manufacturing management, and the parts of HR curricula built around recruiting and managing large young workforces rather than retaining and re-skilling older ones.

(5) Conventional 'Kesejahteraan Sosial' curricula that frame the elderly exclusively as charity recipients (panti-based welfare) rather than as consumers, patients and workers — not obsolete, but obsolete in framing, and directly analogous to China's shift from 养老 to 享老.

(6) Property and marketing curricula built on the nuclear-family starter-home lifecycle, which mis-specifies the fastest-growing housing segment of the 2030s-2040s.

**Jurusan Dibutuhkan**

> (1) Geriatric medicine and gerontology — the single largest capacity gap in Indonesian health education.
> With roughly 14-15 geriatric specialists nationally and about 1.5 per 100,000 elderly, Indonesia needs residency expansion measured in orders of magnitude, plus geriatric sub-specialisation in psychiatry, neurology (dementia), cardiology, orthopaedics (falls and fractures), rehabilitation medicine and pharmacy (polypharmacy).
> (2) Gerontic nursing (keperawatan gerontik) as a genuine specialisation rather than a single course module — UGM has publicly warned that limited gerontic nursing skills threaten the quality of elderly healthcare.
> (3) Elderly care service management — the exact major China created in 2020 (养老服务管理), blending health services, hospitality, facility operations, finance and social work; there is currently no Indonesian equivalent at S1 level.
> (4) Caregiving as a certified vocational pathway at D1/D2/D3 level, articulated with BNSP standards and with overseas placement (Taiwan, Japan, Korea) as an explicit dual outcome — Indonesia already trains for export; it should train for both.
> (5) Physiotherapy, occupational therapy, speech-language pathology and audiology — all critically undersupplied and all central to functional ageing.
> (6) Clinical nutrition and dietetics with a sarcopenia, dysphagia and diabetes-in-ageing focus.
> (7) Actuarial science, insurance and pension economics — Indonesia will need people who can price long-term care risk, design annuities and model a national LTC scheme; this expertise barely exists domestically.
> (8) Health economics and social-protection policy.
> (9) Universal design, gerontechnology and age-friendly architecture within architecture and interior design programmes; age-friendly retrofit is a RMB 200 billion industry in China.
> (10) Biomedical engineering and assistive-device design, plus service robotics and human-robot interaction.
> (11) Health informatics, remote patient monitoring and telemedicine operations.
> (12) Palliative care, hospice and bereavement counselling — almost absent from Indonesian curricula.
> (13) Gerontological social work and case management.
> (14) Senior-focused hospitality, tourism and event management (accessible tourism design).
> (15) Elder law: guardianship, capacity, estate planning, elder-abuse and financial-exploitation law.

**China Education Response**

> China's educational response is the most concrete and fastest-moving of any country facing ageing, and it is directly copyable.

Creation of a dedicated undergraduate major: in 2020 the Ministry of Education formally established 养老服务管理 (Elderly Care Service Management) as a bachelor's-degree major.
> Shanghai University of Engineering Science (SUES) and Shandong Women's University were the pioneers, together enrolling roughly 100 students in 2020.
> By the mid-2020s 44 universities had been approved to offer the major and more than 300 institutions nationwide offered senior-care-related undergraduate programmes.
> The demand signal was unmistakable: SUES's fill rate rose from 34% of slots in 2020 to 126% in 2024, and Shandong Women's University's eldercare-related intake rose from 64 students in 2020 to 473 in 2024.
> Employment outcomes drove the shift — more than 30 eldercare institutions presented over 100 vacancies for just 40 SUES graduates in the first cohort, spanning nursing-home management to individual health consultancy, and the first undergraduate cohort graduated in summer 2024 to intense recruitment.

Vocational layer: a parallel and much larger expansion of 智慧健康养老服务与管理 (smart health and elderly care service and management) at vocational-college level, plus nursing-assistant and caregiver certification pipelines feeding the target of 300,000+ professional eldercare nursing staff.

Education FOR the elderly, not just about them: the National University for the Aged (国家老年大学) was inaugurated in March 2023 as the apex of a nationwide 老年大学 network, treating lifelong learning for seniors as both a welfare service and a consumption category — paid hobby instruction is now a recognised premium segment of the silver economy.

The contraction side, executed simultaneously: as the eldercare pipeline expanded, China shut early-childhood capacity at speed — 21,100 kindergartens closed in 2024, roughly 21,400 in 2025, 241,800 preschool teachers made redundant in 2024, over 30,000 preschools and primary schools closed in 2025, with projections that only about 163,700 kindergartens will remain by 2030 (averaging 15,000 closures a year).
> Some closing kindergartens and vacated school buildings have been converted directly into elderly daycare and community care centres — a literal asset transfer from the young end of the age structure to the old.
> The lesson for Indonesia is that the two moves are one policy: the teacher-training system that shrinks and the care-training system that grows must be planned together, or the transition produces mass graduate unemployment at one end and unfillable vacancies at the other.

### Pelajaran Kebijakan dari China

**Respons Kebijakan China**

> China's policy sequence is unusual in this research set because most of it is *preemptive construction* rather than *post-hoc crackdown* — and that is itself the lesson.
> Six strands.

(1) Reframing ageing as an industry (January 2024): the State Council General Office's 'Opinions on Developing the Silver Economy and Improving the Well-being of the Elderly' — 26 measures across four areas, 10 designated silver-economy industrial parks, explicit calls on both state-owned and private enterprises to serve the elderly market, and support for innovation in elderly products and services.
> Adoptable by Indonesia at near-zero fiscal cost: naming the sector, defining it statistically, and assigning ministerial ownership.

(2) Building the payer before building the beds — belatedly.
> LTC insurance piloted in 49 cities from 2016, reaching about 300 million covered and 3.3 million beneficiaries with designated providers growing tenfold to about 12,000, then nationalised in March 2026 as a 'sixth insurance' with a three-year target of universal coverage by 2028 regardless of employment status, starting with the severely disabled.
> China's own painful lesson — roughly 50% national bed vacancy and 38% Beijing occupancy — is that supply built before payment does not get used.
> Indonesia should invert the sequence: pilot a care benefit before subsidising facilities.

(3) Demand-side vouchers rather than supply-side subsidies (January 2026): monthly e-vouchers up to RMB 800 for 12 months, spendable across meals, bathing, housekeeping, mobility, emergency aid, medical assistance, rehabilitation nursing and daycare — over 1.05 million beneficiaries by March 2026, about 2 million during 2026.
> This is a highly transferable design: it lets consumers choose providers, generates transaction data, and avoids building state facilities.

(4) Labour-supply adjustment (effective 1 January 2025): gradual statutory retirement-age increases (male 60→63; female 55→58 and 50→55) over 15 years, with flexible windows of up to three years earlier or later — the first increase since the 1950s, deliberately incremental (one month every two to four months) to defuse backlash.
> The lesson for Indonesia: raise retirement age early, gradually, and while the electorate is still young, because doing it later is politically impossible.

(5) The 9073 architecture: 90% ageing at home, 7% community-based, 3% institutional — a deliberate refusal to build a bed-heavy system, matched by community canteens, home retrofits and community daycare.
> This aligns with Indonesian family norms and is far cheaper than institutional care.

(6) Post-hoc enforcement against exploitation — the genuine crackdown strand: bans on nursing homes selling expensive pills and false-claim health products; prohibition of financial products marketed to retirees with false return promises; sustained campaigns against elder-targeted fraud.
> These followed disasters that Indonesia can avoid by regulating first: Hunan alone recorded over 70 illegal fundraising cases in eldercare between 2019 and 2021, affecting 90,000 victims and over RMB 8 billion, epitomised by the Golden Sunset Elderly Care Apartment Ponzi scheme in Hengyang, which sold discounted prepaid residency contracts and investment returns and ran for over a decade under official protection.

**Rekomendasi Kebijakan Indonesia**

> (1) Regulate prepaid eldercare contracts BEFORE the industry exists.
> Every rupiah collected in advance for future residency or care must sit in a licensed escrow or trust with independent custody and disclosure.
> China's Hunan experience — 70+ illegal fundraising cases, 90,000 victims, over RMB 8 billion — happened because prepaid membership models outran regulation.
> Indonesia's senior-living market is small enough today that this rule costs nothing and prevents a predictable scandal.
> This is the highest-return preemptive policy available.

(2) Pilot a long-term care benefit now, at small scale, in three to five cities.
> Do not wait for fiscal space.
> Start with a means-tested, disability-assessed home-care voucher modelled on China's RMB 800 e-voucher — perhaps Rp 750,000-1,500,000 per month for severely dependent elders — administered through BPJS Kesehatan or Kemensos with a digital eligibility assessment.
> The purpose is not coverage but institution-building: creating the assessment instrument, the provider registry, the pricing data and the political constituency.
> China needed ten years from pilot to national scheme; Indonesia's clock has not started.

(3) Create a licensing category for assisted living, memory care and home care under Kemenkes, with staffing ratios, clinical standards, incident reporting and inspection.
> The regulatory vacuum is simultaneously deterring good capital and permitting bad operators.

(4) Legislate a modern elderly law to replace UU 13/1998, with budget authority and an accountable lead agency — Perpres 88/2021 has five sound pillars and no money.

(5) Raise and index the retirement age now, gradually, on China's incremental design (one month every few months), while the median voter is around 30.
> Doing this in 2040 will be impossible.

(6) Move toward a universal, tax-financed, low-value social pension for those over 70, as examined in the ILO's October 2025 brief.
> China's rural pension of RMB 123-163/month reaching 180 million people demonstrates that even a very small universal transfer transforms rural elderly welfare and consumption, and it is administratively far simpler than expanding contributory coverage in a 59%-informal labour market.

(7) Name the silver economy as an economic sector, not a welfare programme.
> Assign it to Kemenko Perekonomian as well as Kemenko PMK; have BPS produce an official silver-economy satellite account so investors can size the market; include it in the next RPJMN with targets.

(8) Plan the education transition symmetrically.
> Cap or reduce PGSD/PAUD intake now on published enrolment projections, and simultaneously open geriatric residency slots, gerontic nursing specialisation and an elderly-care-service-management degree.
> China did both at once; Indonesia is doing neither.

(9) Turn the caregiver export programme into dual-purpose infrastructure.
> Indonesia already trains BNSP-certified caregivers at BBPVP and private LSPs for Taiwan and Japan.
> Mandate a domestic-service or return-and-train component, build a returnee registry, and give returning caregivers accelerated pathways into domestic supervisory and training roles.
> This converts a brain drain into a skills pipeline.

(10) Direct OJK to build the financial plumbing: reverse mortgages and home-equity release, retirement annuities, long-term care insurance riders, and elder-specific financial-abuse rules — including a ban on marketing high-yield investment products to over-65s without suitability assessment, which is exactly the abuse China had to prohibit after the fact.

(11) Build the community layer, not beds.
> Fund Posyandu Lansia, 'puskesmas santun lansia', community daycare and home-visit programmes; adopt China's 9073 logic explicitly.
> Institutional beds should be the last thing Indonesia builds, and China's 50% vacancy rate is the evidence.

(12) Commission a national long-term care needs survey.
> Indonesia cannot design or price any of the above without knowing how many elders have ADL limitations and who currently cares for them.

### Peluang & Rekomendasi Aksi

**Peluang Bisnis**

> (1) Home care and companion care agencies — the largest realistic near-term market, because it preserves the family-care norm, requires no real estate, and matches Indonesian willingness to pay (Rp 2-5 million per month for a live-in or day caregiver is already a normal urban middle-class expense paid informally).
> The opportunity is formalisation: background-checked, trained, BNSP-certified, insured, app-scheduled, supervised caregivers replacing the informal 'suster' market.
> Whoever builds the trusted national brand here wins the category.

(2) Adult daycare centres (pusat penitipan lansia) — the highest-return format in the 2027-2035 window.
> Low capex, converts existing buildings, serves dual-income families who cannot institutionalise a parent but cannot supervise one either, and is the format China scaled through community centres.
> Effectively unbuilt in Indonesia outside a handful of Jakarta sites.

(3) Caregiver training, certification and staffing — already commercially proven by LSP Caregiver, Caregiver Indonesia and UI Academy, driven by overseas demand.
> The expansion opportunity is a dual-market operator supplying both Taiwan/Japan placement and domestic agencies, capturing the returnee cohort.

(4) Geriatric clinical services — memory clinics, falls clinics, geriatric day hospitals, post-stroke and post-fracture rehabilitation, home-based rehabilitation.
> Hospital groups (Siloam, Mayapada, Hermina, Bunda) can add these at modest cost with strong differentiation and BPJS-adjacent revenue.

(5) Age-friendly home retrofit — grab bars, non-slip flooring, walk-in showers, ramps, stair aids, lighting, emergency call systems.
> China's 适老化改造 industry reached RMB 200 billion in 2025 from nothing.
> In Indonesia this is a distribution-and-installation business with no incumbent, addressable by existing home-improvement retailers and contractors, and payable out of pocket by adult children.

(6) Assistive-device and elderly-goods distribution — adult incontinence products (a RMB 148.3 billion category in China with 46.8% penetration versus negligible Indonesian penetration), mobility aids, hearing aids, hospital beds, pressure-relief mattresses, fall-detection wearables, medication dispensers.
> Sourced from China, sold via Shopee/Tokopedia/TikTok Shop and pharmacy chains.
> Low barrier, immediate.

(7) Senior-focused financial products — retirement annuities, care-cost savings plans, over-65 health cover, and eventually reverse mortgages.
> Bank Mandiri Taspen's July 2026 move signals the incumbent has spotted it; the gap is a specialist, digitally distributed challenger.

(8) Senior living / CCRC — real but slow, capital-intensive and limited to the top few percent until a payer exists.
> The smarter play is age-adaptable and multigenerational housing product within mainstream developments (wider doors, ground-floor bedrooms, step-free bathrooms) rather than dedicated communities.

(9) Senior tourism and 'living tourism' — escorted, medically supported, slow-paced group travel, and long-stay wellness packages in Bali, Yogyakarta, Bandung, Malang and Lake Toba.
> Bali additionally has a genuine international retirement and medical-tourism opportunity serving Japanese, Korean, Australian and European retirees, plus Indonesian diaspora.

(10) Therapeutic and convenience nutrition — soft-texture, high-protein, dysphagia-friendly and diabetes-appropriate meal delivery; sarcopenia-targeted supplements.
> A large, underserved category with strong repeat purchase.

(11) Telemedicine and remote monitoring for elders, particularly outside Java — the leapfrog play.
> Halodoc/Alodokter-class platforms adding chronic-disease management, medication adherence and family-dashboard features for adult children monitoring parents remotely.

(12) Senior content, community and education — senior creators, hobby classes, digital-literacy training, and 'universitas lansia' style paid learning, which China has proven is a premium rather than charitable category.

(13) Death care and estate services — modern, transparent funeral planning, prepaid funeral products (escrowed), estate and inheritance advisory; a sector with poor incumbents and rising demand.

(14) Elder-fraud protection and guardianship services — financial supervision tools for adult children, transaction monitoring for elderly accounts.
> China's fraud epidemic shows the demand arrives with the wealth.

**Rekomendasi Individu Mahasiswa**

> Build competence at the intersection of health, care operations and money — the three scarcities.
> Concretely: (1) if in medicine, seriously consider geriatrics, geriatric psychiatry, neurology/dementia, rehabilitation medicine or geriatric pharmacy — Indonesia has roughly 14-15 geriatric specialists for a country of 285 million, making this the least competitive and highest-impact clinical niche available; (2) if in nursing, specialise in gerontic nursing, dementia care, wound and pressure-injury care, and palliative care, and get BNSP caregiver certification alongside your degree — it is portable to Taiwan and Japan at multiples of domestic pay and gives optionality; (3) if in allied health, physiotherapy, occupational therapy, speech-language pathology and audiology are all severely undersupplied and directly tied to functional ageing; (4) if in business or economics, learn actuarial science, insurance and pension economics, or health economics — Indonesia will need people who can price long-term care risk and there are almost none; (5) if in engineering or design, learn universal design, gerontechnology, assistive-device engineering, and human-robot interaction; (6) if in IT, focus on health informatics, remote patient monitoring and elder-friendly UX (large-type, voice-first, low-literacy interfaces — the Chinese 'Elder Mode' pattern); (7) if in education, be realistic: PGSD and PAUD face a structural contraction on a 10-15 year horizon following China's pattern, and the durable pivot is toward adult, vocational and senior lifelong learning; (8) whatever the field, add Mandarin or Japanese plus caregiving certification if overseas work is attractive — Taiwan is now the top destination for Indonesian migrant workers and 17.5% of placements are caregivers; (9) cultivate the general-purpose advantage: physical-presence, trust-based, emotionally skilled work is the category most resistant to AI substitution, and eldercare is its largest instance; (10) practically, spend time in a panti or home-care setting before committing — this sector selects hard for people who can tolerate the work, and credentials without stomach are worthless.

**Rekomendasi Perguruan Tinggi**

> Open: (a) an S1 in Manajemen Layanan Lansia / Elderly Care Service Management, directly modelled on China's 养老服务管理 major created in 2020 — blending clinical basics, facility operations, hospitality, finance and social work; China's 44 approved universities and 300+ related programmes, with SUES fill rates rising from 34% to 126% in four years, prove the demand curve exists once employers appear; (b) D3/D4 Caregiver and Gerontic Nursing programmes articulated with BNSP standards and with explicit dual domestic/overseas placement pathways; (c) geriatric medicine residency expansion — the binding national constraint, requiring Kemenkes and the medical colleges to act together, not universities alone; (d) postgraduate programmes in gerontology, health economics and actuarial science for long-term care; (e) palliative care and hospice as taught specialisations; (f) audiology, speech-language pathology and occupational therapy where they do not exist.

Embed rather than create: gerontic modules in all nursing, pharmacy, nutrition, psychology and social work curricula; universal design and age-friendly building standards in architecture and interior design; ageing demography in economics and public policy; elder law in law faculties; senior-consumer and accessible-tourism content in management and hospitality programmes.

Manage down, deliberately and now: PGSD and PG-PAUD intake, using published enrolment projections rather than waiting for the shock.
> China closed 21,100 kindergartens in 2024 and made 241,800 preschool teachers redundant in a single year; Indonesia's LPTKs are still producing primary and early-childhood teachers at scale for a cohort that has stopped growing.
> Redeploy that faculty capacity toward adult, vocational and senior education rather than closing programmes outright — several Chinese kindergartens were physically converted into elderly daycare centres, and the institutional analogue is available here.

Institutional infrastructure: establish university-affiliated teaching nursing homes and home-care services (the model that makes clinical training possible and generates revenue); create ageing research centres tied to BPS and Kemenkes to produce the missing national long-term care needs data; partner with Taiwanese, Japanese and Singaporean institutions for curriculum and clinical placement, which is faster than building from scratch.

### Faktor Risiko & Sisi Gelap

**Dampak Negatif China**

> (1) Rural elderly destitution.
> The rural resident basic pension minimum was RMB 123/month in 2024, RMB 143 in 2025 and RMB 163 in 2026 — roughly US$1 a day — paid to about 180 million people, over 70% of them farmers.
> At about RMB 8 a day elders routinely forgo treatment for minor illness and cannot afford care for serious disease.
> The east-west gap reaches 6.2x (Shanghai about RMB 1,555/month versus Gansu about RMB 249).
> About 82 million farmers aged 60+ are still working, roughly 63% of the rural elderly — 'retirement' does not exist for most rural Chinese.
> China's silver economy is thus a two-tier system in which a coastal urban minority consumes a genuine market while a rural majority subsists.

(2) Systematic financial predation on the elderly.
> Hunan province alone recorded over 70 illegal fundraising cases in the eldercare sector between 2019 and 2021, affecting 90,000 victims and involving over RMB 8 billion.
> The emblematic case — Golden Sunset Elderly Care Apartment in Hengyang — sold discounted prepaid residency contracts and promised investment returns, operated for over a decade under official protection, and collapsed leaving hundreds of elderly investors ruined; a subsequent investigation exposed sustained inaction and corruption among local officials.
> Health-product fraud is endemic in a market for elderly health products estimated at RMB 2.7 trillion as of 2021, forcing bans on nursing homes selling high-priced pills and on false-return financial products marketed to retirees.
> A 2026 investigative report found private psychiatric hospitals admitting people under false pretences to defraud medical insurance, with staff acknowledging some elderly patients were admitted simply 'for elderly care'.

(3) Capital misallocation into unusable capacity.
> Roughly 4.29 million institutional beds against about 2.15 million residents (2020) — about 50% vacancy; national average occupancy about 60%; Beijing at 38% in July 2023.
> Decent-quality institutions charge far above the local average pension, so even reputable operators remain unprofitable and dependent on government subsidy, while rural public homes sit empty.
> Billions were invested against a demand curve that the payment system could not activate.

(4) The care burden fell on women and on a single child.
> The 4-2-1 structure produced a generation of only children carrying two parents and four grandparents, with daughters and daughters-in-law absorbing the unpaid labour — a documented driver of female labour-force exit, delayed marriage and further fertility decline, which compounds the original problem.

(5) Fiscal strain and intergenerational inequity.
> Pension inequality between civil servants/urban employees and rural residents is now a live political controversy in China, and provincial pension funds in the ageing Northeast run structural deficits requiring central transfers.

(6) Collateral damage at the young end.
> The same demographic shift that created the silver economy destroyed the early-childhood sector: 21,100 kindergarten closures in 2024, roughly 21,400 in 2025, 241,800 preschool teachers unemployed in 2024 alone, over 30,000 preschools and primary schools closed in 2025, and about 12 million fewer kindergarten enrolments between 2020 and 2024.

(7) Social isolation.
> Mass rural-to-urban migration produced tens of millions of 'empty-nest' and left-behind elderly living alone in emptying villages, with documented consequences for mental health and mortality.

**Risiko Sosial Indonesia**

> (1) A care crisis with no payer and no floor.
> This is the central risk.
> China entered ageing with near-universal (if minimal) pensions and built LTC insurance over a decade; Indonesia is entering with 15.2 million contributory pension participants, no LTC insurance, roughly 59% informal employment and BPJS Kesehatan under strain.
> The 2045 elderly cohort — today's informal workers — will largely reach 60 with no pension, no savings and illiquid housing.
> The realistic outcome is not a silver economy but mass elderly poverty absorbed silently by families, invisible in national statistics because it takes the form of foregone treatment and unpaid female labour rather than measured expenditure.

(2) Predatory prepaid schemes arriving before regulation.
> Indonesia's senior-living and eldercare market is exactly at the stage — small, unregulated, emotionally charged, targeting people with lump-sum retirement payouts — at which China's Ponzi schemes germinated.
> Indonesian precedent is unfavourable: the country has a long record of investment scams targeting the retired (from koperasi bodong to travel-umrah schemes like First Travel, which specifically exploited older, religiously motivated savers).
> A prepaid senior-residency scandal in Indonesia is not a possibility but a near-certainty absent escrow rules.

(3) Health-product and supplement fraud targeting elders.
> Indonesia already has a large, weakly policed herbal and supplement market with aggressive direct-selling and WhatsApp-group distribution.
> As elderly numbers and anxieties rise, this scales — and China's RMB 2.7 trillion elderly health-product market with endemic fraud shows the ceiling.

(4) Digital financial exploitation.
> Indonesian seniors are entering digital finance (QRIS, e-wallets, online lending) with low digital literacy, in an environment with pinjol harassment, social-engineering scams and weak elder-specific consumer protection.
> This is a fast-moving risk in 2026-2030, well ahead of the care-industry risks.

(5) Women bear the adjustment.
> Without a formal care sector, rising care demand converts directly into women exiting paid work — a hidden tax on household income, on female economic participation and on the very labour supply Indonesia needs as its working-age share declines.

(6) Regional care deserts.
> The oldest populations are in Yogyakarta, Central Java, East Java, Bali and out-migration regions in eastern Indonesia; commercial care will concentrate in Jabodetabek, Surabaya and Bali.
> The mismatch means the most-needy elders live where no provider will ever operate commercially.

(7) Unregulated institutions and abuse.
> With no licensing standards, staffing ratios or inspection regime for assisted living or home care, low-cost unlicensed facilities will emerge to serve families who cannot afford quality — with predictable neglect and abuse outcomes, and no reporting mechanism.

(8) Intergenerational fiscal conflict.
> If a pension or LTC scheme is eventually financed by payroll contributions from a shrinking young workforce already facing high youth unemployment, the resentment dynamic visible in China's pension-inequality debate will appear here too — and Indonesia's version starts from a weaker fiscal base.

(9) Migration whiplash.
> Indonesia is exporting caregivers to societies that are simultaneously automating care (China's eldercare robot programme, Japan's care robotics).
> If overseas demand contracts faster than expected, a large trained cohort returns to a domestic market with no jobs — and remittance-dependent regions lose income.

**Kelompok Rentan**

> (1) Informal-sector workers now aged 45-60 — the single largest at-risk group, numbering in the tens of millions.
> They will reach 60 between 2026 and 2041 with no contributory pension (only 15.2 million Indonesians participate), no employer severance, and savings held in illiquid land or gold.
> They are the cohort that determines whether Indonesia's ageing becomes a fiscal crisis, and there is currently no policy addressing them.
> (2) Rural and left-behind elderly, particularly in Yogyakarta, Central and East Java, NTT, West Sumatra and North Sulawesi, whose children have migrated — China's equivalent group survives on about US$1 a day; Indonesia's has even less institutional support.
> (3) Elderly women — who live longer, are more likely to be widowed, have lower lifetime formal-sector participation and therefore lower pension eligibility, and are more likely to be poor and alone.
> (4) Women aged 35-55 as unpaid caregivers — the adjustment mechanism of a system with no formal care sector; they lose income, career progression and their own future pension entitlement.
> (5) Adult children in the sandwich generation, especially the urban lower-middle class with two children and two unpensioned parents — the group most likely to be pushed down the income distribution by a single parental health event.
> (6) People with dementia and their families — a condition with almost no diagnostic capacity (roughly 14-15 geriatric specialists nationally), no specialist services outside a few Jakarta and Bali facilities, no public awareness, and severe stigma; Indonesia's dementia population will be in the millions by 2040 with essentially no system.
> (7) Elderly people with disabilities requiring ADL support — the exact group China now serves with RMB 800 monthly vouchers and who in Indonesia receive nothing.
> (8) Migrant caregivers abroad — exposed to exploitative conditions, and to displacement by automation in the destination markets.
> (9) Early-childhood and primary teachers — the professional cohort facing structural redundancy on a 10-15 year horizon as the school-age population contracts.
