> (10) Elderly consumers of digital finance — the primary target market for scams, pinjol harassment and investment fraud, with no elder-specific consumer protection regime.

### Contoh Kasus Konkret

**Kasus China**

> (1) Taikang Life / Taikang Community (泰康之家) — the defining business model of China's silver economy and the one Indonesian financial institutions are most likely to imitate.
> Taikang was the first insurer approved by the insurance regulator to build CCRCs, and it fused four businesses into one: pension insurance, health insurance, asset management and physical retirement communities, sold as a membership card conferring residency rights.
> This solved the payment problem privately — customers pre-fund their own care through an insurance product decades in advance.
> Taikang Yanyuan (Beijing) opened in 2015; the network now spans Beijing, Shanghai, Guangzhou, Chengdu and other major cities with independent living, assisted living and on-site medical care.
> The broader insurance-plus-eldercare chain exceeds RMB 500 billion and is projected toward trillion-yuan scale by 2030.
> Bank Mandiri Taspen's July 2026 pivot toward a senior health-and-finance ecosystem is a recognisably early version of the same idea.

(2) National long-term care insurance — the 'sixth insurance'.
> Piloted from 2016 in 49 cities, covering about 300 million people and paying over 3.3 million beneficiaries, with designated providers growing tenfold to about 12,000; nationalised in March 2026 with a three-year target of universal coverage by 2028 regardless of employment status.
> This is the single most consequential eldercare policy any country has attempted, and it took a decade of piloting — the timeline Indonesia should be benchmarking against.

(3) The RMB 800 eldercare consumption voucher (January 2026).
> Ministry of Civil Affairs and Ministry of Finance monthly e-vouchers for 12 months for seniors unable to care for themselves, spendable on meals, bathing, housekeeping, mobility, emergency aid, medical assistance, rehabilitation nursing and daycare; 1.05 million beneficiaries by March 2026, about 2 million during 2026.
> A demand-side, choice-preserving, data-generating design that is directly copyable at Indonesian scale.

(4) Silver trains (银发旅游列车).
> A nine-agency action plan announced February 2025 targets a national senior tourism rail network by 2027 with over 100 routes and 2,500 annual trips; carriages retrofitted with wider berths, larger bathrooms with emergency call buttons, anti-slip grips, onboard medical clinics, reading lounges, games tables and karaoke rooms.
> Over 77% of passengers on China Railway Qinghai-Xizang Group tourism trains are aged 55+; a 15-day Xinjiang tour is a flagship product.
> Over 100 million active senior travellers were projected by end-2025.

(5) Eldercare robotics.
> Beijing launched what state media called the world's first robot- and AI-powered eldercare centre in March 2026; Fourier's GR-3 humanoid, showcased at CES 2026, is positioned as the first full-size robot designed and marketed for eldercare at commercial scale; the Chengdu Humanoid Robot Innovation Center is developing lightweight humanoids to identify seniors, deliver medicine, converse and assist with bathing.
> Market: US$3.14 billion (2025) to US$3.56 billion (2026), projected above US$10 billion by 2035.

(6) The Golden Sunset scandal (Hengyang, Hunan) — the cautionary case.
> A purported non-profit nursing home that became an illegal fundraising scheme before construction even began, selling discounted prepaid residency contracts and promised investment returns for over a decade under official protection before collapsing; Hunan province alone saw over 70 illegal fundraising cases in eldercare between 2019 and 2021, with 90,000 victims and over RMB 8 billion involved.

(7) The education pivot.
> The Ministry of Education created the 养老服务管理 undergraduate major in 2020; SUES and Shandong Women's University enrolled roughly 100 students that year; by the mid-2020s 44 universities were approved and 300+ institutions offered related programmes; SUES's fill rate went from 34% (2020) to 126% (2024) and Shandong Women's University's intake from 64 to 473; over 30 employers presented 100+ vacancies for 40 first-cohort graduates.
> Simultaneously 21,100 kindergartens closed in 2024 and 241,800 preschool teachers lost their jobs.

(8) The vacancy paradox.
> About 4.29 million institutional beds against 2.15 million residents (2020), roughly 60% national occupancy and 38% in Beijing (July 2023) — proof that in eldercare, supply without a payer is dead capital.

**Padanan Indonesia**

> (1) RUKUN Senior Living (Sentul, operating since 2012) — Indonesia's first senior living community, roughly 17 hectares, explicitly built on the CCRC model with tiered services by health status; its CEO Emir Fachry framed the market in May 2026 in exactly the Chinese 享老 register, emphasising quality of life, health, activity and happiness rather than custodial care.
> Notably, RUKUN opened only four years after China's Cherish-Yearn (2008) and three years before Taikang Yanyuan (2015) — Indonesia's format lag is small; its market-depth lag is large.

(2) Hovi Care (Finnish-rooted; Jakarta operations plus Hovi Assisted Saba in Bali) — assisted living and memory care for dementia, Alzheimer's, Parkinson's, post-stroke and post-surgical recovery; recognised at the Global Health Indonesia Awards in February 2025.
> Indonesia's clearest example of specialist clinical eldercare, and evidence that foreign entry is European/Nordic rather than Chinese.

(3) Asosiasi Senior Living Indonesia (ASLI) — a trade body roughly 13 years old, the closest thing to sector self-organisation, in a landscape where Jabodetabek has only about 5 senior living communities, 8 nursing-care facilities and 6 daycare centres against 78 foundation-run and 9 government panti jompo.

(4) Bank Mandiri Taspen (July 2026) — the Taikang analogue in embryo: an institution with a captive base of pensioner customers building outward from pension-backed lending into hospital partnerships, health insurance and new senior financial products, explicitly planning against a 70-million-elderly-by-2045 scenario.
> If any Indonesian institution replicates the insurance-plus-care integrated model, it will be a bank or insurer, not a property developer.

(5) The BNSP caregiver certification industry (LSP Caregiver, Caregiver Indonesia, UI Academy / NTC FIK UI) plus government caregiver training at BBPVP Bekasi — the workforce layer, currently oriented outward.
> Taiwan became the top destination for Indonesian migrant workers in Q1 2026 with 17.5% placed as caregivers; Taipei runs dedicated dementia and elder-care training courses for migrant workers.
> This is Indonesia's genuine comparative advantage in the global silver economy, and it is being spent abroad.

(6) Perpres 88/2021 Strategi Nasional Kelanjutusiaan — the policy analogue, but framed as welfare and rights (five pillars: social protection and income security; health and quality of life; age-friendly communities; institutional strengthening; rights fulfilment) rather than as industrial policy.
> It predates China's January 2024 silver-economy Opinions by more than two years yet has produced far less, because it lacks budget authority and an economic ministry owner.

(7) Insurance products for seniors (Chubb Life 'Asuransi Second Life', Great Eastern and Generali over-60/over-70 health plans) — the retail financial layer, still restrictive on underwriting and priced for the affluent.

(8) What has NO Indonesian equivalent, and this is the point: long-term care insurance, an eldercare consumption subsidy, a universal social pension, a licensing regime for assisted living, an elderly-care-service-management degree, a national silver-economy industrial strategy, or a geriatric workforce of meaningful size.

### Tingkat Keyakinan & Kualitas Sumber

**Catatan Kontradiksi Data**

> (1) China's silver-economy market size varies by more than a factor of two across sources, entirely because of definitional scope.
> The official/international track gives roughly RMB 7 trillion (about US$982 billion, about 6% of GDP) for 2024 and about RMB 8 trillion for 2025, rising to about RMB 30 trillion (about 10% of GDP) by 2035.
> Chinese domestic research houses give roughly RMB 9.8 trillion for 2026 on one series and up to RMB 18.7 trillion for the broadly defined 'elderly industry', while the 康养 health-and-wellness complex is put at RMB 9.5 trillion for 2025.
> A separate series puts 'elderly products' alone at RMB 6.6 trillion for 2026, which is larger than the entire silver economy on the official measure — an obvious inconsistency indicating overlapping and non-comparable definitions.
> Use the RMB 7-8 trillion / 6% of GDP figure for international comparison and treat the larger domestic numbers as promotional.

(2) Indonesia's geriatric specialist count is reported in two mutually incompatible ways: approximately 14-15 gerontology specialists nationally, versus approximately 1.5 geriatricians per 100,000 elderly (which, against roughly 34 million elderly, would imply around 500).
> Both figures appear in credible-looking sources.
> The likeliest reconciliation is that the first counts a narrow sub-specialty registration and the second counts physicians with geriatric competence or training more broadly.
> Either way the shortage is severe; the magnitude is not established.

(3) Indonesia's elderly share is cited as 11.97% (BPS SUPAS 2025), 11.93% (one derivative source) and 12.3% (Bank Mantap/press, 2026), and the absolute count as 34, 35 or 'over 34' million.
> These are reconcilable through different reference dates and whether projections or survey results are used, but they should not be mixed within a single calculation.

(4) Indonesia's 2045 elderly projection ranges from 19.9% to 20.31% of population and from about 57 million (2040, UNFPA-linked) to 61.4 million to 70 million (Bank Mantap's planning assumption).
> The 70 million figure appears to be a rounded upper-bound planning number rather than a demographic projection.

(5) China's nursing-home vacancy is variously reported as roughly 50% (2020 national bed-versus-resident arithmetic), about 40% (implied by 60% national average occupancy) and 62% (Beijing, July 2023, 38% occupancy).
> These are different geographies and years, not contradictions, but they are frequently quoted interchangeably.

(6) China's LTC insurance coverage is reported as about 300 million people across 49 pilot cities — a figure that is the covered *insured* population, not beneficiaries (3.3 million).
> Some secondary coverage conflates the two, dramatically overstating service delivery.

(7) Kindergarten closure figures differ between the MoE statistical series (274,400 to 253,300 in 2024, i.e.
> 21,100 net closures) and press aggregations citing 'over 30,000 preschools and primary schools closed in 2025' (which combines two school types).
> Preschool-teacher redundancies of 241,800 in 2024 come from a single widely republished figure and should be treated as indicative.

(8) Framing conflict on 'ageing before getting rich': Chinese official commentary (Global Times, Justin Lin Yifu) rejects the premise, arguing technological innovation will sustain growth, while external analysts (Newsweek, Asialink, Yi Fuxian) treat it as the central constraint.
> For the Indonesian comparison the more interesting fact cuts against the standard narrative: Indonesia crossed the 10%-elderly threshold at roughly US$4,300 per capita versus China's roughly US$960 in 2000, so Indonesia is *richer* at the equivalent demographic milestone — the risk lies in the growth trajectory afterwards, not the starting level.

(9) Vector assessment tension: this research assumes Chinese trends transfer to Indonesia, but for eldercare specifically the observable foreign entrants are Finnish, Singaporean and Japanese rather than Chinese, and China's flagship models (insurance-linked CCRCs, silver trains, community grid canteens) are the least portable elements of its silver economy.
> The transferable Chinese content is policy design and manufactured product, not business-model entry — a meaningful departure from the pattern in most other items in this research set.

## 16. Gaming & Esports Industry (mobile-first gaming, esports professionalization, and the state's protective regulation of minors in games)
**Kategori**: Digital Economy

📊 MIXED / ASYMMETRIC. Consumption: SIMULTANEOUS (Indonesia is a first-wave market for Chinese mobile games, not a follower). Esports: SIMULTANEOUS-to-slightly-LAGGARD, with a genuine REVERSE element — Indonesia hosted esports as an Asian Games demonstration sport in 2018 before China's Hangzhou 2023 medal event, and Indonesia is MLBB's global number-one market, so Indonesian scene dynamics sometimes lead rather than follow. Protective regulation: clear LAGGARD (5-7 years). Domestic production capability: severe LAGGARD (12-18 years) with no leapfrog visible. The overall label most useful for policy is 'consumption-simultaneous, regulation-laggard, production-laggard' — Indonesia absorbs the full social cost of a mature Chinese industry while capturing almost none of its industrial value. | 🎯 Prob: Tinggi (High) — but with an important qualification: the commercial side has ALREADY transferred completely; what is still in transit is the REGULATORY side, and that is arriving in a diluted, non-Chinese form. | 🔍 Keyakinan: Sedang-Tinggi (Medium-High). HIGH confidence on: China's regulatory chronology and instrument design (Library of Congress, NPPA notices, Niko Partners legal analyses — primary or near-primary sources); China's 2025 market and esports statistics (CADPA Game Publishing Committee + Gamma Data via Xinhua/China Daily, the officially sanctioned statistical series); Indonesia's regulatory chronology (PP 17/2025, Permenkominfo 2/2024, Perpres 19/2024 — verifiable legal instruments with published texts); Indonesia's internet penetration (APJII 2025 survey); the Moonton/Savvy transaction (Bloomberg, March 2026). MEDIUM confidence on: Indonesian market size (sources diverge by a factor of four), Indonesian player counts (definitional), Indonesian esports market size (estimates diverge by two orders of magnitude and should not be relied upon), local developer market share (0.4% vs 0.5% vs 5% depending on year and methodology), and Indonesian hospital data (reported via secondary media rather than a consolidated Kemenkes publication). LOW confidence on: all timeline predictions (tahun_masuk / mainstream / puncak), Indonesia's 2025 GDP per capita (not verified in this research), Southeast Asia's share of Chinese game exports (not broken out in available sources), and Tencent's exact minor-revenue percentage.

> **Status di Indonesia**: SPLIT STATUS — this is the key analytical point. On CONSUMPTION, Indonesia is already massively in (near-zero lag; arguably simultaneous with China, since Mobile Legends launched in Indonesia in 2016, the same year Honor of Kings broke out in China). On ESPORTS, Indonesia is fully mainstream and state-recognized (esports is an official olahraga prestasi under Kemenpora/KONI, with PBESI as the national federation). On DOMESTIC PRODUCTION, Indonesia is a laggard/dependent market — local developers capture under 1-5% of domestic spending. On PROTECTIVE REGULATION OF MINORS — the specific subject of this research item — Indonesia is BARU MULAI (just beginning): PP 17/2025 ('PP Tunas') was signed 28 March 2025 and the Indonesia Game Rating System was relaunched 11 October 2025 with mandatory effect from 2026, roughly six years after China's equivalent 2019 measures and with materially weaker instruments (age tiers and parental consent, but no playtime curfew, no state-run real-name gaming ID, no spending caps).

### Basic Info

**Tahun Mulai China**

> Layered timeline.
> (1) Industry base: online gaming became a mass phenomenon in China from 2001-2005 via PC internet cafes (wangba) and Shanda/NetEase MMOs; esports was recognized by the General Administration of Sport as China's 99th official sport in 2003.
> (2) Mobile-first inflection: 2013-2016, driven by 4G rollout, WeChat/QQ distribution and Tencent's Honor of Kings (launched November 2015, mass breakout 2016).
> (3) Esports institutionalization: 2016 is the pivotal year — the King Pro League (KPL) launched, LPL franchised, and in September 2016 the Ministry of Education added 'Esports and Management' (电子竞技运动与管理) to the vocational higher-education catalogue for implementation from 2017.
> (4) The regulatory/protective phase — the part Indonesia is lagging on — began in 2018 (nine-month approval freeze, August 2018 anti-myopia notice) and hardened in November 2019 (NPPA anti-addiction notice: 90 min/weekday, 3h/holiday, curfew 22:00-08:00, age-tiered spending caps) and definitively on 30 August 2021 (one hour on Fri/Sat/Sun/public holidays only, 20:00-21:00).

**Pemain Kunci China**

> Publishers/developers: Tencent (Honor of Kings, Peacekeeper Elite, League of Legends via Riot, PUBG Mobile via Krafton partnership), NetEase (Identity V, Naraka, Eggy Party), miHoYo/HoYoverse (Genshin Impact, Honkai: Star Rail, Zenless Zone Zero), ByteDance (Nuverse + Moonton/Mobile Legends: Bang Bang, acquired 2021, agreed sold to Saudi Savvy Games Group for >USD 6bn on 20 March 2026), Perfect World, 37 Interactive Entertainment, Lilith Games, XD Inc., Game Science (Black Myth: Wukong, 2024), Century Huatong/Dianhun, Yoozoo, FunPlus, IGG.
> Distribution/streaming: WeChat Mini Games, Douyin mini-games, Huya, DouYu, Bilibili, TapTap.
> Esports: LPL, KPL, EDG (2021 LoL Worlds champion), JD Gaming, Bilibili Gaming, Weibo Gaming, Team WE; host cities Shanghai (declared 'global esports capital', 2017), Hangzhou (Asian Games 2022/2023 medal esports), Chengdu, Xi'an.
> Regulators/industry bodies: National Press and Publication Administration (NPPA — issues banhao/version numbers), Cyberspace Administration of China (CAC), Ministry of Culture and Tourism, Ministry of Education, Ministry of Human Resources and Social Security (MOHRSS), CADPA Game Publishing Committee (GPC) and Gamma Data (伽马数据) as the official statistical authority.

### China Trend Detail

**Apa Yang Terjadi Di China**

> China built the world's largest games market and then deliberately capped its social externalities — a full cycle of boom, backlash, and state-engineered restraint that Indonesia has not yet passed through.

MECHANISM OF THE BOOM (2013-2020): Cheap 4G, a smartphone-only user base skipping consoles, and super-app distribution (WeChat/QQ) made mobile the default.
> Tencent's Honor of Kings turned a 5v5 MOBA into a mass social ritual, and the free-to-play + gacha/battle-pass monetization model replaced upfront purchase.
> Esports was deliberately built as a legitimizing layer on top of gaming: franchised leagues (LPL, KPL), city-based teams with local government subsidies (Shanghai, Hangzhou, Chengdu, Xi'an each issued esports industry policies and built dedicated arenas), and streaming platforms (Huya/DouYu/Bilibili) that converted viewership into the industry's largest revenue line.

MECHANISM OF THE BACKLASH (2018-2021): The state's concern was not economic but demographic and social — youth myopia, academic performance, family conflict, and 'game addiction'.
> Instruments used, in escalating order: (a) the banhao/version-number licensing chokepoint — every commercially monetized game requires an approval number, and approvals were frozen for nine months in 2018 and again from July 2021 to April 2022, which is the single most powerful lever the state holds; (b) mandatory real-name registration against the national ID database, later reinforced by Tencent's facial-recognition 'Midnight Patrol' (2021) that challenges night-time players whose behaviour looks underage; (c) hard playtime windows for under-18s (Nov 2019: 90 min weekdays / 3h holidays, 22:00-08:00 curfew; 30 Aug 2021: one hour on Fridays, Saturdays, Sundays and public holidays only, 20:00-21:00 — roughly 3 hours per week, down from 13.5); (d) age-tiered in-game spending caps for minors; (e) content controls (no blood, no explicit gambling mechanics, historical-accuracy requirements); (f) mandatory loot-box/gacha probability disclosure since the Ministry of Culture's interim measures effective 1 May 2017 — a world-first that predates Western loot-box debates by years; (g) rhetorical shock therapy — a Xinhua-affiliated Economic Information Daily article on 3 August 2021 branded games 'spiritual opium' (精神鸦片) and named Honor of Kings, wiping roughly USD 60bn off Tencent's market value in a day; (h) legal codification — the revised Law on the Protection of Minors (effective 1 June 2021) added an Internet Protection chapter, and the State Council's Regulations on the Protection of Minors in Cyberspace took effect 1 January 2024.

CONSOLIDATION AND RECOVERY (2022-2026): Approvals resumed in April 2022 and are now issued in predictable monthly batches (including regular batches of imported titles), which the industry reads as normalization rather than liberalization.
> A December 2023 NPPA draft ('Measures for the Administration of Online Games') proposing monthly spending caps (~RMB 400), a ban on daily-login and consecutive-recharge rewards, and a ban on item auctions erased roughly USD 80bn from Tencent and NetEase in one session; the draft was pulled from the NPPA website in January 2024 and never enacted — an important signal that even China's regulator now trades off child protection against a strategically valuable export industry.
> The market resumed growth: domestic sales revenue reached RMB 350.79bn in 2025 (+7.68% y/y) with 683m users, and self-developed Chinese games earned USD 20.45bn overseas in 2025.
> Growth has shifted decisively toward (i) mini-games inside WeChat/Douyin (RMB 53.5bn, +34.4% in 2025, over half of all incremental market growth), (ii) premium single-player console/PC titles after Black Myth: Wukong (2024), and (iii) overseas expansion — which is precisely the channel through which the trend reaches Indonesia.

ESPORTS AS A MATURE, PLATEAUED SECTOR: China's esports industry earned RMB 29.33bn in 2025 (+6.4%), but its audience of 495.3m has been essentially flat since 2021 (489.2m), and 80.8% of industry income comes from livestreaming rather than tickets, sponsorship or media rights.
> Mobile titles are 58.6% of esports revenue.
> Esports in China has completed the arc from subculture to state-sanctioned sport (Asian Games medal event, Hangzhou 2023) to a mature, consolidating industry with a well-documented oversupply of aspiring professionals relative to paid roles.

**Fase Tren Di China**

> REGULATED + MATURE, with a re-growth phase inside the regulatory cage.
> The consumption boom peaked around 2020-2021; the backlash phase ran 2018-2022 and culminated in the Aug 2021 minor restrictions and the licence freeze; since April 2022 the sector has been in a 'managed normalization' phase — record revenue (RMB 350.8bn in 2025) but saturated users (+1.35%), consolidated ownership, and growth displaced into mini-games, premium PC/console titles, and exports.
> Esports specifically is MATURE/PLATEAUED (audience flat since 2021, revenue growing single digits, heavy dependence on livestreaming).
> Minor-protection policy is in a STABLE ENFORCED phase — no evidence of relaxation as of mid-2026 — while monetization policy is in a DEREGULATORY PAUSE after the December 2023 draft was withdrawn.

**Puncak Tren China**

> Multiple peaks depending on the dimension.
> (a) User-growth peak: 2020-2021 (COVID lockdowns pushed users past 660m; growth then collapsed to ~1%/year).
> (b) Regulatory-intensity peak: August-September 2021 — the 'spiritual opium' article (3 Aug 2021), the NPPA one-hour rule (30 Aug 2021), and the simultaneous licence freeze; geographically centred on Beijing (NPPA/CAC) and Shenzhen (Tencent).
> (c) Esports peak: 2021-2022 — EDG's LoL Worlds title (November 2021) triggered nationwide campus celebrations and is the cultural high-water mark; audience has been flat since.
> Host-city peak: Shanghai (LPL/KPL hub, 'global esports capital' policy from 2017) and Hangzhou (Asian Games 2023, where esports became a full medal event).
> (d) Revenue peak: not yet reached — 2025 was a record year (RMB 350.8bn), so the industry peak is ahead, but per-user and per-title economics peaked earlier.
> (e) Esports-education peak: 2017-2019, when ~30-50 vocational colleges opened esports programmes; enrolment enthusiasm has since cooled as graduate placement disappointed.

### Status Indonesia Saat Ini

**Status Di Indonesia**

> SPLIT STATUS — this is the key analytical point.
> On CONSUMPTION, Indonesia is already massively in (near-zero lag; arguably simultaneous with China, since Mobile Legends launched in Indonesia in 2016, the same year Honor of Kings broke out in China).
> On ESPORTS, Indonesia is fully mainstream and state-recognized (esports is an official olahraga prestasi under Kemenpora/KONI, with PBESI as the national federation).
> On DOMESTIC PRODUCTION, Indonesia is a laggard/dependent market — local developers capture under 1-5% of domestic spending.
> On PROTECTIVE REGULATION OF MINORS — the specific subject of this research item — Indonesia is BARU MULAI (just beginning): PP 17/2025 ('PP Tunas') was signed 28 March 2025 and the Indonesia Game Rating System was relaunched 11 October 2025 with mandatory effect from 2026, roughly six years after China's equivalent 2019 measures and with materially weaker instruments (age tiers and parental consent, but no playtime curfew, no state-run real-name gaming ID, no spending caps).

**Contoh Konkret Indonesia**

> CONSUMPTION/PLATFORMS: Mobile Legends: Bang Bang (Moonton; Indonesia is MLBB's largest market worldwide, 35m+ MAU, ~40.5% of active Indonesian mobile players), Garena Free Fire (Sea Group), PUBG Mobile, Honor of Kings (Level Infinite/Tencent), Genshin Impact and Honkai: Star Rail (HoYoverse), Roblox, EA FC Mobile.
> ESPORTS: PBESI (Pengurus Besar Esports Indonesia, the Kemenpora-recognized federation), MPL Indonesia (Season 16 ran 22 Aug-2 Nov 2025 with nine franchised teams), Liga Esports Nasional, teams RRQ, EVOS, ONIC, Bigetron, Alter Ego, Aura, Dewa United, Kagendra (sent to Honor of Kings World Cup 2025 with Menpora send-off); EVOS Divine won Free Fire at the Esports World Cup 2025 (USD 300,000).
> PAYMENTS/INFRASTRUCTURE: UniPin (Indonesian top-up gateway), Codashop, warnet/gaming-cafe chains, Telkomsel/Indosat gaming data packages.
> LOCAL STUDIOS: Agate International (Bandung), Toge Productions (Coffee Talk, A Space for the Unbound), Digital Happiness (DreadOut), Mojiken Studio, Ozysoft, Anantarupa (Lokapala — the first Indonesian MOBA, built on local mythology).
> POLICY: Perpres 19/2024 on Acceleration of National Game Industry Development (signed 12 February 2024, eight pillars: research, education, funding, infrastructure, marketing, incentives, IP facilitation, protection of creative output); Permenkominfo 2/2024 on game classification (replacing Permenkominfo 11/2016 which created IGRS); PP 17/2025 'PP Tunas' on child protection in digital space (signed 28 March 2025, effective 1 April 2025, phased platform obligations from 28 March 2026); IGRS enforcement drive from 11 October 2025, mandatory 2026, with Komdigi publicly investigating rating mismatches on Steam.

### Analisis Lag

**Bukti Historical Lag**

> (a) SOCIAL MEDIA / SHORT VIDEO PRECEDENT: China restricted minors on Douyin via 'teen mode' and a 40-minute youth mode (2019-2021); Indonesia only produced binding child-protection rules for high-risk digital platforms with PP 17/2025 (effective platform obligations from March 2026) — a comparable ~6 year regulatory lag, and Indonesia explicitly cited overseas precedent (Australia's under-16 social media ban, EU DSA, China's minor mode) rather than originating the design.
(b) ONLINE GAMBLING: China effectively eliminated consumer-facing online gambling early through payment-rail and ISP blocking; Indonesia's judi online crisis exploded 2023-2025 with hundreds of trillions of rupiah in transactions and required an emergency task force in 2024 — showing Indonesian regulation is reactive (post-harm) rather than preemptive.
(c) FINTECH/P2P LENDING: China's P2P sector peaked 2015-2017 and was fully wound down by 2020 after mass defaults; Indonesia's pinjol boom peaked 2021-2024 and OJK tightening followed the harm — a ~4-6 year lag with the same reactive pattern.
(d) RIDE-HAILING/GIG: Didi's driver-welfare rules (2021) preceded Indonesia's ojol THR/welfare debates (2024-2025) by ~3-4 years.
(e) WITHIN GAMING ITSELF: China's Ministry of Culture mandated gacha probability disclosure effective 1 May 2017; Indonesia's IGRS (introduced 2016 under Permenkominfo 11/2016) sat largely unenforced for nearly a decade until the October 2025 relaunch — showing that Indonesia can adopt the paper instrument early but lags China by many years on enforcement capacity, which is the real binding variable.
(f) The consistent historical pattern: Indonesia imports the consumption trend at near-zero lag but imports the protective regulation at a 5-7 year lag, because the consumption trend arrives through commercial channels (app stores, ads) that require no state action, while regulation requires state capacity that Indonesia builds only after visible harm.

**Tipe Lag**

> MIXED / ASYMMETRIC.
> Consumption: SIMULTANEOUS (Indonesia is a first-wave market for Chinese mobile games, not a follower).
> Esports: SIMULTANEOUS-to-slightly-LAGGARD, with a genuine REVERSE element — Indonesia hosted esports as an Asian Games demonstration sport in 2018 before China's Hangzhou 2023 medal event, and Indonesia is MLBB's global number-one market, so Indonesian scene dynamics sometimes lead rather than follow.
> Protective regulation: clear LAGGARD (5-7 years).
> Domestic production capability: severe LAGGARD (12-18 years) with no leapfrog visible.
> The overall label most useful for policy is 'consumption-simultaneous, regulation-laggard, production-laggard' — Indonesia absorbs the full social cost of a mature Chinese industry while capturing almost none of its industrial value.

### Probabilitas Transfer ke Indonesia

**Probabilitas Transfer**

> Tinggi (High) — but with an important qualification: the commercial side has ALREADY transferred completely; what is still in transit is the REGULATORY side, and that is arriving in a diluted, non-Chinese form.

**Alasan Probabilitas**

> COMMERCIAL SIDE — already 100% transferred, probability moot.
> Chinese-developed or Chinese-owned titles dominate Indonesian mobile gaming (MLBB via Moonton, PUBG Mobile and Honor of Kings via Tencent/Level Infinite, Genshin/Star Rail via HoYoverse, plus a long tail of Chinese-published hyper-casual and 4X titles).
> Chinese exports of self-developed games hit USD 20.45bn in 2025 and Southeast Asia is a priority region because of demographic fit, mobile-only device profiles, and cultural proximity in art style.
> Indonesia's 229m internet users and 80%+ mobile-first access make it the single biggest Southeast Asian prize.

REGULATORY SIDE — high probability of arrival but low probability of arriving in China's form.
> Drivers pushing it: (i) documented and rising harm (28% y/y increase in child psychiatric visits for gadget addiction; ~200,000 children exposed to online gambling); (ii) political salience of judi online, which has made 'games = gateway to gambling' a live parliamentary and DPD issue; (iii) international precedent cascade (Australia's under-16 social media ban, EU DSA, UK Online Safety Act) giving Indonesian regulators cover; (iv) an existing legal vehicle already in place (PP 17/2025 + Permenkominfo 2/2024 + IGRS) that only requires tightening rather than new primary legislation; (v) Komdigi's demonstrated willingness to block platforms, which gives it credible enforcement leverage over app stores.

Counterweights that make full Chinese-style copying unlikely: Indonesia has no equivalent of the banhao licensing chokepoint (games reach Indonesians through Google Play, the App Store and Steam, not a national approval queue); Indonesia has no unified, enforced real-name identity layer binding game accounts to NIK; and Indonesia's political economy treats gaming and esports as a growth sector to be promoted (Perpres 19/2024) rather than a social ill to be suppressed, so the state's own incentives are contradictory in a way China's were not in 2021.

MINI-GAMES / IN-APP GAME PLATFORMS — high probability, medium timeline.
> China's mini-game explosion (RMB 53.5bn, +34.4% in 2025) is the clearest next-wave trend with a real lag, and its natural Indonesian carriers already exist: TikTok's in-app games, WhatsApp/Telegram-adjacent casual play, and super-app surfaces (GoPay/Gojek, Grab, Shopee).
> Expect it in Indonesia in force 2027-2029.

**Vektor Transmisi**

> (a) DIRECT ENTRY BY CHINESE PLAYERS — dominant vector, already complete.
> Tencent (Level Infinite regional publishing, plus a longstanding stake in Sea Group which publishes Garena Free Fire, Indonesia's other top mobile title), HoYoverse (Singapore-based regional HQ serving Indonesia), Moonton (Shanghai-founded, ByteDance-owned 2021-2026, agreed sale to Savvy Games Group announced 20 March 2026 — note this means MLBB's future ownership is Saudi, not Chinese, a genuine change in the transmission map), NetEase, 37 Interactive, Lilith, FunPlus, and dozens of smaller Chinese publishers running Indonesian localization, Indonesian-language community management, and Ramadan/Independence-Day themed events.
> Chinese publishers also run Jakarta-based marketing and community offices and hire Indonesian country managers.

(b) LOCAL COPYCAT / DERIVATIVE PRODUCTION — weak but real.
> Indonesian studios (Anantarupa's Lokapala, an MOBA built on Nusantara mythology) explicitly copy Chinese-validated genre templates with local IP skins.
> The bigger copycat wave is on the business-model side: Indonesian top-up merchants, gacha-style promo mechanics in non-game apps, and battle-pass structures in Indonesian e-commerce and fintech gamification.
> Expect Indonesian mini-game studios cloning Chinese WeChat mini-game hits for TikTok/super-app surfaces from 2027.

(c) ALGORITHMIC CONTENT DIFFUSION — very high intensity.
> TikTok (Indonesia is TikTok's largest or second-largest market), YouTube Shorts, and Chinese-origin livestreaming formats push gacha-pull reaction videos, meta guides, and top-up promos into Indonesian feeds continuously.
> Indonesian gaming creators mirror Douyin/Bilibili content formats.
> This vector transmits the monetization CULTURE (whale spending norms, gacha FOMO, streak mechanics) faster than any company entry.

(d) CHINESE VENTURE CAPITAL — moderate.
> Tencent's stake in Sea Group and historic investments in Gojek/GoTo, Chinese participation in Indonesian esports team and gaming-media funding rounds, and Chinese-backed payment/top-up rails.
> Note the vector is partially diverted: Gulf capital (Savvy Games Group, Qiddiya) is now competing with Chinese capital for Southeast Asian gaming assets, as the Moonton sale shows.

(e) DIASPORA / ALUMNI / TALENT — moderate and growing.
> Indonesian nationals working at Chinese publishers' Singapore and Shanghai offices, Indonesian esports players and coaches in Chinese-run leagues, and Indonesian art/animation outsourcing studios servicing Chinese clients (the Vietnam-style outsourcing path).
> Chinese esports operators also import tournament-production know-how directly.

(f) POLICY DIFFUSION — the vector specific to the regulatory half of this trend.
> Indonesian regulators study China, Australia, the EU and South Korea (which repealed its own shutdown law in 2021 — a cautionary precedent Indonesia is also aware of).
> Komdigi's PP Tunas design borrows the age-tier + parental-consent architecture from the EU/UK rather than China's curfew architecture, which is why the transferred product looks different from the Chinese original.

### Faktor Pendorong

**Indikator Pemantauan**

> REGULATORY TIGHTENING (watch these to know when Chinese-style restriction is actually arriving):
1.
> Publication of implementing regulations (Permen/Kepmen Komdigi) under PP 17/2025 that specify verification methods — especially any requirement to bind game accounts to NIK or to use device-level age signals from Google Play/App Store.
2.
> Any draft mentioning 'batas waktu bermain' (playtime limits), 'jam malam digital' (digital curfew), or 'batas pembelian dalam gim' (in-game spending caps) — the presence of these three phrases in a Komdigi/DPR draft is the single clearest signal of Chinese-style transfer.
3.
> Mandatory gacha probability disclosure requirements appearing in IGRS technical standards.
4.
> Komdigi enforcement actions: number of games delisted, app-store takedown requests, and IGRS non-compliance sanctions issued after the 2026 mandatory date.
> The Steam rating investigation (late 2025) is the baseline case.
5.
> DPR/DPD Panja or RUU on child digital protection or on gaming/judi online convergence.
6.
> Whether Indonesian courts or OJK begin treating gacha/loot boxes as gambling under KUHP/judi online enforcement — a single such ruling would move faster than any Komdigi regulation.

INDUSTRY/COMMERCIAL:
7.
> Chinese publisher local entity registrations (PT PMA) and Jakarta office openings; Level Infinite / HoYoverse / NetEase Indonesian job postings for country manager, community manager, localization lead.
8.
> Trademark filings at DJKI for Chinese game titles and esports league brands.
9.
> Appearance of mini-game surfaces inside Indonesian super-apps (TikTok Indonesia in-app games, GoPay/Shopee/Grab game tabs) — the leading indicator for the mini-game wave.
10.
> Top-up transaction volumes at UniPin/Codashop and telco gaming bundle attach rates.
11.
> Esports franchise slot prices in MPL/Liga Esports Nasional and sponsorship mix shifting from crypto/gambling-adjacent to mainstream FMCG/banking brands (a maturity indicator).

EDUCATION/LABOUR:
12.
> New prodi approvals at Kemendikti Saintek for game technology, game design, and esports management; SMK jurusan gim enrolment numbers.
13.
> Job-posting volume on LinkedIn/Glints for 'Unity developer', 'Unreal', 'technical artist', 'LiveOps', 'game economy designer' based in Indonesia.
14.
> Growth of art/animation outsourcing contracts from Chinese and Japanese publishers to Indonesian studios (the Vietnam path).

HARM/SOCIAL:
15.
> Kemenkes/RSJ quarterly data on child and adolescent admissions for gaming and gambling addiction — currently the fastest-moving indicator (+28% y/y).
16.
> Google Trends volume in Indonesia for 'cara berhenti main game', 'kecanduan game anak', 'top up gratis', 'akun gacor'.
17.
> Number of psychiatric hospitals establishing dedicated behavioural-addiction units (currently ~54 handling addiction cases generally).

### Hambatan & Faktor Pembatal

**Hambatan Transfer**

> FOR THE REGULATORY HALF (why Chinese-style rules are slow to arrive):
- No licensing chokepoint.
> Without a banhao equivalent, Indonesia cannot condition market access on compliance; it can only ask global app stores to cooperate, and app stores answer to their own global policies first.
- No enforceable real-name layer.
> Chinese enforcement rests on a queryable national ID plus facial recognition; Indonesia's IKD/INA Digital is not integrated with game accounts, and pulsa/voucher top-ups are deliberately ID-free.
- Circumvention is trivial and culturally normalized.
> VPNs, third-party APK stores, foreign-region accounts, and account-sharing are already common; even in China, minors routinely borrow adult IDs, and Indonesia has none of China's compensating surveillance.
- Institutional contradiction.
> Perpres 19/2024 makes the state an active promoter of the game industry and esports (Kemenpora, Kemenparekraf/Kemenekraf, Kemenperin), while Komdigi and Kemenkes push restriction.
> There is no single ministry with both mandate and capacity.
- Enforcement staffing and technical capacity at Komdigi is thin relative to hundreds of thousands of distributed titles.
- Political economy of parents.
> In China the 2021 crackdown had broad parental support amid gaokao pressure; in Indonesia, smartphones are often the cheapest childcare available to working-class families, and blanket restriction faces quieter but real resistance.
- Cultural framing.
> Gaming in Indonesia is celebrated as a national-pride vehicle (SEA Games medals, MPL, MLBB world championships) rather than framed as 'spiritual opium'; there is no dominant negative narrative to mobilize.
- Regional cautionary precedent.
> South Korea repealed its Cinderella Law shutdown in 2021 after a decade, which Indonesian policymakers and industry lobbyists cite against curfews.

FOR THE PRODUCTION HALF (why local industry stays small):
- Capital scarcity and no patient funding for 3-5 year dev cycles.
- Talent thinness: shortage of senior engine programmers, technical artists, and game economy designers; brain drain to Singapore.
- No domestic publisher with global distribution or UA (user acquisition) budgets — Chinese publishers spend more on Indonesian user acquisition than Indonesian studios' entire budgets.
- Weak IP monetization ecosystem (merchandise, licensing) and piracy norms.
- Payment friction for premium products; the market is conditioned to free-to-play.

**Faktor Pembatal Transfer**

> Conditions that will prevent China's version of this trend from ever landing in Indonesia in the same form:

1.
> ABSENCE OF A SOVEREIGN DISTRIBUTION LAYER.
> China's entire regulatory architecture is downstream of one fact: the Great Firewall plus the banhao system means the Chinese state controls which games exist domestically.
> Indonesia's games reach users through Google Play, the App Store and Steam — infrastructures Indonesia does not own and cannot license.
> Every Chinese instrument (curfew, spending cap, content edit) depends on the publisher being reachable by the regulator; in Indonesia most publishers are foreign entities with no local establishment.
> This is structural and will not change.

2.
> NO MASS REAL-NAME IDENTITY BINDING, AND CULTURAL RESISTANCE TO IT.
> China's minor restrictions are technically enforceable only because every account maps to a verified national ID and platforms run facial recognition.
> Indonesia's prepaid, cash-and-pulsa digital economy is built on the opposite premise, and post-2021 Dukcapil/BPJS data-leak scandals have made mandatory ID binding politically toxic.
> Without this, playtime curfews would be unenforceable theatre.

3.
> THE STATE HAS THE OPPOSITE ECONOMIC INTEREST.
> China could crush its domestic industry in 2021 because Chinese firms owned the industry — the value destroyed was recaptured domestically and offset by exports.
> Indonesia captures 0.5-5% of its own market's value; restricting play destroys tax revenue and consumer surplus while the profits it might discipline sit offshore.
> The state has little leverage and little to gain, so it will regulate content and age gates rather than time and spend.

4.
> NO GAOKAO-EQUIVALENT SOCIAL PRESSURE.
> China's minor gaming restrictions were coupled to the double-reduction education campaign and a national obsession with a single high-stakes exam.
> Indonesia abolished the UN national exam in 2021 and has a far less zero-sum academic-competition culture, removing the strongest political motive for restricting children's leisure time.

5.
> DEMOGRAPHIC AND FISCAL ASYMMETRY.
> China's crackdown was legible as demographic policy (a one-child generation's health and fertility).
> Indonesia has a demographic dividend and frames youth digital engagement as an asset, not a scarcity to be protected.

6.
> ARCHIPELAGIC AND INCOME STRUCTURE CAPS THE MONETIZATION MODEL, NOT JUST THE REGULATION.
> China's whale-driven gacha economy assumes high disposable income concentrated in dense cities.
> Indonesia's low ARPU, prepaid data, and dispersed geography mean the Indonesian market will skew permanently toward ad-monetized, low-data, low-spec titles.
> So the specific Chinese harm pattern (children spending five- and six-figure sums on gacha, triggering parental outrage and then regulation) will manifest in a muted, distributed form — which paradoxically reduces the political trigger for restriction while the aggregate harm (time, attention, gambling adjacency) still accumulates.

7.
> THE HARM VECTOR HAS ALREADY BEEN CAPTURED BY A DIFFERENT POLICY FRAME.
> In Indonesia, the dominant child-digital-harm narrative is judi online and pornography, not gaming per se.
> Gaming regulation is being pulled along as a rider on gambling and child-safety enforcement, which means Indonesia will likely end up with gambling-adjacency rules and age ratings rather than China's playtime architecture — a different regulatory species entirely.

8.
> OWNERSHIP DRIFT AWAY FROM CHINA.
> The March 2026 agreement to sell Moonton to Saudi Arabia's Savvy Games Group removes Indonesia's single most important game from Chinese ownership.
> Gulf sovereign capital is now a competing transmission channel with different regulatory sensitivities, further weakening the 'China → Indonesia' pipe for governance norms even as content flows continue.

### Prediksi Timeline di Indonesia

**Skenario Percepatan**

> Accelerators for REGULATION: (1) a nationally reported tragedy involving a child and gaming/gacha spending or online gambling — Indonesia's regulatory clock historically starts with a viral case; (2) formal legal classification of gacha/loot boxes as gambling under judi online enforcement, which would instantly drag major titles into an existing enforcement machine; (3) Australia's under-16 social media ban proving operable, giving Indonesian regulators a copyable technical template; (4) a Kemenkes national prevalence study quantifying gaming disorder; (5) integration of INA Digital/IKD with app-store age signals, which removes the enforceability excuse; (6) an election cycle where child digital safety becomes a campaign plank.
> Accelerators for the INDUSTRY/mini-game wave: TikTok Indonesia launching in-app game monetization; a Chinese mini-game publisher establishing an Indonesian entity; Perpres 19/2024 implementing regulations actually releasing fiscal incentives; Gulf capital (post-Moonton) investing in Southeast Asian studios; and cheap AI-assisted content pipelines lowering the cost of shipping a game below the Indonesian studio capital threshold.

### Dampak Sosial-Ekonomi

**Dampak Lapangan Kerja**

> JOBS CREATED (already visible in Indonesia, expanding):
- Esports ecosystem roles: professional players, coaches, analysts, team managers, tournament operations/production crew, casters/shoutcasters, observers, referees, esports venue staff.
> Note the pyramid is brutally narrow — Indonesia has roughly a few hundred salaried tier-1 players against hundreds of thousands of aspirants.
- Content and community: gaming streamers and YouTubers, clip editors, thumbnail designers, community/Discord managers, talent managers and MCN-equivalent agencies, esports journalists.
- Commercial services around foreign titles: localization and Indonesian voice-over, customer support/CS outsourcing, community moderation, user-acquisition and performance marketing agencies, influencer marketing, top-up merchants and payment agents (UniPin/Codashop reseller networks reach into kiosks and warung).
- Compliance and safety, a genuinely new category from 2026: IGRS compliance officers, age-assurance/verification engineers, trust-and-safety analysts, content moderators, child online-safety specialists at platforms and at Komdigi.
- Clinical and educational: behavioural-addiction psychologists and psychiatrists (already capacity-constrained — RSJ Menur has exceeded inpatient capacity), school counsellors specializing in digital wellbeing, parent-education trainers.
- Development-side (small but the highest-value): Unity/Unreal engineers, technical artists, 3D and character artists, animators, level designers, game economy designers, LiveOps managers, QA, build engineers, backend/netcode engineers.
> Art and animation outsourcing for foreign publishers is the most realistic mass-employment path (the Vietnam/Philippines model).

JOBS CHANGED:
- Warnet/internet cafe operators shifting from browsing to gaming cafes and esports venues, and now to console/VR corners.
- Traditional sports coaching and youth-development organizations absorbing esports as a discipline.
- Advertising and media planning, as gaming and streaming take share from TV.
- Telco product managers building gaming-specific data products.

JOBS LOST OR DEVALUED:
- Physical game/DVD retail and console rental (already gone).
- Traditional warnet browsing businesses.
- Generic media/broadcast production roles displaced by streaming-native production.
- Boosting/account-trading grey work, which regulation will criminalize or squeeze.
- In China specifically, the 2021-2022 crackdown eliminated roughly 14,000 gaming-related firms (some counts up to 140,000 including adjacent services) and triggered layoffs at Tencent, NetEase and 37Games — the direct lesson is that this employment is highly regulation-elastic and can vanish in a single policy cycle.

NET ASSESSMENT FOR INDONESIA: as long as Indonesia captures under 5% of its own market's value, gaming creates mostly LOW-VALUE, DOWNSTREAM jobs (top-up agents, streamers, community managers, tournament crew) rather than HIGH-VALUE upstream engineering jobs.
> The employment story is therefore currently a consumption-servicing story, not an industrial one — the opposite of China, where the sector employs hundreds of thousands in development and exports USD 20bn+.

**Dampak Kelas Menengah**

> (1) HOUSEHOLD BUDGET LEAKAGE.
> Gaming top-ups are a small but persistent drain on aspirational middle-class and lower-middle-class households, and unlike China's whale economy the Indonesian pattern is many small, hard-to-notice pulsa-based transactions — which makes it harder for parents to detect and easier to normalize.
> Because most spending flows to foreign publishers, this is a direct consumption leakage out of the domestic economy at a time when Indonesia's middle class is already contracting (the widely reported shrinkage of the aspiring middle class since 2019).

(2) PARENTING BURDEN AND MENTAL-HEALTH COSTS.
> The middle class bears the visible cost first because it is the segment that seeks treatment: the 28% y/y rise in child psychiatric visits for gadget addiction, and the 1,856 cases at RSJ Soeharto Heerdjan, are disproportionately urban middle-class families with the awareness and means to present at a hospital.
> Private behavioural-therapy costs are not covered adequately by BPJS, creating a new out-of-pocket burden.

(3) STATUS AND ASPIRATION DISTORTION.
> Esports offers a visible, aspirational mobility path — 'become a pro player' — that is statistically far worse than the educational paths it competes with.
> This mirrors China's experience where esports vocational programmes drew students who then found few paid roles.
> For middle-class families, the risk is a mis-allocated education decision made at 15-17.

(4) NEW MIDDLE-CLASS OCCUPATIONS.
> Conversely, the sector genuinely creates middle-class-compatible careers: game developers, technical artists, community and marketing managers, tournament producers, and compliance officers.
> Salaries in Indonesian game development are modest but competitive with general IT, and outsourcing work pays in foreign currency.

(5) GAMBLING ADJACENCY IS THE SHARPEST MIDDLE-CLASS RISK.
> The judi online crisis has demonstrated that the same demographic and the same payment rails move fluidly between gaming top-ups and gambling deposits.
> For lower-middle-class households, a gacha habit and a slot-app habit are separated by one advertisement.

(6) TIME-USE.
> Gaming is the cheapest per-hour entertainment available (a Rp 50,000 data package can fill a month), which makes it structurally attractive precisely to households under economic pressure — a demand pattern that will intensify, not weaken, if Indonesian consumer downgrading continues.

**Dampak Daerah Non Jawa**

> HIGHLY RELEVANT OUTSIDE JAVA — arguably more so than in Jakarta, and this is under-appreciated in Indonesian policy discourse.

CONSUMPTION IS NATIONAL, NOT JAVA-CENTRIC.
> Internet penetration is 76.96% in rural areas versus 83.56% urban (APJII 2025) — a gap of under seven points.
> Mobile games require little bandwidth (Free Fire is deliberately low-spec and low-data, which is why it dominates in lower-income and non-Java regions), so the consumption trend has already fully diffused.
> The documented extreme case of a 17-year-old consuming 30GB/month purely on Free Fire came from Bangka Belitung, not Jakarta, and RSJ Sungailiat there recorded 68 new addiction cases in two months (+35%).
> RSJ Lampung and RSJ Menur (Surabaya) report the same trajectory.
> The harm is distributed nationally while treatment capacity (54 psychiatric hospitals, heavily Java-weighted) is not.

WHY NON-JAVA EXPOSURE IS HIGHER, NOT LOWER: fewer alternative leisure and extracurricular options, fewer formal youth employment opportunities, weaker school counselling capacity, lower parental digital literacy, and higher rates of children left with smartphones while parents work.
> Gaming's substitution value is greatest where the substitutes are scarcest.

INDUSTRY AND ESPORTS ARE JAVA-CENTRIC.
> Development studios cluster in Bandung, Jakarta, Yogyakarta and Surabaya; MPL and franchise teams, esports venues, production facilities, publisher offices, and game-related university programmes are almost entirely on Java (with Bali as a small outlier).
> Esports talent from outside Java must migrate to Jakarta/Bandung to turn pro, creating a familiar centre-periphery extraction pattern: the regions supply players and spending, Java captures the salaries and margins.

POLICY IMPLICATION: any protective regulation designed and enforced from Jakarta will bite least where harm is greatest.
> Conversely, the most scalable non-Java opportunity is not esports venues but remote-capable digital work — art outsourcing, QA, localization, community moderation — which can be located anywhere with decent connectivity, and which regional polytechnics could realistically supply.

### Kaitan Pendidikan

**Jurusan Terancam**

> This trend threatens fewer majors by direct substitution than by ATTENTION AND RELEVANCE EROSION, plus one important category of over-supplied new majors:

1.
> ESPORTS-MANAGEMENT AND 'PRO PLAYER' PROGRAMMES THEMSELVES — the single most important warning.
> China opened 'Esports and Management' as a vocational major in 2016-2017; roughly 30 colleges by 2019 and many more later, but placement outcomes disappointed and the pipeline produced far more graduates than the industry's paid roles, with graduates diverted into journalism, casting and event operations.
> Indonesian institutions are now rushing into the same space (UI Vokasi added esports to its curriculum; multiple private campuses market 'jurusan esports').
> Programmes built around competitive play rather than transferable business/production/technical skills will become the clearest example of an over-supplied major.

2.
> TRADITIONAL BROADCAST AND TELEVISION PRODUCTION (Ilmu Komunikasi - Broadcasting, Penyiaran) — audiences and ad budgets have migrated to streaming and gaming content; linear-TV-specific curricula are the most exposed.

3.
> CONVENTIONAL PRINT/SPORTS JOURNALISM — displaced by creator-led coverage.

4.
> GENERIC DESAIN KOMUNIKASI VISUAL / 2D graphic design without real-time 3D, technical art, or engine skills — the entry-level static-design market is being compressed simultaneously by generative AI and by demand shifting toward interactive/real-time assets.

5.
> CONVENTIONAL ILMU KEOLAHRAGAAN / PENJASKES that treats sport purely physically — as esports enters the national sport system, these programmes must absorb it or lose relevance in the youth-sport administration job market.

6.
> GENERAL 'TEKNIK INFORMATIKA' WITHOUT SPECIALIZATION — not threatened by gaming specifically, but the gaming path illustrates the broader point that undifferentiated IT graduates lose to specialists.

7.
> TOURISM/HOSPITALITY AND CONVENTIONAL ENTERTAINMENT MANAGEMENT programmes assuming physical-venue leisure demand from youth.

IMPORTANT CAVEAT: 'threatened' here means reduced relevance and worse placement, not disappearance.
> The honest framing for Indonesian universities is that the threat is to programmes whose graduates cannot do anything a game studio, platform, or regulator will pay for.

**Jurusan Dibutuhkan**

> TECHNICAL / DEVELOPMENT (highest value, scarcest in Indonesia):
- Game programming: C++ and C#, Unity and Unreal Engine, gameplay systems, physics, rendering fundamentals.
- Technical art and real-time 3D: shaders, rigging, optimization for low-spec Android devices (the specific skill Indonesia's own market requires and that Chinese publishers hire for).
- Backend and netcode: distributed systems, matchmaking, anti-cheat, live service architecture, cloud cost engineering.
- Game economy design and monetization analytics — the discipline that actually determines profitability; combines behavioural economics, statistics and product management.
> Almost absent from Indonesian curricula.
- LiveOps and product management for games: cohort analysis, retention/LTV modelling, A/B testing, seasonal content planning.
- Data science applied to player behaviour, churn and fraud detection.
- AI/ML applied to games: procedural content, NPC behaviour, AI-assisted art pipelines, plus the emerging role of AI content-safety tooling.
- Audio design and adaptive music; motion capture and animation.
- QA automation and build/release engineering — the most accessible entry point and the natural base for outsourcing employment.

CREATIVE / NARRATIVE:
- Game design and systems design (distinct from art), level design, narrative design and worldbuilding; adaptation of Indonesian mythology and history into globally legible IP (the Lokapala/Nusantara path).
- Localization and transcreation (Indonesian ↔ Mandarin, English, Japanese) — a direct, immediate earner given Chinese publishers' Indonesian expansion.

BUSINESS / OPERATIONS:
- Esports business management: sponsorship sales, league operations, athlete contracts and welfare, broadcast production management, venue operations.
- Creator/talent management and digital media rights.
- User acquisition and performance marketing for apps.

GOVERNANCE / SAFETY — the fastest-growing new category from 2026:
- Trust and safety, content moderation policy, age assurance and identity engineering.
- Digital child-protection law and platform compliance (IGRS, PP Tunas, DSA-style regimes) — lawyers and compliance officers who understand both code and regulation.
- Clinical and counselling psychology specializing in behavioural addiction (gaming disorder, gambling), plus digital-wellbeing curriculum design for schools.
> Indonesia's psychiatric system is already over capacity on exactly this caseload.
- Data protection and privacy engineering (PDP Law compliance for children's data).

CROSS-CUTTING: for Indonesian students, the highest expected-value combination is a genuine engineering or art-production skill PLUS English/Mandarin PLUS portfolio evidence — because the realistic first employer is a foreign publisher or an outsourcing client, not a domestic studio.

**China Education Response**

> China's education system responded to gaming and esports faster and more institutionally than any other country, then partially corrected:

1.
> VOCATIONAL MAJOR CREATION (2016-2017).
> In September 2016 the Department of Vocational and Adult Education of the Ministry of Education added 'Esports and Management' (电子竞技运动与管理) to the supplementary catalogue of higher vocational majors, for implementation from 2017.
> This is the single clearest instance of a state adding a major specifically in response to a digital-economy trend.
> Hunan Sports Vocational College ran an esports class of 40 students in autumn 2017; roughly 30 colleges offered esports-related programmes by 2019, and the number grew into the hundreds across vocational institutions in subsequent years.

2.
> UNIVERSITY-LEVEL PROGRAMMES (2017 onward).
> The Communication University of China opened a digital media art programme with an esports analysis direction (small cohorts, ~20 students) in 2017; Sichuan Film and Television University, Shanghai institutions and others followed.
> Curricula covered event operations, commentary, data analysis, team management and broadcast production — deliberately NOT 'how to play'.

3.
> OCCUPATIONAL RECOGNITION (2019).
> MOHRSS formally recognized 'esports operator' (电子竞技运营师) and 'esports player' (电子竞技员) as official new occupations in April 2019, creating a formal skills-standard and certification pathway — the step Indonesia has not taken.

4.
> GAME DEVELOPMENT EDUCATION.
> Game programming and art were absorbed into existing digital media technology, digital media art, animation, and software engineering programmes rather than being made a standalone major, supported by a very large CS graduate base (China produces well over a million CS/engineering graduates annually).
> Industry-academia arrangements with Tencent, NetEase and Perfect World (Perfect World Education runs its own training institutes) supplied vocational-to-industry pipelines.

5.
> THE CORRECTION (2019-2022).
> Placement outcomes for esports graduates disappointed: the industry's 'talent gap' rhetoric referred mostly to operations and content roles, while students enrolled expecting to become players.
> After the 2021 crackdown and the 2021-2022 licence freeze and layoffs, enrolment enthusiasm cooled, some programmes were quietly renamed or folded into broader digital-media majors, and messaging shifted toward 'esports industry management' rather than competitive play.
> The lesson China learned and Indonesia has not yet absorbed: create programmes for the industry's actual job pyramid, not for its visible apex.

6.
> THE RESTRICTIVE SIDE OF THE EDUCATION RESPONSE.
> The gaming curbs were designed to sit alongside the 'double reduction' policy (July 2021) limiting private tutoring and homework, and alongside the revised Law on the Protection of Minors (effective 1 June 2021) which added an Internet Protection chapter obliging schools, families and platforms to prevent minors' internet addiction.
> Schools were tasked with digital-literacy and anti-addiction education, and the State Council's Regulations on the Protection of Minors in Cyberspace (effective 1 January 2024) made 'minor mode' obligations explicit across devices, app stores and applications.
> Education policy and platform policy were deliberately coordinated — a coherence Indonesia's fragmented ministries currently lack.

### Pelajaran Kebijakan dari China

**Respons Kebijakan China**

> CHINA'S POLICY TOOLKIT, IN THE ORDER IT WAS DEPLOYED, WITH ADOPTABILITY ASSESSMENT FOR INDONESIA:

1.
> GACHA/LOOT-BOX PROBABILITY DISCLOSURE (Ministry of Culture interim measures, effective 1 May 2017).
> Publishers must disclose the drop rates of random-draw items.
> World-first, low-cost, high-transparency, and it does not restrict anyone's freedom to play.
> HIGHLY ADOPTABLE by Indonesia — could be attached to IGRS technical standards immediately and enforced through app-store listing requirements.
> This is the single best preemptive policy Indonesia could copy.

2.
> REAL-NAME REGISTRATION (from 2007, hardened 2019-2021) plus platform-side facial recognition ('Midnight Patrol', Tencent 2021).
> Enables everything downstream.
> PARTIALLY ADOPTABLE — Indonesia should require age assurance (not necessarily full ID binding), using device/OS-level age signals from Google and Apple, which is far cheaper and privacy-safer than a national game ID.

3.
> AGE-TIERED IN-GAME SPENDING CAPS (2019 notice: monthly caps scaled by age band).
> ADOPTABLE and arguably more urgent for Indonesia than time limits, because the financial-harm channel (and its bleed into judi online) is Indonesia's sharpest documented risk.
> Should be paired with a mandatory refund mechanism for verified minor purchases.

4.
> PLAYTIME CURFEWS FOR MINORS (2019: 90 min/weekday, 3h/holiday, 22:00-08:00 blackout; 2021: 1 hour on Fri/Sat/Sun/holidays only).
> Effective on paper — CADPA/Gamma reported >75% of minor gamers playing under three hours a week by late 2022 — but only because of the real-name substrate.
> LOW ADOPTABILITY for Indonesia without identity infrastructure; would produce circumvention and disrespect for the law.
> Note also the cautionary precedent: South Korea repealed its own shutdown law in 2021 after a decade of poor results.

5.
> LICENSING CHOKEPOINT (banhao) AND APPROVAL FREEZES (2018; July 2021-April 2022).
> The most powerful instrument, and the most economically destructive — roughly 14,000 firms closed (up to 140,000 by broader definitions), Tencent lost close to USD 200bn of market value in 2018 and ~USD 60bn in one day in August 2021.
> NOT ADOPTABLE and should not be copied: Indonesia lacks the sovereign distribution layer, and would destroy its nascent local studios while foreign titles route around it.

6.
> BAN ON ADDICTIVE MONETIZATION MECHANICS (December 2023 draft: monthly spend caps ~RMB 400, ban on daily-login and consecutive-recharge rewards, ban on item auctions).
> Wiped ~USD 80bn off Tencent and NetEase and was WITHDRAWN in January 2024.
> The lesson for Indonesia is about process, not substance: regulate monetization through disclosure and defaults, consult industry before publishing, and never surprise a listed market — otherwise the policy dies and nothing is protected.

7.
> LEGAL CODIFICATION (revised Law on the Protection of Minors, effective 1 June 2021, adding an Internet Protection chapter; State Council Regulations on the Protection of Minors in Cyberspace, effective 1 January 2024; mandatory 'minor mode' across devices, app stores and apps).
> ADOPTABLE — Indonesia's PP 17/2025 is the structural equivalent but currently thinner.
> The specific Chinese innovation worth copying is placing obligations at the DEVICE and APP-STORE layer, not only on individual apps, because that is where enforcement is tractable against foreign publishers.

8.
> CONTENT REVIEW AND CULTURAL REQUIREMENTS.
> Politically specific to China; NOT ADOPTABLE and not desirable.

9.
> INDUSTRY SELF-REGULATION WITH STATE BACKING (CADPA/GPC publishing compliance progress reports, an industry age-rating standard).
> ADOPTABLE and cheap: Indonesia should require a publisher self-declaration regime under IGRS with audit and penalty, rather than trying to review hundreds of thousands of titles centrally.

10.
> SEPARATION OF ESPORTS FROM 'GAMING HARM'.
> China simultaneously restricted minors and promoted esports as a legitimate sport and industry (Asian Games medal event 2023, city-level subsidies).
> ADOPTABLE, and in fact Indonesia is already doing this via Kemenpora recognition and Perpres 19/2024 — but China coupled promotion with restriction, whereas Indonesia has so far only done promotion.

SYNTHESIS OF THE PREEMPTIVE PACKAGE INDONESIA COULD ADOPT NOW: probability disclosure + minor spending caps with refund rights + device/app-store-level age assurance + IGRS enforcement with real penalties + gambling-adjacency rules.
> That package captures most of China's protective benefit while avoiding the instruments (banhao, curfews, facial recognition) that Indonesia cannot enforce and should not want.

**Rekomendasi Kebijakan Indonesia**

> 1.
> MANDATE GACHA/LOOT-BOX PROBABILITY DISCLOSURE via a Permen Komdigi attached to IGRS technical standards, following China's 2017 precedent.
> Cheapest, fastest, least contested protective measure available.
2.
> LEGISLATE MINOR SPENDING CAPS AND A STATUTORY REFUND RIGHT for unauthorized minor in-game purchases, enforced at the payment layer (QRIS, e-wallets, telco pulsa billing) rather than only at the publisher — because the payment rails are domestic and reachable, while publishers are not.
3.
> CLOSE THE GAMBLING-ADJACENCY GAP explicitly.
> Define in regulation the line between gacha, item trading/marketplaces, and gambling; ban cash-out and third-party item resale markets for titles rated below 18+; require publishers to block gambling advertising in-game.
> This is the highest-priority item given ~200,000 children already exposed to judi online.
4.
> PUT OBLIGATIONS AT THE DEVICE AND APP-STORE LAYER.
> Require Google Play and the App Store to transmit a verified age band to apps distributed in Indonesia, and to enforce IGRS ratings at download.
> This is the only enforcement point that scales against foreign publishers, and it is the design China converged on in its 2024 minor-mode regulations.
5.
> RESOURCE IGRS ENFORCEMENT PROPERLY.
> A rating system that sat largely dormant from 2016 to 2025 will not become credible through announcement alone.
> Fund an inspection unit, publish a public compliance register, set escalating administrative fines, and publish enforcement statistics quarterly.
6.
> DO NOT COPY THE CURFEW.
> Without a real-name identity substrate, a Chinese-style playtime limit would be unenforceable, would push minors to VPNs and shared adult accounts, and would delegitimize the rest of the regime — the South Korean shutdown-law repeal (2021) is the cautionary case.
7.
> DO NOT COPY THE LICENSING FREEZE.
> It would kill Indonesian studios and barely touch foreign publishers.
8.
> BUILD CLINICAL CAPACITY AHEAD OF THE CURVE.
> Establish behavioural-addiction units beyond Java, add gaming/gambling disorder to BPJS coverage pathways, publish a national prevalence study, and train school counsellors.
> Hospital data (+28% y/y; RSJ Menur over capacity) shows demand is already outrunning supply.
9.
> MANDATE PLATFORM DATA ACCESS FOR RESEARCH.
> Require large publishers operating in Indonesia to report aggregate minor playtime and spending statistics to Komdigi — China's CADPA progress reports show how much policy legitimacy comes from having the numbers.
10.
> MAKE PERPRES 19/2024 OPERATIONAL.
> Release implementing regulations, a dedicated funding facility for studios, tax incentives tied to Indonesian IP and local employment, and public-procurement demand (educational, health and cultural games).
> Protection without industrial policy just entrenches Indonesia's 95-99% foreign capture.
11.
> CONDITION MARKET ACCESS ON LOCAL PRESENCE.
> Require large foreign publishers above a revenue threshold to register a local entity with a compliance officer — the precondition for any enforcement, and a lever Indonesia already uses for PSE registration.
12.
> REGULATE ESPORTS LABOUR NOW, BEFORE THE BUBBLE DEFLATES.
> Standard player contracts, minimum age, education-continuity requirements for minor athletes, salary escrow, and mental-health provision.
> China's plateau shows the correction comes fast, and Indonesian teenagers signing away years to teams are the ones who will pay for it.

### Peluang & Rekomendasi Aksi

**Peluang Bisnis**

> 1.
> AGE ASSURANCE AND PARENTAL-CONTROL INFRASTRUCTURE (SaaS).
> PP 17/2025 obligations phase in from March 2026 across games, social platforms and app stores, and every foreign publisher operating in Indonesia will need a compliant, low-friction age-signal and parental-consent flow.
> There is currently no dominant Indonesian provider.
> Adjacent: consent management, minor-account dashboards, and audit trails for Komdigi reporting.
2.
> IGRS AND DIGITAL-COMPLIANCE ADVISORY.
> A regulatory-consulting niche serving hundreds of foreign publishers who must classify, label and document their titles from 2026 — analogous to the China-market entry consultancies that grew around banhao.
3.
> LOCALIZATION, CULTURALIZATION AND LIVE COMMUNITY OPERATIONS for Chinese, Korean and now Gulf-owned publishers targeting Indonesia.
> Indonesia is MLBB's largest market and a top-tier market for Free Fire and PUBG Mobile; publishers already outsource Indonesian voice-over, festival event design, creator relations and Discord moderation.
> Low capital, foreign-currency revenue, immediately available.
4.
> ART, ANIMATION AND QA OUTSOURCING (the Vietnam/Philippines path).
> The single most realistic route to mass high-value employment: sell production capacity to foreign studios rather than trying to win the consumer market head-on.
> Requires portfolio-grade technical art training, not new IP.
5.
> MINI-GAMES AND AD-MONETIZED HYPER-CASUAL BUILT FOR SUPER-APP SURFACES.
> China's mini-game segment grew 34.4% to RMB 53.5bn in 2025 and generated over half the market's incremental growth; it is ad-heavy and low-spend, which fits Indonesia's income profile far better than gacha.
> First-mover advantage exists for studios that build for TikTok in-app games, GoPay/Gojek, Shopee, Grab and telco portals.
> This is the clearest 'trend not yet arrived' business opportunity in this domain.
6.
> PAYMENT, TOP-UP AND GAMING-COMMERCE RAILS.
> UniPin proves an Indonesian company can own this layer; adjacent openings include compliant minor-spending controls, family wallets with caps, refund tooling, and gift-card distribution into kiosks and warung across non-Java regions.
7.
> ESPORTS INFRASTRUCTURE AND OPERATIONS OUTSIDE JAVA.
> Regional tournament circuits, school and campus leagues, and modernized warnet-to-esports-venue conversions in Sumatra, Sulawesi and Kalimantan — where consumption is high but organized competition is thin.
> Lower capital than franchise team ownership, which is the part of the value chain most likely to consolidate painfully after ~2028.
8.
> CREATOR AND TALENT MANAGEMENT (MCN-equivalent) specialized in gaming, plus clip/short-form production services — the Chinese MCN playbook applied to Indonesia's streamer base.
9.
> DIGITAL WELLBEING AND BEHAVIOURAL-ADDICTION SERVICES.
> Teletherapy for gaming and gambling disorder, school-based prevention programmes, parent-education products, and corporate/school screening tools.
> Demand is documented and rising 28% y/y while public capacity is exceeded.
10.
> LOCAL IP AND CULTURAL EXPORT.
> Indonesian mythology, history and horror are globally underexploited (Lokapala, DreadOut, A Space for the Unbound prove the concept).
> The realistic path is narrow-scope premium PC/console titles for global storefronts rather than competing with Tencent-scale live services.
11.
> LOW-SPEC DEVICE AND CONNECTIVITY PRODUCTS: gaming-optimized data bundles, device financing for entry-level gaming phones, accessories, and cloud-gaming for spec-constrained users — the largest addressable base in Indonesia is players on sub-USD 150 Android devices.
12.
> ANTI-CHEAT, ANTI-FRAUD AND TRUST-AND-SAFETY TOOLING localized for Indonesian language and scam patterns.

**Rekomendasi Individu Mahasiswa**

> 1.
> CHOOSE A PRODUCTION SKILL, NOT A PLAYING DREAM.
> The esports pyramid in Indonesia supports a few hundred salaried tier-1 players against hundreds of thousands of aspirants; China's esports-major graduates learned this at scale.
> If you want to be in this industry, be the person who builds, operates, analyses or governs the game.
2.
> BUILD ONE DEEP TECHNICAL SPINE: either engine programming (C++/C#, Unity or Unreal) or technical art (shaders, rigging, mobile optimization) or backend/LiveOps.
> Optimization for low-end Android is a specific, marketable Indonesian advantage because it is exactly what publishers targeting this market need.
3.
> LEARN GAME ECONOMY AND ANALYTICS.
> Retention, LTV, cohort analysis, A/B testing, and monetization design are the skills that determine whether a game makes money, and they are almost entirely absent from Indonesian curricula.
> This is the highest scarcity-to-demand ratio in the field.
4.
> SHIP SOMETHING SMALL AND PUBLIC.
> A finished game jam entry, a published mini-game, a mod, or an itch.io release outweighs any transcript.
> Portfolio is the hiring currency; three shipped small things beat one unfinished ambitious thing.
5.
> TREAT THE FOREIGN EMPLOYER AS YOUR REALISTIC FIRST EMPLOYER.
> Domestic studios are few and thinly capitalized; Chinese, Korean, Japanese and Gulf-owned publishers and their outsourcing partners are hiring.
> Therefore: professional English is non-negotiable, and functional Mandarin is a genuine differentiator that very few Indonesian candidates have.
6.
> CONSIDER THE COMPLIANCE AND SAFETY TRACK — it is the newest and least contested.
> Trust and safety, age assurance, child online-protection law, content policy and platform compliance will be hiring from 2026 as PP Tunas and IGRS obligations bite, and there is essentially no trained Indonesian talent pool.
7.
> IF YOU ARE IN PSYCHOLOGY OR MEDICINE, SPECIALIZE IN BEHAVIOURAL ADDICTION.
> Demand is documented, growing 28% y/y, and public capacity is already exceeded — including outside Java, where competition for these roles is lowest.
8.
> LEARN TO WORK REMOTELY AND GET PAID IN FOREIGN CURRENCY.
> Localization, QA, art production and community management can all be done from Makassar or Medan for clients abroad.
> This is the fastest available income arbitrage in the sector.
9.
> DEVELOP AI-ASSISTED PRODUCTION FLUENCY.
> AI art and code assistance are collapsing the cost of small-team game production; the students who compound this advantage will ship more, faster, than any previous Indonesian cohort.
10.
> UNDERSTAND YOUR OWN CONSUMPTION.
> Students in this field are the demographic most exposed to the harms studied here; the practical recommendation is to track your own playtime and top-up spending honestly, because the professional advantage of understanding these systems is worthless if you are captured by them.

**Rekomendasi Perguruan Tinggi**

> OPEN OR STRENGTHEN:
1.
> Game Technology / Game Engineering as a proper concentration inside Informatika or Teknik Komputer — with real engine work (Unity and Unreal), graphics programming, and mobile performance optimization, taught by people who have shipped.
2.
> Technical Art as a distinct track bridging DKV and Informatika.
> This is the highest-demand, lowest-supply role in the region and the natural gateway to outsourcing contracts.
3.
> Game Design and Game Economy Design — systems thinking, behavioural economics, statistics, and monetization ethics.
> Should be taught jointly by design, economics and psychology faculties.
4.
> LiveOps and Product Analytics for digital services — transferable well beyond games.
5.
> Digital Trust, Safety and Child Online Protection — a cross-faculty programme (law, computer science, psychology, communications) producing the compliance workforce that PP 17/2025 and IGRS will require from 2026.
> First-mover advantage for any Indonesian university.
6.
> Clinical concentration in behavioural addiction within psychology and psychiatry residency programmes, with placements at RSJ facilities that are already over capacity.
7.
> Localization and transcreation (Indonesian-Mandarin-English-Japanese) within language faculties, explicitly oriented to games and digital content.

RESTRUCTURE, DO NOT SIMPLY OPEN:
8.
> ESPORTS PROGRAMMES — restructure any 'jurusan esports' around business, event production, broadcast, analytics and athlete welfare, and away from competitive play.
> Publish honest placement statistics.
