> China's 2016-2019 vocational esports expansion is the direct cautionary case: the state created the major, enrolment surged, and graduate outcomes disappointed because students enrolled for the apex of a pyramid whose base was the actual job market.
> Indonesian institutions should learn this without repeating it.
9.
> Broadcasting and DKV curricula — add real-time 3D, interactive media, and streaming production; retire linear-TV-only tracks.
10.
> Ilmu Keolahragaan — add esports administration, sports science for esports athletes (RSI, sleep, cognition), and youth-athlete welfare.

INSTITUTIONAL MEASURES:
11.
> Build studio partnerships and mandatory industry placement (magang) with both Indonesian studios and the Jakarta/Singapore offices of foreign publishers — the Chinese model of Tencent/NetEase/Perfect World industry-academia pipelines is directly copyable.
12.
> Fund and staff a game incubator that can carry a student team through a full ship cycle, since the binding constraint on Indonesian studios is finishing and publishing, not ideating.
13.
> Prioritize regional polytechnics (outside Java) for QA, art production and localization tracks — remote-capable, employment-dense, and located where the consumption (and the harm) is heaviest but the industry jobs currently are not.
14.
> Require ethics and regulation modules in every game programme: gacha probability disclosure, minor protection, gambling adjacency, dark patterns.
> Indonesia's future compliance workforce and its future monetization designers should come out of the same classrooms.

### Faktor Risiko & Sisi Gelap

**Dampak Negatif China**

> 1.
> YOUTH HEALTH AND ADDICTION — the stated trigger.
> Government concern centred on myopia (the August 2018 notice was explicitly framed around deteriorating eyesight), sleep deprivation, academic decline and family conflict.
> State media reported minors playing eight hours a day of Honor of Kings.
> Peer-reviewed meta-analyses of internet gaming disorder prevalence among Chinese adolescents document a substantial affected minority, though estimates vary widely by instrument.
2.
> THE 'SPIRITUAL OPIUM' SHOCK AND MARKET DESTRUCTION.
> The 3 August 2021 Economic Information Daily article cost Tencent roughly USD 60bn of market value in a day.
> The 2018 approval freeze cut close to USD 200bn from Tencent at its trough.
> The December 2023 draft monetization rules erased roughly USD 80bn from Tencent and NetEase before being withdrawn.
> Aggregate shareholder value destroyed by regulatory action across 2018-2024 runs into the hundreds of billions of dollars.
3.
> MASS FIRM CLOSURES AND JOB LOSSES.
> Roughly 14,000 gaming studios and gaming-related firms closed during the 2021-2022 freeze (up to 140,000 by broader definitions including advertising, publishing and merchandising), with layoffs and project cancellations at Tencent, NetEase and 37Games.
> Small studios bore the damage disproportionately: large firms could wait out a licence freeze; small ones could not.
4.
> INDUSTRY CONCENTRATION.
> The licensing chokepoint structurally favours large publishers with compliance departments and cash reserves, entrenching a Tencent/NetEase duopoly and reducing the diversity of Chinese games — an outcome opposite to the stated goal of healthier content.
5.
> CIRCUMVENTION AND A GREY MARKET IN IDENTITY.
> Minors routinely use adult IDs (grandparents' or purchased), account-rental services proliferated, and Tencent had to deploy facial recognition to counter it — creating a normalized surveillance apparatus applied to children, with obvious privacy costs and a chilling precedent now applied well beyond gaming.
6.
> THE RESTRICTION DID NOT PRODUCE THE INTENDED SUBSTITUTION.
> Reporting after the ban found that teenagers were not studying more; freed time migrated to short video, which is at least as attention-capturing and was less regulated at the time.
> The harm was displaced, not eliminated.
7.
> ESPORTS CAREER DISAPPOINTMENT AND EDUCATIONAL MISALLOCATION.
> The esports vocational expansion (2016-2019) produced graduates whose expectations far exceeded available paid roles; the industry's plateau (audience flat since 2021, 80.8% of income from a single livestreaming channel) means the pyramid narrowed further.
8.
> PROFESSIONAL PLAYER WELFARE.
> Short careers, extreme training hours in team houses, repetitive strain injuries, and documented mental-health problems among young Chinese pro players and streamers.
9.
> STREAMING/LIVESTREAM ECONOMY EXCESSES.
> Gambling-adjacent behaviour in gifting, minors spending on streamers, and the concentration of esports economics into a livestreaming layer subject to its own crackdowns — leaving the esports business structurally fragile.
10.
> POLICY UNPREDICTABILITY AS A COST IN ITSELF.
> The withdrawal of the December 2023 draft after a market rout showed that even the regulator can be forced to retreat, which damaged the credibility of future rulemaking and left the underlying monetization harms (login-streak coercion, recharge inducements) unaddressed to this day.

**Risiko Sosial Indonesia**

> 1.
> GAMING AS THE ON-RAMP TO ONLINE GAMBLING — the highest-priority Indonesian risk and the one with no Chinese analogue at this scale.
> China eliminated consumer online gambling early; Indonesia did not, so Indonesian children move between gacha, item trading, and slot apps through the same payment rails, the same advertising surfaces, and the same social groups.
> Komdigi reported in 2026 that nearly 200,000 Indonesian children have been exposed to online gambling, and psychiatric hospitals began handling child gambling-addiction cases in 2025.
> Without a clear regulatory line between gacha and gambling, gaming will keep functioning as a recruitment funnel.
2.
> A MENTAL-HEALTH CAPACITY CRISIS ALREADY IN PROGRESS.
> Child and adolescent psychiatric visits for gadget addiction rose 28% y/y in late 2025; RSJ Soeharto Heerdjan logged 1,856 cases (62% game addiction); RSJ Menur has exceeded inpatient capacity and is queueing patients; RSJ Sungailiat in Bangka Belitung logged 68 new cases in two months (+35%); RSJ Lampung reports the same.
> Indonesia has roughly 54 psychiatric hospitals handling all addiction types for a population of 284m, concentrated on Java.
> Demand is outrunning supply now, before any of the growth this trend still has ahead of it.
3.
> FINANCIAL EXTRACTION FROM POOR HOUSEHOLDS WITH NO REFUND RIGHT.
> Pulsa- and voucher-based top-up requires no ID, no bank account and no parental visibility; a child can spend a household's weekly food budget in an afternoon with no practical recourse against a foreign publisher.
> Indonesia has no statutory minor-refund mechanism and no spending caps.
4.
> UNENFORCEABLE REGULATION BREEDING GENERAL NON-COMPLIANCE.
> If Indonesia adopts age gates it cannot verify, the predictable result is universal false age declaration, normalized VPN use, and a population of minors and parents who have learned that digital law is optional — which will poison enforcement of the PDP Law and future child-safety rules too.
5.
> EDUCATIONAL MISALLOCATION AT SCALE.
> A generation channelled toward an esports career pyramid that cannot support it, encouraged by universities marketing 'jurusan esports' — China ran this experiment from 2016 and the graduate outcomes were poor.
6.
> EXPLOITATION OF MINOR ESPORTS ATHLETES.
> No standard contracts, no minimum age, no education-continuity requirement, no salary escrow, no mental-health provision.
> Teenagers are already signing multi-year agreements with Indonesian organizations.
7.
> CONTINUED VALUE LEAKAGE.
> With 95-99.5% of domestic game spending flowing to foreign publishers, Indonesia absorbs the full social cost of a mature industry while capturing almost none of the tax base or employment that would fund mitigation — the defining asymmetry of this trend for Indonesia.
8.
> NON-JAVA HARM CONCENTRATION WITH JAVA-CONCENTRATED TREATMENT.
> Rural internet penetration (76.96%) is close to urban (83.56%) and leisure substitutes are scarcer outside Java, so exposure is highest exactly where clinical, counselling and school-support capacity is thinnest.
9.
> DATA AND PRIVACY RISK FROM THE REMEDY.
> Any serious age-assurance regime will collect children's identity data.
> Given Indonesia's record of large-scale government and platform data breaches, a poorly designed minor-verification system could itself become the harm — an argument for device-level age signals over centralized ID databases.
10.
> DISPLACEMENT RATHER THAN REDUCTION.
> China's experience shows that restricting games without addressing the attention economy simply moves minors to short video.
> Indonesia, where TikTok penetration is among the world's highest, would see this substitution immediately and more strongly.

**Unintended Consequences**

> IN CHINA (observed):
- Time freed by the gaming ban went to short video rather than study; reporting after the 2021 rules found teenagers were not studying more.
> The state solved a measurable problem by displacing it into a less-measured one, and later had to regulate minor mode across all apps (2024) as a result.
- Enforcement created a grey market in identity: rented and purchased adult accounts, grandparents' IDs, and eventually facial recognition applied to children — normalizing biometric surveillance of minors as a child-protection measure.
- The licence freeze intended to discipline giants instead killed roughly 14,000 small firms and entrenched the Tencent/NetEase duopoly, reducing content diversity.
- Restriction accelerated globalization: shut out of domestic growth, Chinese publishers pushed overseas, reaching USD 20.45bn in export revenue by 2025 — meaning China's domestic child-protection policy directly intensified the commercial pressure on markets like Indonesia.
> Indonesia is, in a real sense, absorbing the displaced output of China's own crackdown.
- The December 2023 monetization draft's withdrawal after an USD 80bn market rout demonstrated regulatory capture-by-market-reaction, leaving the coercive mechanics (login streaks, recharge inducements) legal to this day.
- Esports education created expectations the industry could not meet, producing a cohort of disappointed graduates — a policy-induced labour mismatch.
- Anti-addiction rules pushed some minors toward unapproved foreign titles via VPN accelerators, prompting further enforcement (Tencent cutting off booster access to unapproved games in 2022) — an enforcement spiral.

PREDICTED FOR INDONESIA:
- IGRS enforcement will initially produce labelling compliance without behavioural change, while inadvertently pushing users toward unrated third-party APK distribution — increasing malware and scam exposure, a harm larger than the one being solved.
- Any age gate without verification will train an entire generation to lie about their age, degrading the reliability of all age-based digital policy including gambling and pornography controls.
- Restricting games while leaving short video untouched will shift minors' time to TikTok, where Indonesia's exposure is even greater than China's was.
- Promoting esports (Perpres 19/2024, Kemenpora recognition) while simultaneously warning about game addiction will produce mixed public messaging that undermines both objectives.
- Payment-layer restrictions on top-ups may push transactions to informal reseller networks and crypto, reducing traceability precisely for the judi online cases enforcement is trying to catch.
- A crackdown framed around 'Chinese games' could arrive as economic nationalism rather than child protection, harming Indonesian studios who depend on the same platforms and publishers while doing nothing for children.
- Positive unintended consequence: compliance obligations from PP Tunas and IGRS may create the first genuinely well-paid, non-engineering digital careers in Indonesia (trust and safety, compliance, age assurance) and give local studios a home-field regulatory advantage over foreign publishers who find compliance costly.

**Kelompok Rentan**

> 1.
> CHILDREN AND ADOLESCENTS AGED 7-18, especially boys — the group already appearing in psychiatric hospital statistics (28% y/y increase; 62% of cases at RSJ Soeharto Heerdjan attributable to online games).
> Gen Alpha, at 23.19% of Indonesia's internet users, enters this exposure window with less parental digital literacy than any prior cohort.
2.
> LOW-INCOME AND WORKING-CLASS HOUSEHOLDS where a smartphone is the cheapest available childcare and the cheapest available entertainment.
> These families have the least capacity to absorb a top-up shock, the least access to therapy, and the least ability to supervise.
> The Bangka Belitung case (a 17-year-old consuming 30GB/month on Free Fire) is the archetype.
3.
> CHILDREN OUTSIDE JAVA — rural internet penetration is only ~7 points below urban, but psychiatric, counselling and school-support capacity is far thinner, and there are fewer competing activities.
4.
> ASPIRING PROFESSIONAL PLAYERS AND THEIR FAMILIES — teenagers who defer or abandon education for a career path with a placement rate in the low fractions of a percent, often with informal, unprotective contracts.
5.
> GIG AND INFORMAL WORKERS who game as their primary affordable leisure and are simultaneously the demographic most targeted by judi online advertising — the overlap between gaming top-ups and gambling deposits is highest here.
6.
> CHILDREN OF MIGRANT WORKERS AND SINGLE-PARENT HOUSEHOLDS, where adult supervision is structurally absent for long periods.
7.
> YOUTH WITH EXISTING MENTAL-HEALTH VULNERABILITIES (ADHD, anxiety, depression, social isolation), for whom gaming is both self-medication and accelerant, and for whom Indonesia's adolescent mental-health services are least available.
8.
> SMALL INDONESIAN GAME STUDIOS — vulnerable in the opposite direction: they will bear compliance costs designed to discipline Tencent-scale publishers, and China's freeze showed that regulation aimed at giants kills the small.
9.
> LOW-PAID CONTENT MODERATORS AND CUSTOMER-SUPPORT WORKERS in the outsourcing layer, exposed to psychological harm with minimal protection — a growth occupation with no Indonesian labour standard.
10.
> WOMEN AND GIRLS IN GAMING SPACES, exposed to harassment in voice and text channels with weak Indonesian-language moderation capacity at foreign publishers.

### Contoh Kasus Konkret

**Kasus China**

> CASE 1 — TENCENT / HONOR OF KINGS AS THE POLICY LIGHTNING ROD.
> Honor of Kings (launched November 2015) became China's defining mobile game and the named target of the 3 August 2021 Economic Information Daily 'spiritual opium' (精神鸦片) article, which cited a student playing eight hours a day.
> Tencent lost roughly USD 60bn in market value in a single session; within days it announced deeper self-imposed restrictions for under-18s (90 minutes on ordinary days, 3 hours on holidays) ahead of the regulator.
> Tencent then deployed 'Midnight Patrol' facial recognition to catch minors using adult accounts.
> By the mid-2020s minors accounted for well under 1% of Tencent's domestic games gross receipts [uncertain on exact figure].
> This is the clearest demonstration that in China, anticipatory self-regulation by the dominant firm was faster and more effective than the formal rule that followed.

CASE 2 — THE 30 AUGUST 2021 NPPA NOTICE AND ITS MEASURED EFFECT.
> Under-18s restricted to one hour, 20:00-21:00, on Fridays, Saturdays, Sundays and public holidays only — 3 hours per week, down from the 13.5 hours permitted under the November 2019 rules, a 78% reduction by decree.
> By November 2022 CADPA's Game Publishing Committee and Gamma Data reported that over 75% of minor gamers played under three hours per week and declared the addiction problem 'basically resolved'.
> The counter-case: contemporaneous reporting found that teenagers were not studying more; the time went to short video.

CASE 3 — THE LICENCE FREEZE AND THE 14,000 CLOSURES.
> Approvals were frozen from July 2021 to April 2022 (after an earlier nine-month freeze in 2018).
> Roughly 14,000 gaming studios and gaming-related firms shut down (up to 140,000 by broader definitions), with layoffs and cancellations at Tencent, NetEase and 37Games.
> The regulatory instrument aimed at protecting children destroyed the small-studio layer of the industry.

CASE 4 — THE DECEMBER 2023 DRAFT THAT WAS WITHDRAWN.
> On 22 December 2023 the NPPA published draft 'Measures for the Administration of Online Games' — 8 chapters, 64 articles, roughly 10 of them new — proposing monthly in-game spending caps (~RMB 400), a ban on daily-login, first-recharge and consecutive-recharge rewards, and a ban on item auctions.
> Tencent and NetEase shed roughly USD 80bn combined.
> The consultation closed 22 January 2024 and the draft was quietly removed from the NPPA website; it was never enacted.
> The single most instructive case for Indonesia: the state blinked when the economic cost became visible, and the coercive monetization mechanics remain legal.

CASE 5 — GACHA PROBABILITY DISCLOSURE, EFFECTIVE 1 MAY 2017.
> Ministry of Culture interim measures required publishers to disclose random-draw probabilities — years before Western regulators seriously debated loot boxes.
> Cheap, non-restrictive, and still the best-value protective policy China invented.

CASE 6 — ESPORTS BUILT AND THEN PLATEAUED.
> MOE added 'Esports and Management' to the vocational catalogue in September 2016; MOHRSS recognized esports player and esports operator as official occupations in April 2019; Hangzhou hosted esports as a full Asian Games medal event in 2023.
> Yet the audience has moved from 489.2m (2021) to 495.3m (2025) — 6m in four years — while 80.81% of the RMB 29.33bn industry income comes from livestreaming.
> A fully institutionalized, fully plateaued sector, and the template for where Indonesian esports economics are heading.

CASE 7 — THE 2025 NUMBERS AS THE MATURE-STATE PICTURE.
> Domestic market RMB 350.789bn (+7.68%), 683m users (+1.35%), mini-games RMB 53.535bn (+34.39%) generating over half of all incremental growth, overseas revenue USD 20.45bn.
> Growth now comes from new formats and foreign markets, not new domestic players — the export pressure that lands directly on Indonesia.

**Padanan Indonesia**

> REGULATORY EQUIVALENTS (the lagging half):
- PP 17/2025 'PP Tunas' (Tata Kelola Penyelenggaraan Sistem Elektronik dalam Pelindungan Anak), signed 28 March 2025, effective 1 April 2025, with platform obligations phased from 28 March 2026.
> Age tiers: under 13 restricted to low-risk child-designed services; 13-15 medium-risk with parental consent; 16-17 high-risk with parental supervision; 18+ independent.
> Named platforms in scope include YouTube, TikTok, Facebook, Instagram, Threads, X, Bigo Live and Roblox.
> Crucially it contains NO playtime curfew and NO spending cap — the two instruments that made China's regime bite.
- Indonesia Game Rating System (IGRS): created by Permenkominfo 11/2016, that regulation now revoked and replaced by Permenkominfo 2/2024; relaunched with enforcement intent on 11 October 2025 and mandatory from 2026 with age bands 3+, 7+, 13+, 15+, 18+.
> Komdigi's investigation of rating mismatches on Steam (late 2025) was the first visible enforcement action.
> Indonesia's rating architecture predates China's formal age-rating standard, but sat effectively dormant for nine years — the recurring Indonesian pattern of early adoption, late enforcement.
- Perpres 19/2024 on Acceleration of National Game Industry Development, signed 12 February 2024, eight pillars (research, education, funding, infrastructure, marketing, incentives, IP facilitation, protection of creative output), including a BRIN-managed national game asset store prioritizing Indonesian cultural assets and a mandate to include national games in esports tournaments.
> This is Indonesia's counterpart to China's industrial promotion, not to its restriction — Indonesia currently has the carrot without the stick.

MARKET AND INDUSTRY EQUIVALENTS:
- Mobile Legends: Bang Bang as Indonesia's Honor of Kings — Indonesia is MLBB's largest market worldwide with 35m+ MAU and ~40.5% of active mobile players.
> Ownership passed from Shanghai founders to ByteDance (2021, ~USD 4bn) to Saudi Arabia's Savvy Games Group (agreed 20 March 2026, >USD 6bn, closing expected Q2-Q3 2026).
- MPL Indonesia as the LPL/KPL equivalent: franchised, nine teams, Season 16 ran 22 August-2 November 2025; ONIC finished 14-2.
> Plus Liga Esports Nasional as the tiered domestic pyramid.
- PBESI + Kemenpora/KONI recognition of esports as olahraga prestasi, and Indonesia topping the SEA Esports Nations Cup 2026 — Indonesia's parallel to China's Asian Games institutionalization, achieved on a comparable timeline.
- UniPin as the domestic top-up rail (an Indonesian company owning a real layer of the value chain — the exception that proves the rule).
- Local studios: Agate (Bandung), Toge Productions (Coffee Talk, A Space for the Unbound), Digital Happiness (DreadOut), Mojiken, Anantarupa (Lokapala — Nusantara-mythology MOBA).
> Collectively they hold 0.5-5% of the Indonesian market versus Chinese domestic developers' dominance of their own.
- HARM EQUIVALENT: Indonesia's psychiatric-hospital data is the counterpart to China's 2018-2021 myopia-and-addiction alarm — the 28% y/y rise in child gadget-addiction visits, RSJ Soeharto Heerdjan's 1,856 cases, RSJ Menur's ~3,000 patients and exceeded inpatient capacity, and Komdigi's ~200,000 children exposed to online gambling.
> Indonesia is now approximately where China was in 2018-2019: the harm data has arrived, the political narrative is forming, and the regulatory instruments are being drafted.

### Tingkat Keyakinan & Kualitas Sumber

**Catatan Kontradiksi Data**

> 1.
> INDONESIAN MARKET SIZE VARIES BY 4x.
> USD 4.28bn (2025, Xsolla/industry estimates) vs ~USD 2.0-2.5bn / Rp 41.3tn (Kemenperin-linked industry studies) vs USD 1.117bn (Statista 2023, cited in Perpres 19/2024 commentary) vs a projection of USD 6.66bn by 2034 (which would be inconsistent with a USD 4.28bn 2025 base at 8% CAGR).
> The divergence reflects whether hardware, ad revenue, esports and grey-market top-ups are included.
> Treat USD 2.5-4.3bn as the plausible band; do not cite a single point estimate.
2.
> INDONESIAN ESPORTS MARKET ESTIMATES ARE UNUSABLE.
> Published figures range from USD 1.8bn (2025, 24.1% CAGR) to USD 11.75-18.54m — a difference of two orders of magnitude, indicating that some vendors measure ecosystem spending and others measure only tournament/league income.
> Flagged as uncertain and excluded from analytical conclusions.
3.
> LOCAL DEVELOPER SHARE: 0.4% (Kemenperin, cited 2021) vs 0.5% (October 2025 study) vs 5% (February 2026 report).
> These are not reconcilable as a time series — they likely use different denominators (all consumer spending vs.
> domestically-published titles vs.
> registered-studio revenue).
> The safe statement is 'under 5%, and possibly under 1%'.
4.
> INDONESIAN PLAYER COUNT: 155m (on a 274m population base, an older figure) vs ~190-192m projected for 2025.
> 'Gamer' definitions include anyone who plays any mobile game, which inflates counts relative to China's 683m on a 1.41bn population.
5.
> CHINA FIRM CLOSURES: 14,000 vs 140,000 during the 2021-2022 freeze.
> This is a definitional split (game studios and publishers vs.
> all gaming-related firms including advertising and merchandising), not a factual dispute, but the 140,000 figure is frequently quoted without that qualification.
6.
> CHINA MARKET REVENUE FRAMING: RMB 350.789bn (2025) is 'actual sales revenue of the domestic games market' per CADPA/Gamma; some English-language sources render this as roughly USD 48-50bn while others use different exchange-rate assumptions or add export revenue, producing inconsistent 'China games market' totals.
7.
> EFFECTIVENESS OF CHINA'S MINOR RESTRICTIONS IS CONTESTED.
> CADPA/Gamma (Nov 2022) reported >75% of minor gamers under three hours weekly and declared the problem 'basically resolved' — but the reporting body is the industry association, giving it an interest in demonstrating compliance.
> Independent reporting found time displaced to short video rather than study, and documented widespread use of adult IDs.
> Both can be true: the rule worked on the metric it measured and failed on the outcome it was meant to serve.
8.
> IGRS 'FIRST IN SOUTHEAST ASIA' FRAMING IS MISLEADING.
> Some 2025 coverage described the October 2025 IGRS as the first national game classification system in Southeast Asia; IGRS itself dates to 2016 (Permenkominfo 11/2016).
> The accurate statement is that 2025-2026 marks the first serious ENFORCEMENT of a system that has existed on paper for nine years.
9.
> PP TUNAS TIMELINE: sources variously give 28 March 2025 (signing), 1 April 2025 (entry into force), and 28 March 2026 (phased platform obligations / end of transition).
> All three dates appear in reporting and are not contradictory, but are often conflated.
10.
> MOONTON OWNERSHIP IS IN TRANSITION AS OF THIS RESEARCH DATE.
> The Savvy Games Group acquisition was agreed 20 March 2026 at >USD 6bn but requires regulatory approval expected in Q2-Q3 2026.
> Any statement that MLBB is 'Chinese-owned' or 'Saudi-owned' is timing-sensitive; as of August 2026 the closing status is not confirmed in available sources.
11.
> INDONESIAN HOSPITAL ADDICTION DATA comes from regional media reporting individual facilities rather than a consolidated national Kemenkes dataset; the 28% y/y figure covers a two-month window (Oct-Nov 2025), which is a narrow base for a trend claim.
