## 19. Emotional Economy & Guzi/IP Economy (情绪消费 / 谷子经济) — affect-driven consumption of character IP merchandise: blind boxes, art toys, anime-game-music 'guzi' goods, trading cards, plush charms and fandom collectibles bought for emotional value rather than utility
**Kategori**: Konsumsi & Ritel (Consumption & Retail) — with heavy cross-over into Creative Economy / IP Licensing, Youth Culture & Mental Health, Physical Retail Real Estate, and Consumer Protection Regulation. Structurally it is the 'trading up' twin of the Consumer Downgrade trend: consumers cut big-ticket spending while raising low-ticket affective spending.

⏱ Lag: Split verdict. (a) Consumption of foreign character IP — lag of only about 2-4 years: China's blind-box mass phase was 2019-2021; Indonesia's was 2023-2025 (Pop Mart entry 2023, Labubu mania 2024-2025). Algorithmic diffusion via TikTok/Instagram plus direct entry by the Chinese incumbent compressed this to near-simultaneity in the Labubu wave itself, where Indonesia peaked within months of the global peak. (b) Domestic guzi retail ecosystem (dedicated ACG stores, mall ACG floors, trading-card culture, secondary-market infrastructure) — lag of about 4-6 years; Indonesia in 2026 is roughly where China was in 2020-2021, with pop-up festivals and chain concepts but no 3,000-store national network. (c) Local IP ownership and licensing supply chain — lag of about 8-12 years, and possibly structural rather than temporal: China had Pop Mart, miHoYo and Bilibili producing globally exportable characters by 2020, whereas Indonesia's entire animation industry is worth roughly USD 48 million in 2025, smaller than a single mid-size Chinese IP studio, and still transitioning out of work-for-hire outsourcing. Working headline number: 3 years on demand, 5 years on retail format, 10 years on IP production capability. | 📊 Hybrid: Simultaneous-to-Laggard on consumption (Indonesia joined the global Labubu wave almost in real time, roughly 3 years behind China's domestic blind-box phase), but deep Laggard (8-12 years) on IP ownership, character design capacity and licensing infrastructure. There is no leapfrog: Indonesia is importing the demand side of the trend while remaining a downstream market and, from 2026, a contract-manufacturing site rather than a value owner. | 🎯 Prob: Tinggi (High) — in fact largely already transferred on the consumption side; the open question is not whether but in what form and who captures the value. | 🔍 Keyakinan: Tinggi (High) for China-side market size, company financials and the 2025-2026 downturn, all of which are corroborated by state media, listed-company disclosures and multiple independent research houses. Sedang (Medium) for Indonesia-side sizing — Pop Mart publishes no Indonesia-only revenue, the USD 410m anime-merchandising estimate is a single vendor's number, and there is no official Indonesian statistical series for collectibles or character licensing. Sedang for lag estimates and timeline predictions, which are analytical inferences from adjacent trend transfers (MINISO, TikTok, live commerce, Mixue) rather than measured values.

> **Status di Indonesia**: Sudah masuk masif pada sisi konsumsi, tetapi masih sangat dangkal pada sisi produksi IP — mass-adopted as consumption, embryonic as an industry. Indonesia is a large and fast-growing demand market for Chinese-owned character IP, while local IP monetisation is still at pilot/early stage.

### Basic Info

**Tahun Mulai China**

> Three layered starts.
> (a) 2016-2017 — Pop Mart pivots from a Miniso-style variety retailer to blind-box trend toys after signing designer Kenny Wong for the Molly IP (2016); the first Pop Mart blind-box series sells out and creates the category.
> (b) 2019-2021 — mass-market phase: blind box vending 'roboshops' spread across malls, Pop Mart lists on HKEX in December 2020, and 'blind box economy' (盲盒经济) becomes a mainstream media term.
> (c) 2023-2024 — the true 'guzi economy' (谷子经济) phase, when the ACG merchandise market broadened beyond blind boxes into badges, acrylic stands, trading cards, ita-bags and dedicated 谷子店 retail formats, and the term 情绪消费 (emotional consumption) entered official state-media and industry-report vocabulary.
> 2024 is the year the label 'guzi economy' went national.

**Pemain Kunci China**

> Brand/IP owners: Pop Mart International (9992.HK) — Labubu/The Monsters, Molly, Skullpanda, Crybaby, Dimoo; Letsvan/Shenzhen Yiqi (Wakuku, Ziyuli — controlling stake acquired by NASDAQ-listed QuantaSing in March 2025); 52TOYS; Kayou (卡游) — China's No.1 trading-card firm, revenue near-quadrupled to about USD 1.4bn in 2024, ~80% from collectible cards, filed for a Hong Kong IPO targeting ~USD 500m; TOP TOY (MINISO's trend-toy arm) and MINISO Land IP-concept stores; Bandai Namco/Aniplex licensed goods importers.
> Content/IP upstream: Bilibili (二次元 community and anime licensing), Tencent Animation & Comics, miHoYo (Genshin Impact, Honkai: Star Rail — a top guzi IP), Kuaikan Manhua, Yuewen/China Literature.
> Retail & channel: 谷子店 chains such as 潮玩星球 (Chaowan Xingqiu), 卡通尼 / 漫库 / 抱萌, department-store ACG floors (Shanghai Bailian ZX 创趣场 'the guzi building', Chongqing 超次元X9), Taobao/Xianyu secondary market, Douyin and Xiaohongshu as discovery engines.
> Investors: Sequoia China, Hillhouse, Tencent and CITIC-linked funds in the trend-toy and card segments.

### China Trend Detail

**Apa Yang Terjadi Di China**

> China built the world's first fully industrialised 'emotional consumption' retail complex, in which the product sold is not function but affect — surprise, companionship, identity, belonging and social currency.
> The mechanism has four interlocking layers.
> (1) Product mechanics: the blind box converts a commodity purchase into a probabilistic draw.
> A standard series has 12 regular designs plus a 'secret' chase figure at odds of roughly 1:72 to 1:144, which creates variable-ratio reinforcement — the same reward schedule as slot machines — and drives repeat purchase, set-completion behaviour, and an active secondary market where chase figures resell at 5-50x issue price.
> (2) IP layer: value is captured by owning characters rather than by manufacturing.
> Pop Mart's gross margin reached 72.1% in 2025 because the cost base is vinyl and plush while the price reflects licensed emotional attachment.
> Characters are deliberately designed to be 'ugly-cute' (丑萌) and wordless — Labubu has no canon backstory, so consumers project their own meaning onto it, which is exactly what makes it exportable across cultures.
> (3) Retail layer: from 2023 the format broke out of vending machines into dedicated guzi stores and whole ACG mall floors.
> Shopping-centre landlords, hit by the collapse of apparel and F&B footfall, actively recruited guzi tenants because ACG shops deliver dwell time, photo-sharing and youth traffic — JLL documented ACG retail as a structural rescue for underperforming Chinese malls.
> By January 2025 China had roughly 3,239 guzi stores concentrated in at least 39 cities with 30+ stores each.
> (4) Social layer: consumption is inseparable from posting.
> Unboxing videos on Douyin/Xiaohongshu, 'ita-bag' (痛包) badge displays worn in public, offline 'guzi exchange' meetups and 谷圈 (guzi circles) turn the object into a membership token of a subculture.
> State media reframed the whole thing positively as 情绪消费 / 悦己消费 ('consumption for one's own mood'), which gave the category political cover as a domestic-demand growth story during a deflationary period.
> Crucially, this boomed alongside — not instead of — consumer downgrade: households cut housing, cars and travel while raising spending on cheap high-emotion items, the classic 'lipstick effect' scaled to a RMB 100bn+ industry.
> Since mid-2025 the sector has entered a sharp shakeout, described below.

**Data Skala China**

> Market size: China's guzi (ACG merchandise) market reached RMB 168.9 billion in 2024, +40.63% YoY, with iiMedia and QuestMobile projecting RMB 200-240 billion for 2025 and above RMB 300 billion by 2029.
> The broader ACG (anime-comic-game) market was RMB 597.7 billion in 2024, forecast to RMB 834.4 billion by 2029; the pan-2D plus peripherals market was reported at RMB 652.1 billion in 2025 (+9.1% YoY).
> Users: pan-2D (二次元) user base about 503 million in 2024, projected ~520 million in 2026; Gen Z accounts for roughly 95% of guzi consumption and over 70% of platform guzi transactions were made by post-1995 buyers.
> As of August 2025, active guzi-interest users were about 30.2 million with roughly 12.4 million actual guzi purchasers.
> Taobao guzi-category sales hit 17 million units in 2024, close to 5x YoY.
> Emotional consumption broadly: the 2025 emotional-consumption research report puts the total Chinese 'emotional consumption' market above RMB 2 trillion, growing at ~12% CAGR since 2013; 56.3% of surveyed young people said they buy for emotional value (up 16.2 percentage points from 2024), average monthly emotional-consumption spend RMB 949, with 18.1% spending over RMB 2,000 per month.
> Company scale: Pop Mart FY2025 revenue RMB 37.12 billion (about USD 5.4bn), +184.7% YoY; net profit RMB 13.01 billion, +293.3%; gross margin 72.1% (from 66.8%); the Labubu/The Monsters franchise alone generated RMB 14.16 billion, +365.7%, roughly 38% of group revenue.
> Overseas exceeded 40% of revenue: Americas RMB 6.81 billion (+748.4%, 18.3% of sales), Asia-Pacific ex-China +157.6%, Southeast Asia RMB 2.4 billion (+619.1%, nearly half of overseas revenue); Pop Mart passed 1,000 stores globally by 2026 and scaled plush production toward 30 million units per month.
> Kayou revenue nearly quadrupled to ~USD 1.4bn in 2024, ~80% from trading cards, ranked 66th on the 2025 Hurun Global Unicorn Index.
> Retail footprint: ~3,239 guzi stores across 39+ cities (January 2025).
> Downturn data: at least 155 guzi stores closed or announced closure nationwide during 2025; chain 潮玩星球 shrank from 148 to 99 stores, 抱萌 from 59 to 22 (>60% closure), 漫库 from 44 to 31; CCG EXPO 2025 sold about 48,000 tickets versus over 200,000 in prior years; the July 2026 PTS International Trendy Toy Expo was cancelled; the cultural-and-creative toy sector index fell 16.52% between 1 January and 30 July 2026 (1,193 to 989 points).

**Fase Tren Di China**

> Post-peak correction / early backlash — the consumption behaviour is mature and permanent, but the retail and speculative layer is in an active shakeout.
> Sequence: emerging 2016-2018, booming 2019-2021 (blind box), hyper-boom 2023 to mid-2025 (guzi economy + Labubu global breakout), peak mid-to-late 2025, and from late 2025 through 2026 a visible bust in the physical channel and secondary market: mass guzi-store closures, cancelled expos, collapsing convention attendance, falling resale prices, and a 16.5% sector index drawdown in H1 2026.
> Regulatory scrutiny is running in parallel: the SAMR blind-box guideline has been in force since 2023 and December 2025 Xinhua/China Daily investigations into minors' addiction to 谷圈 signalled the start of a consumer-protection tightening cycle.
> Pop Mart itself is in an IP-concentration crisis: FY2025 results triggered a record 23% single-day share fall in March 2026, Q1 2026 revenue growth decelerated to about 80% from 185%, US sales fell roughly 42-45% YoY in March-April 2026, and Morgan Stanley and Deutsche Bank cut FY2026 growth forecasts to +13% and -2% respectively against management's 'at least 20%' target.
> So: the category survives, the bubble is deflating, and the industry is consolidating toward IP owners with real content pipelines.

**Puncak Tren China**

> Domestic guzi retail peak: late 2024 to H1 2025, centred on Shanghai (the Bailian ZX 创趣场 'guzi building' in Huangpu and the Jing'an/Xujiahui ACG clusters), Chengdu, Chongqing, Wuhan, Guangzhou and Harbin, plus a fast follow-on wave in tier-2/3 cities.
> Global Labubu/emotional-IP peak: August 2025, when worldwide search interest for Labubu topped out (Google Trends interest for 'Labubu figurine' at index 66 in August 2025, down to 6 by March 2026).
> Financial peak: Pop Mart's share price and multiple peaked in H2 2025; the FY2025 results announcement in March 2026 marked the sentiment top.
> Convention/expo peak: 2024, with 2025-2026 showing a collapse (CCG EXPO tickets from 200,000+ to ~48,000; PTS 2026 cancelled).

### Status Indonesia Saat Ini

**Status Di Indonesia**

> Sudah masuk masif pada sisi konsumsi, tetapi masih sangat dangkal pada sisi produksi IP — mass-adopted as consumption, embryonic as an industry.
> Indonesia is a large and fast-growing demand market for Chinese-owned character IP, while local IP monetisation is still at pilot/early stage.

### Analisis Lag

**Estimasi Lag Tahun**

> Split verdict.
> (a) Consumption of foreign character IP — lag of only about 2-4 years: China's blind-box mass phase was 2019-2021; Indonesia's was 2023-2025 (Pop Mart entry 2023, Labubu mania 2024-2025).
> Algorithmic diffusion via TikTok/Instagram plus direct entry by the Chinese incumbent compressed this to near-simultaneity in the Labubu wave itself, where Indonesia peaked within months of the global peak.
> (b) Domestic guzi retail ecosystem (dedicated ACG stores, mall ACG floors, trading-card culture, secondary-market infrastructure) — lag of about 4-6 years; Indonesia in 2026 is roughly where China was in 2020-2021, with pop-up festivals and chain concepts but no 3,000-store national network.
> (c) Local IP ownership and licensing supply chain — lag of about 8-12 years, and possibly structural rather than temporal: China had Pop Mart, miHoYo and Bilibili producing globally exportable characters by 2020, whereas Indonesia's entire animation industry is worth roughly USD 48 million in 2025, smaller than a single mid-size Chinese IP studio, and still transitioning out of work-for-hire outsourcing.
> Working headline number: 3 years on demand, 5 years on retail format, 10 years on IP production capability.

**Bukti Historical Lag**

> Consistent with observed lags in adjacent Chinese consumer trends that reached Indonesia.
> (1) Value retail: MINISO entered China in 2013 and Indonesia in 2017 — a 4-year lag — and by 2024 Indonesia hosted its largest global flagship, showing that Chinese lifestyle retail formats travel to Indonesia in roughly 4 years and can then scale faster than in origin markets.
> (2) Short video: Douyin launched 2016, TikTok Indonesia mass adoption 2018-2020 — 2-4 years.
> (3) Live-commerce and social commerce: China mainstream 2019-2020, Indonesia mainstream 2022-2023 — about 3 years.
> (4) Cheap-tea/coffee chains (Mixue): China scale-up 2018-2020, Indonesian explosion 2022-2024 — 3-4 years.
> (5) Conversely, on the production side the lag has always been much larger: Indonesia adopted Chinese EVs, phones and platforms as a consumer long before acquiring any comparable domestic manufacturing or IP-creation base, which is precisely the pattern repeating here.
> (6) Direct evidence for this specific trend: Pop Mart's Indonesian entry (2023) came three years after its HKEX IPO (December 2020), and Wakuku/Letsvan reached Indonesia in 2025 within a year of its Chinese breakout, showing the transmission window is narrowing as Chinese IP firms internationalise earlier in their life cycle.

**Tipe Lag**

> Hybrid: Simultaneous-to-Laggard on consumption (Indonesia joined the global Labubu wave almost in real time, roughly 3 years behind China's domestic blind-box phase), but deep Laggard (8-12 years) on IP ownership, character design capacity and licensing infrastructure.
> There is no leapfrog: Indonesia is importing the demand side of the trend while remaining a downstream market and, from 2026, a contract-manufacturing site rather than a value owner.

### Probabilitas Transfer ke Indonesia

**Probabilitas Transfer**

> Tinggi (High) — in fact largely already transferred on the consumption side; the open question is not whether but in what form and who captures the value.

**Alasan Probabilitas**

> Five reinforcing reasons.
> (1) It already happened: Pop Mart, MINISO, TOP TOY, OH!SOME, Wakuku and Funism are physically present, and Pop Mart was already the top-performing toy brand in Indonesia by 2024 value-share gain.
> (2) Demographics: Indonesia has the largest Gen Z/millennial cohort in Southeast Asia, extremely high social-media intensity, and one of the world's deepest anime, K-pop and gaming fandoms — the exact substrate the category needs.
> (3) Price architecture: entry price points of IDR 100,000-300,000 sit inside the affordable-treat band even for downgrading consumers, which is why Labubu queues coexisted with weak purchasing power; the same 'trading down + trading up' logic documented in China maps directly onto Indonesia's shrinking middle class.
> (4) Retail pull: Indonesian malls face the same anchor-tenant and footfall problem Chinese malls faced, so landlords have a commercial incentive to import ACG/collectible formats — the Blind Box Festival at Mall of Indonesia and Toys Kingdom's 'Toys Gen' show this is already underway.
> (5) Supply-side commitment: adding Indonesia to Pop Mart's manufacturing network in January 2026 signals long-term local presence rather than opportunistic export.
> The main caveat is timing risk: Indonesia may import the format precisely as the Chinese original enters its shakeout, so what arrives at scale in 2026-2028 could be the post-bubble, consolidated version rather than the mania version.

**Vektor Transmisi**

> (a) Direct entry by Chinese players — the dominant vector and unusually fast here.
> Pop Mart operates its own Indonesian stores, official Shopee/Lazada storefronts and popmart.com/id, keeping brand, pricing, drop calendar and IP entirely under Chinese control; MINISO (300+ stores), TOP TOY, OH!SOME and Wakuku/Letsvan follow the same owned-retail model, and Funism enters via a local distributor (AKG Entertainment).
> From January 2026 Pop Mart also added Indonesian contract manufacturing, deepening the physical footprint.
> (b) Algorithmic content diffusion — the strongest accelerant.
> TikTok, Instagram Reels and YouTube Shorts unboxing content, plus celebrity seeding (Lisa of BLACKPINK's post drove a reported 517% spike in search volume), meant Indonesian demand was manufactured by the same content graph as global demand, with essentially zero lag.
> Indonesia's exceptionally high TikTok penetration makes it one of the most efficient markets in the world for this vector.
> (c) Local copycat and adaptation — visible but shallow: OH!SOME's Owange Boy with Indonesian artist Kong Andri, local blind-box festivals, Toys Kingdom's adult-collector concept, and Indonesian MSMEs producing acrylic stands, keychains and photocard holders for Comifuro.
> Most 'local' products are still licensed foreign IP in local packaging.
> (d) Retail real estate as a carrier — Indonesian mall operators (Mall of Indonesia, Central Park, 23 Paskal, Trans Studio, Grand Indonesia) actively recruit these tenants for footfall, replicating the Chinese mall-rescue mechanism.
> (e) Grey-market and resale channels — Batam/Kepri import routes, Facebook Marketplace, Instagram reseller accounts (e.g.
> labubustore_indo), Tokopedia/Shopee resellers and Discord/Telegram trading groups, including large volumes of counterfeit 'Lafufu' units entering through unofficial channels; BSN has separately flagged counterfeit SNI labels on China-origin toys.
> (f) Diaspora/creator networks — Indonesian illustrators and doujin creators at Comifuro adopting Chinese/Japanese guzi product formats (badges, acrylic standees, ita-bag inserts) as their own merchandising template.
> (g) Chinese venture capital — least developed vector in Indonesia so far; funding flows mostly through the parent companies' own balance sheets rather than local startup investment.

### Faktor Pendorong

**Prasyarat Struktural**

> Threshold conditions and Indonesia's position.
> (1) Income: China's blind-box mass phase (2019-2021) occurred at GDP per capita of roughly USD 10,100-12,600, and the 2024 guzi boom at about USD 13,300.
> Indonesia in 2025 was at about USD 5,083 — roughly 40% of China's level at trend peak.
> This does not block the trend, because the trend is deliberately low-ticket, but it caps average spend per collector and pushes the Indonesian version toward cheaper SKUs, plush charms, cards and secondary-market churn rather than high-end resin figures.
> (2) Urban middle-class density: China's guzi retail concentrated in 39+ cities with 30 or more stores each; Indonesia realistically supports concentrated ACG retail in perhaps 8-12 metros (Jabodetabek, Bandung, Surabaya, Semarang, Yogyakarta, Medan, Makassar, Denpasar, Palembang, Balikpapan), so store-count scale will be an order of magnitude smaller.
> (3) Digital and social penetration: Indonesia is at or above the required threshold — internet penetration around 79-80%, one of the world's largest TikTok and Instagram user bases, and social-commerce familiarity — this prerequisite is fully met and is why the consumption side arrived early.
> (4) Mall infrastructure with surplus capacity: met, especially in Jakarta, Surabaya and Bandung, where landlords need youth-traffic tenants.
> (5) Cashless micro-payment rails: met (QRIS, GoPay, OVO, ShopeePay), plus BNPL and paylater availability, which materially raises impulse conversion.
> (6) A domestic IP content pipeline capable of generating characters with mass emotional attachment: NOT met at scale — Indonesia has one breakout case (Jumbo, 10m+ admissions), 299 registered AINAKI character IPs, and a USD 48m animation industry, versus China's RMB 597.7bn ACG content economy.
> This is the binding constraint on Indonesia capturing value rather than merely spending.
> (7) Licensing and anti-counterfeiting enforcement capability: weakly met — counterfeit SNI labelling and grey imports are documented problems, which suppresses licensor willingness to build local IP-derivative businesses.
> (8) A large fandom base with existing purchase habits: met via anime, K-pop photocard culture, mobile gaming and Comifuro's 40,000+ attendee events.

**Indikator Pemantauan**

> Leading indicators to track quarterly: (1) Pop Mart Indonesian store count and any disclosure of Indonesia-specific revenue in HKEX interim/annual filings; whether the 12-store base moves above 20-25.
> (2) Entry and store openings of second-tier Chinese trend-toy brands — Wakuku/Letsvan, 52TOYS, TOP TOY standalone stores, Kayou trading cards — Kayou's arrival would signal the card sub-category is starting, which in China was the most minor-heavy and most regulated segment.
> (3) Mall leasing data: number of dedicated ACG/collectible tenants and appearance of a whole-floor ACG concept in a Jakarta or Surabaya mall (the Indonesian equivalent of Shanghai's ZX 创趣场).
> (4) DJKI (Directorate General of Intellectual Property) filings: trademark and industrial-design registrations by Chinese trend-toy entities and by Indonesian character-IP holders; a rising local-character filing rate is the key value-capture signal.
> (5) OSS/NIB business-permit registrations under toy retail and licensing KBLI codes.
> (6) Google Trends and TikTok hashtag volume in Indonesia for 'blind box', 'art toy', 'guzi', specific character names, and for 'blind box judi' (the backlash signal).
> (7) Job postings for IP licensing manager, character designer, brand collaboration manager, merchandising manager on Jobstreet/LinkedIn Indonesia.
> (8) Kemenekraf and AINAKI activity: IP licensing programmes, animation industry value updates, and whether a national IP/licensing roadmap or fund is announced.
> (9) Consumer-protection signals: YLKI complaints, Kemendag statements on blind boxes, OJK/PPATK commentary linking blind boxes to gambling behaviour, and any MUI/NU/Muhammadiyah fatwa activity on gharar in mystery-box sales.
> (10) Customs and BSN enforcement actions against counterfeit collectibles — the volume of 'Lafufu' seizures is a proxy for real market size.
> (11) Local licensing deals: whether Jumbo, Si Juki, Nussa or other Indonesian IPs sign merchandising deals with a national retail chain.
> (12) University programme launches in character design, toy design or IP business.

### Hambatan & Faktor Pembatal

**Hambatan Transfer**

> (1) Purchasing power: at USD 5,083 GDP per capita with a middle class that shrank to 46.7 million (16.6% of population) in 2025, the collector base able to spend IDR 500k+ per month is small and concentrated in a few metros; Indonesian collecting will skew heavily to sub-IDR 200,000 items and to resale churn.
> (2) Religious and normative friction: blind boxes sit squarely in the gharar (excessive uncertainty) debate in Islamic commercial ethics, and Indonesia is in an aggressive national anti-online-gambling campaign — PPATK reported gambling as the largest category (47.5%) of suspicious-transaction indications in 2025 — so a mystery-purchase mechanic carries real reputational and regulatory risk that it did not carry in China.
> (3) Price and import friction: import duty, VAT, SNI toy certification requirements and logistics make official products materially more expensive than in China, widening the gap that counterfeits fill.
> (4) Counterfeiting: heavy 'Lafufu' penetration and documented fake SNI labelling erode brand value and licensor confidence.
> (5) Archipelagic logistics: last-mile cost outside Java makes small-parcel collectible commerce expensive and slows the tier-2/tier-3 diffusion that powered China's boom.
> (6) No domestic IP supply: without local characters, virtually all IP margin leaves the country, which limits the multiplier and makes the sector politically easy to characterise as import leakage.
> (7) Weak secondary-market infrastructure: no Indonesian equivalent of Xianyu with authentication and escrow for collectibles, so resale is fragmented across Facebook groups and Instagram with high fraud risk.
> (8) Timing: Indonesia may be scaling the format just as the Chinese original enters shakeout, so investor appetite and IP-owner expansion budgets may contract before Indonesia matures.
> (9) Retail talent gap: few Indonesian professionals have experience in IP licensing, drop-based release management or fandom community operations.

**Faktor Pembatal Transfer**

> Conditions that will prevent the Chinese-form version from ever fully arriving.
> (1) Absence of a domestic content flywheel.
> China's guzi economy is downstream of an enormous domestic anime/comic/game content industry (Bilibili, miHoYo, Tencent Animation, Yuewen web novels) that continuously manufactures characters with pre-existing emotional attachment.
> Indonesia's content base — a USD 48m animation industry, 262 studios, 3,448 workers, largely still doing outsourced service work — cannot generate that character pipeline at comparable rate.
> Without upstream IP, Indonesia can only ever be a distribution market; the RMB 168.9bn structure does not replicate, only its retail veneer does.
> (2) Population and city-density economics.
> China's format depends on 39+ cities each supporting 30+ specialist stores within dense subway-accessible commercial cores.
> Indonesia's urban structure, car-dependent malls and much smaller high-income urban cohort mean specialist single-category ACG stores will be viable in perhaps a dozen locations, so the category will live inside general retailers (MINISO, OH!SOME, Toys Kingdom, e-commerce) rather than as a standalone retail sector.
> (3) Religious-regulatory ceiling on the gambling mechanic.
> Indonesia's combination of Islamic commercial norms around gharar and a state anti-gambling drive gives regulators a ready-made basis to restrict or ban probabilistic sales mechanics; China had no comparable normative brake and only imposed technical rules in 2023.
> If Indonesia acts, it removes the specific mechanic that drives repeat purchase, leaving ordinary licensed merchandise.
> (4) Manufacturing base asymmetry.
> China's Dongguan/Shenzhen toy cluster allows a design-to-shelf cycle of weeks at low MOQ, enabling the drop cadence the model requires.
> Indonesia's toy manufacturing is thin and, ironically, Indonesia is being added as a low-cost assembly site for Chinese IP owners rather than as an independent producer — reinforcing dependency rather than building capability.
> (5) Fandom orientation.
> Indonesian fandom energy is disproportionately allocated to K-pop and Japanese anime, both of whose licensors control merchandising tightly and repatriate margin; the Chinese-style model of domestically-owned original characters has weak precedent.
> (6) Deflation asymmetry.
> China's emotional consumption grew as a substitute for large purchases in a deflationary, high-savings economy; Indonesia has inflation, low household savings and high consumer-credit/paylater exposure, so the same substitution is financially riskier and more likely to end in household debt stress than in China.

### Prediksi Timeline di Indonesia

**Tahun Masuk Indonesia**

> Already entered: 2023 for organised commercial entry (Pop Mart official Indonesian channel and first stores), 2024 for the first mass-visibility moment (September 2024 crowd disturbance at a Jakarta Pop Mart when Labubu sold out).
> Precursors existed earlier — MINISO blind boxes from around 2018-2019 and Bearbrick/gashapon/K-pop photocard collecting well before that — but the recognisable China-style blind-box/IP retail wave dates from 2023-2024.

**Tahun Mainstream Indonesia**

> 2025 — the year Labubu became a general-public phenomenon in Indonesia rather than a subculture item, with national media coverage of queues, resale prices to IDR 4.5 million, and the widely discussed paradox of Labubu queues and sold-out concerts amid weak purchasing power.
> Mainstreaming of the broader guzi format (dedicated ACG retail, trading cards, badge/ita-bag culture beyond convention circles) is expected 2026-2028.

**Skenario Percepatan**

> A domestic breakout character with merchandising rights properly held in Indonesia (a Jumbo sequel or a Visinema/AINAKI character franchise executed with a licensing partner); a Pop Mart-scale flagship or whole-floor ACG concept opening in a Jakarta mall; Kayou or a card brand entering and capturing the schoolchild segment; a major Indonesian celebrity or K-pop-adjacent endorsement cycle; Chinese trend-toy firms redirecting expansion budgets to Southeast Asia as their domestic market shrinks; cheaper local manufacturing from Pop Mart's 2026 Indonesian production base lowering shelf prices; and continued paylater/BNPL penetration lowering the impulse-purchase barrier.

### Dampak Sosial-Ekonomi

**Dampak Lapangan Kerja**

> Jobs created: (1) Specialist retail — store staff, visual merchandisers, queue/drop managers and shift supervisors for Pop Mart, MINISO, TOP TOY, OH!SOME and Toys Kingdom formats; each large store employs roughly 10-25 people, so a 50-store national build-out implies on the order of 500-1,200 direct retail jobs, meaningful but small.
> (2) IP and licensing professions largely new to Indonesia — licensing manager, brand collaboration manager, character designer, 3D sculptor/digital sculptor, toy/product designer, packaging designer, IP legal counsel, royalty auditor, community/fandom operations manager.
> China's guzi chain explicitly generated copyright agency, IP operations and content creation as new professional categories; the same categories are the highest-value jobs and currently the thinnest in Indonesia.
> (3) Creator-economy work — unboxing creators, collectible reviewers, live-selling hosts, custom repaint artists, doujin illustrators and MSME sellers of acrylic stands, badges and photocard holders at Comifuro and online.
> (4) Manufacturing and logistics — from January 2026 Pop Mart added Indonesian contract manufacturing, creating assembly, plush sewing, QC, warehousing and export-logistics jobs; these are labour-intensive but low-margin and directly substitutable, essentially the same category of work as garment assembly.
> (5) Authentication, resale and grading services — a plausible new niche if the secondary market formalises.
> Jobs displaced or degraded: conventional toy retailers and licensed-character shops that cannot secure hot IP; small independent toy importers squeezed by brand-owned retail; and, in the medium term, generic illustration and graphic-design work displaced by generative AI in character-merchandise production.
> Jobs transformed: Indonesian animation and illustration workers currently doing outsourced service work face a fork — either move up into IP ownership and character design (higher pay, scarce skill) or be commoditised further.
> The Indonesia Animation Report 2026 frames this exact transition from 'digital labour' to IP ownership.
> Net assessment: employment gains are real but modest and concentrated in retail and assembly; the high-value IP jobs will only materialise if local IP ownership grows, otherwise Indonesia captures wages while China captures margin.

**Dampak Kelas Menengah**

> This is a middle-class-defining trend under stress.
> With the BPS middle class shrinking from 47.9 million (2024) to 46.7 million (2025) and roughly six in ten consumers reporting pressured purchasing power, Indonesian households are executing the same 'trading down plus trading up' split observed in China: cutting or deferring housing, vehicles, travel and large durables while maintaining or increasing small emotionally-loaded purchases.
> Labubu queues and sold-out concerts amid weak purchasing power are not a contradiction — they are the signature of compensatory consumption, where a IDR 300,000 item substitutes for a IDR 300 million aspiration that has become unreachable.
> Consequences: (1) Positive-adjacent — small affordable purchases genuinely deliver mood regulation, social belonging and identity expression at low absolute cost, and support a domestic creative-retail sector.
> (2) Negative — the blind-box mechanic converts a one-off treat into a repeat-purchase loop; combined with high paylater penetration and low Indonesian household savings rates, this creates a route from 'self-reward' to revolving consumer debt that China's higher-savings households absorbed more easily.
> Nielsen 2024 found 35% of Gen Z and 43% of millennials prioritising entertainment and consumptive goods over saving.
> (3) Distributional — the aspirational-class segment (the ~137 million BPS 'menuju kelas menengah' cohort) is the most exposed, because participation is socially visible on Instagram and TikTok while their income buffer is thinnest.
> (4) Wealth-transfer effect — because the IP is foreign-owned, middle-class emotional spending is a net outflow of discretionary income to Chinese, Japanese and Korean licensors, unlike China where the same spending recirculated domestically and financed a domestic industry.

**Dampak Daerah Non Jawa**

> Asymmetric but not Java-exclusive.
> Physical specialist retail is heavily Java-Bali concentrated — Pop Mart's Indonesian stores cluster in Jakarta, Bandung, Surabaya and Bali, with Trans Studio Mall Makassar as a notable non-Java outlet and Bali positioned as a tourist-driven store rather than a local-demand store.
> MINISO's 300+ stores give the broader category far wider geographic reach, including secondary cities across Sumatra, Kalimantan and Sulawesi, so the entry-level version of the trend (cheap IP plush, licensed blind boxes at IDR 50,000-150,000) is genuinely national.
> E-commerce (Shopee, Tokopedia, TikTok Shop) equalises access to product but not to price: shipping costs and slower delivery outside Java raise effective prices and reduce impulse conversion.
> Grey-market entry points matter regionally — Batam and Riau Islands function as an import and resale node for both genuine and counterfeit units, and border/free-trade-zone dynamics make counterfeit exposure higher outside Java.
> Cultural participation is nationwide via TikTok, but the physical fandom infrastructure (Comifuro at ICE BSD, Indonesia Comic Con, most brand pop-ups) is overwhelmingly Jabodetabek, so non-Java fans participate as online consumers rather than as community members or sellers.
> Opportunity angle: regional character IP rooted in local folklore and identity (Minangkabau, Toraja, Dayak, Balinese, Papuan motifs) is the most plausible route for non-Java regions to move from consumption to production, and it aligns with Kemenekraf's local-IP agenda.

### Kaitan Pendidikan

**Jurusan Terancam**

> Few programmes are outright threatened; more are threatened by irrelevance if they do not adapt.
> (1) Traditional Fine Arts (Seni Rupa Murni) and craft programmes that train studio practice without IP commercialisation, licensing law, or character-franchise thinking — graduates produce art but cannot monetise characters.
> (2) Generic Desain Komunikasi Visual (DKV) tracks focused on print/advertising layout and static branding, where entry-level execution work is now being absorbed by generative AI tools; the commodity end of illustration is the most exposed white-collar creative work in Indonesia.
> (3) Conventional Marketing/Manajemen Pemasaran curricula built on the 4Ps, mass-media advertising and retail funnels, which do not explain drop mechanics, scarcity design, fandom operations, secondary-market management or community-led demand.
> (4) Traditional Retail Management and Manajemen Bisnis Ritel programmes teaching category management and planogram logic for staple goods, poorly matched to experiential IP retail.
> (5) Fashion and product design programmes without licensing/collaboration modules.
> (6) Conventional 2D animation production tracks that train in-betweening and clean-up — precisely the outsourced 'digital labour' the Indonesia Animation Report 2026 warns is being commoditised.
> Important nuance: the threat is not to the disciplines but to their business-illiteracy; a DKV graduate who understands IP ownership and licensing economics is in the scarcest talent category in the country.

**Jurusan Dibutuhkan**

> (1) Character Design and IP Development — explicit training in creating characters designed for merchandisability, cross-media extension and emotional projection, not just illustration.
> (2) Toy/Product Design with 3D digital sculpting (ZBrush, Blender), rapid prototyping, materials science for vinyl/PVC/plush, tooling and DFM (design for manufacture) — the single most concrete new hard skill, and directly employable given Pop Mart's 2026 Indonesian production base.
> (3) IP Law and Licensing Business — trademark, industrial design, copyright, royalty structures, licensing agreements, anti-counterfeiting enforcement; currently taught only fragmentarily inside general law faculties.
> (4) Fandom and Community Management — Discord/Telegram community operations, drop management, KOL seeding, UGC amplification, crisis handling for scarcity-induced backlash.
> (5) Consumer Psychology and Behavioural Economics — variable-ratio reinforcement, scarcity, endowment effect, parasocial attachment; needed both to build responsibly and to regulate.
> (6) Experiential Retail Design and Visual Merchandising for IP flagship formats.
> (7) Creative Business/Producing — financing, revenue-share modelling and multi-window monetisation of an IP across film, game, merchandise and licensing (the Jumbo model).
> (8) Supply Chain and Sourcing for small-batch consumer goods, including QC and compliance (SNI, EN71, ASTM).
> (9) Data and analytics for demand forecasting on drop-based SKUs with extreme demand variance.
> (10) Anti-counterfeiting and brand-protection operations.
> (11) Ethics/consumer-protection specialisation covering gharar, gambling-adjacent mechanics and minor protection — an area where Indonesian expertise could be regionally distinctive.

### Pelajaran Kebijakan dari China

**Respons Kebijakan China**

> China regulated only after the mechanic was already at scale, which is the key transferable lesson.
> (1) August 2022 — SAMR issued draft blind-box operating guidelines.
> (2) June 2023 — SAMR issued the trial 'Blind Box Business Regulation Guidelines' (盲盒经营行为规范指引(试行)), the sector's regulatory floor.
> Core provisions: prohibition on selling blind boxes to children under 8; for minors aged 8 and above, sale only with guardian consent; mandatory disclosure of contents' value, drawing rules and probability of each outcome; prohibition of certain contents (medicines, medical devices, live animals, flammable/explosive items, and content offending public morality); a ban on price manipulation with prices to be set on cost and genuine supply-demand; and encouragement of self-imposed spending caps and purchase-quantity limits to preserve consumer rationality.
> Shanghai issued its own local rules on the under-8 prohibition.
> (3) 2023-2025 — extension of scrutiny to trading cards, with pressure on card firms over minors' spending; Kayou's Hong Kong listing was reportedly delayed in 2024 partly on regulatory grounds.
> (4) December 2025 — Xinhua, China Daily and provincial outlets ran coordinated investigations into minors' addiction in 谷圈, documenting cases of children spending thousands of yuan (one case: RMB 5,000 in half a month), abandoning study, social withdrawal and exposure to online fraud in unregulated resale groups — the standard precursor to a further enforcement round.
> (5) Ongoing consumer-protection enforcement against scarcity manufacturing, scalping and speculative resale pricing.
> What Indonesia can adopt pre-emptively: probability disclosure as a mandatory labelling requirement; a hard minimum-age floor with guardian consent above it; spending caps and purchase limits per customer per drop; a ban on marketing blind boxes through school channels or to primary-school-age children; mandatory display of the secondary-market risk warning; and requiring platforms (Shopee, Tokopedia, TikTok Shop) to police resale listings and counterfeits.
> Indonesia's decisive advantage is that it can impose these rules while the market is still at roughly 12 specialist stores rather than 3,239, at a fraction of the political cost China paid.

**Rekomendasi Kebijakan Indonesia**

> (1) Pre-emptive blind-box rule via Kemendag/BPKN, adapting SAMR's 2023 guideline: mandatory probability disclosure on packaging and product pages, minimum age 12 with parental consent below 17, per-customer purchase caps at drops, a ban on school-adjacent marketing, and a prohibition on manufacturer-driven scarcity pricing — issued now, before the market scales.
> (2) Classify and clarify legal status early: obtain a clear joint position from Kemendag, OJK, Kominfo/Komdigi and, where relevant, MUI/DSN on where mystery-box retail sits relative to maisir/gharar and the online-gambling regime, so businesses have certainty and consumers have protection; ambiguity currently benefits neither.
> (3) Shift the policy objective from restricting consumption to capturing value: make local IP ownership the centrepiece.
> Concretely — a Kemenekraf IP Fund co-financing character development and merchandising for AINAKI's 299 registered IPs; a licensing marketplace matching Indonesian IP holders with retail chains and manufacturers; and tax incentives for royalties earned by Indonesian IP owners.
> (4) Use Pop Mart's 2026 Indonesian manufacturing entry as leverage: negotiate local-design content, technology and QC transfer, and designer apprenticeship commitments as conditions of investment facilitation, so Indonesia does not settle into pure assembly.
> (5) Strengthen DJKI capacity and speed for character/industrial-design registration, plus a fast-track takedown mechanism for counterfeit listings on marketplaces; pair with BSN/Bea Cukai enforcement against fake SNI-labelled toys.
> (6) Mandate financial-literacy and impulse-spending content in secondary schools covering variable-reward mechanics, paylater risk and 'self-reward' framing.
> (7) Require marketplaces to prevent paylater/BNPL use for blind-box purchases by users under 21 [policy proposal, not existing practice].
> (8) Build the retail-format opportunity deliberately: creative-economy grants for MSME collectible producers to occupy mall pop-up space alongside foreign brands, so the Indonesian version has domestic supply, not just domestic demand.
> (9) Establish an official statistical series — Kemenekraf/BPS should measure the character-licensing and collectibles market so policy is not made blind; today Indonesia has no equivalent of China's guzi market data.
> (10) Learn the timing lesson explicitly: China's cost of late regulation was a 155-store closure wave, cancelled expos and documented harm to minors; Indonesia's preemptive-regulation window closes when specialist store count passes roughly 50.

### Peluang & Rekomendasi Aksi

**Peluang Bisnis**

> (1) Local IP creation and licensing — the highest-value and most defensible opportunity.
> Jumbo's 10m+ admissions proved Indonesian characters can command mass emotional attachment; the missing layer is systematic merchandising.
> A studio or licensing agency that builds a franchise pipeline (film/series to game to merchandise to retail) around Indonesian characters captures the margin currently exported.
> AINAKI's 299 registered IPs are largely unmonetised inventory.
> (2) IP licensing agency services — brokering between Indonesian IP holders, manufacturers and retail chains; a role that barely exists domestically and that in China is a recognised profession.
> (3) Contract manufacturing and design-for-manufacture — Pop Mart's January 2026 addition of Indonesian production creates immediate supplier and Tier-2 component opportunities (vinyl moulding, plush sewing, packaging, QC labs); the strategic play is to move from assembly to ODM by adding in-house design.
> (4) Specialist retail and experiential formats — dedicated ACG/collectible stores, mall pop-ups, gachapon corners, and 'guzi floor' concepts for Indonesian mall operators needing footfall; the Blind Box Festival and Toys Kingdom's Toys Gen show landlord appetite is real.
> (5) Trusted secondary market — an Indonesian authentication, grading and escrow platform for collectibles (the gap that Xianyu fills in China); high trust premium given the counterfeit problem.
> (6) Anti-counterfeit and brand-protection services for incoming licensors.
> (7) Accessories and adjacency — ita-bags, display cases, photocard holders, acrylic stands, protective sleeves; low capital, high margin, and already an active MSME segment at Comifuro.
> (8) Fandom event operations — Comifuro-scale conventions, artist alleys, IP roadshows and creator marketplaces, plus ticketing and merchandising services around them.
> (9) Faith-compatible product design — a genuinely differentiated Indonesian/Southeast Asian opportunity: transparent-odds or 'known-content' collectible formats, complete-set pricing and trade-in mechanics that deliver collectibility without the gharar problem, exportable to Malaysia, Brunei and the wider OIC market.
> (10) Regional IP rooted in local folklore and heritage as both a cultural and tourism-merchandise play.
> (11) Creator-economy tooling — small-batch production services letting Indonesian illustrators produce merchandise at low MOQ.

**Rekomendasi Individu Mahasiswa**

> Build the scarce combination: creative craft plus IP business literacy.
> Concretely — (1) master 3D digital sculpting and toy-oriented product design (ZBrush/Blender, plus DFM, tooling and materials for vinyl and plush), which is directly hireable now that manufacturing is landing in Indonesia; (2) learn IP and licensing fundamentals — trademark and industrial-design registration through DJKI, royalty structures, licensing contracts — because almost no Indonesian creative graduate has this and it is where the margin sits; (3) develop character-design thinking rather than illustration alone: study why wordless, ambiguous, ugly-cute characters travel across cultures, and build a portfolio of characters with merchandising extensions, not single images; (4) acquire community and fandom operations skills — running Discord/Telegram communities, managing drops, seeding KOLs, handling scarcity backlash; (5) understand consumer psychology and behavioural economics well enough to build responsibly and to work on the regulation side; (6) get real reps by selling at Comifuro or online — a student who has designed, produced, priced and sold 200 acrylic stands understands this industry better than most graduates; (7) treat AI as a production accelerator for iteration and concepting while investing personal capital in the things it does not replace — character concept ownership, community trust and licensing negotiation; (8) build language and market skills for Mandarin, Japanese or Korean licensing counterparties if aiming at the licensing-agency path; (9) apply personal financial discipline to the trend itself — understand the variable-reward mechanic well enough not to be its victim while studying it.

**Rekomendasi Perguruan Tinggi**

> (1) Open applied concentrations rather than new degrees — add 'Character Design & IP Development' and 'Toy/Collectible Product Design' tracks inside existing DKV, Animation and Product Design programmes; this is exactly how China absorbed the demand, and it is fast.
> (2) Make IP law and licensing a compulsory module in every creative-industries programme, taught with real DJKI filing exercises and real licence agreements.
> (3) Build school-enterprise partnerships on the Chinese model: MoUs with Pop Mart's Indonesian manufacturing partners, MINISO/TOP TOY, OH!SOME, Visinema and AINAKI members for internships, live briefs and capstone commissions.
> (4) Establish shared digital-fabrication studios (3D printing, resin casting, small-batch mould making) at polytechnics and SMK level so students can prototype physically, not only render.
> (5) Add 'Creative Business & IP Producing' to management faculties — franchise financing, multi-window monetisation, royalty modelling — bridging business schools and art schools, which currently barely talk to each other.
> (6) Reposition animation programmes away from outsourced-service training toward IP ownership, in line with the Indonesia Animation Report 2026 roadmap.
> (7) Introduce consumer-psychology and consumer-protection modules covering variable-ratio reinforcement, gharar/maisir analysis and minor protection — a distinctive Indonesian and OIC-relevant research niche.
> (8) De-emphasise or restructure purely executional illustration and layout tracks most exposed to generative AI, redirecting credit hours to concept ownership, direction and business skills.
> (9) Create a national IP incubator across a few leading campuses (ITB, ISI Yogyakarta, Binus, Telkom University) to move student characters into registered, licensable assets.
> (10) Fund research measuring the Indonesian collectibles and licensing market, which currently has no credible domestic statistics.

### Faktor Risiko & Sisi Gelap

**Dampak Negatif China**

> (1) Harm to minors — the most documented damage.
> December 2025 Xinhua/China Daily and Jiangsu media investigations described children spending thousands of yuan on guzi (one documented case: RMB 5,000 in half a month by a child who described 'living on one yuan' otherwise), academic collapse, some suspending schooling, social withdrawal from offline relationships, and exposure to fraud in unregulated resale chat groups.
> This is why the 2023 SAMR rules banned sales to under-8s and required guardian consent for 8-17.
> (2) Speculative bubble and household losses — deliberate scarcity engineering pushed limited editions to extreme secondary prices; when sentiment turned, retail holders and small shop owners were left with inventory bought at peak.
> (3) Small-business destruction — the guzi store gold rush drew thousands of small operators into leases at peak rents; at least 155 stores closed in 2025, chains contracted 33-63% (潮玩星球 148 to 99; 抱萌 59 to 22; 漫库 44 to 31), Harbin's 60+ store cluster went into discounting and lease-transfer distress, and Huxiu documented owners whose monthly income fell from RMB 50,000-60,000 to below rent.
> (4) Ecosystem contraction — CCG EXPO attendance collapsed from 200,000+ to about 48,000 in 2025; the July 2026 PTS Trendy Toy Expo was cancelled; Chongqing's 超次元X9 and Yibin's guzi house closed.
> (5) Investor losses — the cultural-and-creative toy sector index fell 16.52% in H1 2026; Pop Mart fell 23% in a day in March 2026 and about 25% from late March, with US sales down 42-45% YoY.
> (6) Structural fragility of the model — the shakeout exposed homogeneous product, no proprietary IP among most retailers, and dependence on a single character; Pop Mart's 38% revenue concentration in Labubu is itself a systemic risk.
> (7) Counterfeiting and fraud around scarce items, and (8) opportunity cost — capital and youth attention channelled into a speculative merchandise cycle rather than productive sectors, an outcome Chinese commentators increasingly frame as 'the 2D leeks can't be cut anymore' (二次元韭菜割不动了).

**Risiko Sosial Indonesia**

> (1) Gambling normalisation in a country running a national anti-online-gambling emergency — PPATK found gambling to be the largest category (47.5%) of suspicious-transaction indications in 2025.
> A variable-ratio purchase mechanic marketed to teenagers, with a liquid resale market attached, is functionally a gateway habit; without rules, blind boxes normalise the exact reward psychology regulators are trying to suppress.
> (2) Youth debt — Indonesia's combination of high paylater/BNPL penetration, low household savings and 'self-reward' norms makes escalation from treat to revolving debt materially more likely than in high-savings China; documented Indonesian 'doom spending' discourse already frames this.
> (3) Minor harm without any age rule — Indonesia currently has no equivalent of SAMR's under-8 prohibition or guardian-consent requirement, and China's own damage to minors emerged in a market with those rules in place.
> (4) Household financial stress in a shrinking middle class — 46.7 million people, 16.6% of the population, with six in ten reporting pressured purchasing power; discretionary spending on foreign IP is a direct leakage from an already thin buffer.
> (5) Small-business wipeout risk — if Indonesian entrepreneurs pile into guzi-style retail in 2027-2028 at peak rents, the Chinese 155-closure precedent is the base case, and Indonesian operators have less capital cushion.
> (6) Counterfeit and fraud exposure — 'Lafufu' products, fake SNI labelling and unescrowed resale in Facebook/Instagram groups; both safety risk (chemicals, small parts) and financial fraud.
> (7) Social comparison harm — collection display on TikTok/Instagram creates visible status hierarchies among teenagers, with exclusion effects for lower-income peers, and, in the Indonesian school context, potential bullying and theft dynamics.
> (8) Value leakage — without local IP, this is a permanent structural transfer of youth discretionary spending abroad, and unlike garments or electronics it produces no domestic capability.
> (9) Religious-social conflict — unregulated growth invites a hard fatwa or a blunt ban, which would destroy legitimate licensed-merchandise business alongside the problematic mechanic; early rules are the way to avoid that binary.
> (10) Regulatory whiplash risk — Indonesia's pattern of abrupt bans (e.g.
> the 2023 TikTok Shop social-commerce ban) means the industry could face sudden prohibition rather than gradual tightening.

**Unintended Consequences**

> (1) In China, the guzi boom unexpectedly rescued failing shopping malls by supplying youth footfall — an outcome landlords, not toy companies, benefited from most; the same is plausible in oversupplied Jakarta and Surabaya retail.
> (2) It created an entirely new professional class (IP operations, copyright agency, community management) that did not previously exist in Chinese retail.
> (3) It became a soft-power export: Labubu made a Chinese-owned character globally beloved without any state cultural programme, achieving what decades of official cultural diplomacy had not — a lesson Indonesia's creative-economy policy should note.
> (4) Success in a single character created dangerous corporate concentration — Pop Mart's 38% dependence on Labubu turned a triumph into an investor liability within six months.
> (5) Falling resale prices, normally bad news, were publicly welcomed by Pop Mart in September 2025 because scalper-driven prices were damaging genuine-fan access and brand health — an unusual case where a company celebrated its product losing speculative value.
> (6) The trend accelerated 'kidult' normalisation — adults collecting toys shifted from stigma to mainstream identity, changing the entire toy industry's demographic.
> (7) In Indonesia, the counterfeit wave has inadvertently seeded genuine local manufacturing skills (moulding, plush production) that could later serve legitimate local IP.
> (8) Pop Mart's 2026 Indonesian manufacturing decision was driven by global capacity needs and tariff diversification, but has the unintended effect of giving Indonesia physical toy-industry capability years earlier than its domestic IP maturity would have produced.
> (9) The blind-box format is spreading into unrelated Indonesian categories — food, cosmetics, e-commerce mystery bundles — which regulators may not notice until it is embedded across retail.
> (10) Risk of AI-generated character flooding: cheap generative design lowers the barrier to launching characters, which could either democratise Indonesian IP creation or drown the market in undifferentiated product before any local IP achieves scale.

**Kelompok Rentan**

> (1) Children and teenagers aged 8-17 — the group China's own investigations found most harmed, and the group Indonesia currently protects least, with no age floor, no guardian-consent rule and heavy TikTok exposure.
> (2) Lower-middle-income urban youth and the 'menuju kelas menengah' aspirational cohort — highest social pressure to display participation, thinnest financial buffer, highest paylater exposure.
> (3) Young workers and students using BNPL/paylater — the mechanism that converts small emotional purchases into structural debt.
> (4) Parents of collecting children, who absorb the financial cost and the conflict.
> (5) Small retail entrepreneurs entering the category late at peak rents — the direct Indonesian analogue of the Chinese shop owners whose income fell below rent in 2026.
> (6) Resellers and scalpers holding inventory when a character cycle turns, as happened globally with Labubu after August 2025.
> (7) Illustrators and junior animation workers whose executional work is squeezed simultaneously by generative AI and by cheap imported licensed product.
> (8) Consumers outside Java, who pay higher effective prices, face higher counterfeit exposure through grey-import channels, and have least access to authentic retail or redress.
> (9) People using consumption for emotional regulation under genuine psychological distress, for whom the variable-reward loop is least likely to resolve the underlying condition and most likely to compound financial stress.

### Contoh Kasus Konkret

**Kasus China**

> Pop Mart International Group is the definitive case.
> Founded 2010 as a variety retailer, it pivoted to blind-box trend toys after signing designer Kenny Wong for Molly in 2016, listed on HKEX in December 2020, and by FY2025 reported revenue of RMB 37.12 billion (about USD 5.4bn, +184.7% YoY), net profit RMB 13.01 billion (+293.3%) and gross margin of 72.1%, with over 1,000 stores globally by 2026.
> The Labubu/The Monsters franchise alone produced RMB 14.16 billion (+365.7%), about 38% of group revenue; overseas exceeded 40% of sales, with the Americas at RMB 6.81 billion (+748.4%) and Southeast Asia at RMB 2.4 billion (+619.1%), while plush production scaled toward 30 million units per month.
> The same case demonstrates the downside: shares fell a record 23% in a single day in March 2026 on the FY2025 results because of Labubu concentration, Q1 2026 growth decelerated from 185% to about 80%, US sales dropped 42-45% YoY in March-April 2026, and Morgan Stanley and Deutsche Bank cut FY2026 growth forecasts to +13% and -2%.
> Supporting cases: Kayou (卡游), China's No.1 trading-card firm, whose revenue nearly quadrupled to about USD 1.4bn in 2024 with ~80% from cards, targeting a ~USD 500m Hong Kong IPO and expanding to the US in October 2025 with Naruto cards and an NBA card partnership with Fanatics; Letsvan/Wakuku, founded 2020, whose panda character lifted a Beijing MINISO Land store's revenue by over 90% on debut in March 2025 and which QuantaSing took a controlling stake in; and the sector's bust case — at least 155 guzi store closures in 2025, 潮玩星球 contracting from 148 to 99 stores, 抱萌 from 59 to 22, CCG EXPO attendance falling from 200,000+ to about 48,000, the July 2026 PTS expo cancelled, and the cultural-creative toy sector index down 16.52% in H1 2026.

### Tingkat Keyakinan & Kualitas Sumber

**Catatan Kontradiksi Data**

> (1) Unit-scale mistranslation is endemic in English-language coverage of Chinese sources: several outlets render 5.03亿 pan-2D users as '5.03 billion' and 3亿 Gen Z as '3 billion', which are impossible; the correct figures are approximately 503 million and 300 million.
> Similarly some sources render 2000亿元 as '2 trillion yuan' when it means RMB 200 billion.
> Figures in this record have been corrected to the plausible reading, but any downstream use should verify against the Chinese original.
> (2) 2025 guzi market size projections diverge materially: iiMedia-derived estimates cluster around RMB 200 billion while QuestMobile-derived figures reach RMB 240 billion for 2025 and RMB 300 billion for 2027, whereas other sources put RMB 300 billion only by 2029 — a two-year discrepancy on the same milestone.
> (3) Market-boundary inconsistency: 'guzi' (RMB 168.9bn, 2024), 'ACG market' (RMB 597.7bn, 2024) and 'pan-2D plus peripherals' (RMB 652.1bn, 2025) are used interchangeably in some reporting despite measuring different things; the +9.1% growth of the pan-2D aggregate in 2025 sits oddly against the +40% guzi growth in 2024 and suggests either a sharp deceleration or a definitional change.
> (4) Southeast Asia's reported 41.4% share of global Labubu sales appears in secondary aggregators but is not in Pop Mart's audited disclosures, which report Southeast Asia revenue (RMB 2.4bn) rather than character-level regional splits.
> (5) Pop Mart's Q1 2026 growth is variously reported as 'up to 80%' and 'as high as 80%', a guidance-band figure rather than an audited number, and Morgan Stanley (+13%) versus Deutsche Bank (-2%) FY2026 forecasts differ by 15 percentage points — an unusually wide analyst dispersion indicating genuine uncertainty about whether the correction is cyclical or structural.
> (6) Pop Mart Indonesia store count: 12 stores is sourced from a Makassar opening announcement whose date is not precisely established, and the first-Indonesia-store date (2023) could not be confirmed to the month.
> (7) Indonesian middle-class figures vary by definition — 46.7 million (16.6%) and 'about 17.25%' appear in different 2025-2026 reports depending on whether the BPS Aspiring/Middle boundary is applied to the 2025 or 2024 Susenas round.
> (8) No confirmed dedicated 'trend toy design' undergraduate major exists in China's national catalogue despite widespread vocational-level provision; claims to the contrary in industry commentary could not be verified against Ministry of Education documents.
> (9) Comifuro attendance data is sparse — the 40,000 figure dates from CF15 (2022) and no verified recent attendance total was found.
