## 20. Anti-Involution & Platform Backlash Regulation (反内卷 / fan neijuan) — the state-led crackdown on destructive price wars and algorithmic labor exploitation across food delivery, EV, solar/polysilicon, express logistics and platform commerce
**Kategori**: Regulasi & Kebijakan (Regulation & Public Policy) — cross-cutting into Digital Economy, Industrial Policy, and Labor Protection

📊 MIXED — dominantly LEAPFROG on platform-labor and commission regulation (Indonesia legislating before the destructive phase fully matures, and using blunter instruments than China), but LAGGARD on algorithmic governance, fatigue/working-hour standards and general below-cost-pricing law. On industrial overcapacity governance the relationship is REVERSE-DEPENDENT rather than lagging: Indonesia is the destination of China's exported involution (dumped textiles, discounted EVs), so it needs trade-defense instruments, not domestic capacity quotas. | 🎯 Prob: Tinggi (High) — for the regulatory model. Sedang (Medium) — for the full Chinese instrument set including capacity quotas and administrative price floors on manufactured goods. | 🔍 Keyakinan: Tinggi (High) for the China side — the policy instruments, dates, agencies and headline financial figures are documented across regulatory sources, Party media (Qiushi, People's Daily), specialist legal analysis (NPC Observer, King & Wood Mallesons) and independent financial press (Caixin, SCMP, MLex, pv magazine). Tinggi for the Indonesian regulatory instruments (Perpres 27/2026, Permen Komdigi 8/2025, Permen UMKM 3/2026, MK 168) which are all traceable to named legal instruments and mainstream Indonesian legal press. Sedang (Medium) for Indonesian quantitative scale data (driver counts vary widely by source and definition) and for all forward-looking timeline estimates. Rendah-Sedang for the China education-response section, where the link between the anti-involution agenda and specific curricular change is inferential rather than documented.

> **Status di Indonesia**: PARTIAL LEAPFROG IN PROGRESS — Indonesia has entered destructive competition in several sectors (ride-hailing/ojol, e-commerce, express logistics, and now Chinese-brand EVs) but has ALREADY begun issuing anti-involution-style regulation ahead of the damage curve, in some cases with instruments more aggressive than China's. Indonesia is therefore neither 'belum ada' nor 'sudah masuk masif' in the full Chinese sense; it is regulating mid-cycle. Labor/commission regulation: AHEAD (Perpres 27/2026 is arguably stricter than any Chinese take-rate rule). Algorithm governance and working-hours/fatigue standards: BEHIND (no Indonesian equivalent of GB/T 46862-2025 or the CAC algorithm negative list). Industrial overcapacity/price-floor governance: BEHIND and structurally different (Indonesia is the import-receiving end of Chinese involution, not the producer).

### Basic Info

**Tahun Mulai China**

> The underlying destructive-competition problem started with the O2O subsidy wars of 2014-2015 and the solar/EV capacity build-out of 2018-2022.
> The ANTI-involution POLICY response is very recent and datable: July 2024 (Politburo first uses the phrase 'prevent involution-style vicious competition' / 防止内卷式恶性竞争), escalating to a formal national campaign from 1 July 2025 (Central Commission for Financial and Economic Affairs meeting), and hardening into binding law and standards through 2025-2026.

**Pemain Kunci China**

> REGULATORS (the real protagonists): State Administration for Market Regulation (SAMR / 国家市场监督管理总局) — price supervision, anti-unfair-competition enforcement, platform summonses; National Development and Reform Commission (NDRC) — Price Law amendment, capacity governance; Ministry of Industry and Information Technology (MIIT) — sectoral two-year plans for 10 key industries, 60-day supplier payment cap, battery/polysilicon capacity monitoring; Cyberspace Administration of China (CAC) — algorithm governance, 'Life Service Platform Algorithm Negative List' (Jan 2026); Ministry of Human Resources and Social Security (MOHRSS) — new employment forms, occupational injury insurance; All-China Federation of Trade Unions (ACFTU) — collective bargaining over algorithms; State Post Bureau (国家邮政局) and provincial postal administrations — express delivery price floors.
> REGULATED FIRMS: Meituan, Alibaba (Ele.me / Taobao Shangou / Amap), JD.com, Didi, Pinduoduo/Temu, Douyin Life Service; BYD, Geely, Chery, NIO, Li Auto, Xpeng; CATL, BYD, CALB (batteries); Tongwei, GCL, Daqo, Xinte (polysilicon); LONGi, JinkoSolar, Trina, JA Solar (modules); ZTO, YTO, STO, Yunda, J&T/Jitu, SF Express (express delivery).
> INDUSTRY BODIES used as instruments: China Association of Automobile Manufacturers (CAAM), China Photovoltaic Industry Association (CPIA), China Cuisine Association, provincial express delivery associations.

### China Trend Detail

**Apa Yang Terjadi Di China**

> China spent a decade letting hyper-competition run unchecked, then reversed course.
> 'Involution' (内卷 neijuan) describes competition where every player escalates effort and cuts price, but the whole industry ends up worse off — more output, lower prices, thinner or negative margins, and workers absorbing the squeeze.
> By 2024-2025 this had become a macroeconomic problem: producer prices had been falling for 40+ consecutive months, roughly one in five industrial firms was loss-making (a 25-year high), and industrial profits were shrinking even as output grew.
> Beijing reframed price wars from 'consumer benefit' to 'systemic deflation risk' and 'destruction of national industrial value', and built a multi-instrument campaign.

The mechanism has five distinct instruments, and this bundle is what makes the Chinese case a template:
(1) PRICE FLOORS / BELOW-COST BANS.
> The Price Law is being amended for the first time in 27 years (draft published 24 July 2025 by NDRC+SAMR) to sharpen the definition of below-cost dumping and to cover algorithmic pricing, data abuse and price discrimination.
> The revised Anti-Unfair Competition Law (June 2025, in force 15 Oct 2025) added platform-specific provisions banning platforms from forcing merchants to sell below cost.
> Concretely: express delivery price floors were set administratively — Guangdong at RMB 1.4/parcel, Yiwu raised from RMB 1.1 to RMB 1.2/parcel — after Yunda and Baishi were penalized for 'low-price dumping' with partial suspension of sorting centers.
(2) SUBSIDY-WAR BANS IN PLATFORM COMMERCE.
> After JD.com entered food delivery in Feb 2025 and triggered a war in which Alibaba, Meituan and JD burned roughly RMB 157 billion (~USD 22bn) in nine months, SAMR summoned the platforms repeatedly (May 2025, July 2025, Sept 2025, and again Feb 2026 with seven platforms), then issued draft rules banning long-term large-scale subsidies, banning coercive cost-sharing with merchants and riders, requiring 7 days' advance notice of promotions, and capping fee increases.
> The food-delivery price war was named one of SAMR's top-ten 'involutionary competition' enforcement cases in Jan 2026.
(3) SUPPLY-CHAIN PAYMENT DISCIPLINE.
> Because price wars are financed by squeezing suppliers, the revised SME Payment Regulation (effective 1 June 2025) capped payment to SME suppliers at 60 days; 17 major automakers publicly pledged compliance in June 2025, MIIT backed it the same day, and the cap was then extended to batteries (2026) and energy storage.
> Average auto payment cycles fell ~10 days within a year.
(4) CAPACITY GOVERNANCE.
> MIIT wrote two-year (2025-2026) plans for 10 key industries with output growth targets below 2024 levels; Tangshan steel mills were ordered to cut output ~30%; polysilicon producers, backed by NDRC/MIIT, worked on an RMB 50bn (~USD 6.4bn) fund to retire over 1 million tonnes of the ~3.5 million tonnes of capacity; monthly polysilicon output fell 8.3% MoM in Jan 2026 and a further 17.3% in Feb 2026.
(5) LABOR AND ALGORITHM RE-REGULATION — the part most transferable to Indonesia.
> Platforms were pushed to abolish late-delivery fines (Meituan committed Dec 2024 to phase them out by end-2025; by 2026 all three major platforms had essentially removed them and switched to points/training systems).
> A recommended national standard, GB/T 46862-2025 'Basic Requirements for Food Delivery Platform Service Management', was approved in Dec 2025: order-taking capped at 8 hours/day in principle (continuing beyond requires explicit rider confirmation), a fatigue alert plus mandatory 20-minute dispatch pause after 4 continuous hours, delivery-time estimation that must assume safe speeds (e-bike average speed not above 15 km/h), red lights pausing the delivery clock, algorithms that must account for traffic, weather and restaurant prep time, a ban on forcing merchants into promotions, and social insurance for riders in genuine employment relationships.
> In Jan 2026 CAC issued the 'Life Service Platform Algorithm Negative List (Trial)'; major platforms implemented 63 optimization measures and 139 algorithm compliance commitments.
> Then on 26 April 2026 the CPC Central Committee and State Council jointly issued China's first comprehensive labor framework for 'new employment groups' (新就业形态) covering 200+ million platform workers: standardized contracts, pay benchmarked to local minimum wage, holiday premiums, negotiated caps on maximum consecutive order-taking time and maximum daily hours with the system required to STOP dispatching once the cap is hit, and — most radically — the algorithm itself made a subject of collective bargaining with unions, with full compliance required by 2027.

In parallel, Beijing attacked the demand side of involution: the 'unified national market' (全国统一大市场) drive restricts local governments from bidding against each other with tax breaks, fiscal subsidies and procurement favoritism, with a negative list for local fiscal subsidies announced in 2026.
> This matters because much Chinese overcapacity was locally-subsidized duplication.

**Data Skala China**

> MACRO: PPI negative for 40+ consecutive months from Sept 2022; PPI -2.1% YoY in Oct 2025.
> 116,428 loss-making industrial enterprises at end-2024 (>22% of all industrial firms, +9.2% YoY) — share of loss-makers at a 25-year high.
> Industrial profits fell 1.8% YoY in H1 2025 and 1.7% YoY in Jan-Jul 2025 (to RMB 4.02 trillion).
> Post-campaign rebound: industrial profits +15.2% YoY in Jan-Feb 2026, the strongest start since 2018.
FOOD DELIVERY / INSTANT RETAIL: market size RMB 1.64 trillion (~USD 229bn) in 2024, projected RMB 1.96 trillion by 2027; instant delivery orders exceeded 60 billion in 2025, +25% YoY; 553 million active food-delivery users (June 2024, 50.3% of Chinese netizens).
> Subsidy war cost: additional marketing spend Q2-Q4 2025 was Alibaba +RMB 83.7bn (~USD 11.6bn), Meituan +RMB 38.7bn (~USD 5.4bn), JD +RMB 34.7bn (~USD 4.8bn) — ~RMB 156.8bn (~USD 21.8bn) combined.
> Alibaba instant-retail cumulative losses ~RMB 87bn (~USD 12.9bn); JD's new-business unit lost RMB 46.6bn (~USD 6.9bn); Meituan swung to a Q1 2026 net loss of RMB 6.83bn (~USD 1.0bn) on revenue of RMB 91.04bn, versus a RMB 10.06bn profit a year earlier.
LABOR: 13+ million delivery riders; ~84 million workers in 'new employment forms' (truckers, ride-hail drivers, couriers, delivery riders) out of ~402 million employed; the April 2026 CPC/State Council framework covers 200+ million platform workers.
> Meituan rider pension subsidy: pilot from early 2025 in Quanzhou and Nantong (~22,000 riders), national coverage announced 27 Oct 2025 targeting 1m+ riders; by Feb 2026 Meituan had paid RMB 2.77bn in occupational-injury premiums with ~17.28 million rider registrations.
> JD began paying full five-insurances-plus-housing-fund for full-time riders from 1 March 2025.
> Ride-hailing: ~7.48 million licensed drivers; dozens of cities issued 'capacity saturation warnings'.
MERCHANT DAMAGE: China Cuisine Association reported June 2025 revenue for above-designated-size catering down 0.4% YoY during the subsidy war; per-capita spending per restaurant meal fell 23.6% since 2023 to RMB 33 as of Sept 2025; merchants reported ~15% income reduction from forced discounting.
EXPRESS DELIVERY: Yiwu handles ~10% of national parcel volume and saw prices as low as RMB 1.2/parcel against an industry cost benchmark of ~RMB 1.4.
SOLAR: ~3.5 million tonnes polysilicon capacity vs.
> a plan to retire 1m+ tonnes with a proposed RMB 50bn (~USD 6.4bn) fund; polysilicon prices still fell 13%+ YTD as of March 2026, showing enforcement gaps.

**Fase Tren Di China**

> REGULATED / ACTIVE ENFORCEMENT, entering an institutionalization phase.
> The trend has moved through: emerging (July 2024 Politburo language) → booming as a policy campaign (July 2025 onward, sector-by-sector) → codified into binding instruments (Anti-Unfair Competition Law Oct 2025; Internet Platform Pricing Rules Dec 2025; GB/T 46862-2025 Dec 2025; CAC algorithm negative list Jan 2026; CPC/State Council labor framework April 2026 with a 2027 compliance deadline).
> It is NOT yet 'mature' — the Price Law amendment is still being finalized, polysilicon below-cost selling persisted into March 2026, and SAMR had to summon seven platforms again in Feb 2026.
> Best description: the involution PROBLEM is in a late/backlash phase; the anti-involution REGULATORY REGIME is in a booming, mid-implementation phase with a hard 2027 milestone.

**Puncak Tren China**

> Two peaks must be distinguished.
> (a) Peak of DESTRUCTIVE COMPETITION: mid-2025, specifically May-August 2025, in the food delivery/instant retail sector nationwide (peak single-day order records set with Alibaba/Meituan subsidy blitzes in July-August 2025), with a parallel peak in EV price discounting in 2024-2025 and in polysilicon/module below-cost selling in 2024-2025; Yiwu (Zhejiang) was the geographic epicenter for express-delivery price collapse.
> (b) Peak of REGULATORY INTENSITY: expected 2026-2027 — the densest cluster of instruments (CAC algorithm negative list Jan 2026, SAMR top-ten involution enforcement cases Jan 2026, seven-platform summons Feb 2026, national price-supervision conference March 2026, CPC/State Council labor framework April 2026, GB/T standard rollout observed April 2026) with the 2027 full-compliance deadline as the terminal marker.
> Sectoral peak of pain is best dated: food delivery Q3 2025 (Beijing/Shanghai/Guangzhou-Shenzhen), EV 2024-2025 (Shenzhen/Hefei/Shanghai), polysilicon 2024-2025 (Xinjiang/Sichuan/Inner Mongolia), express delivery 2021 and again 2024-2025 (Yiwu).

### Status Indonesia Saat Ini

**Status Di Indonesia**

> PARTIAL LEAPFROG IN PROGRESS — Indonesia has entered destructive competition in several sectors (ride-hailing/ojol, e-commerce, express logistics, and now Chinese-brand EVs) but has ALREADY begun issuing anti-involution-style regulation ahead of the damage curve, in some cases with instruments more aggressive than China's.
> Indonesia is therefore neither 'belum ada' nor 'sudah masuk masif' in the full Chinese sense; it is regulating mid-cycle.
> Labor/commission regulation: AHEAD (Perpres 27/2026 is arguably stricter than any Chinese take-rate rule).
> Algorithm governance and working-hours/fatigue standards: BEHIND (no Indonesian equivalent of GB/T 46862-2025 or the CAC algorithm negative list).
> Industrial overcapacity/price-floor governance: BEHIND and structurally different (Indonesia is the import-receiving end of Chinese involution, not the producer).

**Contoh Konkret Indonesia**

> REGULATION ALREADY IN FORCE: (1) Perpres No.
> 27/2026 on Protection of Online Transportation Workers — announced by President Prabowo at the May Day rally at Monas on 1 May 2026, effective 1 June 2026: platform commission capped at 8% (down from the 20% ceiling under Kepmenhub KP 1001/2022, with drivers reporting effective cuts of 50-70%), a mandated 92:8 revenue split, JKN health coverage and JKK work-accident insurance, religious holiday allowance (THR/BHR).
> Gojek and Grab set implementation for two-wheel passenger transport from 1 July 2026; DPR and driver unions have publicly complained about delayed implementation and Kemenhub's failure to revise the underlying Kepmenhub.
> Notably the Perpres covers only two-wheel ojol, not four-wheel online taxis, and does not address algorithms or working hours.
> (2) Permen Komdigi No.
> 8/2025 on Commercial Postal Services — establishes a cost-plus-margin tariff formula for courier services (labor, transport, application/technology, partner-facility, individual-partner costs), allows the government to set temporary tariff floors/ceilings valid for a maximum of 6 months, with tariff evaluation based on market review, cost study, social impact, financial performance and service sustainability.
> This is a functional analogue of China's express-delivery price floor, issued BEFORE Indonesia's parcel price war reached Yiwu-level destruction.
> (3) Permen UMKM No.
> 3/2026 on Protection and Competitiveness of Micro and Small Enterprises in Electronic Commerce (promulgated 17 June 2026) — requires e-commerce platforms to disclose all seller-facing fees, calculation mechanisms and payment methods transparently; the UMKM Minister publicly ordered Shopee, Tokopedia and TikTok Shop to freeze service-fee increases in May 2026 and said KPPU would be involved.
> (4) MK Decision No.
> 168/PUU-XXI/2023 (31 Oct 2024) requires a wholly new Labour Law separated from the Omnibus Job Creation Law within two years, i.e.
> by 31 October 2026; the DPR working committee began clause-by-clause deliberation on 20 July 2026, and labor coalitions have submitted 16 points.
> Platform-work provisions — algorithm transparency, account suspension/deactivation due process, automated performance scoring, worker data protection, OSH and social security — are explicitly on the table.
DESTRUCTIVE COMPETITION ALREADY VISIBLE: Grab-GoTo merger negotiations through 2025-2026 explicitly framed as ending the subsidy/'bakar uang' war, with Danantara state capital involved and KPPU warning it could unwind a completed merger (Indonesia still uses post-merger notification); KPPU examining TikTok for alleged monopoly and predatory pricing; simultaneous May 2026 fee hikes across Shopee, Tokopedia and TikTok Shop (Shopee twice by mid-2026, TikTok Shop three times), with the per-item commission ceiling jumping from Rp40,000 to Rp650,000 (nearly 15x) and visible seller exit to own-website channels; Chinese EV brands discounting hard (Chery cutting Omoda 5 and E5 prices by Rp50-100 million; BYD Atto 1 around Rp195 million) with GAIKINDO issuing a public warning about the EV price war; textile deindustrialization from dumped Chinese yarn and fabric — 47,115 TPT workers laid off Jan-Oct 2025 and five mills closed with ~3,000 layoffs reported Dec 2025, partly offset by Chinese textile producers relocating INTO Indonesia.

### Analisis Lag

**Bukti Historical Lag**

> (1) Ride-hailing regulation: China issued the Interim Measures on Online Ride-Hailing in July 2016; Indonesia issued PM 32/2016 and then PM 108/2017 for four-wheel online transport, and only reached ojek-specific tariff rules with PM 12/2019 and Kepmenhub KP 348/2019 — a lag of roughly 1-3 years.
> (2) Platform antitrust: China's SAMR fined Alibaba RMB 18.2bn in April 2021 and Meituan RMB 3.44bn in Oct 2021 for 'choose one of two' exclusivity; Indonesia's KPPU only reached comparable enforcement territory around 2023-2024 (Google Play Billing decision, TikTok/Tokopedia scrutiny) — a lag of roughly 2-3 years.
> (3) Social-commerce/live-selling regulation: China regulated livestream e-commerce from 2020-2021; Indonesia's Permendag 31/2023 banning social-commerce transactions came in Sept 2023 — a lag of ~2-3 years.
> (4) Rider social insurance: China's occupational-injury insurance pilot for platform workers started July 2022 in seven provinces; Indonesia's BPJS Ketenagakerjaan coverage for ojol remained largely voluntary until Perpres 27/2026 mandated JKK/JKN in 2026 — a lag of ~4 years.
> (5) Counter-evidence for leapfrog: Indonesia's 8% commission cap (2026) has NO Chinese precedent at all — China regulates algorithms and subsidies but has never capped platform take-rates by decree.
> This is the single strongest data point that Indonesia can, and does, jump straight to blunt preemptive instruments.

**Tipe Lag**

> MIXED — dominantly LEAPFROG on platform-labor and commission regulation (Indonesia legislating before the destructive phase fully matures, and using blunter instruments than China), but LAGGARD on algorithmic governance, fatigue/working-hour standards and general below-cost-pricing law.
> On industrial overcapacity governance the relationship is REVERSE-DEPENDENT rather than lagging: Indonesia is the destination of China's exported involution (dumped textiles, discounted EVs), so it needs trade-defense instruments, not domestic capacity quotas.

### Probabilitas Transfer ke Indonesia

**Probabilitas Transfer**

> Tinggi (High) — for the regulatory model.
> Sedang (Medium) — for the full Chinese instrument set including capacity quotas and administrative price floors on manufactured goods.

**Alasan Probabilitas**

> High, for four reinforcing reasons.
> (1) The trigger conditions are already present in Indonesia: a real subsidy war (Grab/GoTo/Shopee/TikTok), visible driver and seller immiseration, visible merchant fee escalation, and visible dumped-import damage to textiles — all the political inputs that produced China's turn.
> (2) The political economy is favorable: Prabowo's administration has demonstrated appetite for direct, populist, price-and-margin-level intervention (Perpres 27/2026's 8% cap was announced at a May Day rally, not negotiated through a technocratic process), and organized ojol driver unions have proven street-mobilization capacity — the May 2025 and subsequent protests directly produced the Perpres.
> (3) The institutional pipeline is open right now: the MK-mandated new Labour Law must pass by 31 October 2026, creating a once-in-a-generation legislative vehicle into which platform-work, algorithm-transparency and deactivation-due-process clauses can be inserted.
> (4) Indonesian policymakers explicitly benchmark China — Chinese regulatory precedent is cited in Indonesian policy discourse on e-commerce, EVs and platform labor, and Chinese platform operators and investors operating in Indonesia already carry Chinese compliance architecture internally.
> The Medium rating for capacity quotas reflects that Indonesia has no polysilicon/steel/EV overcapacity of its own to ration; it would instead reach for tariffs, safeguards and TKDN — which it is already doing.

**Vektor Transmisi**

> (a) DIRECT ENTRY OF CHINESE PLAYERS carrying Chinese compliance DNA — TikTok Shop/ByteDance, Shopee (Sea, but built on a Chinese playbook and with heavy Chinese-market benchmarking), J&T Express (founded by ex-Oppo Indonesia management, Chinese-model logistics), BYD/Chery/Wuling/Geely, and Chinese solar and battery investors.
> These firms internalize Chinese rules first — a Chinese platform that has already removed late-delivery fines and implemented fatigue pauses domestically can port the same product logic to Indonesia at near-zero cost, and often does so preemptively to avoid regulatory risk.
(b) LOCAL COPYCAT REGULATION / POLICY DIFFUSION — the strongest vector here.
> Indonesian ministries (Komdigi, Kemenhub, Kementerian UMKM, Kemnaker), KPPU and DPR staff actively study Chinese and EU precedents.
> Permen Komdigi 8/2025's cost-plus tariff floor for courier services is functionally the Chinese State Post Bureau model; Permen UMKM 3/2026's fee-transparency mandate mirrors SAMR's fee-disclosure requirements.
> Expect more direct borrowing as the new Labour Law is drafted.
(c) ALGORITHMIC / CONTENT DIFFUSION — Chinese-language and Chinese-origin discourse about 内卷, '困在系统里' (trapped in the system), rider deaths and 'lying flat' circulates through Indonesian TikTok, X and YouTube, seeding public expectation that platforms are exploitative and that the state should intervene.
> This shapes the political demand side even without formal policy transfer.
(d) CHINESE VENTURE AND STATE CAPITAL — Tencent and Alibaba stakes in GoTo/Sea, Chinese LPs in Southeast Asian funds, and now Danantara's involvement in the Grab-GoTo consolidation.
> Capital that has lived through the Chinese crackdown prices regulatory risk into deal structures and pushes portfolio companies toward profitability over share-buying, effectively transmitting the anti-involution norm through the cap table.
(e) DIASPORA / ALUMNI AND MULTILATERAL CHANNELS — Indonesian officials and academics trained in or exposed to Chinese regulatory practice; ILO, ASEAN and G20 platform-work workstreams that carry both the Chinese and the EU Platform Work Directive models; Chinese-Indonesian business networks in logistics and manufacturing.
(f) A SIXTH, NON-CHINESE VECTOR THAT MATTERS: the EU Platform Work Directive (EU 2024/2831, in force 1 Dec 2024, transposition deadline 2 Dec 2026) with its rebuttable presumption of employment and algorithmic-management chapter.
> Indonesian drafters are likely to blend the EU presumption-of-employment approach with Chinese algorithm-governance mechanics — a hybrid that neither source country has.

### Faktor Pendorong

**Prasyarat Struktural**

> For the destructive-competition phase to arrive (it largely has): smartphone penetration above ~60% of population, urban density sufficient for sub-30-minute delivery economics, and abundant cheap labor with weak formal-sector absorption.
> Indonesia: ~79-80% internet penetration and ~58% urbanization (2025), against China's ~65% internet penetration and ~59% urbanization when its O2O subsidy war peaked in 2015 — Indonesia is at or past the threshold.
For the ANTI-involution regulatory response to arrive, four conditions matter: (1) VISIBLE MACRO PAIN attributable to price wars.
> China's trigger was 40 months of PPI deflation, 22%+ loss-making industrial firms, and shrinking industrial profits.
> Indonesia lacks a deflation crisis (CPI has been low but positive; PPI is not in a multi-year slump), so the macro trigger is weaker — Indonesian intervention is driven instead by distributive politics (driver and UMKM anger), which is a faster but shallower trigger.
> (2) STATE CAPACITY AND LEGAL INSTRUMENTS.
> China had SAMR with pre-emptive summons power, a Price Law, a national standards body able to issue GB/T service standards, and CAC's algorithm filing regime.
> Indonesia's KPPU lacks pre-merger notification, has never won a digital predatory-pricing case, and there is no Indonesian equivalent of the algorithm filing regime — this is the binding constraint.
> (3) ORGANIZED WORKER VOICE.
> China used the ACFTU as the counterparty for algorithm bargaining.
> Indonesia has genuinely independent ojol unions (SPAI, Garda, and others) with mobilization power but no statutory collective-bargaining seat for partner-status workers — the MK-mandated Labour Law is the vehicle to create one.
> (4) FISCAL AND POLITICAL WILLINGNESS TO ACCEPT SHORT-TERM CONSUMER PAIN.
> Anti-involution raises consumer prices.
> China accepted this because deflation was the bigger enemy.
> Indonesia, with a squeezed middle class and weak purchasing power in 2025-2026, has less tolerance — this is the main reason to expect Indonesian rules to be labor-side (commission caps) rather than price-side (price floors).
Threshold indicators worth watching for Indonesia: GDP per capita ~USD 5,000 (2025) vs China's ~USD 8,000 in 2015 and ~USD 13,000 in 2024 when anti-involution launched; formal-sector employment share stuck near 40%; e-commerce GMV growth decelerating into single digits (the classic precondition for share wars turning destructive).

**Indikator Pemantauan**

> Regulatory leading indicators: (1) whether the RUU Ketenagakerjaan passed by the 31 Oct 2026 MK deadline contains an explicit platform-work chapter — look for the terms 'transparansi algoritma', 'penonaktifan akun/deactivation', 'penilaian kinerja otomatis' and 'pelindungan data pekerja'; (2) issuance of Kemenhub's revised Kepmenhub replacing KP 1001/2022 to operationalize the 8% cap, and whether it adds working-hour or fatigue provisions; (3) whether Komdigi actually invokes its Permen 8/2025 power to set a temporary courier tariff floor (the 6-month temporary-floor clause being used at all is the signal); (4) KPPU moving from post-merger to pre-merger notification, or opening a formal predatory-pricing case against a platform rather than an inquiry; (5) BSN issuing an Indonesian SNI service standard for food/instant delivery analogous to GB/T 46862-2025; (6) any Indonesian rule requiring algorithm disclosure or filing (there is currently none).
Market leading indicators: (7) resolution of the Grab-GoTo merger and whether KPPU imposes behavioral remedies on commissions, driver incentives or merchant fees; (8) the trajectory of e-commerce seller fees after Permen UMKM 3/2026 — renewed increases would signal enforcement failure; (9) GAIKINDO/Kemenperin statements on EV discounting and any move toward minimum-pricing or anti-dumping action against imported EVs; (10) further BMTP/anti-dumping petitions in textiles, ceramics, steel; (11) courier tariff levels in high-volume corridors (Jabodetabek-Bandung-Surabaya) approaching or falling below cost; (12) job-posting volume for 'competition compliance', 'regulatory affairs', 'algorithm governance' and 'ESG/labor compliance' roles at Indonesian platforms; (13) driver union strike frequency and whether demands shift from tariff/commission to algorithmic issues (order allocation fairness, account suspension) — that shift is the tell that Indonesia has reached China's 2020-2021 stage.

### Hambatan & Faktor Pembatal

**Hambatan Transfer**

> (1) INSTITUTIONAL FRAGMENTATION.
> China concentrated authority in SAMR/NDRC/MIIT/CAC with a Politburo mandate.
> Indonesia splits jurisdiction across Kemenhub (tariffs and ojol), Kemnaker (labor), Komdigi (platforms and post), Kementerian UMKM (seller protection), KPPU (competition) and Kemendag — producing the exact pathology already visible with Perpres 27/2026, where a presidential decree existed for months without the implementing Kemenhub rule needed to make it bite.
> (2) NO PRE-MERGER CONTROL AND WEAK ANTITRUST CASE LAW.
> KPPU's post-merger notification regime and its documented difficulty proving predatory pricing in digital markets (cross-subsidization, algorithmic pricing, opaque cost structures) mean the price-side of anti-involution has no viable enforcement channel today.
> (3) CONSUMER-WELFARE POLITICS.
> Free shipping and discounts are politically popular with a middle class already squeezed by weak purchasing power; any price floor is framed as making life more expensive.
> China could override this because the alternative was deflation; Indonesia cannot make that argument.
> (4) FISCAL AND INVESTMENT DEPENDENCE.
> Indonesia is actively courting Chinese EV, battery, solar and textile investment; aggressive anti-dumping or price-floor action against Chinese-linked players carries FDI cost.
> (5) PARTNERSHIP-STATUS LEGAL FICTION.
> Indonesian platform work is structured as 'kemitraan', outside the Labour Law entirely; until MK 168's mandate is legislated, most protective instruments have no legal hook.
> (6) INFORMALITY AND ENFORCEMENT REACH.
> With ~60% of employment informal and a low-capacity labor inspectorate, rules that require monitoring working hours per worker are close to unenforceable outside big platforms.
> (7) DATA OPACITY.
> Indonesia has no equivalent of China's algorithm filing regime or mandatory platform data reporting, so regulators cannot verify compliance even where rules exist.

**Faktor Pembatal Transfer**

> Several structural features mean the Chinese model will NOT arrive in Indonesia in the same form.
> (1) NO DOMESTIC OVERCAPACITY TO RATION.
> The industrial half of anti-involution — output quotas for steel, polysilicon, batteries, EVs; capacity-retirement funds; MIIT two-year sectoral plans — presupposes that the country OWNS the excess capacity.
> Indonesia does not; it imports the consequences of someone else's.
> Indonesia's functional equivalent will therefore be trade defense (BMTP safeguards, anti-dumping duties, TKDN, import licensing), not domestic capacity governance.
> (2) ARCHIPELAGIC GEOGRAPHY AND LOGISTICS COST STRUCTURE.
> China's express price war was possible because dense inland networks pushed marginal cost toward RMB 1.2/parcel.
> Indonesia's inter-island logistics cost floor is structurally high and heterogeneous, which limits how far below cost anyone can profitably go, but also makes a single national price floor economically incoherent — Indonesia will need zonal tariffs (which Permen Komdigi 8/2025 partly anticipates) rather than one number.
> (3) SCALE.
> China's 60 billion instant-delivery orders in 2025 and 553 million food-delivery users create the density that makes 30-minute delivery and its associated rider brutality viable.
> Indonesia's order density outside Jabodetabek, Bandung, Surabaya and Medan is an order of magnitude thinner, so the 'trapped in the system' extreme of algorithmic time compression will be milder and more geographically confined.
> (4) NO SINGLE-PARTY ENFORCEMENT MACHINE.
> China's ability to summon seven platforms and obtain compliance pledges within an hour, or to have all three delivery majors 'voluntarily' adopt a recommended standard, has no Indonesian analogue.
> Indonesian compliance will be slower, more litigated, and more partial.
> (5) NO STATE-CONTROLLED UNION FEDERATION.
> The ACFTU's role as the algorithm-bargaining counterparty is unreplicable; Indonesia's unions are plural and adversarial, which may actually yield stronger bargaining but far slower institutionalization.
> (6) POLITICAL BUSINESS CYCLE.
> Indonesian intervention arrives in populist bursts tied to May Day and electoral calendars rather than as a multi-year technocratic campaign, so expect headline instruments (an 8% cap) without the surrounding machinery (algorithm filing, standards, cost accounting).

### Prediksi Timeline di Indonesia

**Tahun Masuk Indonesia**

> Already arrived, in two waves.
> Wave 1 (sectoral, 2025-2026): Permen Komdigi 8/2025 (courier tariff formula and temporary floors), Perpres 27/2026 (commission cap and social insurance, effective 1 June 2026), Permen UMKM 3/2026 (platform fee transparency, 17 June 2026), plus continued BMTP safeguards.
> Wave 2 (systemic, 2026-2027): the new Labour Law due by 31 October 2026 and its implementing regulations, which is where algorithmic governance and working-hour protection would enter.
> Treat 2025 as the entry year for anti-involution regulation in Indonesia and 2026 as the year it became visible national policy.

**Skenario Percepatan**

> Acceleration triggers: (1) a high-profile ojol driver death or mass-casualty event attributed to algorithmic time pressure, which is what '外卖骑手，困在系统里' did in China in Sept 2020; (2) Grab-GoTo merger completion forcing KPPU into emergency behavioral remedies; (3) a wave of UMKM seller exits from marketplaces after another fee round, generating parliamentary pressure; (4) a mass layoff event in textiles, ceramics or steel traced to dumped Chinese imports, pushing anti-dumping action into headline politics; (5) the 31 Oct 2026 MK deadline itself, which forces the Labour Law through regardless of readiness; (6) the EU Platform Work Directive transposition deadline of 2 Dec 2026 creating an international benchmark Indonesian drafters can copy; (7) a presidential decision to make platform-worker welfare a signature program ahead of the 2029 electoral cycle.

### Dampak Sosial-Ekonomi

**Dampak Lapangan Kerja**

> JOBS DESTROYED OR DEVALUED BY INVOLUTION ITSELF (the problem being regulated): ojol driver real income erosion as driver supply grows faster than orders — Indonesia already shows the Chinese pattern of 3.7 million registered but only ~700,000-800,000 monthly-active drivers, i.e.
> massive latent oversupply that suppresses per-trip earnings; UMKM seller margins compressed to nothing by platform fee escalation and forced discounting, with brand owners exiting marketplaces; small restaurant and warung margins squeezed by delivery commissions plus mandatory promotion participation — in China per-meal spending fell 23.6% and merchant income fell ~15%; and formal manufacturing jobs destroyed by dumped imports — 47,115 Indonesian textile-sector layoffs in Jan-Oct 2025 alone.
JOBS CHANGED BY THE REGULATION: platform operations roles shift from growth-hacking and subsidy optimization toward compliance, unit economics and merchant success; algorithm and data-science teams acquire an audit and explainability workload; courier network managers must manage to a tariff floor and cost-plus formula rather than to volume at any price; HR/partner-relations functions at Gojek, Grab, Shopee, J&T and SPX must build social-insurance administration and grievance/appeal processes for deactivation.
JOBS CREATED: competition-law and regulatory-affairs specialists (currently scarce in Indonesia); algorithm auditors and AI-governance officers; platform-labor relations and collective-bargaining professionals; cost-accounting and tariff-modelling analysts for the Komdigi cost-plus formula; BPJS/insurance intermediation for gig workers; trade-remedy lawyers and economists for BMTP/anti-dumping petitions; labor inspectors with digital-forensics capability; and, on the state side, a plausible new Indonesian equivalent of SAMR's price-supervision cadre.
NET: anti-involution regulation is mildly job-DESTROYING in the short run (fewer subsidized orders means fewer marginal driver-hours; higher courier tariffs mean lower parcel volumes) and job-QUALITY-improving in the medium run (higher earnings per hour, social insurance, fewer accidents).
> China's own experience shows the trade-off: order volume growth decelerated after subsidy bans, but riders gained pension subsidies and lost the late-fine regime.

**Dampak Kelas Menengah**

> Ambiguous and politically dangerous.
> The Indonesian middle class has been the primary BENEFICIARY of involution — cheap ojol rides, free shipping, subsidized food delivery, and now cheap Chinese EVs are a significant real-income subsidy at a time when middle-class purchasing power is weak and the middle class itself is shrinking.
> Anti-involution regulation directly removes that subsidy: an 8% commission cap raises fares or reduces platform incentives to discount; a courier tariff floor raises shipping costs; a subsidy ban ends the promo economy.
> This is the single biggest political risk of the policy and the reason Indonesia may adopt labor-side rules faster than price-side rules — the former can be framed as taking money from foreign platforms, the latter visibly takes money from consumers.
On the other side, a large and growing share of the Indonesian middle and lower-middle class IS the supply side: ~7 million registered online-transport partners, a majority over 36 and half of them previously laid off or without income, plus millions of UMKM sellers.
> For this group, anti-involution is a direct income transfer.
> It also protects the aspirational-middle-class path of running a small brand or warung, which pure platform involution destroys by making the platform the only viable channel and then taxing it.
Third effect: the middle class as EMPLOYEES of formal manufacturing (textiles, ceramics, steel, automotive components) is being hollowed out by imported involution; trade-defense measures protect these jobs at the cost of higher goods prices — the same trade-off in a different market.

**Dampak Daerah Non Jawa**

> Highly asymmetric, and this is where Indonesian policy must diverge most sharply from China's.
> (1) DELIVERY/RIDE-HAILING INVOLUTION IS A JAVA-AND-BIG-CITY PHENOMENON.
> Order density sufficient to produce the Chinese-style algorithmic time-compression trap exists mainly in Jabodetabek, Bandung, Surabaya, Semarang, Medan, Makassar and Denpasar.
> Outside these, drivers suffer from too FEW orders, not too many under too much time pressure.
> A uniform national working-hour cap or fatigue rule would be irrelevant or even harmful in low-density regions where drivers need long hours to reach subsistence.
> (2) COURIER TARIFF FLOORS CUT BOTH WAYS FOR THE REGIONS.
> Permen Komdigi 8/2025's stated purpose is affordability and service reach to remote areas; a cost-plus formula that permits higher tariffs for eastern Indonesia can improve service availability, but a national floor set at Java's cost level would price out UMKM sellers in Papua, Maluku, NTT and inland Kalimantan whose only market access is e-commerce.
> Zonal tariffs, not a single floor, are the right design.
> (3) UMKM FEE PROTECTION MATTERS MOST OUTSIDE JAVA, because for regional sellers the marketplace is not one channel among many — it is the entire channel.
> A 15x jump in the per-item commission ceiling hits a Makassar or Pontianak seller far harder than a Jakarta seller with offline distribution.
> (4) IMPORTED INVOLUTION IN MANUFACTURING is concentrated in West Java, Central Java and Banten (textiles), so trade-defense benefits are Java-centric, while the consumer cost of tariffs is borne nationally.
> (5) EV price wars are almost entirely Java-metro, given charging infrastructure distribution.
Policy implication: Indonesia should build differentiated, region-aware instruments from the start — something China, as a contiguous landmass with a unified-national-market doctrine, deliberately did NOT do.

### Kaitan Pendidikan

**Jurusan Terancam**

> No major is destroyed by this trend; the threat is to CURRICULA that are obsolete rather than to fields.
> Specifically at risk of irrelevance: (1) conventional Marketing and Business Management programs built around growth-at-any-cost, customer-acquisition-cost and burn-rate logic — the entire 'blitzscaling' orthodoxy taught in Indonesian business schools since the 2015-2021 startup era is precisely what regulators are now criminalizing; (2) Ilmu Hukum programs teaching Competition Law (Hukum Persaingan Usaha) purely through the 1999 Law No.
> 5 framework of physical-market cartels and price-fixing, with no treatment of algorithmic pricing, cross-subsidization, multi-sided markets or below-cost digital pricing; (3) Ilmu Hukum Ketenagakerjaan taught exclusively around the standard employment relationship (PKWT/PKWTT), which cannot see partnership-status platform work at all — and which the new Labour Law will render partially obsolete; (4) Transport/Logistics Management programs teaching freight tariffs as a pure market-clearing outcome rather than a regulated cost-plus structure; (5) Ekonomi Pembangunan curricula that treat FDI and cheap imports as unambiguously welfare-enhancing, with no framework for dumped overcapacity; (6) traditional Public Administration (Administrasi Negara) with no digital-regulation or standards-setting content.

**Jurusan Dibutuhkan**

> (1) DIGITAL COMPETITION LAW AND ECONOMICS — lawyers and economists who can actually prove predatory pricing in a multi-sided market, which is exactly the capability KPPU currently lacks; this requires industrial organization, econometrics and platform cost accounting, not just doctrinal law.
> (2) ALGORITHM GOVERNANCE AND AUDITING — technical-legal hybrids able to audit dispatch, pricing and ranking algorithms for fairness, safety and compliance; China's CAC algorithm filing regime and the EU AI Act/Platform Work Directive both create this profession, and Indonesia will need it the moment any disclosure rule passes.
> (3) PLATFORM LABOR RELATIONS AND SOCIAL PROTECTION DESIGN — actuarial and policy skills for extending BPJS-style coverage to non-employees, plus collective-bargaining capability for partner-status workers.
> (4) REGULATORY ECONOMICS AND TARIFF MODELLING — cost-of-service studies, zonal tariff design, and the impact assessment that Permen Komdigi 8/2025 explicitly requires (market review, cost study, social impact, financial performance, service sustainability).
> (5) TRADE REMEDY AND INDUSTRIAL POLICY ANALYSIS — dumping margin calculation, injury analysis, safeguard petitions, TKDN verification.
> (6) OCCUPATIONAL SAFETY AND HEALTH FOR MOBILE/GIG WORK — road-safety epidemiology, fatigue science, telematics-based risk management.
> (7) DATA SCIENCE FOR REGULATORY SUPERVISION (RegTech/SupTech) — building the state's ability to ingest platform data.
> (8) POLICY EVALUATION / RCT AND QUASI-EXPERIMENTAL METHODS, so Indonesia can actually measure whether an 8% cap raised driver incomes or just shifted the squeeze elsewhere.

### Pelajaran Kebijakan dari China

**Respons Kebijakan China**

> China's instrument set, in the order a country should consider adopting it (this is the core preemptive-policy menu for Indonesia):
A.
> COMPETITION / PRICE INSTRUMENTS.
> (1) Amend the general pricing law to define below-cost dumping operationally and to explicitly cover algorithmic pricing, data abuse and price discrimination — China's Price Law amendment (draft 24 July 2025, NDRC+SAMR, first revision in 27 years).
> (2) Add platform-specific provisions to the unfair-competition statute prohibiting platforms from compelling merchants to sell below cost or to join promotions — China's revised Anti-Unfair Competition Law (adopted June 2025, in force 15 Oct 2025).
> (3) Issue sector rules banning long-duration, large-scale subsidies, banning coercive cost-sharing with merchants and riders, and requiring advance notice (7 days in the Chinese draft) before promotions — SAMR's June/September 2025 food-delivery rules.
> (4) Internet Platform Pricing Rules (NDRC+SAMR+CAC, issued 9 Dec 2025) covering platform pricing conduct.
> (5) Use regulatory summons (约谈) as a fast, pre-litigation compliance tool — SAMR summoned the delivery majors repeatedly in 2025 and seven platforms again on 13 Feb 2026, obtaining same-day compliance pledges.
> (6) Publish 'top-ten involutionary competition enforcement cases' annually as a deterrence and norm-setting device (SAMR, Jan 2026).
B.
> SUPPLY-CHAIN FINANCE INSTRUMENTS.
> (7) Cap payment terms to SME suppliers at 60 days by regulation (China, effective 1 June 2025), with a 7-working-day acceptance deadline for goods, and extend it sector by sector (autos June 2025 → batteries 2026 → energy storage 2026).
> This is the cheapest, highest-leverage anti-involution tool: it removes the supplier float that finances price wars.
C.
> INDUSTRIAL CAPACITY INSTRUMENTS (least transferable to Indonesia).
> (8) MIIT two-year plans for 10 key industries with output targets below prior-year levels; (9) administrative output cuts (Tangshan steel ~30%); (10) industry-funded capacity-retirement vehicles (proposed RMB 50bn polysilicon fund to retire 1m+ of 3.5m tonnes); (11) capacity monitoring and early-warning systems for batteries.
D.
> LOGISTICS PRICE FLOORS.
> (12) Administrative per-parcel price floors set provincially against a costed benchmark (Guangdong RMB 1.4; Yiwu RMB 1.1→1.2), enforced with real penalties (Yunda and Baishi had sorting centres partially suspended for below-cost dumping), backed by industry-association self-discipline pledges.
E.
> LABOR AND ALGORITHM INSTRUMENTS (most transferable).
> (13) Abolish late-delivery fines and replace punitive deduction with points/training systems (Meituan committed Dec 2024, completed across major platforms by 2026).
> (14) Issue a national service standard with hard safety parameters — GB/T 46862-2025: ≤8 hours order-taking per day in principle with explicit rider confirmation to continue, fatigue alert plus mandatory 20-minute dispatch pause after 4 continuous hours, delivery-time estimation constrained by safe speed (e-bike average ≤15 km/h), red lights pausing the clock, algorithms required to account for traffic/weather/restaurant prep time, ban on forcing merchants into promotions, social insurance where an employment relationship exists.
> (15) Algorithm negative list plus mandatory disclosure — CAC's 'Life Service Platform Algorithm Negative List (Trial)', Jan 2026, producing 63 optimization measures and 139 compliance commitments from major platforms.
> (16) Occupational-injury insurance for platform workers (pilot from 2022) and platform-funded pension subsidies (Meituan: 50% premium subsidy for riders meeting an income threshold in 3 of the past 6 months; national coverage from 27 Oct 2025; RMB 2.77bn premiums and ~17.28m registrations by Feb 2026; JD paying full five insurances plus housing fund for full-time riders from 1 March 2025).
> (17) The capstone: CPC Central Committee + State Council framework for 'new employment groups' (26 April 2026) — standardized contracts, pay at or above local minimum wage, holiday premiums, union-negotiated caps on maximum consecutive order-taking and daily hours with mandatory dispatch cut-off, and the algorithm itself as a subject of collective bargaining; full compliance by 2027.
F.
> FISCAL FEDERALISM INSTRUMENT.
> (18) Unified national market drive plus a negative list for local fiscal subsidies (announced 2026), restricting local governments from bidding against one another with tax breaks, subsidies and procurement favoritism — the root cause of much duplicated capacity.
WHAT INDONESIA CAN ADOPT PREEMPTIVELY, ranked by cost-effectiveness: the 60-day SME payment cap (cheap, popular, no consumer price effect); the ban on coercive merchant promotion participation and mandatory fee-change notice periods (extends Permen UMKM 3/2026 from disclosure to conduct); the fatigue/working-hour and safe-speed service standard via BSN (an Indonesian SNI analogue of GB/T 46862-2025); the abolition of punitive late-delivery deductions; algorithm disclosure and a deactivation due-process right; and regulatory summons powers with published enforcement cases for KPPU/Komdigi.
> Indonesia should be far more cautious about administrative price floors on consumer-facing services and should skip capacity quotas entirely.

**Rekomendasi Kebijakan Indonesia**

> (1) INSERT A PLATFORM-WORK CHAPTER INTO THE NEW LABOUR LAW BEFORE THE 31 OCTOBER 2026 MK DEADLINE.
> Minimum content: a rebuttable presumption of employment based on actual control (EU Directive 2024/2831 model) or, if partnership status is retained, a statutory floor of rights attached to the work rather than the contract label; algorithm transparency; due process and a right of appeal against account deactivation; limits on automated performance scoring; worker data protection; OSH duties; and a statutory collective-bargaining seat for partner-status workers.
> This is the single highest-leverage action available and the window closes in months.
(2) OPERATIONALIZE PERPRES 27/2026 IMMEDIATELY AND CLOSE ITS GAPS.
> Issue the revised Kemenhub rule replacing KP 1001/2022 with real penalties; extend coverage from two-wheel ojol to four-wheel online taxis and to courier/instant-delivery partners (currently excluded); and add what the Perpres omits — fatigue limits, order-dispatch cut-offs, a ban on punitive late-delivery deductions, and safe-speed-constrained delivery time estimation.
(3) ISSUE AN INDONESIAN SNI SERVICE STANDARD FOR ONLINE DELIVERY, modelled on GB/T 46862-2025 but density-differentiated: fatigue alerts and dispatch pauses calibrated to metro versus low-density regions, safe-speed parameters appropriate to Indonesian road conditions, and mandatory clock-pausing for traffic conditions outside the rider's control.
(4) ADOPT THE 60-DAY SME PAYMENT CAP.
> Apply to platform payouts to merchants and to large-enterprise payments to SME suppliers in automotive, textiles and electronics.
> It is the cheapest anti-involution instrument, has no consumer-price downside, and directly protects the UMKM working capital that price wars currently expropriate.
(5) UPGRADE KPPU BEFORE, NOT AFTER, THE GRAB-GOTO OUTCOME.
> Move from post-merger to mandatory pre-merger notification with suspensory effect; create an explicit statutory basis for assessing below-cost pricing and cross-subsidization in multi-sided markets; give KPPU a summons/commitment mechanism modelled on SAMR's 约谈 so it can obtain fast behavioral remedies without full litigation; and staff a digital markets unit with economists, not only lawyers.
(6) CONVERT PERMEN UMKM 3/2026 FROM DISCLOSURE TO CONDUCT REGULATION.
> Add: minimum notice periods for any fee change (China used 7 days for promotions; 30-60 days is appropriate for structural fee changes); a ban on compelling sellers to join platform promotions or to fund free-shipping programs; and a ban on retroactive fee changes within an active campaign.
(7) USE PERMEN KOMDIGI 8/2025'S TEMPORARY TARIFF-FLOOR POWER SPARINGLY AND ZONALLY.
> Publish the cost model.
> Set floors per corridor/zone, not nationally.
> Sunset and re-evaluate every 6 months as the regulation already contemplates.
> Avoid the Chinese error of setting a single administrative number that becomes a de facto cartel price.
(8) BUILD A REGULATORY DATA PIPELINE NOW.
> Require platforms to report standardized, audited metrics — active partner counts, hours online, gross and net earnings per active hour, deactivation counts and reasons, accident rates, merchant fee take-rates, and promotion cost allocation — to a single agency.
> Without this, every rule above is unverifiable.
> Indonesia currently has no equivalent of China's algorithm filing regime; a lightweight registration-plus-reporting scheme is the practical first step.
(9) SEPARATE TRADE DEFENCE FROM PLATFORM REGULATION AND RESOURCE IT PROPERLY.
> Indonesia's exposure to Chinese involution is chiefly through dumped goods, not domestic overcapacity.
> Strengthen KADI/KPPI capacity for dumping-margin and injury analysis, keep BMTP instruments current beyond the May 2026 expiries, and pair TKDN enforcement in EVs with a credible verification regime rather than relaxation.
(10) PRE-COMMIT TO THE CONSUMER-PRICE TRADE-OFF PUBLICLY.
> Every anti-involution measure raises some price.
> Publish the expected incidence (who pays, how much) alongside each rule, and pair price-side measures with targeted support for low-income users, or the policy will be reversed at the first political cost.
(11) INSTITUTIONALIZE COORDINATION.
> Create a standing inter-ministerial platform-economy council (Komdigi, Kemenhub, Kemnaker, Kementerian UMKM, Kemendag, KPPU, BPJS) with a single secretariat.
> The Perpres 27/2026 implementation delay is a direct symptom of the coordination failure this would fix.

### Peluang & Rekomendasi Aksi

**Peluang Bisnis**

> (1) REGTECH AND COMPLIANCE SOFTWARE FOR PLATFORMS — fee-disclosure engines meeting Permen UMKM 3/2026, commission-calculation and audit tools for the 8% cap, working-hour and fatigue-tracking modules, deactivation-appeal case management, and standardized regulatory reporting.
> Every Indonesian platform will need this within 24 months and almost none has it.
> (2) ALGORITHM AUDIT AND ASSURANCE SERVICES — an entirely new professional services category in Indonesia; the Big Four and local law firms will build practices, leaving room for specialist boutiques.
> (3) GIG-WORKER FINANCIAL AND INSURANCE PRODUCTS — BPJS enrolment intermediation, income-smoothing and earned-wage-access products, motorcycle maintenance and battery-swap subscriptions, health and accident microinsurance priced on telematics; Perpres 27/2026's mandate creates instant addressable demand across millions of drivers.
> (4) DIRECT-TO-CONSUMER AND OMNICHANNEL ENABLEMENT FOR UMKM — the May 2026 fee shock is pushing brands off marketplaces toward their own websites, WhatsApp commerce and offline; Shopify-equivalents, headless commerce, payment orchestration and independent fulfilment for Indonesian SMEs is a clear opening.
> (5) INDEPENDENT LAST-MILE AND FULFILMENT NETWORKS that can operate profitably at a regulated tariff floor rather than at subsidized rates — a floor is a barrier to entry for burn-financed entrants and a gift to disciplined operators.
> (6) COST-TO-SERVE AND TARIFF ANALYTICS for the courier industry under Permen Komdigi 8/2025's cost-plus formula.
> (7) MERCHANT-SIDE MARGIN TOOLS — menu engineering, promotion ROI analytics and channel-mix optimization for F&B operators squeezed by delivery commissions (a large business in China post-price-war).
> (8) TRADE REMEDY AND TKDN ADVISORY for manufacturers facing dumped imports and for Chinese investors needing local content verification.
> (9) WORKER-VOICE AND GRIEVANCE PLATFORMS — digital infrastructure for driver unions and for platform-union bargaining, a category China built inside the ACFTU and which Indonesia will build in the private/NGO sector.
> (10) CONSOLIDATION PLAYS — as subsidies end, sub-scale players in delivery, logistics and e-commerce become acquisition targets; the Chinese post-war pivot from cash burn to supply-chain M&A (Alibaba bidding ~USD 1.5bn for Pupu; Meituan acquiring Dingdong Maicai) is the template.

**Rekomendasi Individu Mahasiswa**

> Build a hybrid regulatory-technical profile, because Indonesia has almost no one who can do both.
> Concretely: (1) learn platform/multi-sided-market economics well enough to compute unit economics and identify below-cost pricing — this alone makes you employable at KPPU, Komdigi, a platform, or a law firm; (2) learn to read and audit an algorithm at a systems level (how dispatch, pricing and ranking work, what data they use, what fairness and safety failure modes look like) — Python plus applied statistics is sufficient to start; (3) master the actual Indonesian instruments now in force: Perpres 27/2026, Permen Komdigi 8/2025, Permen UMKM 3/2026, UU 5/1999 and the forthcoming Labour Law, and be able to compare them to China's GB/T 46862-2025, the CAC algorithm negative list and the EU Platform Work Directive 2024/2831 — comparative regulatory fluency is rare and highly paid; (4) develop cost-accounting and tariff-modelling skill, since cost-plus regulation is spreading and almost nobody in Indonesia can build a defensible cost-of-service model; (5) learn impact evaluation methods so you can answer 'did the 8% cap actually raise driver incomes'; (6) if entrepreneurial, internalize the strategic lesson rather than the compliance lesson — the era of winning Indonesian markets by burning capital is ending by regulation, so build businesses with positive unit economics, defensible supply-chain positions and merchant/worker goodwill; (7) learn functional Mandarin if you intend to work in policy or industrial strategy, because the primary sources on this trend (SAMR, MIIT, NDRC documents) are Chinese-language and appear 6-18 months before English analysis.

**Rekomendasi Perguruan Tinggi**

> (1) OPEN a graduate concentration or professional certificate in DIGITAL MARKET REGULATION combining competition economics, platform law, algorithm auditing and regulatory data science — jointly run by law, economics and computer science faculties.
> There is currently no Indonesian programme producing the people KPPU, Komdigi and Kemnaker need.
> (2) REWRITE Hukum Persaingan Usaha courses to cover multi-sided markets, algorithmic pricing, cross-subsidization, below-cost digital pricing and merger remedies, using the Grab-GoTo case and the Chinese food-delivery enforcement record as live teaching material.
> (3) REWRITE Hukum Ketenagakerjaan around the MK 168 decision and the forthcoming Labour Law, with a dedicated platform-work module covering algorithmic management, deactivation due process and social protection for non-employees.
> (4) ADD a required unit-economics and regulatory-cost module to Marketing and Business Management programmes, explicitly deprecating growth-at-any-cost and blitzscaling doctrine.
> (5) ADD trade-remedy practice (dumping margin calculation, injury analysis, safeguard petitions) to International Economics and International Law programmes — Indonesia has a chronic shortage of qualified petition drafters.
> (6) BUILD cost-of-service and tariff-regulation capability inside Transport/Logistics and Public Policy programmes to serve the Permen Komdigi 8/2025 regime and its likely successors.
> (7) ESTABLISH a national Platform Economy Observatory hosted at one or more universities (UI, UGM, ITB, Unpad, Prasetiya Mulya) collecting standardized driver-earnings, merchant-fee and safety data — the evidence base that both regulators and unions currently lack, and the single most valuable public good academia can supply here.
> (8) DO NOT copy China's reflex of closing humanities and language programmes to fund technical ones; the Chinese case shows that regulatory capacity failures were legal, economic and institutional, not technical.

### Faktor Risiko & Sisi Gelap

**Dampak Negatif China**

> (1) RIDER SAFETY AND HEALTH.
> A decade of algorithmic time compression produced a documented pattern of speeding, red-light running and traffic fatalities, crystallized by the Sept 2020 investigation 'Delivery Riders, Trapped in the System' (外卖骑手，困在系统里).
> The 2025 GB/T standard's specific parameters — capping the assumed e-bike speed at 15 km/h, pausing the clock at red lights, mandating a 20-minute break after 4 continuous hours — are effectively an admission of how dangerous the prior system was.
> (2) MERCHANT DESTRUCTION.
> Restaurants were compelled into subsidized discounting they did not fund; per-capita restaurant spending fell 23.6% from 2023 to RMB 33 by Sept 2025; merchants reported ~15% income declines during the 2025 war; above-designated-size catering revenue fell 0.4% YoY in June 2025; widespread closures in major cities.
> (3) CAPITAL DESTRUCTION.
> ~RMB 157bn (~USD 22bn) burned in nine months across three platforms; Alibaba instant-retail losses ~RMB 87bn; JD new-business losses RMB 46.6bn; Meituan swung from a RMB 10.06bn quarterly profit to a RMB 6.83bn loss.
> None of this created durable consumer surplus — it bought temporary share.
> (4) MACRO DEFLATION.
> 40+ months of negative PPI, 116,428 loss-making industrial firms (>22% of the total, a 25-year high), falling industrial profits despite rising output — the clearest evidence that involution is not merely a firm-level problem but a macroeconomic one.
> (5) SUPPLIER EXPROPRIATION.
> Price wars were financed by stretching payment terms to SME suppliers far beyond 60 days, transmitting the squeeze down to the smallest, least-capitalized firms — which is why the payment cap became a headline instrument.
> (6) LABOR OVERSUPPLY AND EARNINGS EROSION.
> 7.48 million licensed ride-hail drivers with dozens of cities issuing formal 'capacity saturation warnings' telling residents not to enter the trade.
> (7) LOCAL FISCAL WASTE.
> Years of local governments bidding against each other with subsidies and tax breaks to attract duplicative EV, solar and battery capacity, now being unwound through the unified-national-market drive and a negative list for local subsidies.

**Risiko Sosial Indonesia**

> (1) A PERMANENT UNDERCLASS OF PARTNER-STATUS WORKERS.
> With ~7 million registered online-transport partners in a workforce of ~145-150 million, and half of them ex-laid-off or previously without income, ojol is already Indonesia's shock absorber exactly as delivery is China's.
> Without the new Labour Law giving them a legal status, an 8% commission cap alone will be arbitraged — platforms can restore the squeeze through incentive-scheme changes, priority-order fees, order-allocation discrimination, or by shifting volume to lower-paying order types.
> The risk is a headline victory with no change in take-home pay.
> (2) ROAD DEATHS.
> Indonesia already has extremely high motorcycle fatality rates; layering Chinese-style delivery time compression on top, without the GB/T-equivalent safe-speed and fatigue rules, is the most predictable and most lethal risk of unregulated transfer.
> Indonesia has the commission rule but NOT the safety rule — the reverse of the correct sequencing.
> (3) UMKM CHANNEL CAPTURE.
> If marketplace fee escalation continues unchecked, Indonesian micro-sellers face the Chinese merchant outcome: dependent on a channel that captures all the surplus, with the added Indonesian vulnerability that regional sellers have no offline alternative.
> (4) MONOPOLY REPLACING OLIGOPOLY.
> If Grab-GoTo completes under a post-merger notification regime with weak remedies, Indonesia could exit the subsidy war straight into a dominant-platform regime with pricing and rule-setting power over drivers, merchants and consumers simultaneously — worse than the involution it replaces, and much harder to reverse.
> Maxim and inDrive are too small to constrain it.
> (5) DEINDUSTRIALIZATION BY IMPORTED INVOLUTION.
> 47,115 textile layoffs in ten months of 2025 is the leading edge; ceramics, steel and consumer electronics are exposed.
> Chinese producers relocating into Indonesia while local mills close changes the ownership of the sector without restoring the jobs.
> (6) REGULATORY THEATRE AND DISILLUSION.
> Perpres 27/2026 was announced 1 May 2026 and by mid-2026 the 92:8 split was still not operating — a pattern of announced-but-unimplemented protection that erodes trust and radicalizes driver politics.
> (7) CONSUMER-PRICE BACKLASH.
> Any price-side intervention in a weak-purchasing-power environment risks rapid political reversal, which in turn discredits the whole anti-involution agenda.

**Unintended Consequences**

> IN CHINA: (1) Price floors and subsidy bans functioned as legalized coordination — the state effectively organized what would otherwise be a cartel, raising consumer prices and entrenching incumbents; new entrants can no longer buy share, so JD's disruptive 2025 entry would be impossible under the 2026 rules.
> (2) Capacity cuts without demand stimulus risk being self-defeating: T.
> Rowe Price's assessment is that administrative output cuts in a weak-demand economy simply shrink the economy; fixed-asset investment fell sharply after the campaign launched.
> (3) Enforcement is uneven where the target is private and fragmented — unlike the 2015-16 supply-side reform which targeted SOEs, today's overcapacity sits in private firms in EVs, batteries and solar, and polysilicon below-cost selling persisted into March 2026 despite the rules.
> (4) Abolishing late-delivery fines did not necessarily raise rider income; platforms substituted points and rating systems that can be equally coercive but are less legible to regulators.
> (5) The 60-day payment cap strained small suppliers in a different way — large firms accelerated payment to Tier-1s while pushing complexity down the chain.
> (6) Ending the subsidy war triggered consolidation and M&A, concentrating the market further (Alibaba bidding ~USD 1.5bn for Pupu; Meituan taking Dingdong Maicai) — the cure produces the dominance problem.
> (7) Public 'voluntary' compliance with a recommended (not mandatory) standard means enforcement rests on reputation, which weakens once attention moves on.
PREDICTED FOR INDONESIA: (8) The 8% cap could reduce total driver earnings if platforms respond by cutting incentive pools, raising consumer fares and losing volume, or reclassifying charges outside the capped base — the cap regulates one number in a system with many.
> (9) It may push platforms toward four-wheel and non-covered services, and toward instant-commerce courier models outside the Perpres scope.
> (10) A courier tariff floor could raise UMKM shipping costs enough to depress regional e-commerce participation, hurting exactly the sellers Permen UMKM 3/2026 protects.
> (11) Fee-transparency rules without conduct rules can produce disclosure-then-increase: platforms comply by publishing fees and then raise them anyway.
> (12) Aggressive trade defence invites Chinese retaliation or investment withdrawal at a moment when Indonesia depends on Chinese EV, battery and nickel-downstream capital.
> (13) If the Labour Law imposes employment status too bluntly, platforms may reduce partner headcount sharply, converting an underemployment problem into an unemployment problem.
> (14) Most likely of all: partial implementation produces the worst of both — higher consumer prices, no measurable worker gain, and reduced platform investment.

**Kelompok Rentan**

> (1) OJOL AND ONLINE-COURIER DRIVERS, particularly the ~700,000-800,000 monthly-active drivers who depend on it as primary income, the >50% who are over 36 and have poor formal-sector re-entry prospects, and the ~182,500 registered women partners including single mothers who face additional safety exposure and cannot work the night hours where incentives concentrate.
> (2) FOUR-WHEEL ONLINE TAXI AND INSTANT-DELIVERY COURIERS, explicitly EXCLUDED from Perpres 27/2026 — a regulatory gap that will push volume and risk toward them.
> (3) MICRO-SELLERS ON MARKETPLACES, especially outside Java where the platform is the only market access; the per-item commission ceiling rising from Rp40,000 to Rp650,000 is existential for thin-margin sellers.
> (4) SMALL WARUNG AND F&B OPERATORS compelled into promotion participation and paying commissions they cannot pass through.
> (5) TEXTILE, GARMENT AND CERAMICS WORKERS in West Java, Central Java and Banten — 47,115 TPT layoffs in ten months of 2025 — mostly women, mostly with firm-specific skills and no re-employment path.
> (6) SME SUPPLIERS to large manufacturers and to platforms, whose working capital is the hidden financing of every price war.
> (7) RECENT GRADUATES using ojol as a landing pad, who accumulate no transferable skill or formal work history and whose degree depreciates while they ride — the exact Chinese pattern where associate-degree-or-higher riders rose from 15% in 2018 to nearly 25% by 2020.
> (8) LOW-INCOME CONSUMERS who lose the promo/free-shipping subsidy if price-side rules are applied without compensating support.

### Contoh Kasus Konkret

**Kasus China**

> CASE 1 — THE 2025 FOOD DELIVERY WAR AND ITS SHUTDOWN.
> JD.com entered food delivery in Feb 2025, offering full social insurance to full-time riders as a competitive differentiator; Alibaba retaliated with Taobao Shangou; Meituan defended.
> Between May and August 2025 the three burned roughly RMB 157bn (USD 22bn) in incremental marketing over nine months.
> SAMR summoned the platforms repeatedly, published draft rules on 17 June banning long-term large-scale subsidies and coercive cost-sharing with merchants and riders and requiring 7 days' notice for promotions — all three pledged compliance within an hour.
> SAMR named the war a top-ten involutionary-competition enforcement case in Jan 2026 and summoned seven platforms again on 13 Feb 2026.
> Result: Alibaba's instant retail lost ~RMB 87bn, JD's new business ~RMB 46.6bn, Meituan swung from a RMB 10.06bn quarterly profit to a RMB 6.83bn loss, and the sector pivoted from cash burn to supply-chain M&A.
> Consumers got cheap meals for one summer; restaurants lost ~15% of income; per-meal spend fell 23.6% from 2023 to RMB 33.
CASE 2 — YIWU AND THE PARCEL PRICE FLOOR.
> Yiwu, handling ~10% of China's parcel volume, saw per-parcel prices fall to RMB 1.2 against an industry cost benchmark of ~RMB 1.4.
> Yunda and Baishi were penalized by the Yiwu Postal Administration for below-cost dumping with partial suspension of sorting centres; Zhejiang raised the Yiwu floor from RMB 1.1 to RMB 1.2 and Guangdong set RMB 1.4, with provincial associations in Beijing, Fujian, Hebei and Baoji issuing self-discipline pledges.
> This is the clearest working example of an administrative price floor in a platform-adjacent service industry.
CASE 3 — GB/T 46862-2025 AND THE ALGORITHM.
> Approved by SAMR in Dec 2025: order-taking capped at 8 hours/day in principle with explicit rider confirmation required to continue, a fatigue alert and mandatory 20-minute dispatch pause after 4 continuous hours, delivery time estimated at a safe speed with e-bike average speed capped at 15 km/h, the delivery clock pausing at red lights, algorithms required to factor traffic, weather and restaurant prep time, a prohibition on forcing merchants into promotions, and social insurance where an employment relationship exists.
> Meituan, JD Waimai and Taobao Shangou all announced voluntary adoption.
> Paired with the CAC 'Life Service Platform Algorithm Negative List (Trial)' of Jan 2026 (63 optimization measures, 139 compliance commitments) and the CPC/State Council 'new employment groups' framework of 26 April 2026 — 200m+ workers, union-negotiated hour caps with mandatory dispatch cut-off, minimum-wage floor, algorithm as a subject of collective bargaining, full compliance by 2027.
CASE 4 — THE 60-DAY PAYMENT CAP.
> Revised SME payment regulation effective 1 June 2025; 17 major automakers pledged compliance in June 2025 with MIIT backing the same day; average auto payment cycles fell ~10 days within a year; extended to batteries (CATL, BYD, CALB) and energy storage in 2026.
CASE 5 — POLYSILICON.
> ~3.5 million tonnes of capacity against a proposed RMB 50bn (USD 6.4bn) NDRC/MIIT-endorsed fund to retire 1m+ tonnes; monthly output fell 8.3% MoM in Jan 2026 and 17.3% MoM in Feb 2026 — yet prices still fell 13%+ year-to-date by March 2026, demonstrating that capacity governance without demand support does not restore prices.

**Padanan Indonesia**

> Indonesia's equivalents already exist and are unusually advanced on the labor side.
> (1) PERPRES 27/2026 (announced 1 May 2026 at Monas, effective 1 June 2026): commission cap cut from a 20% ceiling to 8%, mandated 92:8 revenue split, JKN and JKK coverage, THR/BHR — a blunter and more directly redistributive instrument than anything China has issued, since China never capped platform take-rates.
> Implementation lagged: by June 2026 the 92:8 split was still not running, and Gojek and Grab targeted 1 July 2026 for two-wheel passenger transport.
> Covers ojol only, not four-wheel or courier work, and is silent on algorithms and working hours.
> (2) PERMEN KOMDIGI 8/2025 on commercial postal services: cost-plus tariff formula (labor, transport, application/technology, partner facilities, individual partners), government power to set temporary tariff floors/ceilings for up to 6 months, evaluation on five criteria — functionally the Chinese State Post Bureau price-floor model, but issued preemptively rather than after a Yiwu-scale collapse.
> (3) PERMEN UMKM 3/2026 (17 June 2026) on protection of micro and small enterprises in e-commerce: mandatory disclosure of all seller-facing fees, calculation mechanisms and payment methods, after the UMKM Minister summoned Shopee, Tokopedia and TikTok Shop in May 2026 and ordered a freeze on fee increases, with KPPU to be involved — the Indonesian analogue of SAMR's platform-fee rules, at the disclosure stage rather than the conduct stage.
> (4) MK 168/PUU-XXI/2023 and the RUU Ketenagakerjaan due 31 Oct 2026 — the vehicle that could deliver Indonesia's version of the April 2026 CPC/State Council framework.
> (5) GRAB-GOTO / KPPU: the Indonesian analogue of SAMR's platform summonses, except that KPPU's post-merger notification regime means it can only threaten to unwind rather than pre-clear, with Danantara state capital complicating the politics.
> (6) BMTP SAFEGUARDS AND TKDN: Indonesia's substitute for capacity governance — safeguard duties on synthetic staple yarn and on curtains/blinds running to May 2026, PMK 48 and 49/2024 on fabric and floor coverings for three years, CBU EV import tax breaks ended 31 Dec 2025 with 40% TKDN required from 2026 rising toward 60%.
> (7) MISSING ENTIRELY: any Indonesian equivalent of GB/T 46862-2025 (fatigue, safe speed, dispatch cut-off), of the CAC algorithm negative list or filing regime, of the 60-day SME payment cap, or of a general below-cost-pricing statute.
> These four gaps define the preemptive-policy agenda.

### Tingkat Keyakinan & Kualitas Sumber

**Catatan Kontradiksi Data**

> (1) INDONESIAN DRIVER COUNTS ARE INCONSISTENT AND DEFINITIONALLY CONFUSED.
> Sources variously report >7 million online-transport partners nationally, 3.7 million registered with only ~20% active, ~700,000-800,000 monthly-active drivers, ~850,000 slated for the 2026 BHR, and a Coordinating Ministry figure of ~400,000 each for Grab and Gojek plus ~51,000 for Maxim and ~500 for inDrive.
> These cannot all be measuring the same thing — 'registered accounts', 'partners with at least one trip per month', and 'primary-income drivers' differ by an order of magnitude, and one report (3.7 million) appears to be a single platform's registration base rather than a national total.
> Treat any single Indonesian driver number with suspicion; the defensible range for genuinely active primary-income ojol drivers is roughly 0.7-1.5 million with several million more using it as supplementary income.
> (2) CHINA'S '84 MILLION' FIGURE is often quoted as the number of delivery riders; it is actually the total in 'new forms of employment' (truckers, ride-hail drivers, couriers and delivery riders) from the Ninth National Workforce Survey.
> The delivery-rider figure is 13+ million; the April 2026 framework's '200 million+ platform workers' uses a still broader definition.
> (3) THE ANTI-INVOLUTION CAMPAIGN'S EFFECTIVENESS IS GENUINELY DISPUTED.
> Industrial profits rebounded +15.2% YoY in Jan-Feb 2026, the strongest start since 2018, which is cited as success; but polysilicon prices still fell 13%+ year-to-date by March 2026 with below-cost selling persisting, fixed-asset investment fell sharply after the campaign launched, and T.
> Rowe Price argues administrative cuts without demand stimulus are self-defeating and that today's overcapacity sits in private firms rather than the SOEs targeted in 2015-16.
> Both the 'it worked' and 'it cannot work' readings are supportable from 2026 data.
> (4) SUBSIDY-WAR LOSS FIGURES VARY: ~RMB 150bn versus ~RMB 156.8bn burned depending on whether the window is nine months or the calendar year and whether incremental or total marketing spend is measured.
> (5) PERPRES 27/2026 STATUS IS CONTESTED: signed and announced 1 May 2026, stated effective 1 June 2026, but multiple June-July 2026 reports say the 92:8 split was not operating and that Kemenhub had not revised the underlying Kepmenhub; Gojek and Grab separately signalled 1 July 2026 for two-wheel passenger transport.
> The rule exists on paper; its operative date is unclear.
> (6) GB/T 46862-2025 IS A RECOMMENDED (推荐性) NATIONAL STANDARD, not a mandatory one — platforms adopted it 'voluntarily'.
> Sources describing it as a binding requirement overstate its legal force.
> (7) GRAB-GOTO MERGER STATUS is reported inconsistently across 2026 sources (momentum, consultation, no formal KPPU notification); nothing in the sources reviewed confirms completion.

## 21. Embodied AI & Humanoid Robotics (具身智能 / 人形机器人) — the convergence of large AI models with physical robot bodies: general-purpose humanoids, quadruped 'robodogs', wheeled mobile manipulators, dexterous robotic hands, and the Vision-Language-Action (VLA) model stack plus the data-collection/'robot training ground' service layer that feeds them
**Kategori**: Teknologi (Technology / Frontier Industry) — with primary spillovers into Industri & Manufaktur (factory labor and industrial policy), Ketenagakerjaan (labor displacement and new job categories), and Pendidikan Tinggi & Vokasi (new degree programs, curriculum restructuring, vocational retooling). Functionally it is the 'second stage' of the Smart Manufacturing / Industry 4.0 track: fixed industrial automation was stage one, general-purpose embodied agents are stage two.
