> The incentive structure rewards video virality over reliability, and buyers who purchased on the strength of a demo are the ones now reporting dissatisfaction.

(4) THE TRAINING-GROUND LABOUR PARADOX.
> Thousands of young workers in Beijing, Hefei and elsewhere are employed on modest wages to repetitively demonstrate menial tasks — folding, sorting, bolting, bed-making — so that models can learn to do them.
> This is precarious, monotonous, dead-end work whose explicit purpose is to eliminate the category of work it belongs to.
> It is also temporary: demand collapses once models generalise.
> A cohort of young workers is being trained into an occupation with a built-in expiry date.

(5) DISPLACEMENT PRESSURE, SO FAR MASKED.
> Chinese reporting frames humanoid deployment as filling jobs nobody wants — garment factories cannot recruit or retain workers, and annual attrition exceeds robot-substituted positions.
> That is true today because China's demographic decline is doing the displacing.
> But the framing conveniently defers the question of what happens when substitution outpaces attrition, and it exports a dangerously misleading narrative to countries like Indonesia where the demographic conditions are inverted.

(6) STRATEGIC DEPENDENCY DESPITE APPARENT DOMINANCE.
> Per MERICS: continued dependence on Nvidia AI chips and the CUDA ecosystem; continued reliance on US research for VLA-model breakthroughs; and roughly 90% of precision ball screws sourced from Schaeffler, THK and NSK.
> China dominates units shipped while remaining exposed at the two highest-value chokepoints — the intelligence layer and the highest-precision mechanics.

(7) SURVEILLANCE AND DATA ACCUMULATION.
> Humanoids and quadrupeds are mobile, camera- and microphone-equipped, always-on sensor platforms operating in factories, hospitals, homes and public space.
> Their normalisation in China expands the ambient surveillance surface enormously, and the data-lifecycle provisions in HEIS 2026 govern quality and safety more than they constrain collection.

(8) LOCAL-GOVERNMENT FISCAL STRAIN.
> Provincial and municipal competition to host humanoid clusters — funds, parks, training grounds, subsidised scenarios — replicates the fiscal pattern that left local governments over-committed in the EV, solar and semiconductor waves.

**Risiko Sosial Indonesia**

> (1) DISPLACEMENT WITHOUT COMPENSATING JOB CREATION — the central risk, and the way Indonesia's exposure differs fundamentally from China's.
> China displaces factory workers but creates over a million upstream jobs designing, building, training and servicing robots.
> Indonesia will import finished robots and create only a downstream sliver of service and maintenance roles.
> The trend is therefore likely to be net employment-negative for Indonesia in a way it is not for China — and it arrives on top of premature deindustrialisation already in progress (manufacturing GDP share down from ~32% to 18-19%; formal employment elasticity collapsed from 1.77% to 0.58%; ~60 textile factories closed 2022-2024 affecting ~250,000 workers).
> Robots would be accelerating a fire that is already burning.

(2) SAFETY AND LIABILITY VACUUM.
> Indonesia has no SNI for mobile or collaborative robot safety, no K3 framework for human-robot shared workspaces, and no clarity on liability allocation.
> This is acutely dangerous because Indonesia's market is entering via LEASING and RaaS, which separates ownership from operation — when a leased humanoid injures a worker at a Morowali smelter, it is genuinely unclear whether the Chinese manufacturer, the Indonesian importer, the leasing company, the integrator or the operating employer is liable.
> The first serious injury will be litigated into a legal vacuum, and the likely outcome is that the injured worker bears the loss.

(3) THE EDUCATION ENROLMENT BUBBLE — the most predictable harm in this file.
> Viral Chinese robot content plus institutional incentives will drive a rush of new robotics programs and a surge of enrolment far in excess of domestic job creation.
> Families will finance degrees for jobs that do not exist in Indonesia, at institutions without labs, taught by faculty who have never deployed a robot.
> This has a direct Indonesian precedent in the data-science enrolment surge of 2019-2023.

(4) STRANDED-ASSET RISK FROM THE CHINESE SHAKEOUT.
> If the NDRC's warning proves right and 2027-2030 brings mass consolidation, Indonesian buyers — including universities and government agencies that bought on prestige — could be left with unsupported hardware from failed vendors, no spare parts, no firmware updates and no service.
> A visible wave of dead robots in Indonesian universities would poison institutional confidence in automation for a decade.

(5) DATA AND SOVEREIGNTY EXPOSURE.
> Chinese-made robots in Indonesian ports, power plants, smelters, hospitals and government buildings are networked sensor platforms with vendor cloud connectivity.
> Indonesia has no rule requiring data localisation, audit rights or firmware transparency for such devices.
> The risk is not hypothetical — it is the same category of concern that has driven restrictions on Chinese hardware in critical infrastructure elsewhere, and Indonesia is currently walking into it without a policy.

(6) DEEPENED TECHNOLOGICAL DEPENDENCY AND LOCK-IN.
> Universities training students on Chinese platforms and SDKs, industry standardising on Chinese hardware, and a service ecosystem built entirely around Chinese spare parts creates lock-in that is very hard to unwind and that transfers pricing power permanently offshore.
> This is the Huawei-in-telecoms pattern applied to physical labour.

(7) REGIONAL INEQUALITY.
> Robots deployed at non-Java industrial sites, with specification, financing, engineering and high-value roles all captured in Jakarta or Shanghai — the extractive pattern of Indonesian resource industries, reproduced in automation.

(8) INFORMAL-SECTOR SPILLOVER.
> Indonesia's informal sector absorbs workers displaced from formal employment.
> A displacement wave pushes workers into an informal sector that is already crowded and offers no social protection — the visible effect is not unemployment statistics but falling incomes, rising underemployment, and household downgrading.

(9) POLITICAL VOLATILITY.
> Employment is Indonesia's most politically salient economic issue.
> Visible robot-linked layoffs at a large employer would produce union mobilisation, DPR hearings and potentially reactive, poorly designed restrictions — a policy overcorrection that could be as costly as under-regulation.
> The way to avoid it is to regulate calmly now rather than reactively later.

**Kelompok Rentan**

> (1) MANUFACTURING PRODUCTION WORKERS IN LABOUR-INTENSIVE SECTORS — garment, textile, footwear and food-processing operators, disproportionately women, disproportionately with SMP/SMA-level education, concentrated in West Java, Central Java, Banten and East Java.
> This group has already absorbed the closure of ~60 textile factories in 2022-2024 (~250,000 workers affected) from trade and cost pressures; automation adds a second shock to a group with no absorption capacity and limited retraining options.
> Highest-exposure single group in Indonesia.

(2) WAREHOUSE AND LOGISTICS MANUAL LABOUR — pickers, packers and material handlers in e-commerce fulfilment, concentrated in Greater Jakarta and Surabaya.
> These are young workers who entered formal employment through the e-commerce boom; AMR adoption in fulfilment centres is the earliest realistic large-volume displacement in Indonesia, likely 2028-2032.

(3) SECURITY GUARDS AND ROUTINE INSPECTION/PATROL STAFF — one of the largest and least-discussed formal employment categories in Indonesia, and directly substitutable by inspection quadrupeds and autonomous patrol robots.
> Low pay, low bargaining power, and no obvious transition path.

(4) ENTRY-LEVEL SERVICE WORKERS — waiters, food runners, hotel porters and cleaners in urban chains, already partially displaced by Pudu and Keenon service robots since 2021.
> These are the first-job roles through which young Indonesians and rural migrants enter the urban formal economy; removing the bottom rung damages mobility more than the headcount suggests.

(5) SMK GRADUATES FROM UNRETOOLED PROGRAMS — students completing manual machining, manual garment and conventional automotive-repair tracks at schools without robotics or automation equipment.
> Kemendikdasmen has acknowledged the equipment gap; these graduates enter the labour market with credentials for exactly the tasks being automated, and they are disproportionately from lower-income families for whom SMK was the affordable path to formal work.

(6) FAMILIES FINANCING ROBOTICS DEGREES AT UNDER-EQUIPPED INSTITUTIONS — a specifically middle-class and aspiring-middle-class harm: real money spent on a credential that will not convert into a job because Indonesia will not build robots and the program had no lab.

(7) OLDER WORKERS (40+) IN FORMAL MANUFACTURING — the least likely to be retrained, the most likely to be selected for redundancy, and the group for whom re-entry into formal employment after displacement is near-impossible; Indonesia's informal sector is the only landing place and it offers no social protection.

(8) WORKERS IN NON-JAVA INDUSTRIAL ENCLAVES — mining and smelter workers in Morowali, Weda Bay and Kalimantan face the earliest robot deployment in Indonesia, in regions with the fewest alternative formal employers and the weakest labour-inspection capacity.

(9) INFORMAL WORKERS INDIRECTLY — every worker displaced from formal manufacturing enters an informal sector that is already crowded, pushing down incomes for people who were never near a robot.
> The damage propagates well beyond the directly displaced.

### Contoh Kasus Konkret

**Kasus China**

> CASE 1 — UNITREE: THE COST-DISRUPTION PLAY.
> Founded 2016 in Hangzhou.
> Shipped ~5,500 humanoid units in 2025, the world's largest volume; humanoids passed 51% of revenue for the first time; blended gross margin around 60%; cumulative quadruped shipments above 50,000 units with roughly 70% of the global quadruped market.
> Planned capacity: 75,000 humanoids and 115,000 quadrupeds annually.
> STAR Market IPO with subscription in August 2026, having raised over RMB 4.2 billion privately.
> Its cultural breakout came from the CCTV Spring Festival Gala performance in early 2025 — the moment humanoid robots became a mass-consumer concept in China.
> The strategic significance is price: Unitree drove entry humanoid prices into the tens of thousands of dollars, an order of magnitude below Western equivalents, which is what makes export to markets like Indonesia possible at all.

CASE 2 — AGIBOT (ZHIYUAN ROBOTICS): THE SCALE PLAY.
> Shanghai, founded 2023 by a former Huawei 'Genius Youth' engineer.
> Shipped ~5,168 units in 2025, roughly 39% of global humanoid supply.
> Production milestones tell the ramp story: ~1,000 units in 2025, then 5,000, then a 10,000th unit in late March 2026, and 15,000 cumulative by late June 2026.
> Launched a Hong Kong listing process in 2026, debuted four new robots at WAIC 2026 with an explicit global export push, and secured a Singapore foothold via a Singtel enterprise agreement.
> AgiBot is the clearest instance of the export vector reaching Indonesia: the AgiBot Partner Conference Indonesia in Jakarta on 9 June 2026 established Indonesian strategic and leasing partners within roughly a year of the company reaching scale.

CASE 3 — UBTECH: THE INDUSTRIAL DEPLOYMENT PLAY.
> Shenzhen, HKEX-listed.
> Only ~1,000 units in 2025, but the deepest real factory deployments — Walker series humanoids working at BYD, Foxconn, Zeekr and Audi-FAW plants on parts sorting, quality inspection and logistics handling.
> UBTech is the test case for whether humanoids can do production work rather than demonstrations.
> Its advertised chief-scientist package of RMB 15-124 million per year is the sharpest single indicator of how scarce genuine embodied-AI expertise is.

CASE 4 — THE SHIJINGSHAN AND HEFEI TRAINING GROUNDS: THE HIDDEN LABOUR STORY, AND THE MOST TRANSFERABLE PIECE.
> At Beijing's Shijingshan centre, data trainers like 22-year-old Zhao Ran are each paired with a robot and repeatedly guide it through a task so the machine can replicate it; the resulting visual, motion and tactile data are cleaned and labelled into training 'textbooks' for embodied AI models.
> The Beijing Innovation Center's base covers 120+ robot models across 30+ scenarios in six sectors.
> Hefei's facility spans 6,000+ square metres with ~30 simulated environments — kitchens, retail shelves, industrial bays.
> In May 2026 China opened a national vocational training ground for embodied robots.
> Robot training, annotation, testing and operational support are now an emergent service industry, and Chinese projections cite over 1 million new positions across the value chain.
> This is the single most copyable element of the Chinese model for Indonesia — labour-intensive, capital-light, and available now.

CASE 5 — THE MOE CATALOGUE ACTION: EDUCATION AS INDUSTRIAL POLICY.
> April 2026: China's Ministry of Education publishes the 2026 undergraduate catalogue with 38 new majors across 883 total programs, the first year the national program-adjustment ratio exceeded 10%.
> 'Embodied Intelligence' (具身智能) is listed for the first time, in a newly formalised Interdisciplinary Studies category alongside Brain-Computer Science & Technology, Future Robotics and Agricultural Robotics.
> Nine universities including Harbin Institute of Technology and Beihang are approved to launch it first, from a field including Shanghai Jiao Tong, Zhejiang, BIT and Xi'an Jiaotong.
> The mechanism — central definition, new interdisciplinary category, controlled first tranche, paired with national training infrastructure — is the specific thing Indonesia should study.

CASE 6 — THE NDRC BUBBLE WARNING AND HEIS 2026: THE STATE HITTING BOTH PEDALS.
> In the same period that Beijing committed a ~RMB 1 trillion state-backed fund envelope and set a 10,000-unit deployment target for end-2026, the NDRC publicly declared the sector overheated and at bubble risk, and MIIT published the world's first national standard system for humanoid robotics and embodied AI (Feb-March 2026), built with 120+ institutions across six domains including safety and ethics, with a mandatory 'minimum risk condition'.
> China is simultaneously accelerating the industry and pre-building the guardrails and the cooling mechanism — a genuine departure from its own record on fintech, tutoring and gaming, and the strongest argument that preemptive regulation is politically feasible.

**Padanan Indonesia**

> THERE IS NO INDONESIAN EQUIVALENT ON THE PRODUCTION SIDE — the padanan is entirely on the distribution, deployment and education side, and it is very new.

CLOSEST PARALLEL — THE DISTRIBUTOR LAYER: Halo Robotics (Jakarta, operating since 2014, 900+ organisational customers) became Unitree's exclusive Indonesian distributor in May 2026, with local consultation, system integration, operator training, warranty and an official after-sales service centre.
> This is the structural analogue of the early EV distributorships: the Indonesian company captures the channel, service and customer relationship while all technology, IP and margin on the hardware remain Chinese.
> PT Denka Pratama Indonesia plays the same role for AgiBot from June 2026, with PT Robotika Futuristik Indonesia taking the leasing/RaaS position — the latter is genuinely novel and has no Chinese-market equivalent at the same stage.

SERVICE-ROBOT PRECEDENT — THE BEST PREDICTOR: Pudu Robotics service robots distributed by Puri Robotics from around 2021, and Keenon Robotics units (including HolaBot) in Indonesian restaurants, hotels, hospitals and warehouses.
> This is the completed version of the same story: Chinese robot maker, Indonesian distributor, adoption driven partly by efficiency and partly by novelty and 'futuristic' brand value, meaningful quiet displacement of entry-level service jobs, zero technology transfer.
> Everything happening with humanoids in 2026 is this pattern repeating one tier up.

INDUSTRIAL PRECEDENT: automotive assembly in Cikarang and Karawang and electronics in Batam run FANUC, ABB, Omron, Kawasaki and Mitsubishi industrial robots — a Japanese/European installed base with roughly a 20% recent growth rate off a very low denominator.
> Chinese EV plants entering Indonesia (BYD, Wuling, Chery) import their parent-plant automation architecture wholesale, which is the highest-volume and least-visible transfer channel.

LOCAL ECOSYSTEM — THIN: Tracxn lists roughly 15 robotics-application companies in Indonesia including Jumpstart, ATLAS and Karla Bionics (bionics/prosthetics, the most technically distinctive Indonesian robotics venture).
> Integrators and cobot distributors include PT Global Mandiri Instrumentasi (Elite Robot), Weisstech and Netmarks.
> None of these is remotely comparable to a Chinese OEM; the honest reading is that Indonesia has a distribution and integration sector, not a robotics industry.

EDUCATION EQUIVALENT — REAL BUT SHALLOW: UNIKOM Bandung's S1 Teknik Robotika dan Kecerdasan Buatan, approved via Kepmen Dikti Saintek No.
> 454/B/O/2025 in July 2025 with intake from 2025/2026, is Indonesia's answer to China's 具身智能 major — and notably it was approved before China's MOE catalogue action of April 2026.
> Untag Surabaya opened a comparable program.
> The gap is not timing but depth: China approved nine institutions from a competitive field and paired the degree with national training grounds and recognised occupational categories; Indonesia approved individual institutions with no national capability map and an acknowledged shortage of industry-standard labs even at SMK level.
> Kemendikdasmen's July 2026 statement positioning robotics as an SMK career pathway — mapping it onto teknik mekatronika, elektronika industri, otomasi industri, permesinan, ketenagalistrikan, RPL and TKJ — is the most substantive Indonesian policy response to date, and it is rhetorical rather than funded.

POLICY EQUIVALENT — ABSENT: Komdigi's Buku Putih Peta Jalan Kecerdasan Artifisial Nasional (public consultation August 2025) with a Perpres on the National AI Roadmap 2026-2030 targeted for Q1 2026 addresses AI governance, talent, infrastructure and data, but contains no embodied-AI or robotics-manufacturing industrial line, no robot safety standard, and no liability framework.
> Against China's HEIS 2026 six-domain standard system, Indonesia has nothing.

### Tingkat Keyakinan & Kualitas Sumber

**Catatan Kontradiksi Data**

> (1) CHINA'S SHARE OF GLOBAL HUMANOID SHIPMENTS: sources report 'over 80%', '85%', and '~90%'.
> The variation stems from different definitions (shipments vs installations, humanoid vs semi-humanoid, calendar vs fiscal reporting).
> The defensible statement is 85-90% of units in 2025.

(2) WHO SHIPPED MOST IN 2025 — UNITREE OR AGIBOT: Unitree's IPO prospectus claims ~5,500 units; AgiBot claims ~5,168 units and a 39% global share and is described by some trackers as ranking first.
> A separate tracker puts Unitree at 4,200.
> The two companies publicly dispute the top spot, and the discrepancy reflects different recognition points (produced vs shipped vs revenue-recognised).
> Both shipped roughly 5,000+ units; the ranking is unresolved and commercially motivated on both sides.

(3) TOTAL GLOBAL HUMANOID UNITS 2025: estimates range from ~13,000 to ~20,000.
> The 13,000-18,000 band appears in the most careful reporting; some China-focused sources cite ~20,000 for China alone, which cannot be reconciled with a 13,000-18,000 global total and an 85-90% China share.
> Treat the higher figures as including semi-humanoids and educational/toy-class units.

(4) CHINA HUMANOID MARKET VALUE 2025-2030: Morgan Stanley says ~USD 2bn (2026) to USD 15bn (2030); a bottom-up estimate says USD 0.40bn (2025) to USD 2.80bn (2030).
> These differ by roughly 5x at the 2030 endpoint.
> The gap is definitional (whole-market including components and services vs humanoid units only) and directional confidence should be attached only to the growth rate, not the levels.

(5) CHINA GDP PER CAPITA REFERENCE POINTS: one search result reported China's 2016 GDP per capita as USD 14,400, which is the PPP figure; the nominal figure is roughly USD 8,100.
> Nominal figures are used throughout this file for comparability with Indonesia's ~USD 4,900-5,400.

(6) INDONESIA ROBOTICS MARKET SIZE: USD 23.8m (2025) from Mordor is implausibly small relative to Indonesia's industrial base and to other trackers that place Indonesian industrial automation in the hundreds of millions to low billions.
> Almost certainly a narrow segment definition.
> Flagged as uncertain and should not be compared directly to China figures.

(7) INDONESIA'S DEINDUSTRIALISATION: LPEM FEB UI and multiple analysts describe premature deindustrialisation with manufacturing at 18-19% of GDP; Kemenperin publicly rejects the characterisation.
> Both use real data; the disagreement is interpretive.
> The employment-elasticity collapse (1.77%→0.58% formal) is the harder and less disputable evidence.

(8) AGIBOT INDONESIA LAUNCH DATE: one Indonesian outlet carries a URL timestamp of November 2026 while its content and other sources date the AgiBot Partner Conference Indonesia to 9 June 2026.
> The June 2026 date is corroborated by Tek.id and is used here.

(9) NUMBER OF CHINESE HUMANOID COMPANIES: reported variously as 'more than 140', '150', and '>150 companies' (the research brief's figure).
> The distinction is between humanoid OEMs specifically (~140-150) and the broader embodied-AI company population (larger).
> Both are approximately correct at different scopes.

(10) UNIVERSITIES APPROVED FOR THE 具身智能 MAJOR: sources cite both 'seven universities applied' and 'nine universities supported to establish first'.
> These describe different stages (application vs approval) and are not contradictory, but the exact institution list varies by source.

(11) NARRATIVE TENSION WORTH FLAGGING: Chinese state media consistently frame humanoid deployment as filling jobs nobody wants because of labour shortage, while Western coverage frames it as displacement risk.
> Both are accurate for China (where attrition currently exceeds substitution) but the Chinese framing does NOT transfer to Indonesia, whose demographic conditions are the inverse.
> Uncritical import of the Chinese narrative into Indonesian policy discussion is itself a risk identified in this research.

## 22. Low-Altitude Economy (低空经济) — commercial drones/UAS, cargo and delivery drones, agricultural spraying drones, eVTOL air taxis, plus the supporting layer of vertiports, unmanned traffic management (UTM) and low-altitude airspace reform
**Kategori**: Technology & Industry (advanced manufacturing, aviation/transport infrastructure, logistics, agri-tech, and airspace regulation). Cross-cuts Digital Economy (data services, delivery platforms) and Education/Workforce (a brand-new engineering discipline created from scratch).

📊 Laggard with a partial leapfrog window. Laggard on manufacturing, airspace institutions, and the mass logistics layer. Potential leapfrog on two specific fronts: (a) 3T/archipelagic cargo drones, where the absence of roads makes drone logistics economically superior earlier than it was in road-rich China; (b) plantation-scale agricultural drone services, where Indonesia's 16 million ha of oil palm gives a use case China does not have at that scale. Also partly 'importer-simultaneous' on eVTOL: Indonesia is receiving demonstration flights within ~1-2 years of China's own commercial start, because vendors need international showcase markets — but this is deployment simultaneity, not capability simultaneity. | 🎯 Prob: High (for the drone-services and cargo-drone layer); Medium (for a Chinese-style state-orchestrated 'low-altitude economy' policy programme); Low-to-Medium (for mass urban eVTOL air taxis as a mainstream transport mode). | 🔍 Keyakinan: Medium-High overall. HIGH for Chinese policy chronology, CAAC market projections, EHang's certification ladder, education-system response (the 低空技术与工程 major, the six pioneer universities and the 120-university expansion), and Chinese fleet/flight-hour statistics — all traceable to government, state-media or company primary sources. MEDIUM-HIGH for China's operational data (Meituan, SF Express) and the order-bubble evidence, which come from credible industry and securities-research reporting rather than audited disclosure. MEDIUM for Indonesian market sizing, timeline predictions and Indonesian manufacturer specifications, where official statistics are absent and commercial reports conflict. LOW-MEDIUM for quantified Indonesian employment impact, certified-pilot counts, registered-drone counts, and peak-year predictions, where no authoritative published data exists at all.

> **Status di Indonesia**: Early stage / pilot, with a strange top-heavy shape: Indonesia is simultaneously behind on the ordinary drone-services layer and unusually early on the glamorous eVTOL layer (because foreign vendors are using IKN and Jakarta as showcase markets). Practical drone use is already significant but concentrated in extractive and plantation sectors; the policy/airspace architecture (UTM, drone corridors, BVLOS at scale, a national low-altitude strategy) is essentially not yet built.

### Basic Info

**Tahun Mulai China**

> Layered start.
> (1) 2006-2015: DJI's founding (2006) and consumer/industrial drone dominance make China the world's drone workshop.
> (2) 2021: 'low-altitude economy' first appears in a national planning document — the National Comprehensive Three-Dimensional Transport Network Outline (国家综合立体交通网规划纲要, Feb 2021).
> (3) 1 Jan 2024: the Interim Regulations on the Flight Management of Unmanned Aircraft (无人驾驶航空器飞行管理暂行条例) take effect — China's first State Council-level UAS law.
> (4) March 2024: 'low-altitude economy' is written into the national Government Work Report as a 'new growth engine', making 2024 widely called '低空经济元年' (Year One of the Low-Altitude Economy).
> (5) December 2024: NDRC creates a dedicated Low-Altitude Economy Development Department (低空经济发展司).
> So: technology base from ~2010, policy-driven industry take-off from 2024.

**Pemain Kunci China**

> Manufacturing/hardware: DJI (大疆, Shenzhen — >70% of the global consumer drone market and the anchor of the Shenzhen supply chain), XAG (极飞, agricultural drones), EHang (亿航智能, Guangzhou — the pilotless passenger eVTOL leader), AutoFlight (峰飞航空), XPeng AeroHT (小鹏汇天, flying-car spin-off of XPeng), Volant/沃兰特, TCab Tech (时的科技), Vertaxi (御风未来), AVIC subsidiaries, and Wofei Changkong (沃飞长空, Geely-backed).
> Operations/applications: Meituan UAV (美团无人机, food delivery), SF Express Fengyi (顺丰丰翼, logistics), JD Logistics, CITIC Offshore Helicopter (中信海直).
> Infrastructure/airspace: China Mobile/China Telecom low-altitude networks, state-owned low-altitude platform companies set up by city governments (Shenzhen, Hefei, Guangzhou, Chengdu, Suzhou, Wuhan).
> Regulators as active market-makers: CAAC (certification), NDRC (industry policy), PLA Air Force (airspace release), and provincial/municipal governments — 30+ provinces put the low-altitude economy into their 2025 government work reports.

### China Trend Detail

**Apa Yang Terjadi Di China**

> China is deliberately constructing an entirely new economic layer in the airspace below 1,000 m (up to 3,000 m in special cases), treating it the way it earlier treated high-speed rail and new-energy vehicles: a state-designated 'strategic emerging pillar industry' with coordinated policy, certification, infrastructure and capital.

Mechanism, in four connected moves:
(1) LEGAL/AIRSPACE UNLOCK.
> Low-altitude airspace in China was historically military-controlled and effectively closed.
> The Interim Regulations on UAV Flight Management (effective 1 Jan 2024) created a national, risk-tiered legal framework: real-name registration, aircraft classification (micro/light/small/medium/large), operator licensing, and a defined process for releasing airspace.
> Shenzhen went further with the country's first sub-national low-altitude statute — the Shenzhen SEZ Low-Altitude Economy Industry Promotion Ordinance, effective 1 Feb 2024 — covering airspace coordination, infrastructure, and flight services.
(2) CERTIFICATION AS INDUSTRIAL POLICY.
> CAAC moved first in the world on pilotless passenger aircraft: EHang's EH216-S received the world's first Type Certificate (Oct 2023), the world's first Production Certificate for an eVTOL (Apr 2024), a Standard Airworthiness Certificate, and finally the world's first Air Operator Certificates for human-carrying pilotless eVTOL (Mar 2025).
> CAAC also invented scale-friendly licensing for logistics: in April 2025 it granted Meituan's fourth-generation delivery drone a nationwide operating licence, allowing commercial drone delivery across the whole country under one certificate instead of route-by-route approvals.
(3) DEMAND CREATION THROUGH APPLICATIONS.
> Rather than waiting for air taxis, China industrialised the boring use cases first: agricultural spraying (DJI Agras/XAG covering hundreds of millions of mu), power-line and infrastructure inspection, emergency/medical delivery, urban logistics (Meituan food delivery, SF Express parcels), surveying, security, and 'low-altitude tourism' sightseeing flights — which is what the EH216-S actually does commercially today.
(4) LOCAL-GOVERNMENT COMPETITION.
> City governments compete to become 'the low-altitude capital': building vertiports and drone landing points, subsidising manufacturers, setting up guidance funds, and creating standards bodies (Shenzhen created China's first city-level low-altitude standardisation technical committee in 2024).
> This produces very fast build-out but also duplication and order inflation.

Scale and impact: the sector has moved from concept to genuine daily operations in logistics, agriculture and inspection, while the passenger eVTOL leg is still mostly sightseeing and pre-orders.
> It has simultaneously become a labour-market and education event: the Ministry of Education created a brand-new undergraduate major, 低空技术与工程 (Low-Altitude Technology & Engineering), to feed a talent gap officially estimated in the millions.

**Data Skala China**

> Market size: CAAC projects the low-altitude economy at ~RMB 1.5 trillion in 2025, rising to >RMB 3.5 trillion by 2035 (~USD 486 billion) — roughly a sixfold increase over 2023.
> NDRC's 'Two Sessions' framing puts emerging pillar industries (including LAE) at nearly RMB 6 trillion combined output in 2025, doubling to >RMB 10 trillion by 2030.
> Private estimates are much lower and differ in scope: iMedia Research puts the 2025 LAE market at RMB 561.5 billion, reaching RMB 1.39 trillion by 2029.
> Morgan Stanley sizes only the eVTOL segment at RMB 43.4 billion (2025) → RMB 188.3 billion (2030).

Fleet and activity: registered civil drones rose from 1.27 million (2023) to 3.287 million by end-2025 (+51.0% year on year).
> Cumulative civil drone flight hours reached 45.30 million hours in 2025, +69.9% year on year (vs 23.11 million hours in 2023; 24.47 million hours in H1 2025 alone).
> As of July 2025 China had 801 manned general-aviation operators and more than 19,900 registered unmanned-aircraft operating companies.

Firms and capital: over 10,000 low-altitude-related companies were newly registered in 2024, the highest in four years; companies literally named '低空经济' jumped from 20 registrations (2023) to 188 (2024).
> Announced eVTOL order value exceeded RMB 30 billion by November 2025 — but more than 90% of published orders are letters of intent or framework agreements without firm price, delivery date or penalty clauses (AutoFlight: ~2,000 total announced orders vs ~300 confirmed, ≈15% conversion).

Operations: Meituan UAV had 64 routes across Shenzhen, Beijing, Shanghai, Nanjing, Guangzhou, Hong Kong and Dubai and >600,000 cumulative orders by end-June 2025, at ~RMB 7-8 cost per delivery and still loss-making.
> SF Express flew ~190,000 drone sorties delivering ~2.32 million parcels in H1 2025, with 800-2,000 daily take-offs and >12,000 daily deliveries in the Greater Bay Area.
> EHang's EH216 series had logged >60,000 safe flights; it sold only 11 aircraft for RMB 26.1 million (~USD 3.6 million) in Q1 2025 — i.e.
> real revenue is still tiny relative to the trillion-yuan headline.

Local concentration: by end-2024 Shenzhen's Nanshan district alone reported >RMB 550 billion of low-altitude-related output value, with Bao'an and Longgang districts each above RMB 100 billion.
> Infrastructure: 499 public general-aviation airports at end-2023 (vs ~30,000 public airfields in the US), plus city experiments such as Wuhan's 128 autonomous drone hangars and rooftop vertiports in Guangzhou.
> China accounts for over 70% of global drone-related patent applications.

**Fase Tren Di China**

> Split-phase.
> (a) Consumer + industrial/agricultural drones: MATURE, with involution-style price competition and DJI's near-monopoly — this leg is profitable and export-driven.
> (b) Drone logistics/delivery: BOOMING but pre-profit — real volumes, real national licences, negative unit economics.
> (c) eVTOL passenger air mobility: EARLY BOOMING / HYPE PHASE — world-leading certification, but revenue in the tens of millions of RMB against tens of billions in mostly non-binding orders; classic capital-inflation dynamics.
> (d) Policy/institutional layer: PEAK POLICY PUSH, moving toward a REGULATED phase — from 2024's permissive push toward tightening around illegal flying (黑飞), mandatory identification broadcast, and airworthiness codification under the revised Civil Aviation Law.
> Overall label: policy-driven boom entering its first consolidation/shake-out.

### Status Indonesia Saat Ini

**Status Di Indonesia**

> Early stage / pilot, with a strange top-heavy shape: Indonesia is simultaneously behind on the ordinary drone-services layer and unusually early on the glamorous eVTOL layer (because foreign vendors are using IKN and Jakarta as showcase markets).
> Practical drone use is already significant but concentrated in extractive and plantation sectors; the policy/airspace architecture (UTM, drone corridors, BVLOS at scale, a national low-altitude strategy) is essentially not yet built.

**Contoh Konkret Indonesia**

> Regulation: Ministry of Transportation Regulation PM 37/2020 (operation of unmanned aircraft) and PM 63/2021 (CASR/PKPS 107 — remote pilot certification), with a 120 m altitude ceiling and case-by-case BVLOS approval from DGCA.
> In October 2025 the Ministry of Transportation announced a push toward at least one commercial Advanced Air Mobility/cargo-drone operation by December 2026, and joined the international JARUS-linked rulemaking forum.
> eVTOL: EHang's EH216-S completed Indonesia's first pilotless human-carrying flights on 25 June 2025 and received approval for Jakarta flights; Prestige Aviation (Prestige Corp) had pre-ordered 100 EH216 units back at IIMS 2022 — then EHang's largest Asian pre-order.
> Archer Aviation signed with PT IKN in June 2025 for up to 50 Midnight eVTOLs (up to USD 250 million) as a 'Launch Edition' country; the government targets flying-taxi service in Nusantara by 2028.
> Domestic manufacturers: PT Vela Prima Nusantara (Vela Aero, Bandung) with the Vela Alpha 1-pilot/4-passenger eVTOL unveiled with PT Dirgantara Indonesia at Singapore Airshow 2024, plus a large cargo drone prototype; PT Iter Aero Industri (Bandung) with the IA-25 cargo drone, which obtained a Class D Design Organization Approval from the Ministry of Transportation.
> Service/integration firms: Terra Drone Indonesia (agri drones certified for TKDN local-content in October 2025; partnership with PT Yanmar Diesel Indonesia in August 2025), Halo Robotics, Frogs Indonesia, Beehive Drones (remote-area delivery), BETA-UAS, PT Famindo Inovasi Teknologi.
> Community/professional layer: Asosiasi Pilot Drone Indonesia (APDI), legally established 12 Feb 2015, thousands of members across 25 regions, running remote-pilot certification with BNSP-linked schemes.
> Real workhorse use cases: palm-oil plantation mapping, tree census, precision fertilisation and spraying (DJI Agras T-series widely used), mining survey and stockpile volumetrics, telecom tower and power-line inspection, disaster mapping, and 3T (frontier/outermost/underdeveloped) logistics trials including medical supply drops.

### Analisis Lag

**Bukti Historical Lag**

> Comparable China→Indonesia diffusion lags in adjacent hardware-plus-policy sectors: (1) Electric vehicles — China's take-off 2014-2015 (purchase-tax exemption, world's largest NEV market), Indonesia's real policy push 2022-2023 with Wuling/BYD entry: ~8 years.
> (2) QR-code mobile payments — Alipay/WeChat Pay mass adoption 2014-2016, Indonesia's QRIS national standard 2019-2020: ~5 years.
> (3) Livestream commerce — China 2016-2018, Indonesia 2020-2022: ~4-5 years.
> (4) Solar PV manufacturing/deployment — China's scale from 2010-2013, Indonesia still marginal in 2025: 12+ years and widening.
> The pattern is consistent: Indonesia adopts *consumption* of Chinese technology with a 4-8 year lag but adopts *production and institutional capability* with a 10-20 year lag or never.
> Low-altitude economy fits this pattern exactly — Indonesia will buy Chinese airframes quickly and build the regulatory/manufacturing layer slowly.
> Additional direct evidence: China's Interim UAV Regulations (2024) versus Indonesia's PM 37/2020 + PM 63/2021, which cover pilot certification and basic operations but not airspace release, UTM, or scaled BVLOS — an institutional gap of roughly one regulatory generation.

**Tipe Lag**

> Laggard with a partial leapfrog window.
> Laggard on manufacturing, airspace institutions, and the mass logistics layer.
> Potential leapfrog on two specific fronts: (a) 3T/archipelagic cargo drones, where the absence of roads makes drone logistics economically superior earlier than it was in road-rich China; (b) plantation-scale agricultural drone services, where Indonesia's 16 million ha of oil palm gives a use case China does not have at that scale.
> Also partly 'importer-simultaneous' on eVTOL: Indonesia is receiving demonstration flights within ~1-2 years of China's own commercial start, because vendors need international showcase markets — but this is deployment simultaneity, not capability simultaneity.

### Probabilitas Transfer ke Indonesia

**Probabilitas Transfer**

> High (for the drone-services and cargo-drone layer); Medium (for a Chinese-style state-orchestrated 'low-altitude economy' policy programme); Low-to-Medium (for mass urban eVTOL air taxis as a mainstream transport mode).

**Alasan Probabilitas**

> High for the services layer because the enabling hardware is already cheap, imported, and installed: DJI and XAG platforms are sold through Indonesian distributors, palm-oil and mining companies have clear ROI (10-15 ha/hour spraying versus manual labour), and no new institutions are needed beyond existing PM 37/PM 63 permits.
> High also for cargo drones because Indonesia's geography — 17,000+ islands and roadless Papua highlands — makes drone logistics pass a cost test that road-dense China never needed; the Ministry of Transportation has explicitly targeted 3T regions and December 2026 for commercial operation.

Medium for the full Chinese policy programme because Indonesia lacks the three ingredients China used: (i) a military able and willing to release low-altitude airspace on a coordinated national schedule, (ii) fiscally aggressive city governments that compete by building infrastructure, and (iii) a domestic supply chain to capture the value.
> Indonesia can copy the vocabulary ('low-altitude economy roadmap 2026-2045' is already being proposed in policy commentary) faster than the substance.

Low-to-Medium for mass air taxis because at ~USD 1 per passenger-kilometre — roughly double a normal taxi — and with Indonesian GDP per capita around USD 5,000, the addressable market is a thin elite plus tourism (Bali, Jakarta CBD) and state showcase projects (IKN).
> Even in China this leg is still sightseeing-dominated with tiny revenue.
> Indonesian eVTOL therefore arrives as a prestige/tourism product first, and only later — if ever — as transport.

### Faktor Pendorong

**Indikator Pemantauan**

> Leading indicators that the trend is genuinely landing in Indonesia, roughly in the order they should appear: (1) a dedicated Ministerial Regulation or Presidential Regulation replacing/expanding PM 37/2020 with risk-tiered categories, remote-ID and a BVLOS pathway — the single most predictive signal; (2) formal announcement of a National Low-Altitude Economy Roadmap (the 2026-2045 framing already circulating in Indonesian policy commentary) and any inter-ministerial coordinating body spanning Kemenhub, Komdigi, Kemenperin, BRIN, Bappenas, TNI and Polri; (3) AirNav Indonesia procuring or piloting a UTM system, and the designation of the first legal drone corridors (most likely Papua/Maluku or IKN); (4) issuance of the first Indonesian Air Operator Certificate for a cargo-drone or AAM operator — the Ministry's stated December 2026 target; (5) further DOA/POA/TC-track approvals for domestic manufacturers beyond Iter Aero's Class D DOA, and TKDN certifications enabling government procurement; (6) job-posting volume for 'remote pilot', 'drone operator', 'UAV data analyst', 'photogrammetry', 'GIS' on Jobstreet/LinkedIn Indonesia, and enrolment growth in Polman Bandung's D4 Teknologi Rekayasa Sistem Aerial Nirawak plus any new UAS study programmes at ITB, ITS, PENS, ITDA, STTKD or Poltekbang; (7) opening of Chinese vendor offices/service centres (DJI Enterprise, XAG, EHang) and any Chinese joint-venture assembly plant announcement; (8) government budget lines for drone procurement in Kementan (agriculture), Kemenkes (medical logistics), BNPB (disaster) and the police/military; (9) growth in registered drones and RPC holders reported by DGCA — currently not published, so its publication is itself a signal; (10) search-volume and trademark/company registrations containing 'drone', 'UAV', 'aerial' or 'AAM' in AHU/DJKI records.

### Hambatan & Faktor Pembatal

**Hambatan Transfer**

> Regulatory: PM 37/2020 and PM 63/2021 are control-oriented, built around a 120 m ceiling and visual line of sight, with BVLOS granted case-by-case — workable for surveying, structurally incompatible with delivery networks.
> There is no UTM, no remote-ID mandate, no risk-based SORA-style framework, and no eVTOL airworthiness code.
> Institutional: authority is fragmented across Kemenhub/DGCA, AirNav, Komdigi (spectrum), Kemenperin (industry/TKDN), BRIN (R&D), plus TNI and Polri for security — every scaled operation needs multiple sign-offs, and no single ministry owns the outcome.
> Security/political: drones are dual-use, and armed conflict in Papua makes military and police reluctant to liberalise exactly where cargo drones are most economically justified.
> Economic: hardware is imported and priced in USD, capex is heavy relative to Indonesian corporate cost bases outside plantations and mining, and Indonesian labour remains cheap enough that manual spraying and manual surveying still compete in smallholder segments (~40% of oil palm area).
> Infrastructure: no vertiports, weak RTK/CORS outside Java, no charging/battery-swap network, and unreliable connectivity in 3T zones.
> Human capital: very few certified BVLOS operators, almost no airworthiness engineers, and no university pipeline comparable to China's new major.
> Import/customs: drone imports face licensing and lartas-type restrictions and security screening that slow fleet build-up.
> Insurance and liability: no established third-party liability market for BVLOS drone operations.
> Public acceptance: privacy concerns and noise, plus incident risk in dense kampung housing where any crash is politically explosive.

**Faktor Pembatal Transfer**

> Conditions that make a Chinese-shaped low-altitude economy structurally impossible in Indonesia, rather than merely delayed:

1.
> NO MANUFACTURING BASE, AND THE WINDOW HAS CLOSED.
> China's LAE is profitable at the hardware layer because DJI et al.
> own the supply chain.
> Indonesia entering commodity drone manufacture in 2026 faces the same wall as entering commodity solar panels: Chinese cost curves are unbeatable.
> Indonesia will therefore capture only the services and operations margin, which is a fraction of the trillion-yuan headline.
> Any Indonesian target that copies China's *market size* framing is measuring the wrong thing.

2.
> URBAN DELIVERY ECONOMICS DO NOT TRANSFER.
> Meituan's drone delivery costs RMB 7-8 per order and is unprofitable in the richest Chinese cities.
> Indonesia's ground alternative — the ojol/motorcycle courier — costs a fraction of that, is available in seconds, and employs millions.
> In a country with the world's densest motorcycle-courier network, urban drone food delivery has no cost case and never will; this leg of the Chinese model is simply cancelled.

3.
> GEOGRAPHY INVERTS THE USE-CASE ORDER.
> China's model is urban-dense and short-hop.
> Indonesia's real need is long-range, low-frequency, over-water and over-mountain cargo — which requires fixed-wing/VTOL hybrids, long endurance, and BVLOS over uncontrolled terrain: a different aircraft class, different regulation, and much thinner revenue per flight.
> Indonesia cannot import the Chinese template; it must build a different one closer to Zipline's Rwanda model.

4.
> AIRSPACE POLITICS ARE NOT REPLICABLE.
> China released low-altitude airspace through a unified party-military-civil command structure.
> Indonesia's airspace liberalisation must pass through a civilian ministry, a state ANSP, and a military with active internal-security concerns in precisely the target regions.
> There is no Indonesian mechanism to do this on a national schedule.

5.
> NO SUB-NATIONAL FISCAL COMPETITION.
> Shenzhen, Hefei and Chengdu built vertiports and guidance funds because Chinese city governments compete on industrial output.
> Indonesian regencies do not have that fiscal capacity or incentive structure; infrastructure will come from central government or not at all.

6.
> POPULATION AND DENSITY SCALE.
> Even Jakarta cannot generate the flight density that makes a UTM investment pay in Shenzhen.
> The fixed cost of airspace digitalisation is nearly the same; the traffic to amortise it is an order of magnitude smaller.

Net: what will actually arrive in Indonesia is (i) imported drone hardware plus domestic service companies, (ii) plantation/mining/inspection at real scale, (iii) state-subsidised 3T and disaster logistics, and (iv) a small prestige eVTOL tourism/VIP niche.
> What will not arrive is a domestic manufacturing pillar industry or urban drone delivery at Chinese scale.

### Prediksi Timeline di Indonesia

**Tahun Masuk Indonesia**

> Already entered, in stages: 2015-2018 for professional survey/mapping drones (APDI founded 2015, PM 37 drafted from this era); 2019-2023 for agricultural spraying and mining/plantation adoption; 2020 for the first regulatory framework (PM 37/2020) and 2021 for pilot certification (PM 63/2021); June 2025 for eVTOL passenger demonstration flights (EHang EH216-S) and June 2025 for the Archer-PT IKN agreement; 2025-2026 for the state's explicit low-altitude/AAM policy push (Kemenhub's December 2026 commercial-operation target).
> Treat 2025 as the year Indonesia's low-altitude economy became an explicit policy object rather than a collection of private use cases.

**Skenario Percepatan**

> Fastest accelerants, in descending impact: (1) a Presidential Regulation creating a single low-altitude authority with a BVLOS/UTM sandbox — could pull mainstreaming forward 3-4 years; (2) a large state anchor order (Kemenkes vaccine/blood logistics, Kemensos or Bulog food distribution to 3T, BNPB disaster fleet) that guarantees volume and de-risks operators; (3) a major disaster where drone logistics visibly saves lives, collapsing political resistance overnight; (4) IKN mandating drone/AAM operations as part of its build-out, with Danantara or SOE capital behind it; (5) a Chinese or Japanese JV assembly plant with TKDN qualification, which would cut hardware costs and create a domestic lobby; (6) food-security programmes (large-scale rice estates, plantation replanting) subsidising spraying drones the way China subsidised agricultural machinery; (7) bilateral airworthiness validation agreements with CAAC/FAA that let Indonesia accept foreign type certificates instead of building certification capacity from zero.

### Dampak Sosial-Ekonomi

**Dampak Daerah Non Jawa**

> This is one of the few China-origin trends whose economic centre of gravity in Indonesia sits OUTSIDE Java.
> The highest-value use cases are structurally non-Javanese: oil palm in Riau, North Sumatra, Central/West/East Kalimantan and Papua; coal and nickel mining in Kalimantan and Sulawesi; forestry and concession monitoring; and 3T logistics in Papua, Maluku and NTT where the Ministry of Transportation is explicitly directing cargo-drone development and where no road alternative exists.
> Iter Aero's IA-25 and Vela's large cargo drone are aimed at exactly these regions.
> Disaster response — volcanic, seismic and flood mapping — is likewise nationally distributed.
> The Java/Jakarta share of the trend is concentrated in the least economically meaningful parts: eVTOL prestige flights, regulatory offices, and the training/consulting layer.
> Practical implication: regional universities and polytechnics in Pekanbaru, Medan, Samarinda, Banjarmasin, Makassar, Manado and Jayapura have a stronger claim to UAS programmes than most Jakarta campuses do, and regional governments have a stronger interest in drone corridors than the central government has demonstrated.
> Counter-risk: the value capture may still flow to Jakarta and foreign vendors while the regions supply only the field labour — the standard Indonesian extractive-sector pattern repeating in a new industry.

### Kaitan Pendidikan

**Jurusan Dibutuhkan**

> Highest-priority skill clusters, ranked by Indonesian demand realism rather than glamour: (1) UAS/drone operations and maintenance at the vocational (SMK/D3/D4) level — remote-pilot certification, airframe and propulsion maintenance, battery safety, payload integration; China's own numbers suggest maintenance demand exceeds pilot demand roughly 3.5:1, so this is the largest employment pool and Indonesia's most under-served.
> (2) Geospatial data science: photogrammetry, LiDAR and point-cloud processing, multispectral/NDVI analysis, GIS automation, and computer vision for defect and crop detection — this is where the margin sits, above the flying.
> (3) Embedded systems, flight control and autonomy: control theory, sensor fusion, SLAM, ROS, real-time systems, RF/telemetry — the skill base behind PENS-style flight-controller work.
> (4) Electric propulsion and energy systems: battery pack design, thermal management, BMS, power electronics — directly transferable to and from Indonesia's EV/battery downstreaming agenda, which is the strongest synergy argument available.
> (5) Composite materials and lightweight structures manufacturing.
> (6) Aviation safety, airworthiness and certification engineering — SORA/risk-assessment methodology, safety management systems, and regulatory affairs; Indonesia has almost none of this capacity and it is the binding constraint on everything else.
> (7) Airspace/UTM systems engineering: ATM integration, detect-and-avoid, C2 link reliability, cybersecurity of unmanned systems.
> (8) Aviation law and regulatory policy applied to unmanned systems.
> (9) Agribusiness technology management — the bridge role that translates drone data into plantation decisions, which is the actual job most Indonesian employers want to hire for.
> (10) Drone-service entrepreneurship and operations management (fleet economics, DaaS pricing, insurance).

**China Education Response**

> China's response is unusually fast and legible, and is the clearest single piece of evidence that the state treats this as a pillar industry rather than a fad.

UNDERGRADUATE: the Ministry of Education created a wholly new major, 低空技术与工程 (Low-Altitude Technology & Engineering), programme code 083202TK, approved in the 2024 round and entered into the official undergraduate catalogue for 2025.
> The first six universities began enrolling in autumn 2025 — Beihang University (北京航空航天大学), Beijing Institute of Technology, Beijing University of Posts and Telecommunications, Nanjing University of Aeronautics and Astronautics, South China University of Technology, and Northwestern Polytechnical University — all elite 'Double First-Class' institutions, with a combined first-year intake of only ~360 students (BIT 100, NPU 60).
> Then the scale-up: on 14 August 2025 MOE published applications in which 低空技术与工程 was the single most-requested new programme nationally, with 120 universities applying to add it, plus 12 more adding other low-altitude-related majors.
> That is a 20x institutional expansion in one cycle — a speed no other country has matched for any discipline in recent memory.

VOCATIONAL: the larger volume sits below the degree level.
> 无人机应用技术 (UAV Application Technology) at the zhuanke/vocational-college level had reached 237 newly added institutional programmes by 2026, the most of any low-altitude-related vocational major, spread across essentially all provinces; related tracks include 低空装备工程技术 (low-altitude equipment engineering technology) and 无人驾驶航空器系统应用技术 (UAS application technology) at the vocational-undergraduate level.

DRIVER: an officially cited talent shortfall of ~1 million drone operators and ~3.5 million maintenance technicians, roughly 4.5 million total.
> Regional labour markets already show the pull — Shenzhen reports drone-programme graduates being aggressively recruited.

STRUCTURAL LESSON FOR INDONESIA: China did three things in sequence — (i) named the industry in national policy, (ii) created the degree code and let elite universities define the curriculum with small pilot cohorts, (iii) mass-replicated at the vocational level where the actual job volume is.
> The pilot-then-scale sequencing, and the deliberate 1:10 ratio of degree to vocational capacity, is the transferable part.

### Pelajaran Kebijakan dari China

**Respons Kebijakan China**

> China's regulation runs partly *ahead* of the problems, which is unusual and is what makes it useful as a preemptive template.
> Key measures and what Indonesia could adopt before its own problems mature:

1.
> A single national statute for unmanned aircraft — the Interim Regulations on UAV Flight Management (State Council, effective 1 Jan 2024): mandatory real-name registration, aircraft classification by mass/risk (micro/light/small/medium/large), differentiated operator qualification, defined no-fly and approval procedures, and explicit legal liability.
> Indonesia's PM 37/2020 + PM 63/2021 sit a full institutional tier below this; elevating to a Presidential Regulation or law is the single highest-leverage adoptable step.

2.
> Certification designed for scale, not for one-off approval — CAAC's April 2025 nationwide operating licence for Meituan's fourth-generation drone replaced route-by-route permission with a single company-level certificate.
> Indonesia should design its December 2026 commercial framework this way from the start, rather than institutionalising the case-by-case BVLOS habit.

3.
> A full airworthiness ladder for a new aircraft class — TC → PC → AC → OC, executed on EHang, plus codification of drone airworthiness under the revised Civil Aviation Law.
> The lesson is that certification capability *is* industrial policy: whoever certifies first sets the export standard.

4.
> Enforcement against illegal flight (黑飞) — the Ministry of Public Security has published typical criminal cases; unauthorised flights near airports have caused mass delays, and unauthorised imaging has produced privacy and state-secret incidents.
> China's answer is technical rather than purely punitive: mandatory electronic identification/remote-ID broadcast, with non-compliant aircraft effectively disabled from the network.
> Indonesia should mandate remote-ID at the point it liberalises BVLOS, not years afterwards — retrofitting identification onto an installed fleet is far harder.

5.
> Sub-national legislative experimentation — the Shenzhen SEZ ordinance (Feb 2024) let one city test airspace coordination, infrastructure duties and flight-service rules before national rules hardened.
> Indonesia's analogue would be a special-region low-altitude regulation for IKN, Bali or a Papua logistics zone.

6.
> Institutional ownership — NDRC's Low-Altitude Economy Development Department (Dec 2024) gave the sector a single bureaucratic owner.
> Indonesia's fragmentation across Kemenhub/AirNav/Komdigi/Kemenperin/BRIN/TNI/Polri is the mirror image of this and is the main non-technical bottleneck.

7.
> Standards bodies — Shenzhen's city-level low-altitude standardisation technical committee, with local firms leading or contributing to 18 international/national/industry standards.
> Standard-setting is where long-run rent is captured; Indonesia currently contributes none.

WHAT CHINA GOT WRONG AND INDONESIA SHOULD PRE-EMPT: it did not restrain order-announcement inflation (>90% of published eVTOL orders are non-binding intent), nor local-government duplicative infrastructure investment.
> A disclosure rule requiring firm-order definitions, and a central review before subsidising vertiports, would cost Indonesia nothing and prevent the most predictable waste.

**Rekomendasi Kebijakan Indonesia**

> 1.
> Elevate and replace the framework: issue a Presidential Regulation on unmanned aircraft and advanced air mobility that supersedes the operational limits of PM 37/2020, with risk-tiered categories (adopting JARUS/SORA methodology Indonesia has already engaged with), a standing BVLOS authorisation pathway, and mandatory remote-ID from day one.
> 2.
> Create one accountable owner — a low-altitude directorate or inter-ministerial task force chaired at Coordinating-Ministry level, with DGCA, AirNav, Komdigi, Kemenperin, BRIN, Bappenas, TNI and Polri seated permanently.
> 3.
> Sequence use cases honestly: prioritise 3T/disaster logistics, agriculture and infrastructure inspection; treat urban air taxis as a tourism/prestige niche and refuse to build public infrastructure for them.
> 4.
> Regulatory sandbox first: designate 2-3 corridors (Papua highlands, an eastern-island medical route, and one plantation region) with delegated approval authority and published safety data, rather than waiting for a perfect national rule.
> 5.
> Buy the market into existence: multi-year anchor procurement from Kemenkes (vaccine/blood/medicine), BNPB (disaster), Kementan (spraying subsidies analogous to agricultural machinery subsidies) — demand certainty is worth more to domestic manufacturers than tariffs.
> 6.
> Do not attempt commodity hardware import substitution; use TKDN selectively for integration, payloads, software and MRO, where Indonesia can actually hold margin, and avoid protectionism that raises operators' costs.
> 7.
> Build certification capacity: fund DGCA airworthiness engineers and pursue bilateral validation agreements with CAAC/FAA/EASA so foreign type certificates can be accepted while domestic capability is built.
> 8.
> Data sovereignty rules: high-resolution aerial imagery of national strategic assets must be stored and processed domestically, with clear licensing for foreign-operated fleets.
> 9.
> Labour transition: fund BNSP-certified remote-pilot and drone-maintenance training targeted at plantation workers displaced by spraying automation, in the provinces where the displacement occurs.
> 10.
> Anti-hype discipline: require firm-versus-intent disclosure for any publicly announced aircraft order tied to state entities, and require a demand study before any publicly funded vertiport.

### Peluang & Rekomendasi Aksi

**Peluang Bisnis**

> 1.
> DRONE-AS-A-SERVICE FOR PLANTATIONS — the single largest near-term Indonesian opportunity: contract spraying, fertilising, tree census and disease detection across ~16 million ha of oil palm plus rubber, sugarcane and rice.
> Capital-light (an Agras-class unit plus training), recurring revenue, priced against labour cost.
> Regional operators near Riau, North Sumatra and Kalimantan estates have a structural advantage over Jakarta-based firms.
> 2.
> MINING AND ENERGY INSPECTION/VOLUMETRICS — stockpile measurement, pit surveys, haul-road monitoring, flare/pipeline and transmission-line inspection; high willingness to pay, dollar-denominated clients.
> 3.
> 3T AND MEDICAL LOGISTICS — a Zipline-style operator for eastern Indonesia, built around state and donor contracts (vaccines, blood, essential medicines) before commercial parcels; the Ministry's December 2026 target creates a first-mover window.
> 4.
> MAINTENANCE, REPAIR AND SPARE PARTS (MRO) — the least glamorous and most defensible business: China's own 3.5 million-technician gap shows maintenance demand outruns pilot demand roughly 3.5x, and Indonesia currently sends aircraft abroad or cannibalises units.
> 5.
> TRAINING AND CERTIFICATION — approved remote-pilot schools, BVLOS instructor pipelines, and BNSP-aligned maintenance certification; demand is guaranteed by any regulatory liberalisation.
> 6.
> GEOSPATIAL DATA PROCESSING AND ANALYTICS — the software/services layer that converts flights into decisions (yield forecasting, insurance underwriting, illegal-logging and concession-compliance monitoring); exportable to Malaysia, Thailand and Africa.
> 7.
> PAYLOAD AND SUBSYSTEM MANUFACTURING — sprayers, tanks, mounts, ground stations, RTK base networks and tropical-climate-hardened enclosures: real TKDN content without competing head-on with Shenzhen.
> 8.
> INSURANCE AND LIABILITY PRODUCTS for BVLOS operations — a market that does not yet exist in Indonesia and must exist before scale.
> 9.
> GROUND INFRASTRUCTURE — battery-swap stations, drone hangars/docks for autonomous inspection at fixed sites (the Wuhan 128-hangar model applied to mines and plantations).
> 10.
> DISASTER-RESPONSE SERVICES contracted to BNPB and provincial agencies.
> 11.
> TOURISM eVTOL/heli-shuttle joint ventures in Bali and Labuan Bajo — small, high-margin, and the only realistic near-term passenger business.
> 12.
> COUNTER-DRONE AND AIRSPACE SECURITY services for airports, ports, prisons and critical infrastructure — a market China's 黑飞 problem proves arrives automatically after adoption.

**Rekomendasi Individu Mahasiswa**

> Build a stackable, certifiable skill set rather than a hobby.
> Layer 1 (do now, cheap): obtain a legally recognised Remote Pilot Certificate through a DGCA-recognised/APDI-linked scheme, and log real flight hours — certification plus hours is the entry ticket and most competitors have neither.
> Layer 2 (the differentiator): geospatial data processing — photogrammetry, point clouds, QGIS/ArcGIS, multispectral/NDVI analysis, and Python for automating the pipeline; the money is in the deliverable, not the flight.
> Layer 3 (engineering depth, choose one): embedded systems and flight control (C/C++, ROS, sensor fusion, PX4/ArduPilot) OR electric propulsion and battery systems OR composites/structures.
> Layer 4 (scarce and high-leverage): aviation safety, airworthiness and regulation — learn CASR/PKPS 107, ICAO Annex frameworks and SORA risk assessment; Indonesia has almost nobody who combines flying competence with certification literacy, and that combination is what operators and DGCA will both pay for.
> Layer 5 (domain): pick an industry — palm oil agronomy, mining survey, or utility inspection — and learn its vocabulary; generalist drone pilots are commoditised, domain-fluent ones are not.
> Practical moves: join APDI and a campus UAV team, do internships at Terra Drone Indonesia, Halo Robotics, Frogs Indonesia, Iter Aero or Vela Aero, and follow Chinese-language sources on 低空经济 if possible — the Chinese engineering literature and regulatory documents are 5-8 years ahead of anything available in Indonesian.
> Avoid: building an identity solely as a drone videographer (already commoditised) or waiting for an air-taxi industry that will not employ many people this decade.

**Rekomendasi Perguruan Tinggi**

> OPEN/EXPAND: (1) A D3/D4 UAS Operations & Maintenance programme at polytechnics located in the plantation and mining provinces — Riau, North Sumatra, East/Central Kalimantan, South Sulawesi, Papua — not concentrated in Java; this is where the jobs are and where China's vocational-scale lesson (237 vocational programmes versus 6 elite degree programmes) applies most directly.
> (2) Scale and replicate Polman Bandung's D4 Teknologi Rekayasa Sistem Aerial Nirawak, which is already Indonesia's closest analogue to China's new major, and use it as the curriculum reference.
> (3) Add an Aerial Robotics / Unmanned Systems Engineering concentration inside existing aerospace and electrical programmes at ITB, ITS, PENS, UGM, ITDA and STTKD rather than creating stand-alone majors everywhere — Indonesia does not have the faculty depth for 120 new programmes, and China's own sequencing (6 pilot programmes first) argues against premature mass replication.
> (4) Create Indonesia's first Airworthiness & Aviation Safety Engineering track in partnership with DGCA — this is the true national bottleneck and no campus currently owns it.
> (5) Establish a Geospatial Data Science programme or concentration, since the analytics layer employs more people than the flying layer.

REFORM RATHER THAN CLOSE: rebuild Geodesy/Geomatics curricula around photogrammetry, LiDAR and point-cloud processing; embed precision agriculture and remote sensing into agronomy and plantation-management programmes; add electric propulsion, autonomy and battery systems to aeronautical engineering; add UAS law to aviation-law teaching.

INSTITUTIONAL MOVES: dual certification (degree + BNSP/RPC) so graduates leave employable on day one; industry-funded teaching fleets from plantation and mining companies; a shared national UAS test range with delegated BVLOS authority for research flights; and partnerships or student exchange with Beihang, NUAA or NPU to import curriculum design directly from the six Chinese pioneer programmes.
> AVOID: opening dozens of thin 'drone' majors chasing a policy headline — the predictable Indonesian failure mode, and the exact error China avoided by piloting with 360 students before scaling.

### Faktor Risiko & Sisi Gelap

**Dampak Negatif China**

> 1.
> ORDER AND VALUATION INFLATION.
> More than 90% of publicly announced eVTOL orders are letters of intent or framework agreements with no firm price, delivery schedule or penalty clause; AutoFlight's ~2,000 announced orders correspond to roughly 300 confirmed (≈15% conversion).
> Headline order values above RMB 30 billion coexist with actual manufacturer revenues in the tens of millions — EHang sold 11 aircraft for RMB 26.1 million in Q1 2025.
> This is a textbook setup for a sectoral repricing.
2.
> LOCAL-GOVERNMENT DUPLICATIVE INVESTMENT.
> Thirty-plus provinces wrote the low-altitude economy into 2025 work reports and cities raced to build landing points, guidance funds and industrial parks; the predictable outcome is underused vertiports and stranded fiscal capacity in already-indebted localities — the same pattern seen earlier in EV, semiconductor and big-data park build-outs.
3.
> INVOLUTION (内卷) AND MARGIN COLLAPSE.
> Over 10,000 new low-altitude companies registered in 2024 alone, with 188 firms literally naming themselves '低空经济'; commodity drone segments are already in price war, and most entrants have no defensible technology.
4.
> UNPROFITABLE FLAGSHIP OPERATIONS.
> Meituan's drone delivery costs ~RMB 7-8 per order and remains loss-making after eight years and 600,000+ orders — the emblematic use case does not yet work economically even in the best conditions on earth for it.
5.
> ILLEGAL FLIGHT (黑飞) AND AVIATION SAFETY.
> Unauthorised drone flights near airports have caused mass flight delays and significant economic losses; the Ministry of Public Security has had to publish criminal enforcement cases.
> Real-time low-altitude surveillance capability still lags the traffic it must supervise.
6.
> PRIVACY AND SECURITY LEAKAGE.
> Unauthorised imaging of residential buildings and sensitive facilities has produced privacy violations and state-secret exposure incidents; illegal aftermarket modification of drones to defeat geofencing and altitude limits is an acknowledged problem.
7.
> REGULATORY WHIPLASH.
> Having liberalised in 2024, China is now tightening — mandatory electronic identification broadcast with non-registered aircraft effectively grounded — imposing retrofit costs on the very fleet the earlier policy encouraged.
8.
> TALENT MISMATCH.
> A stated 4.5 million-person gap coexists with new degree programmes producing 360 graduates a year, guaranteeing several years of wage distortion and low-quality training-provider proliferation.

**Risiko Sosial Indonesia**

> 1.
> PRESTIGE-PROJECT MISALLOCATION.
> The most likely Indonesian failure is spending public money on IKN air taxis and vertiports — visible, photogenic, and serving a few hundred elite passengers — while 3T medical logistics, the use case with genuine social return, remains unfunded.
> Chinese and US vendors have a commercial interest in encouraging exactly this ordering.
2.
> IMPORT DEPENDENCY WITH NO VALUE CAPTURE.
> Without a deliberate services-and-MRO strategy, Indonesia repeats the solar-panel and EV pattern: buy Chinese hardware, host foreign-operated fleets, and capture only low-margin field labour while the data and software margin leaves the country.
3.
> LABOUR DISPLACEMENT WITHOUT TRANSITION.
> Plantation spraying automation will hit exactly the workers with the least mobility — low-education, often informal, frequently in company towns — in provinces with weak retraining infrastructure.
> Without a funded transition programme this becomes a rural income shock concentrated in Sumatra and Kalimantan.
4.
> SURVEILLANCE AND PRIVACY WITHOUT LEGAL PROTECTION.
> Persistent aerial monitoring of plantations, concessions and neighbourhoods has no clear Indonesian legal boundary; the PDP Law does not address aerial imaging specifically.
> Risk of drones being used to monitor labour, land-rights claimants, and communities in agrarian conflict zones — with no complaints mechanism.
5.
> SECURITY AND CONFLICT SPILLOVER.
> Papua's security situation makes drones dual-use in a live conflict; liberalising airspace where armed groups operate raises real risks of weaponised or smuggling use, and conversely risks the military blocking civilian use entirely.
> Drone-enabled smuggling across maritime borders and into prisons is a documented pattern elsewhere and will arrive.
6.
> AVIATION SAFETY WITHOUT ENFORCEMENT CAPACITY.
> Indonesia already struggles with general aviation oversight; adding tens of thousands of unmanned aircraft without remote-ID, UTM or inspection capacity invites a mid-air or urban crash incident that could trigger a blanket ban — the regulatory whiplash scenario.
7.
> DATA SOVEREIGNTY.
> High-resolution imagery of ports, mines, military-adjacent infrastructure and concession boundaries flowing to foreign cloud platforms is a strategic exposure with no current rule.
8.
> HYPE-DRIVEN EDUCATION MALINVESTMENT.
> Dozens of campuses opening thin 'drone' programmes to chase a policy headline, producing unemployable graduates — the recurring Indonesian pattern after every technology announcement.
9.
> UNREGULATED INFORMAL OPERATORS.
> A large grey market of uncertified pilots undercutting certified operators, degrading safety and making the compliant business model unviable.

**Unintended Consequences**

> IN CHINA: (a) The 'low-altitude economy' label became a financial-market keyword, driving concept-stock speculation and company renaming (20 → 188 firms named after the sector in one year) largely decoupled from operations.
> (b) Certification leadership became a geopolitical asset: by certifying the world's first passenger eVTOL, CAAC positioned itself to export the *standard*, not just the aircraft — an outcome framed as safety policy but functioning as trade policy.
> (c) Liberalising drone flight created a counter-drone industry and a new policing burden, converting a civil-aviation programme into a public-security programme.
> (d) Mandatory identification broadcast, introduced to control illegal flight, effectively grounds non-compliant legacy aircraft — the regulation retroactively destroys installed-base value.
> (e) The delivery-drone flagship trained the public to expect a service that is structurally unprofitable, creating political pressure to sustain it.

PREDICTED FOR INDONESIA: (a) Cargo drones may reduce the political urgency of building roads and airstrips in Papua — a technology substituting for infrastructure the state owes anyway, entrenching rather than closing regional inequality.
> (b) Plantation drone adoption will improve worker health (less pesticide exposure) while eliminating those workers' jobs — a genuine welfare ambiguity that will be argued in bad faith by both sides.
> (c) Cheap aerial monitoring makes concession-boundary and illegal-logging enforcement technically trivial, which could either strengthen environmental governance or expose how much illegality is politically tolerated — the technology forces a choice the state may prefer to avoid.
> (d) The same imagery will strengthen corporate positions in agrarian land disputes against communities that have no comparable evidentiary capability.
> (e) An eVTOL showcase failure at IKN (delayed certification, an incident, or vendor withdrawal) could discredit the entire low-altitude agenda including the useful parts, setting drone logistics back years.
> (f) Insurance markets, not regulators, may end up as the de facto safety authority — as happened with Indonesian ride-hailing.
> (g) Drone imports could be squeezed by geopolitical export controls on Chinese drone technology, an exposure Indonesia has not priced.

**Kelompok Rentan**

> 1.
> Manual plantation sprayers and fertiliser-application crews in oil palm, rubber and sugarcane — the most directly displaced group, typically low-education, often informal or contract labour, concentrated in Riau, North Sumatra and Kalimantan, with minimal realistic path into certified drone work without funded retraining.
> 2.
> Field survey assistants and traditional surveying labour.
> 3.
> Smallholder farmers (roughly 40% of oil palm area) who cannot afford drone services and fall further behind estate productivity — a widening intra-agricultural gap.
> 4.
> Uncertified informal drone operators and small photography businesses, who will be squeezed out when certification is finally enforced and by commoditised pricing.
> 5.
> Remote and indigenous communities in Papua, Kalimantan and Maluku subject to aerial monitoring in land-rights disputes without legal recourse or comparable data capability.
> 6.
> Small Indonesian drone SMEs competing against vertically integrated Chinese vendors bundling hardware, software and service at prices no local assembler can match.
> 7.
> Small logistics operators, boat operators and porters on remote-area supply routes that cargo drones will partially replace.
> 8.
> Vocational graduates of thinly resourced new 'drone' programmes who receive certificates without flight hours or data skills.
> 9.
> Residents under emerging urban flight corridors in Jakarta or Bali who bear noise and safety externalities without benefit — a group with no organised voice in Indonesian aviation policy.

### Contoh Kasus Konkret

**Kasus China**

> CASE 1 — EHANG EH216-S, THE FULL CERTIFICATION LADDER AND ITS REVENUE REALITY.
> Guangzhou-based EHang took a two-seat, pilotless, fully autonomous eVTOL through the world's first complete regulatory ladder: Type Certificate (Oct 2023), the global eVTOL industry's first Production Certificate (Apr 2024), Standard Airworthiness Certificate, and the world's first Air Operator Certificates for human-carrying pilotless aircraft (30 Mar 2025, to EHang and its Hefei JV Hey Airlines).
> It has logged over 60,000 safe flights.
> Yet commercial operations are limited to sightseeing and point A-to-A experience flights, and Q1 2025 revenue was 11 aircraft for RMB 26.1 million (~USD 3.6 million).
> The case is simultaneously the strongest evidence of Chinese regulatory leadership and the clearest evidence that eVTOL revenue is a decade behind eVTOL certification.

CASE 2 — MEITUAN DRONE DELIVERY: OPERATIONAL SUCCESS, ECONOMIC FAILURE.
> 64 routes across Shenzhen, Beijing, Shanghai, Nanjing, Guangzhou, Hong Kong and Dubai; 600,000+ cumulative orders by end-June 2025; and in April 2025 CAAC granted its fourth-generation drone a nationwide operating licence — one certificate for the whole country instead of route-by-route approval, a genuine world-first in regulatory design.
> Cost per delivery remains ~RMB 7-8 and the unit is not profitable after eight years.
> Directly relevant to Indonesia: if this fails economically in Shenzhen, urban drone food delivery cannot work against Indonesian ojol pricing.

CASE 3 — SF EXPRESS FENGYI: THE BORING BUSINESS THAT WORKS.
> ~190,000 drone sorties and ~2.32 million parcels in H1 2025; 800-2,000 daily take-offs and 12,000+ daily deliveries in the Greater Bay Area.
> Freight, not passengers; scheduled corridors, not on-demand — the closest analogue to what Indonesia should build for its islands.

CASE 4 — SHENZHEN AS INSTITUTIONAL PROTOTYPE.
> China's first sub-national low-altitude statute (effective 1 Feb 2024), CAAC designation as a national low-altitude demonstration zone (Mar 2024), a military-civil-commercial coordinated approval mechanism and city flight pilot (Nov 2024), China's first city-level low-altitude standardisation committee, and 18 international/national/industry standards led or co-authored locally.
> Nanshan district alone reported >RMB 550 billion low-altitude-related output by end-2024.
> The case shows the sequence — legislate, designate, coordinate airspace, then set standards.

CASE 5 — THE EDUCATION SHOCK.
> MOE creates 低空技术与工程 (code 083202TK); six elite universities enrol ~360 students in 2025; by 14 August 2025, 120 universities apply to add the same major — a 20x expansion in one cycle, against an official 4.5 million-person talent gap and 237 new vocational UAV programmes.

CASE 6 — THE ORDER BUBBLE.
> >RMB 30 billion in announced eVTOL orders by Nov 2025, of which >90% are non-binding; AutoFlight's ~2,000 announced versus ~300 confirmed (≈15%).
> The counter-case to every other number in this file.
