### Tingkat Keyakinan & Kualitas Sumber

**Catatan Kontradiksi Data**

> 1.
> CHINA MARKET SIZE DIFFERS BY A FACTOR OF ~2.7.
> CAAC/state projections put the 2025 low-altitude economy at RMB 1.5 trillion, while iMedia Research puts it at RMB 561.5 billion for the same year (reaching RMB 1.39 trillion only by 2029).
> The gap is definitional: the official figure appears to include the full ecosystem (manufacturing, operations, infrastructure, airspace management, application services and supporting industries) and possibly induced output, while private estimates count a narrower core.
> Any Indonesian policy document citing 'RMB 1.5 trillion' should be read as an ecosystem-wide, policy-target number, not a revenue measurement.
2.
> ANNOUNCED VERSUS REAL eVTOL DEMAND.
> >RMB 30 billion in announced orders versus >90% non-binding intent, and AutoFlight's ~15% conversion rate, contradict the headline order figures entirely.
> EHang's Q1 2025 revenue of RMB 26.1 million from 11 aircraft is the reality check.
3.
> INDONESIAN MARKET SIZE.
> IMARC gives ~USD 438 million (2025) → ~USD 1.03 billion (2034) at ~10% CAGR; other commercial reports (Statista, Knowledge Sourcing, 6Wresearch, MarketResearchFuture) give materially different bases, segment definitions and growth rates.
> None is an official Indonesian figure, and none was independently verifiable.
4.
> INDONESIAN CARGO DRONE SPECIFICATIONS CONFLICT.
> Reported payloads for domestically developed cargo drones range from ~5 kg (one description of the Iter Aero IA-25, with 45-minute endurance and 60 km range) through 100-150 kg (Indonesian press reports on locally built cargo drones) to ~700 kg (a Vela large-drone prototype).
> These almost certainly describe different aircraft or different development stages being conflated in reporting; treat all specific payload figures as unverified.
5.
> INDONESIAN REGISTRATION AND CERTIFICATION COUNTS ARE UNPUBLISHED.
> No official DGCA figure for registered drones or certified remote pilots was found; APDI reports 'thousands' of members across 25 regions, which is a membership figure and not a certification count.
6.
> GENERAL-AVIATION INFRASTRUCTURE BASELINE.
> China's 499 public general-aviation airports (end-2023) is a widely cited figure but definitions of 'general aviation airport' versus 'landing site' vary across Chinese sources, and 2025-2026 totals were not consistently reported.
7.
> 'TREND START YEAR' IS GENUINELY AMBIGUOUS.
> Depending on whether one dates from DJI's founding (2006), the first national planning mention (2021), the Interim Regulations (2024) or the Government Work Report (2024), the China start year moves by nearly two decades — which correspondingly moves any lag estimate by the same amount.
> The layered dating in this file is deliberate.

## 23. Demographic Crisis (Marriage & Birth Collapse) — the simultaneous breakdown of two linked social institutions: household formation (marriage registrations) and reproduction (fertility). In China this has produced a marriage count 55% below its 2013 peak, births at their lowest level since 1939, and four consecutive years of absolute population decline. The domain is the upstream driver of at least four downstream economies already researched separately in this set: the silver economy, the one-person/solo economy, the pet economy, and the restructuring of the education sector. In Indonesia the same mechanism is running roughly one generation behind at the national level but is already complete in Jakarta, Yogyakarta and most of Java.
**Kategori**: Demografi & Sosial (Demography & Society) — but functionally a meta-category. Unlike a technology trend, this is not a sector; it is a state variable that re-prices every other sector: education (student pipeline), healthcare (obstetrics vs geriatrics), real estate (household formation is the primary demand driver for housing), consumer goods (household size determines pack size), labour markets (workforce entry cohort), fiscal policy (pension and health insurance solvency), and financial services (life-cycle savings). Cross-cuts with: Silver Economy, Real Estate/Housing Crisis, Restrukturisasi Pendidikan Tinggi, Youth Unemployment/Anti-Hustle Culture, Consumer Downgrade, Emotional Economy.

📊 LAGGARD WITH SIMULTANEOUS AND COMPRESSED ELEMENTS — and a critical 'poorer at the same demographic stage' inversion. Laggard on the macro variables (population decline lags by 30-40 years; depth of fertility collapse lags by a generation). Simultaneous on the proximate causes: the 2013 marriage peak, the 50% urbanisation crossing, the smartphone/social-media transition, and the post-2020 housing-affordability shock all hit both countries within a few years of each other, which is why the marriage-decline curves are only 6-9 years apart despite the fertility levels being 30+ years apart. Compressed on the downstream shocks: school closures, PAUD teacher redundancy and silver-economy policy framing arrived in Indonesia only 2-3 years after China. And critically INVERTED on the economic dimension — Indonesia is reaching each demographic milestone at a substantially lower income level than China did. China crossed 12% aged 60+ around 2010-2013 with GDP per capita of roughly US$5,000-7,000 and crossed into population decline in 2022 at roughly US$12,700; Indonesia crossed 11.97% aged 60+ in 2025 at roughly US$5,000 but with a far weaker manufacturing base, a 59% informal labour market, a tax-to-GDP ratio around 10-11% and almost no funded pension coverage. The Chinese phrase 未富先老 ('growing old before growing rich') applies to Indonesia with greater force than to China, because China at least had two decades of 8-10% growth and a state balance sheet capable of absorbing 2.9 trillion yuan of annual social security subsidy. Indonesia will not. | 🎯 Prob: Tinggi (Very High) — but the framing 'transfer' is analytically wrong for this item and should be handled with care. | 🔍 Keyakinan: Tinggi (High) for the core statistics on both sides — Chinese figures come from the National Bureau of Statistics and Ministry of Civil Affairs official releases as reported by Caixin, Xinhua, Reuters and SCMP, and Indonesian figures come from BPS SUPAS 2025 and the BPS marriage/divorce registration series, all of which are primary official sources with consistent cross-reporting. Tinggi also for the downstream education data on both sides (China's Ministry of Education 2025 statistical communique; Indonesia's Dapodik-derived reporting on school mergers and PAUD enrolment).

Sedang (Medium) for: the lag estimates, which depend on which variable is chosen and are explicitly presented as a range with the reasoning shown rather than a single number; the Indonesian timeline predictions for mainstream and peak years; the interpretation of the 2025 Chinese marriage rebound as primarily a registration-reform artefact (well-supported by the city-level pattern and the simultaneous birth decline, but not formally decomposed by any published study); and market-size figures for the solo, pet and eldercare economies, which come from consultancies and vary considerably by methodology and definition.

Rendah (Low) for: the projected Indonesian TFR floor (1.6-1.9), which is a judgement based on religiosity, marriage norms and sex-ratio structure rather than a modelled estimate; specific Indonesian business opportunity sizing, for which no reliable local market data exists; and Indonesian population peak year and level, where different projection vintages (BPS, UN WPP, Bappenas) diverge materially.

> **Status di Indonesia**: ALREADY UNDERWAY AND FASTER THAN OFFICIAL NARRATIVE ADMITS — 'baru mulai' at the national level, but 'sudah masuk masif' in Java, Bali and the metropolitan corridor. Three facts establish this. First, marriage: registered marriages fell from 2,110,776 in 2014 to 1,478,302 in 2024 — a 30% decline in a decade — and 2025 came in essentially flat at 1,480,048, so the level has stabilised at a decade low rather than recovered. Second, fertility: SUPAS 2025 (released by BPS on 5 May 2026) put national TFR at 2.13, essentially at the 2.10 replacement threshold, with NINE provinces already below replacement — DKI Jakarta 1.79, DI Yogyakarta 1.84, East Java 1.95, Banten 1.96, Bali 2.02, West Java 2.05, Central Java 2.05, North Sulawesi 2.07 and East Kalimantan 2.09. That is the whole of Java plus Bali plus the two most urbanised outer-island provinces — around 60% of the national population living in below-replacement territory. Third, the downstream shock has already arrived in the schools: Boyolali regency in Central Java merged 48 state primary schools into 24 in 2026 for lack of pupils; Temanggung recorded 32 schools with fewer than five new entrants; individual schools (SDN Butuh, SDN Kauman 27 Solo) received one or two new pupils; hundreds of primary schools nationwide enrolled between one and five new students in the 2025/2026 academic year. PAUD (early childhood) enrolment fell by 203,936 pupils in 2024 alone and PAUD teacher numbers fell by 5,805 — the largest decline of any education level. Meanwhile Indonesia has already crossed the ageing threshold: 11.97% of the population is aged 60+ (about 33.9 million people) per SUPAS 2025, with sixteen provinces already in the ageing phase, led by DI Yogyakarta at 17.83%. What has NOT arrived: absolute population decline (Indonesia is projected to keep growing into the 2050s-2060s), a collapse in the marriage NORM (marriage remains near-universal and religiously mandated), and any pronatalist policy apparatus.

### Basic Info

**Tahun Mulai China**

> Three distinct inflection points that must not be conflated.
> (a) Policy-forced decline, 1980-2015: the one-child policy (formally launched September 1980) drove TFR from ~2.7 in 1979 to below replacement by around 1991-1992 — this phase was administratively imposed, not voluntary.
> (b) Failure of liberalisation, 2016-2021: the universal two-child policy (effective 1 January 2016) produced one rebound year (18.83 million births in 2016) and then continuous collapse; the three-child policy (May 2021) produced no rebound at all — this proved that Chinese fertility had become behaviourally low, not policy-constrained.
> (c) The visible crisis phase, 2022-present: population decline began in 2022 (-850,000, the first fall since the 1961 famine year), marriage registrations hit a record low of 6.106 million couples in 2024 (-20.5% YoY, the lowest since the series began in 1980), and 2025 births fell to 7.92 million — the lowest annual figure since 1939.
> For the purposes of this research the operative start year is 2013 for marriage (the peak year, 13.47 million couples) and 2017 for births (the start of the eight-year uninterrupted slide).

**Pemain Kunci China**

> This is a state-driven phenomenon rather than a company-driven one, so the 'key players' are institutions and second-order commercial beneficiaries.
> STATE ACTORS: National Bureau of Statistics (NBS, publishes the January population release); Ministry of Civil Affairs (MCA, publishes quarterly marriage/divorce registrations); National Health Commission (NHC, owns fertility-support policy and the childcare subsidy); State Council General Office (issued the October 2024 13-measure birth-support directive and the July 2025 national childcare subsidy); Ministry of Education (manages the school-closure wave); Ministry of Human Resources and Social Security (pension solvency).
> RESEARCH/ADVOCACY: YuWa Population Research Institute (育娲人口研究, founded by Ctrip chairman James Liang / 梁建章 with demographer Ren Zeping — the single most influential non-state voice, author of the 'cost of raising a child' series); Peking University's Institute of Population Research; He Yafu (何亚福), independent demographer; Yi Fuxian (易富贤), the leading external critic who argues official figures overstate the population.
> COMMERCIAL WINNERS: pet-economy firms (Gambol/乖宝, Chinapet/中宠, Yuanfei); solo-dining and small-appliance brands (Bear Electric/小熊电器, Xiaomi ecosystem, Haidilao's single-seat format); eldercare and adult-nutrition pivots by former baby brands (Feihe/飞鹤 launched middle-aged and senior milk powder in 2022; Yili and Mengniu adult nutrition lines); IVF and assisted-reproduction chains (Jinxin Fertility/锦欣生殖).
> COMMERCIAL LOSERS: infant formula, diapers, maternity hospitals, kindergarten chains, K-12 tutoring, children's apparel, wedding services in lower-tier cities.

### China Trend Detail

**Apa Yang Terjadi Di China**

> MECHANISM — a two-stage causal chain that Chinese demographers now describe as 'no marriage, no birth' (不婚则不育).
> Because roughly 95% of Chinese births still occur within registered marriage (non-marital births carry hukou, benefit and social penalties in most provinces), the marriage registration series functions as a leading indicator of births with a lag of one to two years.
> Marriage itself is being suppressed by a stack of reinforcing pressures: (1) the cohort effect — the number of people aged 22-35 is itself shrinking because it is drawn from the small post-1990 birth cohorts, so even a constant marriage propensity produces fewer marriages; (2) the sex-ratio distortion left by the one-child era — roughly 30-35 million surplus males of marriageable age, concentrated in rural and lower-income areas, producing bride-price (彩礼) inflation that in some provinces exceeds several years of household income; (3) female educational attainment — women now outnumber men in Chinese higher education, and the hypergamy norm mathematically strands both high-education women and low-education men; (4) housing — in most tier-1 and tier-2 cities a marital apartment is treated as a precondition for marriage, and the post-2021 property downturn simultaneously destroyed household wealth and left prices unaffordable relative to youth income; (5) youth unemployment — the urban 16-24 rate (excluding students) has hovered in the high teens since 2023, delaying the income stability young men are expected to demonstrate before marriage.

The second stage is fertility within marriage.
> YuWa's cost-of-raising-a-child series is the canonical explanation: raising a child to age 18 costs an average of 538,000 yuan nationally, roughly 6.3 times GDP per capita — the second-highest ratio in the world after South Korea, and far above the United States (4.11x) or Japan (4.26x).
> In cities the figure rises to 667,000 yuan, and in Shanghai to 1.03 million yuan (Beijing 969,000).
> The Chinese internet's term for children — 吞金兽, 'gold-devouring beasts' — captures the framing.
> Layered on top are the 996 work culture, the near-total absence of affordable 0-3 childcare until very recently, employer discrimination against women of childbearing age (which extended maternity leave paradoxically worsened), and the involution (内卷) of the education arms race, which made each child a competitive project rather than a marginal addition.

SCALE OF THE OUTCOME.
> Marriages fell from 13.47 million couples in 2013 to 6.106 million in 2024 — a 55% collapse in eleven years — with the single worst year being 2024 at -20.5%.
> Births fell from 18.83 million in 2016 to 7.92 million in 2025, a 58% collapse in nine years.
> The population has now declined four years running: -850,000 (2022), -2.08 million (2023), -1.39 million (2024), -3.39 million (2025), ending 2025 at 1.40489 billion.
> In 2025 deaths (11.31 million) exceeded births by 3.39 million.
> The birth rate of 5.63 per 1,000 is the lowest since the founding of the PRC in 1949, and the absolute birth count is the lowest since 1939.
> Twenty-four of thirty-one provincial-level jurisdictions reported population declines for end-2025; only seven grew.

THE 2025 MARRIAGE REBOUND AND WHY IT IS MOSTLY ARTEFACT.
> Marriages rose 10.76% in 2025 to 6.76 million couples (+657,000).
> This is heavily driven by (a) the revised Marriage Registration Regulation effective 10 May 2025, which abolished the requirement to register in a spouse's hukou location and removed the hukou booklet requirement entirely — a migrant population of roughly 250 million people could suddenly register where they actually live, pulling forward and capturing marriages that were previously deferred or unrecorded; (b) a zodiac/calendar effect — 2024 was a 'no-spring year' (无春年), traditionally considered inauspicious for weddings, which artificially depressed 2024 and flattered the 2025 comparison; and (c) the first wave of provincial marriage subsidies.
> Registration surges were concentrated in migrant-receiving cities: Shanghai +38.7% to 125,102 couples, Shenzhen +28.5% to 118,900, Fuzhou +20.4% to 37,887 — precisely the pattern a registration-location reform would produce.
> Critically, the marriage rebound did not stop the birth collapse: 2025 births still fell 17% to 7.92 million.
> The 2024 birth uptick to 9.54 million had been a Year-of-the-Dragon effect and fully reversed.

DOWNSTREAM RESTRUCTURING ALREADY VISIBLE.
> Education: China closed nearly 30,000 kindergartens and primary schools in a single year in 2025 — 21,400 kindergartens (an average of 59 per day, leaving 231,900) and roughly 8,000 primary schools.
> Preschool enrolment fell 10% (-3.58 million) to 32.25 million, down from a 2020 peak of 48.18 million — a one-third contraction in five years.
> Primary school admissions fell 9.6% to 14.61 million, 22% below the 2023 recruitment peak.
> Total K-12 teaching staff fell to 15.68 million, a second consecutive annual decline, with losses concentrated in early education.
> The wave is moving up the age ladder: senior high school intake still rose 3.7% in 2025 and the high-school-age population is expected to peak around 2029, after which the shock hits universities.
> Healthcare: the 'obstetric winter' (产科寒冬) — dozens of public hospitals have shut delivery wards, obstetricians are retraining into other specialties, and Shanghai deliveries fell from about 34,000 to 20,000.
> Consumption: household size has fallen from 3.10 to about 2.62 persons; one-person households exceed 125 million (nearly 20% of households in 2024, projected above 30% — 150 to 200 million people — by 2030); the solo-dining market reached roughly 800 billion yuan in 2025; the pet economy reached about 811.4 billion yuan and Goldman Sachs projects urban pets will outnumber young children by 2030.
> Fiscal: social security subsidies consumed 2.9 trillion yuan in 2025, 10.1% of general budget spending, and the pension fund would have run a 1.4 trillion yuan shortfall in 2024 without them.

POLICY RESPONSE — LATE, LARGE, AND SO FAR INEFFECTIVE.
> October 2024: State Council directive with 13 targeted measures on childbirth support, childcare, education, housing and employment.
> March 2025: 'childcare subsidies' entered the annual Government Work Report for the first time, with an explicit instruction to use financial incentives.
> July 2025: the first nationwide, tax-exempt childcare subsidy — 3,600 yuan per child per year for every child under three, backdated to 1 January 2025, covering more than 20 million families annually.
> Autumn 2025: free preschool phased in, starting with waived fees for the final kindergarten year.
> December 2025: moves toward effectively free childbirth by folding delivery costs into maternity insurance.
> At least 23 provincial-level regions run their own birth subsidies; Hohhot's is the most aggressive — 10,000 yuan for a first child, 10,000 yuan a year until age five for a second (50,000 total), and 10,000 yuan a year until age ten for a third (100,000 total).
> The 2025 result — births down 17% despite all of this — is the single most important policy datapoint in the entire domain: at 3,600 yuan against a 538,000 yuan cost of raising a child, the subsidy covers roughly 1.2% of the total cost, and cash transfers of this magnitude have nowhere in the world reversed a fertility collapse.

**Data Skala China**

> MARRIAGE (Ministry of Civil Affairs, couples registered): 2013 peak 13.47 million | 2019 9.27 million | 2020 8.13 million | 2021 7.64 million | 2022 6.83 million | 2023 7.68 million (post-COVID rebound) | 2024 6.106 million, -20.5% YoY, lowest since the series began in 1980 | 2025 6.76 million, +10.76% (+657,000), driven by the 10 May 2025 registration reform.
> City detail 2025: Shanghai 125,102 (+38.7%), Shenzhen 118,900 (+28.5%), Fuzhou 37,887 (+20.4%).

DIVORCE: 2024 2.82 million (+1.1% YoY) | 2025 2.743 million.
> Divorce/marriage ratio 2024: 46%.

BIRTHS (NBS): 2016 18.83 million (two-child policy peak) | 2019 14.65 million | 2020 12.02 million | 2021 10.62 million | 2022 9.56 million | 2023 9.02 million | 2024 9.54 million (Year of the Dragon rebound) | 2025 7.92 million, -1.62 million (-17%), the lowest since 7.57 million in 1939.
> Crude birth rate 2025: 5.63 per 1,000 (2024: 6.77; a decade earlier: 11.99).
> Total fertility rate estimated at roughly 1.0-1.1, among the lowest in the world.

DEATHS AND POPULATION: deaths 2025 11.31 million.
> Population end-2025 1.40489 billion.
> Annual change: -850,000 (2022), -2.08 million (2023), -1.39 million (2024), -3.39 million (2025) — four consecutive declines, accelerating.
> Twenty-four of thirty-one provinces shrank in 2025; seven grew.
> Women of childbearing age: 213.7 million, down 13% over the decade.

PROJECTIONS (Rhodium Group, 2026): China loses about 60 million people between 2026 and 2035 — roughly the population of France or Italy; annual decline reaches 7.6 million per year by 2035; deaths reach about 15 million per year by 2035.
> Worker-to-retiree ratio: 4.4 (2024) → 3.5 (2030) → 2.8 (2035).
> Long-run GDP growth projection downgraded to 4.2% annually through 2035 from 4.8%.

COST OF CHILDREN (YuWa Population Research Institute): 538,000 yuan to raise a child to 18 nationally, 6.3x GDP per capita (US 4.11x, Japan 4.26x, Australia 2.08x); urban average 667,000 yuan; Shanghai 1.03 million yuan; Beijing 969,000 yuan.
> China ranks second globally behind South Korea.

MARRIAGE BEHAVIOUR: unmarried share 51.3% at ages 25-29, 18.4% at 30-34, 8.0% at 35-39 (2023).
> Mean age at first marriage has risen to roughly 28.1 for women and 29.3 for men, from 25.3 overall in the 2020 census baseline.
> Expected years spent single from birth (2020 census): 33.6 years for males, 29.6 for females.

EDUCATION SHOCK (Ministry of Education, 2025): 21,400 kindergartens closed (about 59 per day), leaving 231,900; roughly 8,000 primary schools closed; nearly 30,000 institutions in total.
> Preschool enrolment 32.25 million (-3.58 million, -10%), down from 48.18 million in 2020.
> Primary intake 14.61 million (-9.6%, -22% vs the 2023 peak); the primary student body shrank by 4.06 million.
> K-12 teaching staff 15.68 million (second consecutive decline).
> Counter-trend: senior high intake 10.74 million (+3.7%); 3,167 higher education institutions; gross tertiary enrolment 61.3%; master's graduates exceeded 1 million and doctorates 100,000 for the first time.
> High-school-age population peaks around 2029.

DOWNSTREAM CONSUMER ECONOMY: one-person households exceed 125 million, nearly 20% of all households in 2024, projected above 30% (150-200 million people) by 2030; average household size 2.62 persons, down from 3.10.
> Solo-dining market roughly 800 billion yuan (about US$115 billion) in 2025.
> Small appliances market roughly US$60 billion in 2025 (CAGR 3.8% to 2030).
> Pet economy roughly 811.4 billion yuan in 2025, up 68% from 494 billion.
> Infant formula market roughly RMB 129 billion (US$18 billion) in 2025 — still the world's largest by revenue but structurally shrinking in volume; the maternity-and-baby online channel still grew 12.6% to RMB 223.78 billion as brands trade volume for premiumisation.

FISCAL: social security subsidy 2.9 trillion yuan in 2025 = 10.1% of general budget spending; pension fund shortfall of 1.4 trillion yuan in 2024 absent subsidies.
> National childcare subsidy: 3,600 yuan per child per year under age three, covering 20+ million families.

**Fase Tren Di China**

> PHASE: Full-blown crisis with an institutionalised, escalating but so-far-failing state response — best described as 'declining fundamentals + booming policy response + booming compensatory economies'.
> Decompose by layer: (1) Marriage and fertility fundamentals — DECLINING, and the 2025 marriage uptick is an administrative artefact rather than a behavioural reversal, since births still fell 17% in the same year.
> (2) Policy response — BOOMING/ESCALATING: 2024-2025 saw the first universal cash subsidy, the first free-preschool commitment, the first move toward free childbirth, and a registration-law liberalisation; expect further escalation (housing-linked incentives, longer paid leave, tax credits) through the 15th Five-Year Plan period.
> (3) Downstream compensatory economies — BOOMING: silver economy, solo economy, pet economy, adult nutrition, IVF/assisted reproduction, eldercare robotics.
> (4) Downstream contracting sectors — IN ACTIVE LIQUIDATION: preschools, primary schools, obstetrics, infant formula volume, children's apparel, K-12 tutoring, lower-tier wedding services.
> (5) Public discourse — BACKLASH/CONTESTED: state pronatalist messaging collides with a young-adult cohort that reads marriage and children as financial liabilities, and heavy-handed local measures (officials phoning newlyweds about pregnancy plans, restrictions on non-medically-necessary abortions) generate visible online resistance, particularly among women.
> The crucial analytic point is that this phase is irreversible on a multi-decade horizon: the women who will bear children in 2045 have already been born, and their cohort is 13% smaller than a decade ago.

### Status Indonesia Saat Ini

**Status Di Indonesia**

> ALREADY UNDERWAY AND FASTER THAN OFFICIAL NARRATIVE ADMITS — 'baru mulai' at the national level, but 'sudah masuk masif' in Java, Bali and the metropolitan corridor.
> Three facts establish this.
> First, marriage: registered marriages fell from 2,110,776 in 2014 to 1,478,302 in 2024 — a 30% decline in a decade — and 2025 came in essentially flat at 1,480,048, so the level has stabilised at a decade low rather than recovered.
> Second, fertility: SUPAS 2025 (released by BPS on 5 May 2026) put national TFR at 2.13, essentially at the 2.10 replacement threshold, with NINE provinces already below replacement — DKI Jakarta 1.79, DI Yogyakarta 1.84, East Java 1.95, Banten 1.96, Bali 2.02, West Java 2.05, Central Java 2.05, North Sulawesi 2.07 and East Kalimantan 2.09.
> That is the whole of Java plus Bali plus the two most urbanised outer-island provinces — around 60% of the national population living in below-replacement territory.
> Third, the downstream shock has already arrived in the schools: Boyolali regency in Central Java merged 48 state primary schools into 24 in 2026 for lack of pupils; Temanggung recorded 32 schools with fewer than five new entrants; individual schools (SDN Butuh, SDN Kauman 27 Solo) received one or two new pupils; hundreds of primary schools nationwide enrolled between one and five new students in the 2025/2026 academic year.
> PAUD (early childhood) enrolment fell by 203,936 pupils in 2024 alone and PAUD teacher numbers fell by 5,805 — the largest decline of any education level.
> Meanwhile Indonesia has already crossed the ageing threshold: 11.97% of the population is aged 60+ (about 33.9 million people) per SUPAS 2025, with sixteen provinces already in the ageing phase, led by DI Yogyakarta at 17.83%.
> What has NOT arrived: absolute population decline (Indonesia is projected to keep growing into the 2050s-2060s), a collapse in the marriage NORM (marriage remains near-universal and religiously mandated), and any pronatalist policy apparatus.

### Analisis Lag

**Bukti Historical Lag**

> SUPPORTING EVIDENCE FROM PRIOR DEMOGRAPHIC AND POLICY TRANSITIONS.

(a) The family-planning programme itself is the cleanest precedent.
> China launched 'later, longer, fewer' (晚稀少) in 1971 and the one-child policy in 1980; Indonesia launched BKKBN in 1970 with 'Dua Anak Cukup'.
> The two started almost simultaneously, yet China's TFR fell below replacement around 1991 while Indonesia's took until 2026-2028 — a 35-year divergence driven entirely by coercion intensity, not by lagged diffusion.
> This is the strongest evidence that the fertility lag is NOT a normal technology-diffusion lag and should not be modelled as one.

(b) Urbanisation as the transmission channel.
> China's urbanisation crossed 50% in 2011; Indonesia crossed 50% around 2010-2012 — essentially SIMULTANEOUS.
> Yet Chinese urban fertility fell much faster because of hukou-driven separation of migrant families, the housing-as-marriage-precondition norm and the education arms race.
> Indonesia's urbanisation delivers the same fertility-suppressing effect but with a weaker multiplier, which supports a shorter lag on the social manifestations and a longer lag on the depth of the collapse.

(c) Marriage peak synchronicity.
> Both countries peaked in 2013.
> This is not coincidence: both peaks were driven by the last large birth cohorts (China's 1985-1990 echo boom; Indonesia's 1985-1995 cohorts) reaching marriage age simultaneously, and both declines are driven by the same post-2013 combination of urban housing costs, female tertiary enrolment overtaking male, and the arrival of smartphone-mediated social life.
> Where the CAUSE is contemporaneous rather than diffusive, the lag collapses.

(d) Education-sector shock precedent.
> China's kindergarten closures began 2022-2023; Indonesia's PAUD contraction began 2024 and SD regrouping 2025-2026 — a 2-3 year gap.
> Compare with the prior wave: China's K-12 tutoring boom peaked in 2020-2021 and Indonesia's edtech (Ruangguru, Zenius) peaked in 2021-2022 with Zenius shutting down in 2023 — a 1-2 year gap.
> Education-sector shocks propagate to Indonesia much faster than the underlying demography, because they respond to enrolment growth rates and capital-market sentiment, not to population levels.

(e) Ageing services precedent.
> China's silver economy was formalised by the January 2024 State Council document; Indonesia's national population authority themed its 2026 symposium on the silver economy — a two-year policy-framing lag, despite Indonesia's elderly share being where China's was roughly a decade earlier.
> Policy narratives travel much faster than the demography they describe.

(f) Counter-evidence for a long lag.
> Indonesia has no one-child legacy: its sex ratio at birth is normal (about 105) versus China's peak of 111-118, so Indonesia will not experience the 30-35 million surplus-male marriage squeeze that mechanically suppresses Chinese marriage.
> Indonesia also has an eastern-region fertility reserve (Papua Pegunungan 2.78, NTT, Maluku above 2.4) that China's ethnic-minority regions were too small to provide.
> Both argue for a slower, shallower Indonesian decline than a naive lag model would predict.

**Tipe Lag**

> LAGGARD WITH SIMULTANEOUS AND COMPRESSED ELEMENTS — and a critical 'poorer at the same demographic stage' inversion.
> Laggard on the macro variables (population decline lags by 30-40 years; depth of fertility collapse lags by a generation).
> Simultaneous on the proximate causes: the 2013 marriage peak, the 50% urbanisation crossing, the smartphone/social-media transition, and the post-2020 housing-affordability shock all hit both countries within a few years of each other, which is why the marriage-decline curves are only 6-9 years apart despite the fertility levels being 30+ years apart.
> Compressed on the downstream shocks: school closures, PAUD teacher redundancy and silver-economy policy framing arrived in Indonesia only 2-3 years after China.
> And critically INVERTED on the economic dimension — Indonesia is reaching each demographic milestone at a substantially lower income level than China did.
> China crossed 12% aged 60+ around 2010-2013 with GDP per capita of roughly US$5,000-7,000 and crossed into population decline in 2022 at roughly US$12,700; Indonesia crossed 11.97% aged 60+ in 2025 at roughly US$5,000 but with a far weaker manufacturing base, a 59% informal labour market, a tax-to-GDP ratio around 10-11% and almost no funded pension coverage.
> The Chinese phrase 未富先老 ('growing old before growing rich') applies to Indonesia with greater force than to China, because China at least had two decades of 8-10% growth and a state balance sheet capable of absorbing 2.9 trillion yuan of annual social security subsidy.
> Indonesia will not.

### Probabilitas Transfer ke Indonesia

**Probabilitas Transfer**

Tinggi (Very High) — but the framing 'transfer' is analytically wrong for this item and should be handled with care.

**Alasan Probabilitas**

> This is not a trend that diffuses from China to Indonesia the way short video, EV manufacturing or quick commerce do.
> It is an ENDOGENOUS transition that Indonesia is generating from its own internal conditions, arriving at the same destination by the same mechanism roughly one generation later.
> The probability that Indonesia's national TFR falls below replacement is effectively 100% and imminent — it is already at 2.13, nine provinces including all of Java are already below, and no country in history has reversed a below-replacement TFR back above replacement on a sustained basis.
> What actually 'transfers' from China is threefold and each has a different probability.

(1) THE DOWNSTREAM ECONOMIES — probability high.
> Silver economy products, eldercare technology and services, single-serving consumer formats, small appliances, pet economy goods, adult nutrition, IVF technology and assisted-living formats are all commercial categories with Chinese firms holding cost and product leadership.
> These will enter Indonesia through normal commercial channels and are already entering.

(2) THE POLICY PLAYBOOK — probability medium-high for the framing, low for the fiscal content.
> Indonesia's population ministry has already imported the vocabulary (its 2026 symposium is themed on the silver economy).
> But Indonesia cannot import a universal 3,600-yuan-per-child subsidy: at Indonesia's tax ratio and with 4.4 million annual births, an equivalent per-child transfer scaled to income would still cost tens of trillions of rupiah annually against a budget already absorbed by free nutritious meals (MBG), fuel and energy subsidies, and IKN.
> The likelier import is the cheap, symbolic end of China's playbook — marriage-registration simplification, wedding-cost campaigns, exhortation — rather than the expensive end.

(3) THE MISTAKE — probability high, and this is the real warning.
> China's central error was acting only after the collapse: it maintained anti-natalist enforcement until 2015 and did not deploy meaningful pronatalist money until 2025, by which time the childbearing-age female cohort had already shrunk 13%.
> Indonesia is currently at the exact policy moment China occupied around 2012-2014 — TFR at the threshold, institutional muscle memory oriented toward birth CONTROL, and an official narrative still celebrating the demographic dividend.
> The base rate for governments recognising this window in time is very poor; every East Asian precedent (Japan, Korea, Taiwan, Singapore, Thailand, China) missed it.

The one genuine uncertainty is DEPTH, not direction.
> Indonesia's religiosity, near-universal marriage norm, normal sex ratio at birth, and eastern-region fertility reserve all argue that Indonesia stabilises somewhere around 1.6-1.9 rather than falling to China's 1.0-1.1 or Korea's 0.72.
> That is the difference between a manageable ageing society and a demographic emergency.

### Faktor Pendorong

**Prasyarat Struktural**

> THRESHOLD INDICATORS AND INDONESIA'S POSITION VERSUS CHINA WHEN THE CHINESE TREND BROKE.

(1) FEMALE EDUCATIONAL ATTAINMENT.
> The single most reliable global predictor of fertility decline.
> China: women surpassed men in tertiary enrolment around 2009-2010; by 2016 women were over half of undergraduates.
> Indonesia: women already exceed men in tertiary enrolment (roughly 52-55% of university students) and female secondary completion is near-universal in Java.
> STATUS: THRESHOLD ALREADY CROSSED.
> This alone makes continued fertility decline near-certain.

(2) URBANISATION.
> China was about 50% urban in 2011 and 66% by 2024 when its births collapsed to 9.5 million.
> Indonesia crossed 50% around 2010-2012 and is roughly 58-60% urban in 2025, projected above 70% by 2045.
> STATUS: CROSSED, still rising — each additional percentage point of urbanisation mechanically drags TFR down.
> Jakarta's 1.79 is the preview of what the national figure becomes as urbanisation continues.

(3) GDP PER CAPITA.
> China's marriage peak (2013) occurred at roughly US$7,000 per capita; its population decline began (2022) at roughly US$12,700.
> Indonesia is at roughly US$5,000 in 2025.
> STATUS: BELOW the level at which China's crisis peaked — but Indonesia's marriage decline started at a LOWER income level than China's, confirming that the marriage strike is driven by relative cost-of-family-formation, not absolute income.
> Housing price-to-income ratios in Jakarta already exceed 10-15x, comparable to or worse than many Chinese tier-2 cities.

(4) HOUSING AFFORDABILITY AND THE MARRIAGE PRECONDITION.
> In China the marital-apartment norm made housing a binding constraint on marriage.
> Indonesia's equivalent is the combination of wedding-cost expectations (resepsi, mahar, extended-family obligations) plus a backlog of roughly 9-12 million households without adequate housing and a mortgage market reaching only a thin formal-sector slice.
> STATUS: THRESHOLD CROSSED IN THE METROS — the UNFPA 2026 finding that 57% of young adults cite housing scarcity confirms it.

(5) FEMALE LABOUR FORCE PARTICIPATION WITHOUT CHILDCARE INFRASTRUCTURE.
> This is the key gap-driver.
> China had roughly 60-70% FLFP and near-zero formal 0-3 childcare until the 2021-2025 build-out; that combination is the classic 'gender-equity mismatch' recipe for very low fertility.
> Indonesia has lower FLFP (roughly 54%) but even less formal childcare, offset by extended-family caregiving (grandmothers, ART/domestic help).
> STATUS: PARTIALLY CROSSED — the extended-family buffer is Indonesia's main remaining fertility support and it erodes with nuclear-family urban migration.

(6) SOCIAL SECURITY AND PENSION COVERAGE.
> Determines whether children remain an old-age insurance asset.
> China's rural pension (NRPS) rollout from 2009 measurably reduced the old-age motive for children.
> In Indonesia only about a third of elderly have any pension income and BPJS Ketenagakerjaan coverage of informal workers is thin.
> STATUS: NOT CROSSED — children still function as retirement insurance for most Indonesians, which is a fertility SUPPORT and a reason Indonesia's decline should be slower than China's.
> But it is also the reason Indonesia's ageing will be far more painful when it arrives.

(7) CONTRACEPTIVE ACCESS AND STATE CAPACITY.
> Indonesia's BKKBN built one of the developing world's most effective family-planning systems; contraceptive prevalence is high.
> STATUS: CROSSED DECADES AGO.
> The apparatus that was built to lower fertility is now perfectly positioned as the institutional chassis for the opposite mission — which is exactly what the ministry reorganisation into Kemendukbangga enables.

(8) RELIGIOSITY AND MARRIAGE NORM STRENGTH.
> The main brake.
> China is a secular society with no religious mandate to marry; Indonesia's marriage norm is reinforced by Islam, Christianity, adat and legal structures (there is no legal framework for cohabitation or non-marital childbearing).
> STATUS: NOT CROSSED and unlikely to be crossed.
> This is the primary reason to expect Indonesian TFR to stabilise around 1.6-1.9 rather than 1.0.

(9) SEX RATIO AT BIRTH.
> China's 111-118 peak produced a structural marriage squeeze; Indonesia's is a normal ~105.
> STATUS: NOT APPLICABLE — a China-specific accelerant Indonesia does not carry.

(10) COST OF CHILD-REARING RELATIVE TO INCOME.
> China's 6.3x GDP-per-capita cost is the proximate trigger.
> Indonesia has no equivalent authoritative national estimate, but the drivers are assembling: private-school premiums, tutoring, urban housing, and the middle-class expectation of tertiary education.
> STATUS: RISING, not yet at Chinese levels — the absence of an Indonesian YuWa-equivalent study is itself a policy gap.

**Indikator Pemantauan**

> LEADING INDICATORS THAT THE TREND IS DEEPENING IN INDONESIA, ordered by signal quality.

TIER 1 — DIRECT DEMOGRAPHIC.
> (1) Number of provinces with TFR below 2.10 in each Susenas/SUPAS round — nine in 2025; crossing 15 would signal the national figure is structurally below replacement.
> (2) National TFR crossing below 2.10 (expected 2026-2028) and then below 2.00 (the psychologically decisive threshold).
> (3) Monthly/annual KUA and Dukcapil marriage registrations (Kemenag + BPS) — watch whether the 2025 flattening at 1.48 million holds or resumes falling; a break below 1.4 million confirms continuation.
> (4) Median age at first marriage for women (BPS Susenas) — every year of delay costs roughly 0.1 of TFR.
> (5) Share of 16-30 year olds unmarried (71.04% in 2025) — crossing 75% is a major signal.
> (6) Divorce-to-marriage ratio (29.6% in 2025).

TIER 2 — DOWNSTREAM INSTITUTIONAL, the fastest-moving indicators.
> (7) Count of SD/MI schools with zero or under-five new entrants in each PPDB/SPMB cycle, and the number of regrouping/merger decrees issued by kabupaten education offices — Dapodik is the underlying dataset and is public.
> (8) PAUD/TK enrolment change and PAUD teacher headcount change (already -203,936 pupils and -5,805 teachers in 2024).
> (9) PPPK/ASN teacher formation quotas for SD versus SMA/SMK — a shift of quota upward through the age ladder mirrors China exactly.
> (10) University enrolment in PGSD and PG-PAUD programmes and the number of LPTK study programmes closing or merging.
> (11) Number of hospital maternity units closing or converting, and BPJS Kesehatan claims volume for persalinan — the Indonesian analogue of China's 'obstetric winter'.

TIER 3 — COMMERCIAL.
> (12) Infant formula and baby-diaper volume (not value) from Nielsen/Kantar Indonesia, and the ratio of adult-diaper to baby-diaper sales — in China this ratio crossing is a widely cited demographic marker.
> (13) Growth of pet food and pet care retail versus baby care retail.
> (14) IVF cycle volumes and new fertility clinic openings.
> (15) Share of one-person and two-person households in Susenas, and the share of new apartment supply in studio/one-bedroom formats in Jabodetabek.
> (16) Single-serving pack-size share in FMCG.

TIER 4 — DISCOURSE AND POLICY.
> (17) Google Trends Indonesia for 'childfree', 'tidak mau menikah', 'biaya nikah', 'gaji tidak cukup untuk menikah'.
> (18) Whether Kemendukbangga's public messaging retires 'Dua Anak Cukup' — the single clearest policy inflection to watch.
> (19) Appearance of pronatalist line items in APBN/APBD: birth grants, childcare subsidies, wedding-cost assistance, regional insentif kelahiran (a kabupaten offering a birth bonus would be the first hard signal).
> (20) Trademark filings and business-licence (OSS/KBLI) registrations in eldercare, home care, pet services and co-living.
> (21) Entry of Chinese, Japanese or Korean eldercare and age-tech firms into Indonesia.

### Hambatan & Faktor Pembatal

**Hambatan Transfer**

> Barriers here mean forces that SLOW Indonesia's demographic decline or slow the arrival of the Chinese-style downstream economy — some of which are genuinely protective.

SLOWING THE FERTILITY DECLINE ITSELF: (1) Religious and normative pressure toward marriage and childbearing across Islam, Christianity, Hinduism and adat — marriage is near-universal and there is no legal or social framework for non-marital childbearing; the nikah siri channel also absorbs couples deterred by registration costs.
> (2) The extended-family caregiving system — grandmothers and affordable domestic help substantially reduce the opportunity cost of children compared with China's atomised urban households.
> (3) Eastern Indonesia's fertility reserve (Papua Pegunungan 2.78, NTT, Maluku, Papua provinces above 2.4) plus internal migration from high- to low-fertility regions, which cushions the national average and repopulates Java's cities.
> (4) Children as old-age insurance in the absence of pension coverage — a rational fertility support that will persist as long as BPJS Ketenagakerjaan coverage of informal workers stays low.
> (5) Lower female labour force participation than China (roughly 54% vs 60-70%), reducing the work-family conflict intensity.

SLOWING THE DOWNSTREAM ECONOMY'S ARRIVAL: (6) Income — the silver and solo economies require discretionary spending Indonesia's elderly and singles largely do not have; only about a third of Indonesian elderly have pension income.
> (7) Fragmented archipelagic geography raises the cost of the dense, city-scale service networks that make Chinese eldercare and instant-delivery formats viable.
> (8) Weak long-term-care financing — no LTC insurance, minimal formal home-care market, and a strong cultural preference for family care that stigmatises institutional eldercare.
> (9) Health workforce constraints — Indonesia has among the lowest doctor-per-capita ratios in ASEAN and almost no geriatric specialists.
> (10) Data infrastructure — Indonesia lacks a timely monthly demographic release comparable to China's MCA quarterly marriage data; SUPAS is quinquennial and Susenas annual, so the crisis is always observed with a 12-24 month lag, which itself delays policy response.
> (11) Political economy — the 'demographic dividend' narrative is embedded in Indonesia Emas 2045 messaging, and admitting fertility decline is politically awkward while the official story is about a young workforce.
> (12) Fiscal space — a tax ratio of roughly 10-11% and an APBN already committed to free nutritious meals, energy subsidies and IKN leaves little room for Chinese-scale pronatalist transfers.

**Faktor Pembatal Transfer**

> STRUCTURAL REASONS INDONESIA'S DEMOGRAPHIC CRISIS WILL NOT TAKE THE SAME FORM AS CHINA'S — these are not delays, they are permanent divergences, and getting them wrong is the main way analysts misapply the China template.

(1) NO ONE-CHILD POLICY LEGACY.
> This is the decisive difference.
> China's crisis carries three artefacts Indonesia will never have: (a) a distorted sex ratio at birth that peaked at 111-118 and left roughly 30-35 million surplus males of marriageable age, mechanically capping marriages regardless of preferences and inflating bride prices in rural areas; (b) the 4-2-1 family structure, in which a single adult child carries two parents and four grandparents — Indonesia's larger sibling sets distribute elder care across multiple children; (c) a generation raised as only children with no experience of siblings, which independently depresses desired family size.
> Indonesia's sex ratio at birth is a normal ~105 and its cohorts have siblings.
> Indonesia's decline is therefore voluntary and preference-driven, which makes it shallower and more responsive to policy than China's, which is partly structural and irreversible.

(2) RELIGION AND THE MARRIAGE NORM.
> China is a secular society where non-marriage carries diminishing stigma.
> Indonesia's legal system does not recognise cohabitation, there is no civil marriage outside religious frameworks, and Islamic and Christian institutions actively promote marriage.
> The practical consequence is that Indonesian fertility decline will express itself as LATER and SMALLER marriage-based families rather than as mass permanent non-marriage.
> This is the strongest argument for an Indonesian floor around 1.6-1.9 rather than China's 1.0-1.1 or Korea's 0.72.

(3) EXTREME INTERNAL HETEROGENEITY AND NO HUKOU.
> China's crisis is relatively uniform (24 of 31 provinces shrinking).
> Indonesia's spans 1.79 in Jakarta to 2.78 in Papua Pegunungan simultaneously, and internal migration is completely unrestricted.
> Java will age and shrink while eastern Indonesia continues growing — meaning Indonesia will experience an INTERNAL demographic redistribution problem (fiscal transfers, DAU/DAK formulas, labour migration, regional political representation) where China experiences a national contraction.
> Policy must be provincial, not national.
> A single national pronatalist policy would be simultaneously too late for Yogyakarta and actively harmful in Papua Pegunungan, where the binding constraint is stunting and maternal mortality, not fertility.

(4) NO ABSOLUTE POPULATION DECLINE FOR DECADES.
> Indonesia's population will keep growing to roughly 320-330 million into the 2050s-2060s on standard projections.
> The entire class of China-specific phenomena that depend on absolute shrinkage — ghost cities, nationwide housing oversupply driven by household-formation collapse, systemic labour shortage — will not appear in Indonesia on this horizon.
> Indonesia's problem is the SPEED of ageing and the LOW INCOME at which it occurs, not shrinkage.

(5) NO STATE CAPACITY FOR CHINESE-SCALE INTERVENTION IN EITHER DIRECTION.
> China could impose a one-child policy and can now write a universal 3,600-yuan cheque to 20 million families and absorb a 2.9 trillion yuan social security subsidy.
> Indonesia can do neither.
> Its pronatalist toolkit is limited to cheap instruments: messaging, marriage-registration simplification, maternity-leave law, and possibly targeted regional incentives.
> Correspondingly, Indonesia's ageing crisis cannot be papered over with fiscal transfers — it must be solved through labour-force participation, productivity and informal-sector pension coverage, not cash.

(6) DIFFERENT ECONOMIC BASE.
> China's demographic decline collides with a manufacturing economy that needs a large industrial workforce and has been automating in response (see Smart Manufacturing and Embodied AI items).
> Indonesia's economy is commodity- and services-weighted with a large informal sector and a persistent employment DEFICIT — Indonesia's problem for the next 15 years is too few jobs for too many young people, not too few workers.
> The Chinese logic 'population decline forces automation' does not apply to Indonesia in this window and may invert: premature automation into a labour-surplus economy is the risk.

(7) THE MIGRATION VALVE.
> Indonesia is a labour EXPORTER (roughly 4-5 million citizens working abroad) and could become a destination for regional labour; China is neither.
> This gives Indonesia a policy option China lacks.

### Prediksi Timeline di Indonesia

**Tahun Masuk Indonesia**

> ALREADY ARRIVED — the entry point is 2014 for marriage and 2024-2025 for the visible crisis.
> Precise markers: 2014 is the peak year of registered marriages (2,110,776), after which the series declined every year through 2024.
> 2020-2021 marks acceleration, as pandemic income shocks and remote work compounded the underlying trend.
> 2024 is the year the decline became undeniable — marriages hit a decade low of 1,478,302 and PAUD enrolment fell by over 200,000 pupils.
> 2025-2026 is the year the crisis became institutionally visible: SUPAS 2025 (published May 2026) confirmed national TFR at 2.13 with nine provinces below replacement and elderly at 11.97%; mass SD regrouping (Boyolali, Temanggung, Solo) hit the national press; and Kemendukbangga reframed its national symposium around the silver economy.
> For a research-outline 'entry year' the defensible answer is 2024 — the first year in which all three indicators (marriage at a decade low, PAUD enrolment contracting, urban TFR confirmed below replacement) were simultaneously true.

**Skenario Percepatan**

> Factors that would pull Indonesia's fertility decline forward and deepen it: (1) a prolonged youth unemployment episode or recession — the single most reliable fertility depressant, and Indonesia's youth unemployment is already among ASEAN's highest; (2) continued urban housing-price inflation outpacing wages in Jabodetabek, Bandung and Surabaya, making the marital-home precondition binding as it became in China; (3) expansion of gig and platform work without social protection, which removes the income stability young men are expected to demonstrate before marriage; (4) further female tertiary enrolment gains without any corresponding childcare infrastructure — the classic gender-equity mismatch; (5) viral normalisation of childfree and solo-living content through TikTok and Instagram, which travels in months; (6) rising wedding-cost expectations amplified by social media (the Indonesian equivalent of Chinese bride-price inflation); (7) any cut or failure of maternal-child support programmes; (8) rapid nuclearisation of urban households that removes the grandmother childcare buffer; (9) middle-class education-cost escalation reproducing Chinese-style involution.
> Conversely, decelerators: a large-scale affordable-housing-for-young-couples programme, enforceable parental leave extending into the informal sector, subsidised daycare (TPA/PAUD repurposed from closing schools), and pension coverage that reduces the tension between having children and saving for old age.

### Dampak Sosial-Ekonomi

**Dampak Lapangan Kerja**

> JOBS DISAPPEARING — the contraction is already measurable and follows the age ladder upward with a predictable lag.

(a) EARLY CHILDHOOD AND PRIMARY EDUCATION.
> This is the first and largest casualty.
> Indonesia lost 5,805 PAUD teachers in 2024 alone — the largest decline of any education level — as PAUD enrolment fell by 203,936 pupils.
> Boyolali's merger of 48 SDN into 24 implies dozens of displaced teaching and administrative posts in one regency alone.
> Because 21% of Indonesian educators are on non-permanent status (honorer/GTT) and PAUD teachers are overwhelmingly in this category with sub-minimum-wage pay, the adjustment falls almost entirely on the most precarious workers, exactly as China's 21,400 kindergarten closures fell on private-sector teachers (private kindergartens are 52.1% of Chinese facilities).
> Expect the wave to reach SMP around 2030-2033 and SMA/SMK in the mid-2030s, with LPTK (teacher-training) faculty and PGSD/PG-PAUD lecturers affected last and hardest.

(b) MATERNAL AND CHILD HEALTH.
> Indonesia produces very large numbers of midwives (bidan) through hundreds of diploma and undergraduate programmes; a 30% decline in annual births over two decades removes the demand base.
> China's 'obstetric winter' — dozens of delivery wards closed, Shanghai deliveries down from 34,000 to 20,000, obstetricians retraining — is the template.
> Indonesian obstetricians, midwives, neonatal nurses and posyandu cadres face the same squeeze, though delayed by Indonesia's still-high maternal mortality, which sustains demand for quality rather than quantity.

(c) CHILD-ORIENTED CONSUMER SECTORS.
> Infant formula, baby diapers, children's apparel, toys, child-focused retail and family-format food service face structural volume decline.
> The Chinese lesson is that VALUE can hold up while VOLUME collapses (China's maternity-and-baby online channel still grew 12.6% in 2025 on premiumisation), so the jobs lost are in mass-market manufacturing and distribution, not in premium brand and marketing roles.

(d) WEDDING SERVICES IN LOWER-INCOME REGIONS.
> A 30% decline in registered marriages hits the mass-market wedding economy — catering, tent/dekorasi, rias pengantin, gedung, undangan printing — hardest outside the metros, while premium urban wedding services grow on higher per-event spend.
> IBISWorld's China data shows exactly this bifurcation: couples down sharply, market value still up.

JOBS BEING CREATED — the compensating demand is real but in different places, requiring different skills, and typically located in cities.

(e) ELDERCARE AND GERIATRIC HEALTH.
> The largest single job-creation category.
> With elderly rising from 33.9 million (2025) to 63-66 million (2045), Indonesia needs home-care workers, caregivers/perawat lansia, geriatric nurses, physiotherapists, occupational therapists, geriatric physicians (Indonesia has almost none), palliative and hospice staff, care coordinators and assisted-living managers.
> Japan, Taiwan, Hong Kong, Singapore and increasingly China are also net importers of Indonesian caregivers, making this simultaneously a domestic and an export labour market — the strongest single labour-market opportunity in this entire research set for lower-middle-income Indonesian workers.

(f) DAYCARE AND CHILDCARE — counterintuitive but real.
> Fewer children but far higher female labour force participation and nuclear-family living means demand for FORMAL 0-6 childcare rises even as the child population falls.
> China's build-out of 托育 (0-3 care) capacity from near zero since 2021 is the model, and closing PAUD/SD buildings are the obvious physical asset for conversion.

(g) ASSISTED REPRODUCTION AND FERTILITY MEDICINE.
> Later marriage and later first birth mechanically raise infertility.
> China's IVF sector boomed and is now covered by provincial insurance in many regions; Indonesia's clinics (Morula, Bocah Indonesia, Bunda) are scaling.
> Embryologists, reproductive endocrinologists, andrologists and fertility counsellors are a growing shortage occupation.

(h) PENSION, INSURANCE AND ACTUARIAL SERVICES.
> Annuities, long-term-care insurance, retirement planning, reverse mortgages and pension fund management — Indonesia has a severe actuary shortage (a few hundred fully qualified actuaries for a 285-million population).

(i) THE PET, SOLO AND EMOTIONAL ECONOMY.
> Veterinary services, pet grooming, pet food, pet hotels; single-serving food production and delivery; co-living management; companionship and mental-health services.
> China's pet economy at 811.4 billion yuan and solo-dining at 800 billion yuan indicate the scale these categories can reach.

(j) DEMOGRAPHIC DATA AND POLICY ANALYSIS.
> Demographers, health economists, actuarial modellers and regional planning specialists — currently a very thin Indonesian bench.

NET ASSESSMENT: this is a REALLOCATION, not a net destruction — eldercare demand alone plausibly exceeds education job losses in headcount.
> But the reallocation is brutally mismatched in skill, geography and gender: a 45-year-old honorary PAUD teacher in Boyolali cannot become a geriatric nurse in Jakarta without retraining that currently does not exist, and the eldercare jobs created are lower-status and often lower-paid than the education jobs lost.

**Dampak Kelas Menengah**

> The Indonesian middle class is both the primary DRIVER and the primary VICTIM of this transition, and it is already shrinking as a share of the population — which compounds every mechanism below.

(1) THE MIDDLE CLASS IS WHERE FERTILITY FALLS FIRST AND FASTEST.
> Jakarta at 1.79 and Yogyakarta at 1.84 are not poor provinces; they are the most educated and most urban.
> Middle-class Indonesians face a specific arithmetic: to reproduce their class position they must buy private schooling, tutoring, English, a house in a good zone, and a university education — the same involution logic that produced China's 538,000-yuan (6.3x GDP per capita) child cost.
> Each additional child is a direct threat to the family's class position, so the rational response is one or two children, late.

(2) THE SANDWICH GENERATION IS THE DEFINING MIDDLE-CLASS BURDEN.
> Indonesian urban professionals in their 30s and 40s are already supporting parents with no pension while raising children in an expensive city, on incomes squeezed by housing costs.
> As the elderly share goes from 12% to 20% by 2045 and family sizes shrink, the burden per adult child rises sharply — Indonesia's version of China's 4-2-1 problem, mitigated by larger sibling sets today but worsening for every subsequent cohort.
> This is the single largest driver of middle-class financial fragility over the next two decades and the reason Indonesian household savings rates are unlikely to rise.

(3) DELAYED HOUSEHOLD FORMATION RESHAPES MIDDLE-CLASS CONSUMPTION.
> Later marriage means a longer single or DINK phase, which shifts spending from family durables (7-seater cars, large houses, family-pack FMCG) toward experiences, travel, pets, personal services, gadgets and premium single-serving goods — the mechanism that produced China's solo economy at 800 billion yuan in solo dining and 811 billion yuan in pets.
> Indonesian brands built for the family household will lose share to those built for one or two people.

(4) HOUSING DEMAND CHANGES SHAPE, NOT JUST SIZE.
> Household formation, not population, drives housing demand — and household COUNT keeps rising even as size falls, so Indonesia will not see a Chinese-style demand collapse for decades.
> But the product mix shifts decisively toward studio and one-bedroom formats, co-living, and later toward age-adapted housing.
> Developers building 3-4 bedroom landed housing for a two-child family are building for a shrinking segment.

(5) THE MIDDLE CLASS BEARS THE PENSION GAP.
> Because Indonesia's formal pension system covers only a fraction of workers and BPJS Ketenagakerjaan replacement rates are low, middle-class households must self-fund retirement while also supporting parents.
> Combined with a shrinking number of children to rely on, this drives demand for private retirement products, annuities, health insurance and reverse mortgages — a genuine growth market, but one that also crowds out current consumption.

(6) A POSITIVE CHANNEL: PER-CHILD INVESTMENT RISES.
> Fewer children means more spending per child.
> Premium education, enrichment, health, children's travel and safety products grow even as the child population shrinks.
> This is exactly the pattern in China's maternity-and-baby online market, which grew 12.6% in 2025 on a shrinking birth base.

(7) A NEGATIVE MACRO CHANNEL: the middle class's own children will enter a labour market with a smaller domestic consumer base per worker and a heavier fiscal burden from ageing — meaning the intergenerational bargain (invest heavily in your one child, they support you) is weakening at exactly the moment families are betting everything on it.

**Dampak Daerah Non Jawa**

> This trend is emphatically NOT Java-only, but it splits Indonesia into three distinct demographic regimes that require opposite policies — the most consequential regional differentiation in this entire research set.

REGIME A — ALREADY BELOW REPLACEMENT AND AGEING (Java, Bali, plus two outer-island outliers).
> DKI Jakarta 1.79, DI Yogyakarta 1.84, East Java 1.95, Banten 1.96, Bali 2.02, West Java 2.05, Central Java 2.05, North Sulawesi 2.07, East Kalimantan 2.09.
> DI Yogyakarta already has 17.83% of its population aged 60+, followed by East Java and Bali.
> Note that North Sulawesi and East Kalimantan are NOT in Java — the driver is urbanisation, education and out-migration of young adults, not geography.
> These regions need: school consolidation frameworks, teacher redeployment, eldercare infrastructure, long-term-care financing, age-friendly transport and housing, and a reversal of anti-natalist messaging.
> Yogyakarta is Indonesia's demographic future arriving twenty years early and should be treated as the national pilot site for ageing policy.

REGIME B — TRANSITIONING, AT OR JUST ABOVE REPLACEMENT (most of Sumatra, South Sulawesi, West Nusa Tenggara, urban Kalimantan).
> TFRs in the 2.1-2.4 range and falling.
> These provinces will cross below replacement in the late 2020s and early 2030s.
> They face the sharpest ADJUSTMENT because their infrastructure and teacher pipelines were built for growth.
> Riau, North Sumatra, South Sumatra and South Sulawesi are the ones to watch.
> A distinctive feature: high out-migration of young adults to Java and abroad accelerates local ageing beyond what fertility alone would produce — the same mechanism that hollowed out China's Northeast, where Heilongjiang, Jilin and Liaoning combined low fertility with mass youth out-migration to produce the country's most stressed provincial pension funds.
> Indonesian provinces with high out-migration should study the Dongbei case specifically.

REGIME C — STILL HIGH FERTILITY WITH DEVELOPMENT DEFICITS (Papua Pegunungan 2.78, the other Papua provinces, NTT, Maluku, parts of Sulawesi).
> Here the binding constraints are stunting (national prevalence still around 19-20%), maternal and infant mortality, poverty and educational access — NOT fertility.
> Applying a pronatalist frame here would be actively harmful; the correct policy is exactly what Kemendukbangga's 2026 symposium articulated — human capital development, health access and poverty reduction.
> These regions are also Indonesia's demographic reserve: their young cohorts will supply labour to ageing Java for decades, meaning internal migration policy becomes a core instrument of national demographic management.

CROSS-CUTTING FISCAL IMPLICATION: Indonesia's intergovernmental transfer formulas (DAU, DAK, Dana Desa) are population-weighted.
> As Java's school-age population shrinks and its elderly population grows while eastern Indonesia's child population keeps growing, the allocation formulas will produce increasingly perverse results — funding schools where there are no children and underfunding eldercare where the elderly are concentrating.
> Reforming transfer formulas to be age-structure-weighted rather than headcount-weighted is a concrete, unglamorous, high-leverage policy action that should happen before 2030.
> This is also where the archipelagic structure genuinely matters: Indonesia will run a national ageing policy and a national child-health policy simultaneously, in different provinces, forever — something China never had to do.

### Kaitan Pendidikan

**Jurusan Terancam**

> PROGRAMMES WITH STRUCTURALLY DECLINING DEMAND.
> These are ranked by the directness and immediacy of the demographic hit.

(1) PG-PAUD (Pendidikan Guru Pendidikan Anak Usia Dini) — the most immediately threatened programme in Indonesian higher education.
> PAUD enrolment fell 203,936 pupils and PAUD teacher headcount fell 5,805 in 2024 alone.
> China's precedent is unambiguous: 21,400 kindergartens closed in a single year and preschool enrolment fell from 48.18 million (2020) to 32.25 million (2025), a one-third contraction that made 学前教育 one of China's most oversupplied majors.
> Indonesian LPTKs are still expanding PG-PAUD intakes into a market that is contracting.
> This should be the first programme subject to intake caps.

(2) PGSD (Pendidikan Guru Sekolah Dasar) — next in line, with a 3-6 year lag behind PG-PAUD.
> Hundreds of Indonesian primary schools received 1-5 new entrants in 2025/2026; Boyolali merged 48 schools into 24.
> China's primary intake fell 9.6% in 2025 and is 22% below its 2023 peak.
> PGSD is one of the highest-volume programmes in Indonesian higher education and is producing graduates into a shrinking market — while the government simultaneously reports a 498,000 teacher shortfall, which is a distribution and status problem (21% of educators are non-permanent), not a volume problem.
> Graduates will find the shortage is in remote postings at honorarium pay, not in the urban positions they trained for.

(3) KEBIDANAN (Midwifery) at D3/D4/S1 level — Indonesia has an unusually large number of midwifery programmes producing far more graduates than a shrinking birth cohort can absorb.
> Births are around 4.44 million in 2025 and falling.
> China's 'obstetric winter' shows the endpoint: delivery wards closing, obstetricians retraining.
> Midwifery will not disappear — Indonesia's maternal mortality is still high and quality of care must improve — but the VOLUME of practitioners needed will fall sharply while the QUALITY bar rises.

(4) SECONDARY-LEVEL TEACHER EDUCATION (Pendidikan Matematika, Pendidikan Bahasa, Pendidikan IPA and similar) — safe for roughly a decade, then hit in the mid-2030s as the shock climbs the age ladder.
> Institutions should plan now, not react later.

(5) CHILD-ORIENTED APPLIED PROGRAMMES: children's apparel and toy design, child-focused product design, and child-market-focused segments of marketing and retail management.

(6) PEDIATRIC SPECIALISATION as a growth field (the specialty itself remains essential, but pediatric hospital capacity expansion will stop; specialist training slots should be capped and rebalanced toward geriatrics).

(7) LONGER-TERM, 2035+: general higher education capacity itself.
> Indonesia has over 4,000 higher education institutions, most of them small private ones already struggling to fill seats.
> The Chinese sequence — kindergartens first, then primary, then the university enrolment cliff in the early-to-mid 2030s — is arriving in Indonesia in the late 2030s and will trigger a private-campus consolidation wave.
> This connects directly to the Restrukturisasi Pendidikan Tinggi item in this research set: Indonesia's private-university shakeout will be demographically driven, and the institutions most exposed are the ones most dependent on teacher-education enrolment.

IMPORTANT CAVEAT: 'threatened' means declining DEMAND VOLUME, not declining social value.
> Early childhood education is where the returns to human capital investment are highest, and Indonesia's stunting and learning-poverty problems argue for MORE quality-focused early education even as the child population falls.
> The right response is intake reduction plus quality upgrading, not abolition.

**Jurusan Dibutuhkan**

> PROGRAMMES AND SKILLS WITH STRUCTURALLY RISING DEMAND, ranked by the size of the current supply gap.

(1) GERONTOLOGY AND GERIATRIC HEALTHCARE — the largest gap in Indonesian higher education.
> Needed: geriatric medicine specialisation (Indonesia has a critically small number of geriatricians for 33.9 million elderly rising to 63-66 million by 2045), geriatric nursing, gerontological social work, geriatric pharmacy (polypharmacy management), and dementia care.
> Almost no Indonesian university offers a dedicated gerontology degree.
> China opened dedicated smart elderly care service and management programmes (智慧养老服务与管理) across its vocational system and inaugurated a National University for the Aged in 2023 — Indonesia has no analogue.

(2) LONG-TERM CARE AND CAREGIVING (vocational/D3 level) — the highest-volume job creation category, and dual-purpose: domestic demand plus export to Japan, Taiwan, Hong Kong, Singapore, South Korea and increasingly China, all of which are net importers of Indonesian caregivers.
> Curriculum needs: personal care, mobility and transfer technique, dementia communication, palliative basics, plus destination-country language (Japanese N4-N3, Mandarin).
> This is the single most accessible upgrade path for the honorary PAUD and SD teachers being displaced.

(3) REHABILITATION AND ALLIED HEALTH — physiotherapy, occupational therapy, speech-language pathology, audiology, prosthetics and orthotics, and podiatry.
> All are severely undersupplied in Indonesia and all scale directly with the elderly population.

(4) ACTUARIAL SCIENCE, PENSION AND INSURANCE — Indonesia has only a few hundred fully qualified actuaries for a 285-million population facing a pension, health-insurance and long-term-care financing problem.
> Add: health economics, social-insurance design, longevity risk modelling, and retirement financial planning.

(5) DEMOGRAPHY AND POPULATION POLICY — Indonesia needs analysts capable of doing what YuWa does in China: producing an authoritative national estimate of the cost of raising a child, provincial fertility projections, and age-structure-weighted fiscal transfer modelling.
> Existing capacity at UI's Lembaga Demografi and UGM's PSKK should be expanded, not treated as a niche.

(6) EARLY CHILDHOOD CARE (0-3) AS DISTINCT FROM EARLY EDUCATION (4-6) — counterintuitive growth area.
> Fewer children but far more working mothers and nuclear households means formal daycare (TPA/penitipan anak) demand rises even as PAUD enrolment falls.
> China built its 托育 sector essentially from zero after 2021.
> Indonesian PG-PAUD programmes should pivot toward infant-toddler care, childcare centre management and childcare regulation rather than shrink outright — the physical assets (closing PAUD and SD buildings) and the human capital (displaced PAUD teachers) are already in place.

(7) ASSISTED REPRODUCTIVE TECHNOLOGY — embryology, reproductive endocrinology, andrology, fertility counselling and genetic counselling, driven by rising maternal age.

(8) AGE-TECH, ASSISTIVE ROBOTICS AND BIOMEDICAL ENGINEERING — mobility aids, fall detection, remote monitoring, exoskeletons, hearing and vision assistance.
> Connects to the Embodied AI and Health Tech items in this research set; Chinese suppliers will dominate the hardware, so Indonesian value capture is in integration, service and clinical validation.

(9) AGE-FRIENDLY AND SMALL-FORMAT ARCHITECTURE AND URBAN PLANNING — universal design, aging-in-place retrofit, co-living and studio-format residential design, and the adaptive reuse of closing school buildings.

(10) FAMILY SOCIOLOGY, COUNSELLING AND MENTAL HEALTH — marriage and family counselling, grief and hospice counselling, loneliness and social isolation intervention, and the psychology of single-person living.
> Indonesia's psychologist-to-population ratio is among the worst in the region.

(11) VETERINARY MEDICINE AND ANIMAL SERVICES — small-animal practice, veterinary nursing, pet nutrition and pet behaviour, tracking the pet economy that in China reached 811.4 billion yuan.

(12) DATA SKILLS ACROSS ALL OF THE ABOVE — health informatics, care-quality analytics and claims analytics, which are what make eldercare systems financially sustainable at scale.

**China Education Response**

> China's education system did not plan for this; it is being restructured by force, and the response has been reactive triage rather than strategy.
> That reactive quality is itself the most transferable lesson.

WHAT CHINA ACTUALLY DID.

(1) MASS CLOSURE AND CONSOLIDATION, NOT PLANNED WIND-DOWN.
> In 2025 alone China closed 21,400 kindergartens (about 59 per day, leaving 231,900) and roughly 8,000 primary schools — nearly 30,000 institutions in one year.
> Preschool enrolment fell 10% (-3.58 million) to 32.25 million, down from 48.18 million in 2020; primary intake fell 9.6% to 14.61 million, 22% below the 2023 peak.
> Private kindergartens, 52.1% of facilities, absorbed a disproportionate share of the closures because they had no public subsidy floor.
> Teaching staff fell to 15.68 million, a second consecutive annual decline, concentrated in early education.
> The closures happened faster than any redeployment programme could absorb, and displaced private-sector early-childhood teachers largely exited the profession.

(2) REPURPOSING FACILITIES: 'INTEGRATED CHILDCARE' AND 'CARE FOR BOTH ENDS'.
> Rather than demolish capacity, many localities converted surplus kindergarten space into 托育 (0-3 infant-toddler care) under a 托幼一体化 (integrated childcare-preschool) policy, and a growing number of pilots merge eldercare and childcare in shared facilities (养老托育一体) offering intergenerational programming.
> This is the single most directly copyable Chinese innovation for Indonesia: a closing SD building in Boyolali is a functioning daycare, posyandu lansia and community centre with minimal capital expenditure.

(3) UPWARD REALLOCATION OF CAPACITY.
> While the bottom of the ladder liquidates, the top expands to absorb the earlier birth peaks: senior high intake rose 3.7% to 10.74 million in 2025, regular high schools increased by 300 to 16,100, and China now has 3,167 higher education institutions with a gross tertiary enrolment rate of 61.3%, producing over 1 million master's graduates and over 100,000 doctorates for the first time.
> The high-school-age population peaks around 2029, after which the same liquidation logic climbs into higher education.

(4) MAJOR-LEVEL ADJUSTMENT.
> The Ministry of Education's annual undergraduate major adjustment process has been used to add elderly-care, health-management and smart-eldercare programmes across the vocational and applied-undergraduate system while implicitly squeezing preschool-education intakes as employment outcomes deteriorated.
> Vocational colleges have been the fastest-moving layer, adding elderly care alongside robotics and other priority fields.
> China also inaugurated a National University for the Aged in 2023 — a lifelong-learning institution for the elderly themselves, which is simultaneously an education service, a social-isolation intervention and a silver-economy business.

(5) TEACHER WORKFORCE MANAGEMENT — the weakest part of the response.
> There is no national redeployment or retraining scheme of adequate scale; the adjustment has fallen on individual teachers, with quality metrics improving (85.3% of primary teachers now hold a bachelor's degree or higher, up from 70.3% in 2021) partly because the least-qualified were the first to be shed.

WHAT INDONESIA SHOULD LEARN.
> Positive: repurpose facilities rather than close them (childcare, eldercare, community health, intergenerational centres); use the demographic window to raise per-student quality since smaller cohorts make higher spending per child affordable; move capacity up the age ladder deliberately; and open eldercare and gerontology programmes NOW, before the shortage bites.
> Negative — the mistakes to avoid: do not let intake into PG-PAUD and PGSD continue expanding while the market shrinks; do not let the entire adjustment burden fall on non-permanent teachers (21% of Indonesian educators are non-permanent, an even more precarious base than China's private kindergarten sector); and do not wait for the crisis to force consolidation, because reactive consolidation destroys community trust and strands assets.

### Pelajaran Kebijakan dari China

**Respons Kebijakan China**

> CHINA'S POLICY RESPONSE — chronology, content, and the verdict on effectiveness, which is the most policy-relevant finding in this item.

CHRONOLOGY OF PIVOT.
> 1980-2015: one-child policy, enforced with fines, sterilisation quotas and hukou penalties.
> 2013: 'selective two-child' (couples where one parent was an only child).
> 1 January 2016: universal two-child policy — one rebound year (18.83 million births), then eight consecutive years of decline.
> May 2021: three-child policy plus removal of social maintenance fees — no measurable effect.
> July 2021: the 'double reduction' (双减) crackdown on K-12 tutoring, partly justified as a fertility measure to reduce child-rearing costs.
> 2021-2023: provincial extensions of maternity leave (to 158-190 days in most provinces), paternity and parental leave, and childcare tax deductions.
> October 2024: State Council directive with 13 targeted measures spanning childbirth support services, childcare expansion, and support in education, housing and employment, plus a mandate to build a 'birth-friendly social atmosphere'.
> March 2025: 'childcare subsidies' entered the annual Government Work Report for the first time, with an explicit instruction to use financial incentives.
> 10 May 2025: the revised Marriage Registration Regulation took effect, abolishing the hukou-location requirement and the household register document — the most operationally successful single measure, producing a 10.76% marriage increase.
