> July 2025: the first NATIONWIDE childcare subsidy — 3,600 yuan per child per year for every child under three, tax-exempt, backdated to 1 January 2025, covering 20+ million families annually.
> Autumn 2025: free preschool phased in, beginning with the final kindergarten year.
> December 2025: moves toward effectively free childbirth by absorbing delivery costs into maternity insurance.
> Throughout: at least 23 provincial-level regions run their own birth subsidies, with Hohhot the most aggressive (10,000 yuan for a first child; 10,000 yuan a year to age five for a second, 50,000 total; 10,000 yuan a year to age ten for a third, 100,000 total).
> Many provinces have also brought IVF and assisted reproduction into medical insurance coverage.

THE VERDICT.
> 2025 births fell 17% to 7.92 million — the lowest since 1939 — in the very year the national subsidy, free preschool and marriage-registration reform all took effect.
> This is the most important single data point for Indonesian policymakers.
> Diagnosis: (a) SCALE MISMATCH — 3,600 yuan per year against a 538,000 yuan cost of raising a child to 18 covers roughly 1.2%; cash of this magnitude changes timing at most, not completed family size.
> (b) TIMING — the measures arrived after the childbearing-age female cohort had already shrunk 13% in a decade, so even a propensity increase cannot offset the base effect.
> (c) WRONG TARGET — the binding constraints are housing cost, job insecurity, employer discrimination against women of childbearing age, and the opportunity cost of women's careers, none of which a per-child cash transfer addresses.
> (d) MEASURES THAT DID WORK were administrative, not fiscal: removing the hukou requirement for marriage registration produced an immediate 10.76% increase because it removed a genuine friction rather than trying to change a preference.

WHAT INDONESIA CAN ADOPT AS PREEMPTIVE POLICY.
> The China lesson is that pronatalist cash arrives too late and works too weakly, so the actionable agenda is different from copying the subsidy.
> (1) REMOVE FRICTIONS NOW — simplify and reduce the cost of marriage registration; the Chinese registration reform is the highest return-per-rupiah intervention available and Indonesia has its own frictions (registration cost outside KUA office hours, documentation, the nikah siri gap).
> (2) BUILD THE 0-3 CHILDCARE SYSTEM WHILE THE BUILDINGS EXIST — China had to build 托育 from zero after the collapse; Indonesia has thousands of soon-to-be-surplus PAUD and SD buildings and a displaced PAUD teacher workforce, right now.
> This is the single most time-sensitive opportunity in this item.
> (3) ATTACK HOUSING, NOT BIRTHS — housing for young couples addresses the actual stated constraint (57% in the UNFPA 2026 survey).
> (4) DO NOT REPEAT CHINA'S EXTENDED-MATERNITY-LEAVE-WITHOUT-COST-SHARING ERROR — long leave financed by employers increased discrimination against women in hiring; Indonesia's UU 4/2024 six-month provision must be socially financed or it will reduce female employment.
> (5) BUILD THE PENSION AND LONG-TERM-CARE SYSTEM BEFORE THE ELDERLY SHARE HITS 15% — China is now spending 2.9 trillion yuan (10.1% of general budget) on social security subsidies and would have run a 1.4 trillion yuan pension shortfall without them; Indonesia has neither the coverage nor the fiscal space and must build contributory coverage of informal workers in the 2020s.
> (6) AVOID COERCION — Chinese local officials phoning newlyweds about pregnancy plans and restricting non-medically-necessary abortions generated visible backlash without raising births.

**Rekomendasi Kebijakan Indonesia**

> TEN CONCRETE RECOMMENDATIONS, ordered by time-sensitivity rather than importance — several have hard expiry dates.

(1) RETIRE 'DUA ANAK CUKUP' AND REFRAME KEMENDUKBANGGA'S MISSION (do this in 2026-2027).
> Indonesia is running anti-natalist messaging into a below-replacement urban population.
> The ministry reorganisation and the 2026 silver-economy symposium show the pivot has started; complete it.
> Replace with a neutral 'families get support to have the number of children they want' frame, with differentiated provincial messaging — family support in Java and Bali, maternal-child health and stunting reduction in Papua, NTT and Maluku.
> Do NOT adopt coercive or shaming pronatalism; it fails everywhere and would fall hardest on women.

(2) CONVERT CLOSING SCHOOLS INTO CHILDCARE AND ELDERCARE INFRASTRUCTURE — THE HIGHEST-RETURN, MOST TIME-LIMITED ACTION.
> Boyolali merged 48 SDN into 24; hundreds more will follow.
> Issue a Kemendikdasmen-Kemendukbangga-Kemenkes joint regulation NOW establishing a default repurposing pathway: surplus PAUD/SD buildings become TPA (0-3 daycare), posyandu lansia, day-care centres for the elderly, or integrated intergenerational centres, with displaced honorary PAUD teachers given a funded retraining route into infant-toddler care or caregiving certification.
> China had to build its 0-3 childcare sector from zero after 2021; Indonesia can build it from assets it already owns.
> This window closes as buildings are sold, repurposed ad hoc, or fall derelict.

(3) COMMISSION AN AUTHORITATIVE NATIONAL COST-OF-RAISING-A-CHILD STUDY.
> YuWa's 538,000 yuan / 6.3x GDP per capita figure is the single most influential demographic statistic in China and drove the entire subsidy debate.
> Indonesia has no equivalent.
> BPS with UI's Lembaga Demografi and UGM's PSKK should produce one, disaggregated by province and income decile, and update it annually.
> Without it, Indonesian policy debate has no anchor.

(4) FIX THE MATERNITY LEAVE FINANCING IN UU 4/2024 BEFORE IT BACKFIRES.
> Six months of leave financed primarily by employers replicates China's error and will increase hiring discrimination against women aged 20-35.
> Shift the financing to BPJS Ketenagakerjaan or a dedicated social insurance pool, and add meaningful paid paternity leave — the evidence that paternal leave uptake supports both fertility and female employment is among the strongest in the field.

(5) REFORM FISCAL TRANSFER FORMULAS TO BE AGE-STRUCTURE-WEIGHTED (target 2028).
> DAU, DAK and Dana Desa are population-weighted; as Java's child population shrinks and its elderly population grows while eastern Indonesia's child population grows, headcount weighting will fund empty schools and starve eldercare.
> This is unglamorous, cheap and high-leverage.

(6) BUILD LONG-TERM-CARE FINANCING AND EXTEND CONTRIBUTORY PENSION COVERAGE TO INFORMAL WORKERS WHILE THE DEPENDENCY RATIO IS STILL FAVOURABLE (before 2035).
> Study China's LTC insurance pilots (Qingdao, Shanghai) and Japan's Kaigo Hoken.
> Every year of delay raises the eventual contribution rate.
> Indonesia's dependency ratio is at its most favourable around 2030-2035; after that, building a contributory system becomes politically and arithmetically much harder.

(7) MAKE HOUSING FOR YOUNG COUPLES AN EXPLICIT DEMOGRAPHIC POLICY, NOT JUST A HOUSING POLICY.
> 57% of young Indonesians in the UNFPA 2026 survey cite economics and housing scarcity as the reason for delaying cohabitation.
> Link FLPP/subsidised mortgage access, rental assistance and transit-oriented small-format housing explicitly to newly married and young households.

(8) CAP AND REDIRECT TEACHER-EDUCATION INTAKE, EXPAND GERONTOLOGY (start with the 2027/2028 intake).
> Kemendikti Saintek should place enrolment caps on PG-PAUD and PGSD at institutions in below-replacement provinces, tie accreditation renewal to graduate employment outcomes, and fast-track approval and funding for gerontology, geriatric nursing, long-term care, rehabilitation science and actuarial science programmes.

(9) TREAT CAREGIVER EXPORT AS STRATEGIC INDUSTRIAL POLICY.
> Japan, Taiwan, Hong Kong, South Korea, Singapore and increasingly China are structurally short of caregivers and Indonesia is already a supplier.
> Build a certified, language-trained, protected caregiver pipeline through BP2MI and the vocational system — this simultaneously creates jobs for displaced education workers, generates remittances, and builds the domestic caregiving workforce Indonesia will itself need after 2040.

(10) UPGRADE DEMOGRAPHIC DATA FREQUENCY.
> China publishes marriage registrations quarterly and population annually within three weeks of year-end; Indonesia observes its own demographic turning points 12-24 months late.
> Publish monthly KUA/Dukcapil marriage registrations and annual provincial birth estimates.
> You cannot manage a turning point you only see two years after it happens.

OVERARCHING PRINCIPLE: Indonesia's advantage over China is roughly a decade of warning and a TFR still at the threshold rather than at 1.0.
> Every East Asian precedent — Japan, Korea, Taiwan, Singapore, Thailand and now China — squandered exactly this window.
> The realistic goal is not to keep TFR above 2.1 (no country has done this once it started falling) but to stabilise it around 1.7-1.9 rather than let it fall to 1.2, and to build the ageing infrastructure while the dependency ratio still allows it.
> The difference between 1.8 and 1.2 compounds into tens of millions of people and determines whether Indonesia's 2060s are Japan-like (manageable) or Korea-like (existential).

### Peluang & Rekomendasi Aksi

**Peluang Bisnis**

> BUSINESS OPPORTUNITIES OPENED BY THE INDONESIAN DEMOGRAPHIC TRANSITION, with the Chinese analogue and market size that validates each.

(1) ELDERCARE SERVICES — the largest and most durable.
> Home care agencies, day-care centres for the elderly, assisted living, memory/dementia care, geriatric clinics, and care-coordination platforms.
> Indonesian elderly go from 33.9 million (2025) to 63-66 million (2045).
> Entry is capital-light at the home-care end (matching, training, scheduling, quality assurance) and capital-heavy at the residential end.
> The Chinese lesson from Taikang and Cherish-Yearn is that pure residential CCRC models struggle on unit economics; the winners are asset-light service networks plus insurance tie-ins.
> Note the cultural constraint: institutional eldercare is stigmatised in Indonesia, so home-based and day-care formats will scale years before residential ones.

(2) THE 0-3 CHILDCARE MARKET — counterintuitive, underappreciated, and time-limited.
> Fewer children plus more working mothers plus nuclear urban households equals rising demand for formal daycare even as PAUD enrolment falls.
> China built 托育 from near zero after 2021 into a national policy priority.
> In Indonesia the physical assets (closing PAUD/SD buildings) and the workforce (5,805 PAUD teachers displaced in 2024 alone) are available cheaply right now.
> First movers who consolidate closing PAUD into professionally run TPA chains in Jabodetabek, Bandung and Surabaya are buying assets at their cyclical low.

(3) THE SOLO / ONE-PERSON ECONOMY.
> China's solo dining reached roughly 800 billion yuan in 2025 and small appliances roughly US$60 billion, driven by 125 million+ one-person households and average household size falling to 2.62.
> Indonesian analogues: single-serving ready meals and delivery formats, compact kitchen appliances, studio and co-living residential formats, small-format grocery, laundry and cleaning services for singles, solo travel packages, and self-storage.
> Chinese suppliers already dominate the hardware; Indonesian value capture is in retail format, food service and property.

(4) PET ECONOMY.
> China reached roughly 811.4 billion yuan in 2025, up 68%, with Goldman Sachs projecting urban pets to outnumber young children by 2030 — driven directly by singles and the elderly.
> Indonesia's pet market is small but compounding fast in Jabodetabek.
> Opportunities: premium pet food manufacturing (currently import-dependent), veterinary clinic chains, pet insurance, grooming and boarding, and pet e-commerce.

(5) ASSISTED REPRODUCTION.
> Later marriage plus later first birth equals rising infertility.
> China's IVF sector boomed and moved into insurance coverage; Indonesia's clinics (Morula IVF, Bocah Indonesia, Bunda Medik) are scaling but capacity is far below latent demand and concentrated in Jakarta and Surabaya.
> Expansion into tier-2 cities, plus fertility preservation (egg freezing) marketed to professional women, is a clear white space — with the caveat that regulatory and religious frameworks around ART in Indonesia are restrictive and must be navigated carefully.

(6) SENIOR NUTRITION AND ADULT INCONTINENCE PRODUCTS.
> Feihe's pivot into middle-aged and senior milk powder is the exact playbook available to Kalbe, Sari Husada/Danone and Nutrifood.
> In China adult diaper volumes are approaching and in some channels exceeding baby diapers — the same crossover will occur in Indonesia in the 2030s and manufacturers should be building the line now.

(7) RETIREMENT AND LONGEVITY FINANCIAL PRODUCTS.
> Annuities, private pension (DPLK), long-term-care insurance, critical illness cover, and eventually reverse mortgages.
> Indonesia's severe actuary shortage is itself a services opportunity.

(8) AGE-TECH AND ASSISTIVE DEVICES.
> Fall detection, remote vital monitoring, medication management, mobility aids, hearing aids, home safety retrofit.
> Hardware will be imported from China; the Indonesian business is distribution, installation, clinical integration and service.

(9) ADAPTIVE REUSE OF EDUCATION REAL ESTATE.
> Thousands of surplus school buildings in Java over the next fifteen years, on well-located community land.
> Repurposing into daycare, eldercare, community clinics, co-working and training centres is a specialised property play with an unusually clear supply pipeline.

(10) PREMIUM CHILD PRODUCTS AND SERVICES — fewer children, more spending per child.
> China's maternity-and-baby online channel grew 12.6% to RMB 223.78 billion in 2025 on a shrinking birth base.
> Premium education, enrichment, child health, safety products and children's travel all grow in Indonesia even as births fall.

(11) WEDDING INDUSTRY REPOSITIONING.
> Fewer marriages but higher spend per event: China's wedding services market kept growing while couples fell 55%.
> The mass-market wedding business shrinks; premium, destination and small-format 'intimate wedding' services grow.
> Bali is already positioned for the regional destination-wedding market.

(12) CAREGIVER TRAINING AND PLACEMENT.
> Structurally short markets in Japan, Taiwan, Hong Kong, Korea, Singapore and China plus a growing domestic market.
> Language-plus-skills academies with placement pipelines are a high-margin, policy-supported business.

**Rekomendasi Individu Mahasiswa**

> FOR STUDENTS AND YOUNG PROFESSIONALS DECIDING WHAT TO BUILD NOW.

AVOID OR HEDGE: do not enter PG-PAUD or PGSD expecting an urban teaching career — the pupil base is contracting and 21% of Indonesian educators are already on non-permanent status.
> If you are already in these programmes, add a certification that transfers: infant-toddler (0-3) care, childcare centre management, special-needs education (demand is rising as diagnosis improves and cohorts shrink), or caregiving.
> Midwifery students should add geriatric or critical-care competencies and target quality-driven roles rather than volume-driven ones.

HIGH-CONVICTION SKILL BETS.
> (1) Geriatric and long-term care competence in any health-adjacent field — nursing, physiotherapy, occupational therapy, pharmacy, nutrition, social work.
> This is the deepest and most durable shortage in the Indonesian labour market for the next thirty years, and it is portable internationally.
> (2) Actuarial science, health economics and social-insurance design — Indonesia has a few hundred qualified actuaries facing a national pension and long-term-care problem; the scarcity premium is extreme.
> (3) Demography and applied population analysis paired with data skills — Indonesia needs analysts who can do provincial fertility projection, age-structure fiscal modelling and cost-of-child estimation; almost no one can.
> (4) Care-sector operations and quality management — the eldercare and childcare industries will be built by operators, not clinicians, and Indonesia has no trained bench of care-facility managers.
> (5) Japanese, Mandarin or Korean language plus a caregiving certification — the single fastest route from a low-income background to a high-remittance career, with structurally guaranteed demand.
> (6) Product and service design for one-person and elderly households — a differentiator in FMCG, food service, property and retail careers.
> (7) Veterinary and animal health, small-animal focus.
> (8) Assistive technology and biomedical engineering, oriented toward integration and service rather than component manufacture.

MINDSET.
> Two general points.
> First, this is the rare trend where the direction is essentially certain — the people who will be 40 in 2045 have already been born, and the elderly of 2045 are alive today.
> Skills aligned to it carry unusually low forecast risk compared with, say, betting on a specific AI toolchain.
> Second, do not read 'declining births' as 'declining opportunity in children' — read it as a shift from volume to quality and from education to care.
> The money moves from teaching many children to caring for a few children and very many old people.

PERSONAL FINANCIAL PLANNING.
> Assume you will support parents with little or no pension while having fewer siblings to share the burden and fewer children of your own to rely on later.
> Build independent retirement savings early, buy health and critical-illness cover for parents, and treat 'sandwich generation' exposure as the central financial risk of an Indonesian professional career born after 1990.

**Rekomendasi Perguruan Tinggi**

> FOR UNIVERSITIES, LPTK AND THE HIGHER-EDUCATION REGULATOR.

OPEN OR EXPAND (urgent, 2026-2029 intake cycles): gerontology and geriatric nursing (currently near-absent in Indonesia); long-term care and caregiving at D3/D4 level with destination-country language tracks; rehabilitation sciences — physiotherapy, occupational therapy, speech-language pathology, audiology; geriatric medicine as a recognised specialty pathway with expanded residency slots; actuarial science, health economics and social insurance; applied demography and population policy; care-facility and health-services management; assistive technology and biomedical engineering; small-animal veterinary medicine and veterinary nursing; family, grief and hospice counselling; and universal-design architecture and age-friendly urban planning.

CAP, MERGE OR REPOSITION: PG-PAUD — cap intake immediately in below-replacement provinces and reposition curriculum toward 0-3 infant-toddler care, childcare centre management and childcare regulation rather than 4-6 preschool teaching; PGSD — cap intake and add multi-grade, small-school and school-consolidation management competencies plus special-needs and remedial specialisation; midwifery — consolidate the excessive number of programmes and raise the quality bar rather than the volume; secondary teacher education — begin planned reduction from around 2030; small private campuses dependent on teacher-education enrolment should plan for merger now rather than face the late-2030s enrolment cliff unprepared.

STRUCTURAL AND REGULATORY ACTIONS.
> (1) Kemendikti Saintek should tie accreditation renewal for teacher-education programmes to graduate employment outcomes, which would automatically throttle oversupply without a political fight over closures.
> (2) Create a national funded retraining pathway — micro-credentials in caregiving, 0-3 care and rehabilitation aide work — targeted at displaced PAUD and SD teachers, delivered through the same LPTKs whose enrolment is falling, which converts a threat into a revenue line for those institutions.
> (3) Establish at least one national centre of excellence in ageing research and policy, modelled on the analytical role YuWa plays in China and Japan's gerontology institutes, ideally at UI or UGM, with a standing mandate to publish provincial fertility projections and an annual cost-of-raising-a-child estimate.
> (4) Build a caregiver-export academy model — certification plus Japanese/Mandarin/Korean language plus placement — in partnership with BP2MI and destination-country employers.
> (5) Introduce demographic literacy into the general curriculum across business, economics, health and public administration programmes; every Indonesian professional entering the workforce now will spend their career inside this transition.
> (6) Use closing school assets as teaching sites: university-run demonstration daycare and elder day-care centres in repurposed SD buildings would provide clinical placement capacity, community service and a revenue stream simultaneously.

### Faktor Risiko & Sisi Gelap

**Dampak Negatif China**

> DAMAGE ALREADY DONE IN CHINA — much of it irreversible, and much of it caused by the policy response rather than the demography itself.

(1) THE 30-35 MILLION SURPLUS MALE PROBLEM.
> The one-child policy interacting with son preference and sex-selective abortion produced a sex ratio at birth peaking at 111-118 and left tens of millions of men who will never marry, concentrated in poor rural areas.
> Consequences: bride-price (彩礼) inflation that in some provinces consumes several years of household income and drives rural indebtedness; trafficking of women from Southeast Asia into forced marriage; and a large population of permanently single, low-income rural men — a well-documented social stability concern in Chinese policy literature.
> This damage is permanent and cannot be undone by any future policy.

(2) THE 4-2-1 CARE BURDEN.
> A single adult child supporting two parents and up to four grandparents, with the state pension system already requiring 2.9 trillion yuan of annual subsidy (10.1% of general budget spending) and facing a 1.4 trillion yuan shortfall without it.
> Rural elderly poverty and elderly suicide rates in rural China are documented concerns, and the burden falls disproportionately on daughters and daughters-in-law.

(3) EDUCATION SECTOR DEVASTATION.
> Nearly 30,000 institutions closed in one year, K-12 teaching staff down two consecutive years, and the burden concentrated on private-kindergarten teachers (private facilities are 52.1% of the total) who had no public-sector protection.
> An entire profession's employment base evaporated within five years, with no national redeployment programme.

(4) OBSTETRIC AND PEDIATRIC CAPACITY DESTRUCTION.
> Dozens of delivery wards closed, obstetricians retraining out of the specialty, Shanghai deliveries down from 34,000 to 20,000.
> The dangerous part is irreversibility: once a hospital closes obstetrics and its specialists disperse, rebuilding capacity takes a decade, and rural women face longer travel to deliver — a maternal safety risk created by a fertility problem.

(5) INTENSIFIED DISCRIMINATION AGAINST WOMEN.
> Extended maternity leave (158-190 days in most provinces) financed largely at employer level made women of childbearing age measurably more expensive to hire, worsening hiring discrimination and the gender pay gap — a textbook case of a pronatalist policy reducing women's economic position without raising births.
> Add coercive local practices: officials contacting newly married couples about pregnancy plans, pressure on women's reproductive choices, and 2021 guidance to reduce 'non-medically necessary abortions'.
> The result has been visible online feminist backlash and, if anything, further reduced marriage willingness among educated women.

(6) REGIONAL HOLLOWING-OUT.
> The Northeast (Heilongjiang, Jilin, Liaoning) combined low fertility with mass youth out-migration to produce shrinking cities, stranded infrastructure and the country's most stressed provincial pension funds.
> Twenty-four of thirty-one provinces shrank in 2025.

(7) ECONOMIC DRAG.
> Rhodium's assessment: Beijing has downgraded long-run GDP growth projections to 4.2% through 2035 from 4.8%, with the worker-to-retiree ratio compressing from 4.4 (2024) to 2.8 (2035).
> Demographic decline also interacts with the property downturn, since household formation is the primary driver of housing demand.

(8) THE PSYCHOLOGICAL AND CULTURAL COST.
> The rise of 躺平 (lying flat), 不婚不育 (no marriage, no children) and the framing of marriage and children as 'liabilities' and 'overdrafts from the future' reflects a generation that has concluded family formation is economically irrational.
> Once that belief becomes a social norm, it is extremely resistant to policy — which is precisely why the 2025 subsidy failed.

**Risiko Sosial Indonesia**

> RISKS SPECIFIC TO INDONESIA IF THIS TRANSITION PROCEEDS WITHOUT PREEMPTIVE POLICY.

(1) AGEING WITHOUT A PENSION SYSTEM — the dominant risk.
> China at least entered ageing with near-universal basic pension coverage and a state balance sheet capable of a 2.9 trillion yuan annual subsidy.
> Indonesia has roughly a third of its elderly receiving any pension income, BPJS Ketenagakerjaan coverage of informal workers is thin, and the tax ratio is roughly 10-11%.
> Indonesia will hit 20% elderly by 2045 at a fraction of China's per-capita income.
> The risk is not slow growth; it is mass old-age poverty.
> Yogyakarta at 17.83% elderly today is the preview.

(2) THE SANDWICH GENERATION SQUEEZE ON A SHRINKING MIDDLE CLASS.
> Indonesia's middle class is already contracting as a share of population.
> Loading it with unfunded elder care plus urban housing costs plus per-child education inflation produces a class that cannot save, cannot invest and cannot have children — a self-reinforcing loop that accelerates fertility decline precisely in the segment the economy depends on.

(3) STRANDED EDUCATION ASSETS AND A DISPLACED, PRECARIOUS TEACHING WORKFORCE.
> 21% of Indonesian educators are non-permanent, and PAUD teachers — already the lowest-paid — took the largest hit in 2024.
> Without a funded transition pathway, tens of thousands of predominantly female, predominantly rural honorary teachers will be pushed into informal work.
> Simultaneously the state will keep funding a reported 498,000-position 'shortage' that is actually a distribution failure, wasting fiscal resources on both ends.

(4) A PRONATALIST BACKLASH THAT TARGETS WOMEN.
> This is the most likely form of policy error in the Indonesian context.
> If fertility decline becomes a moral panic, the politically cheapest responses available are religious and social pressure on women, revival of early-marriage advocacy (Indonesia already grants thousands of marriage dispensations for under-19s annually, and child marriage is a live problem), restriction of reproductive health access, and polygamy discourse framed as demographic solution.
> All would damage women's welfare and education without raising completed fertility — and would likely lower it by raising the perceived cost of marriage for educated women.
> This risk deserves explicit preemptive guarding.

(5) REGIONAL POLITICAL FRICTION.
> As Java ages and eastern Indonesia stays young, population-weighted fiscal transfers and parliamentary apportionment will produce visible unfairness in both directions, with a real risk of the demographic issue being racialised or regionalised.

(6) COLLAPSE OF THE INFORMAL CARE SYSTEM WITHOUT A FORMAL REPLACEMENT.
> Indonesia currently runs on family care — grandmothers, daughters, daughters-in-law, and cheap domestic help.
> Urbanisation, smaller families and rising female labour force participation are dissolving that system, while institutional eldercare remains stigmatised and formal home care barely exists.
> The gap between the informal system failing and a formal one existing is where the real human damage occurs, and on current trajectory that gap opens in the 2030s.

(7) PREMATURE DEINDUSTRIALISATION MEETING PREMATURE AGEING.
> Indonesia's demographic dividend window closes around 2035-2040.
> If manufacturing employment has not absorbed the current youth bulge by then — and youth unemployment is already among ASEAN's highest — Indonesia arrives at ageing with neither the industrial base nor the accumulated savings to fund it.
> This is the true 'middle-income trap' mechanism and it is demographic, not just industrial.

(8) HEALTH SYSTEM MISMATCH.
> Indonesia's health system, BPJS financing model and medical training pipeline are all built around maternal-child health and infectious disease.
> Non-communicable disease and geriatric care have a completely different cost curve, and BPJS Kesehatan is already under financial strain — an ageing population will stress it structurally within a decade.

(9) LONELINESS AND MENTAL HEALTH AT SCALE.
> Rising single-person households and elderly living alone in a country with one of the region's worst psychologist-to-population ratios.
> China's 'loneliness economy' is a commercial response to a genuine public health problem; Indonesia will have the problem with neither the commercial nor the clinical response in place.

**Kelompok Rentan**

> (1) HONORARY AND NON-PERMANENT TEACHERS, ESPECIALLY IN PAUD — the most immediately and severely affected group.
> 21% of Indonesian educators are non-permanent, PAUD teachers are the lowest-paid segment, 5,805 PAUD teaching positions vanished in 2024 alone, and the workforce is overwhelmingly female, often rural, and typically without alternative qualifications.
> They have no severance protection and no retraining pathway.

(2) THE ELDERLY POOR WITHOUT PENSION COVERAGE — roughly two-thirds of Indonesian elderly have no pension income.
> As family sizes shrink and children migrate to cities, the informal support system that has substituted for a pension system erodes.
> Rural elderly in Yogyakarta, Central Java and East Java — the provinces that are ageing fastest — are the front line.

(3) THE URBAN SANDWICH GENERATION — professionals aged 30-50 in Jabodetabek, Bandung and Surabaya, supporting parents without pensions while paying metropolitan housing costs and per-child education inflation, with fewer siblings to share the load each cohort.

(4) WOMEN GENERALLY, AND EDUCATED URBAN WOMEN SPECIFICALLY — they bear the physical cost of childbearing, the overwhelming majority of elder and child care, the career penalty of maternity leave (which UU 4/2024 may worsen if employer-financed), and would bear the brunt of any pronatalist moral pressure.
> China's experience shows both the discrimination effect and the backlash effect clearly.

(5) MIDWIVES, OBSTETRIC NURSES AND MATERNAL-HEALTH WORKERS — an oversupplied profession facing a shrinking birth base, with skills that do not transfer automatically to geriatric care without funded retraining.

(6) YOUNG MEN IN LOW-INCOME REGIONS — less severely than in China, since Indonesia's sex ratio is normal, but the same economic mechanism applies: men unable to meet the income and housing expectations attached to marriage face involuntary singlehood, and this population is a well-documented source of social alienation.

(7) SINGLE WOMEN OVER 30 AND CHILDLESS COUPLES — facing intensifying social and religious stigma in a society where marriage is a near-universal norm, likely to worsen if fertility decline becomes a public moral concern.

(8) CHILDREN IN HIGH-FERTILITY, HIGH-POVERTY REGIONS — Papua Pegunungan, NTT, Maluku.
> If national policy attention and budget pivot toward ageing in Java, the regions where the binding constraints remain stunting, maternal mortality and educational access risk being deprioritised precisely when they most need investment.

(9) SMALL PRIVATE UNIVERSITIES AND THEIR STUDENTS — the late-2030s enrolment cliff will close institutions, and students enrolled at closing campuses lose credential value and continuity.

(10) INFORMAL WORKERS APPROACHING RETIREMENT — the roughly 59% of the labour force outside formal employment who will reach old age in the 2030s and 2040s with no contributory pension entitlement whatsoever.
> This is numerically the largest vulnerable group and the one with the least policy attention.

### Contoh Kasus Konkret

**Kasus China**

> CASE 1 — THE 2024 MARRIAGE CRASH AND THE 2025 'RECOVERY' THAT WASN'T.
> In 2024 China registered 6.106 million marriages, down 20.5% year-on-year, the lowest since the series began in 1980 and 55% below the 2013 peak of 13.47 million.
> In 2025 marriages rebounded 10.76% to 6.76 million (+657,000) after the 10 May 2025 revised Marriage Registration Regulation abolished the hukou-location requirement, with the surge concentrated in migrant-receiving cities: Shanghai +38.7% to 125,102, Shenzhen +28.5% to 118,900, Fuzhou +20.4% to 37,887.
> Yet in the same year births fell 17% to 7.92 million.
> This is the definitive case study of the domain: an administrative reform can move the marriage number, and it changes nothing about fertility.
> Any Indonesian policy that targets the marriage statistic rather than the underlying economics of family formation will produce the same result.

CASE 2 — THE 3,600 YUAN SUBSIDY VERSUS THE 538,000 YUAN CHILD.
> In July 2025 China launched its first nationwide childcare subsidy: 3,600 yuan per child per year for every child under three, tax-exempt, backdated to 1 January 2025, covering more than 20 million families — the largest universal pronatalist cash transfer ever attempted at that population scale.
> YuWa Population Research Institute's estimate of the cost of raising a child to 18 is 538,000 yuan nationally (6.3x GDP per capita, second-highest in the world after South Korea), 667,000 yuan in cities, 1.03 million yuan in Shanghai and 969,000 yuan in Beijing.
> The subsidy covers roughly 1.2% of the total.
> Births in 2025: down 17%, to the lowest level since 1939.
> The lesson for Indonesia is not 'subsidies don't work' — it is that a subsidy an order of magnitude below the cost it is meant to offset, deployed after the childbearing cohort has already shrunk 13%, cannot work.

CASE 3 — 59 KINDERGARTENS A DAY.
> In 2025 China closed 21,400 kindergartens (leaving 231,900) and roughly 8,000 primary schools — nearly 30,000 institutions in twelve months.
> Preschool enrolment fell from a 2020 peak of 48.18 million to 32.25 million, a one-third contraction in five years; primary intake fell 9.6% to 14.61 million, 22% below the 2023 peak; K-12 teaching staff fell to 15.68 million for a second consecutive year, with losses concentrated in early education and in private kindergartens (52.1% of facilities).
> This is the most operationally transferable case: it maps exactly onto Boyolali merging 48 SDN into 24, Temanggung's 32 schools with under five entrants, and Indonesia's 203,936-pupil PAUD enrolment drop in 2024.
> China did this reactively and destroyed a profession's employment base; Indonesia has roughly a five-year head start to do it deliberately.

CASE 4 — HOHHOT'S 100,000 YUAN BABY.
> Hohhot, capital of Inner Mongolia, offers 10,000 yuan for a first child, 10,000 yuan annually to age five for a second (50,000 total) and 10,000 yuan annually to age ten for a third (100,000 total) — among the most aggressive subnational birth incentives in the world, in a province with a shrinking population.
> The pattern replicated across 23+ provincial-level regions.
> The results have been modest and localised, and there is evidence of subsidy-shopping and administrative gaming rather than genuine fertility increase.
> Relevant to Indonesia because subnational birth incentives are the most politically attractive and least effective instrument, and Indonesian bupati and governors will be tempted by them.

CASE 5 — FEIHE'S PIVOT AND THE PET ECONOMY.
> Feihe (飞鹤), China's largest domestic infant formula producer, launched middle-aged and senior milk powder lines in 2022 as its core market structurally shrank; Chinese dairy companies broadly are redirecting capacity toward adult nutrition.
> Simultaneously the pet economy reached roughly 811.4 billion yuan in 2025, up 68% from 494 billion, with Goldman Sachs projecting urban pets to outnumber young children by 2030, and the solo-dining market reached roughly 800 billion yuan.
> The corporate sector adapted to the demographic transition faster, and more profitably, than the state did — which is the clearest signal to Indonesian businesses about where the next two decades of consumer demand sit.

CASE 6 — THE OBSTETRIC WINTER.
> Dozens of Chinese public hospitals closed delivery wards over 2023-2025; obstetricians retrained into other specialties; Shanghai deliveries fell from about 34,000 to 20,000.
> The capacity destruction is hard to reverse and creates maternal safety risk in less-served areas.
> Indonesia's midwifery oversupply and still-elevated maternal mortality mean the correct Indonesian response is consolidation with quality upgrading rather than the uncoordinated capacity exit China experienced.

**Padanan Indonesia**

> DIRECT INDONESIAN COUNTERPARTS, mapped to the Chinese cases above.

MARRIAGE COLLAPSE: registered marriages fell from 2,110,776 (2014) to 1,478,302 (2024) and 1,480,048 (2025) — a 30% decade decline, versus China's 55%.
> Divorce-to-marriage ratio rose from 16.3% (2020) to 29.6% (2025).
> 71.04% of 16-30 year olds were unmarried in 2025 versus 59.5% in 2016.
> Indonesia sits roughly where China sat in 2019 on this curve.

BELOW-REPLACEMENT URBAN FERTILITY: SUPAS 2025 puts DKI Jakarta at 1.79 and DI Yogyakarta at 1.84, with nine provinces below the 2.10 replacement threshold and national TFR at 2.13.
> Jakarta is Indonesia's Shanghai, arriving roughly two to three decades later.

SCHOOL CLOSURES — the closest one-to-one match with China: Boyolali (Central Java) merged 48 state primary schools into 24 in 2026; Temanggung recorded 32 schools with fewer than five new entrants; SDN Butuh enrolled two pupils and SDN Kauman 27 Solo enrolled one; hundreds of primary schools nationwide enrolled 1-5 new students in 2025/2026, spanning Java to Lampung.
> PAUD enrolment fell 203,936 pupils and PAUD teachers 5,805 in 2024.
> This is China's 2022-2023 moment, arriving in Indonesia in 2025-2026 — a two-to-three year lag on the downstream shock despite a 30-year lag on the underlying fertility level.

INSTITUTIONAL PIVOT: BKKBN became Kementerian Kependudukan dan Pembangunan Keluarga (Kemendukbangga) in October 2024; its 2026 National Population Symposium was themed 'Transformasi Kebijakan Kependudukan Menyambut Silver Economy'.
> This is Indonesia's analogue of China's January 2024 State Council silver-economy document — a two-year framing lag.

POLICY: UU No.
> 4/2024 on Maternal and Child Welfare in the First 1,000 Days (extended maternity leave to a baseline three months with up to three more on medical grounds, plus paternity leave) is Indonesia's first substantively family-supportive labour legislation — structurally similar to China's provincial maternity leave extensions, and carrying the same employer-financing risk of increased discrimination against women.

ATTITUDES: IDN Research Institute's Indonesia Millennial and Gen Z Report 2025 found 68% of millennials and 63% of Gen Z deprioritising marriage and children because of job-market unpredictability and living costs — the Indonesian expression of China's 不婚不育 discourse, arriving through the same social-media channels.

AGEING: elderly (60+) at 11.97% (about 33.9 million) in 2025, sixteen provinces already ageing, DI Yogyakarta highest at 17.83%, projected to reach roughly 20% (63-66 million) by 2045.
> Yogyakarta today is roughly where China was around 2010-2013.

COMMERCIAL: fertility clinic expansion (Morula IVF, Bocah Indonesia, Bunda Medik) mirrors China's IVF boom; adult and senior nutrition lines at Kalbe, Sari Husada/Danone and Nutrifood mirror Feihe's pivot; pet care growth in Jabodetabek mirrors the early phase of China's pet economy; co-living, premium kos and studio-format housing mirror the Chinese solo economy.

WHAT HAS NO INDONESIAN COUNTERPART YET, AND SHOULD BE WATCHED AS THE NEXT MARKER: no maternity ward closures reported at scale; no birth subsidy from any level of government; no authoritative national cost-of-raising-a-child study; no gerontology degree programme of national standing; no long-term-care insurance scheme; and no retirement of the 'Dua Anak Cukup' message.
> The first Indonesian kabupaten to announce a birth incentive, and the first hospital to close its maternity ward for lack of deliveries, will each be significant threshold events.

### Tingkat Keyakinan & Kualitas Sumber

**Catatan Kontradiksi Data**

> (1) 'LOWEST SINCE 1986' IN THE RESEARCH OUTLINE IS INCORRECT.
> The outline description states China's 2024 marriage figure of 6.106 million was the lowest since 1986.
> Ministry of Civil Affairs data and all major reporting (SCMP, CNN, Reuters) state it was the lowest since the current series began in 1980.
> The 6.106 million and -20.5% figures in the outline are correct; only the historical reference year is wrong.

(2) 'POPULATION DECLINED FOUR CONSECUTIVE YEARS' IN THE OUTLINE NOW UNDERSTATES THE SITUATION AS OF LATE 2025 DATA.
> When the outline was written this referred to 2022-2025 as of the 2024 data release.
> The January 2026 NBS release confirms the fourth consecutive decline was 2025, at -3.39 million — more than double the 2024 decline and the largest yet.
> The outline's framing remains directionally correct but the magnitude has worsened materially.

(3) 2025 CHINESE BIRTH FIGURES CONFLICT ACROSS SOURCES.
> NBS official: 7.92 million.
> Some market-research and industry sources cite 8.2 million.
> The NBS figure is authoritative and is used throughout this analysis.
> Note also the standing external critique from demographer Yi Fuxian that official Chinese population and birth figures are systematically overstated; if correct, the actual situation is worse than reported.

(4) CHINESE DIVORCE FIGURES FOR 2025 ARE INTERNALLY INCONSISTENT IN REPORTING.
> One report states divorces fell to 2.743 million, 'down by 770 thousand' from 2024.
> The 2024 figure was 2.82 million, so the arithmetic implies a decline of about 77,000, not 770,000.
> The 2.743 million level figure is used here; the stated change magnitude appears to be a reporting error.

(5) INDONESIAN 2025 MARRIAGE FIGURE CONFLICTS WITH THE PREVAILING HEADLINE NARRATIVE.
> The BPS series shows 1,478,302 in 2024 and 1,480,048 in 2025 — a marginal INCREASE.
> Numerous Indonesian media outlets in 2025-2026 reported 'marriages continue to decline' and cited approximately 1.4 million for 2025.
> The most defensible reading is that the decade-long decline has flattened at a low plateau rather than continued falling, which is materially different from the media framing and is important for the lag analysis.
> Note also that registered marriages exclude nikah siri, so the true level is higher and the true decline likely gentler.

(6) THE INDONESIAN 'CHILDFREE' STATISTIC IS INTERNALLY INCONSISTENT.
> A widely cited figure states 'about 8%, or 71,000 Indonesian women, choose to be childfree'.
> Eight percent of Indonesian women of reproductive age would be several million, not 71,000.
> The two numbers cannot both be correct; the underlying BPS statistic likely refers to a specific narrower sub-population.
> This statistic should not be used without verification against the original BPS source.

(7) INDONESIAN TFR VARIES BY SOURCE AND VINTAGE.
> SUPAS 2025: 2.13.
> SP2020 long-form: 2.18.
> BKKBN has cited 2.14 in various communications.
> World Bank and UN WPP estimates cluster around 2.1-2.2.
> These differences reflect methodology and reference period rather than genuine conflict, but they matter when assessing exactly when Indonesia crosses below 2.10.

(8) CHINESE TFR ESTIMATES RANGE FROM 1.0 TO 1.2 depending on source and adjustment method; China does not publish an official annual TFR, so all figures are derived.
> The 1.0-1.1 range used here reflects the consensus of independent demographers.

(9) CHINESE MEAN AGE AT FIRST MARRIAGE FIGURES CONFLICT.
> The 2020 census yields a mean of 25.33 overall (26.32 male, 24.44 female) on one calculation basis, while other analyses of the same census report 28.14 for women and 29.3 for men.
> The discrepancy arises from different computational methods (singulate mean age at marriage versus mean age of those marrying in the reference period).
> Both are cited in the literature; direction of travel (rising) is unambiguous.

(10) THE INDONESIAN '498,000 TEACHER SHORTAGE' COEXISTS WITH DOCUMENTED MASS SCHOOL MERGERS AND TEACHER REDUNDANCY.
> This is not a data error but a genuine structural paradox — the shortage is geographic (remote postings) and status-based (permanent versus honorary), while the surplus is demographic and concentrated in Java.
> Any policy analysis quoting either number alone will reach the wrong conclusion.

(11) CHINA'S 2025 MARRIAGE INCREASE IS CAUSALLY AMBIGUOUS.
> The +10.76% could reflect the registration reform (capturing previously deferred or displaced registrations), the zodiac calendar effect (2024 was a 'no-spring year'), genuine policy-induced behaviour change, or some combination.
> No published decomposition exists.
> The simultaneous 17% fall in births strongly suggests the administrative explanation dominates, but this is inference, not established fact.
