> Open or scale: Robotics and Autonomous Systems Engineering as a full S1 programme, consolidating what ITB, ITS, UI and UGM already do in fragments; a Perception and Machine Vision track within electrical engineering and informatics; Intelligent Transportation Systems as a graduate specialisation in transport engineering, with mixed-traffic and motorcycle-dominated flow modelling as its distinctive Indonesian research agenda; Functional Safety and Automotive Software Engineering as a certificate and graduate track (ISO 26262, SOTIF, cybersecurity regulation) — the scarcest competence in the country and a prerequisite for Indonesia ever homologating an autonomous vehicle; and Technology Law and Algorithmic Liability within law faculties, because Indonesia will need drafters and adjudicators before it needs engineers.
> Vocational tier, most urgent because it is where demand already exists: D3/D4 Mining Automation and Autonomous Systems Technician programmes sited in Kalimantan and Sulawesi near the operations that are automating now, covering fleet management systems, sensor maintenance, calibration and remote-operations support; AV/ADAS maintenance and calibration modules added to existing SMK TKRO and automotive diplomas; and teleoperation as an occupational programme with SKKNI competency standards.
> Restructure rather than close: heavy-equipment operator training should be rebuilt as heavy-equipment systems and automation, converting a threatened programme into the pipeline for the jobs that replace it; SMK TKRO/TBSM should add sensors, networks and vehicle software alongside the electrification content already needed; Teknik Mesin should add controls, mechatronics and embedded systems; transport-management programmes should replace manual dispatch content with fleet autonomy and systems economics.
> Delivery reforms that matter more than the programme list: shared regional AV laboratories rather than duplicated per-institution facilities, since sensor rigs and test vehicles are expensive; industry co-design with mining contractors (Pamapersada, Petrosea, BUMA, Thiess), Grab and Chinese OEMs on China's order-class (订单班) model, including equipment donation and instructor secondment; simulation-first pedagogy, because CARLA and open-source Apollo/Autoware stacks let Indonesian students reach production-grade skill without a vehicle; a national Indonesian traffic-scenario dataset built by universities as shared research infrastructure and a genuine international asset; instructor retraining, since most automotive and transport lecturers have no perception or controls background; and a published national AV/automation workforce assessment to coordinate the whole response — the instrument China used to pull its vocational system into line.

### Faktor Risiko & Sisi Gelap

**Dampak Negatif China**

> (1) Income destruction for taxi and ride-hailing drivers, now measured rather than alleged: peer-reviewed research finds robotaxi entry reduces traditional taxi drivers' average daily income by about 10.9%, while increasing their working hours and job stress, decreasing job satisfaction, and pushing them to seek alternative employment.
> This is against a driver population that had already doubled from 3.51 million (July 2021) to more than 7 million (May 2024), i.e.
> a labour market already in oversupply.
> (2) The Wuhan backlash of 2024 — a local taxi company's open letter stating that the technology 'led those at the bottom of society to starve', driver protests whose scale is unknown because coverage was quickly censored, and a municipal government forced to quietly slow Apollo Go's expansion.
> The episode showed that below-cost pricing (RMB 4 base fare against RMB 18 for a human taxi) is not a neutral consumer benefit but a direct transfer from the poorest workers to passengers and platform shareholders.
> (3) The March 2026 systemic failure — roughly 100 Apollo Go vehicles stalled simultaneously in Wuhan from a cloud outage, passengers trapped for up to two hours, vehicles paralysed in traffic.
> No injuries, but it revealed a single-point-of-failure architecture that a human-driven fleet cannot have, and it cost the whole industry a nationwide permit freeze from 29 April 2026 with only selective resumption from late June.
> (4) Consumer harm from assisted-driving overclaiming — the fatal Xiaomi SU7 crash in late March 2025 and the marketing environment that preceded it, which MIIT judged serious enough to ban an entire vocabulary on 16 April 2025; drivers had been sold 'smart driving' and were operating L2 systems.
> Analysts estimated the compliance response would add 10-15% to production costs.
> (5) Surveillance normalisation — the December 2023 national guidelines mandate audio and video recording inside autonomous vehicles, meaning every robotaxi ride in China is recorded; this was accepted with little debate and is now a settled feature of the technology as exported.
> (6) Capital intensity and competitive attrition — robotaxi is far more capital-hungry than ride-hailing, and the same involution dynamics visible in Chinese EVs (fare undercutting, negative unit economics sustained by investor capital) are present here; only a handful of city-level operations have reached breakeven and most operators remain loss-making.
> (7) An unaddressed transition — China built a large technical education pipeline for intelligent connected vehicles but has no national reskilling programme for the drivers being displaced; the backlash was managed by slowing deployment and suppressing protest rather than by supporting affected workers, which is a policy debt rather than a policy solution.

**Risiko Sosial Indonesia**

> (1) Premature deployment into a labour market with no floor.
> Indonesia's roughly 7 million ojol drivers have no minimum income, no employment status, no unemployment insurance and average net earnings around Rp 1.7 million a month already down from Rp 2.9 million in 2023.
> China could absorb a 10.9% income hit to taxi drivers; Indonesia's equivalent population is closer to subsistence and would not.
> (2) Political instability, which is not hypothetical.
> The July 2025 national action drew an estimated 50,000 drivers, and the death of driver Affan Kurniawan under a police vehicle on 28 August 2025 triggered nationwide unrest.
> A visible driverless deployment in Jakarta while driver incomes are falling is a plausible flashpoint, and Indonesia has no censorship mechanism comparable to the one that contained Wuhan.
> (3) Deployment without a legal framework.
> If a pilot goes ahead under an ad-hoc dispensation in a special zone, Indonesia will have driverless vehicles on roads with no liability doctrine, no insurance product, no event-data recording requirement and no incident-investigation capability — meaning the first serious crash has no defendant and no evidentiary basis.
> This is the most likely concrete failure mode and it is entirely preventable.
> (4) Unregulated L2+ assisted driving, which is the live risk today.
> Chinese-brand vehicles with advanced driver assistance are already sold in Indonesia with no terminology rules, no driver-monitoring mandate and no OTA verification requirement — precisely the conditions MIIT judged unacceptable after a fatality in March 2025.
> Indonesia is currently exposed to a risk China has already regulated.
> (5) Silent displacement in mining.
> Autonomous haulage is arriving in Kalimantan and Sulawesi with no regulatory attention, no transition planning and no reporting requirement, removing some of the best-paid blue-collar jobs available to non-Java workers in regions with the thinnest alternatives.
> The national conversation is fixated on ojol while the actual displacement happens elsewhere.
> (6) Sovereignty and data risk — offshore remote operations centres supervising Indonesian vehicles, perception and in-cabin data stored abroad, and a foreign operator able to disable an Indonesian fleet remotely; nothing in current Indonesian law addresses any of this.
> (7) Systemic fragility on weaker infrastructure.
> The Wuhan outage happened in a country with near-universal 5G; Indonesia targets 32% 5G coverage by 2030.
> A comparable failure here would be more likely, more prolonged and harder to recover.
> (8) Elite-capture geography — robotaxi would serve Jakarta, Bali and gated developments first, reinforcing the perception of technology as something done for the affluent and to everyone else.
> (9) Prestige procurement repeating the IKN ART failure — buying flagship autonomous systems for symbolic purposes, discovering they do not work in Indonesian conditions, and absorbing the fiscal and reputational cost.
> (10) Misdirected policy panic — a public debate that treats robotaxi as an imminent threat to ojol may produce restrictive or performative regulation while leaving the real near-term issues (assisted-driving marketing, mining automation, gig-worker protection) untouched.

**Kelompok Rentan**

> (1) Mining heavy-equipment operators in East and South Kalimantan, Central and Southeast Sulawesi and North Maluku — the first and most certain Indonesian casualties of vehicle autonomy, holding well-paid formal jobs in regions with almost no comparable alternatives, and currently protected by no policy whatsoever.
> (2) Ojol drivers, roughly 7 million people — largely insulated from robotaxi for a decade or more because their vehicle is a motorcycle, but already suffering falling real incomes (Rp 2.9 million in 2023 to about Rp 1.7 million in 2025) from platform dynamics alone, with no employment status or social protection, so any additional shock lands on people with no buffer.
> Their four-wheel counterparts (GrabCar, GoCar) are considerably more exposed.
> (3) Conventional taxi drivers and taxi companies — the group that bore the first hit in Wuhan, and in Indonesia already squeezed by ride-hailing; Bluebird-class operators would face the same margin compression.
> (4) Long-haul truck and intercity bus drivers on the Trans-Java and Trans-Sumatra corridors, whose routes are the most automatable public-road work in the country.
> (5) Port equipment operators and yard workers at automating terminals.
> (6) SMK and BLK heavy-equipment and driver-training graduates entering pipelines aimed at shrinking occupations, with curricula that have not been rebuilt.
> (7) Residents and road users generally, if L2+ assisted driving continues to be sold in Indonesia without terminology rules, driver monitoring or OTA verification — the population exposed to exactly the risk that killed a Xiaomi driver in China in March 2025 and prompted MIIT's intervention.
> (8) Passengers and pedestrians in any early Indonesian deployment conducted before liability, insurance and incident-investigation frameworks exist.
> (9) Non-Java regions generally — bearing the automation job losses years before Java sees any of the mobility benefit or the new technical employment.
> (10) Informal roadside economies dependent on driver traffic — warung, parking attendants, small repair shops and fuel stops along automating corridors, a diffuse group that appears in no impact assessment.

### Contoh Kasus Konkret

**Kasus China**

> (1) Wuhan and Apollo Go / 萝卜快跑, 2024 — the defining case of the entire domain.
> Baidu scaled to roughly 400 vehicles with a target of 1,000, priced base fares as low as RMB 4 against RMB 18 for a human taxi, and made more than 70% of rides fully driverless by April 2024.
> The result was a viral consumer phenomenon and a labour crisis: a local taxi company's open letter saying the technology 'led those at the bottom of society to starve', protests that were censored, and a municipal government that quietly slowed the rollout.
> This is the single most transferable case for Indonesia and the clearest evidence that robotaxi is a labour-policy question before it is a technology question.
> (2) The Apollo RT6 at RMB 204,600 (~USD 28,600) — the cost breakthrough that made the whole industry viable, bringing amortised monthly vehicle cost (~RMB 4,166) below tier-1 driver wages (~RMB 8,000).
> It is also the number that explains why the model does NOT transfer to Indonesia, where the wage being replaced is roughly one-fifth as large.
> (3) The Ministry of Transport Guidelines for AV Transport Safety Services, effective December 2023 — the first national rules anywhere legalising commercial driverless operation at scale, including the 3:1 remote-operator ratio, mandatory in-vehicle audio and video recording, and designated-area restriction.
> The 3:1 ratio is the most important single design decision in the domain: it converts the driver from an eliminated job into a supervisory job at one-third density.
> (4) The Xiaomi SU7 fatal crash of late March 2025 and MIIT's directive of 16 April 2025 — a fatality caused in part by consumer misunderstanding of an L2 system, followed within weeks by a ban on 'autonomous driving' and 'smart driving' marketing, mandatory SAE terminology, driver monitoring with 60-second hands-off warnings, prohibition of remote valet parking, and OTA restrictions.
> The most directly and urgently applicable Chinese policy for Indonesia today.
> (5) The Beijing Autonomous Vehicle Regulation, effective 1 April 2025 — the first comprehensive AV law in China, assigning primary liability to manufacturers for vehicle quality, consistency, functional safety and software-update management, and operational liability to fleet operators; the model liability architecture Indonesia lacks entirely.
> (6) The Wuhan cloud outage of 31 March 2026 — roughly 100 Apollo Go vehicles stalled simultaneously, passengers stranded up to two hours, followed by three ministries ordering industry-wide rectification and a nationwide suspension of new AV permits on 29 April 2026, lifted only selectively from late June.
> The definitive demonstration that fleet-level software creates fleet-level failure, and the most important cautionary case for any country with weaker connectivity.
> (7) Pony.ai's unit-economics breakeven — Guangzhou in November 2025 and Shenzhen in February 2026, with robotaxi revenue rising 128.6% to USD 16.6 million in FY2025 and 395.4% year on year in Q1 2026, and fully driverless commercial permits in all four tier-1 cities.
> The proof that the business works, in the specific conditions of a dense, wealthy, well-regulated Chinese metro.
> (8) The WeRide-Grab Singapore deployment — Grab's strategic equity investment in August 2025 and the Ai.R public service in Punggol from 1 April 2026 after roughly 30,000 km of autonomous mileage, with an explicit commitment to retrain and transition Grab driver-partners.
> This is simultaneously a Chinese case and the direct mechanism by which the trend will reach Indonesia.
> (9) The intelligent-connected-vehicle talent gap — a published net R&D shortfall of 13,000-37,000 by 2025 (about 69.4% of the existing R&D stock), a full-caliber gap near 1.03 million, only three relevant vocational majors producing about 120,000 graduates a year, and an ICV undergraduate cohort of only ~7,300 in 2025; the case showing that even a determined state cannot close a skills gap as fast as it can build an industry.
> (10) The 2026 export wave — Apollo Go in Hong Kong, Dubai, Abu Dhabi (Yas Island), Switzerland (PostBus AmiGo) and South Korea with Germany and the UK planned, and Pony.ai targeting 3,500 vehicles across 20+ cities; Chinese robotaxi is globalising while still immature at home, partly because domestic permitting was frozen.

**Sumber Data Kunci**

### Tingkat Keyakinan & Kualitas Sumber

**Catatan Kontradiksi Data**

> (1) The research brief states that 'China's national autonomous vehicle regulation took effect in April 2025'.
> This is not accurate as stated.
> Two distinct April 2025 events exist and neither is a national AV regulation: the Beijing Autonomous Vehicle Regulation (北京市自动驾驶汽车条例), which is MUNICIPAL, took effect 1 April 2025; and MIIT's directive of 16 April 2025, which is national but governs assisted-driving marketing, driver monitoring and OTA updates rather than autonomous vehicle operation.
> The genuine national operational framework is the Ministry of Transport's Guidelines for AV Transport Safety Services (Trial), effective December 2023, and the genuine national mandatory safety standard is still only a draft circulated in February 2026 with a target effective date of 1 July 2027.
> Several sources explicitly note that China still has no nationwide mandatory AV safety regulation in force.
> This correction materially changes the lag calculation and should be carried into any report.
> (2) Indonesian ojol driver counts are irreconcilable: roughly 7 million per Ministry of Transport figures cited in May 2025, versus 850,000 drivers covered by Grab and Gojek holiday bonuses in 2026, versus 'more than 1 million' active drivers added by one platform.
> The 7 million figure almost certainly counts registered accounts including highly occasional drivers; the 850,000 approximates full-time-equivalent drivers on the two largest platforms.
> Both are used in public debate without distinction.
> (3) Ojol income data conflict sharply: IDEAS research puts 2025 average net income at about Rp 1.7 million a month (down from Rp 2.9 million in 2023), while Grab's own December 2025 data describes a 'primary livelihood' tier earning above Rp 10 million.
> These are not contradictory so much as measuring different populations (all drivers vs high-intensity full-time drivers), but they are routinely presented as if comparable.
> (4) China robotaxi fleet estimates vary by source and definition — Goldman's ~5,000 (2025) and 14,000 (2026) are analyst estimates, while company-reported fleets (Pony.ai >1,700, WeRide ~1,000, Apollo Go across 20+ cities) do not sum transparently to those totals and mix permitted, delivered and actively operating vehicles.
> (5) Robotaxi market-size estimates differ by an order of magnitude between consultancies (roughly USD 0.56 billion for China in 2026 in one series, versus much larger 'robotaxi market' totals in others that include hardware and services); these were not reconciled and should not be quoted interchangeably.
> (6) The Chinese ride-hailing driver figure of 'more than 7 million as of May 2024' is a registered-driver count from the Ministry of Transport; active drivers are fewer, and the coincidental similarity to Indonesia's 7 million ojol figure is misleading because Indonesia's is overwhelmingly two-wheeled and China's overwhelmingly four-wheeled.
> (7) The 'Autonomous Vehicle Roadmap 2025-2035' with four detailed phases could not be traced to any primary Kemenhub or Kemenperin publication; it appears only on commercial and aggregator websites and is marked uncertain throughout.
> (8) Reports of a Hyundai-Gojek robotaxi trial in SCBD Jakarta and of Risetcar launching a Jakarta robotaxi in 2026 come from low-quality secondary sources and could not be corroborated by any company statement or regulatory filing.
> (9) The number of stalled Apollo Go vehicles in the 31 March 2026 Wuhan outage is reported as 'nearly 100' and 'more than 100' in different accounts; passenger delay is reported as up to two hours.
> (10) Reports differ on whether the April 2026 permit suspension was formally nationwide or an informal halt in new approvals; sources agree on the effect but not the instrument, and no primary regulatory text was located.
> (11) Apollo RT6 vehicle cost is cited as RMB 204,600 in Baidu's own announcement but also as 'RMB 250,000 production cost' in unit-economics analyses; the RMB 4,166 monthly amortisation figure derives from the higher number.
> (12) Indonesian autonomous haul-truck deployment is well attested at the market-analysis level but no source provides an Indonesian unit count, operator list or displaced-worker estimate — a significant evidence gap given that this is argued here to be the most consequential near-term autonomy effect in Indonesia.
